en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
[This is] the work called the *Aṭṭhasālinī* in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.
In the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā*,
the Introduction to the Work:
The Great Sage, whose wisdom toward sentient beings was like compassion;
Regarding all things that are to be known, he proceeded according to his own inclination.
With a mind inspired by such compassion for sentient beings,
he dwelt in the abode of the Thirty-three at the conclusion of the miracles.
Seated upon a stone throne named Paṇḍukambala at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree,
he was like the sun over Mount Yugandhara.
Having come from all ten thousand world-systems in every way, [the devas gathered there].
Surrounded by a host of deities seated together,
and placing his mother at their head, he set forth the path of the Abhidhamma discourse for the gods through her wisdom and splendor.
Having paid homage at the feet of that glorious, perfectly enlightened Buddha,
having honored the True Dharma and extended his joined palms in reverence to the Saṅgha,
he performed this act of prostration toward the Triple Gem.
Having dried up all obstacles by his spiritual power,
at the earnest request of the bhikkhu Buddhaghosa— one of purified conduct and virtue, and possessed of subtle and stainless intelligence— [this work was composed].
That which the God of Gods, the Guide, having taught to the gods, again explained to the Elder Sāriputta;
after performing service to the Great Sage at Lake Anotatta.
Having heard it and brought it down to the surface of the earth,
that Elder recited it to the monks; thus it was preserved by the monks and further chanted at the time of the Council by the Sage of Videha.
Of that Abhidhamma, which is profound in its knowledge, frequently plunged into,
and variegated by manifold methods— from its very beginning,
there was formerly the commentary on the eight treatises (*aṭṭhakathā*) composed by the masters Mahākassapa and others.
Chanted and recited again by the sages in the past,
this supreme [Dhamma] was brought here by the Elder Mahinda and composed in the language of those who dwell on the Island.
Having removed from it the vernacular speech of the inhabitants of Tambapaṇṇi,
and having introduced faultless language that follows the method of the canonical texts—
unmixed with the tenets of other schools and free from confusion.
Illuminating the adjudication of the Mahāvihāravāsins,
I shall clarify the meaning by taking what is to be taken even from the commentaries on the Āgamas, thus pleasing those who possess discerning vision.
All meditation subjects— whether of temperament, direct knowledge, or insight—
are indeed fully elucidated in this *Visuddhimagga*.
Therefore, without taking up that entire body of tradition, [I shall proceed].
Following the very sequence of the words, we shall provide a commentary on the meaning.
Therefore, as I speak this discourse on the Abhidhamma,
listen with undistracted minds, for this teaching is indeed difficult to encounter.
The Nidānakathā:
In this context, in what sense is it the Abhidhamma? It is in the sense of being a dhamma that exceeds and is distinct from [other] dhammas.

Here, the prefix *abhi-* signifies the meaning of excess and distinction, as in such examples as: “My painful feelings are increasing (*abhikkamanti*), not subsiding,” and “of surpassing beauty (*abhikkantavaṇṇā*).”
Thus, just as among many parasols and banners raised together,

that which is of superior size and distinguished by its particular color and shape is called an "over-parasol" (*aticchattra*), and that banner which is of superior size and endowed with various beautiful colors is called an "over-banner" (*atidhvaja*);
and just as among many princes gathered together from one side...
Furthermore, among gods, a prince who is more preeminent and distinguished by his excellence in birth, enjoyment, power, sovereignty, and so forth, is called a "super-prince" (*atirājakumāra*);
likewise, a god who is more preeminent and distinguished by his excellence in lifespan, beauty, power, fame, and so forth, is called a "super-god" (*atideva*); such is also the case with Brahmā.
Just as one is called "surpassing Brahmā" (*atibrahmā*), so too this Dhamma is called "Abhidhamma" in the sense of being a Dhamma that surpasses and distinguishes itself from other Dhammas.
For when reaching the Suttanta, the five aggregates are analyzed only partially and not exhaustively;
but when reaching the Abhidhamma, they are analyzed exhaustively by way of the methods of the *Suttanta-bhājaniya*, the *Abhidhamma-bhājaniya*, and the *Pañha-pucchaka*.
They have been analyzed. Likewise, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the four truths, the twenty-two faculties, and the twelvefold formula of conditions have been analyzed.
For indeed, in the *Indriyavibhaṅga*, there is no *suttantabhājanīya*; and in the *Paccayākāra*, there is no *pañhapucchaka*.
Furthermore, when reaching the discourses (*suttanta*), the four foundations of mindfulness have been analyzed only partially.
Not in their entirety; however, upon reaching the Abhidhamma, they are analyzed as being exhaustive by way of all three methods.

Likewise, there are the four right endeavors, the four bases of psychic power, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the four jhānas, the four immeasurables, the five training rules, and the four analytical insights.
However, here in the *Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga*, there is no *suttantabhājanīya*. And when it comes to the *Suttanta*, knowledge (*ñāṇa*) is analyzed only partially and not exhaustively;

likewise for the defilements (*kilesa*). But when one reaches the *Abhidhamma*, having established a matrix (*mātikā*) by way of "the basis of knowledge as a singlefold," etc., they are analyzed exhaustively. Likewise from the "singlefold" onwards...

Starting from there, the defilements are analyzed through numerous methods. Upon reaching the Suttanta, the delimitation of the planes (bhūmantara-pariccheda) is explained only partially, not exhaustively;
however, upon reaching the Abhidhamma, the delimitation of the planes is explained exhaustively by way of all three methods.
Thus, it should be understood that it is called "Abhidhamma" in the sense of being a distinction of the Dhamma that exceeds the [ordinary] Dhamma.

Furthermore, from the perspective of its sections (*pakaraṇa*), this work is established by way of the seven treatises: the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, the *Vibhaṅga*, the *Dhātukathā*, the *Puggalapaññatti*, the *Kathāvatthu*, the *Yamaka*, and the *Paṭṭhāna*. This is the consensus among the teachers on this point. However, the caviller (*vitaṇḍavādī*) says:
"Why was the *Kathāvatthu* included? Was it not more than eighteen years after the Parinibbāna of the Perfectly Enlightened One?"
“Was this established by the Elder Moggaliputtatissa after two hundred years had passed? Therefore, since it was spoken by a disciple, you should discard it.
“But are the six treatises (Chappakaraṇa) the Abhidhamma? “I do not say so. “Then what do you say?
“The seven treatises (Sattappakaraṇa). “Which one do you take as the seventh? “The Mahādhammahadaya.”
“There is a work called the *Kathāvatthu*; with that, there are seven [books]. “In the *Mahādhammahadaya* there is nothing new;
only a few sections on questions remain; it is with the *Kathāvatthu* alone that there are seven. “Not with the *Kathāvatthu*;
there is a work called the *Mahādhātukathā*; with that, there are seven. “In the *Mahādhātukathā* there is nothing new; it is merely a short text.”
"The remainder [is] together with the *Kathāvatthu*— thus [it is said].
For when the Perfectly Enlightened One was teaching the seven treatises (*sattappakaraṇa*), having reached the *Kathāvatthu*,
he began with that eightfold method of debate which exists in the section on the person (*puggala-vāra*) regarding the four questions by way of two pentads."
On all the paths of discourse, he established a matrix (*mātikā*) consisting of a portion of the canonical text (*pāḷi*) amounting to an incomplete recitation-section (*bhāṇavāra*).
That [matrix] begins: "The person (*puggala*) is apprehended in the sense of a real and ultimate fact (*saccikaṭṭha-paramattha*)? Yes.
Is that person apprehended in the sense of a real and ultimate fact from that which is the real and ultimate fact? It should not be said so. Understand the refutation... [etc.]..."

"Does a person exist at all times? Does a person not exist at all times? Does a person exist in all things?

Does a person not exist in all things? [Does this hold] in the sense of a real and ultimate fact?"—thus, by demonstrating the first refutation based on the first thesis, the second refutation based on the second, and so on up to the eighth refutation based on the eighth.
It was established by the Teacher. In this manner, the establishment of the *mātikā* (table of contents) is to be understood in all instances.

Now, when establishing this *mātikā*, he did so having seen this: at the end of two hundred years plus eighteen years after my Parinibbāna, a monk named the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, seated in the midst of a thousand monks, [will establish] his own doctrine...
"By compiling five hundred suttas from the opposing doctrines and five hundred suttas [from our own],
he will distribute the *Kathāvatthu* treatise, equal in extent to the *Dīghanikāya*. Thus,
when the Elder Moggaliputtatissa taught this treatise, he did not teach it by means of his own knowledge, but rather by that of the Teacher.
However, he taught by means of the matrix (mātikā) established according to the method given by the Teacher.

Thus, because it was taught by means of the matrix established according to the method given by the Teacher, this entire treatise is indeed known as "spoken by the Buddha. How so? Just like the *Madhupiṇḍika Sutta* and others.
For in the *Madhupiṇḍika Sutta*, the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhu, from whatever source a person's proliferation-perception-conceptualization..."

Having established the outline: "They practice these things; and herein, if there is nothing to be delighted in, nothing to be welcomed, and nothing to be clung to, this is the very end of the underlying tendencies of lust," the Elder Mahākaccāna rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
Then the monks who were recipients of the Dhamma approached the Elder Mahākaccāna regarding the outline established by the One of Ten Powers.
They asked about the meaning. Without speaking immediately upon being asked, the Elder, for the sake of showing honor to the One of Ten Powers, brought forward the simile of the heartwood, beginning:
"Just as if, friends, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood... He explained that the Blessed One is like a heartwood tree and the disciples are like the branches and foliage, saying:
"For, friends, that Blessed One knows what should be known and sees what should be seen."
Having praised the Teacher, saying, "The Tathāgata is become vision, become knowledge, become Dhamma, become Brahma;

he is the speaker, the proclaimer, the guide to the goal, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of Dhamma," and having been requested again and again by the elders, the Teacher analyzed the meaning of the summary (mātikā) he had established, saying:
"And if you wish, venerable ones, [approach] the Blessed One himself..."
Having approached him, you should inquire about this matter;

if it accords with and is consistent with his omniscient knowledge, you may accept it, but if not, do not accept it. With this intention, he said, “You should retain it exactly as the Blessed One explains it,” and then dismissed them.
They approached the Teacher and questioned him. Instead of saying, "Kaccāna has spoken poorly," the Teacher raised his neck like one lifting a golden statue;

filling his great mouth, which was as beautiful as a full-blown hundred-petaled lotus, he let forth a Brahma-voice and gave the Elder his approval, saying, "Excellent, excellent! Monks, Mahākaccāna is wise."
“Monks, Mahākaccāna is of great wisdom; if you were to ask me about this matter, monks, I too would have answered it exactly as it was answered by Mahākaccāna,” he said.
And from the time the Teacher thus expressed his approval, the entire sutta is known as the word of the Buddha.
It was born. This same method applies even to the suttas elaborated by the Elder Ānanda and others.

In this very way, while teaching the seven treatises (sattappakaraṇa), the Fully Enlightened One, upon reaching the *Kathāvatthu*, established the matrix (mātikā) according to the manner already described. And while establishing it, he saw this:
"At the end of two hundred years plus eighteen years after my Parinibbāna, the Elder Moggaliputtatissa..."
The monk named [Moggaliputta] Tissa, seated in the midst of a thousand bhikkhus, will compile five hundred suttas from his own school and five hundred from opposing schools—
totaling one thousand suttas— and distribute the treatise *Kathāvatthu*, which is equal in extent to the *Dīghanikāya*. Furthermore,
when the Elder Moggaliputtatissa teaches this treatise, he does not teach it by means of his own knowledge, but rather by that of the Teacher.
However, he taught by means of a table of contents (mātikā) established according to the method provided by the Teacher.
Thus, because it was taught by means of a table of contents established according to the method given by the Teacher, this entire treatise became the very word of the Buddha.
In this way, the seven treatises together with the *Kathāvatthu* are what is called the Abhidhamma.

In that regard, there are four expositions in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* treatise: the exposition of consciousness, the exposition of matter, the collection of matrices (*nikkheparāsi*), and the extraction of meanings (*atthuddhāra*).
Therein, from the wholesome of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) there are eight; from the unwholesome, twelve; from the wholesome resultant, sixteen;
from the unwholesome resultant, seven; and from the functional (*kiriyā*), eleven. From the wholesome of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), five; from the resultant...
Five from the functional; four from the wholesome of the formless realm, four from the resultant, and four from the functional;
and four from the wholesome supramundane, four from the resultant—these ninety-nine consciousnesses are called the "Analysis of Consciousness" (*cittavibhatti*).

It is also known by the name "The Section on the Arising of Consciousness" (*cittuppādakaṇḍa*). From the perspective of the path of recitation, it consists of more than six *bhāṇavāras*; when expanded in detail, [it is even longer].
However, it is infinite and immeasurable.

Immediately following that, having established the matrix (mātikā) by way of "in one way, in two ways," and so forth, and having shown it by analyzing it in detail, there is what is called the "Analysis of Matter" (rūpavibhatti).
Its other name is the "Matter Section" (Rūpakanda). From the perspective of the path of recitation, it exceeds two bhāṇavāras.
When expanded, however, it becomes infinite and immeasurable.

Immediately following that, the "heap of exposition" (nikkheparāsi) is that which is taught by way of laying out [the teaching] through its roots and so forth—namely, by way of root, trunk, door, plane, meaning, phenomenon, name, and gender. It is as follows:
By way of root, and also by way of trunk, And also by way of door, and by way of plane;
Because it is taught by setting aside [the subject] according to its meaning, its nature, its name, and its gender, it is called "The Section on Setting Aside" (*Nikkhepa*).

It is also known by the name *Nikkhepakaṇḍa*. From the perspective of the path of recitation, it consists of approximately three *bhāṇavāras*; however, when expanded in detail, it becomes infinite and immeasurable.

Following that, however, there is the section known as the *Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa*, which constitutes the extraction of the meaning (*atthuddhāra*) of the Buddha’s word consisting of the Three Piṭakas, and which extends as far as the *Saraṇaduka*.
It is from this that the monks of the *Mahāpakaraṇiya* school bring their enumeration of the *Mahāpakaraṇa* into alignment when they do not perceive the sequence of the enumeration therein.
From the perspective of the path of recitation (*vācanāmagga*), it consists of approximately two *bhāṇavāras*; however, when expanded, [it is much more extensive].
It is infinite and immeasurable.

Thus, the entire *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* treatise consists of more than thirteen recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*) according to the path of oral transmission. When expanded, however, it is infinite and immeasurable. Thus it is said:
The Analysis of Consciousness, Matter, The Enumeration, and the Exposition of Meaning;
The profound and subtle state was also taught by the Buddha.

Following that is the section known as the Vibhaṅga (Analysis). It consists of: the Analysis of the Aggregates, the Analysis of the Bases, the Analysis of the Elements, the Analysis of the Truths, the Analysis of the Faculties, the Analysis of the Modes of Conditionality, the Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness, and the Analysis of the Right Exertions.

It is analyzed in eighteen ways: the analysis of the bases of psychic power, the analysis of the factors of enlightenment, the analysis of the factors of the path, the analysis of the meditative absorptions,
the analysis of the immeasurables, the analysis of the training rules, the analysis of the analytical knowledges, the analysis of knowledge, the analysis of the minor matters,
and the analysis of the heart of the Dhamma.

Therein, the Analysis of the Aggregates (*khandhavibhaṅga*) is analyzed in three ways: by way of the Suttanta-exposition (*suttantabhājanīya*), the Abhidhamma-exposition (*abhidhammabhājanīya*), and the interrogation (*pañhapucchaka*).
From the perspective of the recitation path, it consists of about five recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*); however, when expanded, it becomes infinite and immeasurable.
Following that, the Analysis of the Bases (*āyatanavibhaṅga*) and the others are also analyzed by these same three methods. Among those—

The Analysis of the Bases (*Āyatanavibhaṅga*) is more than one recitation section (*bhāṇavāra*) from the path of oral transmission; the Analysis of the Elements (*Dhātuvibhaṅga*) is about two recitation sections.
Likewise for the Analysis of the Truths (*Saccavibhaṅga*). In the Analysis of the Faculties (*Indriyavibhaṅga*), there is no "Exposition according to the Suttas" (*suttantabhājanīya*);

however, from the path of oral transmission, it is just over one recitation section. The Analysis of the Modes of Conditionality (*Paccayākāravibhaṅga*) is six recitation sections, and here there is the "Interrogation of Questions" (*pañhapucchaka*).

There is none. The Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness (*Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga*) is about one recitation-section (*bhāṇavāra*) in length; likewise for the Analyses of the Right Efforts, the Bases of Psychic Power, the Factors of Enlightenment, and the Factors of the Path.

The Analysis of the Meditations (*Jhānavibhaṅga*) is about two recitation-sections in length; the Analysis of the Immeasurables (*Appamaññāvibhaṅga*) is about one recitation-section in length. In the Analysis of the Training Precepts (*Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga*), there is no "Exposition according to the Discourses" (*suttantabhājanīya*);
however, from the perspective of the textual tradition, it is about one recitation-section in length; likewise for the Analysis of the Analytical Knowledges (*Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅga*).
The Analysis of Knowledge (Ñāṇavibhaṅga) is analyzed in ten ways; as for its recitation path, it consists of approximately three recitation sections (bhāṇavāra).
The Analysis of Minor Matters (Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga) is also analyzed in ten ways; as for its recitation path, it consists of approximately three recitation sections.

The Analysis of the Heart of the Dhamma (Dhammahadayavibhaṅga) is analyzed in three ways; as for its recitation path, it consists of a little more than two recitation sections. All of these, when expanded in detail...
They are infinite and immeasurable. Thus, this Vibhaṅga treatise consists of approximately thirty-five recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*) according to the path of oral transmission;
however, in its detailed extent, it is infinite and immeasurable.
Immediately following that is the treatise called the Dhātukathā. It consists of: inclusion and non-inclusion; that which is included and that which is not included.
The uncomprised by the comprised; the comprised by the comprised; the uncomprised by the uncomprised;
association and dissociation; the associated by the dissociated; the dissociated by the associated; the associated by the associated;
the dissociated by the dissociated; the associated with the comprised; the comprised by the associated.

It is analyzed in fourteen ways: that which is not included, associated with what is not included and dissociated from it, dissociated from what is not included and included in it, and both included and not included in it.
From the perspective of the path of recitation, this amounts to more than six recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*);
however, when expanded in detail, it becomes infinite and immeasurable.

Following that is the *Puggalapaññatti* (Designation of Persons). It is analyzed into six types: "designation of aggregates, designation of bases, designation of elements, designation of truths, designation of faculties, and designation of persons.
From the perspective of the path of recitation, it consists of more than five *bhāṇavāras*; however, when explained in detail, it is truly infinite and immeasurable.

Following that is the work named *Kathāvatthuppakaraṇa*. It is analyzed by compiling five hundred suttas from the side of one's own school (*sakavāda*) and five [hundred] from the side of the opposing school (*paravāda*), thus totaling one thousand suttas.
From the perspective of the oral tradition, it has not yet been committed to writing in books;
however, according to the method established at the Council (*saṅgīti*), its extent is equal to the *Dīghanikāya*. When expanded in detail, however, it becomes infinite and immeasurable.

Following that is the Yamaka (Pairs). It is analyzed into ten types: the Root Yamaka, the Aggregate Yamaka, the Base Yamaka, the Element Yamaka, the Truth Yamaka, the Formations Yamaka, the Latent Dispositions Yamaka, the Consciousness Yamaka, the Dhamma Yamaka, and the Faculty Yamaka.
From the perspective of the path of recitation, it consists of one hundred and twenty recitation sections; however, in its full extent, it is infinite and immeasurable.
Following that is the *Mahāpakaraṇa*, which is also known by the name *Paṭṭhāna*. It consists of:

the root condition (*hetu-paccaya*), the object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), the predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*), the proximity condition (*anantara-paccaya*), the contiguity condition (*samanantara-paccaya*), the co-nascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*), the mutuality condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*), the support condition (*nissaya-paccaya*), the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*), the prenascence condition (*purejāta-paccaya*), the postnascence condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*), and the repetition condition (*āsevana-paccaya*).

The conditionality is analyzed into twenty-four kinds by way of conditions as follows: kamma-condition, vipāka-condition, nutriment-condition, faculty-condition, jhāna-condition, path-condition, association-condition, dissociation-condition, presence-condition, absence-condition, disappearance-condition, and non-disappearance-condition.
Thus it is analyzed first by way of conditions into twenty-four types.
At this point, however, the *Paṭṭhāna* (Conditional Relations) should be brought together.

There are twenty-two triplets, beginning with the wholesome triplet (*kusalattika*), and one hundred pairs, beginning with "states that are roots" and "states that are not roots," up to "states with conflict" and "states without conflict.
There are also forty-two other pairs, beginning with "states on the side of true knowledge" and "states on the side of ignorance," up to "knowledge of destruction" and "knowledge of non-arising."

These are called the Suttantika-dukas. Among them, the two hundred and twenty-three groups of three (tikas) and one hundred groups of two (dukas) constitute what is known as the *mātikā*—the matrix—of the seven treatises;
it was spoken directly by the Conqueror, is the word of the Jina, and was taught by the Omniscient Buddha.

Now, as for the other forty-two Suttantika-dukas: from where did they originate, by whom were they established, and by whom were they taught? They originated from the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma.
"By him they were established; by him they were taught. However, when the Elder established these, he did not do so through his own independent knowledge (*sāmukkaṃsika*).

Rather, having compiled the recitation of the *Ekuttariya*—the first and second chapters—by harmonizing them with the *Dasuttara-suttanta*, and having reached the Suttanta portion for the Abhidhamma Elders, they were established without weariness. These, moreover, are contained within a single section on "Arrangement" (*nikkhepa-khaṇḍa*).
Having reached the conclusion, it was analyzed. In the remaining sections, the Abhidhamma was analyzed up to the *Saraṇa-duka*.
For indeed, by the Fully Enlightened One, based on twenty-two triads (*tika*) in the *Anuloma-paṭṭhāna*, that which is called the *Tika-paṭṭhāna* was demonstrated;
and based on one hundred dyads (*duka*), that which is called the *Duka-paṭṭhāna* was demonstrated. Following that, taking twenty-two triads...
Having placed the hundred dyads (duka) within [the dyads], what is called the "Establishment of Dyads and Triads" (dukatikapaṭṭhāna) was shown.

Following that, having taken the hundred dyads and placed them within the twenty-two triads (tika), what is called the "Establishment of Triads and Dyads" (tikadukapaṭṭhāna) was shown. Furthermore, having placed the triads within the triads themselves, what is called the "Establishment of Triads and Triads" (tikatikapaṭṭhāna) was shown.
And having placed the dyads within the dyads themselves, the "Establishment of Dyads and Dyads" (dukadukapaṭṭhāna) [was shown].
Thus the name has been shown:
“The excellent Paṭṭhāna, the supreme Duka, the Tika,
the Duka-Tika, and the Tika-Duka.”
"The three triads and the two pairs—
these six methods in the *anuloma* (direct order) are profoundly deep.
In the *paccanīya-paṭṭhāna* (inverse order), the *Tika-paṭṭhāna* (Analysis of Triads) is based on twenty-two triads, and the *Duka-paṭṭhāna* (Analysis of Pairs) is based on one hundred pairs.
The *Dukatika-paṭṭhāna* is so called because the two hundred and twenty-two *dukas* are inserted into the *tikas*.

The *Tikaduka-paṭṭhāna* is so called because the one hundred *dukas* are inserted into the twenty-two *tikas*. The *Tikatika-paṭṭhāna* is so called because the *tikas* are inserted into the *tikas* themselves.
The *Dukaduka-paṭṭhāna* is so called because the *dukas* are inserted into the *dukas* themselves. Thus, in the reverse order as well, there are six methods.
The *Paṭṭhāna* has been explained. Therefore it was said:
"The excellent *Paṭṭhāna*, the supreme among dyads, the triad, the dyad-triad, and the triad-dyad;"
"The threefold and the twofold-by-twofold—these six methods in the negative sequence are very profound.
Thereafter, by this same method, the six methods in the positive-negative sequence are also shown. Therefore he said:
The excellent and most supreme *Paṭṭhāna* consists of the three triads, the two triads,
the three dyads, and the two dyads.
"The six methods in the Positive-Negative (Anuloma-Paccanīya) are very profound.
Immediately following that, the Negative-Positive (Paccanīyānuloma) is also demonstrated by these same six methods. Therefore he said:
"The excellent Paṭṭhāna, the supreme Duka and Tika..."
The dyads-and-triads and the triads-and-dyads,
the triads-and-triads and the dyads-and-dyads—
these six methods in the positive-negative (paccanīyānuloma) sequence are most profound.

Thus, there are six *paṭṭhānas* in the forward order (*anuloma*), six in the reverse order (*paṭiloma*), six in the forward-reverse order (*anulomapaccanīya*), and six in the reverse-forward order (*paccanīyānuloma*). This compendium of twenty-four *samanta-paṭṭhānas*, known as the *Paṭṭhāna Mahāpakaraṇa*, is now complete.

Now, in order to understand the profound nature of this Abhidhamma, four oceans should be known: the ocean of *saṃsāra*, the ocean of water, the ocean of methods (*naya*), and the ocean of knowledge (*ñāṇa*). Therein, the "ocean of *saṃsāra*" refers to:
The succession of the aggregates (*khandha*), and of the elements (*dhātu*) and sense-bases (*āyatana*).
"When the process is uninterrupted, it is called 'saṃsāra' (the wandering). Thus has the cycle of existence been described.
Now, as for this cycle, no prior limit to the arising of these beings is discerned—whether it be so many hundreds of years, thousands of years, or hundreds of thousands of years.
There is no such limitation as to whether beings have arisen at the end of a hundred eons, a thousand eons, or a hundred thousand eons, or whether they did not exist prior to that;

nor is there a limitation as to whether they arose during the time of a certain king or during the time of a certain Buddha, or whether they did not exist prior to that. For it is said: "Bhikkhus, the prior limit..."

"By this method—that ignorance is not perceived, such that 'ignorance did not exist before this, and then it subsequently came into being'—the ocean of saṃsāra is indeed without discoverable beginning.
However, the great ocean should be understood as the 'ocean of water. It is eighty-four thousand yojanas deep."
In that regard, there is no measure of water in terms of hundreds of *āḷhakas*, thousands of *āḷhakas*, or hundreds of thousands of *āḷhakas*.
Rather, it is reckoned simply as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of water.
This is what is called the "Ocean of Water."
What is the ocean of method? It is the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas.
For indeed, when noble sons who are endowed with faith, full of serene confidence, and supreme in knowledge, reflect upon even two of these collections, infinite joy and gladness arise within them.
Which two? The Vinaya and the Abhidhamma. For when bhikkhus who are masters of the Vinaya reflect upon the Vinaya collection...
The laying down of training rules in accordance with the fault means:
the laying down of training rules such that "for this fault, for this transgression, there is this [penalty]"—this is not within the domain of others, but is the domain of the Buddhas alone.

This applies to those reflecting on the series of superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*), those reflecting on the series of blue lotuses (*nīlapeyyāla*), and those reflecting on the series concerning acting as a go-between (*sañcaritta*).
Boundless joy and happiness arise. Even for the bhikkhus learned in the Abhidhamma, as they grasp the form and formless phenomena—

distinguishing between the aggregates, bases, elements, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, kamma, and its result, and discerning the subtle and refined phenomena through their divisions and sections,
just as one perceives the forms of stars across the vault of the sky— [boundless joy and happiness arise].
Having done so, he showed it by analyzing it, saying, "Behold, our Teacher has appeared! As they reflect upon this lineage of the Abhidhamma, infinite joy and gladness arise.
Furthermore, this story regarding its origin should be understood: the Elder Mahāgatigamiyatissadatta...
It is said that, thinking "I shall worship the Mahābodhi," as he was traveling to the opposite shore seated on the upper deck of a ship, he gazed upon the great ocean.

At that moment, neither the opposite shore nor this shore appeared to him; rather, it was only the great ocean that was visible, strewn with sprays of water tossed up by the force of the waves, resembling a spread carpet of jasmine flowers or a sheet of silver laid out. He...
He reflected: "Which is more powerful—the force of the waves in the great ocean, or the 'gateways of method' in the twenty-fourfold *Samantapāṭhāna*?
Then the boundaries of the great ocean became apparent to him:
it is bounded below by the great earth, above by space, on one side by the Cakkavāḷa mountains, and on the other side by the shoreline.
It was clearly defined; however, because no limit could be perceived for the *Samantapāṭhāna*, a powerful rapture arose as he reflected upon that subtle and delicate phenomenon.

Suppressing that rapture and increasing his insight, even while remaining seated as he was, he exhausted all defilements, established himself in the supreme fruit of Arahantship, and uttered this inspired utterance:
That which has gone so deep and is so difficult to awaken to—
having personally realized through direct knowledge its arising with its cause—
he taught it in its entirety, according to the proper sequence.
"By the Great Seer, one sees it as merely a form"—this is called the Ocean of Methods.
What is the Ocean of Knowledge? Omniscient knowledge is called the Ocean of Knowledge. This is called the Ocean of Saṃsāra; this...
For it cannot be known by anyone else that "this is named Jalasāgara" or "this is named Nayasāgara";
it can only be known through omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). Thus, omniscient knowledge is called the "Ocean of Knowledge.
Among these four oceans, it is the Ocean of Methods (*nayasāgara*) that is intended here. Indeed, only the omniscient Buddhas penetrate this.
This Blessed One too, while sitting at the foot of the Bodhi tree, reflected upon the Dhamma he had penetrated:
"Having sought and searched for this Dhamma, four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons have passed;
now, while sitting on this very seat, having exhausted one thousand five hundred defilements, this Dhamma has been penetrated by me. Thus he contemplated the Dhamma he had realized.
Reflecting thus, he sat for seven days in a single cross-legged posture.
Then, rising from that seat, thinking, "In this very seat, indeed, omniscient knowledge was realized by me," he stood for seven days gazing at the seat with unblinking eyes.
Thereupon, the deities thought, "Surely there is still some duty to be performed by Siddhattha even today."
The thought arose: "Indeed, he does not abandon his attachment to the *pallaṅka* (throne).
The Teacher, knowing the thoughts of the deities, immediately ascended into the air to suppress their reflections and displayed the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*).
[He displayed] the miracle performed at the Great Bodhi Throne (*mahābodhipallaṅka*) and [the one] at the assembly of kinsmen.
The miracle performed at Kaṭapāṭihāriya and the miracle performed at the assembly of Pāṭiyaputta were both exactly like the twin miracle performed at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree.

Having thus performed the twin miracle, he descended from the sky into the space between his seat and the place where he had stood, and walked back and forth for seven days. And during these twenty-one days, not even for a single day—
No rays issued forth from the Teacher’s body.
However, on the fourth week, he sat in the Jewel House in the northwestern direction.
The so-called "Jewel House" was not a dwelling made of the seven precious gems; rather, it was the place where he had mastered the seven treatises (pakaraṇa).
It should be understood as follows: while he was contemplating the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, no rays issued from his body.
While he was contemplating the *Vibhaṅga-pakaraṇa*, the *Dhātukathā*, the *Puggalapaññatti*, the *Kathāvatthu-pakaraṇa*, and the *Yamaka-pakaraṇa*, no rays issued from his body.
But when he descended into the *Mahāpakaraṇa* and [contemplated] "the root-condition (*hetu-paccayo*)..."
He began his synthesis with "the object-condition... [and so on] ...the non-disappearance-condition.
As he synthesized the twenty-four modes of the *Paṭṭhāna*, the knowledge of omniscience found its exclusive place within the *Mahāpakaraṇa* itself.
For just as the great fish Timirapiṅgala finds its place only in the great ocean, which is eighty-four thousand yojanas deep, even so did the knowledge of omniscience find its place.
He obtained an opportunity only for the *Mahāpakaraṇa* itself.
As the Teacher, having thus gained this opportunity, was at his ease comprehending the subtle and delicate Dhamma with his omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*),
six-colored rays— blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and brilliant— issued forth from his body.
From his hair and beard, as well as from the dark places of his eyes, blue rays issued forth; by means of these, the vault of the sky became as if strewn with powdered collyrium,
as if covered with the petals of flax-flowers and blue lotuses, as if hung with whirling jeweled fans,
and as if spread with a wide-spread black cloth.
From the yellow parts of his skin and eyes, yellow rays issued forth;
by means of which the quarters of space shone as if being sprinkled with streams of liquid gold, as if spread over with golden cloth, and as if strewn with saffron powder and *kaṇikāra* flowers.
From the fleshy parts and the red parts of his eyes, red rays issued forth, by means of which...

The various quarters shone as if colored with Chinese lac powder, as if being sprinkled with the juice of well-boiled lac, as if draped with red woolen cloths, and as if strewn with *jayasumana*, *pāribhaddaka*, and *bandhujīvaka* flowers.
From the bones, the teeth, and the white parts of the eyes, white rays issued forth; by means of which—

The quarters of the sky shone as if drenched by streams of milk poured from silver jars, as if covered by canopies of spread-out silver cloth, as if fanned by silver palm-leaf fans, and as if strewn with *kunda*, *kumuda*, *sinduvāra*, *sumana*, and *mallikā* flowers.
Furthermore, rays of deep crimson light issued forth from various parts of his body; thus those six-colored rays, having emerged, enveloped the solid great earth.
The great earth, two hundred and forty million *yojanas* in thickness, became like a mass of refined gold.
Then, having split the great earth, they took up the water below.
The water supporting the earth, four hundred and eighty million *yojanas* in thickness, became like molten gold being poured from golden jars. Having pierced through the water...
They seized the wind. The wind, nine hundred and sixty thousand yojanas in thickness, became like a towering mass of gold.
Having pierced through the wind, they plunged into the cloudless space below.
Rising up by way of the upper regions, they seized the gods of the Four Great Kings. Having pierced through them, [they went] from there to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
From there they passed through Yāma, then Tusita, then Nimmānarati, then Paranimmitavasavatti, then the nine Brahmā-worlds, then Vehapphala,
and having pierced through the five Suddhāvāsa heavens, they seized the four formless realms.
Having pierced through the four formless realms as well, they entered the unblemished space.
Infinite world-systems in the horizontal directions were pervaded [by light].
In all these places, there was no lunar radiance in the moon, no solar radiance in the sun, and no radiance from the forms of the stars in the starry bodies;
furthermore, there was no radiance at all in the parks, celestial mansions, wish-fulfilling trees, bodies, or ornaments of the deities.
Even the Great Brahmā, who is capable of pervading the light throughout the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system, became like a firefly at the rising of the sun.
Only the mere outlines of the moon, the sun, the stars, the forms of deities, celestial chariots, palaces, and the wish-fulfilling trees (kapparukkha) were discernible.
This entire extent of space was completely overspread by the rays of the Buddha alone. And this [light] was not... of the Buddhas.
This was the miracle of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāniddhi*), not the miracle produced by meditation (*bhāvanāmayiddhi*).

However, as the Lord of the World contemplated the subtle and delicate phenomena, his blood became serene, his physical basis (*vatthurūpa*) became serene, and the complexion of his skin became serene.
The color-element (*vaṇṇadhātu*) originating from the mind remained motionless for a distance of eighty cubits all around. In this manner, he contemplated for seven days.
"How much Dhamma was there that he comprehended during those seven days and nights? "It was infinite and immeasurable.

This, first of all, is what is called the "mental teaching. However, when the Teacher, having thus contemplated the Dhamma with his mind for seven days, taught it by means of vocal expression, he reached its ultimate limit even in a hundred years, a thousand years, or a hundred thousand years.
It should not be said that he is unable to teach. For later on, as well,

while seated upon the yellow sandalwood stone at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven amidst ten thousand deities of the world-systems, the Tathāgata made his mother a witness with his own body and taught the Dhamma—
namely, wholesome states, unwholesome states, and indeterminate states— by means of a hundredfold [analysis].
Moving from one point of the Dhamma to another by increments of a thousandth and a hundred-thousandth part,
he taught. For three months, the continuous teaching that proceeded without interruption became infinite and immeasurable, like the celestial Ganges flowing with speed,
or like a stream of water pouring from a jar turned upside down.
For when the Buddhas offer their expression of gratitude (*anumodana*) after a meal, even as they extend it slightly, their teaching reaches the length of the *Dīgha Nikāya* and *Majjhima Nikāya*.
However, when they teach the Dhamma to an assembled assembly after the meal, their teaching is only the length of the *Saṃyutta*, *Aṅguttara*, and the two great *Nikāyas*. Why is this?
Because for the Buddhas, the latency of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) is light, their lips are well-polished, and their intake of food is moderate.
His tongue was smooth and soft, his voice sweet, and his speech quick in its delivery. Therefore, even the Dhamma he taught in that single moment was so vast;
yet the Dhamma he taught over three months was truly infinite and immeasurable.
For the Elder Ānanda was of great learning, a bearer of the Three Piṭakas, possessing fifteen thousand stanzas and sixty thousand phrases.
Standing on his very feet as if pulling up creepers and flowers, he would grasp, recite, or teach [the text].
This much constitutes one "path of recitation" for the Elder. Indeed, no one else could possibly provide a word-for-word recitation to the Elder;
they would not be able to reach it. Only the Perfectly Enlightened One himself could reach it. Thus was he possessed of such supreme mindfulness.

Even a disciple possessing supreme progress and supreme fortitude, though learning for a hundred years or a thousand years the teaching taught by the Teacher in this manner over three months, would not be able to reach its culmination.
Yet, while the Tathāgata was thus teaching uninterruptedly for three months, his acquired body remained bound to material food.
"How did he pass the time? "By means of tending [to him] alone. For the respective times of the Buddhas are well-established, well-delimited, and clearly manifest.
Therefore, while teaching the Dhamma, the Blessed One observes the time in the world of humans.
Having noted the hour for the alms-round, he creates a manifested Buddha and [observes] the manner of this one’s taking of the robe and the taking of the bowl."
Having resolved, "Let my deportment be such as this, and let me teach only so much of the Dhamma," he took his bowl and robe and went to Lake Anotatta. Deities gave him a tooth-stick of nāgalatā;
having chewed it and attended to his body at Lake Anotatta, he stood upon a slab of emerald, put on his bright red undergarment, and donned his upper robe.
Taking a stone bowl given by the Four Great Kings, he goes to Uttarakuru.
Having brought back almsfood from there, he sits on the bank of Lake Anotatta; after partaking of it, he goes to the Sandalwood Grove for his midday rest.
The Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, also goes there, performs his duties toward the Perfectly Enlightened One, and [sits] to one side.
He sits down. Then the Teacher gives him a method, declaring: "Sāriputta, this much of the Dhamma has been taught by me.

Thus, while the Perfectly Enlightened One is giving a method, it is like the gift of a method shown by the Chief Disciple—who has attained the analytical knowledges—standing on the shore and stretching out his hand to point toward the ocean.
For the Elder as well, [it is shown] by means of a hundred methods and a thousand methods.
The Dhamma taught by the Blessed One through hundreds of thousands of methods indeed remains present before him.
The Teacher, having sat for his midday rest, asks: "At what time does he go to teach the Dhamma?
There is a specific time for the teaching of the Dhamma when the sons of good family residing in Sāvatthī have assembled; it is at that time that he goes. The Dhamma...
When he has given the instruction and is either departing or arriving, who knows [this] and who does not know? Devas of great power know;
devas of little power do not know. Why do they not know? Because there is no diversity in the rays and so forth of either the Perfectly Enlightened One or the emanated Buddha.
For indeed, there is no difference between the rays, the sounds, or the words of both of them.
The Elder Sāriputta, too, having brought forth the Dhamma taught by the Teacher, taught it to his five hundred co-resident bhikkhus.

This was their prior practice: it is said that in the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, they were reborn as small bats and, while hanging from a mountain cave, [listened] to two bhikkhus learned in the Abhidhamma.
While reciting the Abhidhamma, they grasped the signs in the sounds;
even though they did not understand the dark and light sides [of the syllables], by the mere grasping of the signs in the sounds, they passed away and were reborn in the world of the gods.

Having dwelt in the world of the gods for the duration of an interval between Buddhas, they were reborn in the human world at that time, and having gained faith through the Twin Miracle, [they approached] the Elder.
They went forth into the presence [of the Teacher]. The Elder brought forward the Dhamma as it had been taught by the Teacher and taught it to them.
At the very same moment that the Perfectly Enlightened One finished his teaching of the Abhidhamma, those bhikkhus completed their mastery of the seven treatises.
In the Abhidhamma, the method of recitation known as *vācanāmaggā* originated from the Elder Sāriputta.
Even the system of numerical progression (*gaṇanacāra*) in the *Mahāpakaraṇa* was established by that same Elder.

For the Elder established this numerical progression so that others might easily grasp, retain, master, and recite the Dhamma without confusing it with other doctrines. This being the case, the Elder himself was the very first to [do so].
Is he an Abhidhammika? No, he is not. Only the Perfectly Enlightened One is the first Abhidhammika;

for it was he who, having sat upon the Great Enlightenment Seat, penetrated it. And having become a Buddha, while sitting for seven days in a single cross-legged posture, he uttered this inspired utterance:
“When, indeed, phenomena become manifest to the ardent, meditating brahmin,
then all his doubts vanish away.”
Since he understands phenomena together with their causes:
“When phenomena indeed become manifest to the ardent, meditating brahmin;”
Then all his doubts fade away,
since he has understood the destruction of conditions.
"When phenomena indeed become manifest..."
"For the brahmin who meditates with ardor,
standing having shaken off Māra’s host,
he illuminates the sky like the sun."
This is known as the first word of the Buddha. However, the reciters of the *Dhammapada* say:
“Through the wandering through the cycle of many births, seeking the builder of the house, I have run on, finding no rest; birth again and again is suffering.”
“House-builder, you have been seen; you shall build no house again.
All your rafters are broken, the ridgepole is shattered.
The mind has reached the unconditioned; it has attained the destruction of craving.”
They say that this is called the first word of the Buddha.

The words spoken at the time of his final passing away, while reclining between the twin *sāla* trees—"Now, monks, I address you: all conditioned phenomena are subject to decay; strive with diligence"—are called the last word of the Buddha.

Between these two, for forty-five years, as if stringing together a garland of flowers or weaving a string of jewels, he proclaimed the True Dhamma that reveals the Deathless; this is called the middle word of the Buddha.

When all of this is summarized, it consists of three Piṭakas by way of Piṭaka, five Nikāyas by way of Nikāya, nine Aṅgas by way of Aṅga, and eighty-four thousand Dhamma-kkhandhas by way of Dhamma-kkhandha. How so?
For all of this, when classified by way of Piṭaka, consists of only three divisions: the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Suttanta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Therein...
The two Pātimokkhas, the two Vibhaṅgas, the twenty-two Khandhakas, and the sixteen Parivāras—this is called the Vinaya Piṭaka.
The Dīghanikāya is the collection of thirty-three suttas beginning with the Brahmajāla. The Majjhimanikāya is the collection of one hundred and fifty-two suttas beginning with the Mūlapariyāya.
The Saṃyuttanikāya is the collection of seven thousand seven hundred and sixty-two suttas beginning with the Oghataraṇa.
The *Saṃyutta Nikāya*. The *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, which comprises nine thousand five hundred and seventy-seven discourses beginning with the *Cittapariyādāna Sutta*.

The *Khuddaka Nikāya*, which has fifteen divisions according to the *Khuddakapāṭha*, *Dhammapada*, *Udāna*, *Itivuttaka*, *Suttanipāta*, *Vimānavatthu*, *Petavatthu*, *Theragāthā*, *Therīgāthā*, *Jātaka*, *Niddesa*, *Paṭisambhidā*, *Apadāna*, *Buddhavaṃsa*, and *Cariyāpiṭaka*—this is what is called the *Suttanta Piṭaka*. [Furthermore,] there are the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* and so forth...
The seven treatises constitute what is called the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Regarding that:

Because it possesses various specific methods, because it disciplines both body and speech, and because it is known by those who understand the meaning of discipline—this is declared as "Vinaya" by the experts in the Vinaya.
For herein there are various methods, distinguished by the fivefold recitation of the Pātimokkha, the analysis of the seven classes of offenses beginning with the Pārājikas, and so forth;
and there are methods of subsequent ordinances (anupaññatti-naya) intended for the purposes of strengthening or relaxing [the rules].

Because it restrains misconduct of body and speech, it disciplines both body and speech. Therefore, due to its manifold methods, its distinguished methods, and its disciplining of body and speech, [it is called the Vinaya].
"This is called the Vinaya, the Vinaya. For the sake of proficiency in the meaning of this term, it has been said:
"Because of its manifold and specific methods, and because of the disciplining of body and speech, This is declared by those who know the meaning of Vinaya as 'Vinaya,' the Discipline."
Furthermore,
it is called "Sutta" because it indicates meanings, because it is well-spoken, because it is heard, because it flows forth,
because it is a guiding thread, and because it shares the characteristics of a thread.

For it indicates meanings distinguished as one’s own welfare, the welfare of others, and so forth. And herein, the meanings are well-spoken because they are spoken in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*).
It "flows" toward these meanings; that is to say, it brings them forth, just as a crop [brings forth] fruit.
It "exudes" these [meanings], just as a cow exudes milk; that is to say, it flows forth. And it thoroughly protects and guards them; thus it is said.
It exists. And this is similar to a string (sutta). For just as a string is a means of measurement for carpenters, so too is this for the wise.
And just as flowers gathered by a string are not scattered or destroyed, so too are the meanings gathered by this [work].
Therefore, this was stated for the sake of skill in understanding its meaning:

“Because it indicates the meaning, because it is well-spoken, because it is heard, because it leads forth, because of its instruction, and because of its similarity to a thread—therefore it is called ‘Sutta.
The explanation of the term for the Abhidhamma has already been stated. Here is another method:
Because the phenomena herein are superior, characterized, honored, delimited, and stated in addition [to those in the Sutta], it is therefore called Abhidhamma.
For this prefix *abhi-* is seen in the senses of superiority, characteristic, honored, delimited, and additional. Thus, for example, it is used in "bāḷhā... [meaning intense].
In such passages as “My painful feelings increase, they do not subside,” it occurs in the sense of growth.

In such passages as “Those nights which are well-known and well-characterized,” it occurs in the sense of a characteristic mark (*lakkhaṇa*). In such passages as “The King of Kings, the Lord of Men,” it occurs in the sense of being honored.
In such passages as “Able to guide in the Abhidhamma and the Abhivinaya,” it occurs in the sense of being delimited—that is, in phenomena that are free from mutual confusion.

And it is said in the Vinaya: “With surpassing beauty,” and so forth; here, [the word] refers to that which is superior. Furthermore, in this context, even phenomena characterized by growth are spoken of in such a manner as:
“He develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, dwelling having pervaded one direction with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness,” and so on.
Or [it refers to] the object of visible forms, the object of sounds...

They are "characterized" (*salakkhaṇā*) because they are to be defined by their objects and so forth, according to the method beginning with the words "or. They are "honored" (*pūjitā*) because they are revered according to the method beginning with "the states of those in training, the states of those beyond training, and supramundane states"; the intended meaning is that they are worthy of honor.
They are "delimited" (*paricchinnā*) because their individual natures are circumscribed according to the method beginning with "there is contact, there is feeling. "Lofty states..."
Furthermore, even more categories of phenomena have been taught according to such methods as "immeasurable phenomena" and "unexcelled phenomena.
Therefore, this was stated for the sake of skill in the meaning of these terms:
"That which herein possesses growth, has its own characteristic, is honored, and is delimited;"
“And the teachings spoken in addition [to those in the Sutta Piṭaka]—therefore they are called Abhidhamma.
As for what is not distinguished here: “Those who know the meaning of the Piṭakas say that ‘Piṭaka’ is so called from the sense of ‘learning’ and ‘receptacle.’”
Having thus synthesized [the meanings], the three—Vinaya and the others—should be understood as "piṭaka.
For the "pariyatti" (the teaching) is also called "piṭaka" in such passages as, "Do not [be satisfied] with the acquisition of the Piṭakas.

In such passages as, "Then a man might come carrying a spade and a basket," it refers to any kind of container. Therefore, those who know the meaning of "piṭaka" say that "piṭaka" signifies both the teaching (*pariyatti*) and a container (*bhājana*).
Now, having combined these, those three—the Vinaya and the others—are also to be known as "piṭakas.

By forming a compound with the word *piṭaka* in its two aforementioned senses, it is called the *Vinayapiṭaka*, because it is both the Vinaya and a *piṭaka* (basket) by virtue of being the state of the teaching (*pariyatti*), and because it contains (*bhājana*) the respective meanings.
In the same manner as stated above, it is called the *Suttantapiṭaka*, because it is both the Suttanta and that *piṭaka*.
And since it is both the Abhidhamma and a Piṭaka, it is called the Abhidhamma Piṭaka; thus these three, beginning with the Vinaya, are to be known.
Having understood them in this way, furthermore, for the sake of proficiency in their various aspects within those very Piṭakas:
"The distinctions of teaching, dispensation, and discourse therein, as appropriate;"
One should also illuminate the profound nature of the abandonment of training.
One should likewise analyze everything regarding the divisions of the scriptures,
as well as the success and failure that a bhikkhu attains in each respective case.

In this regard, here is the exposition and analysis: These three Piṭakas are, respectively, called the teaching of the command (*āṇā*), the teaching of conventional usage (*vohāra*), and the teaching of ultimate meaning (*paramattha*);

the instruction according to offense (*yathāparādha*), according to conformity (*yathānuloma*), and according to the Dhamma (*yathādhamma*); and the discourse on restraint (*saṃvara*), non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), the unraveling of views (*diṭṭhiviniveṭhana*), and the delimitation of mind-and-body (*nāmarūpapariccheda*).
For herein, the Vinaya Piṭaka is the teaching of the command, because it was taught by the Blessed One, who is worthy of commands, primarily as a command. The Suttanta Piṭaka...
It is called a "teaching on conventional usage" because it was taught by the Blessed One, who is skilled in conventional usage, for the most part in terms of conventional usage;

and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka is called a "teaching on the ultimate meaning" because it was taught by the Blessed One, who is skilled in the ultimate meaning, for the most part in terms of the ultimate meaning.
Likewise, it is a "discipline according to offenses" because those beings who frequently commit offenses are disciplined herein according to their respective offenses.
The second is called the "Teaching in Accordance with the Natural Order" (*yathānulomasāsana*) because beings who possess various inclinations, latent tendencies, temperaments,

and dispositions are here taught in accordance with those [traits]. The third is called the "Teaching in Accordance with the Dhamma" (*yathādhammasāsana*) because beings who perceive a mere heap of phenomena as "I" and "mine" are here taught in accordance with the true nature of things (*yathādhamma*).
Likewise, first, because here restraint and non-restraint—which are the opposites of misconduct—are discussed, it is called the "Discussion of Restraint and Non-restraint";
"restraint and non-restraint" refers to both minor and major forms of restraint and non-restraint, just as there are right and wrong actions, and right and wrong fruits;
secondly, because here the unraveling of views—which is the opposite of the sixty-two views—is discussed.

The Discourse on the Unraveling of Views; and the Discourse on the Analysis of Name-and-Form, so called because herein the analysis of name-and-form—which serves as the antidote to lust and the other defilements—is explained.
In all three of these, the three trainings, the three abandonments, and the fourfold profundity are to be understood. Likewise...

For in the Vinaya Piṭaka, the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) is specifically taught; in the Sutta Piṭaka, the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā); and in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā).
Furthermore, in the Vinaya Piṭaka, there is the abandoning of transgression, because virtue is the antidote to the transgression of the defilements (kilesa);

in the Sutta Piṭaka, there is the abandoning of the obsessions (pariyuṭṭhāna), because concentration is the antidote to the obsessions; and in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, there is the abandoning of the underlying tendencies (anusaya).
Because wisdom is the antidote to the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).

In the first [truth], there is the abandonment of defilements by way of their specific factor (*tadaṅga*); in the others, there is abandonment by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*) and eradication (*samuccheda*). In the first, there is the abandonment of the defilement of misconduct; in the others, there is the abandonment of the defilements of craving and views.
Furthermore, in each one of these, the fourfold profundity—of the phenomenon (*dhamma*), the meaning (*attha*), the teaching (*desanā*), and the penetration (*paṭivedha*)—is to be understood.

In this context, "Dhamma" refers to the *tanti* (the textual tradition). "Meaning" (*attha*) is the meaning of that very same [text]. "Teaching" (*desanā*) is the teaching of that *tanti* as it has been determined by the mind.

"Penetration" (*paṭivedha*) is the realization, according to reality, of both the *tanti* and the meaning of the *tanti*. And these—namely, Dhamma, meaning, teaching, and penetration—are present in all three [types of suttas].
Because they are difficult for those of dull intellect to fathom, like the great ocean for crocodiles and other such creatures.

And because it has no foothold that can be gained, it is therefore profound. Thus, in each single instance here, the fourfold profundity is to be understood. Another method: "Dhamma" means cause. For this has been said:
"Knowledge regarding the cause is the analytical knowledge of Dhamma (dhamma-paṭisambhidā). "Attha" means the fruit of the cause. For this has been said:
"Knowledge regarding the fruit of the cause is the analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā). "Desanā" means designation (paññatti).

The intended meaning is "the expression of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma"; or alternatively, it is the speaking [of it] by way of direct order, reverse order, summary, detailed exposition, and so forth.
"Penetration" (paṭivedha) means realization (abhisamaya). And that is both mundane and supramundane. It is an awakening, both in terms of its object and in terms of non-delusion:
an understanding of phenomena in accordance with their meanings, of meanings in accordance with phenomena, and of designations in accordance with the paths of designation.
The unerring intrinsic nature, characterized by specific marks, of those various phenomena taught in their respective places must be penetrated.
Now, since within these Piṭakas, whatever kind of phenomenon or category of meaning there may be,
and whatever meaning is to be made known in such a way that it stands before the knowledge of the listeners, the teaching serves to illuminate that very meaning accordingly.

And herein, penetration—which consists in unerring comprehension, or the unerring intrinsic nature consisting of the specific characteristics to be penetrated regarding those various phenomena—is profound in its entirety;
for those of poor wisdom who have not accumulated the requisites of merit, it is difficult to fathom and provides no foothold, like the great ocean to frogs and the like. Therefore, it is profound.
Thus, in each of these cases, the fourfold profundity should be understood. And to this extent:
"One should clearly illustrate, as appropriate among them, the distinctions between the teaching, the dispensation, and the discourse, as well as the profundity of training and abandoning."
This verse has its meaning already explained:
"Explain in full how a bhikkhu attains every kind of excellence, whether in the divisions of the scriptures, or in success and failure, wherever it may occur."

In this context, however, the threefold classification of the scriptures (*pariyatti*) within the Three Piṭakas should be understood. For there are three kinds of scripture: that which is like a water-snake, that for the sake of escape, and the scriptural treasury.
Among these, that which is wrongly grasped and studied for the sake of criticism and so forth is "like a water-snake. With reference to this, it was said:
"Just as if, monks, a man needing a water-snake, seeking a water-snake, searching for a water-snake..."
While walking, he might see a large snake and seize it by its coils or by its tail;
that snake, having turned back upon him, might bite his hand, his arm, or some other limb, and because of that, he would meet death or suffering amounting to death. Why is that?
What is the reason? It is because of the wrong grasp of the water-snake, monks. In the same way, monks, here certain foolish men master the Dhamma—the discourses...
[and so on] ...the expositions; yet having mastered that Dhamma, they do not examine the meaning of those teachings with wisdom.
As they do not examine the meaning of those teachings with wisdom, [they fall into ruin].
They do not find satisfaction in reflective contemplation; they master the Dhamma for the sake of finding fault and for the sake of escaping through mere verbal disputation.
They do not experience the purpose for which they mastered the Dhamma.
Those teachings, being wrongly grasped by them, lead to their harm and suffering for a long time. Why is that? Because they have been wrongly grasped.
“...of phenomena, monks.

However, that which is well-learned by one desiring only the fulfillment of the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth, and is mastered not for the sake of criticism and the like, but for the sake of deliverance (*nissaraṇa*), is [well-learned].
With reference to this, it was said: “Those teachings were well-learned by them for a long time...”
“...they conduce to welfare and happiness. For what reason? Because, monks, the teachings have been well grasped.

Furthermore, when one who has fully understood the aggregates, abandoned the defilements, developed the path, penetrated the unshakable, realized cessation, and exhausted the taints, learns [the teachings] solely for the purpose of preserving the tradition and maintaining the lineage, this is the “learning as a storekeeper.”

Furthermore, a bhikkhu who has practiced well in the Vinaya attains the three types of higher knowledge (tisso vijjā) by relying on the perfection of virtue (sīlasampadā), because their specific classifications are explained therein.

One who has practiced well in the Sutta attains the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiññā) by relying on the perfection of concentration (samādhisampadā), because their specific classifications are explained therein.
One who has practiced well in the Abhidhamma [attains] the perfection of wisdom (paññāsampadā).
Relying on this, one attains the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), because their detailed classification is explained right there.

Thus, one who practices correctly toward these [three trainings] attains, in due order, this excellence consisting of the threefold clear knowledge (*vijjāttaya*), the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*), and the four analytical knowledges.
However, one who practices incorrectly regarding the Discipline (*vinaya*) [does so] by way of the commonality of tactile contact with permitted pleasant objects such as rugs and coverlets.
He perceives as blameless those things such as tactile contact that have been rejected though they are subject to grasping. For this has been said:
“I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that these things called ‘obstructive states’ by the Blessed One are not actually able to obstruct one who indulges in them.
Thereby he falls into a state of immorality. Being ill-practiced regarding the Suttas, it is said: “These four...”
Not understanding the intended meaning in such passages as, "Bhikkhus, these persons are found existing in the world," one grasps it wrongly.
With reference to this, it was said: "By his own wrong grasp, he misrepresents us, injures himself, and produces much demerit.
Thereby, he falls into false view. One who has practiced wrongly regarding the Abhidhamma...
One who runs too far ahead in reflecting on the Dhamma reflects even upon what should not be reflected upon; from that, he reaches a state of mental derangement. For it has been said:
"Bhikkhus, there are these four things that should not be reflected upon; one who reflects upon them would partake of madness and distress.
Thus, one who practices wrongly with respect to these [four] successively incurs this corruption of character, which is distinguished by its divisions of wrong view and mental derangement.
"He meets with failure. And to this extent:
"In whatever way a bhikkhu attains excellence through the divisions of the scriptures, as well as whatever failure he may meet, let all that be made clear."
This verse also has its meaning already explained. Having thus understood the Piṭakas in their various aspects, all of this, when classified according to them, constitutes the three Piṭakas.
How, by way of Nikāya, are there five Nikāyas? For all of this consists of five divisions:
the Dīghanikāya, the Majjhimanikāya, the Saṃyuttanikāya, the Aṅguttaranikāya, and the Khuddakanikāya. Among these, what is the Dīghanikāya?
The thirty-four discourses beginning with the Brahmajāla,
which comprise the three groups— these thirty-four suttas whose collection consists of three groups—
this is the Dīghanikāya, the first [collection] in forward order.

Why, then, is this called the *Dīghanikāya* (Long Collection)? It is because it is a collection (*samūha*) and a dwelling place (*nivāsa*) for suttas of long extent. For collections and dwellings are called *nikāyas*. As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, I do not see even a single other *nikāya* so full of mind as this, namely, the *poṇika-nikāya* and the *cikkhallika-nikāya* among animals."

And here, these and other such proofs are found both from the teaching itself and from the world. In this same way, the etymological meaning of the remaining [collections] as "nikāyas" should be understood.

What is the *Majjhima Nikāya*? It consists of discourses beginning with the *Mūlapariyāya Sutta*, which are of middle length, comprised in fifteen sections, and numbering one hundred and fifty-two suttas.
Where there are one hundred and fifty suttantas and two suttas, that is [the Majjhima Nikāya].
The *Majjhima Nikāya* consists of five [collections], comprising ten chapters (*vagga*).

What is the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*? It consists of seven thousand, seven hundred and sixty-two discourses (*sutta*) arranged according to the *Devatā-saṃyutta* and other groupings, such as the *Oghataraṇa*.
Seven thousand, seven hundred [discourses]...
There are sixty-two discourses; this is the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*.

What is the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*? It consists of nine thousand five hundred and fifty-seven discourses, beginning with the *Cittapariyādāna*, arranged according to the progressive increase of single factors.
There are nine thousand five hundred and fifty-seven discourses.
The number of suttas in the Aṅguttara is fifty-seven. What is the Khuddakanikāya?

It consists of the entire Vinaya Piṭaka, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the Khuddakapāṭha, and the fifteen divisions previously shown beginning with the Dhammapada—namely, all the word of the Buddha excluding the four Nikāyas.
Excluding these four Nikāyas, beginning with the Dīgha, the remainder is the Khuddakanikāya.
"Whatever else is the word of the Buddha is considered the Khuddaka Nikāya.
Thus, by way of *nikāya*, there are five *nikāyas*.
How, by way of *aṅga*, are there nine *aṅgas*? For all of this consists of: Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā...
It consists of nine divisions: Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla.

Among these, the Ubhatovibhaṅga, Niddesa, Khandhaka, and Parivāra, as well as the Maṅgalasutta, Ratanasutta, Nālakasutta, Tuvaṭṭakasutta in the Suttanipāta, and whatever other words of the Tathāgata are titled "Sutta," should be understood as Sutta.
All of this, including that which contains verses, [is included].
It should be understood that the Sutta and Geyya [are included]. Specifically, the entire Sagāthāvagga in the Saṃyuttanikāya; the entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka;
all Sutta that is without verses (niggāthaka); and whatever other word of the Buddha is not comprised within the eight factors (aṅga)—that should be understood as Veyyākaraṇa.
[Also included are] the Dhammapada, the Theragāthā, the Therīgāthā, and those sections in the Suttanipāta that do not bear the name "Sutta."
The *Suddhikagāthā* and the *Gāthā* should be understood as such. The eighty-two discourses associated with verses consisting of joy and knowledge should be understood as the *Udāna*.
The one hundred and ten discourses proceeding by way of the formula beginning with “This was said by the Blessed One” should be understood as the *Itivuttaka*.
The five hundred and fifty *Jātaka*s, beginning with the *Apaṇṇakajātaka*, should be understood as the *Jātaka*.

It should be understood that all discourses proceeding in the manner beginning with, “Monks, there are these four wonderful and marvelous qualities in Ānanda,” which are connected with wonderful and marvelous qualities, are to be known as the *abbhutadhamma* (Marvels).
These include the *Cūḷavedalla*, *Mahāvedalla*, *Sammādiṭṭhi*, *Sakkapañha*, *Saṅkhārabhājaniya*, *Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta*, and others.

All those discourses consisting of questions and answers, wherein both Veda and Tuṭṭhi have been received repeatedly, should be understood as Vedalla. Thus, according to its constituent parts, it consists of nine divisions (navāṅga).
How, according to the categories of Dhamma (dhammakkhandha), does it consist of eighty-four thousand units of Dhamma? All this indeed is the word of the Buddha:
"I received eighty-two [thousand units] from the Buddha, and two thousand from the monks."
“The eighty-four thousand teachings that have been expounded by me.
Thus, according to the classification of the aggregates of Dhamma thus elucidated, there are eighty-four thousand divisions.

Therein, a single discourse with a single sequence of connection constitutes one aggregate of Dhamma; whereas that which has multiple sequences of connection, the count of aggregates of Dhamma is determined according to those sequences.
In the *Gāthābandha* (the Versified Section), the posing of questions constitutes one *dhammakkhandha*, and the answering constitutes another.
In the *Abhidhamma*, each individual analysis of triplets (*tika*) and dyads (*duka*), as well as each individual analysis of mental cycles (*cittavāra*), constitutes one *dhammakkhandha*.

In the *Vinaya*, there is the *vatthu* (the narrative background), there is the *mātikā* (the matrix), there is the *padabhājanīya* (word-by-word commentary), there is the *āpatti* (offense), there is the *anāpatti* (non-offense), and there is the *antarāpatti* (intermediate offense).
There is the "cutting of the triads. In this context, each individual section should be understood as a single aggregate of the Dhamma (*dhammakkhandha*).
Thus, from the perspective of aggregates of the Dhamma, there are eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma.
In this way, all of this word of the Buddha was recited during the Council of Five Hundred by those headed by Mahākassapa.
By means of the assembly of masters, this is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya; this is the first word of the Buddha, this is the middle word of the Buddha, this is the final word of the Buddha;
this is the Vinaya Piṭaka, this is the Sutta Piṭaka, this is the Abhidhamma Piṭaka; this is the Dīghanikāya...
[and so on] ...this is the Khuddakanikāya; these are the nine divisions beginning with the Suttas, and these are the eighty-four thousand [teachings].
It was recited after defining this specific classification as "the thousands of Dhamma-aggregates.
Furthermore, not only this, but also many other types of classifications found within the Three Piṭakas— such as the Uddāna-collection, the Vagga-collection,
the Peyyāla-collection, the Ekanipāta, Dukanipāta, and so forth, as well as the Saṃyutta-collection and the Paṇṇāsa-collection— were recited only after defining these various modes of classification.
The rehearsal was completed in seven months.
At the conclusion of the rehearsal, the Elder Mahākassapa rendered this teaching of the One Possessing Ten Powers capable of enduring for a period of five thousand years;
thus, the great earth, filled with joy as if giving a cry of "Well done!", shook.
Making the ocean its boundary, it quaked, trembled, shook, and vibrated in many ways;
and many wonders appeared.

Thus, in this recitation, this Abhidhamma is the Abhidhamma Piṭaka by way of Piṭaka, the Khuddaka Nikāya by way of Nikāya, the Vyākaraṇa by way of Aṅga, and consists of several thousand Dhamma-khandhas by way of Dhamma-khandha.
While the bhikkhus were maintaining that [tradition], formerly one bhikkhu, having sat in the assembly of all sects, would bring forth a discourse from the Abhidhamma and preach the Dhamma, saying:
"The aggregate of form is indeterminate; the four aggregates may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate;
ten bases are indeterminate; two bases may be wholesome or unwholesome."
There may be indeterminate [factors]: sixteen elements are indeterminate; two elements may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate;
the truth of the origin is unwholesome; the truth of the path is wholesome; the truth of cessation is indeterminate;
the truth of suffering may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate; ten faculties are indeterminate; the faculty of mental grief...

“Unwholesome [states], the faculty of ‘I shall come to know the unknown’ is wholesome, four faculties may be either wholesome or indeterminate, and six faculties may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. Thus he delivered a discourse on the Dhamma.
At that point, a certain monk sitting there said, “O preacher of the Dhamma, you are like one who, while encircling Sineru, [recites] a long sutta...”
“You are reciting; what is the name of this sutta? he asked. “It is called the *Abhidhammasutta*, friend,” [the other] replied.
“Why are you reciting the *Abhidhammasutta*? Is it not proper to recite some other sutta spoken by the Buddha?
“By whom was the Abhidhamma spoken? “It was not spoken by the Buddha. “But have you, friend, mastered the Vinaya Piṭaka?”
“I have not memorized it, friend. “Then, I suppose, you say this because you do not know the Discipline (vinaya). “I have only memorized the mere words of the Discipline, friend.
“That too has been wrongly grasped by you; it must have been memorized while you were sitting on the edge of the assembly hall and falling asleep.
For one who ordains or grants full admission to someone like you commits an offense of transgression.”
‘For what reason? Because even a slight misapprehension of the Vinaya [leads to this]. For it has been said: “In that case there is no offense if he says:
‘Come now, friend, first master the Suttanta, the Gāthās, or the Abhidhamma; afterwards you shall master the Vinaya.
Or if, having made him master the Suttanta, he says: ‘Master the Abhidhamma or the Vinaya... [and so forth].
Or, if he asks about the Abhidhamma, [the opponent] grants him leave and then asks about the Suttanta or the Vinaya;
