or, if he asks about the Vinaya, [the opponent] grants him leave and then asks about the Suttanta or the Abhidhamma.
By saying, “But you do not even know this much,” the proponent of the opposing view is thus defeated.
The Mahāgoṇisiga Sutta, however, is even more powerful than this.

For there, the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, having gone into the presence of the Teacher to report both the questions asked and the answers given to one another, while reporting the answer of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, said:
"Here, friend Sāriputta, two bhikkhus were discussing the Abhidhamma..."
“They ask one another questions; when asked a question by another, they answer and do not falter, and their discourse proceeds in accordance with the Dhamma.
It is by such a bhikkhu, friend Sāriputta, that the Gosiṅga Sāl Grove would be illumined.
The Teacher, without saying, “Those called Abhidhammikas are outsiders to my teaching,” [spoke] like a golden image.
Lifting up his neck and filling his great mouth, which was as beautiful as the full moon, he let out a Brahma-voice, saying, "Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!

Having thus given his applause to the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, he said, "Just as Moggallāna would speak when speaking correctly, for Moggallāna, Sāriputta, is a preacher of the Dhamma. [He spoke] only to the bhikkhus versed in the Abhidhamma.
It is said that those who are called *dhammakathikas* (preachers of the Dhamma) are not truly *dhammakathikas* even though they preach the Dhamma. Why?

Because when they preach the Dhamma, they speak by mixing up different types of kamma, different results (*vipāka*), the analysis of the material and immaterial, and different categories of phenomena (*dhamma*).
However, the masters of the Abhidhamma do not mix up different categories of phenomena. Therefore, one is a true master of the Abhidhamma.
Whether a bhikkhu speaks on the Dhamma or not, he will certainly speak when questioned;
it is for this reason that he is called an "unfailing speaker of the Dhamma. It was with reference to this that the Teacher, having given his approval, said: "Well spoken by Moggallāna!"
One who rejects the Abhidhamma strikes a blow at this wheel of the Conqueror; he obstructs omniscient knowledge,
turns back the Teacher’s knowledge of fearlessness, deceives an assembly desirous of hearing the Dhamma, creates an obstruction on the Noble Path, and among the eighteen grounds for schism,
he corresponds to one who is deserving of the act of suspension (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*) and the act of censure (*tajjanīya-kamma*).
[It] exists. Having performed that particular deed, he should be dismissed with the words: "Go, you shall live as a scavenger-eater.

Furthermore, he might say this: "If the Abhidhamma was spoken by the Buddha, then just as in many thousands of Suttas a prologue is prepared in the manner beginning, 'At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha,' so too [should there be one for this]."

“...the introduction would have been prepared. He should reject this, saying, “There is no such introduction for the *Jātaka*, *Sutta Nipāta*, *Dhammapada*, and so forth, yet these were not spoken by the Buddha. Having rejected it thus, he should further be told:
“Wise man, this which is called the Abhidhamma is the domain of the All-Knowing Buddhas alone; it is not the domain of others. For the descent of the Buddhas...”
The birth was manifest, the manifestation of the noble lineage was manifest, the full enlightenment was manifest, and the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma was manifest.
The Twin Miracle was manifest, the ascent to the Heaven of the Thirty-Three was manifest, the teaching given in the world of the gods was manifest, and the descent from the heavens was manifest.
It is just as if the elephant-treasure or the horse-treasure of a wheel-turning monarch were stolen and used to draw a carriage while wandering about.
It is impossible and out of place for the Wheel-Treasure to be stolen and hung from a straw cart;

it is impossible and out of place for the Jewel-Treasure, capable of illuminating a distance of a league, to be placed in a wicker basket and used as such. Why? Because they are treasures worthy of a king. Even so...
"The Abhidhamma is not the domain of others; it is the domain of the Omniscient Buddhas alone. It is according to them that the teaching should be taught.
For the descent of the Buddhas is manifest... [and so on] ...the descent from the deva-world is manifest.
There is no need for a 'source-narrative' (nidāna) for the Abhidhamma, O wise one. When this was said, the opponent was unable to provide a scripturally valid example in response.

The Elder Tissa-Bhūti, a resident of Maṇḍalārāma, however, in order to show that this Abhidhamma has its origin in the Great Enlightenment, brought forward and expounded the Padesavihāra Sutta, saying:
"Monks, I dwelt in a portion of that same dwelling in which I dwelt when first fully enlightened.
For there are ten kinds of "portions": the portion of the aggregates (*khandhapadesa*),...

The section on the bases (*āyatana*), the section on the elements (*dhātu*), the section on the truths (*sacca*), the section on the faculties (*indriya*), the section on the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*), the section on the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), the section on the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), the section on names (*nāma*), and the section on phenomena (*dhamma*).
Among these, the Teacher fully penetrated the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*) at the seat of Great Enlightenment;
during these three months, he dwelt by way of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) alone. [He likewise dwelt by way of] the twelve bases (*dvādasāyatana*).

He penetrated the eighteen elements without exception; for these three months, he dwelt in the sense-base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) by way of feeling, and in the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*) likewise by way of feeling alone. He penetrated the four truths without exception;
for these three months, he dwelt in the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) by way of feeling alone. He penetrated the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*) without exception.
During these three months, he dwelt by way of the five faculties beginning with feeling.
He penetrated, without exception, the twelvefold cycle of conditions; during these three months, he dwelt precisely by way of feeling conditioned by contact.
He penetrated, without exception, the four foundations of mindfulness; during these three months, he dwelt precisely by way of the foundation of mindfulness regarding feeling.
He penetrated the four jhānas without exception; during these three months, he dwelt by way of feeling alone among the factors of jhāna.
He penetrated name without exception; during these three months, he dwelt therein by way of feeling alone. He penetrated phenomena without exception;
during these three months, he dwelt by way of the three feelings alone. Thus, according to the *Padesavihāra Sutta*, the Elder [dwelt].
He related the introduction to the Abhidhamma.
Meanwhile, the Elder Sumanadeva, a village-dweller, while reciting the Dhamma on the lower iron palace, [remarked]:
"This opponent is like one weeping in the forest with arms outstretched, or like one making a claim without witnesses regarding the Abhidhamma."
Having said, "He does not even know the existence of a cause," he spoke thus while explaining the cause:
"At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Tāvatiṃsa gods, at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree on the yellow sandalwood stone.
There, the Blessed One delivered a discourse on the Abhidhamma to the Tāvatiṃsa gods: 'Wholesome states, unwholesome states...'"
“...phenomena, indeterminate phenomena.
However, in other suttas there is only one nidāna. In the Abhidhamma there are two nidānas: the nidāna of realization (adhigama-nidāna) and the nidāna of teaching (desanā-nidāna).
Therein, the nidāna of realization extends from the time of the Great Hero Dīpaṅkara up until the Great Seat of Enlightenment (mahābodhi-pallaṅka).
This should be understood. The source of the teaching extends as far as the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma.
Now, for the sake of proficiency regarding the source of this Abhidhamma—which is thus endowed with both sources—the following method of inquiry should be understood:
By whom was this Abhidhamma brought forth? Where was it matured? Where was it attained? When was it attained?
By whom was it realized? Where was it sought? When was it sought? By whom was it sought? Where was it taught?
For whose sake was it taught? For what purpose was it taught? By whom was it received? Who trains in it? Who has completed their training?
Who preserves it? Whose word is it? By whom was it brought here?
Herein, this is the answer: By what was it brought forth? It was brought forth by the faith of the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhābhinīhāra*).
Where was it matured? In the six hundred and fifty Jātaka tales. Where was it attained? At the foot of the Bodhi tree. When was it attained?
On the full moon day of the month of Visākha. By whom was it attained? By the Omniscient Buddha. Where was it displayed? At the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
When was it recited? On the seventh day after the Ratana Sutta. By whom was it recited? By the Omniscient Buddha. Where was it taught?
Among the Tāvatiṃsa gods. For whose sake was it taught? For the sake of the deities. For what purpose was it taught?

For the purpose of pulling [beings] out of the four floods. By whom was it received? By the gods. Who train in it? Those in training (sekkhā) and the virtuous worldlings (puthujjanakalyāṇā). Who have completed their training? [The Arahants.]
The *arahants* are those whose taints are exhausted. Who maintains [this]?: Those for whom it is appropriate maintain it. Whose word is it?:
It is the word of the Blessed One, the *arahant*, the Perfectly Enlightened One. By whom was it brought?: By way of the succession of teachers.
For this Elder Sāriputta, Bhaddaji, Sobhita, Piyañjaha, Piyaḷāla, Piyaṃdasa, Kosiya-putta, and Siggava...
From Sandhāna, Moggaliputta, Sudatta, Dhammiya, Dāsaka, Soṇaka, Revata, and others, it was transmitted down to the time of the Third Council.

From then on, it was transmitted through their own successive disciples and grand-disciples; thus, for the time being, it was transmitted on the mainland of Jambudīpa by way of the succession of teachers.
As for this island [Lankā]:
Then Mahinda, Iṭṭhiya, Uttiya, and likewise Sambala,
as well as Paṇḍita and Bhadda— these Nāgas of great wisdom came here from Jambudīpa.
It was brought down by these Great Nāgas. Thenceforth, it has been brought down through their very lineage of teachers—consisting of disciples and grand-disciples—down to the present day.
Regarding the account of Sumedha:
thus, from the time of the Ten-Powered Dīpaṅkara up until the Great Seat of Enlightenment (Mahābodhipallaṅka), this [lineage] has been transmitted.
The cause of his attainment and the cause of his teaching, up to the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, have been stated;
in order to clarify that, this sequential narrative (anupubbikathā) should be understood:
It is said that at the head of four incalculable eons (asaṅkhyeyya), plus one hundred thousand eons from now, there was a city named Amaravatī.

There was a city. Therein dwelt a brahmin named Sumedha, well-born on both sides, from his mother’s side and his father’s side, of pure descent back through seven generations of ancestors, unblemished and irreproachable by birth;
he was handsome, pleasing, attractive, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion. He [performed] no other work...
Without practicing the craft of a brahmin, he mastered it instead. While he was still in his childhood, his parents passed away.
Then the treasurer-minister brought forth the register of assets and, opening the storehouses filled with gold, silver, gems, pearls, and other treasures, said:
"So much, prince, belongs to your mother; so much belongs to your father; so much belongs to your paternal and maternal grandfathers."
"This wealth belongs to you," he said, "and it has been declared to extend as far as the seventh generation of your family; therefore, take possession of it.
The wise Sumedha thought: "When my father, grandfather, and their ancestors passed away to the next world, they did not go taking even a single kahāpaṇa with them.
However, it is fitting that I should now take this and provide for the cause of my own departure. Having informed the king, he...
Having caused the drum to be beaten in the city and having given alms to the great multitude, he went forth into the ascetic life of a forest-dweller.
At this point, however, the story of Sumedha should be told. For it is said in the *Buddhavamsa*:
"In a hundred thousand aeons and four incalculable aeons ago..."
There was a city named Amara, beautiful to behold and delightful to the mind.
It was never devoid of ten kinds of sounds and was well-provided with food and drink:
the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, and the sounds of drums, conchs, and chariots.
"Eat and drink indeed, for the city has been proclaimed with food and drink!
It is a city endowed with all its parts, where every task is accomplished;
it is possessed of the seven treasures and crowded with various people."
Like a prosperous city of the gods, it was a dwelling for those who perform meritorious deeds.
In the city of Amarāvatī, there lived a brahmin named Sumedha,
who possessed a hoard of many millions and was rich in wealth and grain.
A reciter of the Vedas, a bearer of mantras, one who had mastered the three Vedas,
and who had reached the perfection of the science of marks, of history, and of our own sacred doctrine—
sitting down in seclusion, I then reflected thus:
Rebirth is indeed suffering, as is the breaking up of the body.
Subject to birth, subject to aging, and likewise subject to sickness at that time;
I shall seek the deathless, the secure, the peace of Nibbāna.
"What if I were now to cast aside this putrid body, filled with various kinds of filth, and go away without longing or seeking it?
There must be a path; it is not impossible for me."
I shall seek that path for liberation from existence.
Just as when suffering exists, happiness also exists;
so too, while existence exists, non-existence (liberation) must also be sought.
Just as when heat exists, coolness also exists;
so too, while the three fires exist, Nibbāna is to be sought.
Just as when evil exists, goodness also exists.
In the same way, while birth exists, one should seek non-birth.
Just as a man who has fallen into excrement, upon seeing a full pond,
does not search for that pond— it is no fault of the pond.
Thus, while washing away the stains of defilement, even though the lake of the Deathless exists, one does not seek that lake; there is no fault in the lake of the Deathless.
Just as one besieged by enemies, even when a path for escape exists—
That man does not flee; it is no fault of the straight path.
Likewise, one who is obstructed by defilements, while the auspicious path exists, does not seek that way; it is no fault of the straight path to peace.
Just as when a man who is diseased, though a physician is available,
does not have that disease treated, the fault lies not with the physician;
so too one who is afflicted and oppressed by the diseases of the defilements—
He does not seek out that teacher; there is no fault in such a guide.
Just as a man, loathing a corpse tied around his neck, might set it free and go away happy, independent, and self-mastered.
In the same way, having cast aside this putrid body— a heap of various filths—
I would depart, indifferent and without desire for it,
just as men and women leave excrement behind in a place of defecation.
Having abandoned it, they go away, indifferent and having no further need for it. Even so shall I go,
having abandoned this body filled with various kinds of filth,
just as one leaves a hut after having used the latrine.
Just as people abandon a dilapidated boat, leaking with water,
and depart without looking back or desiring it,
even so do I regard this body— with its nine openings and its constant flow.
I shall go having abandoned it, just as owners leave behind a worn-out boat.
Just as a man traveling with thieves, taking his goods along,
sees the danger of his goods being seized and goes on after abandoning them.
In this very way, this body is like a great thief;
having abandoned it, I shall depart for fear of the destruction of my wholesome roots.
Having reflected thus, [I gave away] wealth amounting to many hundreds of millions.
Having given [the kingdom] to my sons and grandsons, I went to the Himalayas.
Not far from the Himalayas is a mountain named Dhammika;
there my well-constructed hermitage stands, with its leaf-hut beautifully laid out.
There I had a walking path constructed, free from the five defects and endowed with eight qualities;
I brought forth the power of supernormal knowledge.
There I cast off my garment, which had come to possess nine defects.
I wore garments of bark, having attained twelve virtues.
I abandoned the leaf-hut, which was beset by eight faults;
I approached the foot of a tree, which possesses ten virtues.
I abandoned without remainder the grain that had been sown and planted,
and instead took up fruits that ripened spontaneously and were endowed with manifold virtues. There,
I applied myself to exertion while sitting, standing, and walking.
"Within seven days, they attain the power of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).

Regarding the passage, "There my hermitage is well-prepared, the leaf-hut is well-constructed," this is stated as if the wise Sumedha had personally built the hermitage, the leaf-hut, and the walking-path. This, however, is the meaning here: for the Great Being—
Seeing him set out with the thought, "Having plunged into the Himālaya mountains, today I shall enter the Dhammika mountain," Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the young deva Vissakamma:
"Go, dear son, and prepare a dwelling place for this wise Sumedha, who has set out thinking, 'I shall go forth into homelessness.
Having accepted his word, he [created] a delightful [hermitage].
He constructed a well-guarded hermitage, a leaf-hut, and a delightful walking-path.
Then the Blessed One, referring to that hermitage site produced by the power of his own merit, said:
"Sāriputta, on that Dhamma Mountain—my hermitage is well-constructed, my leaf-hut is beautifully laid out."
"I had a walking path constructed there, free from five defects," he said.
"In that place, my hermitage was well-constructed" means it was well-built by me. "The leaf-hut was well-erected" means a hut covered with leaves was also well-erected by me.
"Free from five defects": these five are indeed the defects of a walking path—namely, being hard, unevenness, having trees inside, being overgrown with thickets, and [the fifth defect]...

Excessive narrowness and excessive width. For when one walks on a walkway where the ground is hard and uneven, the feet ache, blisters arise, the mind does not attain one-pointedness, and the meditation subject fails.
But by resorting to a comfortable dwelling on soft, level ground, the meditation subject succeeds. Therefore, [one should avoid] hardness and unevenness of the ground.

One fault should be understood as follows: if there is a tree at the end, in the middle, or at the edge of the walking path, the forehead or head of one who is walking may strike it through negligence; thus, having a tree within [the path] is the second fault.

Furthermore, on a walking path covered by a thicket of grass, creepers, and so forth, one who is walking might step on or kill creatures such as snakes during the time of darkness, or be bitten by them.
"One encounters suffering" refers to the third fault: being covered by dense vegetation. The fourth fault is excessive narrowness;
when walking on a walkway that is too narrow—whether one *ratana* or half a *ratana* in width—one stumbles against the boundaries, and even the nails and fingers are broken.
When walking on an excessively wide walkway, the mind wanders, and one-pointedness [of mind] is lost.
"It is not obtained" refers to excessive width; this is the fifth fault.

As for the walking path (*caṅkama*), it should be one and a half *ratanas* in breadth, with a narrow walkway of just one *ratana* on both sides, sixty cubits in length, with a soft surface and evenly strewn sand, such as the walking path of the Elder Mahinda, the illuminator of the Island, at Cetiyagiri. Such [a path] is required.
That came to pass. Therefore he said: “There I had a walking path constructed, free from the five faults.

“Endowed with eight qualities” means endowed with the eight kinds of happiness of a recluse (samaṇa). These eight so-called happinesses of a recluse are: the absence of concern for wealth, grain, and possessions;
the state of seeking almsfood blamelessly; the state of consuming almsfood with a sense of peace; [and] the state of not oppressing the kingdom to extract its wealth and essence...
In royal households that take silver coins, copper coins, and so forth, there is an absence of the affliction of oppressing the realm;
among one's requisites, there is an absence of desire and attachment; in the face of a bandit’s plunder, there is fearlessness; there is no intimacy with kings, royal ministers, or great officials;
and there is an unimpeded state in the four directions. This is what is meant: "Just as for one dwelling in that hermitage..."
"These eight ascetic joys can be experienced; thus he built that hermitage endowed with these eight qualities. Regarding the phrase "he brought forth the power of direct knowledge":

while dwelling later in that hermitage, having performed the preliminary work on the *kasiṇas*, he began insight meditation (*vipassanā*) by way of impermanence, suffering, and so forth, for the purpose of producing the direct knowledges and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), until he reached the stage of firm strength.

"I brought forth the power of insight (vipassanā-bala). The meaning is that he built that hermitage, making it suitable for the power of insight required for higher knowledge (abhiññā), so that while dwelling there, I would be able to bring forth that power.

Regarding the phrase 'I abandoned my garment there, having reached the age of nine,' this is the sequential account: at that time, it is said, [the place] was adorned with huts, caves, walking-paths (caṅkama), and so forth."
Having constructed a delightful hermitage— densely covered with trees bearing flowers and fruits, possessing pools of sweet water,
free from the terrifying wild beasts and birds, and suitable for seclusion— and having provided supporting planks at both ends of a decorated walkway,
he fashioned a level stone slab the color of green mung beans in the middle of the walkway for the purpose of sitting, within the leaf-hut.
Having fashioned all those things that are useful for renunciants— such as matted locks, circles of hair, bark garments,
staffs, water-pots, and so forth, as well as water-jars, conch shells, and bowls in the pavilion, and charcoal basins, wood,
and other items in the fire-hall— and having thus prepared everything, he wrote on the wall of the leaf-hut: "Whoever desires to go forth, these requisites..."
When the divine son Vissakamma had carved these words and departed for the world of the gods, the wise Sumedha,
following the mountain caves at the foot of the Himālayas in search of a suitable and comfortable place to dwell,
saw a delightful hermitage built by Vissakamma and gifted by Sakka at a bend in the river; and he went to the end of its walking path.
Not seeing any footprints, he thought, "Surely the renunciants, having sought alms in the village ahead, must have returned weary and entered the leaf-hut to sit down.
After waiting a short while, thinking, "They are taking far too long;
I shall find out," he opened the door of the leaf-hut, entered within, and looked here and there.
Looking about and reading the letters on the great wall, [I thought], "These are my lawful requisites;
having taken these, I shall go forth," and I discarded the pair of cloths I was wearing. Therefore he said:
"There I discarded the cloth. Thus, Sāriputta, having entered that leaf-hut, I discarded the cloth.
"Abandoning the garment that has come to possess nine faults" means he abandons it having seen those nine faults;
this explains that for those who have gone forth into the ascetic life, nine faults manifest regarding the garment. Among these, its high value is one fault;
its liability to arise [only] through dependence on others is one; its liability to become quickly soiled by use is one; and when soiled—
For it must indeed be washed and dyed; through use, its state of weariness is easily brought about, for when it is worn out, either mending or the patching of seams must be done.
Furthermore, there is the difficulty of having to seek it again; there is the unsuitability of it for the ascetic life of renunciation;
and there is the fact that it is common to one's enemies—just as [in the following].
For indeed, enemies do not seize what is thus guarded; it must be protected in this way.

For one who enjoys [luxuries], there is the state of being an object of adornment on the one hand, and for one who goes about carrying [it] after having taken it up, there is the state of a burden on the shoulders and the state of a burden on the back on the other.
"I put on a garment of bark," Sāriputta—having seen these nine faults at that time, I abandoned my lower garment and put on a garment of bark.

The meaning is that he wore muñja grass, having taken up a bark garment (*vākacīra*) made by weaving it after repeatedly pulling it out, for the purpose of wearing as an undergarment and an upper robe.
"Endowed with twelve qualities" means possessed of twelve advantages; for there are twelve advantages in a bark garment:
first, it is inexpensive, beautiful, and allowable—this is one advantage; it can be made with one's own hands—this is...
The second [advantage] is that it becomes gradually soiled through use; the third is that there is no fuss even when it is being washed;
the fourth is that there is no need for sewing even when it has become worn through use; the fifth is that it can be easily made by one who seeks to obtain it again;
the sixth is that it is suitable for the ascetic life of renunciation; and the seventh is that it is of no use to one's enemies.
The eighth is the absence of ornamentation while wearing it; the ninth is its lightness when worn;
the tenth is having few desires regarding the requisite of robes; the eleventh is its being righteous and blameless in producing speech;
and the twelfth is the state of non-attachment even if the bark-fiber robe is lost.
"He abandoned the leaf-hut filled with eight faults"— how did he abandon it? It is said that,
taking off his pair of fine garments, he took a red bark-cloth (*vākacīra*) hanging on the robe-stand which resembled a garland of *anoja* flowers,
put it on as an undergarment, and over that, he donned another golden-colored bark-cloth which was like a carpet of *punnāga* flowers.
Placing the deer skin with its hooves over one shoulder, fastening his circle of matted hair, and inserting a metal pin into the topknot to keep it steady,
he hung a coral-colored water-pot from a carrying-net resembling a lattice of pearls; then, taking a tripod stand with three curved legs,
he placed the water-pot on one end and the hook, the sacrificial ladle, the staff, and other implements on the other.

Having hung [his belongings] and placed his carrying-pole upon his shoulder, he took a walking-stick in his right hand, emerged from the leaf-hut, and while pacing back and forth on the great walkway sixty cubits long, he looked at his own appearance and thought:
"My heart's desire has reached its fulfillment; my renunciation truly shines, like that of the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and others."
"This renunciation is praised and extolled by all wise men; the bonds of household life have been abandoned by me;
I have gone forth into homelessness; I have obtained the supreme renunciation; I shall practice the duty of a recluse;
I shall attain the bliss of the highest fruit"—thus inspired, he set down his load on his head and stood upon the bean-colored stone slab in the middle of the walkway.

Sitting like a golden statue, he spent the day; then, at evening time, having entered the leaf-hut and lain down on a wooden mat by the side of a bed of palm leaves, he allowed his body to take on its natural temperature.
Waking at the powerful dawn, he reflected upon his own arrival: "Having seen the peril in household life, [I left] immeasurable wealth and boundless treasure..."
Having abandoned [the world] and entered the forest, I have gone forth as one seeking renunciation;
from this moment on, it is not fitting to engage in heedless conduct. For the flies of wrong thoughts devour one who wanders about having abandoned seclusion.
Now it is fitting for me to cultivate seclusion, for I have departed from the household life seeing it as a hindrance.

"This leaf-hut is pleasing; the ground is plastered with the color of ripe *veluva* fruit, the white walls are silver-colored, the thatched roof is the color of pigeon’s feet, and the bed of split bamboo has the appearance of a variegated rug.
It is a dwelling place comfortable for living; indeed, no excellence of a house appears to me to be superior to this," [he said, regarding] the faults of the leaf-hut.
Searching [for faults], he saw eight defects.
For there are eight disadvantages in the use of a leaf-hut: first, the disadvantage of having to seek out and assemble the building materials through great exertion;
second, the disadvantage of having to repeatedly replace the grass, leaves, and clay whenever they fall away.
The state of being bound to wakefulness is the second; the fact that a senior monk obtains the lodging is the third, as there is no one-pointedness of mind for one who is roused at an improper time;
the state of making the body delicate by warding off cold and heat is the fourth;
and the state of concealing reproach—the notion that "when one has entered a house, it is possible to do whatever evil"—is the fifth.
The sixth [disadvantage] is the state of making it one's own by thinking “it is mine. The seventh is the fact that the house exists as a second dwelling, just like a second hut.
The eighth is the state of being shared with many, due to its commonality with bedbugs, ants, crickets, and so forth.
Having seen these eight disadvantages, the Great Being abandoned the leaf-hut. Therefore he said: “I abandoned the leaf-hut, which was filled with eight faults.”
“I have approached the foot of a tree, endowed with ten qualities”: having rejected [the other] coverings, he says, “I have approached the foot of a tree possessed of ten qualities.
Herein, these are the ten qualities: (1) little effort is one quality, for there is only the act of approaching it;
(2) lack of maintenance is the second, for even if it is not swept, whether it be well-swept or not, it is still comfortable for use.
The state of not being made to stand [in opposition] is the third. Not concealing blame is the fourth; for one who commits evil therein feels shame, thus there is the state of not concealing blame.
The state of the body not being stiffened—like living in the open air—is the fifth. The absence of making a possession is the sixth; it is the rejection of dwelling in a home.
Seventh, the absence of the need for removal—like in a house shared by many, thinking, "I shall look after it; you may go out.

Eighth, the state of being joyful while dwelling there. Ninth, the lack of concern due to the ease of finding a tree-root dwelling wherever one goes. Tenth, [the lack of concern] because of the availability of such dwellings at every place one travels.
Having seen these ten qualities, he says, "I have approached the foot of a tree."
Having observed these reasons, on the following day the Great Being entered the village for alms.
Then, in the village he had reached, the people gave him alms with great enthusiasm.
Having finished his meal and returned to the hermitage, he sat down and reflected: "I did not go forth into homelessness thinking, 'I shall not obtain food.'"
“Indeed, this smooth food increases pride, intoxication, and human arrogance. There is no end to the suffering rooted in food;
what if I were to abandon food that produces grain through sowing and planting, and instead become one who eats only wild fruits that grow spontaneously?
From then on, acting accordingly and striving with diligence, within seven days alone—
He produced the eight attainments and the five superknowledges. Therefore it was said:
“The grain that had been sown and planted, I abandoned without remainder;
I took instead the fruit that ripens spontaneously, endowed with manifold virtues.”
“Therein I applied myself to effort— sitting, standing, and walking—
and within seven days I attained the power of direct knowledge.
Thus it was for me, who had achieved success and become masterful in the Teaching.
The Conqueror named Dīpaṅkara, the Leader of the World,
appeared. While he was appearing, being born, awakening, and teaching the Dhamma, I—
absorbed in the delight of jhāna— did not perceive the four signs.
Having invited the Tathāgata to a borderland region,
with joyful minds they cleared the path for his arrival.
At that time, having departed from my own Sakka realm, I—
Shaking off my bark garments, I then traveled through the sky.
Seeing the people filled with wisdom, joyful, delighted, and exultant,
I descended from the heavens and immediately questioned the people.
“With joyful hearts, elated and thrilled, a great multitude has arisen in wonder:
‘Whose path is being cleared—the straight way, the path of travel?
When they were thus questioned by me, they replied: ‘The Buddha is the unsurpassed one in the world;’”
“The Victor named Dīpaṅkara, the Leader of the World, has arisen;
his path is being cleared, the straight way for traveling.
Upon hearing the word “Buddha,” joy arose at that very moment.
Uttering "Buddho, Buddho," I proclaimed my joy.
Standing there, with a heart full of gladness and agitation, I reflected:
"I shall plant seeds here; let not the opportune moment pass me by."
"If you would clear the way for the Buddha, grant me a single space;
I too shall clear the straight path, the way of travel.
Then they gave me the space to clear that straight path.
Thinking, “Buddho, buddho,” I was then clearing the path.
Before my release was completed, the Great Sage Dīpaṅkara,
together with four hundred thousand [monks] who were such-like and possessed of the six higher knowledges—
The Conqueror proceeded along the straight path with those stainless ones whose taints were destroyed.
Welcoming processions took place, many drums resounded, and humans and gods, filled with joy, raised shouts of "Excellent! (Sādhu).
The gods see humans, and humans also see the deities;
both of them, with palms joined in reverence, follow after the Tathāgata.
The gods with divine musical instruments and the humans with human ones—
Avoiding both of those, they follow after the Tathāgata.
Having ascended into the sky, the devas scatter divine mandārava flowers, lotuses,
and pārichattaka trees in every direction.
The gods, having ascended into the sky, scattered divine sandalwood powder and pure, excellent perfumes in every direction;
as well as campaka, salala, nīpa, nāga, punnāga, and ketaka flowers.
People standing on the ground threw up soil from all sides.
Having loosened my hair there and spread out my bark garment and hide upon the mud, I lay down face downwards.
"Having stepped on me, may the Buddha go along with his disciples;
let him not step on the mud—it will be for my benefit.
As I lay upon the earth, such was the thought in my mind.
“If I so desired today, I could burn away my defilements.
But what need have I for this state of anonymity?
Having realized the Dhamma here, and having attained omniscience, I shall become a Buddha in the world with its devas.”
“What is the use of my alone crossing over, as a man who perceives his own strength?
Having attained omniscience, I shall ferry across the world together with its gods.
By this service rendered by me to the Supreme Man,”
“Having attained omniscience, I shall deliver the vast multitude of people.
Having cut the stream of saṃsāra and shattered the three realms of existence,
I shall board the ship of the Dhamma and safely ferry across the world together with its devas.”
Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World, the recipient of offerings,
stood at my head and spoke these words:
“Behold this ascetic, the matted-hair ascetic who practices fierce austerities.”
"In an immeasurable aeon from now, a Buddha will appear in the world.
Having gone forth from the delightful city called Kapila, the Tathāgata,
after exerting himself in striving and performing difficult austerities..."
“Having sat at the foot of the Ajapāla tree, the Tathāgata will take his meal of milk-rice there and proceed to the Nerañjarā River.
On the bank of the Nerañjarā, that Conqueror will eat the milk-rice.”
By the prepared supreme path, he will approach the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Then, having circumambulated the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) to the right,
the unsurpassed one of great renown will awaken at the foot of the Assattha tree.
“His mother who gave him birth shall be named Māyā;
his father shall be named Suddhodana, and he himself shall be Gotama.
Free from taints, devoid of passion, with peaceful minds and concentrated, they shall be.”
Kolita and Upatissa shall be the foremost disciples;
he named Ānanda shall be the attendant who will serve this Conqueror.
Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā shall be the foremost female disciples.
Free from taints, devoid of passion, with peaceful minds and concentrated, they said:
"The enlightenment of that Blessed One is called 'Assattha';
Citta and Hatthāḷavaka shall be the foremost attendants."
"And Uttarā and Nandamātā shall be the foremost among those who provide service.
Having heard these words of the Peerless Great Sage,
humans and gods were filled with joy, thinking, "Truly, this one is the seed of a Buddha."
Cries of "Bravo! resound; they clap their hands and laugh;
with palms joined in reverence, the ten thousand worlds together with the devas pay homage.
If we should fail in the teaching of this Lord of the World, [we shall suffer].
In a future time, we shall stand face to face with this [teaching].
Just as people crossing a river, having missed a convenient ford,
take hold of a lower landing and cross over the great river.
"In the same way, if we all release this Conqueror,
in a future time we shall stand face to face with him.
Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World, the recipient of offerings— "
Having proclaimed my deed, he raised his right foot.
All those sons of the Conqueror who were there circumambulated me;
men, nāgas, and gandhabbas, having paid homage, departed.
When the Leader of the World, together with his Saṅgha, had passed beyond my sight,
I rose from my seat with a heart joyful and elated.
I became happy through happiness, and gladdened by rapture.
Suffused with rapture, I then folded my legs crosswise.
Having sat down cross-legged, I then reflected thus:
“I have attained mastery in jhāna and reached the perfection of direct knowledge.”
“In the ten-thousandfold world system, there are no seers equal to me;
peerless in the powers of psychic attainment, I have obtained such happiness as this.
While I sit cross-legged, the inhabitants of the ten-thousandfold world system [are present].”
They raised a great cry: "Surely you will become a Buddha!
Those signs which appeared in the past when Bodhisattas sat upon the excellent throne—those very same signs appear today."
The cold has vanished and the heat is stilled;
these signs are visible today, so surely you will become a Buddha.
The ten-thousandfold world system is silent and free from agitation.
Those [signs] are visible today; surely you will become a Buddha.
The great winds do not blow, and the rivers do not flow;
those [signs] are visible today; surely you will become a Buddha.
All flowers born on land and born in water bloom for only so long;
today they have all blossomed, so you will surely become a Buddha.
Whether they be creepers or trees, they bear fruit for only so long.
Today all three have borne fruit; surely you will become a Buddha.
The jewels dwelling in the sky and those dwelling on the earth shine forth;
today these jewels shine forth; surely you will become a Buddha.
Human and divine musical instruments resound at that time;
both together they cry out joyfully: "Surely you will become a Buddha.
At that time, various flowers rain down from the sky.
The rain falls on all sides today; surely you will become a Buddha.
The great ocean heaves, and the ten-thousandfold world system trembles;
both sides resound with joy; surely you will become a Buddha.
Even in the ten thousandfold world-system of hells, the fires were extinguished at that moment;
today those fires have been extinguished—surely you will become a Buddha.
The sun has become stainless, and all the stars are visible.
The signs appear today; surely you will become a Buddha.
Just as water, though not rained down, sprang up from the earth at that time, so too does it spring up from the earth today; surely you will become a Buddha.
The hosts of stars shine brightly, the constellations in the circle of the sky;
Viśākhā is joined with the moon—surely you will become a Buddha.
Those who dwell in caves and those who dwell in mountain clefts are emerging from their own abodes.
Today these three aspirations have been fulfilled; surely you will become a Buddha.
No discontent arises among beings; they are all content for the time being;
today all are content; surely you will become a Buddha.
Diseases are then pacified, hunger is destroyed, and those very [signs] appear before you; surely you will become a Buddha.
Then illness becomes slight, and hatred and delusion are destroyed.
Today all [fears] have departed; surely you will become a Buddha.
Fear does not exist then, yet today it is seen here;
by this sign we know that surely you will become a Buddha.
Dust does not rise upward from you; even today this is clearly seen.
By this sign we know: you will certainly become a Buddha.
An unpleasant odor departs, and a divine fragrance wafts forth.
A fragrance wafts forth today; surely you will become a Buddha.
All the gods are visible today, with the exception of those who are formless;
all of them are seen today; surely you will become a Buddha.
As many hells as there are, all of them are visible at once;
today they are all visible—surely you will become a Buddha.
Then walls, doors, and rocks shall no longer be obstructions.
Having become like space today, you will surely become a Buddha.
Death and rebirth do not exist at this moment;
yet these two are visible today—surely you will become a Buddha.
Exert firm energy; do not turn back, but press forward!
We too recognize this: you will certainly become a Buddha.
Having heard the words of the Buddha, the ten thousand worlds on both sides—
Joyful, elated, and filled with gladness, I then thought thus:
"The Buddhas speak words that are never double-dealing; the Conquerors speak words that are never in vain.
There is nothing false about the Buddhas; surely I shall become a Buddha."
Just as a clod of earth thrown into the sky will certainly fall to the ground,
so too the word of the Best of Buddhas is certain and eternal.
Just as death is certain and inevitable for all living beings, so too is the word of the Buddha.
In the same way, the word of the Best of Buddhas is firm and eternal.
Just as the rising of the sun is certain when the night has ended,
so too the word of the Best of Buddhas is firm and eternal.
Just as the roar of a lion who has emerged from his lair is certain,
so too the word of the Supreme Buddhas is certain and eternal.
Just as the laying down of the burden by those pregnant with a child is certain;
In that same way, the word of the Best of Buddhas is firm and eternal.
Come now, I shall search here and there for the qualities that make one a Buddha—
upward and downward, throughout the ten directions, as far as the element of phenomena extends.
Searching through them, I then beheld the first perfection of giving—
the great path practiced by the great seers of old.
First of all, you must firmly undertake this.
Go to the perfection of giving if you wish to attain awakening.
Just as a full jar, when turned upside down, pours out its water entirely without retaining any of it; so too should you give.
In the same way, seeing beggars— whether low, high, or middling—
give them gifts without remainder, like a jar turned upside down.
These qualities of a Buddha will not remain merely at this level.
"I shall search for other qualities that ripen enlightenment.
While searching, I then beheld the second perfection, that of virtue (sīla),
which had been practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old.
First, having firmly undertaken this second [perfection],
go forth to the perfection of virtue (sīlapāramitā) if you wish to attain enlightenment.
Just as a yak-cow, when her tail has become entangled anywhere, [will not let it go].
One meets death there without having the tail torn out.
In the same way, fulfill the precepts in the four stages;
always protect your virtue as the yak protects its tail.
"The qualities of a Buddha will not be limited to just these;
I shall seek out others as well, those qualities that ripen into enlightenment.
While seeking, I then beheld the third perfection: renunciation."
This has been practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old.
Therefore, first of all, take up this third perfection with firm resolve;
go forth to the perfection of renunciation if you desire to attain enlightenment.
Just as a man who has lived long in a prison and is afflicted by suffering does not conceive passion for it, but seeks only liberation; even so,
you should view all states of existence as if they were that very prison.
He is intent upon renunciation for the sake of liberation from existence.
These alone will not be all the qualities of a Buddha;
I shall seek out others as well, those qualities that ripen into enlightenment.
Searching, I then beheld the fourth perfection of wisdom,
which was practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old. Therefore,
you too should first undertake this fourth perfection, making it firm.
Go to the perfection of wisdom if you wish to attain enlightenment.
Just as a monk, while wandering for alms, maintains his livelihood by not avoiding families—
whether low, high, or middling— so too shall you succeed.
In the same way, at all times, by constantly questioning wise people,
you will reach the perfection of wisdom and attain full enlightenment.
For these qualities of a Buddha will not remain merely at this number.
"I shall investigate other qualities as well that ripen enlightenment.
While investigating, I then beheld the fifth perfection, vigor—
that which was practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old.
First, having firmly undertaken this fifth perfection,
go forth to the perfection of energy if you wish to attain enlightenment.
Just as Sīha, the king of beasts, whether sitting, standing, or walking;
He is one whose vigor does not falter, always with a mind of exertion.
In the same way, you too must exert firm vigor toward all states of existence;
having reached the perfection of vigor, you will attain full enlightenment.
"The qualities of a Buddha will not be limited to just these;
I shall seek out others as well, those qualities that ripen into enlightenment.
While searching, I then beheld the sixth perfection: patience."
This has been practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old.
Now, having firmly undertaken this sixth [perfection], with a mind free from doubt,
you shall attain full enlightenment therein.
Just as the earth, indeed, endures the depositing of both the pure and the impure,
and does not harbor resentment toward you; even so,
may you too be patient with the honor and dishonor of all.
Having reached the perfection of patience, you will attain full enlightenment.
These alone will not be all the qualities of a Buddha;
I shall also seek out those other qualities that bring enlightenment to fruition.
Searching through them, I then beheld the seventh perfection of truth,
which was practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old. Therefore,
you too should now undertake this seventh perfection with firm resolve.
In that regard, being one whose word is free from duplicity, you shall attain perfect enlightenment.
Just as the constellation known as Osadhi, which serves as a standard for the world including the gods,
does not deviate from its course during the proper seasons or the rains.
In the same way, you too must not deviate from the path of the truths;
having reached the perfection of truth, you will attain full enlightenment.
For these qualities of a Buddha will not remain merely at this level.
"I shall search for other qualities that ripen enlightenment.
While searching, I then beheld the eighth perfection, the perfection of resolve,
which had been practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old.
First, having firmly undertaken this eighth [precept], remain unshakable therein; thus you shall attain full enlightenment.
Just as a rocky mountain is immovable and well-established, so too shall you stand firm.
It does not shake in violent winds, but remains firmly in its own place.
In the same way, you too should always be unshakable in your resolve;
having reached the perfection of resolve, you will attain supreme enlightenment.
The qualities of a Buddha will not be limited to just these;
I shall seek others as well, those qualities that ripen into enlightenment.
While seeking, I then beheld the ninth perfection: loving-kindness.
This has been practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old.
Now, having firmly undertaken this ninth [practice],
be peerless in loving-kindness if you wish to attain enlightenment.
Just as water, toward both good and evil people alike,
bestows its coolness equally and washes away dust and dirt,
even so you too should cultivate loving-kindness equally toward those who are beneficial and those who are harmful.
Having reached the perfection of loving-kindness, you will attain full enlightenment.
These qualities of a Buddha will not be limited to these alone;
I shall seek out others as well, those factors that ripen for enlightenment.
Searching through them, I then beheld the tenth perfection, equanimity (upekkhā),
which was practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old. Therefore, you too,
having firmly undertaken this tenth perfection, [should practice it].
Becoming firm like a scale, you shall attain perfect enlightenment.
Just as the earth, indeed, remains indifferent toward both the impure and the pure that are cast upon it,
free from both aversion and attachment.
In the same way, you too should always remain like a scale in the face of pleasure and pain;
having reached the perfection of equanimity, you will attain supreme enlightenment.
These alone are the factors in the world that ripen for enlightenment.
There is nothing higher than this; stand firm therein.
As one comprehends these phenomena, characterized by their intrinsic nature and essential quality, the earth of the ten-thousandfold world system trembles through the power of that Dhamma.
The earth resounds with a trembling, like a field of sugarcane being crushed; as a wheel turns upon its pivot, so does the earth quake.
As far as the assembly was gathered at the Buddha’s meal-offering, [so did it tremble].
Trembling there, she lay unconscious upon the ground.
Thousands of jars and many hundreds of pots were crushed and mangled there,
clashing against one another.
Agitated, trembling, and afraid, their minds bewildered and distressed,
the great masses of people gathered together and approached Dīpaṅkara,
wondering: "What will happen to the world— will it be auspicious or evil?"
"The whole world is distressed; dispel that, O Visionary One!
Then Dīpaṅkara, the Great Sage, reassured them:
"Be confident, do not fear this shaking of the earth."
Today I have prophesied that he will become a Buddha in the world;
he is now comprehending the Dhamma, the ancient one practiced by the Conquerors.
As he comprehends the Dhamma in its entirety, reaching the stage of a Buddha, he will attain it without remainder.
Therefore this earth, together with its ten thousand worlds and its gods, trembled.
Having heard the Buddha’s word, my mind was instantly extinguished;
all of them approached me and once again paid homage.
Having resolved upon the qualities of a Buddha and made my mind firm,
I then rose from my seat after paying homage to Dīpaṅkara.
Both gods and humans offered celestial and human flowers.
They sprinkle flowers upon him as he rises from his seat.
Both gods and humans alike proclaim his well-being:
"Great is that which you have sought; may you obtain it just as you desire."
May all calamities be avoided; may sorrow and disease perish.
May no obstacles arise for you; may you quickly touch supreme enlightenment.
Just as when the proper season has arrived, the flowering trees burst into bloom.
In that same way, O Great Hero, you shall blossom with the wisdom of a Buddha.
Just as all those who were perfectly awakened fulfilled the ten perfections,
so too, O Great Hero, may you fulfill the ten perfections.
Just as all those who were perfectly enlightened awakened at the seat of enlightenment,
so may you too, O Great Hero, awaken to the enlightenment of the Conqueror.
Just as all those who were perfectly enlightened set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion...
In that same way, O Great Hero, set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.
Just as the moon on the full-moon night shines forth perfectly pure, so may you,
with a mind full of virtue, shine throughout the ten thousandfold world-system.
Just as the sun, freed from Rāhu, shines forth with its heat, even so,
having been released from the worlds, you shine with glory.
Just as whatever rivers there may be flow toward the great ocean, [so do all virtues flow toward you].
Thus may the worlds, including the devas, come into your presence.
Praised and extolled by them, he undertook ten qualities;
fulfilling those qualities, he then entered the forest.
The Story of Sumedha is finished.
Then, having fed the Leader of the World together with his Saṅgha,
they went for refuge to that Teacher Dīpaṅkara.
The Tathāgata established some in the going for refuge,
some in the five precepts, and others in the tenfold morality.
To some he gave the state of a recluse, and to others the four supreme fruits.
To some he gives the unequalled states that are the analytical knowledges;
to some the Bull among Men grants the eight sublime attainments;
to some he bestows the three true insights and the six direct knowledges.
By that method, the Great Sage exhorted the multitude of people;
by that means, the teaching of the Lord of the World became widespread.
He who was named Dīpaṅkara had great jaws and the shoulders of a bull.
He delivers many people and liberates them from miserable rebirths.
Seeing those capable of being awakened, even if they are a hundred thousand yojanas away,
the Great Sage approaches in an instant and awakens them.
At the first realization of truth, the Buddha awakened one hundred koṭis;
at the second realization, the Protector awakened ninety koṭis.
And when the Buddha taught the Dhamma in the celestial realm,
There was a third realization for ninety thousand koṭis.
There were three assemblies for the Teacher Dīpaṅkara;
the first gathering consisted of one hundred thousand koṭis.
Again, when the Conqueror had gone to seclusion on Mount Nāradakūṭa,
one hundred koṭis of those whose taints were destroyed and who were free from stain gathered together.
At that time, the Great Hero was on the Sudassana mountain.
The Great Sage offered alms to ninety thousand times ten million [monks].
At that time, I was a matted-hair ascetic practicing fierce austerities,
traveling through the sky and having reached the further shore of the five supernormal powers.
There was the realization of the Dhamma by twenty thousand;
the realizations of one and two were beyond counting.
At that time, it was widespread, well-known, prosperous, and flourishing.
The teaching of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara was thoroughly purified.
Four hundred thousand [monks], possessing the six higher knowledges and great psychic power,
constantly surrounded Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World.
Whoever at that time abandons human existence—
those trainees who have not yet attained their goal— are censured.
The well-flowered word of the Dhamma has been proclaimed by the Tathāgatas, the Arahants.
It shines with those whose taints are destroyed and who are stainless, in this world including the devas.
The city was named Ramyavatī; the kshatriya king was named Sudeva;
and the mother of the Teacher Dīpaṅkara was named Sumedhā.
Sumaṅgala and Tissa were the two chief disciples;
the attendant of the Teacher Dīpaṅkara was named Sāgata.
Nandā and Sunandā were the two chief female disciples.
The enlightenment of that Blessed One is called Pipphali.
Dīpaṅkara, the Great Sage, was eighty cubits in height;
he shone like a lamp-tree, like a flowering king of sāl trees.
His radiance streamed forth for twelve leagues in every direction.
The lifespan of that Great Seer was one hundred thousand years;
remaining for that long, he delivered many people across [the flood].
Having kindled the True Dhamma and having delivered the great multitude of people,
he— like a blazing mass of fire— has attained Nibbāna together with his disciples.
That supernatural power, that fame, and those wheels of treasure upon his feet [have all vanished].
"All that has vanished; are not all conditioned things empty?
After the passing of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, once an incalculable aeon had elapsed, a Teacher named Koṇḍañña appeared.
He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one hundred thousand koṭis.
In the second [assembly], there were one thousand koṭis; in the third, ninety koṭis.

At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a wheel-turning monarch named Vijitāvī, gave a great almsgiving to a Saṅgha of bhikkhus numbering one hundred thousand koṭis, headed by the Buddha. The Teacher, having prophesied of the Bodhisatta, "He will become a Buddha,"...
He taught the Dhamma. Having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he handed over his kingdom and went forth.
Having mastered the Three Piṭakas and developed the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the five higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), he was reborn in the Brahma-world with his jhāna unimpaired.
As for Buddha Koṇḍañña, however, his city was named Rammavatī, and his father was the Kṣatriya Sunanda.
His mother was named Sujātā; his two chief disciples were Bhadda and Subhadda; his attendant was named Anuruddha;
his two chief female disciples were Tissā and Upatissā; his Bodhi tree was the Sāla-kalyāṇī; his body was eighty-eight cubits in height;
and the measure of his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
After that, when one incalculable aeon had passed, four Buddhas appeared in a single aeon:
Maṅgala, Sumana, Revata, and Sobhita. During the first assembly of disciples of the Blessed One Maṅgala, there were one hundred thousand times ten million monks;
in the second, one thousand times ten million; and in the third, ninety times ten million.
Now his half-brother, the prince named Ānanda, together with a retinue numbering ninety crores, went into the presence of the Teacher for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.

The Teacher preached a gradual discourse to him. Together with his retinue, he attained Arahantship along with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). The Teacher, looking back at the former conduct of those sons of noble family—
Seeing the supporting conditions for robes and bowls made of supernormal power, he extended his right hand and said, "Come, monks.
At that very moment, they all became endowed with proper deportment, wearing robes and bowls made of supernormal power like elders of sixty years' standing;
having paid homage to the Teacher, they surrounded him. This was his third assembly of disciples.
However, unlike other Buddhas whose bodily radiance extends only eighty cubits all around, it was not so for that Blessed One.
The bodily radiance of that Blessed One stood pervading the ten-thousandfold world system at all times.
Trees, the earth, mountains, oceans, and so forth—even down to the smallest items such as cooking pots—appeared like a golden cloth.
They were as if shrouded in darkness. His lifespan, however, was ninety thousand years.
During that time, the moon, sun, and other luminaries were unable to shine by their own light, and the distinction between night and day was not perceived.
Beings moved about constantly by the light of the Buddha alone, just as they do by the light of the sun during the day. In the evening...
The world discerned the divisions of day and night by means of the blooming flowers and the birds that call out at dawn.
But is this supernatural power not possessed by other Buddhas as well? It is not that they lack it;
for if they so desired, they too could pervade a ten-thousandfold world system, or even more than that, with their radiance. This was the case with Maṅgala.
However, by virtue of the Blessed One’s former aspiration, his bodily radiance— unlike that of others, which is limited to one fathom—
remained constantly pervading the ten-thousandfold world system.
It is said that during his time as a Bodhisatta, while established in an existence such as that of Vessantara, together with his children and wife on a mountain like Vaṅka...

He lived on a mountain. Then a certain yakkha named Kharadāṭhika, having heard of the Great Being’s inclination toward giving, approached him in the guise of a brahmin and asked the Great Being for his two children.

The Great Being, with a joyful and exultant heart, saying, “I give these two little sons to the brahmin,” gave both children away, making the earth tremble as far as its watery boundaries. The yakkha—
While the Great Being stood watching, leaning against the support-board at the edge of the walkway,
the yakkha devoured the two children like a bundle of lotus stalks.
Even when the Great Man looked at the yakkha and saw its mouth disgorging streams of blood like a mass of flames the very moment it opened, not even a hair’s breadth of dejection arose within him.
As he reflected, "Truly, my gift was well-bestowed," a great surge of rapture and joy arose within his body.
He made this aspiration: "By the result of this, in the future, may rays of light issue forth from my body in this very manner.
Based on that aspiration, when he became a Buddha, rays of light issued forth from his body.
They pervaded that much space.

Furthermore, there is another account of his former conduct: it is said that in the time of his existence as a Bodhisatta, upon seeing the stupa of a certain Buddha, he thought, "It is fitting for me to sacrifice my life for this Buddha," and according to the manner of wrapping a torch-wick around a staff—
Having wrapped his entire body [in cloth], he filled a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand—adorned with jewels the size of jujube fruits—with ghee;
having lit a thousand wicks therein, he took it upon his head, wrapped his entire body in flames, and spent the whole night circumambulating the Cetiya.
Thus, even as he exerted himself until the rising of the dawn, for him too...
Not even the slightest warmth was felt from the pores of his skin; it was as if he had entered the interior of a lotus.
Indeed, this Dhamma protects the one who protects themselves. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"The Dhamma truly protects the one who lives according to the Dhamma."
“Dharma well-practiced brings happiness;
this is the benefit when Dharma is well-practiced:
one who lives according to Dharma does not go to an evil destination.”
Through the result of this very deed, the radiance of that Blessed One’s body remained pervading the ten-thousandfold world system.
At that time, our Bodhisatta, having been born as a brahmin named Suruci, approached the Teacher with the thought, "I shall invite the Teacher.
Having heard a sweet discourse on the Dhamma, he said, "Venerable sir, please accept alms from me tomorrow. [The Teacher asked: "Brahmin, how many..."
The monks said, "There is business for us," and asked, "But how many monks, venerable sir, are in your retinue? At that time, it was the very first assembly of the Teacher;
therefore, he replied, "One hundred thousand crores. He said, "Venerable sir, please accept alms from me along with all of them.
The Teacher consented. Having invited [the Teacher] for the following day, the brahmin went to his home.
He thought, "I am not unable to provide such a great number of monks with rice gruel, alms-food, robes, and so forth;

but how will there be a place for them to sit? That thought produced a sense of heat in the stone throne of Paṇḍukambala belonging to the King of the Devas, which was situated eighty-four thousand yojanas away. Sakka [wondered], "Who indeed is it that [disturbs] me from this..."
Desiring to displace him from his position, he looked with his divine eye and saw the Great Man;

seeing that the brahmin Suruci had invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha and was contemplating a place for seating, [the deity] thought, "It is fitting that I too go there and take a portion of merit.
Thereupon, assuming the form of a carpenter, he appeared with an axe and a hatchet in hand.
He appeared before the Great Being and said, "Is there perhaps any work to be done for hire?
When the Great Being saw him, he asked, "What work will you do? He replied, "There is no craft I do not know;
whether it be a house or a pavilion, whatever anyone has made, I know how to make that. [The Great Being said,] "In that case, do work for me."
“There is. “What is it, noble sir? “I have invited one hundred thousand million bhikkhus for tomorrow;
you shall build a pavilion for them to sit in. “I would indeed do so, if you could provide me with wages. “I can, dear man.
“Very well, I will do it,” he said, and having gone there, he surveyed a certain spot.
An area measuring twelve or thirteen yojanas became level like a *kasiṇa* disk.
He thought, "Let a pavilion made of the seven precious gems arise in this much space," and he looked upon it.
At that very moment, the earth split open and the pavilion arose. Its pillars were made of gold with capitals of silver, and its pillars of silver...
On the golden pillars were [vases] made of gold; on the jeweled pillars, those made of coral; on the coral pillars, those made of jewels;
and on the pillars made of the seven precious gems, there were vases likewise made of the seven precious gems. Then he looked, thinking, "Let a network of small bells hang within the pavilion.
At the very moment of his looking, a network of small bells hung down, which, when stirred by a gentle breeze—
A sweet sound issued forth from the fivefold musical instruments; it was as if the time for celestial music had arrived.
He thought, "Let fragrant garlands and flower wreaths hang down here and there," and at that very moment, the garlands hung down.
"May seats and footstools for one hundred thousand times ten million monks burst forth from the earth."
"Let them rise," he thought; and immediately they rose. "Let one water-jar arise in every corner," he thought; and immediately the water-jars arose.
Having constructed this much, he went into the presence of the brahmin and said, "Come, noble sir, look at your pavilion and give me my wages. The Great Being went and [looked at] the pavilion.
He looked out. As he was looking, his entire body became suffused without interruption by five-colored rapture (*pīti*).
Then, having looked at the pavilion, this thought occurred to him: "This pavilion was not made by a human being;
rather, it was surely because of my own intention and my own virtue that Sakka’s abode became hot. Thereupon, by Sakka..."
“This pavilion must have been built by the king of the gods.
He thought, “It is not fitting for me to give alms in such a pavilion for only a single day; I shall give them for seven days.
For even an external gift, however extensive it may be, is unable to bring satisfaction to the Bodhisattvas. [His] head was adorned...
But when one has cut off [the limbs], plucked out the eyes that were anointed with ointment, or torn out the heart-flesh and given them away— at that time,
there arises what is called joy based on the generosity of the Bodhisattvas. For even in our own Bodhisattva’s *Sivi Jātaka*,
as he was bestowing five hundred thousand kahāpaṇas daily at the four city gates and in the center of the city, giving that gift brought him joy.

He was unable to pluck them out. However, when Sakka, the king of the gods, came in the guise of a brahmin and asked for his eyes, even as he was plucking them out and giving them away, joy arose within him; there was not even a hair’s breadth of change in his mind.
Thus, for Bodhisattvas, there is no such thing as satiety based on giving. Therefore, that Great Being too—
Thinking, "It is fitting that I give alms for seven days to a number of monks amounting to hundreds of thousands of millions," he had the Saṅgha of monks,
headed by the Buddha, seated in that pavilion and gave them what is called *gavapāna* for seven days.
*Gavapāna* means filling large jars with milk, placing them on hearths, and cooking them until they are thick and well-baked.
Food prepared with a small amount of milk and rice, mixed with cooked honey, sugar powder, and ghee, is what is being described.
However, humans alone were unable to serve it; even the devas served it in alternating turns.
Even an area measuring twelve or thirteen yojanas was not sufficient for the bhikkhus to occupy. Those bhikkhus—

They sat down by means of their own supernatural power. On the final day, having had the bowls of all the bhikkhus washed and filled with ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses for medicinal purposes, he gave them along with three robes.
The sets of three robes and garments received by the most junior bhikkhu in the Sangha were worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold. The Teacher [then delivered] the blessing of thanksgiving.
While reflecting, "This man has given such a great gift; who indeed will he become?
and investigating further, he saw that "in the future, at the conclusion of two incalculable eons plus one hundred thousand kalpas, there will be a Buddha named Gotama.
Having seen this, he addressed the Great Man: "After you have passed through so much time, you will be Gotama..."
“You shall indeed become a Buddha,” he prophesied.
Having heard this prophecy, the Great Being thought, “I am indeed to become a Buddha; what need have I for the life of a householder?
I shall go forth. Thinking thus, he abandoned such magnificent prosperity as if it were a globule of spittle and went into the presence of the Teacher.

He went forth. Having gone forth and mastered the word of the Buddha, he attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), and at the end of his life, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.
For the Blessed One Maṅgala, however, there was a city named Uttara. His father was also a kshatriya named Uttara.
His mother was named Uttarā; his two chief disciples were Sudeva and Dhammasena; his attendant was named Pālita;
his two chief female disciples were Sīvalī and Asokā; his Bodhi tree was the Nāga tree; his body was eighty-eight cubits in height.
Having remained for ninety thousand years, when he passed away into Parinibbāna, ten thousand world-systems simultaneously—
All became shrouded in darkness. In all the world-systems, there was great weeping and lamentation among human beings.
Thus, after that Blessed One had passed away into Parinibbāna, having cast darkness over the ten-thousandfold world-system, at a later time a Teacher named Sumana appeared.
He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one hundred thousand koṭis of bhikkhus.
There were [nine hundred thousand crores]. On the second Golden Mountain there were ninety thousand crores, and on the third eighty thousand crores.
At that time, the Great Being was a Nāga king named Atula, possessed of great psychic power and majesty;
hearing that "a Buddha has appeared," he emerged from the Nāga realm surrounded by his retinue of kinsmen, accompanied by a company of one hundred thousand crores of bhikkhus.

Having caused offerings to be made to that Blessed One with celestial musical instruments, having distributed a great almsgiving, and having presented pairs of garments to each [of the monks], he established himself in the refuges.
That Teacher also prophesied of him: "In the future, you shall become a Buddha.
The city of that Blessed One was named Mekhalā; his father was King Sudatta, and his mother was named Sirimā.
His mother was Saraṇā; his two chief disciples were Bhāvitatta and Udena; his two chief female disciples were Soṇā and Upasoṇā;
his Bodhi tree was the Nāga tree; his body was ninety cubits in height; and the measure of his lifespan was ninety thousand years.
In a later period, a teacher named Revata appeared. He too had three assemblies of disciples:
in the first assembly there was no counting them; in the second there were one hundred thousand koṭis of bhikkhus, and likewise in the third.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a brahmin named Atideva, heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma and took refuge.
Placing his joined palms upon his head, he spoke in praise of that Teacher’s abandonment of the defilements and made an offering with his upper robe.
That Teacher also prophesied of him, "You shall become a Buddha.
The city of that Blessed One was named Sudhaññavatī, and his father was a kshatriya named Vipula.
His mother was named Vipulā; Varuṇa and Brahmadeva were his two chief disciples; Sambhava was his attendant;
Bhaddā and Subhaddā were his two chief female disciples; the Bodhi tree was a nāga-tree; his body was eighty cubits in height;
and his lifespan was sixty thousand years.
At a later time, a teacher named Sobhita appeared. He also had three assemblies of disciples:
in the first assembly there were one hundred koṭis of bhikkhus; in the second, ninety koṭis; and in the third, eighty koṭis.

At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a brahmin named Ajita, heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, established himself in the refuges, and [approached] the community headed by the Buddha...
He gave a great almsgiving to the community of monks. He, too, prophesied of him: "You will become a Buddha.
That Blessed One's city was named Sudhamma; his father was King Sudhamma, and his mother was also named Sudhammā.
Asama and Sunetta were his two chief disciples, Anoma was his attendant, and Nakulā...
Sujātā and two chief female disciples were his attendants; his Bodhi tree was a *nāga* tree; his body was eighty-eight cubits in height;
and the measure of his lifespan was ninety thousand years.
After him, having passed one incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeyya*), three Buddhas appeared in a single aeon.
Anomadassī, Paduma, and Nārada. Under the Blessed One Anomadassī, there were three assemblies of disciples:
in the first, there were eight hundred thousand bhikkhus; in the second, seven; and in the third, six.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was a single yakkha general, possessed of great psychic power and majesty, the lord of many hundreds of thousands of millions of yakkhas. He [thought]: "A Buddha..."
Having heard that [the Buddha] had appeared, he came and offered a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.
The Teacher also prophesied of him, "In the future you will become a Buddha.
As for the Blessed One Anomadassi, his city was named Candavatī, and his father was King Yasavā.
His mother was named Yasoḍharā; his two chief disciples were Nisabha and Anoma; his attendant was named Varuṇa;
his two chief female disciples were Sundarī and Sumanā; his Bodhi tree was the Ajjuna tree; his body was eighty-eight cubits in height;
and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
At a later time, a Teacher named Paduma appeared. He too had three assemblies of disciples:

in the first assembly there were one hundred thousand koṭis of bhikkhus; in the second, three hundred thousand; and in the third, two hundred thousand bhikkhus dwelling in a great forest grove in a wilderness devoid of villages. At that time, while the Tathāgata was dwelling in that very forest grove, the Bodhisatta—
Having become a lion, he saw the Teacher absorbed in the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti);
with a mind full of faith, he paid homage, circumambulated him, and, filled with joy and gladness, let out a lion’s roar three times.
Without abandoning the joy directed toward the Buddha for seven days, and departing from his feeding ground solely out of joy and happiness, he remained in attendance, having renounced his life.
After seven days had passed, the Teacher emerged from cessation (*nirodha*).

Looking at the lion, he thought, “He will gladden his heart in the Saṅgha of monks and pay homage to the Saṅgha,” and so he thought, “Let the Saṅgha of monks come. At that very moment, the monks arrived.
The lion gladdened his heart in the Saṅgha. The Teacher, observing his mind, prophesied: “In the future, you shall become a Buddha.”
For the Blessed One Paduma, the city was Campaka; his father was the king named Asama, and his mother was named Asamā.
His two chief disciples were Sāla and Upasāla; his attendant was named Varuṇa; his two chief female disciples were Rāmā and Surāmā.
His Bodhi tree was named Soṇarukkha; his body was eighty-eight cubits in height, and such was his lifespan.
"A hundred thousand years.
After that, a teacher named Nārada appeared. He too had three assemblies of disciples:
in the first assembly there were one hundred billion bhikkhus; in the second, ninety billion; and in the third, eighty billion.

Then the Bodhisatta, having gone forth as an ascetic and attained mastery over the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments, gave a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha and performed worship with red sandalwood.
He, too, prophesied of him: "In the future, you shall become a Buddha."
The city of that Blessed One was named Dhaññavatī; his father was the kshatriya Sudeva, and his mother was Anomā.
His two chief disciples were Bhaddasāla and Jitamitta; his attendant was Vāsiṭṭha, and his two chief female disciples were Uttarā and Phaggunī.
His Bodhi tree was the Mahāsoṇa tree, and his body was eighty-eight cubits in height.
The lifespan was ninety thousand years.

Then, after the time of Buddha Nārada had passed and one incalculable aeon (asaṅkhyeyya) had elapsed, at the end of a hundred thousand aeons from now, in a single aeon, there arose a single Buddha named Padumuttara. He too had three assemblies of disciples.
