At the first assembly, there were one hundred billion monks; at the second on Mount Vebhāra, ninety thousand million; and at the third, eighty thousand million.

At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a great royal chaplain named Jaṭila, gave a gift of robes to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. He, too, prophesied of him: "In the future, you will become a Buddha."
In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, there were no so-called "heretics" (titthiyā); all gods and humans took refuge in the Buddha alone.
His city was named Haṃsavatī; his father was the kṣatriya Ānanda, and his mother was Sujātā.
Devala and Sujāta were his two chief disciples (aggasāvakā), Sumana was his attendant (upaṭṭhāka), and Amitā and Asamā were his two chief female disciples (aggasāvikā).
The Bodhi tree was a *salala* tree; his body reached a height of eighty-eight cubits; his bodily radiance extended twelve *yojanas* all around;
and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
After him, when seventy thousand *kappas* had passed, and at the end of thirty thousand *kappas* from now...
In one eon, two Buddhas were born: Sumedha and Sujāta. Sumedha also had three assemblies of disciples;
in the first assembly at the city of Sudassana, there were one hundred billion who had destroyed the taints (*āsava*); in the second, ninety billion; and in the third, eighty billion.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been a brahmin student named Uttara, [found] exactly what had been left buried and stored away.
Having spent eighty koṭis of wealth, he gave a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha;
having heard the Dhamma, he established himself in the refuges, went forth, and was ordained. He too prophesied of him: "In the future, you will become a Buddha.
For the Blessed One Sumedha, there was a city named Sudassana; his father was King Sudatta, and his mother was...
His two chief disciples were named Sudatta and Saraṇa Sabbakāma; his attendant was named Sāgara;
his two chief female disciples were Rāmā and Surāmā; his Bodhi tree was the Mahānīpa tree; his body was eighty-eight cubits in height;
and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.
At a later time, a teacher named Sujāta arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples:
in the first assembly there were six million monks; in the second, fifty thousand; and in the third, forty thousand.

At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a wheel-turning monarch, heard that "a Buddha has appeared," and having approached him and heard the Dhamma, [he offered it] to the community headed by the Buddha.
Having given the kingdom of the four great continents along with the seven treasures to the community of monks, he went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher.
The inhabitants of the entire realm, having taken up the office of royal stewards, constantly provided a great almsgiving for the community of monks headed by the Buddha.
The Teacher also made a prediction concerning him.
The city of that Blessed One was named Sumaṅgala; his father was King Uggata, and his mother was Pabhāvatī.
His two chief disciples were Sudassana and Sudeva; his attendant was named Nārada; his two chief female disciples were Nāgā and Nāgasamālā.
His Bodhi tree was the Mahāveḷu tree, which, it is said, had few gaps and a thick trunk, with branches extending upward.
With its great branches, it shone like a peacock’s tail-feather fan. The body of that Blessed One was fifty cubits in height, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.
Following him, within a single eon eighteen hundred kalpas ago from now, there appeared Piyadassī and Atthadassī.
Three Buddhas were born named Dhammadassi. Piyadassi also had three assemblies of disciples:
in the first there were one hundred thousand koṭis of bhikkhus, in the second ninety koṭis, and in the third eighty koṭis.

At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a young brahmin named Kassapa who had mastered the three Vedas, heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma and, through the renunciation of wealth amounting to one hundred thousand koṭis, [became a follower].
Having had a monastery built, he established himself in the refuges and the precepts. Then the Teacher prophesied of him:
"After the passing of eighteen hundred aeons, you will become a Buddha.
That Blessed One's city was named Anoma; his father was King Sudinna, and his mother was named Candā.
Pālita and Sabbadassī were the two chief disciples; his attendant was named Sobhita; Sujātā and Dhammadinnā were the two chief female disciples;
his Bodhi tree was the Piyaṅgu tree; his body was eighty cubits in height; and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.
After him, the Blessed One named Atthadassī appeared. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first...
There were eight million nine hundred thousand bhikkhus; in the second assembly, eight million eight hundred thousand; likewise in the third.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a powerful ascetic named Susīma, brought a parasol of mandārava flowers from the world of the gods and honored the Teacher.
The Teacher also made a prediction concerning him.
The Blessed One’s city was named Sobhana; his father was King Sāgara, and his mother was Sudassanā.
His two chief disciples were Santo and Upasanto; his attendant was named Abhaya;
his two chief female disciples were Dhammā and Sudhammā. His Bodhi tree was a Campaka tree, and his body was eighty cubits in height. The radiance of his body...
It stood pervading an area of one *yojana* all around at all times; its lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
Later than him, a Teacher named Dhammadassī appeared. He too had three assemblies of disciples:
in the first assembly there were one hundred *koṭis* of bhikkhus, in the second ninety *koṭis*, and in the third eighty *koṭis*. At that time, the Bodhisatta—
Having become Sakka, the king of the gods, he made offerings with celestial scented flowers and celestial musical instruments. The Teacher also prophesied concerning him.
That Blessed One had a city named Saraṇa; his father was King Saraṇa, and his mother was Sunandā.
Paduma and Phussadeva were his two chief disciples, Sunetta was his attendant, and Khemā and Sabbanāmā were his chief female disciples.

He had two chief female disciples; his Bodhi tree was the Rattaṅkura tree—also called the Kakudha tree or the Bimbijāla—and his body was eighty cubits in height, while his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
Subsequently, ninety-four aeons ago from now, in a single aeon, there appeared only one [Buddha] named Siddhattha.
A Buddha appeared. He too had three assemblies of disciples: in the first assembly there were one hundred thousand times ten million bhikkhus;
in the second, ninety crores; and in the third, eighty crores. At that time, the Bodhisatta, possessing great majesty and endowed with the power of higher knowledge, became an ascetic named Maṅgala;
he brought a large rose-apple fruit and gave it to the Tathāgata. The Teacher [accepted] it...
Having consumed the fruit, he prophesied of the Bodhisatta: "At the end of ninety-four aeons, you will become a Buddha.
That Blessed One's city was named Vebhāra; his father was King Jayasena, and his mother was Suphassā.
Sambala and Sumitta were his two chief disciples, Revata was his attendant, and Sīvalā and Surāmā were [his chief female disciples].
His two chief female disciples were Kaṇikārā and Uppalavaṇṇā; his Bodhi tree was the Kaṇikāra; his body was sixty cubits in height; and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
Subsequently, ninety-two aeons ago from now, two Buddhas named Tissa and Phussa appeared in a single aeon.
Of the Blessed One Tissa, there were three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were [eighty million] bhikkhus...
In the first [assembly] there were one billion; in the second, nine hundred million; and in the third, eight hundred million.

At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been born as a noble of great wealth and great fame named Sujāta, went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, attained great psychic power (*mahiddhika*), and upon hearing that "a Buddha has arisen," took celestial mandārava, paduma, and pāricchattaka flowers and [approached] the midst of the fourfold assembly.
He honored the Tathāgata as he was walking, and [the flowers], having become a canopy of blossoms in the sky, remained suspended there.
The Teacher also prophesied of him: "In the ninety-second aeon from now, you will become a Buddha.
That Blessed One had a city named Khema; his father was a kṣatriya named Janasandha, and his mother was Padumā.
His two chief disciples were named Brahmadeva and Udaya; his attendant was named Samaṅga; his two chief female disciples were Phussā and Sudattā;
his Bodhi tree was the Asana tree; his body was sixty cubits in height; and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
After him, a Teacher named Phussa arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples; in the first assembly—
There were six million monks in the first assembly, five million in the second, and thirty-two million in the third.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been a kshatriya named Vijitāvin, renounced great sovereignty and went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher.
Having mastered the Three Pitakas, he preached the Dhamma to the great multitude and fulfilled the perfection of virtue (sīlapāramī). The Teacher also declared of him: "He shall become a Buddha..."
"You shall become [an enlightened one]," he prophesied.
The city of that Blessed One was named Kāsī; his father was King Jayasena, and his mother was named Sirimā.
Surakkhita and Dhammasena were his two chief disciples, Sabhiya was his attendant, and Cālā and Upacālā were his chief female disciples.
There were two chief female disciples, the Bodhi tree was an *āmalaka* tree, his body was fifty-eight cubits in height, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.
After him, in this same ninety-first aeon from now, the Blessed One named Vipassī appeared. He too had three assemblies of disciples.
At the first assembly there were six million eight hundred thousand bhikkhus; at the second, one hundred thousand; and at the third, eighty thousand.

At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become the Nāga king named Atula, possessed of great psychic power and majesty, presented to the Blessed One a great golden throne inlaid with the seven precious gems. The Teacher, too, accepted it.
He prophesied: “In this very ninety-first aeon, you shall become a Buddha.
That Blessed One’s city was named Bandhumatī; his father was King Bandhumā; his mother was named Bandhumatī;
Khaṇḍa and Tissa were his two chief disciples; his attendant was named Asoka; and Candā and Candamittā were [his chief female disciples].
He had two chief female disciples, his Bodhi tree was the *pāṭali*, and his body was eighty cubits in height.
The radiance of his body remained pervading seven *yojanas* at all times, and his lifespan was eighty thousand years.
After him, in the thirty-first aeon from now, there were two Buddhas named Sikhi and Vessabhū. Of Sikhi also...
The Blessed One had three assemblies of disciples: in the first assembly there were one hundred thousand monks; in the second, eighty thousand;

and in the third, seventy thousand. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been a king named Arindama, offered a great almsgiving including robes to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, and [gave] the elephant-treasure adorned with the seven jewels.

Having given it and fashioned it to the size of an elephant, he presented it as an allowable article (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*). He, in turn, prophesied of him: "In the thirty-first aeon from now, you shall become a Buddha.
That Blessed One’s city was named Aruṇavatī; his father was the kṣatriya Aruṇavā, and [his mother was] Pabhāvatī.
His mother was named Nāmā; Abhibhū and Sambhava were his two chief disciples; Khemaṅkara was his attendant;
Sakhilā and Padumā were his two chief female disciples; the Puṇḍarīka tree was his Bodhi tree; his body was seventy cubits in height;
the radiance of his body remained pervading three yojanas; and his lifespan was seventy thousand years.
In a later period, a Teacher named Vessabhū arose. He also had three assemblies of disciples:
in the first assembly there were eighty thousand bhikkhus; in the second, seventy; and in the third, sixty.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been King Sudassana, gave a great almsgiving of robes and other requisites to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, and then to the Teacher...
Having gone forth in his presence, he became endowed with virtuous conduct and qualities, and was filled with great reverence and joy toward the Jewel of the Buddha. He, too, prophesied of him:
"In the thirty-first aeon from now, you shall become a Buddha.
Furthermore, that Blessed One had a city named Anoma; his father was King Suppatīta, and [his mother was] Yasavatī.
His mother was named Mātā; his two chief disciples were Soṇa and Uttara; his attendant was named Upasanta; his two chief female disciples were Dāmā and Samālā;
his Bodhi tree was the Sāla tree; his body was sixty cubits in height; and his lifespan was sixty thousand years.
Subsequently, in this eon, four Buddhas appeared: Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, and [Gotama].
"Our Blessed One. The Blessed One Kakusandha had one assembly of disciples; therein there were forty thousand bhikkhus.

At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been King Khema, gave a great almsgiving of robes and medicinal requisites such as ointments to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, and having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching, [he attained the fruit of stream-entry].
He went forth as a monk. The Teacher also made a prediction concerning him.
Now, for the Blessed One Kakusandha, there was a city named Khema;
his father was the brahmin Aggidatta, his mother was the brahmin lady Visākhā, his two chief disciples were Vidhura and Sañjīva, and his attendant was named Buddhija.
Sāmā and Campā were his two chief female disciples; his Bodhi tree was the Mahāsiri-sarukkha;
his body was forty cubits in height; and his lifespan was forty thousand years.
Subsequently, in a later age, a Teacher named Koṇāgamana appeared. He too had one assembly of disciples; therein—
There were thirty thousand bhikkhus. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been King Pabbata, went into the presence of the Teacher surrounded by his retinue of ministers;

having heard the preaching of the Dhamma, he invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, and after providing a great almsgiving, he offered fine cotton, Chinese silk, Koseyya, Kambala, and Dukūla cloths, as well as golden sandals.
Having given [these gifts], he went forth in the presence of the Teacher.
The Teacher also made a prediction concerning him. That Blessed One had a city named Sobhavatī;
his father was a brahmin named Yaññadatta, his mother was a brahmin woman named Uttarā, his two chief disciples were Bhiyyosa and Uttara, and his attendant was named Sotthija.
Samuddā and Uttarā were his two chief female disciples; his Bodhi tree was the Udumbara; his body was thirty cubits in height;
and his lifespan was thirty thousand years.
After him, a Teacher named Kassapa arose. He too had only one assembly of disciples; therein—

There were twenty thousand bhikkhus. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a young brahmin named Jotipāla, a master of the three Vedas, renowned both on earth and in the sky, and a friend of the potter Ghaṭīkāra;
having approached the Teacher with him and heard a discourse on the Dhamma, he went forth and applied himself with energy.
Having mastered the Three Piṭakas, he adorned the Buddha’s dispensation through his perfection in conduct. The Teacher also made a prediction concerning him.
The birthplace of that Blessed One was the city named Bārāṇasī.
His father was a brahmin named Brahmadatta, and his mother was a brahmin woman named Dhanavatī. Tissa and Bhāradvāja were his two chief disciples, and Sabbamitta was his attendant.
His attendants were Anulā and Uruvelā, his two chief female disciples; his Bodhi tree was the Nigrodha tree;
his physical body was twenty cubits in height, and his lifespan was twenty thousand years.

Beyond that Blessed One, there is no other Buddha who appeared after this Sammasambuddha. Thus, having received the prophecy in the presence of the twenty-four Buddhas beginning with Dīpaṅkara, the Bodhisatta—
“Human birth, possession of the male organ, the cause, seeing the Teacher,
going forth, possession of virtues, the requisite qualification, and zeal—
through the convergence of these eight factors, the resolution succeeds.”
Having combined these eight qualities and having made his resolve at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha, he exerted himself with the thought:
"Come now, let me search here and there for the qualities that produce a Buddha. While searching, he saw first the Perfection of Giving;
thus, he beheld the qualities that produce a Buddha, beginning with the Perfection of Giving. Fulfilling them, he proceeded until he reached the state of existence as Vessantara.
And as he was coming, there were those benefits described for Bodhisattvas who have made their resolution:
"Thus, men endowed with all factors are certain of enlightenment,
even while wandering through the long course of existence for hundreds of millions of eons."
“They are not reborn in Avīci, nor likewise in the Lokantara hells;
they are free from parching thirst and hunger, and do not become Kālakañjika spirits.
They are not reborn as small creatures in states of woe.”
Being born among human beings, they are not born blind.
They have no deficiency in hearing, nor are they mute;
they do not become female, nor are they hermaphrodites or eunuchs.
“Those men destined for enlightenment do not belong to the mundane realm;
they are freed from the deeds of immediate retribution and are pure in their conduct in every respect.
Seeing the efficacy of kamma, they do not pursue wrong views.”
Even though they dwell in the heavens, they do not take rebirth among the non-percipient beings.
Among the gods of the Pure Abodes, no cause for such rebirth exists;
these true persons are inclined toward renunciation and are detached from existence after existence.
“They practice deeds for the welfare of the world and fulfill all the perfections.

Having attained these very benefits, he has come here. And while he was fulfilling the perfections—during his time as the brahmin Akitti, during his time as the brahmin Saṅkha, during his time as King Dhanañjaya, during his time as King Mahāsudassana, during his time as Mahāgovinda, during his time as King Nimi, and during his time as Prince Canda—
There is no limit to the number of existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of giving during the time of the merchant Visayha, the time of King Sivi, and the time of King Vessantara.
However, it was specifically during the time of the *Sasapaṇḍita-jātaka* that he said:
“Seeing one who had come for alms, I surrendered my own self.”
“There is no one equal to me in giving; this is my perfection of giving. (Cariyāpiṭaka 1.143) [Its summary:
Thus, for one who practices the sacrifice of oneself, the perfection of giving becomes what is called the ultimate perfection (*paramatthapāramī*).
Likewise [it was fulfilled] during the time of the virtuous Nāga King, the time of the Campēyya Nāga King, the time of the Bhūridatta Nāga King, and the time of the Chaddanta Nāga King.
During the time of Prince Jayaddisa and the time of Prince Alīnasattu, there was no limit to the number of existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramitā*).
However, it was specifically during the time of the Saṅkhapāla Jātaka that he said:
“Even while being pierced by spears and struck by javelins, ... [the thought never arose: ‘I am suffering.’”
“I am not angry with the son of the Bhojas;
this is my perfection of virtue (sīlapāramī). Thus, for one who makes such a sacrifice of self, the perfection of virtue becomes what is called the ultimate perfection (paramatthapāramī).
Likewise, during his time as Prince Somanassa, as Prince Hatthipāla, and as the wise Ayoghara, he renounced great sovereignty.

There is no limit to the number of existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhammapāramitā*). However, at the time of the *Cūḷasutasoma Jātaka*, it was said of him with absolute certainty:
“I cast away great sovereignty that had come into my hand like a lump of spittle;
for one who renounces, there is no clinging—this is my perfection of renunciation.”
Thus, for him who renounced his kingdom out of detachment and went forth, the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhammapāramitā*) became known as a perfection of the ultimate sense (*paramatthapāramī*).
Likewise, the number of existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramitā*) during the times of the wise Vidhura,
the wise Mahāgovinda, the wise Kudāla, the wise Araka, the wandering ascetic Bodhi, and the wise Mahosadha is immeasurable.
There was no such thing. However, in the *Sattubhasta Jātaka* during the time of the wise Senaka, it is said:
"By investigating with wisdom, O Brahmin, I liberated the brahmin from suffering;
there is none equal to me in wisdom—this is my perfection of wisdom."
For one who showed a snake that had been placed inside a bag, the perfection of wisdom (*paññā-pāramitā*) became known as the supreme perfection (*paramattha-pāramī*).
Likewise, there is no limit to the number of existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of energy (*vīriya-pāramitā*) and the others. Specifically, regarding him in the *Mahājanaka-jātaka*:
"Those men, unable to see the shore, were all destroyed in the midst of the water."
“There is no other way for my mind; this is my perfection of energy.
Thus, for one crossing the great ocean, the perfection of energy became known as the ultimate perfection (*paramattha-pāramī*).
In the *Khantivādī Jātaka*:
“Even as they were hacking at me with a sharp axe as if I were insentient,
I felt no anger toward the King of Kāsi; this is my perfection of patience.”—
Thus, for one who endures great suffering as if it were insentience itself, the perfection of patience becomes what is called the ultimate perfection (*paramattha-pāramī*).
In the Mahāsutasoma Jātaka:
“Protecting my word of truth, even at the cost of my own life, I liberated one hundred kṣatriyas; this is my perfection of truth.”
Thus, having sacrificed his life while guarding the truth, the perfection of truth (saccapāramitā) became known as a perfection of the ultimate goal (paramatthapāramī).
As it is said in the Mūgapakkha Jātaka:
“My mother and father are not to be given away, nor is great fame to be given away;”
“Omniscience is dear to me; therefore, I resolved upon the vow.
Thus, for one who, having renounced life, resolves upon the vow, the perfection of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna-pāramitā*) becomes what is called the perfection in the ultimate sense (*paramattha-pāramī*).
In the *Ekarāja-jātaka*:
“‘No one terrifies me, nor do I fear anyone at all;
supported by the power of loving-kindness (mettā), I then delight in the forest.
Thus, for one who does not look back upon life and practices loving-kindness, the perfection of loving-kindness (mettā-pāramitā) arises as a perfection in the ultimate sense.”
In the *Lomahaṃsa Jātaka*:
“I make my bed in the charnel ground, with a skeleton for my pillow;
village girls come and display their forms, not at all meager.”

Thus, even when village boys cause him pleasure and pain by spitting on him and so forth, or by offering garlands, perfumes, and the like, he who does not overstep his equanimity has fulfilled the perfection of equanimity (upekkhā-pāramitā), which is called the ultimate perfection (paramattha-pāramī).
This is the summary here; however, this matter should be understood in detail from the Cariyāpiṭaka.
Having thus fulfilled the perfections while established in the Vessantara existence, he declared:
“This earth is insentient, it does not perceive pleasure or pain;
yet even it shook seven times by the power of my giving.”
Having thus performed great meritorious deeds that caused the great earth to tremble, at the end of his lifespan, passing away from there, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven.
There, surpassing other devas in ten respects and enjoying divine prosperity for the duration of his life, [the devas] said:
"In human reckoning, his lifespan will now reach its end in seven days. Thus they spoke regarding his robes.
They become defiled, their garlands wither, sweat breaks forth from their armpits, a change of color comes over their bodies,
and a deity no longer remains steady in his divine seat. When these five portents have arisen, and having seen them, the deities—
stricken with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) thinking, "Alas, the heavens will surely become empty"— [perceive] the Great Being’s fulfillment of the perfections (*pāramitā*).

Having understood this, he thought: "Now, without going to another world of the devas, when humans are born in the human world and attain Buddhahood, they will perform meritorious deeds and, passing away again and again, fill the world of the devas. Then he said:
"Since I was in the Tusita host, I was then named Santusita; ... [the rest of the verse follows]"
Ten thousand [gods] gathered together and, with palms joined, entreated me:
“It is time, O Great Hero, O Lord! Arise within a mother’s womb;
saving the world including the gods, awaken to the deathless state.”

Thus, having been requested for the sake of attaining Buddhahood, and having performed the five great observations— regarding the time, the continent, the country, the family, and the lifespan of his mother—
and having made his resolve, he passed away from that state and took rebirth in the Sakyan royal family.
There, being raised with great prosperity, he gradually reached auspicious youth.

The detailed account of this interval should be understood from the Sutta passages such as, “Mindful and clearly comprehending, Ānanda, the Bodhisatta passed away from the Tusita realm and descended into his mother’s womb,” as well as from their respective commentaries.
During that time, he enjoyed the glory of sovereignty in three palaces suited to the three seasons, like the splendor of the deva-world.

At the time of going for a pleasure excursion to the park, having gradually seen the three divine messengers known as the old, the sick, and the dead, he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and turned back;
on the fourth occasion, seeing one who had gone forth (*pabbajita*), he conceived a desire for the life of renunciation, thinking, "Excellent is the going forth!
Having gone to the park and spent the day there, he [stood] on the bank of the Maṅgala lotus pond.
Having sat down, adorned and prepared by the divine son Vissakamma, who had arrived assuming the guise of a barber,

he heard the news of Rāhula’s birth; perceiving the intensity of his paternal affection, he thought, “I shall cut this bond while it has not yet grown strong,” and as he was entering the city in the evening—
“Truly extinguished is that mother; truly extinguished is that father;
truly extinguished is that woman who has such a husband as this.
Having heard this verse spoken by her paternal aunt’s daughter named Kisāgotamī, [he thought], “I am [the one] for whom she uses the word ‘extinguished’...”
Saying "Sāvitrī," he loosened a pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold and sent it to her;
then, having entered his own palace and sat upon his royal couch, he saw the disorder of the dancers while falling into a light sleep.
With a heart weary of the world, he roused Channa, had Kaṇḍaka brought, mounted Kaṇḍaka, and together with Channa as his companion, [departed] amidst the ten thousand deities of the world-system.
Having departed on the Great Renunciation accompanied by his retinue, and having traversed three great kingdoms during the remainder of that very night, he went forth on the bank of the Anomā River.
Proceeding by stages to Rājagaha, he wandered for alms there and sat in a mountain cave on Mount Paṇḍava; though invited by the King of Magadha to accept the kingdom, he declined it.
Having attained omniscience, he made a promise to them for the sake of coming to their realm;
having approached Āḷāra and Udaka and remained unsatisfied with the distinction he had achieved in their presence, he exerted himself in the Great Struggle for six years;
then, on the morning of the full moon day of Visākha, he consumed the milk-rice offered by Sujātā in the village of Senā.

Having cast a golden bowl into the river Nerañjarā, and having spent the day on the bank of the Nerañjarā in a great forest grove by means of various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), he took at the time of evening the eight handfuls of grass given by Sotthiya;
his virtues being extolled by the Naga king Kāḷa, he ascended the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), spread out the grass, and [resolved]: “Not until this—”
Having made the vow, "I shall break this cross-legged posture until my mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging," he sat facing the eastern direction;
and even before the sun had set, having shattered the host of Māra,
he attained the knowledge of past lives in the first watch, the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings in the middle watch, and at the conclusion of the final watch—

While penetrating the omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) adorned with all the qualities of a Buddha, such as the ten powers (*dasa-bala*) and the four grounds of self-confidence (*catu-vesārajja*), he reached this ocean of Abhidhamma methods. Thus should his source of attainment be understood.
Having thus attained the Abhidhamma, he remained for seven days seated cross-legged, for seven days with unblinking eyes, and for seven days walking back and forth.
Having passed that time, during the fourth week, he investigated the Abhidhamma attained through the realization of self-existent knowledge;
then, after spending another three weeks in the Ajapāla and Mucalinda groves,
on the eighth week, while seated at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree, he fell into a state of inactivity as he reflected upon the profundity of the Dhamma.
Requested by Sahampati Brahmā, who was accompanied by a retinue of ten thousand Great Brahmas, the Buddha—
having surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye and having accepted Brahmā’s entreaty— looked to see for whom he should first teach the Dhamma;
perceiving that Āḷāra and Uddaka had passed away, he recognized the great service rendered by the monks of the group-of-five.
Having recollected this, he rose from his seat and, traveling toward Kāsi-pura, consulted with Upaka along the way.
On the full moon day of Āsāḷhī, having reached the dwelling place of the group of five monks at Isipatana in the Deer Park,
and having instructed them after they had behaved in an unseemly manner, he set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion for those headed by the Elder Aññā-Koṇḍañña.
He caused eighteen koṭis of Brahmās to drink the beverage of the Deathless. In this way, the origin of the teaching should be understood as extending up to the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma.
This is the summary here. The detailed account, however, should be understood by means of the *Ariyapariyesana Sutta*, the *Pabbajjā Sutta*, and so forth, together with their commentaries.
Furthermore, for this Abhidhamma, which is thus endowed with both the origin of its realization and the origin of its teaching, there is yet another distant origin.
The distant cause (*dūranidāna*), the proximate cause (*santikenidāna*), and the immediate cause (*avidūranidāna*)—these are the three causes.

Therein, from the time [the Bodhisatta] was at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha up until his arrival in the Tuṣita heaven, it should be understood as the distant cause. From the Tuṣita heaven up until the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), it is the proximate cause.
“At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Tāvatiṃsa devas, at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree upon the yellow sandalwood stone.”
"Therein, the Blessed One delivered a discourse on the Abhidhamma to the Tāvatiṃsa devas"—this is its proximate cause.
This concludes the introductory narrative.
The introductory narrative is finished.
1. Cittuppādakaṇḍa: Commentary on the Words of the Triple Matrices (Tikamātikā).
Now...
“Thus, as I speak this discourse on the Abhidhamma, listen with undistracted minds; for rare indeed is this teaching.
When the discourse on the Abhidhamma had been thus promised, the occasion for its delivery arrived. In that regard, since the Abhidhamma...

The "Name" refers to the seven treatises beginning with the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*. The *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* itself consists of four sections (*kaṇḍa*), such as the Section on the Arising of Consciousness (*Cittuppādakaṇḍa*).
The Section on the Arising of Consciousness is twofold, by way of the Schemas (*mātikā*) and the Exegesis (*bhājanīya*). Among these, the Schemas come first. That [Schemas] is also twofold:
the Threefold Schema (*tikamātikā*) and the Twofold Schema (*dukamātikā*). Among those, the Threefold Schema comes first. Regarding the Threefold Schema as well—
In the "Triplet of the Wholesome" (kusalattika), within the wholesome triad itself, there is this term: "wholesome states" (kusalā dhammā). Therefore:
"From here onwards, listen with one-pointed attention to this profound discourse on the Abhidhamma as it is being spoken; well done, well done, O virtuous ones!"
1. “Wholesome states, unwholesome states, and indeterminate states”—this is first the triad of the wholesome (kusalattika), named after its initial term.
“States associated with pleasant feeling, states associated with painful feeling, and states associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling”—this is [the triad] named after all its terms.
This is called the "Feeling Triplet. In this way, the name for all triplets and dyads should be understood either by way of the first term or by way of every term.
All of these are established through fifteen chapters: there is one chapter for the triplets and fourteen for the dyads.
For the six dyads beginning with "states that are roots" and "states that are not roots" are [found] in the text.

Furthermore, because they exist in mutual connection both in meaning and in substance—standing like the central hub of a wheel or like a cluster of pots—they are called the "Cluster of Causes" (*hetugocchaka*).
Beyond those, there are seven dyads (duka) such as "conditioned phenomena" and "unconditioned phenomena," which are not mutually connected;
rather, having been selected solely on the basis of their commonality as dyads, they have been placed separately within different clusters.
Because they are minor compared to other major dyads (*mahantaraduka*), they should be understood as the “Minor Intermediate Dyads” (*cūḷantaradukā*).

Following that, by way of the six dyads beginning with the taints (*āsava*), there is the “Cluster of Taints” (*āsavagocchaka*); likewise, by way of the dyads beginning with the fetters (*saṃyojana*), there is the “Cluster of Fetters” (*saṃyojanagocchaka*);

likewise, by way of the dyads beginning with the knots (*gantha*), floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), and hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), there are the “Clusters of Knots, Floods, Yokes, and Hindrances”; [and finally] the dyads beginning with the perversions (*parāmāsa*).
By way of these five, there is the "Cluster of Misapprehensions" (*parāmāsa-gocchaka*). All seven clusters (*gocchaka*) should be understood in this manner.
Following that, the fourteen dyads beginning with "states that have an object" (*sārammaṇā dhammā*) are called the "Great Intermediate Dyads" (*mahantara-duka*).

Next, the six dyads beginning with the "dyad of clinging" (*upādāna-duka*) are called the "Cluster of Clinging" (*upādāna-gocchaka*). Then, the eight dyads beginning with the "dyad of defilements" (*kilesa-duka*) are the "Cluster of Defilements" (*kilesa-gocchaka*).

Next, the eighteen dyads beginning with "those to be abandoned by vision" (dassanena-pahātabba-duka) are called the "Back Dyads" (*piṭṭhiduka*) because they are placed at the conclusion of the Abhidhamma matrix (*mātikā*).

Furthermore, the forty-two dyads beginning with "states partaking of true knowledge" (*vijjābhāginō dhammā*) and "states not partaking of true knowledge" (*avijjābhāginō dhammā*) are called the "Sutta Dyads" (*suttantikaduka*). Thus, all these [dyads] consist of fifteen sections.
They should be understood as being thus determined.
When determined in this way, these fall into two groups by way of being with reference (sappadesa) and without reference (nippadesa).
Among them, the nine triads and seventy-two dyads are called "with reference" because they include material and immaterial phenomena that possess spatial location.
The remaining thirteen triplets (tīka) and seventy-one dyads (duka) are called "without exception" (nip-padesa). Among them, first regarding the triplets:

the triplet of feeling (vedanā), the triplet of applied thought (vitakka), the triplet of rapture (pīti), the triplet of what has arisen (uppanna), the triplet of the past (atīta), and the four triplets of objects (ārammaṇa)—these nine triplets are called "with exception" (sa-padesa).
Regarding the dyads, there are nine groups (gocchaka) beginning with the group on causes (hetu) and ending with the group on clinging (upādāna).
At the end [of the section on the aggregates], there are three dyads; at the end of the group on the defilements (*kilesagaṇa*), there are four dyads; two great dyads:
"states associated with consciousness" and "states dissociated from consciousness," and "states conjoined with consciousness" and "states not conjoined with consciousness";

and among the Suttanta dyads, the dyad of designation (*adhivacanaduka*), the dyad of etymological expression (*niruttiduka*), the dyad of description (*paññattiduka*), and the dyad of name-and-form (*nāmarūpaduka*).
Excluding these four dyads, the remaining thirty-eight dyads are called "with reference" (sappadesa).
It should be understood that all the remaining triads and dyads mentioned [in the matrix] are "without reference" (nippadesa).
Now follows this sequential word-commentary on the matrix headings beginning with "wholesome states" (kusalā dhammā): the word "wholesome" (kusala)—

It is seen in the sense of health, blamelessness, skillfulness, and pleasant ripening. For this [term] is seen in the sense of health in such passages as: “I hope, sir, you are well; I hope you are free from illness.
And it is seen in the sense of blamelessness in such passages as: “But what, venerable sir, is wholesome bodily conduct?
That bodily conduct, Great King, which is blameless,” and: “Furthermore, venerable sir, this is unsurpassed...”
In such passages as, “Just as the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*),” it means blameless.
In such passages as, “You are skilled (*kusala*) in the parts of a chariot,” or “The four types of women are skilled and trained in dance and song,” it means clever or expert.
In such passages as, “Bhikkhus, it is due to the undertaking of wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*),” or “Because of having performed wholesome karma (*kusala-kamma*),” [it means skillful].
In such passages as "because of being accumulated," it refers to a pleasant result (*sukhavipāka*). Here, however, this term applies to health, to what is blameless, and to a pleasant result.

Furthermore, this word *dhamma* is seen in the senses of scripture (*pariyatti*), cause (*hetu*), quality (*guṇa*), insentience (*nissatta*), lifelessness (*nijjīvatā*), and so forth. Indeed, in such passages as "he masters the *dhamma*:

the Sutta, the Geyya," it is seen in the sense of scripture. In such passages as "knowledge regarding the cause is the analytical knowledge of *dhamma* (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*)," it is seen in the sense of a cause.
“In neither Dhamma nor non-Dhamma do both have the same ripening;
non-Dhamma leads to hell, while Dhamma brings one to a happy destination”—in such passages, it refers to a quality (*guṇa*).

“At that time, indeed, there are phenomena (*dhammā*); “he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena”—in such passages, it refers to the absence of a sentient being or a soul (*nissatta-nijjīvatā*). This [meaning] is also appropriate here, precisely as the absence of a sentient being or a soul.
The meaning of the words here is as follows: they are called *kusala* because they "make firm" (*salayanti*), move, shake, and destroy base and evil states (*dhamma*).
Alternatively, they are *kusā* because they lie in a base manner (*kucchitena ākārena*). They are *kusala* because they "mow down" (*lunanti*) and cut those weeds (*kusa*) known as the unwholesome.
Or else, knowledge that brings about the end of, thins out, and exhausts what is base is called *kusa*. By means of that *kusa*, [they are *kusala*].
They are "wholesome" (*kusala*) because they are to be cut (*lātabba*); the meaning is that they are to be grasped and put into practice.
Or, just as a sickle (*kusa*) cuts both parts of the area of the hand it reaches, so too these [states] cut the side of the defilements—comprising both the arisen and the unarisen.
Therefore, they are "wholesome" because they cut like a sickle. Furthermore, they are "phenomena" (*dhamma*) because they bear their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

They are called *dhammas* because they are sustained by conditions (*paccaya*) or because they are sustained according to their own intrinsic nature (*yathāsabhāva*). They are not wholesome (*kusala*) nor unwholesome (*akusala*).

Just as "non-friends" (*amitta*) are the opposites of friends, and "non-greed" (*alobha*) and so forth are the opposites of greed (*lobha*) and so forth, the meaning here is that they are the opposites of the wholesome.

They are "indeterminate" (*abyākata*) because they are not described as being either wholesome or unwholesome; the meaning is that they have not been stated as having the nature of either the wholesome or the unwholesome. Among them, those characterized by blamelessness and pleasant fruition are—

The wholesome (kusala) have the characteristic of being blameless and having pleasant results; the unwholesome (akusala) have the characteristic of being blameworthy and having painful results; the indeterminate (abyākata) have the characteristic of having no result.
Now, are these terms—“wholesome,” “states” (dhamma), and so forth—synonymous, or do they have different meanings? What is the point here?
If they were synonymous, then the expression “wholesome states” (kusalā dhammā) would be identical to the expression “wholesome and unwholesome” (kusalākusalā) as it was previously stated. Or else...
Otherwise, the sets of three and two would result in being six and four [respectively], and there would be a lack of connection between the words.

For just as when one says "wholesome," "form," and "possessing eyes," there is no connection whatsoever among those words if they do not look toward one another by way of their meaning, so too here a lack of connection between the words would result. [Thus,] they would be devoid of any prior-posterior relationship.
Furthermore, these words would become meaningless. Moreover, this would also result in a contradiction with the subsequent question:
“Which states are wholesome? For it would follow that states are not wholesome at all, and yet this is said:
“Which states are wholesome? Another way: if these [terms] have the same meaning, then because of the unity of the three “states,” there would be only one state.
It also results in the oneness of the wholesome and so forth. For there is an oneness in the state of being "dhamma" among all three "dhammas," namely the wholesome and the rest.
Therefore, it results in the oneness of the wholesome and so forth—which are not different in meaning from the perspective of their actual referent—along with the triad of dhammas [as categories].
[One might say: "That which is wholesome is unwholesome, and that is indeterminate. Furthermore, regarding the three dhammas...

If you do not accept unity, but say that the state characterized by the wholesome is one thing, the state characterized by the unwholesome is another, and the state characterized by the indeterminate is yet another—

this being so, "dhamma" would mean an existent (bhāva), and non-existence (abhāva) would be something other than an existent; thus, the states characterized by the wholesome, which are reckoned as existents, would be one thing,
while the state characterized by the unwholesome would be a different thing, a non-existent, and likewise for the state characterized by the indeterminate.

And by those [terms], another wholesome [dharma] would also [be negated]. Thus, since wholesome dharmas and the rest would not be different from those dharmas that have reached the state of non-existence, they too would simply be non-existent.
All of this is without reason. Why? Because conventional expression is established according to how it is intended. For conventional expression, in whatever way it applies to things—
It is approved and accepted, and is established exactly as such.

Furthermore, this expression "dhamma" preceded by "kusala" in phrases such as "wholesome states" (kusalā dhammā), and the expression "kusala" following "dhamma," are not accepted by the wise as being identical in meaning—like the repetition "wholesome, wholesome"—because they lack any specific distinction in their own referents;
nor do they have mutually unrelated meanings, like the words "kusala" and "rūpa" or "cakkhu" and "māsa."
In this context, the word *kusala* is accepted as signifying the sense of being blameless and having a pleasant result;
the word *akusala* signifies the sense of being blameworthy and having an unpleasant result; the word *abyākata* signifies the sense of not having a result;
and the word *dhamma* signifies such senses as intrinsic nature and persistence. When it is spoken immediately after any one of these [terms], [it is understood accordingly].
It illustrates their commonality of meaning. For all these are *dhammas* by virtue of the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) of maintaining their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and so forth.
Furthermore, when terms such as "wholesome" (*kusala*) and the like are spoken before the word *dhamma*, they illustrate their respective specific meanings for that [word].
For a *dhamma* is either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. Thus, when these are spoken separately...

They are accepted by the wise in the world as being indicated by their respective individual meanings when used alone; and when spoken together with the word *dhamma*, they are accepted as indicating either the commonality of their respective meanings or their specific meanings.
Therefore, all that has been stated here regarding the attribution of faults by positing a difference in meaning where there is actually a single meaning is entirely without foundation.
This, then, is the word-by-word commentary on the sequence for the wholesome triad (*kusalattika*). By this same method, the method for the remaining tetrads and dyads should also be understood.
Hereafter, however, we shall explain only the specific distinctions.

2. Regarding the phrases beginning with "for pleasant feeling" (*sukhāya vedanāya*), first, the word "pleasant" (*sukha*) refers to: pleasant feeling, the root of pleasure, the object of pleasure, the cause of pleasure, the condition of pleasure, the state of pleasure, non-affliction, Nibbāna, and so forth.
It is seen [in various senses]. For this term is seen in the sense of pleasant feeling in such passages as, “With the abandoning of pleasure” (*sukhassa ca pahānā*).

It is seen in the sense of the root of pleasure in such passages as, “The arising of Buddhas is pleasant,” and “Pleasant is dispassion in the world. It is seen in the sense of an object of pleasure in such passages as, “Because, Mahāli, form is pleasant, followed by pleasure, and immersed in pleasure.
And it is seen in the sense of a designation for pleasure in such passages as, “This, bhikkhus, is a designation for pleasure.”
In such passages as "namely, merits," it refers to the cause of happiness.

In such passages as "To this extent, monks, it is not easy to reach through description how happy the heavenly realms are," and "Those who do not see Nandana do not understand happiness," it refers to the state that is the condition for happiness.
In such passages as "These states are dwellings in happiness in the present life," it refers to the absence of affliction (*abyābajjha*). [And] "Nirvana..."
In such passages as “the supreme bliss,” it refers to Nibbāna; however, here it should be understood as referring specifically to pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*).

The word “feeling” (*vedanā*) occurs in the sense of that which is felt (*vedayita*) in such passages as “felt feelings arise. The word “suffering” (*dukkha*) occurs in the sense of painful feeling, the basis for painful feeling, the object of painful feeling, the condition for painful feeling, the state of being a condition for painful feeling, and so forth.
It is seen [in various senses]. For this term is seen in the sense of painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*) in such passages as “with the abandoning of suffering” (*dukkhassa ca pahānā*);

in the sense of the basis of suffering (*dukkhavatthu*) in such passages as “birth, too, is suffering” (*jātipi dukkhā*); in the sense of an object of suffering (*dukkhārammaṇa*) in such passages as “Because, Mahāli, form is suffering, beset by suffering, immersed in suffering”;

in the sense of a condition for suffering (*dukkhapaccaya*) in such passages as “the accumulation of evil is suffering”; and in such passages as “To this extent, monks... [it is seen in the sense of the state of being suffering itself].
In such passages as “it is not easy to reach [the end] by description, so painful are the hells,” it refers to the state of being a condition for suffering.
Here, however, this should be understood as referring specifically to painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).

As for the etymological meaning here: it causes happiness, thus it is pleasant (*sukhā*); it causes pain, thus it is painful (*dukkhā*); that which is neither painful nor pleasant is neither-painful-nor-pleasant (*adukkhamasukhā*).

"Neither-painful-nor-pleasant. [Note: The syllable "ma" is used here for the sake of euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*). All [feelings] are called "feeling" (*vedanā*) because they feel and experience the flavor of their respective objects.
Among them, that which has the characteristic of experiencing what is desirable is pleasant; that which has the characteristic of experiencing what is undesirable is painful;
and that which has the characteristic of experiencing what is contrary to both is neither-painful-nor-pleasant. As for the term "associated" (*sampayutta*) found in all three instances:
Its meaning is as follows: they are "associated" (sampayutta) because they are joined together by certain modes. By which modes? By such modes as arising together (ekuppādatā), and so forth.
For, in the refutation of the question, "Are there no states that are associated with any other states? [the answer is] "Yes," and in response to this, it is said:
"Is it not the case that there are some states that are co-existent (sahagata), conascent (sahajāta), conjoined (saṃsaṭṭha), arising together, and ceasing together with other states?"
"Having a single basis and a single object"—thus the meaning of association has been stated by way of simultaneous arising and so forth.
Therefore, they are "associated" (sampayutta) because they are joined together in these ways, such as simultaneous arising. 3.

In the triad of resultants: the "resultants" (vipāka) are the ripenings of wholesome and unwholesome states that are distinguished from one another; they are those that have attained the state of having fully ripened.
This is a designation for immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*). "Phenomena subject to result" (*vipākadhammadhamma*) means phenomena whose intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is result.

Just as beings whose nature and constitution is birth and aging are called "subject to birth" and "subject to aging," so too, in the sense of producing a result, phenomena whose nature and constitution is result are meant by this term.
The third phrase is stated by way of negating both of these natures.

4. Regarding the triad of "clung-to and subject to clinging" (*upādinnupādāniya*): they are "clung-to" (*upādinna*) because they have been taken up by karma associated with craving and views through the act of making them an object, and because they have been grasped as the state of a fruit.
They are "subject to clinging" (*upādāniya*) because, having become objects, they are beneficial to the clingings (*upādāna*) by way of their connection to clinging.
This is a designation for those things that serve as the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) for clinging. And [the term] *upādiṇṇa*...

"Those which are subject to clinging" (*upādāniya*) means "clung-to and subject to clinging" (*upādiṇṇupādāniya*); this is a designation for those material and immaterial phenomena produced by tainted (*sāsava*) karma.
Thus, in the same manner, the meaning of the remaining two terms should also be understood as being accompanied by negation.
5. In the triad of "defiled and defiling" (*saṃkiliṭṭha-saṃkilesika*): it defiles, thus it is "defiling" (*saṃkileso*); it afflicts and causes torment.

The meaning is as follows: "Possessed of defilement" means defiled (*saṃkiliṭṭha*). They are called "defiling" (*saṃkilesika*) because they are worthy of defilement by way of occurring with themselves as their object, or because they are engaged in defilement, since they do not transcend the state of being its object.
This is a designation for those things that serve as the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) for defilement. And these are both defiled and defiling.

And these are defiled and subject to defilement. The remaining two pairs should also be understood according to the method explained for the first triad. 6. In the triad of applied thought (*vitakka*):

those that occur together with applied thought by way of association are "with applied thought" (*savitakka*). Those that occur together with sustained thought (*vicāra*) are "with sustained thought" (*savicāra*).

Those that are both with applied thought and with sustained thought are "with applied thought and sustained thought" (*savitakkasavicāra*). Those devoid of both are "without applied thought and without sustained thought" (*avitakka-avicāra*).
"Vicāra-only" (*vicāramatta*) means that among applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), these have *vicāra* alone as their measure (*mattā*) or standard (*pamāṇa*).

The meaning is that they do not associate with applied thought beyond the level of sustained thought. "Without applied thought and having sustained thought-only" (*avitakkavicāramatta*) means those which are without applied thought and possess sustained thought-only.

7. In the triad concerning rapture (*pīti*), "accompanied by rapture" (*pītisahagata*) means having attained the state of arising together with rapture, etc.; the meaning is that they are associated with rapture (*pītisampayutta*).
The same method applies to the other two terms as well. Here, "equanimity" (*upekkhā*) refers to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*adukkhamasukhā vedanā*).
For this feeling "looks on" (*upekkhati*) at the occurrence of the modes of pleasure and pain; because it is established in a neutral mode, it occurs in that manner, and thus it is called equanimity.

Thus, by taking only two terms from the triad of feelings, this triad is stated in order to show the distinction of happiness free from rapture (*nippītika sukha*) from happiness accompanied by rapture (*sappītika sukha*).
8. In the "Triplet on Seeing," "by seeing" means by the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*). For that [path] is called "seeing" because it sees *nibbāna* for the first time.
As for the change-of-lineage consciousness (*gotrabhu*), although it sees [the truth] even earlier, it is like a man who has come to a king’s presence on some business:
even though he sees the king from afar seated upon the neck of an elephant as he moves along the road, [he does not yet truly see him].
When asked, "Have you seen the king?", although he had indeed seen him, he replied, "I have not seen him," because the duty that ought to be performed [upon seeing him] had not been done.
In the same way, although Nibbāna has been seen, it is not called "seeing" because the abandonment of defilements (*kilesappahāna*) which ought to be performed is still absent.
For that knowledge stands in the position of the path's adverting (*āvajjana*). By "development" (*bhāvanāya*) is meant by means of the remaining three paths. For the remaining three paths...
It arises by way of development (bhāvanā) regarding that very phenomenon already seen through the first path; it does not see anything previously unseen.
Therefore, it is called "development" (bhāvanā). The third term is stated by way of the negation of both [seeing and development]. 9. In the triad of "immediately following that":
those whose causes (hetu) are to be abandoned by seeing are "those whose causes are to be abandoned by seeing" (dassanena pahātabbahetuka).

The same method applies to the second term as well. Regarding the third term, one should not take the meaning to be "those for whom the cause is to be abandoned neither by vision nor by cultivation," but rather the meaning should be taken as "those who possess a cause that is to be abandoned neither by vision nor by cultivation.
Otherwise, there would be no inclusion of those states that are rootless (*ahetuka*); for in their case, there is simply no cause whatsoever.
It may be abandoned by seeing and by cultivation. Even among those states accompanied by roots, it follows that there is abandonment of those excluding the roots, but not of the roots themselves;
for it is the roots alone among these that are said to be "not to be abandoned either by seeing or by cultivation," and not those other phenomena.
And both of these [interpretations] are unintended. Therefore, the root among these is neither to be abandoned by seeing nor by cultivation.
The meaning to be understood here is: "They exist" means they have roots that are to be abandoned neither by vision nor by cultivation.
10. Regarding the category of "leading to accumulation" (*ācayagāmin*): it is called "accumulation" (*ācaya*) because it is accumulated by kamma and defilements.

This is a name for rebirth-linking, death, and the course of existence (*pavatta*). They go toward that accumulation by way of being its cause through the state of producing it, or else they proceed within it.

They are called "leading to accumulation" (*ācayagāmin*) because they cause that person to go toward accumulation exactly as previously described; this is a designation for wholesome and unwholesome states associated with the taints (*sāsrava*).
Precisely for that reason, because they have departed from "accumulation"—which is to say, from what is termed "piling up"—Nirvana is "without accumulation" (*apacaya*).
Because they proceed by taking that [Nirvana] as their object, they are called "leading to non-accumulation" (*apacayagāmin*); this is a designation for the Noble Paths (*ariyamagga*).

This is a designation (*adhivacana*). Furthermore, they are "tending toward accumulation" (*ācayagāmin*) because, like a mason building a wall with bricks, they proceed by accumulating the process of occurrence.
They are "tending toward diminution" (*apacayagāmin*) because, like a person dismantling each brick already piled up, they proceed by diminishing that very same process of occurrence.
The third term is stated as a negation of both.

11. Regarding the "Threefold Training" (Sekkhattika): they are called *sekkhā* because they are born within the three trainings (*sikkhā*). They are also called *sekkhā* because they belong to the seven types of trainees (*sekkha*).

Furthermore, they are called *sekkhā* because they train by themselves due to their training being not yet completed. They are called *asekkhā* because there is no further training to be undertaken; thus they are "non-trainees.
Alternatively, they are called *asekkhā* because they have reached the culmination of the trainings. This is a designation for the states of the fruit of arahantship (*arahatta-phala-dhamma*).
The third term is stated by way of negating both. 12.
In the triad of the limited (*paritta*): because it is broken on all sides, that which is small is called "limited" (*paritta*), as in the expressions "a limited lump of cow dung" and so forth.
These [states] are also called "limited" because they are, as it were, limited due to their lack of power; this refers to the states belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
This is a synonym. They are called "lofty" (*mahaggata*) because they have attained greatness through their capacity to suppress the defilements, their great fruitfulness, and their long duration;
or alternatively, because they are practiced by those who possess greatness—that is, by those endowed with sublime zeal, energy, mind, and wisdom.
Defilements such as lust and the like are what constitute a "measure. However, these [states] have no measure either in terms of their object or in terms of their association.
They are "immeasurable" (*appamāṇā*) because they are the opposites of what is measurable.

13. Regarding the triad of limited objects: those which have a limited object are "limited-objected" (*parittārammaṇā*). The same method applies to the other two terms as well. 14. Regarding the triad of the inferior:

"inferior" (*hīnā*) refers to base, unwholesome states. Those that exist between the inferior and the sublime are "middling" (*majjhimā*). The remaining states belonging to the three planes are "sublime" (*paṇītā*) in the sense of being excellent and unsurpassed; these are the supramundane states.

15. Regarding the triad of wrongness (*micchattattika*): they are called "wrongnesses" (*micchattā*) because, even when one desires, "May these bring me benefit and happiness," they do not exist in that way, and because they proceed erroneously by perceiving the foul and so forth as beautiful.

They are "fixed" (*niyata*) because, once they have begun to yield their result, they must yield that result immediately after the breaking up of the aggregates. Since they are both wrongnesses and fixed, they are "fixed wrongnesses" (*micchattaniyatā*).

They are "right" (*sammatta*) because their nature is right, being the opposite of what was previously stated. And because they are both right and fixed in delivering their fruit immediately thereafter, they are "right-and-fixed" (*sammattaniyata*).
Those that are not fixed in either way are "indefinite" (*aniyata*). 16.

In the triad of objects of the path (*magga*), Nibbāna is called the "path" (*magga*) because it is sought (*maggati*) or searched for (*gavesati*), or because it goes while slaying the defilements (*kilesa*).

"Having the Path as their object" means those for which the Path is the object (*ārammaṇa*). "Having the Path as their cause" (*maggahetuka*) means that even the Eightfold Path is their cause in the sense of a condition (*paccaya*).
Alternatively, the causes associated with the Path, or the causes within the Path, are the "Path-causes. Since these are their causes, they are also "having the Path as their cause.
Right View (*sammādiṭṭhi*) is itself both the Path and the cause; thus, because the Path is their cause, they are also "having the Path as their cause."
Those for whom the Path (*magga*) is predominant (*adhipati*) in the sense of proceeding after having overcome [the defilements] are "those for whom the Path is predominant" (*maggādhipatino*).

17. Regarding the triad of the arisen (*uppanna*): from the moment of arising until the point of dissolution, it has already occurred and passed away; thus, it is "arisen. That which is not arisen is "unarisen" (*anuppanna*). Because they are a portion of the causes that have reached completion, they will necessarily arise;

thus, they are "bound to arise" (*uppādino*). 18. Regarding the triad of the past (*atīta*): having reached their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) or the moments of arising and so forth, they have transcended them; thus, they are "past. Both of these [the unarisen and the bound to arise] have not yet arrived; thus, they are "future" (*anāgata*). Having arisen in dependence upon this or that cause, they are "present" (*paccuppanna*).
19. In the triad of "immediate" (*anantara*), those whose object is the past are called "having a past object" (*atītārammaṇā*). The same method applies to the other two pairs of terms as well.

20. In the triad of "internal" (*ajjhatta*): the grasping [of an object] with the thought, "We are the self (*atta*) thus proceeding," or that which proceeds by making the self its primary reference (*adhikāra*) with the intention, as it were, "we shall go"—this is "internal. Furthermore, this word "internal" (*ajjhatta*)...
The term *ajjhatta* is seen in four senses: as the objective sphere (*gocara-ajjhatta*), as one's own (*niyaka-ajjhatta*), as internal (*ajjhatta-ajjhatta*), and as the domain (*visaya-ajjhatta*).

In such passages as, "Therefore, Ānanda, that bhikkhu should steady his mind right within upon that very same original sign of concentration," and "Delighting in the internal, composed," this term is seen in the sense of the objective sphere. [And in] "Internal confidence... [it is seen in the sense of one's own].

In such passages as “he dwells contemplating phenomena in internal phenomena,” it refers to one’s own internal [self]. In such passages as “the six internal sense bases,” it refers to what is internal within the internal.

In such passages as “This, Ānanda, is the dwelling awakened to by the Tathāgata, namely, by not attending to any signs, he enters and dwells in internal emptiness,” it refers to... [internal emptiness].
"Within the object" (*visayajjhatte*); the meaning is "in the place of mastery. For the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) is indeed called the place of mastery for Buddhas.
However, in this context, what is intended is that which is within one's own [personal] sphere.

Therefore, it should be understood that individual phenomena (*dhammā*) occurring within one's own continuum (*santāne*) are "internal" (*ajjhatta*). But those that are external to it, whether bound to the sense faculties (*indriyabaddhā*) or not bound to the sense faculties (*anindriyabaddhā*), are "external."
Or "external" (bahiddhā). The third term is stated by way of both [internal and external]. 21.
The triad of "immediate" (anantara) is stated by way of occurring after having made those same three kinds of phenomena the object (ārammaṇa). 22.

In the triad beginning with "visible" (sanidassana), they are "with visibility" (sanidassanā) because they possess visibility (nidassana), which is defined as the state of being visible; and because they possess "impingement" (paṭigha), which is defined as the state of resistance...
"With resistance" means possessing resistance (*sappaṭigha*). "Visible and possessing resistance" means those which are both visible and possess resistance.

"Invisible" means that for these [phenomena], there is no visibility (*nidassana*) characterized by the state of being seen. "Invisible and possessing resistance" means that they are invisible and, according to the method already stated, possess resistance. The third term is stated by way of the negation of both. This...
Thus concludes the word-commentary on the triple matrix (tikamātikā) in successive order.
The word-commentary on the triple matrix is finished.
Now follows the word-commentary on the double matrix (dukamātikā).
1–6. In the Duka-mātikā, however, we shall provide an explanation only for those terms not already included among the Tika (triads). First, regarding the Hetu-gocchaka (Cluster of Roots):

"Root-dhammas" refers to those phenomena designated as roots in the sense of being a foundation (*mūlaṭṭhena*). There is also a reading: "Roots that are dhammas. "Not roots" is the term used to negate those very same [root-dhammas].
"With root" (*sahetukā*) means accompanied by a root as it occurs through association (*sampayogato*). It occurs in exactly that same way.
They are "rootless" (*ahetuka*) because they have no roots. They are "associated with roots" (*hetusampayutta*) because they are associated with roots by way of simultaneous arising and so forth.

They are "dissociated from roots" (*hetuvippayutta*) because they are dissociated from roots. Although there is no difference in meaning between these two pairs, they were stated as such either for the sake of the Teacher’s pedagogical skill or to suit the inclinations of those individuals who understand through such explanations.
Following that, having combined the first dyad with the second and third,
three further dyads are stated according to possibility by way of such terms as “roots” and “not roots. In this regard, just as it is possible to say,
“states that are both roots and accompanied by roots,” so too is it possible to say, “states that are both roots and not accompanied by roots.”
And just as it is possible that "states which are both with-cause and not themselves causes" exists, so too does "states which are both without-cause and not themselves causes.
This same method applies when connecting this with the "pair of states associated with a cause.
In that context, once it is established that "states which are not causes are both with-cause and without-cause," [it follows that] "states which are indeed not causes..."
The phrase “but moreover” (*atirittaṃ kho pana*) has been stated; by virtue of this, it should be understood that this additional meaning is included.
How so? It is not only the case that “states which are not roots, and furthermore, others which are neither with-cause nor without-cause,” but rather, “and also otherwise.
This is what is meant: just as “states which are not roots are both with-cause and without-cause,” [so too is the case here].

Thus, "states that are roots are both with-root and rootless. And just as "states that are not roots are both with-root and rootless," so too "states that are not roots are both associated with roots and dissociated from roots.
7–13. In the *Cūḷantaraduka*, they are "with-condition" (*sappaccaya*) because they possess their own productive condition. There is no [condition] for these...
Those which have no conditions for their arising or persistence are "unconditioned" (*appaccayā*). Those that are made by coming together through conditions are "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*).
That which is not conditioned is "unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*). Those that possess form (*rūpa*) in the sense of being inseparable from it are "material" (*rūpino*).
Those that do not possess such form are "immaterial" (*arūpino*). Alternatively, "form" (*rūpa*) has the characteristic of being afflicted (*ruppana*); those that possess this are "material."
"Neither material nor immaterial. "Worldly phenomena": the world (*loka*) is said to be the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) in the sense of breaking up and disintegrating;
those things are "worldly" (*lokīya*) because they are connected to the world by virtue of being included within it. "Supramundane" (*lokuttara*): they have "crossed over" (*uttinna*) from that;

they are supramundane because they have transcended the world by virtue of not being included within it. "Cognizable by anyone": by any one [of the consciousnesses], such as eye-consciousness among the eye-consciousnesses and so forth.
Or they are to be cognized by ear-consciousness. "Not to be cognized by anything" means not to be cognized by that very eye-consciousness or ear-consciousness.
This being so, because there is a difference in meaning between the two terms, it constitutes a dyad (duka).
14–19. In the group concerning the taints (*āsava*): they flow, hence they are called taints (*āsava*). They stream forth and proceed from the eye... [and so on] ...up to the mind.

This is what is meant. They are called *āsava* (taints) because they flow (*savanti*) from the perspective of the phenomena (*dhamma*) down to the stage of the lineage (*gotrabhū*), or from the perspective of space (*okāsa*) up to the peak of existence (*bhavagga*).
The meaning is that they proceed by encompassing these phenomena and this space; for this syllable "ā" has the sense of encompassing.

In the sense of having been stored for a long time, wine and the like are called *āsava*. Alternatively, they are called *āsava* because they are like *āsava* (liquor). For in the world, those things that have been stored for a long time...
Wines and the like are called *āsava*. And if they are *āsava* in the sense of having been stored for a long time, then only these [fermented liquors] ought to be so;
for this has been said: "Bhikkhus, no prior limit of ignorance is known, that before this there was no ignorance," and so forth.

Alternatively, they are called *āsava* because they flow (*savanti*) and pour out long-lasting suffering in *saṃsāra*. Other than those, there are no such things as *āsava*. [They flow] toward the self...

They are "with taints" (sāsava) because they proceed together with the taints by taking them as their object. They are "without taints" (anāsava) because, while proceeding in this way, there are no taints within them.
The rest should be understood according to the method explained in the *Hetugocchaka* (Cluster on Causes). However, this is the distinction:
just as there, in the first pair, the second phrase of the concluding dyad is, "States that are not causes are both with-cause and without-cause."
It was stated [in the previous section] by setting aside the first case; thus, here it is not stated as “states that are outflows are both with-outflow and without-outflow.
Although it is not stated, nevertheless, this and other classifications should be understood according to the method already explained there.
20–25. Regarding the group on fetters (*saṃyojana*): those which exist in a person fetter and bind that individual to the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

Fetters (*saṃyojana*). Other than those, there are things called "not fetters. They are "fetterable" (*saṃyojaniya*) because they are conducive to the binding by means of the fetters once they have entered into the state of being an object (*ārammaṇa*).
This is a designation for those things that serve as the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) for a fetter.
"Not fetterable" (*asaṃyojaniya*) means not conducive to fettering. The remainder should be applied according to the same method explained in the "Cluster on Causes" (*hetu-gocchaka*).
26–31. In the Group on Ties (*ganthagocchaka*): those that are found in a person tie and bind them to the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) by way of death and rebirth-linking;

thus they are called "ties" (*gantha*). Others than these are not ties. Because they are to be tied by the ties by way of being made into objects (*ārammaṇakaraṇa*), they are "objects of the ties" (*ganthaniya*).
The remainder should be applied according to the method already stated in the Group on Causes (*hetugocchaka*). And as it is here, so it is from here [onward].
In other cases as well, the remainder should be understood according to the method explained in various places [elsewhere].
32–37. In the group on the floods (*ogha-gocchaka*): those that exist in someone "flood" or cause them to sink within the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) are called floods.

Because they must be crossed by making them the object of focus, they are "to-be-crossed-by-the-floods" (*oghaniya*). It should be understood that these are simply the phenomena that serve as the objects of the floods.

38–43. In the group of the *yogas*, they are called *yogas* because they yoke one to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). They should be understood as being like the floods (*ogha*), which also yoke. 44–49.
In the group of the *nīvaraṇas*, they are called *nīvaraṇas* because they obstruct and envelop the mind. They should be understood as being like the fetters (*saṃyojana*), which also obstruct. 50–54.
In the group of the *parāmāsas*, [they are so called because] they transcend the true nature of phenomena—the aspects such as impermanence—and instead [cling to them] as "permanent."

They are called *parāmāsā* (misapprehensions) because, while occurring by way of their initial mode, they further grasp (*āmasanti*) from beyond. They are called *parāmaṭṭhā* (misapprehended) because they have been grasped by misapprehensions through the act of making them an object.
In the "Great Pairs" (*mahantaraduka*), they are called *sārammaṇā* (with an object) because they do not occur without taking an object.
They are "without an object" (*anārammaṇa*) because they have no objective support. They are "consciousness" (*citta*) in the sense of cognizing, or in the sense of being variegated (*vicitta*).
They are "mental factors" (*cetasika*) because they are bound to the mind by way of non-separation.

They are "conjoined with consciousness" (*cittasaṃsaṭṭha*) because they reach a state of immediate contiguity with consciousness from its arising until its dissolution. Although they proceed together as one, they maintain a state of immediate contiguity.
"Detached from the mind" (*cittavisaṃsaṭṭhā*) means they are dissociated from the mind by way of non-association (*anupagamanatāya*). "Origination" (*samuṭṭhānaṃ*) means that by which [they] arise.
"Mind-originated" (*cittasamuṭṭhānā*) means those for which the mind is the origin. "Co-existent" (*sahabhuno*) means they exist together.

"Co-existent with the mind" (*cittasahabhuno*) means co-existent with the mind. "Concomitant" (*anuparivattino*) means they revolve along with [it]. What do they revolve along with? The mind. Of the mind...
They follow along with the mind and revolve in accordance with the mind. They are both conjoined with the mind and originated by the mind; thus, they are "conjoined-and-originated-by-the-mind.
They are both conjoined with the mind and originated by the mind, and they are also co-existent with the mind; thus, they are "conjoined-and-originated-and-co-existent-with-the-mind.

They are both conjoined with the mind and originated by the mind, and they are also revolving in accordance with the mind; thus, they are "conjoined-and-originated-and-revolving-in-accordance-with-the-mind."
All the remaining terms should be understood by way of the negation of the terms already stated.
Regarding the internal triad, "internal" (ajjhattika) means simply "internal" (ajjhatta) as explained therein; those existing outside of that are "external" (bāhira).

They cling to the primary elements (bhūta), but they do not cling in the same manner as the primary elements themselves; thus they are "derived" (upādā). Those which do not cling at all are "non-derived" (noupādā).

69–74. In the group on clinging (*upādāna-gocchaka*), they are called "clinging" (*upādāna*) because they grasp intensely; the meaning is that they take hold with a firm grip. Those other than these are "non-clinging" (*noupādāna*). 75–82.
