In the group on defilements (*kilesa-gocchaka*), the meaning should be understood in the same manner as explained in the section on the triad of the defiled (*saṃkiliṭṭhattika*).

83–100. In the subsequent pairs (*piṭṭhiduka*): they move within sense-desires, thus they are "belonging to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*); they move within the fine-material realm, thus they are "belonging to the fine-material sphere" (*rūpāvacara*); [they move] within the immaterial realm, thus [they are] "belonging to the immaterial sphere" (*arūpāvacara*).
They are called "belonging to the formless realm" (*arūpāvacara*) because they range within it. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, will be made clear later.

They are "included" (*pariyāpanna*) because they are comprised within and contained in the round of existence consisting of the three planes. They are "unincluded" (*apariyāpanna*) because they are not included in that [round].
They are "leading out" (*niyyānika*) because, cutting the root of the round, they lead away from the round by making Nibbāna their object. By this—

They are "non-leading" (*aniyyānika*) because they do not lead out by means of their characteristics. They are "fixed" (*niyata*) because they are certain to yield their fruit immediately after death or immediately after their own occurrence;
they are "unfixed" (*aniyata*) because they are not so certain. They are "surpassable" (*uttara*) because other states surpass or abandon them.

They are "with-surpassable" (*sauttara*) because they are accompanied by those things capable of surpassing themselves. They are "unsurpassable" (*anuttara*) because there is nothing superior to them.
They are called *raṇā* because beings cry out and lament in various ways when overcome by them;
this is a designation for lust and the other [defilements]. They are "with conflict" (*saraṇā*) because they are associated with conflict and because they must be abandoned together with it.
They are "without conflict" (*araṇā*) because they possess no conflict in that manner.
Commentary on the Words of the Matika of the Suttanta Pairs, 101–108.
Regarding the Suttanta Pairs: they are "associated with true knowledge" (*vijjābhāgin*) because they partake of true knowledge by way of association;

alternatively, they are "associated with true knowledge" because they function within the sphere of true knowledge, that is, within the division of true knowledge. Therein, [they include] insight-knowledge, mind-made psychic power, and the six...
"Higher knowledge" (*abhiññā*) refers to the eight types of clear knowledge (*vijjā*). In the former sense, the states associated with them are also "partaking of clear knowledge.

In the latter sense, any one among those is itself "clear knowledge," while the rest are "partaking of clear knowledge. Thus, it should be understood that both clear knowledge and the states associated with clear knowledge are indeed "partaking of clear knowledge.
However, in this context, only the associated states are intended, by virtue of their association alone.

They partake of ignorance (*avijjā*), thus they are "partakers of ignorance" (*avijjābhāgin*). Alternatively, they are "partakers of ignorance" because they exist within the portion of ignorance, that is, within the division of ignorance.
In this context, there are four types of ignorance: that which conceals suffering, and those which conceal origination and so forth.

By the same method as before, the states associated with these are also "partakers of ignorance. Among them, any one of these [four] is simply "ignorance," while the rest are "partakers of ignorance."
In this way, ignorance (*avijjā*) and the phenomena associated with ignorance (*avijjā-sampayutta-dhammā*) should be understood as belonging to the category of ignorance.
However, here it is specifically the associated phenomena that are intended.
Furthermore, because it is incapable of dispelling the darkness of the defilements by virtue of its non-pervasive nature, lightning is used as a simile.
"These are like lightning" means they are like lightning because of their capacity to shatter everything without exception. "Like a thunderbolt" means they are like a thunderbolt for the same reason.
They are called "fools" (bāla) either because they abide among fools—using the location for the person—or because they cause foolishness;
they are called "wise" (paṇḍita) because they abide among the wise, or because they cause wisdom. "Dark" (kaṇha) means black, as they cause the mind to lose its luminosity.

"White" means pure, because they cause the mind to become luminous. Or, they are "black" because they are the cause for birth in a black lineage, and "white" because they are the cause for birth in a white lineage.
They are called "tormenting" (*tapanīya*) because they torment both in this world and in the future life. That which does not torment is "non-tormenting" (*atapanīya*).
The three sets beginning with the "synonym-duads" (*adhivacanaduka*) do not differ in meaning; here there is only a difference in phrasing. (Thus spoke) Sirivaḍḍhaka.
Terms such as *dhanavaddhakoti* (the treasurer’s crore) and so forth are called "designations" (*adhivacanā*), as they function by taking a mere word as their basis.

The "paths of designations" (*adhivacanapathā*) are the ways of these designations. "They construct, O monks, therefore they are 'formations' (*saṅkhārā*)"—expressions stated in this way, having been determined and established with their causes, are called "language" (*nirutti*). The "paths of language" (*niruttipathā*) are the ways of these languages.
"Paths of expression" (*niruttipathā*): because they make known [things] in such and such a manner—as "reasoning," "applied thought," or "intention"—they are called "designations" (*paññatti*).

The paths of these designations are "paths of designation" (*paññattipathā*). And here, although only one dyad has been mentioned, the purpose for stating the others should be understood in the same way as was explained in the section on the "Cluster of Causes" (*hetugocchaka*).
109–118. In the dyad of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*): "name" (*nāma*) is so called in the sense of bending, in the sense of inclining, and in the sense of naming.

"Form" (*rūpa*) is so called in the sense of being affected by change (*ruppana*). This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, will be made clear in the Section on Enumeration (*Nikkhepakaṇḍa*).

"Ignorance" (*avijjā*) is non-knowing regarding suffering and the other [truths]. "Craving for existence" (*bhavataṇhā*) is the longing for existence. "View of existence" (*bhavadiṭṭhi*): "existence" (*bhava*) refers to eternalism; by way of eternalism—
The view that arises [regarding non-existence] is the view of non-existence (*vibhavadiṭṭhi*). "Non-existence" (*vibhava*) refers to annihilation; it is the view that arises by way of annihilation.
The view that occurs as "the self and the world are eternal" is the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*).

The view that occurs as "it will be annihilated" is the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*). The view that occurs as "it is finite" is the view of finitude (*antavādiṭṭhi*). The view that occurs as "it is infinite" is the view of infinity (*anantavādiṭṭhi*).
A view that follows after the past is a "view regarding the past" (*pubbantānudiṭṭhi*). A view that follows after the future is a "view regarding the future" (*aparantānudiṭṭhi*).
Shamelessness (*ahirika*) is the lack of modesty, explained in detail as that by which one does not feel shame where one ought to feel shame.

Fearlessness of wrongdoing (*anottappa*) is the state of being devoid of dread, explained in detail as that by which one does not feel dread where one ought to feel dread. *Hirī* is the act of being ashamed (*hiriyanā*).
*Ottappanā* is *ottappa* (moral dread). Regarding *dovacassatā* and so forth: one who is contrary, antagonistic, hostile, and disrespectful has "bad speech" (*dubbaco*) directed toward him;
his action is *dovacassa*; the state of that is *dovacassatā*. One whose friends are evil persons—such as those lacking faith—is a "bad friend" (*pāpamitto*);
the state of that is *pāpamittatā*. *Sovacassatā* (the state of being easy to speak to) is the opposite of this.
And the state of having good friends (kalyāṇamittatā) should be understood by way of the opposite of what has been stated [in the previous section].

119–123. Regarding the offenses mentioned as “the five classes of offenses are offenses” and “the seven classes of offenses are offenses,” skillfulness regarding these offenses is skillfulness with regard to offenses (āpattikusalatā).
Skillfulness regarding the emergence from those offenses is skillfulness with regard to emerging from offenses (āpattivuṭṭhānakusalatā).

Skillfulness regarding the meditative attainments is proficiency in attainment (*samāpatti-kusala-tā*). This is a designation for the wisdom that discerns the absorption and the limits of the attainments.
Skillfulness regarding emergence from the meditative attainments is proficiency in emerging from attainment (*samāpatti-vuṭṭhāna-kusala-tā*).

Skillfulness regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) is proficiency in the elements (*dhātu-kusala-tā*). Skillfulness regarding the attention directed toward those very same elements is proficiency in attention (*manasikāra-kusala-tā*).

Skillfulness regarding the sense bases, such as the eye base and so forth, is skillfulness in the sense bases (*āyatana-kusala-tā*). Skillfulness regarding dependent origination with its twelve factors is skillfulness in dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda-kusala-tā*).
Skillfulness regarding each respective point is skillfulness in the points (*ṭhāna-kusala-tā*). "Point" (*ṭhāna*) is said to mean a cause;
for it is because the fruit abides depending upon that [cause]—as its existence is contingent upon it—that it is called a "point. Therefore, it is a "point."
It has been said. Skillfulness regarding what is improper is *aṭṭhānakusalatā*.
124–134. Uprightness is *ajjava*. Softness is *maddava*. The state of forbearance, characterized by endurance, is *khanti*.
The state of being well-disposed is *soracca*. The state of being kindly, characterized by friendliness and softness, is *sākhalya*. Just as...
"Patisanthāra" (hospitality) is the act of welcoming others with the gifts of the Dhamma so that there is no deficiency in oneself compared to them.

"Indriyesu aguttadvāratā" (unrestraint of the sense faculties) is the state of not guarding the doors of the six sense faculties, with the mind as the sixth, which is characterized by the breaking of restraint over the senses.

"Bhojane amattaññutā" (lack of moderation in eating) is the state of not knowing the proper measure in food, both in terms of receiving it and consuming it. This concludes the pair of terms immediately preceding.
It should be understood by way of the opposites of what has been stated. The state of being muddled in mindfulness, which is reckoned as the lapse of mindfulness, is *muṭṭhassacca*.
The state of lacking clear comprehension is *asampajañña*. One remembers, thus it is *sati* (mindfulness). One comprehends clearly, thus it is *sampajañña* (clear comprehension).
In the sense of being unshakable in the absence of reflection, the power reckoned as reflection is *paṭisaṅkhānabala* (the power of reflection). [The rest] under the heading of energy... seven.

The power that arises in one developing the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) is the power of development (bhāvanābala). It is called serenity (samatha) because it subdues (sameti) opposing states.
It is called insight (vipassanā) because it sees in various ways by way of impermanence and so forth.

Serenity itself, having taken up that mode [of calm], is the sign of serenity (samathanimitta) by virtue of being the cause for the further occurrence of serenity. The same applies to the sign of exertion (paggāhanimitta).
This is the method. It grasps associated states, thus it is "exertion" (*paggāha*). It does not cause distraction, thus it is "non-distraction" (*avikkhepa*).
135–142. The failure of virtue, characterized by non-restraint, which destroys virtue, is the "failure of virtue" (*sīlavipatti*).
The failure of view, characterized by wrong view, which destroys right view, is the "failure of view" (*diṭṭhivipatti*). Since it accomplishes virtue, it is indeed "moral conduct" (*soracca*).

The perfection of virtue (*sīlasampadā*) is the accomplishment of virtue through the fulfillment of virtue. Knowledge that has reached the fulfillment of view is the accomplishment of view; thus, it is the perfection of view (*diṭṭhisampadā*).
The purification of virtue is virtue itself, designated as "virtue," which has attained the state of purity; thus, it is the purification of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*).
The purification of view is view itself, designated as "view," which is capable of leading to the purification known as *nibbāna*; thus, it is the purification of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*).
"Furthermore, purification of view and the striving of one who has seen":

this refers both to the purification of view—consisting of the knowledge of the ownership of kamma and so forth—and to the striving associated with that very view, which is appropriate to what has been seen, namely, the wholesome view of one who has seen accordingly.
"A sense of urgency" is the state of being stirred by fear arising in dependence on birth and the other [stages of suffering]. "An object that inspires urgency" is...
The cause of birth and so forth is that which generates a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).

"And for one who is urgent, the proper application" means the application of skillful means by one who has thus become spiritually urgent. "And dissatisfaction with regard to wholesome states" refers to the state of being insatiable in fulfilling wholesome qualities.
"And non-retrogression in striving" refers to the state of not turning back or not withdrawing from striving until one has attained *arahantship*.

It is "clear knowledge" (*vijjā*) because of its knowing; it is "liberation" (*vimutti*) because of its liberating. "Knowledge of destruction" (*khaye ñāṇa*) is the knowledge regarding the Noble Path that effects the destruction of the defilements.

"Knowledge of non-arising" (*anuppāde ñāṇa*) is the knowledge regarding the Noble Fruit that has arisen at the conclusion of the non-arising of those various defilements to be abandoned by each respective path, which has occurred by way of non-relinking. This is the word-by-word commentary on the sequence of terms in the matrix (*mātikā*).
The commentary on the words of the two-fold matrix is finished.
The detailed exposition of the wholesome states of the sense-sphere.
Now, in order to show the classification of the phenomena included in the matrix as it has been set forth: "Which phenomena..."

The analysis of the term "wholesome" (*kusala*) has now begun. Therein, regarding that which was first shown as "at whatever time a wholesome consciousness of the sense-sphere has arisen," there are three great sections in its exposition:

the section on the determination of phenomena (*dhammavavatthāna*), the section on inclusion (*saṅgaha*), and the section on emptiness (*suññata*). Among these, the section on the determination of phenomena consists of both the enumeration (*uddesa*) and the exposition (*niddesa*).

It is established in two ways. Among those, there are four sections: the inquiry of the summary (uddesavāra), the description of the occasion (samayaniddesa), the summary of phenomena (dhammuddesa), and absorption (appanā).
Among these, “Which phenomena are wholesome? is called the inquiry. “At whatever time one [engages] in the sense-sphere realm...
at that time” is called the description of the occasion. “Contact exists... non-distraction exists” is this—

This is called the "Exposition of Phenomena" (*dhammuddesa*). “Or whatever other immaterial phenomena that are dependently arisen exist at that time—these phenomena are wholesome”: this is called "Absorption" (*appanā*).
Thus, regarding the section on the Exposition established by way of the four delimitations, this is the first delimitation of the inquiry.
In this context, "Which states are wholesome? is a question motivated by a desire to explain. There are five kinds of questions:

a question for the purpose of revealing what has not been seen, a question for the purpose of correlating what has been seen, a question for the purpose of cutting through doubt, a question for the purpose of seeking approval, and a question motivated by a desire to explain. This is their distinction.
What is a question for the purpose of illuminating what has not been seen? There is a characteristic that is by nature unknown—unseen, unweighed, unexamined, unmanifested, and unclarified.

One asks a question for the sake of knowing it, for seeing it, for weighing it, for examining it, for its manifestation, and for its clarification. This is a question for the purpose of illuminating what has not been seen.
What is the question for the purpose of verifying what has been seen? One has naturally known the characteristic; it has been seen, weighed, judged, clarified, and fully discerned.
He asks a question together with other wise people for the sake of verification.
This is the question for the purpose of verifying what has been seen.
What is a question for the purpose of cutting through doubt? One is by nature prone to uncertainty, prone to perplexity, and full of hesitation, thinking:
“Is it thus? Is it not thus? What indeed? How indeed? Such a person asks a question for the purpose of cutting through doubt.
This is a question for the purpose of cutting through doubt.
What is a question asked for the sake of obtaining consent? The Blessed One asks a question of the bhikkhus with their consent: “Bhikkhus, what do you think:
is form permanent or impermanent? “Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness? “Suffering, venerable sir. “But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—”
“Is it right to regard this as: ‘This is mine, this am I, this is my self’? “No, venerable sir. This is a question for assent. What is a question from a desire to speak?
The Blessed One asks a question because he desires the monks to speak: “Monks, there are these four foundations of mindfulness. Which four? This is a question from a desire to speak.
In that regard, the Buddhas do not have the first three types of questions. Why? Because for the Buddhas, regarding the three periods of time, nothing...
There is nothing—whether conditioned or unconditioned, whether liberated from time or not—that is unseen, unknown, unillumined, unmeasured, uninvestigated, unmanifested, or unrevealed.
Therefore, they have no questions regarding the illumination of what has not been seen.
However, as for that which has been penetrated by the Blessed One through his own knowledge, [no other] ascetic, brahmin, or deva...
There is no need for him to consult with Māra or Brahmā; therefore, he has no inquiry regarding the verification of what has been seen.
Since he is free from doubt, has crossed over uncertainty, and has destroyed all hesitation concerning all phenomena, he has no inquiry regarding the removal of doubt.
However, the other two inquiries belong to the Blessed One. Of these, this should be understood as the inquiry arising from a desire to speak.
In this context, by the word “which” (*katame*), he asks about the phenomena (*dhammā*) that are to be demonstrated.
For by the mere statement “wholesome phenomena” (*dhammā kusalā*), it is not possible to know “what has been done” or “what they do.

However, when “which” is stated, their state of being questioned becomes evident. Therefore it was said: “By the word ‘which,’ he asks about the phenomena to be demonstrated. By the two-word phrase “wholesome phenomena,”...
It shows the phenomena (dhammas) as they were asked about in the questions. Their meaning has already been explained above.
But why, instead of saying "wholesome phenomena" (*kusalā dhammā*) as in the matrix (*mātikā*), is the word-order here made as "phenomena that are wholesome" (*dhammā kusalā*)?
It is for the purpose of showing the possessor of the classification after first demonstrating the teaching of the phenomena by way of their classifications. For in this Abhidhamma...

Only phenomena (dhammas) are to be taught. And these are of many varieties through their classifications such as the wholesome and so forth. Therefore, it is only phenomena that are to be taught here; this is not a teaching by way of conventional terminology.
Furthermore, they are to be taught according to their many varieties, not merely as "phenomena" in the abstract.
For a teaching given according to their specific varieties brings about the analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa) that resolves the compact mass [of experience]. Thus: "Wholesome phenomena..."
Having thus illustrated the teaching of phenomena by way of their classification, it should now be understood that this sequence of terms beginning with “Which phenomena are wholesome?
has been established in order to show those phenomena that are to be taught through that classification.
For when those possessing the classifications have been shown, the classification itself becomes appropriate and easy to understand.
Now, regarding the phrase "at whatever time wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere":
here, the Sage indicated the consciousness by means of the occasion, and the occasion by means of the consciousness;
having thus delimited them, he explains them there according to their specific distinctions.
When the Blessed One describes it as "at whatever time there is wholesome consciousness pertaining to the sense sphere," he is describing consciousness by way of its occasion.

For what reason? Because by means of that consciousness delimited by the occasion, and having thus fixed the occasion at the conclusion with the words "at that time," he does so even though there is a diversity of occasions; for at whatever time there is consciousness, it is at that very [time].

"At the time there is contact, there is feeling"—this means that when the mind has been thus determined, at that time one understands these phenomena, such as contact and feeling, which are difficult to comprehend due to their manifold distinctions, by way of the density of the continuity, the aggregate, the function, and the object.
Now follows this word-by-word commentary on the passage beginning with "at whatever time. "At which" (*yasmim*) is an indefinite locative designation.
"Samaya" is an indication of what is unspecified. Up to this point, the "occasion" (samaya) has been indicated in its unspecified sense. In that regard, the word *samaya* is seen to apply to:
a collection, a moment, time, a multitude, a cause, and views;
as well as to acquisition, abandonment, and penetration.
For instance, in such passages as “Perhaps tomorrow we might approach him, taking into account the time and the occasion,” the meaning is *samavāya* (conjunction).
In such passages as “Monks, there is indeed but one moment and one occasion for living the holy life,” it means *khaṇa* (moment).
In such passages as “The season of heat, the season of feverish distress,” it means *kāla* (time). In such passages as “A great assembly in the forest,” it means *samūha* (multitude).

“Bhaddāli, you also failed to realize this circumstance: ‘The Blessed One is staying at Sāvatthī, and the Blessed One will know me as the bhikkhu named Bhaddāli who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s dispensation.
This circumstance, too, Bhaddāli, was not realized by you. In such passages, it is the *hetu* (cause/reason). “Now at that time... [etc.]

In such passages as, "The wanderer Uggāhamāna, son of Samaṇa Muṇḍikā, was residing at the Mallikā Park in the single-sālaka Tindukācīra grove, which was frequented by those who propound various doctrines," it refers to *diṭṭhi* (view). [And as it is said:
"Whatever benefit there is in this present life, and whatever benefit there is in the future life..."
In such passages as, “The steadfast one, through the realization of the goal (attha-abhisamaya), is called wise,” it refers to attainment.
In such passages as, “Through the right realization of conceit (māna-abhisamaya), he made an end of suffering,” it refers to abandoning.

In such passages as, “The meaning of suffering is oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of burning, the meaning of change, and the meaning of realization (abhisamaya),” it refers to penetration.
Thus, among the many meanings—
conjunction, moment, time, collection, and cause—
these five should be understood here by the wise as the meanings of *samaya*.

Regarding the phrase "at whatever time wholesome [kamma] of the sense-sphere," within this section on the wholesome, among those nine occasions, these five occasions—conjunction and so forth—should be understood by the wise.

Among them, the ninth alone is to be known as the occasion of the convergence of conditions (*paccayasāmaggī*), or alternatively, as the four wheels. *Paccayasāmaggī, samavāyo, khaṇo pana;* *Eko eva navamo ñeyyo, cakkāni caturopi vā.*
Indeed, that harmony of conditions which exists by way of producing a common fruit should be understood here as "conjunction" (*samavāya*).

However, when it is said, "Monks, there is indeed but one moment and one occasion for living the holy life," this should be understood as the "one moment" being the ninth moment itself. Or else, those [moments] which were stated as: "Monks, these four... [and so forth].

Regarding the statement, “The four wheels turn for those gods and humans who possess these wheels,” it is here that the four wheels—namely, dwelling in a suitable locality, relying on true persons, right self-application, and merit performed in the past—are mentioned.

Alternatively, these should be understood as the “opportunity” (*khaṇa*) in the sense of being the occasion (*okāsa*), taken together as one; for they constitute the occasion for the arising of the wholesome.
Having thus understood both the combination and the moment, one understands others as follows:
"Time is merely a conventional designation established in dependence upon this or that;
it is analyzed as a heap, a collection of phenomena such as contact."

By way of such expressions as “the time of consciousness” and “the time of form,” one understands either the phenomena (*dhamma*) themselves; or by way of such expressions as “the past” and “the future,” one understands the occurrence of phenomena (*dhammavutti*);

or by way of such expressions as “the time of the seed” and “the time of the sprout,” one understands the sequence of phenomena (*dhammapaṭipāṭi*); or by way of such expressions as “the time of arising” and “the time of aging,” one understands the characteristics of phenomena (*dhammalakkhaṇa*);
or by way of such expressions as “the time of feeling” and “the time of perceiving,” one understands the functions of phenomena (*dhammakicca*).
Or, by way of the duties of beings such as “time for bathing, time for drinking,” etc.;
or by way of the postures such as “time for walking, time for standing,” etc.; or by way of the revolution of the moon, sun, and so forth such as “forenoon, afternoon, day, night,” etc.;
or by way of the accumulation of time reckoned as days and nights such as “fortnight, month,” etc.—thus that [time]...

Time is designated in dependence upon that [aggregation]. However, because it does not exist by way of its own intrinsic nature, it should be understood as being merely a conceptual designation (*paññatti*).
Furthermore, that which is an aggregate of phenomena such as contact and feeling is analyzed here as a "collection" (*samūha*).
Having thus understood both time and the collection, the other—
"Here, 'cause' (hetu) is indeed a condition (paccaya); its manifold nature is to be understood either by way of its doors or by way of the conditions themselves.
For here, 'condition' is what is called 'cause'; its manifold nature is to be known either through its doors or through the various conditions."
How so? For the conditions for eye-consciousness and the rest arising at the doors of the eye and so forth are the eye-faculty, visible form, light, attention, and so on;
and in the *Mahāpakaraṇa*, twenty-four conditions have been stated in the manner beginning with "root-condition" (*hetupaccaya*) and "object-condition" (*ārammaṇapaccaya*).
Among these, excluding the ripening-condition (*vipākapaccaya*) and the postnascent-condition (*pacchājātapaccaya*), the remaining ones [are] wholesome states.

They certainly exist as conditions. All of these are intended here by the term "root" (*hetu*). Thus, its manifold nature should be understood either by way of these doors or by way of these conditions.
In this way, it should be understood that these five meanings—beginning with "conjunction" (*samavāya*)—are encompassed here by the word "occasion" (*samaya*).
"But why, instead of selecting any one of these, has the inclusion of all been made?

"Because each one illustrates a specific aspect of its meaning. For among these, 'occurrence' (*samaya*), which is synonymous with 'coincidence' (*samavāya*), illustrates arising from multiple causes.
By this, the doctrine of a single cause is refuted. And as for what is called 'coincidence,' it [refers to] the production of a common result..."

It is mutually dependent. Therefore, it also illustrates this point: "There is no such thing as a single agent. For when a cause exists by its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), dependence on another cause is illogical.
Thus, by demonstrating the absence of any single cause whatsoever, the views that "pleasure and pain are self-made" and so forth are refuted.
In this regard, it might be argued: “What was stated—that [the cause] illustrates occurrence from multiple causes—is not tenable. Why?
Because even when there is a combination of non-causes, the state of being a non-cause would still result. For a hundred blind people cannot see when a single blind person is unable to see.
[Reply: This is not untenable. For their status as established [causes] exists by virtue of their producing a common fruit.
It is *sāmaggī* (conjunction); it is not merely the coming together of many things. Furthermore, seeing by the blind is not a common fruit [of their conjunction].
Why? Because even when there is a hundred blind people, that [seeing] is absent. However, for the eye and so forth, that is a common fruit, because it exists when they exist.
Thus, the status of being a cause is established both in the case of non-conjunction and in the case of the conjunction of non-causes. This very [non-conjunction], in the state of non-conjunction...

It is to be understood by way of the absence of the fruit and the presence of its completeness. For the world, it is established by direct perception that when there is a deficiency in the eye and so forth, there is an absence of eye-consciousness and the rest, whereas when there is no deficiency, they are present.
This, first of all, is the meaning illustrated by the term *samaya* in the sense of "assemblage."

Furthermore, this ninth opportunity, which is free from the eight inopportune moments (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*), and the "opportunity" consisting of the four wheels beginning with dwelling in a suitable locality—referred to here in the sense of a "moment"—does not exist without the convergence of the moments such as being human, the appearance of a Buddha, and the persistence of the True Dharma.
Moreover, the rarity of these factors, such as being human, is illustrated by similes such as that of the blind turtle. Thus, because of the rarity of this opportunity...
Wholesomeness (*kusala*), which is even more dependent upon the opportune moment (*khaṇa*) and serves as a support for supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*), is indeed difficult to obtain.
Thus, this "time" (*samaya*), in the sense of the opportune moment, illustrates the rarity of the arising of wholesomeness.

By illustrating it in this way, he shows that for those who, having obtained such moments, waste them by failing to practice that very wholesomeness dependent on the moment, there is a dwelling in negligence (*pamāda-vihāra*).
It is thus prohibited. This meaning is illustrated by the term "occasion" (*samaya*), which refers to a moment (*khaṇa*).
However, the duration of time during which this wholesome consciousness actually occurs is exceedingly brief. And as for that extreme brevity of its duration, it is said:
"Monks, just as the speed of that man, just as the speed of the moon and the sun..."

"And the speed of those deities who run before the moon and sun—the life-formations (āyusaṅkhārā) perish even more swiftly than that"—this should be understood according to the commentary on this sutta.
For there, the time for the material life-faculty (rūpajīvitindriya) is stated to be merely brief; it lasts only as long as the present material form persists.
Sixteen consciousnesses arise and perish; thus, because their duration is so brief, there is not even a simile for them. For this very reason it was said:
"Bhikkhus, it is not easy to find a simile for how quickly the mind revolves.

By illustrating it in this way, the term "time" (samaya), which denotes a period of time, demonstrates the extreme brevity of the duration of a wholesome state of consciousness. By demonstrating it thus—
And by this [simile], because of its extremely brief duration—like the heating of pearls by a flash of lightning—it is shown that this mind is difficult to penetrate;
therefore, the instruction is given: "Great effort and reverence must be applied toward its penetration.
This explains the meaning of "time" (samaya) as what is reckoned as time.

Furthermore, the term "simultaneity" (*samaya*), understood as a collection, indicates the simultaneous arising of many factors. For a mass or aggregate of phenomena such as contact and the rest is what is called a "collection.
And since the consciousness arising within that collection arises together with those phenomena, the simultaneous arising of many factors is thereby indicated.
By indicating this, the arising of a single phenomenon alone is precluded.
This meaning is illustrated by "time" (samaya) in the sense of a collection.
However, "time" in the sense of a cause (hetu) illustrates dependence on another. For the phrase "at whatever time" (yasmiṃ samaye) has the meaning:
"when which cause exists, [it] has arisen. Therefore, because it occurs when a cause exists, there is a state of dependence on another.
It is thus illuminated. By illuminating it in this way, the conceit that phenomena possess independent self-sovereignty is refuted.

Herein, the meaning is illuminated by means of the term "occasion" (samaya), which is synonymous with "cause. In that context, "at whatever occasion" (yasmiṃ samaye) refers to an occasion reckoned as time; thus, the meaning is "at whatever time."

Regarding the phrase “in which aggregate” (*yasmiṃ samūhe*), this refers to that which is designated as a collection. Regarding the phrases “at which moment,” “by which combination,” and “when which cause exists,” the meaning should be understood as follows:
when a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen—at that very [moment], at that very [combination], and when that very [cause] exists—then contact and the other [mental factors] also exist.
For the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is here designated as time.
And "time" (*samaya*) is reckoned as a collection. Here, the locative case in the phrase "of the states mentioned therein" (*tattha vuttadhammānaṃ*) is used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

Furthermore, since the state of those [states] is characterized by the state of "time"—which is reckoned as a moment, a coincidence, or a cause—the locative case here is used in the sense of characterizing a state by another state (*bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇa*).
Regarding "belonging to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*): "Which states belong to the sense-sphere? From the Avīci hell below up to the Paranimmitavasavatti heaven above..."
It is included among the sense-sphere phenomena (*kāmāvacara-dhamma*) described by way of the method beginning with “having made a limit,” and so forth.

Herein, this is the etymological explanation: in brief, there are two kinds of desire (*kāma*): objective desire (*vatthu-kāma*) and defilement-desire (*kilesa-kāma*). Therein, defilement-desire is, in meaning, simply zeal and lust (*chanda-rāga*);
objective desire is the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) belonging to the three planes. And herein, defilement-desire is called *kāma* because it desires (*kāmeti*); the other, however—
It is called *kāma* because it desires (*kāmiyati*).
That region in which these two kinds of *kāma* move about by way of their activity is an elevenfold region, consisting of the four woeful states, the human world, and the six heavenly worlds.
It is called *kāmāvacara* because *kāma* moves about therein, just as one speaks of a "region frequented by weapons" (*sasatthāvacara*). For just as in whatever region weapons...
Just as a place where men frequent is called "frequented by men with weapons" because they are particularly conspicuous there,
even though other bipeds and quadrupeds are also present and frequenting it; so too, even though other realms such as the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) exist and beings frequent them,
this particular sphere is called "the sense-sphere realm" (*kāmāvacara*) because those [beings] are particularly conspicuous there.
Just as *rūpabhava* (the existence of form) is called simply "form" (*rūpa*) by eliding the latter member of the compound, so too this [consciousness] is called simply "sensual desire" (*kāma*).
Thus, because this consciousness moves within this "desire" (*kāma*), which is reckoned as eleven bases, it is called "belonging to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*).
For although it also moves within the realms of form and formlessness, it is nevertheless called "belonging to the battle-sphere" (*saṅgāmāvacara*) because it moves within a battle.
Just as a nāga who has received the name “Saṅgāmāvacara” (Warrior) is called by that very name even while wandering in the city,
and as creatures that move on land or in water are called “land-dwellers” or “water-dwellers” even when they are situated on dry land or out of water,

so too this [dhamma] should be understood as “belonging to the sense-sphere” (*kāmāvacara*) even though it occurs elsewhere. Alternatively, it may be understood that here the sense-desire (*kāma*) moves within its range (*avacara*) by way of being made an object (*ārammaṇa*).
It belongs to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). Granted that this [being] also courses in the fine-material and immaterial spheres, yet it is called a "calf" (*vaccha*) because it behaves in such a way;
and when one says "a buffalo" (*mahīṃsa*) because it lies on the earth, that name does not apply to every single being that speaks or lies on the earth.

It should be understood that this case is exactly like that. Furthermore, it takes rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in "sense-desire," which is designated as the existence of sense-desire (*kāmabhava*).
It is called "belonging to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*) because it operates within the sense-sphere.

It is "wholesome" (*kusala*) in the sense of flowing away from things that are base (*kucchita*), and so forth. Furthermore, it is wholesome in the sense of health (*ārogya*), in the sense of blamelessness (*anavajja*), and in the sense of being produced by skill (*kosallasambhūta*).
For just as one asks, "Is your physical body (*rūpakāya*) well?"— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.*
The wholesome (*kusala*) is described in the sense of health, in the sense of being free from illness, in the sense of being without disease, and in the sense of well-being.

Likewise, among immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*), the wholesome should be understood in the sense of health, by way of the absence of the illness of the defilements, the sickness of the defilements, and the disease of the defilements.
Furthermore, it is wholesome in the sense of blamelessness, due to the absence of the blameworthiness of the defilements, the fault of the defilements, and the distress of the defilements.
Skill (kosalla) is said to be wisdom (paññā); because it arises from skill, in the sense of being produced by skill, it is wholesome (kusala).

Let it be so for that which is associated with knowledge (ñāṇasampayutta); but how is it so for that which is dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇavippayutta)? That too is wholesome by way of conventional usage (ruḷhīsadda).
For just as even that which is made not of palm leaves but of reeds and the like is still called a "palm-leaf fan" (tālavaṇṭa) due to its similarity to one, by way of conventional usage.

Thus, even that which is dissociated from knowledge should be understood as wholesome (*kusala*) in this very sense. However, in the non-figurative sense, that which is associated with knowledge receives the name "wholesome" by way of three aspects:
in the sense of health, in the sense of blamelessness, and in the sense of being produced through skill;
whereas that which is dissociated from knowledge receives it by way of only two. Thus, both according to the method of the Jātaka and according to the method of the Bāhitika Sutta...
And whatever is called "wholesome" (kusala) by way of the Abhidhamma method—all that is found in this consciousness through all three meanings.

By way of its characteristics and so forth, it has the characteristic of being blameless and having a pleasant result; its function is the destruction of the unwholesome; its manifestation is purification;
and its proximate cause is wise attention. Or alternatively, the wholesome has the characteristic of being blameless simply because it is the opposite of what is blameworthy.
Its essence is the state of purification; its manifestation is desirable result; and its proximate cause is precisely as stated above. Regarding the characteristics and so forth:
the specific or general nature of various phenomena is called their characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*). Their function or accomplishment is called their essence (*rasa*).
Their mode of appearance or fruit is called their manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*). And the immediate cause is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*).
[This is] the name. Thus, wherever we shall explain the characteristics and so forth, their diversity should be understood by this very method.
"Citta" (mind) is called *citta* because it thinks (*cinteti*) upon an object; the meaning is that it cognizes (*vijānāti*). Or, because "citta" is common to all states of consciousness...

This is the meaning of the word; therefore, whatever mundane wholesome, unwholesome, or functional consciousness is here, it is called *citta* because it accumulates (*cinoti*) its own continuity by way of the cognitive process (*javanavīthi*).

It is called *citta* because it is accumulated (*citam*) by kamma and defilements as their result. Furthermore, all [consciousness] is *citta* by virtue of its being variegated (*cittatā*) according to its respective nature.
It is called *citta* because it causes variegation (*cittakaraṇatā*). Thus should the meaning be understood here. In that regard, since—

The mind with lust is one thing, that with hatred another, and that with delusion another; the mind of the sense-sphere is one thing, and that divided into the fine-material sphere and so forth is another;

the mind with a visible-form object is one thing, and that with sound or other objects is another; even among those with visible-form objects, the mind with a blue object is one thing and that with yellow or other objects is another;
the same principle applies to those with sound and other objects; and among all these, the inferior is one thing.

One is different from the middling, and another from the sublime; even among the inferior and so forth, one is dominated by desire (*chandādhipateyya*), another by energy (*vīriyādhipateyya*), another by consciousness (*cittādhipateyya*), and another by investigation (*vīmaṃsādhipateyya*). Therefore, its state as "consciousness" (*cittatā*) should be understood by way of these factors: association, plane, object, and the dominance of the inferior, middling, sublime, or dominant.
Although, in this context, there is not actually only a single such consciousness, yet among the various states of consciousness...
Because they are included therein, it is appropriate to call even any one of them "mind" (*citta*) due to its nature as mind. Thus, first, it is "mind" by way of its nature as mind.
How is it "mind" by way of being the maker of mind? In this world, indeed, there is no other thing called "mind" superior to the craft of painting.
Even in that [craft], what is called the "footing" (the base) is itself an exceedingly fine mind. For the painters who create it, [they produce] such [forms]...

The mental perception arises: "In this place, forms are to be made. From that mental perception, mental activities arise which accomplish the drawing of lines, coloring, illuminating, turning, and so forth.
Thereupon, a particular variegated form is produced within the mind, which is designated as "footing.
Then, having thought, "Let this be above this form, this below, and this on both sides," according to what was thus intended—

Through the sequence [of moments], the production of the remaining consciousnesses and material phenomena occurs; thus, whatever diverse craft exists in the world, all that is performed by consciousness alone.
Therefore, by virtue of this diversity of performing agents, the consciousness that produces each respective consciousness is likewise itself a consciousness.
Or, because there is no production of everything exactly as it was intended, for that reason too—
Mind alone is more mind than anything else. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Bhikkhus, have you seen that which is called ‘conduct’ as being mind? “Yes, venerable sir.
“That conduct, bhikkhus, which is called mind, was thought out by mind alone. And by that conduct-mind, bhikkhus, mind itself is even more mind.”

Likewise, that internal consciousness which, within the various destinies of gods, humans, hell-beings, and animals, is differentiated by way of karma, gender, perception, and conventional designation—that too is produced solely by consciousness.

For the diversity of karma—consisting of bodily actions and so forth, proceeding in the manner of giving, virtue, cruelty, deceit, and so on, whether wholesome or unwholesome—is produced by consciousness.
And it is precisely through this diversity of karma that, in those respective [destinies]...
In the various realms of existence, there is a diversity of gender (*liṅga-nānatta*) distinguished by the specific shapes of the hands, feet, ears, belly, neck, mouth, and so forth.

From this diversity of gender, there arises a diversity of perception (*saññā-nānatta*), consisting of the perceptions that arise according to the shapes as they were grasped, such as "this is a woman" or "this is a man.
From this diversity of perception, there arises a diversity of conventional expression (*vohāra-nānatta*) among those who, in accordance with their perceptions, designate someone as "woman" or "man."

Furthermore, because by way of diversity in conventional expression one performs the karma that produces this or that individual existence (attabhāva), thinking, “I shall become a woman, I shall become a man;
I shall become a khattiya, I shall become a brahmin,” therefore there is a diversity of karma due to the diversity of conventional expression.
And this diversity of karma, producing existence (bhava) according to what was aspired for, [arises].
Because it produces [rebirth] by way of the destiny (gati), there is a diversity of destinies due to the diversity of kamma.
And by that very diversity of kamma, there arises for those various beings the state of being footless, two-footed, and so forth, in their respective destinies;

the state of being high or low in their respective births; the state of being beautiful or ugly in this or that individual existence (attabhāva); and the state of gain, loss, and so forth, amidst the worldly conditions (lokadhamma).

And it is discerned. Therefore, all this—consisting of the distinctions of karma, signs, perceptions, and conventional designations within the various realms of existence, such as those of gods, humans, hell-beings, and animals—should be understood as internal mind produced by mind alone.
This meaning is to be understood by means of this discourse (*sutta*) which has not yet been included in the *Saṅgīti*; for it has been said:
“Through the determination of the diversity and multiplicity of kamma, there comes about the determination of the diversity and multiplicity of gender;
through the determination of the diversity and multiplicity of gender, there comes about the determination of the diversity and multiplicity of perception;
through the determination of the diversity and multiplicity of perception, there comes about the determination of the diversity and multiplicity of conventional expression.”
Through the determination of the diversity and multiplicity of conventional usage, there comes to be the determination of the diversity and multiplicity of kamma.
Depending on the diversity of kamma, the diversity of the destinies of beings is discerned:
footless, two-footed, four-footed, many-footed; material, immaterial; percipient, non-percipient, and neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient. [This is] through the diversity of kamma.
Depending on karma, the differentiation of beings in their rebirth is discerned: high and low, inferior and superior, well-born and ill-born, happy and miserable.
Depending on the differentiation of karma, the differentiation of beings in their individual forms is discerned:
beautiful and ugly, well-proportioned and ill-proportioned, well-formed and ill-formed. Depending on the differentiation of karma, [the differentiation of beings] in worldly conditions...
"A distinction is perceived—in gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain.
Furthermore, it has been said:
"From karma and from gender-signs, the designation of gender arises."
Through perception they come to distinction, thinking "this is a woman" or "this is a man.
"The world is led by karma; by karma the multitude is led.
Beings are bound by karma, like the linchpin of a moving chariot."
Through action one gains fame and praise;
through action one incurs loss, death, and bondage.
Having understood this diversity of action, [one should act with discernment].
"Why do you say that there is no such thing as karma in the world?

'Young man, beings are owners of their karma, heirs of their karma, born of their karma, bound by their karma, and have karma as their refuge; it is karma that divides beings into the inferior and the superior.
Thus, through this very state of being made by the mind, the mindedness of the mind is to be understood. For all these [states] are indeed manifold."

They are made by the mind alone. However, for a mind that has not obtained an opportunity, or for one that is deficient in other remaining conditions, there is an absence of the production of certain states of mind;
therefore, even compared to that internal mind which is said to be "made by the mind," this [mind] is simply the mind, the very essence of mind.
Thus the Blessed One said:

“Bhikkhus, I do not see even a single other class of beings whose minds are so fickle as those of animals... Indeed, bhikkhus, among those animal beings, the mind itself is more fickle. Regarding the phrase “it has arisen” (*uppannaṃ hoti*):

here, “arisen” is of many varieties according to its occurrence by way of being present (*vattamāna*), having been [previously] (*bhūta*), having passed away (*apagata*), being occasioned (*okāsakata*), or having obtained its plane (*bhūmiladdha*). Among these, that which is characterized by the possession of arising, aging, and dissolution is called “presently arisen” (*vattamānuppanna*).

[It is] called "name" (*nāma*). That which has ceased after experiencing the flavor of the object, known as "that which has been experienced and passed away," refers to wholesome and unwholesome [kamma];
that which has ceased after reaching the three characteristics of arising and so forth, known as "that which has arisen and passed away," refers to the remaining conditioned phenomena;
and that which has arisen and passed away is called "name. Furthermore, the kamma described in such passages as, "Those kammās which were performed by him in the past," is also [included as] past.
It is "equal" because it remains having warded off another result and made room for its own result;
and since that result, though as yet unarisen, will necessarily arise when such room has been made, it is called "arisen by way of making room.
Unwholesome states that have not been eradicated in their respective planes are called "arisen by way of obtaining the plane. And here, regarding the plane—
And the distinction of what has "reached the plane" (bhūmiladdha) should be understood. "Plane" (bhūmi) refers to the five aggregates of the three planes that have become the object of insight.
"Reached the plane" means the class of defilements capable of arising within those aggregates;
for by them, this plane is said to be "reached," and therefore it is called "reached the plane. Thus, when these four have arisen—
Here, "arisen" (uppanna) is intended in the sense of "presently occurring.
Its etymological meaning is as follows: it is called "arisen" because it has gone forth (panna) from the past toward arising and so forth. Furthermore, this word "arisen" is used in many senses:

for what is past, for what has been acquired, for what has arisen, for what is unobstructed, for what is not cut off, and for that which has reached the three moments [of arising, presence, and dissolution].

It is seen in the sense of "objects" (*attha*). For this [word] occurs in the past tense in the passage: “Now at that time, monks, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had arisen in the world.
It occurs in the sense of "obtained" in the passage: “An extra robe had been obtained for the Venerable Ānanda.
And it occurs in the sense of "arisen" (as in a cloud) in the passage: “Just as, monks, when a great cloud has arisen...”
In the passage, “A great wind causes that which has arisen to vanish right there,” it refers to what has already arisen. In the passage, “The mind set on wandering is difficult to dispel;
one causes evil, unwholesome states that have arisen, as they arise, to vanish from their very place,” it refers to what has not yet been suppressed.
[And] in the passage, “Developing and cultivating the Noble Eightfold Path, one causes evil, unwholesome states that have arisen... [to vanish].
In the passage, “It makes it vanish right on the spot, even while it still exists,” this refers to [a state] that has not yet been cut off.

In the passage, “Is that which is arising what has arisen? Yes,” this refers to that which has reached the three moments. This [state] here too should be understood as having reached the three moments.
Therefore, in the phrase “it has arisen,” it has reached the three moments; it is present; it is currently existing. This is the summary meaning.
The phrase "a consciousness has arisen" is merely a conventional mode of teaching. For consciousness does not arise alone; rather, it arises together with more than fifty wholesome states.

Therefore, just as when it is said, "the king has arrived," one understands that he has not come alone, setting aside his retinue, but has indeed arrived together with the royal entourage, so too this [consciousness] has arisen together with more than fifty wholesome factors.
This should be understood. However, in the sense of being the precursor, it is simply stated: "consciousness has arisen.
For when reaching mundane states, consciousness is the chief, consciousness is the leader, and consciousness is the precursor.
But when reaching supramundane states, wisdom is the chief, wisdom is the leader, and wisdom is the precursor. For this very reason, the Blessed One, in the method of the Vinaya—
Having reached the question, instead of asking, "What is your contact? What is your feeling? What is your perception?
What is your consciousness?", he asks by making consciousness itself the primary focus: "Bhikkhu, what is your mind?

And when it is replied, "My mind is not thieving, Blessed One," rather than saying, "There is no offense for one whose contact is not thieving," and so forth, he says, "There is no offense, bhikkhu, for one whose mind is not thieving."
And not only when teaching the method of the Vinaya, but even when teaching other worldly discourses, he teaches making the mind alone the primary factor.
As it is said: "Bhikkhus, whatever states are unwholesome, partaking of the unwholesome, and belonging to the side of the unwholesome—all these are preceded by the mind.
The mind arises first among those states."
“Mental phenomena are preceded by the mind, led by the mind, and made of the mind.
If one speaks or acts with a corrupted mind,
then suffering follows him, even as the wheel follows the hoof of the draught-ox.”
“Mind precedes all phenomena; mind is their chief, they are all mind-wrought.
If one speaks or acts with a pure mind, happiness follows them, like a shadow that never departs.”
“The world is led by the mind; by the mind it is drawn along.
All follow under the sway of this one thing: the mind.
“Bhikkhus, through the defilement of the mind, beings are defiled; through the purification of the mind, they are purified.”
“Bhikkhus, this mind is luminous, but it is defiled by adventitious defilements.
“Householder, when the mind is unprotected, bodily action is unprotected, verbal action is unprotected, and mental action is unprotected;
householder, when the mind is protected... [and so on] ...householder, when the mind is protected...”
“Householder, when the mind is malevolent… [and so on] … when the mind is not malevolent… [and so on] … when the mind is lustful… [and so on] … when the mind is not lustful,
householder, bodily action is also not lustful, verbal action is also not lustful,
and mental action is also not lustful.”
Thus, it should be understood that having encountered worldly phenomena, the mind is the chief, the mind is the burden-bearer, and the mind is the forerunner. Furthermore,
it should be understood that among these suttas, all of them have been cited— not just one or two—
for the purpose of preserving the integrity of the suttas.
But when asking about the supramundane state (*lokuttaradhamma*), he does not ask, "Which contact have you attained?
Which feeling, which perception, which volition, or which consciousness? Instead, he asks: "Bhikkhu, what kind of wisdom have you attained?
Have you attained the wisdom of the first path, or the second... [and so on]... or the third... or the fourth path-wisdom?"
He asks, making wisdom the foremost and wisdom the burden. All wholesome states have wisdom as their chief;
they do not decline. But for what purpose is wisdom? "Monks, for the noble disciple who possesses wisdom, faith follows and becomes established;
energy follows and becomes established; mindfulness follows and becomes established."
Furthermore, suttas such as "concentration becomes established" should be seen here.
Thus, having reached the supramundane state, it should be understood that wisdom is the eldest, wisdom is the leader, and wisdom is the precursor. However, this is a mundane teaching;
therefore, teaching while making the mind the primary factor, he said, "the mind has arisen."

“Accompanied by joy” (*somanassasahagata*) means having come into a state of simultaneous arising and so forth with that which is called joy (*somanassa*), characterized as pleasant and sweet feeling.
Now, this word *sahagata* is seen in these senses: identity, being mixed, support, object, and associated.
Among these, in the passage, “This craving, which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust,” it should be understood in the sense of identity.

The meaning is "consisting of delight and lust. Regarding the statement, “Bhikkhus, that investigation which is accompanied by indolence, associated with indolence,” it should be understood as being mixed;
the meaning here is that it is mixed with indolence arising from time to time.

Regarding the statement, “He develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor accompanied by the perception of a skeleton,” it should be understood as being based upon; [the meaning is] the perception of a skeleton...

The meaning is: "having attained [it] by developing the perception of the skeleton as a support. Regarding the phrase "he is an obtainer of attainments accompanied by the form realm or the formless realm," the meaning is that they have the form and formless realms as their objects (*ārammaṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "this happiness is accompanied by this rapture—co-arisen, conjoined, and associated with it"—the meaning is "in association" (*saṃsaṭṭha*).
In this passage as well, this very same meaning is intended. For here, that which is "associated with joy" (*somanassa-saṃsaṭṭha*) is stated as being "accompanied by joy" (*somanassa-sahagata*).
Furthermore, this word *saṃsaṭṭha* is seen in many senses: in similarity, in being impassioned, in friendship, and in co-nascence.
Indeed, it occurs in the sense of similarity in the verse: "Having avoided the thin and the fat, the horses are yoked in association (*saṃsaṭṭhā*)."
“Live in association, noble ladies,” [is said] regarding one who is lustful. “A householder lives in association,” [is said] regarding friendship.
“This happiness is accompanied by this rapture; it is co-nascent, associated, and conjoined,” [is said] regarding co-nascence (*sahajāta*).
Here too, it is co-nascence that is intended. In that context, “accompanied” means not co-nascent, not associated, and not conjoined.
There is no such thing [as association] here. However, that which is co-nascent (*sahajāta*) may or may not be associated (*saṃsaṭṭha*) and conjoined (*sampayutta*).
For among material and immaterial phenomena that arise together, matter is co-nascent with the immaterial, but it is neither associated nor conjoined;
likewise, the immaterial is so with matter; and matter is co-nascent with matter. But the immaterial is necessarily accompanied by, and co-nascent with, the immaterial.
It is associated only with that which is conjoined; it is with reference to this that it is said to be "accompanied by joy.
"Associated with knowledge" means conjoined with knowledge; the meaning is that it is joined with it in such ways as arising simultaneously and so forth.

Whatever else might need to be said here follows the same method already explained in the commentary on the matrix (mātikā) under the triad of feeling (vedanāttika). Therefore, [they share] a simultaneous arising...
By this characteristic—that they have a single cessation, a single basis, and a single object—it should be understood that this is associated.
This is an exalted description; however, in the formless realm, association is found even without having a single basis.
What has been stated thus far? Among the wholesome states of the sense-sphere, that which is accompanied by joy, possesses three roots, and is associated with knowledge.
The great unprompted consciousness has been explained. For in the unqualified question, “Which states are wholesome? all wholesome states of the four planes are included.

However, by the statement, “A wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere has arisen,” wholesome states of the three higher planes are excluded, and only the eightfold wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere is taken. By the phrase, “accompanied by joy,”...
Then, having excluded the fourfold [consciousness] accompanied by equanimity, only the fourfold accompanied by joy is taken.
By the expression "associated with knowledge," having excluded from that the two types dissociated from knowledge, only the two associated with knowledge are taken.
However, the state of being unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*) is not included precisely because it was not brought forward [in the previous context].

Although it was not explicitly mentioned here, since the word "with volitional effort" (*sasankhārena*) occurs later, the state of being "without volitional effort" (*asankhārika*) should be understood even though it is not stated here as such.
For the Fully Enlightened One began this teaching precisely by first analyzing and defining this "great consciousness";
thus, it should be understood that a definitive conclusion has been reached in this matter.
Now, in order to show that very same consciousness by way of its object, he says: "Or having a visible form as its object," and so forth.

For when the Blessed One demonstrates an immaterial state (*arūpadhamma*), he does so either by means of its basis (*vatthu*), or by means of its object (*ārammaṇa*), or by means of both its basis and its object, or by means of its own essential nature (*sarasabhāva*).
"Eye-contact... [and so on] ...mind-contact; feeling born of eye-contact... [and so on] ...feeling born of mind-contact."
In such passages as "feeling; eye-consciousness... mind-consciousness," immaterial phenomena are shown by means of their basis (*vatthu*).
In such passages as "perception of forms... perception of mental objects; volition regarding forms... volition regarding mental objects," they are shown by means of their object (*ārammaṇa*).
[And in such passages as]: "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact... mind and..."

In such passages as, "Dependent on the eye and forms, mind-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact," [the immaterial states] are shown by way of the physical basis (*vatthu*) and the object (*ārammaṇa*).

In such passages as, "With ignorance as condition, monks, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises," the immaterial states are shown by way of their own essential nature (*sarasabhāva*).
However, in this present instance, showing them by way of the object, he says, "having visible form as its object," and so forth.
Therein, visible form itself—arising from four causes and belonging to the past, future, or present—is the object of visible form.
Sound itself—arising from two causes and belonging to the past, future, or present—is the object of sound.

Odor itself—arising from four causes and belonging to the past, future, or present—is the object of odor. Taste itself—arising from four causes and belonging to the past, future, or present—is the object of taste.
The tangible object itself—whether past, future, or present—is the objective support for the tangible, and it arises from four origins.
Mental states and mental factors—whether arising from one origin, two origins, three origins, or four origins; whether they cannot be so classified;
or whether they are past, future, or present—and the remaining phenomena not yet mentioned, which are reckoned as the domain of consciousness, constitute the objective support for mental objects.
Furthermore, those who claim that even visible forms and other objects which have not come within range are "mental objects" (dhammārammaṇa) should be refuted by this Sutta. For it is said:

"Friends, these five faculties have different domains and different ranges; since they do not experience each other's domain and range, the mind is their resort, and the mind experiences their domain and range.

Indeed, for these [faculties], visible forms and so forth are called their "domain and range. Even when those very same visible forms and so forth are being experienced by the mind, they remain simply "visible forms as objects" and so on.
This point is established. Furthermore, because the knowledge of the divine eye and so forth have visible forms and the like as their objects, this point is likewise established.
For it is only visible forms and other such objects that have not come within the range [of the senses] which serve as the objects for the divine eye and so forth;
they do not have mental phenomena (dhamma) as their objects. Thus, the determination of the objects should be understood according to the method already stated.
In this context, each individual object enters the range of two doors. For a visible-object object, having struck the sensitive eye, enters the range of the mind-door at that very moment;
the meaning is that it becomes a condition for the vibration of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
The same method applies to sound, odor, flavor, and tangible objects. Just as a bird, having come through the air...
Just as one perched on the top of a tree might touch a branch while its shadow strikes the ground—

such that the touching of the branch and the spreading of the shadow occur not before or after, but simultaneously— in the same way, the simultaneous occurrence of the eye-sensitivity’s contact with present visible forms and so forth,
and their arrival at the threshold of the mind-door through the capacity to stir the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), is unprecedented.
The final [moment] occurs at one and the same instant. Then, having interrupted the life-continuum (bhavaṅga),

immediately after the moments beginning with adverting (āvajjana) that have arisen through the eye-door and so forth and ending with determining (voṭṭhabbana), this "great consciousness" arises with respect to one of those objects.
However, in the pure mind-door (*manodvāra*), there is no function of striking the sensitive matter (*pasāda*).
These objects come into the range of the door by way of what is naturally seen, heard, smelled, tasted, or touched. How so?

Here, someone [sees] a building whose plaster work has been completed, variegated with colors such as yellow orpiment and red arsenic, with various kinds of flags and banners hoisted, entwined with garlands and wreaths, surrounded by rows of lamps, and exceedingly beautiful.
Having circumambulated the Great Cetiya, which was resplendent with glory and adorned for the occasion, he paid homage at the sixteen footprints with the fivefold prostration.
Raising his hands in añjali and looking upward, he stood there, seizing upon joy inspired by the Buddha.
After he had thus beheld the Cetiya and generated joy inspired by the Buddha, later on—
Wherever he may go, whether sitting in night-quarters or day-quarters, as he reflects, the Great Shrine, adorned and prepared, appears as if it had just entered the range of his visual faculty;
it is as if it were the very moment of performing a circumambulation and paying homage to the Shrine.
In this way, first of all, a visible object enters the range of his perception by way of what has been seen.
Furthermore, having heard the sound of a preacher of the Dhamma speaking with a sweet voice,
or a reciter of the scriptures reciting with a melodic chant, at a later time, while sitting anywhere and reflecting,
that preaching of the Dhamma or that scriptural recitation seems as if it has entered the door of his ear; and he gives a cry of approval.
It is as if it were the time for hearing. Thus, by way of what has been heard, the sound-object comes into the range of perception.

But having obtained a fragrant scent or a garland, and having performed an offering with a mind focused on that fragrance-object at a seat or a shrine, later on, while sitting anywhere and reflecting upon it, that fragrance-object [comes into the range of perception].
It is as if it has come within range at the nose-door; it is as if it were the time for making an offering. Thus, by way of smelling, the scent-object comes into the field of awareness.
But having shared out exquisite solid food or soft food with one's fellow celibates and having partaken of it—
Later on, when he obtains some food such as kudrūsaka at any place whatsoever,
as he reflects, "At such-and-such a time I enjoyed exquisite food after sharing it with my fellow celibates," that object of taste seems to enter the range of the tongue-door as if it were right now,
and it becomes as if it were the very moment of eating. Thus, by way of having tasted it.
The object of taste comes into range.

Having previously enjoyed a soft and pleasant-to-the-touch bed, chair, rug, or coverlet, one later lies down in some place on a painful bed and thinks: "At such-and-such a time, my soft bed or chair..."
For one who adverts [to the thought], "The rug and cloak have been used," that tactile object (phoṭṭhabba-ārammaṇa) becomes as if it has entered the range of the door of the body (kāyadvāra).
It is as if there were a moment of experiencing a pleasant touch. Thus, by way of contact, the tactile object enters the range [of consciousness].
In this way, in the pure mind-door (manodvāra), there is no function of striking the sensitivity (pasāda).
It should be understood that these objects come into the range of the senses precisely through the modes of what is naturally seen, heard, smelled, tasted, and touched.
Now, regarding the way they enter the range of the senses by way of what is naturally seen and so forth, there is this further method not found in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathāmuttaka*).
First, "the seen," "the heard," and "that connected with both" are to be understood as the categories beginning with the seen. Therein, "the seen":
The term "seen" (*diṭṭha*) refers to what was previously apprehended by way of the five doors.

"HearD" (*suta*) refers to those same objects, such as visible forms and so forth, which were apprehended not through direct perception but by way of hearsay. The connection between these two is called "connection with both.
Thus, it should be understood that these [objects] also come into the range of the mind-door by way of what has been seen and so forth. In that regard, first, by way of what has been seen:
The coming into range has already been explained by the five methods below.
However, someone hears: "The Blessed One’s physical form is produced from such an abundance of merit;
his voice is exceedingly sweet; in a certain place, there is the most delightful fragrance of certain flowers and the most sweet [savor] of certain fruits."
"the taste, or the extremely pleasant touch of certain garments and such.
Even without the contact of the sensitive eye-organ and so forth, those [objects] reach the range of his mind-door merely by being heard.

Then, that consciousness [arises] toward that visible form or sound either by way of the sensitive organ, or toward odors and so forth by way of the noble ones' desire to give, or by way of rejoicing in what has been given by others.
Or it proceeds. Thus, by way of what has been heard, these [objects] come into the range of the mind-door.
Alternatively, those aforementioned forms and so forth have been seen or heard.
Then, for him, in the manner of "Such a form will also belong to the Buddha who arises in the future," and so on, even without the stimulation of the eye-sensitivity and the other [sensitivities],...
These objects enter the range of the mind-door precisely through their connection with what has been seen or heard.
Then, in the manner described below, this great consciousness occurs with one of those as its object.
Thus, by way of both connections, these objects enter the range of the mind-door.

This too is merely a brief illustration. However, it should be understood that, in detail, these [objects] come within the range of the mind-door by way of faith, inclination, mode of reflection, speculative thought, contemplation of views, patience, and so forth.
Yet, because such objects may be both real and unreal as they thus enter the range of the mind, this method was not included in the Commentary.
Thus, it should be understood that a javana with a single object arises at each of the two doors.
For a javana having a visible-form object arises both at the eye-door and at the mind-door. The same method applies to objects such as sound and the rest.
Among these, the javana with a visible-form object arising at the mind-door may consist of giving, consisting of virtue, or consisting of meditation.

It is threefold. Among those, each one—bodily action, verbal action, and mental action—is itself threefold. The same method applies to those having sound, odor, taste, tangible object, and mental phenomena as their objects.

Therein, when this great wholesome consciousness arises taking visible form as its object, it takes as its object any one among the desirable, lovely, pleasing, and enticing signs of beauty known as the "signs of the beautiful" (subhanimitta) found within the colors blue, yellow, red, and white, or within flowers, clothes, or the elements.
It arises having taken visible form as its object. But is this not a desirable object, a basis for greed?
How then can this consciousness be called wholesome (*kusala*)? It is so by way of determination, by way of transformation, by way of manifestation, and by way of inclination.
For when one’s mind is determined toward the performance of what is wholesome, thinking, "Only the wholesome must be done by me," [then it is wholesome].
It exists; having turned one away from the occurrence of unwholesome states, it has been directed solely toward the performance of wholesome deeds;

through constant practice, it has been practiced as the very manifestation of the wholesome; and through supporting conditions such as dwelling in a suitable locality, reliance upon virtuous friends, hearing the true Dhamma, and merit performed in previous lives, as well as through wise attention (*yoniso ābhoga*), it proceeds.
For him, by way of this restriction and by way of this direction—
It is called "wholesome" (kusala) by way of its manifestation and its inclination.
However, in this context, the state of being accompanied by joy (somanassa-sahagata) should be understood by way of the object.

For it has arisen in respect to a desirable object, and thus it has become accompanied by joy. Furthermore, the abundance of faith and so forth are themselves the causes here; for those who lack faith...
Even upon seeing the physical form of the Tathāgata, which is an exclusively desirable object for those of wrong view, joy does not arise.
And for those who do not perceive the benefit in the occurrence of wholesome states, joy does not arise even when they perform wholesome deeds after being encouraged by others.
Therefore, there must be abundance of faith, purity of view, and the perception of benefits.
In this way, the state of being accompanied by joy should be understood here. Furthermore, eleven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of rapture:

recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, recollection of the deities, recollection of peace, avoidance of persons who are harsh, association with persons who are gentle, and reflection on discourses that inspire confidence.
"Because of being resolved upon that": by these reasons also, the state of being accompanied by joy (somanassa) should be understood here.
