However, the detailed explanation of these will be made clear in the *Bojjhaṅgavibhaṅga*.

Furthermore, by these reasons—namely, from the perspective of karma, from the perspective of rebirth, from the perspective of the ripening of the faculties, and from the perspective of the remoteness of defilements—it should be understood here.
One should understand this as being associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayuttatā*). For whoever teaches the Dhamma to others, trains them in blameless fields of craft,
fields of action, and branches of science, causes a preacher of the Dhamma to preach the Dhamma after having honored him,

and gives various kinds of gifts while establishing the aspiration, "May I be wise in the future"— for such a person, wholesome [kamma] arises based upon that very action as its decisive support (*upanissaya*).
When it arises, it arises associated with knowledge. Furthermore, for one born in a world free from affliction—or even by way of rebirth, according to the method stated:

"For him who is happy there, the words of the Dhamma flow forth... slow, O monks, is the arising of his mindfulness, yet that being quickly becomes one who attains distinction"—the wholesome [state] that arises is associated with knowledge.

Likewise, for those who have reached the full maturity of the faculties and attained the "wisdom-decade" (paññādasaka), wholesome states arising in dependence on that maturity of the faculties arise associated with knowledge.

Furthermore, for those by whom the defilements have been suppressed, wholesome states arising in dependence on that remoteness from defilements also arise associated with knowledge. And this has also been said:
“Through yoga, indeed, much is born; through non-yoga, the destruction of much.
Thus, association with knowledge should be understood by way of these causes: by way of action, rebirth, the ripening of the faculties, and the distancing of the defilements.
Furthermore, seven factors lead to the arising of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor: being one who asks questions thoroughly, ...
Purification of the basis, balancing of the faculties, avoidance of persons of poor wisdom, cultivation of association with persons of wisdom,
reflection on the conduct of those possessing deep knowledge, and devotion thereto— by these reasons also,
association with knowledge should be understood. The detailed explanation of these, however, will be revealed in the *Bojjhaṅgavibhaṅga*.

Thus, being associated with knowledge, this [consciousness] that has arisen is called "without volitional effort" (*asaṅkhāra*) because it arises without prompting, without application, and without contrived reflection.

As it arises having a pleasing color as its object, it arises according to a threefold determination: it is either consisting of giving (*dānamaya*), consisting of virtue (*sīlamaya*), or consisting of meditation (*bhāvanāmaya*).

How so? When, having obtained one of the flowers or other items—blue, yellow, red, or white—one turns toward them by way of their color and honors the Buddha-jewel and the others, thinking, "This is my gift of color," then it is "consisting of giving. Here is an example:
it is said that Saṅghamitta, the storekeeper, having obtained a cloth inlaid with gold, [thought], "Even this cloth..."
"It is gold-colored; the Perfectly Enlightened One is also gold-colored. A gold-colored cloth is suitable for one who is gold-colored, and it will serve as a gift of color for us.
Thinking thus, he offered it at the Great Cetiya.
It should be understood that such an occasion constitutes "merit consisting of giving" (*dānamaya*). However, when one has obtained such a gift-object (*deyyadhamma*) and [thinks], "For me..."
When one worships the Buddha-jewel and the other jewels, thinking, "This is the family lineage, the family tradition, the family succession;

this is the family duty," then it consists of virtue (sīlamaya). But when, having performed worship of the Triple Gem with such a material object, one establishes the contemplation of decay and fall, thinking, "This complexion will go to destruction, it will go to decline," then it consists of meditation (bhāvanāmaya).

Furthermore, although it exists as something consisting of giving (*dānamaya*), when it proceeds for one who personally worships the Three Jewels with one's own hand, then it is bodily action (*kāyakamma*).

When, while worshipping the Three Jewels, one commands one's children, wife, slaves, laborers, servants, and so forth, to cause them to worship, then it is verbal action (*vacīkamma*). When that same aforementioned existing material object—
When one thinks, "I will give a gift of beauty," that is mental action (*manokamma*).
According to the method of the Vinaya, a gift is defined by this characteristic: once the speech has been uttered, such as "I will give" or "I will do," it becomes [a formal act].
However, according to the method of the Abhidhamma, from the moment one thinks in the mind, "I will give," with respect to an existing object, it is wholesome (*kusala*).
It exists. It is said that at a later time, one will perform what is to be done by means of body or speech.
Thus, giving consisting of material things (*dānamaya*) is threefold precisely through the modes of bodily, vocal, and mental action.
However, when one has obtained such a basis as described above, and [having considered] one’s own family lineage and so forth, personally offers the Three Jewels—
When one worships [the shrine] oneself, it is bodily action consisting of virtue (*sīlamaya-kāyakamma*).
When, by means of one's family lineage and so forth, one commands one's children, wife, and others to worship and has them perform the worship, it is vocal action (*vacīkamma*).
When, regarding an existing object, one thinks—based on the thought, "This is my family lineage, this is the family tradition, this is the family custom"—"I shall give a gift of praise," then...
There is mental action (*manokamma*). Thus, virtue-born action (*sīlamaya*) is threefold by way of bodily, verbal, and mental action.

But when, having obtained such a basis as described and having worshipped the Three Jewels, one establishes [the contemplation of] destruction and fall while walking up and down, then there is bodily action consisting in development (*bhāvanāmaya*).
For one who establishes the investigation of the Dhamma through speech, there is verbal action.
There is mental action for one who, without moving any part of the body or speech, initiates contemplation by means of the mind alone.
Thus, that which consists in development is threefold according to bodily, verbal, and mental action.

In this way, the Dhamma King demonstrated how this wholesome state with visible form as its object is divided into nine doors of action by way of the three bases for performing merit. This same method applies to objects such as sounds and the rest.
For in the case of the sound of drums and so forth, by taking a pleasing sound as the object, wholesome consciousness arises through the three aforementioned conditions.
In this context, it is not possible to give a gift of sound by uprooting it like a tuber and placing it in one's hand like a blue lotus;
rather, one gives a gift of sound by giving it while keeping it based upon its source.
...so it is called. Therefore, when one makes an offering to the Three Jewels with any musical instrument such as a kettle-drum or a drum, thinking, "I shall give the gift of sound";
or when one has drums and other instruments set up, thinking, "May there be the gift of sound for me";

or when one gives honey-medicine, oil, molasses, and so forth, to monks who preach the Dhamma; or when one proclaims a recitation of the Dhamma, recites the *sara-bhañña*, or delivers a discourse on the Dhamma—
When one speaks, engages in conversation while seated, or offers words of appreciation, it consists of giving (*dānamaya*).
When one performs this very same practice by way of family lineage, tradition, or custom, it consists of virtue (*sīlamaya*).
When, having performed all of this, one thinks: "This sound, though as vast as the Brahma-world, will come to destruction and will pass away," [it consists of wisdom].
When one establishes full comprehension (*sammasana*), it then consists of the quality of development (*bhāvanāmaya*).
In this context, first, that which consists of giving (*dānamaya*) occurs when one takes drums and other such instruments and makes an offering with one’s own hand;

or when one sets them out for the purpose of a constant offering, setting them out with one’s own hand; or when one goes to announce the hearing of the Dhamma, thinking, "I am giving the gift of sound," or [to give] a discourse on the Dhamma.
When he goes to perform the *sara-bhañña* (the chanting of the Dhamma), that is bodily action (*kāyakamma*). When he commands, "Go, dear ones,
and make an offering to the Three Jewels with music," or when he commands at the temple courtyards,
"Place this drum and this small drum here for my musical offering," or when he himself proclaims the call for the hearing of the Dhamma— [these are bodily actions].
When one delivers a discourse on the Dhamma or recites the sacred texts, that is verbal action (*vacīkamma*).
When, without moving any part of the body or voice, one mentally renounces an existing object with the thought, "I shall give the gift of sound," that is mental action (*manokamma*).
Even the virtue consisting of giving sound [is established] by means of drums and so forth, thinking, "The gift of sound is my family lineage, my family tradition, and my family heritage."
Bodily action consists of making offerings with one's own hands; personally placing drums and other instruments in the temple courtyards and similar places;

personally giving medicinal tonics to preachers of the Dhamma; and going for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma, proclaiming it, preaching the Dhamma, or reciting the *sara-bhañña* (eloquent chanting) as part of one’s duties.
One thinks: “The tradition of giving sound is our family lineage, our family custom, and our family heritage.”
“Go, dear ones, and make offerings to the Jewel of the Buddha and the others”—this is verbal action for one who gives such a command;
and it is also verbal action for one who, by virtue of his family lineage, himself delivers a Dhamma discourse or a *sarabhañña* recitation.

“The tradition of my family is the giving of sound; I shall give the gift of sound”—this is mental action for one who, without moving body or speech, [intends] toward an existing object by means of the mind alone.
For one who relinquishes, there is mental action (*manokamma*).
When, while walking, one establishes the contemplation of the waning and passing away of sounds, even though it consists of development (*bhāvanāmaya*), there is bodily action (*kāyakamma*).
For one who contemplates with speech without moving a limb of the body, there is vocal action (*vacīkamma*). Without moving either a limb of the body or a limb of speech—
For one who comprehends the sound-base with the mind, there is mental action.
Thus the Dhamma-King demonstrated how even a wholesome object consisting of sound is divided into nine doors of action by way of the three bases for the performance of merit.
In the case of roots, scents, and so forth as well, by taking a pleasing scent as the object, this should be determined by the same three rules as explained above.

Wholesome [kamma] arises. In that regard, when one obtains any kind of fragrance from among root-fragrances and so forth, and having directed the mind toward it by way of the fragrance, worships the Buddha-jewel and the others with the thought, "This is my gift of fragrance," then it is "consisting of giving" (dānamaya).

All of this should be understood in detail according to the same method explained under the "gift of color" (vaṇṇadāna). Thus, even wholesome kamma with fragrance as its object is [classified] by way of the three bases for the performance of merit.
The Dhamma King showed [the process] by dividing it according to the nine doors of action.
However, regarding the root-juices and so forth, when one takes a pleasing flavor as the object, wholesome consciousness arises in the manner already explained below through three determinations.
In that context, whenever one obtains any kind of pleasing flavorful substance among the root-juices and so forth—
Having relished it by way of its flavor, when one gives and relinquishes it thinking, "This is a gift of flavor for me," then it is "consisting of giving" (dānamaya);
all this should be understood in detail according to the very method already stated regarding the "gift of color" (vaṇṇadāna).

Regarding the "consisting of virtue" (sīlamaya), however, he had twelve thousand bhikkhus provided with [the food], saying: "It is not our custom to consume [this] without first giving to the Saṅgha."
Beginning with the story of King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya, who enjoyed delicious flavors, various stories have been recorded in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.

This is the only distinction. Thus, the Dhamma King demonstrated how even wholesome action with flavor as its object is divided into nine doors of kamma by way of the three bases for the performance of merit.
Regarding the tangible object as well, the three great elements—namely, the earth element, the fire element, and the air element—are what is called the "tangible object.
In this context, one should not apply the analysis by way of these [elements], but rather by way of beds, chairs, and so forth.
For when one encounters any pleasant tangible thing among beds, chairs, and the like, by way of that tangible object...
When one folds [the cloth] and gives it away, relinquishing it with the thought, "This gift of a touchable object is for me," then it is "consisting of giving.
All this should be understood in detail according to the very method already stated regarding the gift of color.
Thus the Dhamma-King demonstrated that even wholesome kamma having a tangible object is divided into nine doors of action by way of the three bases for the performance of merit.

Regarding the mental object (dhammārammaṇa), the six internal sense bases, the three characteristics, the three formless aggregates, the fifteen subtle forms, and the designation of Nibbāna—these phenomena included within the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana) are both "included" (pariyāpanna) and "unincluded" (apariyāpanna);

these are what is called the mental object. However, in this context, instead of making the application by way of these, [it is done] by way of the gift of vitality, the gift of drink, and the gift of life.

It should be performed. For when one takes as an object a delightful mental state (*dhammārammaṇa*) such as nutritive essence (*ojā*), wholesome consciousness arises according to the three rules explained below.

In that context, when one gives ghee, fresh butter, and so forth, thinking, "This gift of nutritive essence is for me," or when one gives the eight kinds of drinks, thinking, "This is a gift of drink"—
He gives; "giving of life" means he gives such things as tickets for meals or communal meals for the Saṅgha; he gives medicine to monks who are unwell;
he attends upon physicians; he has fishing nets torn up; he has fish-traps destroyed; he has bird-cages demolished; he has prisoners released;
he has the drum beaten for the Great Sacrifice (Māghāta); and other such acts for the purpose of protecting life.
When one performs such deeds, it is then "consisting of giving" (dānamaya).

However, when one carries out the giving of nutritive essence, the giving of drink, and the giving of life under the pretext of a formal obligation, thinking, "These are my family lineage, my family tradition, and my family custom," it is then "consisting of virtue" (sīlamaya).
When one establishes the contemplation of destruction and vanishing regarding the object of the Dhamma, it is then "consisting of meditation" (bhāvanāmaya).
Furthermore, although it occurs as consisting in giving (*dānamaya*), when one gives with one’s own hand gifts of strength, drinks, or life, then it is bodily action (*kāyakamma*).
When one causes children, wives, and so forth to give by commanding them, then it is verbal action (*vacīkamma*).
When, without moving the limbs of the body or the organs of speech, one intends with respect to an existing object—by way of giving strength, drinks, or life—saying, “I shall give,”...
When one thinks it with the mind, then it is mental action (*manokamma*).
But when one gives with one's own hand an existing object of the kind described above by way of family lineage and so forth, then it is bodily action consisting of virtue (*sīlamaya-kāyakamma*).
When, by way of family lineage and so forth, one causes children, wife, and others to be commanded and makes them give, [then it is bodily action consisting of virtue].

At that time, it is verbal action. When one merely thinks in the mind, "I shall give such an existing object as previously described," simply by way of family lineage and so forth, at that time it is mental action.
However, for one who, having walked up and down, establishes the contemplation of destruction and fall regarding the Dhamma as an object, there is bodily action consisting of meditation.
For one who establishes the contemplation of decay and fall through speech alone, without moving a limb of the body, there is verbal action.
For one who establishes the contemplation of decay and fall regarding the mental object through the mind alone, without moving either a limb of the body or a limb of speech, there is mental action.

Thus, that which consists of meditation is threefold by way of bodily, verbal, and mental action. In this way, even though it has a mental object, this wholesome state is threefold by way of the bases for performing meritorious deeds.
The Dhamma King demonstrated this by dividing it according to the nine doors of action.
Thus, this consciousness has been illustrated in various ways through various objects;
however, this [variety] is indeed obtainable even within a single object. How so? For among the four requisites, there are six objects in the case of the robe.
They are obtained as follows: for a newly dyed robe, the color is pleasing and beautiful to behold;

this is the object of visible form (*rūpārammaṇa*). At the time of use, it makes a rustling sound; this is the object of sound (*saddārammaṇa*). Whatever odor of mold or the like is present therein, this is the object of smell (*gandhārammaṇa*).
As for the object of taste (*rasārammaṇa*), it is spoken of by way of the flavor of its use. And whatever quality of pleasant touch (*sukhasamphassatā*) is found therein—
This is an object of tangible form (*phoṭṭhabbārammaṇa*). Pleasant feeling arising in dependence upon a robe has mental phenomena as its object (*dhammārammaṇa*).

In the case of almsfood, the object of taste (*rasārammaṇa*) is obtained in the direct sense alone. Thus, having applied the analysis according to various objects within the four conditions, the classification beginning with "consisting of giving" (*dānamaya*) should be understood.

However, for this consciousness, the object alone is fixed, because it does not arise without an object. The door, on the other hand, is not fixed. Why? Because of the non-fixity of kamma. For when kamma is not fixed, the door is likewise not fixed.
This concludes the discussion on the doors of sense-sphere wholesome kamma; specifically, the discussion on the door of bodily action.
To clarify this matter, the "Discourse on the Doors" (Dvārakathā) is set forth in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* at this point.
Therein are mentioned: three types of kamma, three doors of kamma; five consciousnesses, five doors of consciousness;
six contacts, six doors of contact; eight non-restraints, eight doors of non-restraint; and eight restraints.
The eight doors of restraint, the ten courses of wholesome action, and the ten courses of unwholesome action—
this much is called the laying down of the table of contents for the discourse on the doors.
In that regard, although the three types of kamma were mentioned first, setting those aside for now, first [we shall consider] the three...
The doors of action have been shown by dividing them. Which three? The door of bodily action, the door of verbal action, and the door of mental action.
Therein, the body is fourfold: that which is clung-to (upādinnaka), that produced by nutriment, that produced by temperature, and that produced by consciousness.
Therein, the eight types of form beginning with the eye-base and ending with the life-faculty, though they are forms produced by action, are indeed only those produced by action.
The four elements—color, odor, taste, and nutritive essence—are called the eightfold body of the clung-to (*upādinnaka*).

Those same eight born of nutriment are called the body originated by nutriment (*āhārasamuṭṭhānika*). The eight born of temperature are called the body originated by temperature (*utusamuṭṭhānika*). The eight born of consciousness are called the body originated by consciousness (*cittasamuṭṭhānika*).
Among these, the "door of bodily action" (*kāyakammadvāra*) is neither a name for the body that is subject to clinging (*upādinnaka*), nor for other [material phenomena].

However, among the eight types of matter originated by consciousness (*cittasamuṭṭhāna*), there is one kind of intimation (*viññatti*); this is what is called the door of bodily action. With reference to this, it was said:
"What is that matter which is bodily intimation? It is that which belongs to a wholesome mind, or an unwholesome mind, or an indeterminate mind..."
Or, whether moving forward or moving backward, looking ahead or looking aside,
contracting or extending a limb— the stiffening, the bracing, the state of being braced of the body, the intimation, the intimating, the state of having been intimated—
this is that material form which is bodily intimation. [Thinking] ‘I shall move forward,’ ‘I shall move backward’...
For the mind, when arising, produces matter. In that regard, among these eight groups of matter— namely, the earth element, water element, fire element, and air element,
as well as color, odor, flavor, and nutritive essence—
the air element produced by the mind stiffens and supports the material body co-nascent with itself.
It causes movement, causing one to advance and to retreat. Therein,
within a single process of adverting (*ekāvajjana-vīthi*), during the seven impulsive moments (*javana*),
the air element (*vāyodhātu*) arising from the first consciousness is able to stiffen and sustain the material body co-nascent with itself, but it is not yet able to move it back and forth.
It is capable [of doing so]. The same method applies to the second consciousness and those that follow.

However, the air element produced by the seventh consciousness, having received the condition of support from the air elements produced by the six preceding consciousnesses, is able to stiffen, sustain, move, cause to advance, cause to retreat, and cause to illuminate the material body co-nascent with itself.
It is able to cause looking, contracting, and extending.

By means of that, what is called "going" arises, what is called "coming" arises, and what is called "going and coming" arises; it brings about the state of being describable as "having gone a league" or "having gone ten leagues.
For just as in a cart that is to be pulled by seven yokes, the oxen yoked to the first yoke must first steady the yoke itself.
They are able to bear the burden, yet they do not turn the wheel; the same principle applies to the second pair and those following.

However, when oxen are yoked in the seventh team and a skilled charioteer sits on the pole, takes up the reins, and from the very front begins to strike the oxen with a goad-stick, then all together, becoming as one force, they both bear the pole and turn the wheel.
And they cause the wheels to turn; they bring about the state of being called "having taken the cart and gone ten yojanas or twenty yojanas"—this should be understood as being exactly like that.

In this context, that body which originates from consciousness (*cittasamuṭṭhānika*) is not intimation (*viññatti*); rather, it is the air-element originating from consciousness (*cittasamuṭṭhānā vāyodhātu*).
There is a certain modification of form (ākāra-vikāra) capable of acting as the condition for stiffening, sustaining, and moving the co-nascent material body;
this is called intimation (viññatti). Unlike the eight types of material phenomena, it is not produced by consciousness (citta-samutthāna).
Just as aging and death are the nature of phenomena such as impermanence and so forth, [it is said]: "Aging and death, monks, are impermanent and conditioned," and so on.
It has been said that, because it is a manifestation of mind-originated material phenomena, it too is called "mind-originated.
However, it is called "manifestation" (*viññatti*) because it makes something known. What does it make known? A single bodily action.
For when one standing within the range of vision raises a hand or a foot, or moves the head or the eyebrows—this [action] of the hand and so forth...
The physical form (*ākāra*) is cognizable by the eye; however, intimation (*viññatti*) is not cognizable by the eye, but only by the mind.
For with the eye, one sees only the object of color as it moves through hand gestures and so forth.
But having reflected upon the intimation with a mind-door consciousness, one knows: "He is making me do this and that."
For just as in the forest during the heat of summer, people tie palm leaves and such to the tops of trees at a place where there is water,
thinking, "By this sign, people will know that water exists here," or they raise a flag at the entrance to a tavern,
or a tall tree is shaken by the wind, or fish move within the water and bubbles appear on the surface—
They arise; at the limit of the path traversed by the great flood, a mass of grass, leaves, and straw is cast up.

There, seeing the movement of palm-leaf banners, the tossing of branches, bubbles, and the mass of grass and leaves, one infers—even if not seen with the eye—that "there must be water here," or "there must be liquor," or "this tree must have been struck by the wind."
"Just as one knows by means of mental consciousness: 'There will be a fish in the water;
the current has flowed over such a distance,' even so, intimation (*viññatti*) is not cognizable by the eye-faculty, but is cognizable only by the mind-faculty.
For with the eye, one sees only the object of color-form (*vaṇṇa*) as it moves through the gestures of the hands and so forth. But intimation is [perceived] by a mind-door consciousness."
Having reflected, one knows: "He is having this and that done," as it were.
This is called *viññatti* not only because of its making known (*viññāpanato*), but also because it is something to be known (*viññeyyato*).
For this is manifest even to others, down to the animals. Those gathered here and there...

For dogs, jackals, crows, oxen, and the like, when they see someone brandishing a staff or a clod and making a gesture of striking, they know, "This person wishes to strike us," and flee in whatever direction possible.

However, there is also a time when another person is not visible from behind a wall, a rampart, or a similar obstruction. Even though [the assailant] is invisible at that moment, because he becomes visible to those who are present face-to-face, [the fear arises].
It is simply called "intimation" (viññatti).
But when the body originated by mind moves, does that which is originated by the three [kamma, mind, and nutriment] move or not? It too moves in exactly the same way;
it follows that [body] and conforms to it. For just as dry sticks, grass, leaves, and so forth, which have fallen into water, move when the water flows—
They follow the course of water; when that [water] goes, they go; when it stands still, they stand still—it should be understood that this is exactly how it is.
Thus, among material phenomena produced by consciousness, this intimation should be understood as the "door of bodily action.
Furthermore, the volition established in that door—by which one kills a living being, takes what is not given, or engages in sexual misconduct—[is the action itself].
When one acts, abstaining from killing living beings and so forth—this is what is called bodily action (*kāyakamma*).
Thus, when there is an opponent, the body is the door; the volition established through that door must be classified as either "wholesome" or "unwholesome.
However, when there is no opponent, it must be classified by completing the triad as "indeterminate" (*abyākata*). In this regard, just as...
The city gate stands right where it was built; it does not shift even a finger’s breadth from one place to another, yet by that very gate the great multitude of people passes through.
In the same way, the door does not move to another door, but karma "moves" because it arises at this or that door. Thus the ancients have said:
"Karmas move through the doors; the doors do not move through the doors.
Therefore, by means of the doors, karmas are established as distinct from one another.

In this context, the door receives its name from the karma, and the karma [receives its name] from the door. For just as there are locations for the arising of consciousness and so forth, [so too are there locations for the arising of karmas].

They receive the names "door of consciousness," "door of contact," "door of non-restraint," and "door of restraint"; likewise, the place where bodily action arises receives the name "door of bodily action.
The same principle applies to the doors of vocal and mental action.
Just as, for example, the deities residing in various trees are called the "simbali-tree deity," the "palāsa-tree deity," or the "pucimanda-tree deity," [so too are these doors designated].

Just as a deity is given a name according to whichever tree it inhabits—such as "Phandanadevatā"—in the same way, an action performed through the door of the body receives the name "bodily action" (kāyakamma) because of that door.
The same principle applies to vocal action and mental action. In this context, the body is one thing and the action is another;
however, because it is performed by means of the body, it is called "bodily action. Thus say the teachers of the commentaries:
If an action is performed by means of the body, it is called "bodily action";
the body and bodily action are established as distinct from one another.
If an action is performed by means of a needle, it is called "needle-work."
The needle and the needle-work are established as distinct from one another.
If the work is done with an axe, it is called "axe-work";
the axe and the axe-work are established as distinct from one another.
If an action is performed by a man, it is called "a man's action";
the man and the man's action are established as distinct from one another.
It is just so.
"If an action is performed by means of the body, it is called 'bodily action';
thus, the body and bodily action are established as distinct from one another.
This being the case, neither the definition of the door nor the definition of the action is tenable. How so? For in the case of bodily intimation...
“Because of the statement, ‘Kamma operates at the door,’ verbal kamma also occurs; therefore, it is not appropriate to define that [verbal intimation] as the door of bodily kamma.
And since bodily kamma also occurs in verbal intimation, it is not appropriate to define that [verbal intimation] as bodily kamma.
“It is not inappropriate. Why? Because of its predominant occurrence and because of its frequent occurrence.”

For bodily action (*kāyakamma*) generally proceeds as bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*), whereas the others do not; therefore, because it occurs predominantly as bodily action, its status as the "door of bodily action" is established.

This determination of the doors is logical, just as the designation of "Brāhmaṇa village," "mango grove," or "elephant grove" is applied to those respective places. However, bodily action itself exists only within the door of the body.
It occurs predominantly through the body-door and only slightly through the door of speech.

Therefore, because it occurs predominantly through the body-door, its status as bodily action (kāyakamma) is established, just as those who frequent the forest—such as hunters and young girls—are designated by the terms "forest-dweller" and so forth. Thus, the determination of action is also logical.
The discussion on the door of bodily action is concluded.
The Discussion on the Door of Verbal Action.
In this discussion on the door of verbal action, speech is said to be threefold by way of volition (*cetanā*) and abstinence (*virati*). Regarding that:
"Bhikkhus, speech endowed with four factors is well-spoken, not ill-spoken; it is blameless and beyond reproach."
And [the phrase] "of the wise"—this is called the expression of volition (*cetanā-vācā*). That which is said, "Abstention from, and refraining from, the four types of verbal misconduct...

this is called right speech (*sammā-vācā*)"—this is called the expression of abstinence (*virati-vācā*). "Speech, utterance, discourse, enunciation, sound, the act of sounding, speech, and the differentiation of speech"—this is called the expression of sound (*sadda-vācā*).
Among these, the door of verbal action (*vācī-kamma-dvāra*) is neither [identical with] volition...
The name does not belong to the abstention (*virati*). However, because of the word "together" (*saha*), there is a single intimation (*viññatti*);
this is what is called the door of verbal action (*vacīkammadvāra*). With reference to this, it was said: "What is that material form which is verbal intimation?

It is the speech, the utterance, the discourse, the enunciation, the sound, the vocal act, the speech, the differentiation of speech, belonging to a wholesome mind, an unwholesome mind, or an indeterminate mind."

“This is called speech (*vācā*). That which is the intimation (*viññatti*), the making known (*viññāpanā*), and the state of being made known (*viññāpitatta*) by that speech—this is the material form (*rūpa*) called vocal intimation (*vacīviññatti*).
For when one who is thinking, “I shall say this,” or “I am saying this,” there arises what is called the sound of the expansion of thought (*vitakkavipphārasaddo*).
This is not to be cognized by the ear, but is to be cognized by the mind; thus it is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. However, in the commentaries on the *Āgamas*,...
‘The sound of the diffusion of thought’: this refers to the sound of those who are prattling due to the diffusion of thought, such as those who are asleep or heedless.
‘Having heard’: having heard that sound which arose for one who was thinking; having said that “on account of that, one declares:
‘Such is your mind, even so is your mind,’” the illustrative instances (*vatthu*) have also been told. In the *Paṭṭhāna* as well:
It is stated: “The sound-base originated by mind is a condition for ear-consciousness by way of the object-condition.
Therefore, there is no such thing as a sound produced by the diffusion of applied thought (*vitakka*) that arises without the impact of intimation (*viññatti*) and is not cognizable by the ear.
However, the earth element and the water element [are present] in the mind that arises with the intention, “I shall speak this; I shall speak that.”
The fire element, the air element, color, odor, flavor, and nutritive essence—these eight material phenomena produce [the sound].
Within them, the consciousness-originated earth element arises while striking the clung-to (upādinnaka) matter. Together with that impact of the elements, sound arises.
This is what is called "sound originated by consciousness. This is not intimation (viññatti). Of that...
However, there is a certain formal modification that serves as the condition for the impact of the appropriated earth-element produced by consciousness;

this is called vocal intimation (*vacīviññatti*). From here on, everything—such as how it does not originate from consciousness like the eight [other] material phenomena—should be understood according to the method already stated below.
For here too, having heard the sound of someone calling out, "Tissa! Datta!
Mittā!", one reflects upon that intimation with a mind-door consciousness and knows, "He is likely making me do this and that. And like bodily intimation, this is also evident even to animals.
For having heard the sounds "Come! or "Go!", even animals think, "He is likely making me do this."
Having known [the object], they both come and go. As for the phrase "it moves or does not move the body produced by three origins," this section is not applicable here.
Furthermore, there is no function of support originating from the preceding consciousness.
However, that volition which is established in that door of speech—by means of which one speaks falsehood, speaks slander, or speaks harsh words...
Speaking, idle chatter, and abstaining from false speech and so forth—this is called verbal action (*vacīkamma*).
From here on, all determinations of action (*kammavavatthāna*) and determinations of doors (*dvāravavatthāna*) should be understood according to the method already explained below.
The discussion on the door of verbal action is finished.
The Discourse on the Door of Mental Action.
In this discourse on the door of mental action, "mind" refers to the fourfold mind according to the planes of existence, beginning with the sense-sphere.
Therein, the sense-sphere mind is of fifty-four kinds; the fine-material-sphere mind is of fifteen kinds; and the immaterial-sphere mind is of twelve kinds.
The supramundane is eightfold; thus, all together there are eighty-nine types. In this regard, it cannot be said that this particular mind is not the mind-door.

For just as it cannot be said that this particular volition is not karma—even volition associated with the fivefold sensory consciousness is designated as "karma" in the Great Treatise—so too is this [mind].
It should not be said that what is called "mind" is not the mind-door.
Here it is asked: "What does this 'kamma' do? It accumulates, it constructs, it forms a mass, it intends, it plans, it designs.
This being so, what does the volition of the fivefold sense-consciousness accumulate or construct?

Does it "make a mass," "intend," "fashion," or "arrange"? [It does so] with respect to co-nascent states. For that [volition] also, in relation to the co-nascent associated aggregates, collects them, conditions them, makes a mass, intends, fashions, and arranges.
Or rather, what is the use of this discussion? This was stated by way of a comprehensive inclusion.
However, the definitive conclusion here is this: wholesome and unwholesome [volition] belonging to the three planes...
The twenty-ninefold mind is called the door of mental action (*manokammadvāra*).

Furthermore, the volition established in that door of mind—which includes both covetousness, ill-will, and wrong view, as well as non-covetousness, non-ill-will, and right view—this is called mental action (*manokamma*).
Hereafter, all the determinations of action and the determinations of the doors [will follow] as explained below.
It should be understood in the manner already stated. These are called the three doors of action.
The discussion on the door of mental action is finished.
The Discussion on Action.
Now, having set aside the three types of kamma, these doors of kamma have been shown;

beginning with those, this is the detailed exposition for establishing the matrix of the remaining discussion on the doors. For there are three kinds of kamma: bodily kamma, verbal kamma, and mental kamma.
But what is this that is called "kamma"? It is volition itself, as well as certain factors associated with volition.
...phenomena (*dhammā*). In this regard, concerning the status of volition (*cetanā*) as action (*kamma*), there are these discourses:
“Bhikkhus, I say that volition is action; having willed, one performs action by way of body, speech, and mind.
“For when there is a body, Ānanda, internal pleasure and pain arise with bodily volition as their cause; [likewise] with speech...”
“Or, Ānanda, when there is speech, internal pleasure and pain arise with volition regarding speech as their cause;
or, Ānanda, when there is mind, internal pleasure and pain arise with volition regarding the mind as their cause. “Bhikkhus, threefold is bodily volition:
unwholesome bodily action with suffering as its outcome, suffering as its result. Fourfold, bhikkhus, is verbal volition... [and so on]...”
“Monks, there are three kinds of mental volition that are unwholesome mental actions with a painful outcome and a painful result.
Monks, there are three kinds of bodily volition that are wholesome bodily actions with a pleasant outcome and a pleasant result.
Monks, there are four kinds of verbal volition... [and so on] ... Monks, there are three kinds of mental volition that are wholesome mental actions.”
“Having a pleasant outcome, having a pleasant ripening. “If, Ānanda, this foolish man Samiddhi, when asked thus by the wanderer of Pāṭaliputta, were to answer thus:

‘Friend Pāṭaliputta, having performed an intentional deed by body, speech, or mind that is to be experienced as pleasant, one experiences pleasure... [and so on] ...or a deed to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant,’...”
“He experiences neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Ānanda, if the foolish man Samiddhi were to answer correctly when asked by the wanderer of Pāṭaliputta, he would answer in this way.

These, first of all, are the suttas regarding the status of volition as action (kamma). However, the status of the factors associated with volition as action is illustrated by the fourfold classification of action (kammacatukka). For this has been said:
“Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of kamma that have been realized by me through direct knowledge and proclaimed.
What are the four? There is, bhikkhus, black kamma with black result; there is, bhikkhus, white kamma with white result;
there is, bhikkhus, black-and-white kamma with black-and-white result; there is, bhikkhus, [white kamma with white result].”
“Monks, there is action that is neither dark nor bright, with neither-dark-nor-bright result, which leads to the destruction of action.
… And what, monks, is the action that is neither dark nor bright, with neither-dark-nor-bright result, which leads to the destruction of action?
It is these seven factors of enlightenment: the mindfulness factor of enlightenment … [and so on] … the equanimity factor of enlightenment. This, monks, is called…”

Kamma that is neither dark nor bright, with neither-dark-nor-bright result, leads to the destruction of kamma. … And what, bhikkhus, is the kamma that is neither dark nor bright, with neither-dark-nor-bright result, which leads to the destruction of kamma?

It is this very Noble Eightfold Path—namely, right view … right concentration. This is called [the kamma that is neither dark nor bright, with neither-dark-nor-bright result, leading to the destruction of kamma].
“Monks, there is action that is neither dark nor bright, with neither-dark-nor-bright result, which leads to the destruction of action.
Thus, these fifteen states, categorized according to the factors of enlightenment and the factors of the path, have been illustrated by the fourfold classification of action.
Furthermore, together with these six—covetousness, ill will, wrong view, non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view—[the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are complete].
Twenty-one states associated with volition (cetanā) should be understood.
In that context, when the supramundane path (lokuttara-magga) is analyzed, it comprises the three types of action (kamma), beginning with bodily action.
For whatever misconduct one commits with the body, the restraint from that is to be understood as bodily [action]. Whatever misconduct one commits with speech...
Therefore, restraint from that [mental misconduct] should be understood as verbal restraint. Thus, right action is bodily action, and right speech is verbal action.
When these two are taken, right livelihood is already included because it belongs to that same category.

Furthermore, whatever immorality one commits through the mind, restraint from that should be understood as mental restraint. This [restraint] occurs by way of right view, intention, effort, mindfulness, and concentration.
It is fivefold. This fivefold [action] is also called mental action (*manokamma*). Thus, when the supramundane path (*lokuttaramagga*) is cultivated, it partakes of the three types of action.

At this point, there is what is called the "conjunction of doors" (*dvārasaṃsandana*). For, having reached the stage of "touching" (*copana*) through the doors of body and speech, it reaches the course of action (*kammapatha*).
There is that which has not yet reached [the path of action], and there is also that which, having reached its manifestation in the mind-door, has not yet reached the path of action;
taking this into account, they classified it according to each respective door.
Herein is the method: one who, thinking "I will go hunting," strings his bow, winds the bowstring, and fixes an arrow—
He eats his meal and puts on his clothes; up to this point, there is contact and acquisition at the door of the body.
If he wanders through the forest all day long and does not obtain even as much as a hare or a cat, is this called unwholesome bodily action or not? It is not. Why?
Because it has not reached the level of a course of action (*kammapatha*). However, it is simply bodily misconduct (*kāyaduccarita*).
It should be understood that it is called [a preparatory action]. The same principle applies even to well-directed activities such as catching fish.

Regarding the door of speech as well, although one has reached the stage of verbal transgression by commanding, "I will go hunting" or "Quickly prepare the bow and so forth," for one who finds nothing in the forest as previously described, it does not reach the level of a full course of kamma.
However, it is not bodily action; it should be understood that it is merely called verbal misconduct.
In the mind-door, however, the breach of the course of action occurs at the mere arising of the volition of killing.
And that occurs by way of ill will, not by way of the destruction of life. For unwholesome bodily action originates in the doors of body and speech.

Not at the mind-door; likewise for unwholesome verbal action. Unwholesome mental action, however, originates through all three doors; and the same applies to wholesome bodily, verbal, and mental actions. How so?
For instance, the action of one who kills a living being with his own hand, takes what is not given, or engages in sexual misconduct [originates through the body door].
It is bodily action alone. The door is also the body-door alone. Thus, first of all, unwholesome bodily action originates at the body-door.
Furthermore, the covetousness, ill-will, and wrong view that arise together with those consciousnesses either belong to the side of volition or are indeterminate (abbohārika).
[For example: "Go, deprive such-and-such a person of life; take such-and-such a person's goods..."
But for one who commands, "Seize it!", the action is a bodily action (*kāyakamma*), while the door is the verbal door (*vacīdvāra*).

Thus, unwholesome bodily action arises through the verbal door. Furthermore, the covetousness, ill will, and wrong view that arise simultaneously with those consciousnesses are either included within the category of volition (*cetanā*) or are not so designated.
This much is the teachers' "Exposition of Common Meaning" (*samānatthakathā*).
The caviller, however, says: "Unwholesome bodily action also originates at the mind-door. When told, "Bring a sutta included among the three compendia," he brings this so-called Kulumba Sutta:

"Furthermore, monks, here some ascetic or brahmin, possessing psychic power and attained to mastery over the mind, regards with an evil mind the embryo in another's womb, thinking: 'Oh, may this one in the womb...'"
‘The fetus will not emerge safely. Thus, monks, there is the destruction of the family.
Having cited this sutta, he said: “As soon as such a thought is conceived in the mind, the fetus within the womb dissolves like a lump of foam.
In this case, where is there any physical assault or verbal assault? It is in the mind-door alone...”
"However, this unwholesome bodily action arises [from it].
Then, saying, "We shall weigh the meaning of your sutta," they weighed it thus: "You speak of injuring others through psychic power (iddhi).

Now, this so-called psychic power consists of: the psychic power of resolution (adhiṭṭhāniddhi), the psychic power of transformation (vikubbaniddhi), and the psychic power of the mind-made body (manomayiddhi)."

There are ten kinds of success (iddhi): success through the expansion of knowledge, success through the expansion of concentration, noble success, success born of the ripening of karma, success belonging to one who possesses merit, success consisting of science (vijjā), and success in the sense of succeeding through the condition of right application here and there.
"Among these, what kind of success do you claim? "Success consisting of development (bhāvanāmaya). "But can one perform an act of harming others with success consisting of development?"
“Does it happen? “Yes, some teachers say it happens once.

They say that just as when one wishing to strike another throws a water-filled jar, both the jar breaks and the water is lost, even so, through the power of spiritual development (*bhāvanāmaya-iddhi*), an act of harming another occurs only once.
From that point on, however, that power is lost. Then, regarding that power of spiritual development...
Having said, "An act of harming others does not occur even once, nor twice," they asked him as he approached that invitation:
"Is the psychic power consisting of meditation wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?
Is it associated with pleasant feeling, associated with painful feeling, or associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling? Is it accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought?"
"Are they with applied thought and sustained thought only, or without applied thought and sustained thought only? Are they of the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the immaterial sphere?
Now, whoever understands this question will say: "The supernormal power consisting in development is either wholesome or indeterminate;
it is experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant only, is without applied thought and sustained thought only, and belongs to the fine-material sphere only. He should be told:
—“To which category among the wholesome and so forth does the volition of taking life belong? Knowing [the answer], he would say:

“The volition of taking life is exclusively unwholesome, exclusively to be experienced as painful, exclusively accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and exclusively belonging to the sense-sphere.
“If that is so, your question does not accord with the triad of the wholesome, nor with the triad of feeling, nor with the triad of applied thought, nor with the classification of planes.”
"But is such a vast discourse as this meaningless? "It is not meaningless; however, you do not know its meaning.

For here, in the phrase 'one possessing psychic power, attained to mastery over mind,' neither the psychic power consisting of meditation is intended, but rather the psychic power of sorcery (*āthabbaṇiddhi*) is intended.
That indeed is what is found to be present here. But that [power], having released the doors of body and speech..."

It is not possible to do so. For beings who practice the *āthabbaṇa* (sorcery) arts must eat saltless food for seven days, spread out on darbha grass, and lie upon the bare earth while performing austerities.

On the seventh day, having prepared a cemetery ground and standing on the seventh footprint, they rotate their hands again and again and mutter the spell with their mouths. Only then does their ritual succeed. Thus...
This psychic power (iddhi) also cannot be performed by releasing the doors of body and speech. One must reach the conclusion here that "bodily action does not originate in the mind-door.
However, when one speaks falsehoods and so forth by means of hand gestures (hatthamuddā), the action is verbal action (vacīkamma), while the door is the body-door (kāyadvāra).
Thus, unwholesome verbal action also originates at the door of the body.
Furthermore, the covetousness, ill will, and wrong view that arise simultaneously with those consciousnesses either belong to the side of volition or are indeterminate (*abbohārika*).
However, for one who utters speech and speaks falsehoods and so forth, the action is indeed verbal action, and the door is likewise the door of speech. Thus...

Unwholesome verbal action arises at the door of speech. However, the covetousness, ill will, and wrong view that arise simultaneously with those consciousnesses are either on the side of volition or are not included [in the formal classification]. This much is the teachers’ common exposition.
But the caviller says: "Unwholesome verbal action also arises at the door of mind. When told, "Bring a sutta included in the three compendiums," he brings this sutta from the Uposatha Khandhaka:
“But whichever bhikkhu, when the proclamation has been made up to the third time, being conscious of an existing offense, does not reveal it, there is an intentional falsehood for him.
Having cited this sutta, he said: “In this way, while not revealing the offense, one remains silent and incurs another offense;
herein, where is there any movement of the body or movement of speech? It is only in the mind-door that—”
‘This unwholesome verbal action arises. He should be asked:
‘Is this sutta of interpretable meaning (neyyattha) or of definitive meaning (nītattha)? [If he says: ‘This sutta of mine is of definitive meaning,’ he should say:
‘Do not speak thus; we shall weigh its meaning,’ and then he should ask as follows: ‘In the case of intentional lying...’
"What happens? [If he asks this,] knowing the answer, one should say: "In the case of a deliberate lie, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Then he should be told: "The Vinaya has two roots: body and speech. For the Fully Enlightened One has prescribed all offenses through these very two doors;
there is no such thing as the prescription of an offense in the mind-door. You [are being too] excessive regarding the Vinaya..."
Having rebuked him with such words as, “You are one who knows what has been done; you have laid down an offense in a matter not laid down by the Teacher;
you misrepresent the Perfectly Enlightened One and strike at the Wheel of the Conqueror,” he should then be asked a further question:
“Does deliberate lying arise from action or from non-action? Knowing [the answer], he will say, “From action. Then he should be told:
“If he does not reveal it, what kind of action does he perform? Indeed, failing to see the action, he will fall into distress.
Therefore, he should be convinced by the meaning of this sutta. This is the meaning here:
that which is called “intentional lying,” from what offense does it arise? The meaning is: “What kind of offense is it? “It is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).”

And this should be understood as an offense originating from non-action at the door of speech by virtue of the Blessed One’s word, rather than by the characteristic of false speech itself. For it has been said:
“Not conversing with any person...”
Even if others should speak harsh words to us,
one might incur a verbal offense but not a bodily one;
this question has been pondered by those skilled in wholesome states.
Thus, it must be concluded that unwholesome verbal action does not originate at the mind-door.

However, when one moves a limb of the body with a mind accompanied by covetousness and performs acts such as grasping the hand, or with a mind accompanied by ill-will and performs acts such as seizing a staff,

or with a mind accompanied by wrong view and thinks, "Khaṇḍa, Siva, and others are supreme"— [The remainder of the sentence would continue to explain how these actions originate through the body-door.]

When one performs such acts as bowing to them, joining the palms in salutation, preparing seats, or decorating the surroundings, at that time the action is mental action (manokamma), while the door is the bodily door (kāyadvāra).
Thus, unwholesome mental action arises through the bodily door. However, in this context, volition (cetanā) is not included in the conventional designation.
But when, with a mind accompanied by covetousness, one utters a vocal act and covets another's wealth and requisites, thinking, "O, may what belongs to another be mine";
or when, with a mind accompanied by ill will, one says, "May these beings be slain, or bound, or destroyed, or may they not exist at all"; or [when] with a mind accompanied by wrong view—
When one says such things as “there is no gift, there is no sacrifice,” then the action is mental action (*manokamma*), while the door is the door of speech (*vacīdvāra*).
Thus unwholesome mental action originates at the door of speech. However, in this case, volition (*cetanā*) is not included in the conventional classification [of the three courses of action].
But when, without moving the limbs of the body or the members of speech, one sits in private accompanied by covetousness, ill will, and wrong view—
When one arouses such thoughts, then the action is mental action (manokamma) and the door is likewise the mind-door (manodvāra). Thus, unwholesome mental action originates in the mind-door.
Furthermore, in this context, both volition (cetanā) and the mental states associated with volition originate in the mind-door alone.
In this way, it should be understood that unwholesome mental action originates through all three doors.
As for what was said regarding “likewise wholesome bodily, verbal, and mental actions,” this is the method:

when someone, being unable to speak due to some cause, takes up these training precepts— “I abstain from killing living beings, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct”— by means of a hand gesture,
then the action is bodily action and the door is likewise the bodily door.

Thus, wholesome bodily action arises at the door of the body. Accompanying those consciousnesses, non-covetousness and the other factors are either on the side of volition (*cetanā*) or are indeterminate (*abbohārika*).
However, when one undertakes those very training rules by means of vocal expression, then the action is bodily action, and [the body] is the door.
...but there is also the door of speech. Thus, wholesome bodily action originates at the door of speech.
Accompanying those consciousnesses, states such as non-covetousness are either on the side of volition (*cetanā*) or are indeterminate (*abbōhārika*).

However, when those training rules (*sikkhāpada*) are being given, if one does not move the limbs of the body or the organs of speech but [refrains] by means of the mind alone from "killing living beings" (*pāṇātipāta*)...
When one undertakes the training, thinking, ‘I shall abstain from taking what is not given and from sexual misconduct,’ then the action is bodily action, yet the door is the mind-door.
Thus, wholesome bodily action originates in the mind-door.
The volitions associated with those consciousnesses—such as non-covetousness and so forth—belong either to the category of volition or are beyond such classification.
Furthermore, it should be understood that for one who undertakes the four training rules beginning with “abstaining from false speech” in the manner already described,
wholesome verbal action arises through the three doors. Here too, non-covetousness and the others belong either to the category of volition or are indeterminate.

However, for one who performs such acts as sweeping the precincts of a shrine, worshipping with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, or venerating the shrine, by means of bodily action accompanied by thoughts free from covetousness and the like, the deed is mental action (*manokamma*), while the door is the body-door (*kāyadvāra*). Thus, wholesome mental action originates at the body-door.
In this context, however, volition (*cetanā*) is not included in the conventional reckoning. [Likewise,] by means of speech accompanied by a mind free from covetousness...
When one has cultivated [the mind] and, being free from covetousness, thinks, "Oh, may what belongs to another's wealth and requisites not be mine," with a mind accompanied by non-ill-will;
or when one says, "May all beings be free from enmity, free from affliction, free from distress, and may they maintain themselves in happiness," with a mind accompanied by right view;
or when one utters such words as "There is giving," etc., that action is mental action (manokamma).

However, the door is the door of speech (*vacīdvāra*). Thus, wholesome mental action (*manokamma*) originates at the door of speech. But here, volition (*cetanā*) is not included in the conventional designation [of that specific door].

On the other hand, for one who sits in private without moving the limbs of the body or the members of speech, and who arouses states of consciousness accompanied by non-covetousness and so forth solely by means of the mind—that action is mental action, and the door is likewise the door of mind (*manodvāra*) alone. Thus is wholesome mental action.
It originates at the mind-door (*manodvāra*). However, in this context, both the volition (*cetanā*) and the mental states associated with volition originate at the mind-door alone.

Therein, regarding killing and taking what is not given that originate through an order, one who says that the action is bodily action and the door is the body-door by virtue of the action itself protects the action but "breaks the door.
This is so in the case of those [actions] originating through a hand gesture (*hatthamuddā*).

Regarding lying and the other [unwholesome deeds], although the door is the body-door, one who speaks of the action as "bodily action" by way of the door is said to "protect the door and break the action.
Therefore, thinking "I shall protect the action," one must not break the door;
thinking "I shall protect the door," one must not break the action. However, according to the method already stated, both the action and the door—
It should be understood in this way, for by speaking thus one neither violates the action nor the door.
The Discussion of Action is finished.
Now, regarding such passages as "the five consciousnesses are the five doors of consciousness," [we shall explain] eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness...

Tongue-consciousness and body-consciousness—these are called the five types of consciousness. The eye-consciousness-door, the ear…, nose…, tongue…, and body-consciousness-door—these are called the five doors of consciousness.
Volition arising by way of these five doors is neither bodily action nor verbal action; it is exclusively mental action.
It should be understood that they "arise. These six types of contact—eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact—are called the six contacts.

These six doors of contact—the door of eye-contact, the door of ear-contact, the door of nose-contact, the door of tongue-contact, the door of body-contact, and the door of mind-contact—are called the six doors of contact.

Restraintlessness of the eye, restraintlessness of the ear, restraintlessness of the nose, restraintlessness of the tongue, restraintlessness of the sensitive body, restraintlessness of the physical body, restraintlessness of speech, and restraintlessness of the mind—these are called the eight kinds of non-restraint.
In terms of their essential nature, these consist of five factors: immorality, forgetfulness, ignorance, impatience, and laziness.
Among these, even a single factor [is present] in the consciousnesses that conclude with the stage of determining at the five sense doors.

It does not arise [at that time]; it arises only at the moment of impulsion (*javana*). Even though it has arisen during the impulsion, it is called "non-restraint" (*asaṃvara*) in the five sense-doors.
For contact co-nascent with eye-consciousness is called "eye-contact," volition is called "mental action" (*manokamma*), and that consciousness is called the "door of mental action.
Herein, the fivefold non-restraint does not exist. [That which is] co-nascent with the moment of receiving (*sampaṭicchana*)...
Contact is called mental contact; volition is called mental action; that consciousness is called the door of mental action.
Herein also, there is no lack of restraint. The same method applies to investigating and determining as well.
Furthermore, the contact co-arising with the impulsion is called mental contact; the volition is called mental action; and that consciousness is called the door of mental action.
Herein, non-restraint is what is called "non-restraint of the eye. The same method applies to the doors of the ear, nose, tongue, and sensitive body.

However, when a javana consciousness belonging to the mind-door arises—taking any one of the objects such as visible forms as its object—without the vocal door, but causing the mere impulsion reckoned as the bodily door to occur, then the contact co-nascent with that consciousness [is non-restraint].
Contact of the mind is called *manosamphassa*; volition is called bodily action (*kāyakamma*).

However, that consciousness is not included in the formal enumeration [of the doors], and because it has arisen as a mere stirring (*copana*), it does not receive the designation of the "mind-door. Herein, non-restraint is called non-restraint of the stirring body.
When such a process of impulsion (*javana*) occurs without the body-door, causing a mere stirring designated as the pure "door of speech" to arise—
When such a javana-citta arises, the contact (phassa) co-nascent with that citta is called "mental contact" (manosamphassa); the volition (cetana) is called "verbal action" (vacīkamma).
However, that citta is not designated as [a full cognitive process], because it arises merely as a stirring and thus does not receive the designation of a "mind-door" (manodvāra).
In this context, non-restraint (asaṃvara) refers to verbal non-restraint (vācā-asaṃvara). But when such a javana-citta occurs without the doors of body or speech—

When it arises as the pure mind-door itself, then the contact co-nascent with that consciousness is called "mind-contact," the volition is called "mental action" (*manokamma*), and that consciousness is called the "door of mental action. Herein, non-restraint is called "mental non-restraint.
Thus, by way of these eight types of non-restraint, there is the door of eye-non-restraint... [and so forth].

The ear... the nose... the tongue... the body of sensitive matter... the body of non-sensory matter... speech... and the mind-door—these eight should be understood as the doors of non-restraint (*asaṃvaradvāra*). Restraint of the eye... restraint of the ear...

restraint of the nose... restraint of the tongue... restraint of the body of sensitive matter... restraint of the body of non-sensory matter... restraint of speech... and restraint of the mind—these [are the doors of restraint].

Furthermore, there are what are called the eight types of restraint (*saṃvara*). In terms of their actual nature, these consist of five factors: virtue (*sīla*), mindfulness (*sati*), knowledge (*ñāṇa*), patience (*khanti*), and energy (*vīriya*).
Not even one of these factors arises in the moments of consciousness ending with the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*) in the five sense doors.
They arise only at the moment of the impulsion (*javana*). Even though they arise during the impulsion, they are called "restraint" in relation to the five sense doors. Of that [restraint]...
Furthermore, the arising of contact co-nascent with all eye-consciousness— termed "eye-contact" and so forth— should be understood according to the method already explained regarding non-restraint.
Thus, by way of these eight types of restraint, one should understand the eight doors of restraint,
beginning with the door of eye-restraint and ending with the door of mind-restraint.
The Discussion of the Unwholesome Courses of Action:

Killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view—these are called the ten unwholesome courses of action.
Therein, the "over-stepping" (*atipāta*) of a living being (*pāṇa*) is called killing (*pāṇātipāta*); it is meant as the slaying or the slaughter of a living being. A "living being" (*pāṇa*)...
And here, from the conventional standpoint (*vohāra*), it is a "being," while from the ultimate standpoint (*paramattha*), it is the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).

Now, taking that living being as a living being, the volition of killing—which arises through either the door of body or the door of speech and instigates the action that cuts off the life-faculty—is the destruction of life (*pāṇātipāta*).
This is less blameworthy when directed toward small living beings among animals and so forth who lack special qualities, but more blameworthy when directed toward a large-bodied being. Why?
It is due to the greatness of the application (*payoga*). Even when the application is equal, it is due to the greatness of the object (*vatthu*).

Among humans and others who possess qualities, it is less blameworthy when they have few qualities and more blameworthy when they have great qualities. However, when there is equality in the bodily qualities, it should be understood that it is less blameworthy when the defilements (*kilesa*) and the efforts (*upakkama*) are mild, and more blameworthy when they are intense.
It has five constituent factors: a living being, the perception of it as a living being, the intention to kill, the means employed, and death by that means.
There are six modes of application: by one's own hand, by command, by relinquishing (an object), by immobilization, by means of spells, and by means of psychic power (*iddhi*).
However, if this matter were explained in detail, it would become excessively prolix; therefore, we shall not elaborate upon it. Nor shall we explain other matters of a similar kind.
Those who seek [clarity], however, should consult the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya, to grasp the meaning.
Taking what has not been given is "adinnādāna"; it is said to be the seizing of another's property, theft, or robbery.

In this context, "what has not been given" (*adinnam*) refers to that which is owned by another, such that one who exercises control over it according to their own will would be subject to punishment and liable to reproach.

And it occurs as follows: when something is possessed by another, for one who perceives it as being possessed by another, the volition of theft—which originates from the act of taking that object—is *adinnādāna* (taking what is not given).
This is less blameworthy when the property of another is inferior, and more blameworthy when it is superior. Why?
Because of the superiority of the object (*vatthu*). When the value of the object is equal, it is more blameworthy in the case of an object belonging to those who possess superior qualities.
Taking into account that which possesses a particular quality in excess, there is little blame in taking from an object belonging to one who has inferior qualities compared to that [superior one].

This [offense] has five constituent factors: the object being possessed by another, the perception that it is possessed by another, the intention to steal, the effort, and the removal by means of that effort.
There are six modes of application: those beginning with "by one's own hand," and so forth; and these, according to their respective suitability, constitute the act of stealing.
They occur by way of these five types of theft: open theft, concealed theft, theft by artifice, and theft by fraud. This is the summary here;
the detailed explanation, however, is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*.

Regarding the phrase "misconduct in sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu micchācāro*): here, "in sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu*) refers to sexual intercourse; "misconduct" (*micchācāro*) refers to that which is utterly censured.

It is base conduct. By way of its characteristic, however, sexual misconduct is the volition of transgressing against an improper place, proceeding through the door of the body with the intention of an unrighteous state (*asaddhamma*).

In this context, an "improper place" refers to—firstly, regarding men—the woman protected by her mother, protected by her father, protected by both parents, protected by her brother, protected by her sister, protected by her relatives, protected by her clan, protected by her Dhamma, or protected by [the threat of] punishment; and so forth.

The ten [types of women] protected by their mothers and so forth are those with a staff [to punish them for misconduct]. The ten beginning with those purchased with wealth—namely, the one who lives according to her own will (*chandavāsinī*), the one who lives for enjoyment (*bhogavāsinī*), the one who wears fine cloth (*paṭavāsinī*), the one who shares the water-pot (*odapattakinī*), the one whose head-covering has been removed (*obhaṭacumbaṭā*), a female slave as a wife, a female servant as a wife, one captured under a banner (*dhajāhaṭā*), and a momentary wife (*muhuttikā*)—these are the twenty types of women.
Among women, however, of the two types who are protected by their mothers and those with a staff...
For the other twelve women, including those purchased with wealth and so forth, this is called an "unapproachable object" for other men.

Furthermore, this misconduct is less blameworthy when committed toward an unapproachable object that lacks qualities such as virtue (*sīla*), but it is greatly blameworthy when committed toward one endowed with such qualities.
It has four constituent factors: the unapproachable object, the intention to pursue it, the effort of pursuit, and [the consummation].
The path, the practice of the path, and endurance. One application is that which is performed by one's own hand alone.
"Falsehood" (*musā*) is a verbal or bodily application that destroys the welfare of another, preceded by the intention to deceive.

However, lying (*musāvāda*) is the volition that, with the intent to deceive, originates a bodily or verbal application intended to mislead another. According to another method—"falsehood" (*musā*)—is...
An unreal and untrue matter. "Speech" (*vāda*) is the making known of that [matter] as real and true.
By way of its characteristic, however, false speech (*musāvāda*) is the volition that originates such a communication from one who desires to make another understand an untrue matter as being true.
It is less blameworthy when the matter it destroys is small, and more blameworthy when it is great. Furthermore—
For householders, it is a minor offense when it proceeds in such a manner as saying "there is none" out of a desire not to give what belongs to them.
It is a major offense when spoken by one acting as a witness for the purpose of subverting the truth.

For renunciants, even having obtained a small amount of oil or ghee, to speak with a motive of amusement according to the method of exaggeration—saying, "Today in the village there seems to be an oil-river flowing"—is likewise [an offense].
When it occurs in the manner of saying "I saw" regarding what was not actually seen, and so forth, it is a grave offense (*mahāsāvajja*).
It has four constituent factors (*sambhāra*): a basis that is not as it appears, the intention to deceive, the corresponding effort, and the other person’s understanding of that meaning.
There is a single mode of application (*payoga*), which is exclusively by means of one's own hand; and that [effort] is either by way of the body or by way of something connected to the body.
Or it should be understood as the act of deceiving another by means of speech.
If the other person understands that matter because of that act, this person is bound by the kamma of false speech at the very moment of the volition that originates the act.
For just as one deceives another through bodily actions or speech connected to the body, so too does one instruct this person, saying, "Speak thus."
Whether one causes [something] to be brought, or places a written notice before [someone], or writes on a wall or similar surface and leaves it there saying,

"This matter is to be understood in this way"— therefore, in this case, the applications (payoga) of verbal command (āṇattika), relinquishment (nissaggiya), and fixedness (thāvara) are all appropriate. However, since they have not been mentioned in the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā), they should be adopted after careful investigation.

Regarding the terms beginning with “pisuṇavācā” (slanderous speech): that speech by which one creates a state of affection for oneself and a state of emptiness [or lack of regard] for another in the heart of the person to whom that speech is addressed is “pisuṇavācā.
Furthermore, that speech by which one makes both oneself and another harsh, or which is itself harsh—neither pleasant to the ear nor touching the heart—is “pharusavācā” (harsh speech).
That by which one prattles nonsense, which is meaningless, is "frivolous speech" (*samphappalāpa*).
The volition that is the root of these [other unwholesome actions] also receives the very name of "malicious speech" (*pisuṇavācā*) and so forth; and it is precisely this that is intended here.
In that regard, it is the volition of one with a defiled mind that originates the bodily and vocal exertion for the purpose of dividing others or out of a desire for one's own favor.
Volition is what is called malicious speech (*pisuṇavācā*). It is less blameworthy when directed toward one who has few virtues, and more blameworthy when directed toward one who has great virtues.
Its four constituent factors are: either the intention to cause division, thinking “the other person should be split,” “these two shall become divided,” or “they shall be separated”;
or the desire for intimacy, thinking “thus I shall become dear and trustworthy”; or [the corresponding]...
Viriya is the knowing of that purpose. However, when others have not yet been divided, there is no breach of the path of action; it occurs only when they are divided.
Harsh speech (*pharusavācā*) is an exclusively cruel volition that originates from bodily and verbal exertion intended to pierce the vital parts (*mamma*) of another.
To illustrate this, there is the following account: it is said that a certain boy, disregarding his mother’s words, went into the forest...
He went away. His mother, unable to turn him back, cried out, "May that fierce buffalo pursue you!
Then, right there in the forest, a buffalo rose up before him. The boy made an act of truth, saying, "May that which my mother spoke with her mouth not come to pass;
may that which she thought in her heart come to pass. The buffalo was bound right where it stood.
