He stood as if [he were] a living being. Thus, even an action that would cut through a vital organ does not constitute harsh speech if there is gentleness of mind.
For parents sometimes say to their children, “May robbers cut you into pieces,” yet they do not wish for even a single lotus leaf to fall upon them.
And teachers and preceptors sometimes speak thus to those under their care:
—‘Why do these shameless and fearless ones wander about? Drive them out! And yet they desire their success in study and realization.
Just as harsh speech does not occur because of gentleness of mind, so too gentle speech does not occur because of gentleness of words.
For the words “Lay this man down comfortably” spoken by one wishing to have him killed are not considered gentle speech.

This harshness of mind, moreover, is itself harsh speech. Depending on the person toward whom it is directed, it is slightly blameworthy if that person has few virtues, and greatly blameworthy if they have great virtues.
It has three constituent factors: another person who is to be reviled, a mind of anger, and the act of reviling.
Unprofitable volition that communicates what is harmful and gives rise to bodily and verbal exertion is "frivolous talk" (*samphappalāpa*). Due to its weak habituation...
It is slightly blameworthy. It becomes greatly blameworthy through the magnitude of its habitual practice. Its two constituent factors are:

a preoccupation with useless talk such as the Mahābhārata war or the abduction of Sītā, and the actual delivery of such talk. However, if others do not take up that talk, there is no breach of the course of kamma;
it constitutes frivolous chatter only when another person takes up that talk.
It is called *abhijjhā* because one covets (*abhijjhāyati*). The meaning is that it occurs by being directed toward another's property and leaning toward it.
Its characteristic is the coveting of another's property, thinking, "O, may this belonging to you be mine.
Like the taking of what is not given, it is both slightly blameworthy and greatly blameworthy. It has two constituent factors: another's property and the intention of appropriating it for oneself.
For even when greed arises with respect to another's property, there is as yet no breach of the path of action until one appropriates it for oneself, thinking, "O, may this be mine!

Malice (*vyāpāda*) is so called because it intends to destroy the welfare and happiness of others; its characteristic is mental corruption directed toward the ruin of others. Harsh speech (*pharusavācā*).
It is of two kinds: slight offense and grave offense. It has two constituent factors: another being and the thought of their destruction.
For even when anger arises toward another being, there is as yet no breach of the path of action so long as one does not think of their destruction, such as:
"Oh, would that this person were cut off, would that they were destroyed!"
It is called "wrong view" (*micchā-diṭṭhi*) because one sees wrongly due to the absence of grasping things as they truly are.

Its characteristic is a distorted perception, according to the method beginning with "there is no giving," and so forth. Like frivolous chatter, it is both slightly blameworthy and greatly blameworthy.

Furthermore, it is slightly blameworthy when indeterminate, and greatly blameworthy when determinate. It has two constituent factors: the object itself, and the distortion of the mode in which that object is grasped.

And just as one grasps it, so does it appear to one through its actual nature. In this regard, the breach of the courses of kamma occurs only through the views of nihilism, causelessness, and non-action, and not through other views.

Furthermore, the exposition of these ten unwholesome courses of kamma should be understood by way of five modes: according to their intrinsic nature (*dhamma*), their classification (*koṭṭhāsa*), their object (*ārammaṇa*), their feeling (*vedanā*), and their root (*mūla*).

In this context, "by way of dhamma" means that among these, according to their sequence, there are seven dhammas consisting of volition (*cetanā*), while the three beginning with covetousness (*abhijjhā*) are associated with volition.
"By way of factors" means that the first seven and wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*)—these eight—are exclusively courses of action (*kamma-patha*);
they are not roots (*mūla*). Covetousness and ill will (*vyāpāda*) are both courses of action and roots. For when covetousness reaches the state of being a root, it is called "greed" (*lobha*).
Greed is an unwholesome root; ill will is the hatred-unwholesome root.
Regarding "by way of object": killing has the life-faculty as its object and thus has formations as its object.
Taking what is not given has either beings or formations as its object. Sexual misconduct has formations as its object by way of the tangible.
It exists; some say it has sentient beings as its object. False speech has either sentient beings or formations as its object.

So too with malicious speech. Harsh speech has only sentient beings as its object. Frivolous chatter has either sentient beings or formations as its object, by way of what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized.
So too with covetousness. Ill will has only sentient beings as its object. Wrong view has only formations as its object, by way of the phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence.

‘From the standpoint of feeling’: killing living beings is accompanied by painful feeling. For even though kings, upon seeing a thief, may say with a smile, “Go, kill him,” their volition of instigation is nevertheless associated only with pain.
Taking what is not given is associated with all three feelings; for when one seizes another’s property while joyful and delighted at the sight of it, there is pleasant feeling.

For one who takes [an object] while terrified and trembling, there is a painful feeling. Likewise, for one reflecting upon the results of kamma as result (vipāka) and outflow (nissanda), there is a painful feeling.

However, for one who remains in a state of equanimity at the time of taking, there is a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Thus, sexual misconduct is associated with two feelings by way of pleasure and equanimity;
however, in the mind that brings about the final decision, it is not associated with the feeling of equanimity.

False speech (*musāvāda*) has three kinds of feeling (*vedanā*), according to the method already explained for taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*); likewise for malicious speech (*pisuṇavācā*). Harsh speech (*pharusavācā*) is painful feeling.

Frivolous talk (*samphappalāpa*) has three kinds of feeling. For when others are giving applause, throwing up their robes, and so forth, at the time of telling stories such as the *Sītāharaṇa* or the *Bhārata-yuddha*, one who is joyful and delighted experiences pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*). [This applies] to one who has first received his wages...

When one person has come later and says, "Tell it from the beginning," the other feels a painful feeling at the time of speaking while thinking, "Shall I tell a disconnected, miscellaneous story or not? For one who speaks with equanimity, there is a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Covetousness possesses two feelings by way of pleasure and equanimity; likewise...
Wrong view. Ill will is associated with painful feeling.
Regarding "by way of root": killing living beings has two roots, namely hatred and delusion. Taking what is not given has either two roots—hatred and delusion—or two roots—greed and delusion.
Sexual misconduct has two roots: greed and delusion. False speech has either two roots: hatred and delusion, or greed and delusion.
Likewise, malicious speech and frivolous chatter [arise] from greed and delusion. Harsh speech arises through hatred and delusion.
Covetousness has a single root, which is delusion; likewise for ill will. Wrong view has two roots: greed and delusion.
The discussion on the unwholesome courses of action is finished.
The Discussion of the Wholesome Courses of Action:
The ten wholesome courses of action consist of the abstinences from killing living beings and so forth, along with non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view.
Among these, killing living beings and the others have already had their meanings explained. By means of this [abstinence], one refrains from killing living beings and the rest; oneself—
Or it is *virati* because one desists (*viramati*), or because this is merely the act of desisting.

That *virati* associated with wholesome consciousness, which is described as "the abstention (*ārati*) and desisting (*viratī*) from killing at that time" for one who is desisting from killing, is threefold by way of its classification:
*sampattavirati* (abstention by chance), *samādānavirati* (abstention by undertaking), and *samucchedavirati* (abstention by eradication).

In this context, "abstention from what is encountered" (sampattavirati) should be understood as the refraining that arises in those who have not formally undertaken the training rules, yet—having reflected upon their own birth, age, learning, and so forth, and thinking, “It is unbecoming for us to commit such an evil”—do not transgress the object that has presented itself;
such as in the case of the lay follower Cakkana in the Island of Sri Lanka. It is said that even in his youth...
A sickness arose in his mother’s body, and the physician declared, “It is necessary to obtain fresh hare-flesh.
Thereupon, Cakkana’s brother sent Cakkana, saying, “Go, dear one, and roam through the fields. He went there.
At that moment, a hare had come to eat the young grain; seeing him, [Cakkana] ran after it with speed.
Bound by the vine, he made the sound "kirī, kirī. Hearing that sound, Cakkana went to him, seized him, and thought:
"I shall prepare medicine for my mother. Then he thought again:
"It is not fitting for me to deprive another of life for the sake of my mother's life. Thereupon he said to him: "Go, [live] with the deer in the forest."
"Let him subsist on grass and water," he released. When his brother asked, "Father, was a hare caught? he explained what had happened. Then his brother rebuked him.

He went to his mother and stood there, speaking the truth: "Since I was born, I do not recall ever intentionally depriving a living being of life. At that very moment, his mother became free from her illness.

However, the abstinence that arises for those who have undertaken the training rules (*sikkhāpada*)—who, having renounced even their own lives both at the time of undertaking the training rules and thereafter, do not transgress the basis of the precepts—should be understood as "abstinence by undertaking" (*samādānavirati*). This is like the case of the lay follower (*upāsaka*) who lived on Mount Uttaravaḍḍhamāna.
It is said that he received the training rules from the Elder Piṅgalabuddharakkhita, who resided at the Ambariya Monastery.
Having taken it, he ploughed the field. Then his ox went astray. While searching for it, he climbed Uttaravaḍḍhamāna Mountain.
There a great serpent seized him. He thought, “I will cut off its head with this sharp axe.
Then he thought again, “It is not fitting that I should [break] the training rules in the presence of my venerable teacher, who is worthy of respect.”

Having thought thus up to three times, “I shall take it and break it,” and resolving, “I would rather give up my life than the training rule,” he cast away the sharp wooden axe he had placed on his shoulder in the forest. At that very moment, a great wild beast released it and departed.

However, the abstinence associated with the Noble Path should be understood as “abstinence by eradication” (*samucchedavirati*), for from the moment it arises, even the thought “I shall kill a living being” does not occur to Noble Persons.

Now, just as it was for the unwholesome courses of action, so too for these wholesome courses of action, the exposition should be understood by way of five aspects: by way of nature (*dhammata*), by way of constituent parts (*koṭṭhāsato*), by way of object (*ārammaṇato*), by way of feeling (*vedanāto*), and by way of root (*mūlato*).

In this context, "by way of nature": among these, in their respective order, the first seven may be either volitions (*cetanā*) or abstinences (*virati*); at the end, the three are associated only with volition. "By way of constituent parts":
in their respective order, the first seven are courses of action (*kammappatha*) alone, not roots; at the end, the three are both courses of action and roots.
And as for the roots: having reached non-covetousness as its root, it becomes "non-greed, the wholesome root"; non-ill-will becomes "non-hatred, the wholesome root";
and right view becomes "non-delusion, the wholesome root.
Regarding "by way of object": the objects of these [wholesome states] are precisely the same objects as those of killing and so forth, because they are exactly what must be transgressed.

For this is indeed called abstinence (*veramaṇī*). Just as the Noble Path, having Nibbāna as its object, abandons the defilements (*kilesa*), so too these courses of action (*kammapatha*), having the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) and so forth as their objects, should be understood to abandon the unwholesome conduct of killing living beings and the rest.

As for "from the perspective of feeling" (*vedanāto*): all [the associated mental states] are either pleasant feelings or neutral feelings; for once the wholesome has been reached, there is no such thing as a painful feeling.

"From the root": when one abstains from the seven courses of action in sequence with a consciousness associated with knowledge, they have three roots by way of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion;

for one abstaining with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge, they have two roots. Non-covetousness has two roots when abstaining with a consciousness associated with knowledge, and one root when abstaining with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge. But non-greed itself [is its own root] by its very nature.
There is no root [of unwholesomeness]. This same method applies to non-ill will as well. Right view has only two roots, by way of non-greed and non-hatred.
These are called the ten courses of wholesome action.
The Discussion on the Concordance of the Courses of Action.
Now, at this point, what is called the "concordance of the courses of action" (kammapathasaṃsandana) should be understood.

For non-restraint that arises by way of the five doors of contact is exclusively unwholesome mental action (manokamma). That which arises by way of the door of mental contact consists of all three types of action;
for when it reaches the stage of actual execution (copana) at the bodily door, it becomes unwholesome bodily action, and at the vocal door...
Unwholesome verbal action; and unwholesome mental action that has not yet reached the point of contact in either case.
Even when it arises by way of the five doors of non-restraint, it is still merely unwholesome mental action.

When it arises by way of the door of bodily non-restraint involving contact, it is merely unwholesome bodily action; when it arises by way of the door of verbal non-restraint, it is merely unwholesome verbal action.
That which arises by way of the door of non-restraint of mind is precisely unwholesome mental action.
The threefold misconduct of body is precisely unwholesome bodily action; the fourfold misconduct of speech is precisely unwholesome vocal action;
and the threefold misconduct of mind is precisely unwholesome mental action.
Restraint arising by way of the five doors of contact is also wholesome mental action alone.
However, that which arises by way of the door of mental contact—like non-restraint—is all three types of action.

That which arises by way of the five doors of restraint is also wholesome mental action alone; that which arises by way of the door of bodily restraint consisting of volition is wholesome [bodily action].
That which arises by way of the door of restraint of body is simply wholesome bodily action; that which arises by way of the door of restraint of speech is simply wholesome verbal action;
and that which arises by way of the door of restraint of mind is simply wholesome mental action. The threefold good conduct of body is simply wholesome bodily action;
the fourfold good conduct of speech is simply wholesome verbal action; and the threefold good conduct of mind—
Wholesome mental action alone occurs.
Unwholesome bodily action does not arise by way of the five doors of contact; it arises solely by way of the door of mind-contact.
Likewise for unwholesome verbal action. However, unwholesome mental action arises by way of all six doors of contact.
That unwholesome bodily or verbal action which has reached the doors of body and speech is *copana*; that unwholesome mental action which has not reached them is *manokamma* alone.
And just as it is by way of the five doors of contact (*phassadvāra*), so too, unwholesome bodily action does not arise by way of the five doors of non-restraint (*asaṃvaradvāra*);
rather, it arises by way of the door of bodily non-restraint and the door of verbal non-restraint.

It does not arise by way of the door of non-restraint of mind. Unwholesome verbal action also does not arise by way of the five doors of non-restraint, but it arises by way of the doors of non-restraint of the body and speech; it does not arise by way of the door of non-restraint of mind.
Unwholesome mental action arises indeed by way of all eight doors of non-restraint. This same method applies to wholesome bodily action and the rest as well.

But this is the distinction: unlike unwholesome bodily and verbal actions, which do not arise by way of the door of mental restraint (*manoasaṃvara*), these [wholesome ones] do not follow that same pattern.

Rather, for one who undertakes the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) without moving the limbs of the body or the members of speech, these [wholesome states] certainly arise even at the door of mental restraint.
In that regard, wholesome consciousness of the sense-sphere arises by way of the three doors of action.

It does not arise by way of the five doors of consciousness; rather, it arises by way of the six doors of contact according to this method: "Whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
It does not arise by way of the eight doors of non-restraint, but it arises by way of the eight doors of restraint.
It does not arise by way of the ten unwholesome courses of action; it arises by way of the ten wholesome courses of action.

Therefore, whether this consciousness has arisen by way of the three doors of action, or by way of the six doors of contact, or by way of the eight doors of restraint, or by way of the ten wholesome courses of action—it is a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness.

When it is said, “There arises [consciousness]…pe… having visible form as its object, or…pe… having mental phenomena (dhamma) as its object,” everything that was previously stated is thereby included.
The Discussion of the Doors is finished.

Regarding the phrase “whatever [object] one takes as a basis,” the construction here is as follows: among the objects of visible form and so forth mentioned below, [it refers to] the object of visible form.
"Having taken as an object" means having made it the focal point. It arises having taken as its object a sound-object... pe... or a mental-object (dhamma).
To this extent, for this consciousness, any one of these objects is similar to what has been permitted.
And this [consciousness] arises at one time for a single person, having taken a visible-form-object as its object.
Furthermore, at another time, it certainly arises again with respect to one or another object among sounds and so forth, or for another person.

And as it thus arises, there is no fixed sequence such that within a single existence its occurrence first takes place by way of a visible-form object and subsequently by way of a sound object. Nor is there a fixed order even among the visible forms and other objects.
There is no fixed rule that the object must first be blue and subsequently yellow.

Thus, in order to show both this universality of objects and the absence of a sequence, as well as the lack of restriction regarding blue, yellow, and so forth even when there is no sequence, he said: "Whatever [object] one takes as a basis.
This is what is meant: among these [objects] such as visible forms and the rest, it is not just any single one; rather, whatever indeed one takes as a basis—

It arises. And even as it thus arises, it does not arise by thinking, "First the visible-object object, afterwards the sound object," nor does it arise by depending on whatever object it may be—whether in reverse order, in direct order, or by skipping one or two intervals—among the objects such as the visible-object and so forth. Whatever object [it arises] from...

The meaning is: “it arises having made [something] its object. Regarding visible-form objects as well, it does not arise according to the restriction that “first the blue object, afterwards the yellow object”; rather, the meaning is:
“having taken whatever [object], that is, having taken any particular visible-form object among the blue, yellow, and so forth, it arises. The same applies to sound-objects and the rest.
This is one method of interpretation. But there is this other:

"That which has form as its object (ārammaṇa) is 'with form as object' (rūpārammaṇa)... [and so on] ... that which has mental phenomena (dhamma) as its object is 'with mental phenomena as object' (dhammārammaṇa).
Thus, a consciousness arises having either form as its object... [and so on] ...or having mental phenomena as its object.
Having said this, he further stated, “Whatever [object] one takes as a basis. Its meaning is:

“Whatever among these [objects] such as form (rūpa) and so forth has arisen by the very method explained below. However, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: “There is nothing new in the inclusion;
what was already included below is indeed included here,” and then: “Whether taking form as a basis... pe ...or taking mental phenomena (dhamma) as a basis.”
Regarding the statement "referring to this or that," only as much as "this was said" has come down.
This concludes the section on the Enumeration of Phenomena (Dhammuddesa-vāra), specifically the commentary on the "Contact-as-the-Fifth-Rat" (Phassapañcamaka-rāsi).
"At that time" is a definitive restatement of a "time" that was previously indicated without such restriction. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as follows:
"At whatever time a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen, at that very same time there is contact...
[and so on] ...there is non-distraction. In this context, just as it is with consciousness, so it is with contact and the other factors.

There is contact. What is it? The application should be made according to the terms available in such a manner as: "it belongs to the sense-sphere," "it is wholesome," "it has arisen," "it is accompanied by joy," and so forth.

For in the case of feeling, the term "accompanied by joy" is not found, and in the case of the faculty of wisdom, the term "associated with knowledge" is not found; therefore, it is said, "according to the terms available."
This is the opinion of the teachers outside the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*); however, this should not be regarded as the essential truth.
Why, then, is contact (*phassa*) mentioned first here? Because it is the mind’s first impact.
For contact arises by first making an impact upon the object, thereby touching the object; therefore, it is mentioned first.
It has been said: "Having touched by means of contact, one feels by means of feeling, perceives by means of perception, and volitions by means of volition.
Therefore it was said: "Touched, monks, one feels; touched, one perceives; touched, one volitions.
Furthermore, this so-called contact is, just as a pillar upon reaching a palace becomes a powerful support for all other building materials, [the primary condition for the remaining mental factors].

Just as the rafters, wall-plates, pillars, ridge-poles, gable-ends, side-beams, and the mouth-projections are bound to the pillars and rest upon the pillars, even so [ignorance] is a powerful condition for the co-nascent associated states. For this [ignorance] is like the pillar, while the remaining [mental factors] are like the building materials.
Therefore, it was mentioned first. But this is not the reason.
For it is not possible to say of the phenomena that have arisen within a single moment of consciousness, "this one arose first" or "this one arose later.

Even though contact possesses a powerful conditionality, no other cause for it is seen. However, in the order of the teaching, contact was mentioned first: "there is feeling, there is contact; there is perception, there is contact; there is volition..."
It might indeed have been appropriate to list them as: "there is contact, there is mind, there is contact, there is feeling, there is perception, there is volition, there is applied thought";
however, it should be understood that within this particular teaching sequence, contact alone is stated first.

And just as it is here, so too in the case of the remaining phenomena, one need not seek out a specific order of priority; [they are to be understood] by way of their etymological meaning, characteristics, functions, and so forth.

But only phenomena (dhammas) are to be sought after. They are as follows: it touches, thus it is contact (phassa). This contact has the characteristic of touching; its function is impingement; it is manifested as the meeting [of sense organ, object, and consciousness]; its proximate cause is the object that has come into the range [of the senses].
For although it is an immaterial phenomenon, it occurs by way of the very mode of touching the object; thus it has the characteristic of touching.

And because it strikes consciousness and its object together—just as the eye [strikes] form and the ear [strikes] sound—even though it does not merge with them part by part, it has the function of striking together (*saṅghaṭṭana-rasa*).

Alternatively, it should be understood as having the function of striking together in the sense of "attainment" (*sampatti*), because it arises from the striking together of the physical basis (*vatthu*) and the object (*ārammaṇa*). For this has been said in the Commentary: "Contact of the four planes..."
"For there is no such thing as a characteristic of contact that does not involve impact. However, the function of impact belongs only to that which operates through the five doors.

For what operates through the five doors has both the name 'characteristic of contact' and the name 'function of impact'; but for what operates through the mind-door, it has only the name 'characteristic of contact,' not the function of impact."
Having said this, he cited this sutta: “Great King, just as two rams might fight, so should the eye be regarded as one ram and the visible form as the second ram;
just as their collision, so should contact be regarded. Thus, contact has the characteristic of touching and the function of impact.
And: “Just as, great king, two sticks might rub together… [as it is said]… two hands might rub together:
just as one hand is to be regarded, so should the eye be regarded; just as the second hand is to be regarded, so should visible form be regarded;
just as their meeting is to be regarded, so should contact be regarded. Thus, contact has the characteristic of touching and the function of impact,” and so on in detail.

Or, just as in passages such as "having seen a form with the eye," the eye-consciousness and so forth are expressed by the names "eye" and so on, so too here they should be understood as being expressed by the names "eye" and so on.
Therefore, in phrases such as "thus the eye should be seen," the meaning should be understood according to this method:
"thus eye-consciousness should be seen. This being so, [it follows that] from the impact of the mind and the object...
In this sutta as well, contact is established as having the function (*rasa*) of "striking together" precisely in the sense of what is to be done (*kicca*).
However, because it is described by way of its own cause—which is the so-called "conjunction of the triad"—it has "conjunction" as its manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*).
For it is described there and elsewhere by way of its cause thus: "The meeting of the three is contact."
And regarding this passage of the Sutta, the meaning is that contact (*phassa*) is the coming together of the three; it is not merely the coming together itself that is contact.
However, because it is declared in this way, it manifests in that very manner, and thus it is called "manifestation as a conjunction" (*sannipāta-paccupaṭṭhāna*).
But in terms of its fruit, by way of manifestation, it is called "manifestation as feeling" (*vedanā-paccupaṭṭhāna*), for it brings feeling into manifestation.

The meaning is "it produces. And while producing [heat], just as heat—though dependent on a substance called lac, which is itself dependent on something external—produces softness in its own support (the lac), but not in the external state of heat consisting of glowing embers which serves as its condition;
even so, although it has other conditions consisting of the physical basis (*vatthu*) and the object (*ārammaṇa*), because it is dependent on the mind, its own...
It should be understood that this producer of feeling arises only in the mind which serves as its support, and not in the physical basis (*vatthu*) or the object (*ārammaṇa*),

even though these serve as its conditions. However, because it arises immediately following an object that has been prepared by the appropriate attention (*tajjā-samannāhāra*) and the sense faculty (*indriya*),
it is said to have "the object that has come into range" as its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*).

It feels, thus it is feeling (*vedanā*). Its characteristic is that which is felt; its function is experiencing, or its function is the enjoyment of a desirable aspect; it is manifested as the mental relish of feeling; its proximate cause is tranquility.
Having stated, "Indeed, there is no feeling belonging to the four planes that does not have the characteristic of being felt;
however, the quality of having experiencing as its function is found only in pleasant feeling," he then rejects that position, saying: "Whether it be pleasant feeling or painful feeling..."
Or, having said, "Whether it be pleasant feeling, painful feeling, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, all have the function of experiencing," this meaning is illustrated:
once they have reached the state of experiencing the flavor of the object, the remaining associated states experience only a mere portion of it. For contact has only the function of touching;
perception has only the function of perceiving; volition has only the function of intending; and consciousness has only the function of cognizing.
But exclusively by virtue of its sovereignty, its lordship, and its status as master, feeling alone experiences the flavor of the object.
For feeling is like a king, while the remaining phenomena are like a cook.
Just as a cook, having prepared a meal of various flavors, places it in a casket, seals it, presents it before the king, and then breaks the seal and [opens] the casket...
Having opened [the vessel], he takes the very best portion of all the curries and condiments, places it in a bowl, and consumes it for the purpose of testing whether it is tainted or untainted;
thereafter, he serves the king various kinds of exquisite food.

There, the king—being a master, a lord, and a sovereign by virtue of his power and authority—eats whatever he desires. For in that case, the cook’s act is merely a test of the food, whereas for the remaining phenomena...
It is the experiencing of a single portion of the flavor of the object (*ārammaṇa-rasa*).
For just as a cook examines only a small portion of the meal, so too do the remaining mental factors experience only a single portion of the flavor of the object.
But just as a king, by virtue of his sovereignty and authority, being the master, eats whatever he desires, so too does feeling (*vedanā*), by virtue of its sovereignty and authority...
It experiences the flavor of the object by way of its own nature; therefore, it is called "having the function of experiencing.

According to the second interpretation of the meaning, this feeling intended here is said to have "the function of enjoying the desirable aspect" because it enjoys only the desirable aspect of the object, whether in one way or another.
Furthermore, from the perspective of its mental essence, it [experiences] by its own individual nature.

With reference to its presence, it is said to have "mental enjoyment" as its manifestation. However, because "one whose body is tranquil experiences happiness," it should be understood to have "tranquility" as its proximate cause.
Perception (saññā) is so called because it perceives an object distinguished by blue and other colors; it has the characteristic of perceiving and the function of recognition.
Indeed, among the perceptions belonging to the four planes, there is none that does not have the characteristic of perceiving;
all have the characteristic of perceiving. However, that which perceives by means of a sign (*abhijñāṇa*) has the function (*rasa*) of subsequent recognition (*paccābhijñāṇa*).
For example, when a carpenter has made a mark on a piece of wood and later recognizes it by means of that very mark.
When, having observed the distinctive marks of a man such as black moles and so forth, one subsequently recognizes him by those very marks,
thinking, "This is the person named so-and-so"; or when a treasurer who guards the king’s ornaments has tied a name-tag to each ornament and,
upon being told, "Bring such-and-such an ornament," he lights a lamp and [enters] the jewel-chamber...
Having entered [the house] and read the leaf, the occurrence [of perception] should be understood at the time of taking each respective ornament.

Another method: in its all-encompassing aspect, perception has the characteristic of perceiving. Its function is to provide the sign as a condition for subsequent perception, just as carpenters and others do with wood and such materials.
Its manifestation is the act of fixing upon an object according to the sign as it was grasped.
It is like the blind men who saw the elephant. Because it does not penetrate deeply into the object, its manifestation is one of non-persistence, like a flash of lightning.
Its proximate cause is the appearance of the object as it presents itself, like the perception of "men" that arose in young deer regarding blades of grass shaped like human figures.
Furthermore, when this perception is associated with knowledge, that perception follows after knowledge itself.
In the case of the earth and other elements together with their requisites, the remaining phenomena should be understood as being like the earth and the rest.
It "wills" (*cetayati*), which means it directs the associated phenomena along with itself toward the object. Its characteristic is that which is willed;
the meaning is that its characteristic is the state of volition (*cetanā*). Its function is exertion (*āyūhana*). This refers to volition belonging to the four planes.

Indeed, there is nothing that does not have the characteristic of volition; all things indeed possess the characteristic of volition. However, the function of "exertion" (āyūhana) occurs only in wholesome and unwholesome states.
For when reaching the point of exerting wholesome or unwholesome kamma, the other associated mental factors perform only a partial function.
Volition, however, possesses superior zeal and superior effort; it has double the zeal and double the effort. Therefore, they say:
The Ancients say: "And this volition is established in a stable nature. "Stable" (thāvariya) refers to the owner of a field.
Just as a man who is the owner of a field takes fifty-five strong men with him and enters the field together [with them], thinking, "I shall reap," his effort is excessive, his exertion is excessive;
his effort is doubled, his exertion is doubled, [and he works] continuously.
One should understand this matter as being analogous to the following: [The field-owner] says, "Take [it]," and so forth; he points out the boundary;
he recognizes their liquor, food, perfumes, garlands, and so on; and he levels the path. In this way, it should be understood. For the volition (*cetanā*) is like the man who owns the field.
The fifty-five wholesome states (*kusalā dhammā*) that arise by way of the mental factors (*cittanga*) are like the fifty-five strong men. The man who owns the field...

Just as at the time of exerting double the enthusiasm and double the effort, when one has reached the place for the accumulation of wholesome and unwholesome kamma, volition possesses double the enthusiasm and double the effort. In this way, its function of accumulating should be understood.
Furthermore, it is manifested as coordinating; for it appears while coordinating, accomplishing both its own task and the tasks of others.
It is like the chief pupil, the master carpenter, and others.
For just as the chief pupil, seeing his preceptor approaching from afar, continues his own recitation and sets the other boys to their respective tasks of study;
for when he has begun to recite, they too recite, following his lead. And just as the master carpenter, while cutting himself...
The others also engage in their respective carpentry work;
for when the carpenter has begun to work, they too carve, following his lead.
And just as a military commander, while fighting himself, causes the other soldiers to engage in the act of combat, for when he has begun to fight, they too fight without retreating.

Because it follows that [preceding state]. In this way, while this [consciousness] itself proceeds toward its object by means of its own function, it also causes the other associated states to proceed by means of their respective functions. For when its own function has begun, those associated with it also begin theirs.
Therefore it is said: “They accomplish both their own functions and the functions of others, like an elder, a pupil, and a master carpenter.”

Furthermore, it should be understood that this [consciousness] becomes manifest when it occurs with the quality of instigating its associated mental states during urgent tasks, recollection, and so forth.
As for the etymological meaning of *citta*, it has already been stated according to the method: "It thinks of the object, thus it is consciousness.

However, from the perspective of its characteristics and so on: consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing; its function is to be the forerunner; its manifestation is cohesion; and its proximate cause is name-and-form.
Indeed, among the consciousnesses of the four planes, there is none that does not have the characteristic of cognizing;
all have the characteristic of cognizing alone. However, having reached the door, at the place where the object is manifested, consciousness is the precursor and the leader.
For the visible-object condition seen by the eye is cognized by consciousness alone... and so on... the mental-object condition cognized by the mind is [cognized] by consciousness alone.

It cognizes. For this should be understood as being just like a city guard who, sitting at a crossroads in the middle of the city, observes and identifies each person as they arrive, thinking, "This one is a resident; this one is a newcomer.
And this was said by the Great Elder: "Just as, O King, a so-called city guard [in the middle of the city]..."
Just as one sitting at a crossroads might see a man coming from the eastern direction... from the western direction... from the southern direction... or from the northern direction;

even so, great king, what one sees with the eye as a form, that one cognizes by consciousness; what one hears with the ear as a sound... [what one smells] with the nose... [what one tastes] with the tongue... [what one touches] with the body... [what one cognizes] with the mind...
"One smells an odor with the nose, tastes a flavor with the tongue, touches a tangible object with the body, and cognizes a mental phenomenon with the mind;
one cognizes that by means of consciousness. Thus, having reached the door, it is consciousness alone that is the precursor and forerunner in the place where the object is manifested.
Therefore, it is called "the precursor's function."
Since each subsequent [moment] arises by making each preceding one its immediate antecedent, it appears as a continuous connection;

thus, it has "continuity" as its manifestation (*sandahanapaccupaṭṭhāna*). Its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) is, in the five-aggregate existence, invariably name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), while in the four-aggregate existence, it is name alone. Therefore, it is said to have "name-and-form" as its proximate cause.
But is this consciousness the very same as the consciousness previously specified, or is it something else?
It is the very same. Then why was what was previously specified stated again? This has not been investigated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). However, the reasoning here is as follows:
just as the sun and so forth, which are designated in dependence upon visible form and other phenomena, do not exist as entities distinct from those visible forms and so forth; [so too is this case].
For at the very same time that the sun rises, its material form (rūpa), which is reckoned as heat (tejo), also exists.
Even though it is spoken of in this way, there is no such thing as a "sun" other than the material form and so forth. It is not so with the mind (citta);

[the mind] is designated by depending upon states such as contact (phassa) and the rest, yet in terms of its actual essence (attha), it is indeed something other than them. Therefore, when it is said, "At whatever time the mind has arisen..."

It should be understood that this was stated again for the purpose of illustrating the meaning: "At that time, it is in one sense indeed something other than contact and the rest in terms of its actual referent. And just as:
"At whatever time one develops the path for rebirth in the form realm... [omission] ...the earth-kasina, at that time..."

But in such passages as "there is contact, there is feeling," when [the factors] have been defined by one who is developing [the meditation], that which develops does not actually arise in a literal sense;

for that very reason, it is not stated therein that "he who develops is [himself] what arises," in the same way that it is said, "there is contact, there is feeling. "At whatever time a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness..."
However, in such passages as "arisen," when the mind has been defined by way of time, the mind defined by that time does not fail to arise in its actual sense.

But it should be understood that this was stated again for the purpose of illustrating the meaning "there is also mind," just as at that time it is said "there is contact" and "there is feeling. This, moreover, is [the point] here:
The determination: In the section on the enumeration (*uddesavāra*), it is for the purpose of inclusion; and in the section on the exposition (*niddesavāra*), it is for the purpose of analysis.
For by the preceding word "consciousness" (*citta*), only the momentary occasion was defined.

However, in order to show those phenomena that exist within that occasion defined by consciousness, the passage beginning with "there is contact" (*phasso hoti*) is commenced. And consciousness, too, in that [occasion]...
It is indeed present at that time. Therefore, this is stated again for the purpose of including it as well.
And in this context, if this were not mentioned, it would not be possible to analyze "What is the consciousness at that time? in the section on exposition (niddesa).
Thus, its analysis would be omitted. Therefore, this is also [stated] for the purpose of analyzing it in the section on exposition.
It should be understood that it is so stated. Or alternatively,
since in the passage "it has arisen" (*uppannaṃ hoti*), the term "consciousness has arisen" (*cittaṃ uppannaṃ*) is merely a conventional mode of expression (*desanāsīsa*),

and not that "a single consciousness arises alone"— as has been analyzed in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*)— therefore, in this case as well, [the phrase] "consciousness has arisen" (*cittaṃ uppannaṃ*)...
Without taking the mind alone, the mind is taken together with more than fifty wholesome states.

Thus, having briefly included all mental states and mental factors therein, the passage beginning with "there is contact" is commenced here to show them in their specific nature and detailed classification.
Therefore, it should be understood that the mind has already been mentioned just like contact and the other factors.
The Section on the Enumeration of Dhammas: Explanation of the Factors of Jhāna.

It is called *vitakka* because it "thinks upon" (*vitakketi*); or rather, *vitakka* is the act of thinking (*vitakkana*). What is meant is that it "investigates" (*ūhana*). This [factor], with respect to its object—
It has the characteristic of directing the mind onto its object. For it causes the mind to ascend toward the object.

Just as someone, by relying on a relative or a friend who is a favorite of the king, gains access to the royal palace, so too, by relying on applied thought (*vitakka*), the mind ascends toward the object.
Therefore, it is said that its characteristic is the directing of the mind onto the object. —Thera Nāgasena.
He further said: "Initial application (vitakka) has the characteristic of striking. 'Just as, great king, when a drum is struck, it subsequently reverberates and resounds;

even so, great king, initial application should be seen as the striking itself, while sustained application (vicāra) should be seen as the subsequent reverberation and resonance. Thus, its function is that of striking and repeatedly beating.
For it is said that by means of this, the practitioner of yoga makes the object struck by thought and overwhelmed by thought.
It has the manifestation of leading the mind toward the object.
It is called *vicāra* because by means of it the mind moves about upon the object; or rather, *vicāra* is the act of moving about (*vicaraṇa*). It is described as "moving along" (*anusañcaraṇa*).

It exists. This [vitakka] has the characteristic of repeatedly rubbing against the object. In this context, its function is to apply itself simultaneously [with the other mental factors]. Its manifestation is the continuous succession of consciousness.

And although there is no dissociation between them in certain instances, vitakka is the first impact of the mind, in the sense of being gross, in the sense of being a precursor, and in the sense of directing [the mind] toward the object, like the striking of a bell. Vicāra, however, is characterized by subtle refinement and the nature of repeated rubbing.
And sustained application (*vicāra*) is a continuous succession, like the resonance of a bell. Furthermore, initial application (*vitakka*) is expansive;

at the time of its first arising, it is a state of agitation in the mind, like the flapping of wings by a bird wishing to fly into the sky, or like the descent of a bee toward a lotus whose mind is attached to its fragrance.
Sustained application (*vicāra*), however, has a peaceful mode of occurrence and lacks such excessive agitation.
It is like the spreading of the wings of a bird that has flown up into the sky, and like the hovering above a lotus of a bee that has fallen toward the lotus;
however, in the Commentary it says: "As a great bird moving through the sky takes up the wind with both its wings..."
*Vitakka* (initial application) is that which proceeds by way of directing the mind onto the object, like the act of making [a bird] settle down before its flight.
For it settles the mind once it has become one-pointed, just as the movement of one who flaps his wings for the purpose of taking flight.
*Vicāra* (sustained application) proceeds by way of continuous rubbing. For it is said that it "continuously rubs" the object; it does so by means of following after that [object].
This is highly appropriate in the context of the actual practice. Furthermore, that distinction between them becomes evident in the first and second jhānas.
Moreover, it is like a person who, holding a tarnished bronze vessel firmly with one hand, rubs it all over with a cloth soaked in powder and oil with the other hand:
the hand that holds it firmly is like *vitakka* (initial application), and the hand that rubs it is like *vicāra* (sustained application). Likewise...
Just as the hand that presses down while a potter turns the wheel with a blow from his staff to fashion a vessel is like initial application (vitakka),
and the hand that moves it here and there is like sustained investigation (vicāra); likewise, for one drawing a circle,
the thorn fixed in the center is like the initial application of directing the mind, and the thorn moving around the outside...
Investigation is that which examines closely, as it were.
It gladdens, thus it is *pīti* (rapture). Its characteristic is the act of gladdening. Its function is to refresh the body and mind, or its function is pervading.
It is manifested as elation. Furthermore, this rapture is fivefold: minor rapture, momentary rapture, showering rapture, uplifting rapture, and pervading rapture.
Therein, minor rapture (*khuddikā-pīti*) is able to cause only a bristling of the body hairs. Momentary rapture (*khaṇikā-pīti*) occurs like the flashing of lightning from moment to moment.
Overwhelming rapture (*okkantikā-pīti*) descends upon the body again and again and breaks up, like a wave on the shore of the ocean.
Transporting rapture (*ubbegā-pīti*) is powerful; it raises the body upward and reaches the point of making one leap into the air.
For instance, the Elder Mahātissa, a resident of Puṇṇavallika, went to the courtyard of the Cetiya on the evening of the full moon day.

Seeing the light of the moon, he stood facing the Mahācetiya and, thinking, "At this very hour, the four assemblies are surely worshipping the Mahācetiya," he generated an intense joy directed toward the Buddha by means of an object previously seen. Then, upon the plastered floor...
Like a painted ball struck by a stick, it leapt into the air and came to rest right upon the courtyard of the Mahācetiya.

Likewise, in the village of Vattakālaka, which was near the Girikaṇḍaka Monastery, a certain daughter of a noble family also leaped into the air through the intense joy of uplifting rapture directed toward the Buddha as its powerful object.
It is said that her parents [were about to go] to the monastery in the evening for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.
As they were going along, they said, “Mother, you are heavily burdened; you cannot travel at this hour.
We will wait for you and listen to the Dhamma. Although she wished to go, being unable to refuse their words, she remained behind at home;
standing at the door of her house, she looked toward the courtyard of the Ākāsa Cetiya on Mount Girika by the light of the moon.

She saw the offering of lamps at the cetiya. She also heard the four assemblies performing circumambulations after having made offerings of garlands, perfumes, and other things to the cetiya, and she heard the sound of the communal recitation (*gaṇasajjhāya*) of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Then it occurred to her:
"Blessed indeed are those people who, having gone to the monastery, may wander upon such a cetiya courtyard and hear such sweet discourse on the Dhamma."
Thinking, "May we obtain the opportunity to hear it," as she beheld the shrine resembling Mount Meru, a rapturous joy arose within her.
Leaping into the air, she descended from the sky onto the courtyard of the shrine even before her parents;
having paid homage to the shrine, she stood listening to the Dhamma. Then her parents approached her and asked, "Dear child, by which path did you come?"
They asked, "Have you come? She replied, "I have come through the air, not by way of the path. When they asked, "Sister, those whose taints are exhausted travel through the air; how did you come?
she said, "As I stood gazing at the shrine by the light of the moon, a powerful rapture (pīti) directed toward the Buddha arose within me. Then, I was no longer aware of my own standing position..."
"I was not aware of my sitting posture; rather, having leaped into the air by means of the very sign grasped [in meditation], I landed upon the terrace of the shrine.
In this way, the rapture of uplifting (ubbegā-pīti) has as its measure the ability to leap into the air.
But when the rapture of pervasion (pharaṇā-pīti) arises, it blows through the entire body until it is filled like a leather bag or by a great flood of water.
And it becomes completely pervasive, like the interior of a mountain that has split open.
This fivefold joy, taking conception and reaching maturity, fulfills two kinds of tranquility: bodily tranquility and mental tranquility.
Tranquility, taking conception and reaching maturity, fulfills two kinds of happiness: bodily...

And as for the mental factor: pleasure, when it takes conception and reaches maturity, fulfills three kinds of concentration—momentary concentration (*khaṇika-samādhi*), access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*), and absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*).
Among these, with the exception of that which fulfills absorption concentration, the other two are also applicable here.
It is called *sukha* because it pleases (*sukhayati*); the meaning is that it makes happy that person in whom it arises.
Or, it is *sukha* because it thoroughly consumes (*suṭṭhu khādati*) and digs away (*khanati*) afflictions of body and mind. This is the name for the feeling of mental joy (*somanassavedanā*).
Its characteristic and other features are to be understood in the same manner as explained under the section on feeling (*vedanāpada*).
Another method: happiness has the characteristic of being agreeable; its function is to nourish associated states; it is manifested as assistance.

And although there is sometimes no dissociation between these two—rapture and happiness—nevertheless, rapture is satisfaction at obtaining a desirable object, while happiness is the experiencing of the flavor of what has been obtained.
Where there is rapture, there is happiness; where there is happiness, there [is rapture].

It is not necessarily so. Joy (*pīti*) is included within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), while pleasure (*sukha*) is included within the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*).
Joy is like seeing and hearing about water at the edge of a forest when one is exhausted in a desert; pleasure is like entering the forest shade and enjoying the water.
For example, it is as if a man traveling along a great desert road, oppressed by heat, parched and thirsty, were to meet someone on the way...
Seeing a man, he might ask, "Where is there water? He would reply, "Having crossed the forest, there is a grove of natural ponds;
go there and you will find it. Having heard his words, the man would become exceedingly joyful.
Then, as he went along, seeing lotus petals, stalks, and leaves fallen upon the ground, he would become even more certain.
Walking along, he might see men with wet clothes and wet hair; he might hear the cries of wild cocks, peacocks, and other birds;
he might see a dark green forest thicket resembling a net of jewels growing on the edge of a lake;
he might see blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, and other such flowers grown in the lake; and he might see water that is clear and serene.
Becoming more and more delighted, he descended into the lake of birth; having bathed and drunk as he pleased, his fatigue subsided.

He ate lotus roots, stalks, and lotuses, adorned himself with blue water-lilies and other flowers, and placing the roots of *mandālaka* on his shoulder, he climbed out, put on his cloth, and left his bathing garment in the sun.
Lying down in cool shade with a gentle breeze blowing, he would say, "Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss!
This should be understood as being exactly like that.
For that man’s state of extreme joy lasted from the moment he heard about the forest thicket until the moment he saw the water.
Joy (*pīti*) is the state of being exultant with respect to the object during its preliminary stage.

Pleasure (*sukha*) is the state established as the experience of the flavor of the object when it has reached its peak, like the time when one who has bathed and drunk lies down in cool shade while a gentle breeze blows, saying, "Oh, what bliss!
Oh, what bliss! This is because it becomes manifest at each respective moment.
It should be understood that this has been stated. Furthermore, it has already been stated that wherever there is joy (*pīti*), there is also happiness (*sukha*).
"One-pointedness of mind" (*cittassekaggatā*) is the state of the mind being one-pointed; this is a name for concentration (*samādhi*).

Regarding its characteristics and so forth, it is first stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*): "Concentration has the characteristic of predominance and the characteristic of non-distraction. Just as...

Just as the pinnacle of a gabled house is the foremost because it binds together all the remaining building materials, even so, because all wholesome states succeed through the mind of concentration, concentration is the leader of all those states. Therefore it was said:
"Great King, just as whatever rafters there are in a gabled house, they all go toward the peak, incline toward the peak..."

“Just as the peak is declared to be the foremost among the summits of a mountain, even so, Great King, whatever wholesome states there may be, they all incline toward concentration, lean toward concentration, and tend toward concentration; concentration is declared to be their foremost.
And just as a king, having reached his army, goes to whichever place the army is faltering, so too...
Wherever he goes, his army becomes complete, and the enemy army breaks apart and follows the king alone;
in the same way, because it does not allow co-nascent states to be distracted or scattered, concentration is said to have non-distraction as its characteristic.
Furthermore, there is another method: this so-called concentration, which consists of one-pointedness of mind, has non-diffusion or non-distraction as its characteristic.
Or, it has the function of unifying co-nascent states, like water for bath-powders;
its manifestation is tranquility or knowledge, for it is said: “One who is concentrated knows and sees things as they really are.
In particular, it should be understood as having happiness as its proximate cause, being the stability of the mind like the steadiness of a lamp’s flame in a windless place.
**Commentary on the Faculty of Faith (Saddhindriya):** It is called *saddhā* because by means of it one has faith, or because it itself has faith, or because its very nature is simply faith.

That same [faith] is a faculty (*indriya*) in the sense of being predominant (*adhipati*), owing to its overcoming of lack of faith (*assaddhiya*). Alternatively, it exercises the function of a lord (*indaṭṭha*) with respect to the characteristic of resolution (*adhimokkha*).

Faculty. Faith itself as a faculty is the faith-faculty (*saddhindriya*). Now, this faith has the characteristic of serene confidence (*sampasādana*) and the characteristic of leaping forward (*sampakkhandana*).
For just as when the water-clearing gem of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*) is thrown into water, it [clears] the mud, moss, duckweed, and silt...
It causes [the mud] to settle, making the water clear, serene, and undisturbed;
even so, when faith arises, it suppresses the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), settles the defilements (*kilesa*), gladdens the mind, and makes it undisturbed.
With a gladdened mind, the clansman who is a practitioner of yoga gives gifts, undertakes moral discipline (*sīla*), and performs the observance-day rites (*uposathakamma*).
He undertakes the cultivation [of the mind]. In this way, first of all, faith should be understood as having the characteristic of serene confidence. Therefore, the Venerable Nāgasena said:
"Great King, it is just as if a Wheel-turning Monarch, traveling along a road together with his fourfold army, were to cross a small body of water;
that water would be agitated by the elephants, the horses, the chariots, and the infantry."
It would become turbid, stirred up, and muddy. And the wheel-turning monarch, having emerged, would command his men:
“Bring water, I say! I shall drink it. Now, there would be a water-clearing gem belonging to the king.
“Very well, Your Majesty,” those men would reply to the wheel-turning monarch, and taking that water-clearing gem—

They would throw it into the water. As soon as it is thrown into that water, the mud, algae, and moss would disappear, the silt would settle, and the water would become clear, serene, and undisturbed;
then they would offer the drinking water to the Wheel-turning Monarch, saying, “May Your Majesty drink the water.”
“Great King, just as water is, so should the mind be regarded. Just as those men are, so should the practitioner be regarded.
Just as the mud, the moss, the water-weeds, and the silt are, so should the defilements be regarded.
Just as the water-clearing gem is, so should faith be regarded. Just as, the moment the water-clearing gem is placed [in the water], the mud, the moss, the water-weeds...”
"The mud disappears and settles; the water becomes clear, serene, and undisturbed.
Even so, Great King, when faith arises, it suppresses the hindrances, and the mind becomes free from hindrances—clear, serene, and undisturbed."
Just as a timid person, having approached a great river filled and teeming with crocodiles, makaras, sea-monsters, and rākṣasas, stands on both banks;
but a great warrior, a hero in battle, having arrived and asked, "Why do you stand?
and being told, "Because of the state of fear, we cannot venture down," takes up a well-sharpened sword and says, "Behind me..."

Saying, "Come here, do not be afraid," he descends into the river and, warding off the crocodiles and other predators as they arrive one after another, leads the people from this bank to the opposite bank, ensuring their safety. He likewise brings them safely back from the opposite bank to this side.
In the very same way, for one who gives gifts, guards morality, performs the observance-day duties, and undertakes meditation—
Faith is preceded by and goes before [the other faculties]. Therefore it is said:
“Faith has the characteristic of leaping forward. Another method: faith has the characteristic of believing, or the characteristic of conviction.
Its function is to clarify, like a water-clearing gem, or its function is to leap forward, like one crossing a flood. It is manifested as untroubledness, or it is manifested as resolve.

Or rather: it has the state of being a matter to be believed as its proximate cause, or it has the factors of stream-entry as its proximate cause; it should be regarded as being like hands, wealth, or seeds.
Viriya is the state of a hero (vīra), or the action of heroes is viriya. Or, viriya is that which is to be set in motion or put forth by way of method, principle, or means.
That very same [quality], because it overcomes laziness, is a faculty (indriya) in the sense of predominance.
Or, it is called a faculty (*indriya*) because it exercises the function of a lord (*indaṭṭha*) in the act of exertion. Energy itself as a faculty is the energy-faculty (*vīriyindriya*).
Furthermore, this energy has the characteristic of supporting and the characteristic of exerting.
For just as an old house stands by means of a newly erected pillar for support, even so the practitioner (*yogāvacara*) is supported by the support of energy.
Having offered it, one does not diminish or decline in all wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*). In this way, its characteristic of providing support should be understood.
Therefore, the Elder Nāgasena said:
"Just as, O Great King, a man might prop up a house that is collapsing with another piece of wood, and once it has been propped up..."
“In that case, the house would not collapse; even so, Great King, energy has the characteristic of providing support.
When all wholesome states are supported by energy, they do not decline nor do they diminish.
Or again, just as when a battle is joined between a small army and a large army, the small army might falter.
Then one should inform the king; the king would dispatch a powerful army, and supported by that, his own army would defeat the enemy army.
In the same way, energy does not allow the co-arising and associated states to slacken or retreat;
it uplifts and exerts them. Therefore it is said: “Energy has the characteristic of exertion.”
Another method: Energy has the characteristic of exertion; its function is to support conascent states; it is manifested as non-collapse.
According to the statement, “One who is stirred strives wisely,” it has spiritual urgency as its proximate cause, or else the basis for the arousal of energy.
It should be understood that when rightly undertaken, it is the root of all success.
It is *sati* because by means of it one remembers, or it itself remembers, or it is merely a remembering (*saraṇamatta*).

That very same [mindfulness] is a faculty (*indriya*) in the sense of being predominant (*adhipati*) because it overcomes forgetfulness; or, it exercises the function of a lord (*indaṭṭha*) regarding the characteristic of establishing, thus it is a faculty.

Mindfulness itself as a faculty is the "faculty of mindfulness" (*satindriya*). Furthermore, this mindfulness has the characteristic of not wobbling (*apilāpana*) and the characteristic of grasping (*upaṅgahaṇa*).
And it is just as the king’s treasurer, guarding the ten kinds of treasure, reminds and makes the Wheel-turning Monarch aware of his sovereign prosperity morning and evening;
even so, mindfulness reminds and makes one aware of wholesome states. Therefore the Elder said:
"Just as, O Great King, the treasurer of a Wheel-turning Monarch [reminds] the Wheel-turning Monarch morning and evening..."

He reminds one of one’s reputation, saying: “Sire, there were so many elephants, so many horses, so many chariots, so many foot-soldiers, so much bullion, so much gold, and so much total property; may Your Majesty remember that.
In the same way, Great King, when wholesome states are present, mindfulness does not allow them to slip away, thinking: “These are the four foundations of mindfulness,” these...
"The four right efforts, these four bases of psychic power, these five faculties, these five powers, these seven factors of enlightenment,
this noble eightfold path, this serenity, this insight,
this true knowledge, this liberation— these are the supramundane states. Thus, Great King, mindfulness has the characteristic of non-confusion."
Just as the counselor-treasure of a wheel-turning monarch, having understood what is harmful and what is beneficial to the king,
causes him to avoid the harmful and approach the beneficial, even so mindfulness, having investigated the courses of wholesome and unwholesome states,
dispels those unwholesome states, thinking: "These states, such as bodily misconduct, are harmful," and [promotes] those such as bodily good conduct...
“Dhammas are beneficial,” he thus takes up those dhammas that are beneficial. Therefore the Elder said:
“Just as, Great King, the counselor-treasure of a wheel-turning monarch knows what is beneficial and what is harmful for the king—‘These are beneficial to the king, these are harmful;
these are helpful, these are unhelpful’—and so he removes what is harmful and takes up what is beneficial...”
"In the same way, Great King, when mindfulness arises, it investigates the courses of beneficial and unbeneficial states:
'These states are beneficial; these states are unbeneficial; these states are helpful; these states are unhelpful.
Thereupon, it dispels unbeneficial states and embraces beneficial states. Thus, Great King, mindfulness has the characteristic of embracing."
Another method: Mindfulness has the characteristic of not floating away; its function is non-forgetfulness;
it is manifested as guarding or as the state of being directed toward the object; its proximate cause is firm perception or the foundations of mindfulness such as the body;
and it should be regarded as like a pillar because it is firmly established upon the object, and like a gatekeeper because it guards the eye-door and so forth.
Concentration (*samādhi*) is so called because it rightly concentrates and places the mind upon its object.

That same state is a faculty (*indriya*) in the sense of predominance, because it overcomes distraction; or else, it is a faculty because it exercises lordship over the characteristic of non-distraction.
Concentration itself as a faculty is the "concentration faculty. Its characteristics and other qualities should be understood in the same manner as explained below.
It understands, thus it is wisdom (*paññā*). What does it understand? It understands the Noble Truths by way of the method beginning with “This is suffering.
In the Commentary, however, it is said: “It makes known, thus it is wisdom. How does it make known? It makes known [them] as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
That very same [wisdom] is a faculty in the sense of sovereignty because of its overcoming of ignorance; or else, it exercises the lordship of a ruler (*inda*) in the characteristic of seeing.
It causes [one] to act, thus it is a faculty (*indriya*). Wisdom itself as a faculty is the "faculty of wisdom" (*paññindriya*).

Now, this wisdom has the characteristic of illuminating and the characteristic of understanding. For just as in a house with four walls, when a lamp is lit during the night, darkness ceases and light becomes manifest, even so is wisdom characterized by illuminating. There is no illumination equal to the illumination of wisdom.
There is no such thing. For one possessed of wisdom, when seated cross-legged, the ten-thousandfold world system becomes a single expanse of light. Therefore the Elder said:

"Just as, O Great King, if a man were to bring a lamp into a house in darkness, the lamp, once brought in, would dispel the darkness, produce radiance, manifest light, and make visible forms clear—just so..."

“Indeed, Great King, when wisdom arises, it shatters the darkness of ignorance, generates the light of true knowledge, reveals the radiance of understanding, and makes the Noble Truths manifest. Thus, Great King, wisdom has the characteristic of illumination.
Furthermore, just as a skilled physician knows which foods are suitable and which are unsuitable for his patients, so too does wisdom.

As they arise, one understands wholesome and unwholesome states, those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated, the inferior and the superior, the dark and the bright, and those with a counterpart and those without a counterpart.

And this was said by the General of the Dhamma: "One understands, one understands—therefore, friend, one is called 'possessed of wisdom. And what does one understand? One understands: 'This is suffering,'" and so on in detail.
Thus its characteristic of understanding should be known.

Another method: wisdom has the characteristic of penetrating things according to their true nature; or it has the characteristic of unerring penetration, like the penetration of an arrow shot by a skilled archer.
Its function is to illuminate the object, like a lamp. It is manifested as non-delusion, like a guide who has entered a forest.
It is called *mano* because it "measures" (*manatīti*); the meaning is that it cognizes. However, the teachers of the Commentaries say:
"It measures and understands the object as if measuring with a nali-measure or weighing with a great balance, thus it is *mano*.

That very same [consciousness] exercises the function of lordship (*indaṭṭha*) in the characteristic of measuring, thus it is a faculty (*indriya*). The mind itself as a faculty is the "mind-faculty" (*manindriya*). This is a synonym for the "consciousness" mentioned above.
Because it is associated with joy (*pīti*) and gladness (*somanassa*), it is "beautiful mind" (*sumana*); the state of being such is "gladness" (*somanassa*).
It exercises lordship (*indaṭṭha*) over the characteristic of satisfaction; thus, it is a "faculty" (*indriya*). Gladness itself as a faculty is the "faculty of gladness" (*somanassindriya*).
This is a synonym for the very same feeling (*vedanā*) mentioned previously.
It is called *jīvita* (life) because the states associated with it live by means of it.

It is called *indriya* (faculty) because it exercises lordship (*indaṭṭha*) over the characteristic of preservation. Life itself as a faculty is the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). It is the dominant influence over the continuity of the process of existence.
Furthermore, in terms of its characteristics and so forth, the life-faculty has the characteristic of preserving those states that are inseparable from itself.
Their function is to cause those very states to proceed; their manifestation is the stabilization of those same states;

their proximate cause is the phenomena that are to be maintained. Furthermore, although there are other modes such as the characteristic of preservation, it is only at the moment of existence that it preserves those states, just as water preserves lotuses and the like, and just as a nurse protects a child even though the child has arisen from its own respective conditions.
It proceeds solely by way of its connection with the dhamma that has already arisen, like a pilot;
it does not cause it to proceed after the moment of dissolution, because of the absence of both itself and that which is to be caused to proceed.

Nor does it establish it at the moment of dissolution, because it is itself dissolving, like the wick-oil of a lamp as it is being consumed [extinguishing] the flame. And yet, it is not devoid of the power of preservation, proceeding, establishing, and maintaining.
It should be understood that at the moment described, each [factor] acts as a means to its respective [result].
In the commentary on the collection of path factors:
among right view and the others, it is "right view" in the sense of seeing; it is "right intention" in the sense of directing toward; it is [right effort] in the sense of exerting.
Right effort, right mindfulness in the sense of establishing, and right concentration in the sense of non-distraction are to be understood thus. As for the etymological meaning:

one sees rightly, or by means of it one sees rightly, thus it is right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*). One intends rightly, or by means of it they intend rightly, thus it is right intention (*sammā-saṅkappo*).
One exerts oneself rightly, or by means of it they exert themselves rightly... [thus it is right effort].
Right effort (*sammāvāyāma*). One remembers rightly, or one remembers by means of that [faculty] rightly, thus it is right mindfulness (*sammāsati*).

One concentrates rightly, or one is concentrated by means of that [faculty] rightly, thus it is right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*). Furthermore, praised or beautiful view is right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*).
The meaning of these terms should be understood according to this same method. As for their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth, they have already been explained below.

The commentary on the powers of the young boy (*balarāsivaṇṇanā*): Regarding the power of faith and the others as well, faith and the rest have already been explained in their respective places. However, they should be understood as "powers" (*bala*) in the sense of being unshakable.
Thus, among these, it is the power of faith because it is not shaken by lack of faith; it is the power of energy because it is not shaken by indolence.
"It does not waver in the state of forgetfulness" refers to the power of mindfulness (*satibala*). "It does not waver in restlessness" refers to the power of concentration (*samādhibala*).

"It does not waver in ignorance" refers to the power of wisdom (*paññābala*). "It does not waver in shamelessness" refers to the power of moral shame (*hiribala*). "It does not waver in fearlessness of wrongdoing" refers to the power of moral dread (*ottappabala*).
This is the commentary on the meaning according to both terms.

Among these, the first five have already been explained below by way of their characteristics and so forth. Regarding the final pair: one feels shame (*hiriyati*) because of bodily misconduct and the like;

thus it is *hirī*, which is a designation for modesty (*lajjā*). One feels dread (*ottappati*) because of those very same things; thus it is *ottappa*, which is a designation for the sense of alarm regarding evil. To illustrate the distinction between them:
"The origin, the dominant influence, modesty, and the characteristic of fear... [is said].
Having established this matrix (*mātikā*) with the words "and so forth," this detailed exposition has been stated:
conscience (*hirī*) is that which originates from within; shame (*ottappa*) is that which originates from without. Conscience is that which has oneself as its sovereign;
shame is that which has the world as its sovereign. Conscience is established in the nature of modesty; shame is established in the nature of fear.
Shame (*hirī*) is characterized by a sense of self-respect. Moral dread (*ottappa*) is characterized by the perception of fear regarding what is blameworthy.
In this context, one arouses shame originating from within oneself through four causes:
by reflecting on one’s birth, by reflecting on one’s age, by reflecting on one’s courage, and by reflecting on one’s great learning. How so?
“This performance of evil is not the work of those endowed with noble birth; it is the work of low-born people such as fishermen.

It is not fitting for one like me, who is endowed with noble birth, to do this deed. In this way, first of all, by reflecting upon birth, one who refrains from evil such as the taking of life arouses a sense of shame (*hiri*). Likewise, “This performance of evil is [the work] of the young...”

"This is a deed that ought to be done; it is not fitting for one established in my age to do this"—reflecting thus on his own age, he arouses a sense of shame (*hiri*) by refraining from evil such as the taking of life. Likewise:
"This kind of evil deed is the work of those who are weak-natured, not of those who possess courage. This deed is not fit for one like me, who is endowed with courage."
Reflecting on his own courage in this way—thinking, "It is not fitting for me to do so"—he arouses a sense of shame (*hiri*) by refraining from evil deeds such as killing living beings.
Likewise, reflecting on his great learning (*bāhusacca*)—thinking, "This kind of evil deed is the work of blind fools, not of the wise;
it is not fitting for a wise and learned person like me to perform such an act"—he arouses a sense of shame.
