By refraining from evil deeds such as the taking of life, one arouses moral shame (*hiri*). Thus, one arouses this internally-aroused moral shame through four causes.
Having aroused it and having caused moral shame to enter one’s own mind, one does not commit an evil deed.
This is what is called internally-aroused moral shame.
What is called "moral dread" (ottappa) arising from the external? It is this: "If you commit an evil deed, you will become an object of reproach among the four assemblies.
Wise people will censure you, saying: 'How can this man act like a monk when he is devoid of virtue, like an impure layman?
Thus you will be shunned by those possessed of moral conduct."
Reflecting in this way, one does not commit an evil deed through a sense of shame (*ottappa*) that arises from the external world. Thus, this is what is called "shame arising from the external.
How is it that "self-mastery" (*attādhipati*) is called moral dread (*hirī*)? Here, a certain son of good family, making himself his own master and leader, reflects:
"It is not fitting for one like me—who has gone forth out of faith, is learned, and maintains the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*)—to commit an evil deed."
One does not commit evil, thinking, "I shall do it. Such is what is called *hirī* (moral shame) having oneself as its own authority. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Having made oneself alone one's own authority and leader, one abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome;
one abandons the blameworthy and develops the blameless; one maintains oneself in purity."

What is called moral dread with respect to the world as authority (*lokādhipati-ottappa*)? Here, a certain son of good family, making the world his authority and his elder, does not commit an evil deed.
As it has been said: "Great indeed is this world-dwelling.
In this great world-dwelling there are recluses and brahmins who possess psychic power, have the divine eye, and are knowers of the minds of others."
They see from afar, yet they are not seen when close at hand; they understand the mind with their own minds.
They will know of this [monk]: "Look, sirs, at this clansman who, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, dwells mired in evil, unwholesome states.
There are deities possessed of psychic power and divine vision.
There are those who know the minds of others. They see from afar, yet they are not seen even when nearby; they understand the mind with their own minds.

They too will know of me: “Look, sirs, at this clansman! Having gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, he dwells mired in evil, unwholesome states. … Thus, he makes the world itself his master and his chief.
"Having done unwholesome [deeds], he abandons them and develops the wholesome; he abandons the blameworthy and develops the blameless; he maintains himself in purity.
Thus, *ottappa* (moral dread) is called "lord of the world.
*Hirī* (moral shame) is established in the nature of modesty; *ottappa* is established in the nature of fear. Herein, "modesty" (*lajjā*) is the mode of being modest.
*Hirī* (moral shame) is established by way of that intrinsic nature. *Bhaya* means the fear of the states of misery (*apāya*); *ottappa* (moral dread) is established by way of that intrinsic nature.

Both of these become manifest in the avoidance of evil. For just as a certain son of good family, while performing the functions of defecation and urination, might experience a sense of shame upon seeing someone who ought to be shunned, becoming overcome with a feeling of loathing and abashed—even so [is it with moral shame].
Having internalized the sense of shame, one does not commit an evil deed. Another person, being terrified by the fear of the states of misery, does not commit an evil deed.
Here is an illustration: suppose there were two iron balls; one might be cold but smeared with excrement, while the other...
The fire is hot. In this regard, the wise man does not take it because he feels disgust at being smeared with cold excrement; the other [the fool] does not take it out of fear of being burned.

Therein, the non-taking of the cold [fire] due to the disgust of being smeared with excrement is like the non-committing of evil after having entered into a sense of moral shame (*lajjā*) within oneself.
The non-taking of the hot [fire] out of fear of being burned is like [the non-committing of evil] out of fear of the states of deprivation (*apāya*).
Non-doing is to be understood.
*Hirī* has the characteristic of having a sense of shame; *ottappa* has the characteristic of seeing fear in what is blameworthy.
This pair also becomes manifest precisely in the avoidance of evil. For some, through the reflection on the greatness of their lineage and the reflection on the greatness of the Teacher...
By reflecting on four causes— the greatness of the inheritance, the greatness of one’s fellow celibates, the fear of self-reproach, and the fear of reproach by others—
one arouses *hiri*, characterized by a sense of shame, and does not commit evil. By reflecting on four causes— the fear of blame by oneself, the fear of blame by others, the fear of punishment,
and the fear of an unhappy rebirth— one arouses *ottappa*, characterized by the perception of danger and dread of faults.
One does not commit evil. In this regard, one should explain in detail the reflections on the greatness of one’s birth and so forth, as well as the fear of self-reproach and so forth.
Commentary on the Root Section.

It is called *alobha* (non-greed) because by means of it one does not become greedy, or because it itself is not greedy, or because its nature is simply non-greed. The same method applies to *adosa* (non-hatred) and *amoha* (non-delusion).
Among these, non-greed has the characteristic of the mind’s lack of attachment to an object, or the characteristic of non-clinging, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf.
Its function is non-appropriation, like a monk who has renounced his robes. It is manifested as a state of non-attachment.
It is like a man who has fallen into filth. Non-hatred (adosa) has the characteristic of being non-cruel, or the characteristic of non-opposition, like a compliant friend.
Its function is the removal of resentment, or the removal of feverish burning, like sandalwood. It is manifested as a state of gentleness, like the full moon.
Non-delusion (amoha) has already been explained by way of its characteristics and other features in the section on the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) above.
Among these three, non-greed (*alobha*) is the opposite of the stain of stinginess (*maccheramala*); non-hatred (*adosa*) is the opposite of the stain of immorality (*dussīlyamala*);

and non-delusion (*amoha*) is the opposite of the lack of cultivation regarding wholesome states (*kusalesu dhammesu*). Furthermore, among these, non-greed is the cause for giving (*dānahetu*), non-hatred is the cause for morality (*sīlahetu*), and non-delusion is the cause for cultivation (*bhāvanāhetu*).
And therein, by means of non-greed one takes no more than is necessary, because a greedy person takes too much; by means of non-hatred one takes no less, because a hater...
Because of grasping what is deficient. Through non-delusion, one perceives things without error, for one who is deluded grasps things erroneously.
And herein, through non-greed, one proceeds toward fault by holding a fault that exists to be a fault; for one who is greedy conceals a fault.
Through non-hatred, one proceeds toward virtue by holding a virtue that exists to be a virtue; for one who is hateful...
“He anoints with virtue”: by means of non-delusion (*amoha*), one who maintains the true nature of things as they truly are proceeds in accordance with that true nature.
For one who is deluded perceives the real as unreal and the unreal as real. Furthermore, through non-greed (*alobha*), there is no suffering from separation from the beloved;
for one who is greedy has a disposition toward what is dear and is unable to endure separation from it.

Through non-hatred (*adosa*), the suffering of association with the unpleasant does not arise, for one who is free from hatred does not possess an unpleasant nature and is unable to endure such association.

Through non-delusion (*amoha*), the suffering of not obtaining what is desired does not arise, for in one who is undeluded, reflections such as "How could that possibly be obtained here? become possible.
And through non-greed (*alobha*), the suffering of birth does not arise here, because non-greed is the direct opposite of craving and because [birth] is rooted in craving.
Through non-hatred, the suffering of aging does not arise, because for one with sharp hatred, aging occurs quickly.
Through non-delusion, the suffering of death does not arise, for the suffering of death is that which occurs with delusion, and this does not happen to one who is undeluded.
Furthermore, through non-greed there is pleasant companionship for householders, through non-delusion for those who have gone forth, and through non-hatred for all alike.
And here, in particular, rebirth in the realm of the *petas* does not occur through non-greed (*alobha*).

For, as a general rule, beings are reborn in the realm of the *petas* by means of craving (*taṇhā*), and non-greed is the direct opposite of craving. Rebirth in hell does not occur through non-hatred (*adosa*).
For, due to a fierce nature born of hatred, beings are reborn in hell, which resembles hatred; and non-hatred is the direct opposite of hatred.

Non-hatred (*adosa*). Through non-delusion (*amoha*), rebirth in the animal realm does not occur. For it is through delusion that beings are born into the animal realm, which is characterized by constant bewilderment.
And non-delusion is the direct opposite of delusion. Among these, non-greed (*alobha*) prevents approaching [an object] by way of lust;
non-hatred (*adosa*) prevents departing [from an object] by way of hatred; and non-delusion (*amoha*) prevents a state of indifference by way of delusion.

Furthermore, by means of these three in their respective order—namely, the perception of renunciation (*nekkhamma-saññā*), the perception of non-ill will (*abyāpāda-saññā*), and the perception of non-cruelty (*avihiṃsā-saññā*)—there are also these three perceptions:

the perception of the foul (*asubha-saññā*), the perception of the immeasurable (*appamāṇa-saññā*), and the perception of elements (*dhātu-saññā*). By means of non-greed (*alobha*), there is the avoidance of the extreme of devotion to sensual pleasure (*kāmasukhallikānuyoga*);
and by means of non-hatred (*adosa*), there is the avoidance of the extreme of devotion to self-mortification (*attakilamathānuyoga*).
Through non-delusion, one practices the middle way of practice. Likewise, through non-greed there is the breaking of the bodily tie of covetousness;
through non-hatred, the bodily tie of ill will; and through non-delusion, the remaining two bodily ties.
Furthermore, the first two foundations of mindfulness succeed through the power of the first two [roots], while the latter ones succeed through the power of the last one alone.
In this context, non-greed (*alobha*) is the condition for health; for one who is not greedy does not indulge even in unwholesome things that provoke greed, and by that means he remains healthy.
Non-hatred (*adosa*) is the condition for youthfulness; for one who is not hateful is not consumed by the fire of hatred—which brings on wrinkles and grey hair—and thus remains young for a long time.
Non-delusion (*amoha*) is the condition for long life; for one who is undeluded, having understood what is beneficial and what is harmful, avoids the harmful.
And by practicing what is beneficial, one becomes long-lived.
Furthermore, non-greed (*alobha*) is the condition for the attainment of wealth, for one who is not greedy gains wealth through generosity.

Non-hatred (*adosa*) is the condition for the attainment of friends, because through loving-kindness (*mettā*) one both acquires friends and does not lose them. Non-delusion (*amoha*) is the condition for the attainment of self.
For one who is undeluded, performing only what is beneficial for oneself, perfects the self.
Non-greed is a condition for the divine abiding (*dibbavihāra*), non-hatred for the sublime abiding (*brahmavihāra*), and non-delusion for the noble abiding (*ariyavihāra*).
And herein, through non-greed, one becomes extinguished regarding the beings and formations belonging to one's own side; by their destruction, [one is freed] from the cause of attachment.
Through non-hatred (*adosa*), there is the absence of the perception of enmity even toward those who are hostile, because one who is free from hatred lacks the perception of others as enemies.
Through non-delusion (*amoha*), there is the absence of attachment to all things regarding neutral parties, because one who is undeluded lacks all forms of clinging.

Furthermore, through non-greed (*alobha*), there is the vision of impermanence; for a greedy person, due to the hope for enjoyment, does not see conditioned phenomena as impermanent even when they are impermanent.

He does not see [them as pleasant]. Through non-hatred (*adosa*), there is the vision of suffering: for one whose underlying tendency toward non-hatred has abandoned the objects of resentment, he sees even conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) as suffering. Through non-delusion (*amoha*), there is the vision of non-self:

for one who is undeluded and skilled in grasping things as they truly are, he awakens to the five aggregates—which lack a leader—as being without a leader. And just as through these [three roots] there are the visions of impermanence and so forth...
In this way, these too arise through the vision of impermanence and so forth. For through the vision of impermanence, non-greed arises; through the vision of suffering, non-hatred;
and through the vision of non-self, non-delusion arises. For who, indeed, having rightly understood that "this is impermanent," would generate a longing for its sake?
Or how could one who knows conditioned phenomena to be "suffering" [give rise to] further, utterly sharp, painful anger?
Could one who has awakened to the emptiness of self fall back into delusion again?
Commentary on the Section on the Path of Action:
"Non-covetousness" (*anabhijjhā*) means not coveting. It is bodily and mental happiness, beneficial for this world and the next, obtained through the power of one's virtues.
It does not cause ill will toward fame; thus, it is non-ill-will (*abyāpāda*). It sees rightly, or it is a beautiful view; thus, it is right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*).

These are indeed the names for non-greed and the other [wholesome roots]. However, it should be understood that these states were previously taken in terms of their roots, whereas here they are taken in terms of the courses of action (*kamma-patha*).
Commentary on the Pair of World-Guardians (*Lokapāla-duka*)

The two qualities of moral shame (*hirī*) and moral dread (*ottappa*) were previously included by way of their strength; here, they are included by way of being the guardians of the world (*lokapāla*).
For these two qualities guard the world. As it is said: "Monks, these two bright qualities guard the world. Which two? Moral shame and moral dread.
These, monks, are the two bright qualities that guard the world. If, monks, these two bright qualities..."

If these two bright qualities did not protect the world, then "mother" would not be known here, nor "maternal aunt," nor "uncle's wife," nor "teacher’s wife," nor "the wives of those worthy of respect.
The world would fall into promiscuity, like goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, dogs and jackals.
But because, monks, these two bright qualities protect the world, therefore "mother" is known.
“Or as an aunt, or as a maternal uncle’s wife, or as a teacher’s wife, or as the wife of one’s elders.
Commentary on the Pairs beginning with Tranquillity:
Tranquillity of the body is *kāyapassaddhi*. Tranquillity of the mind is *cittapassaddhi*. “Body” means...

And here, the three aggregates beginning with feeling are included. Taken together, these two—tranquillity of body and tranquillity of mind—are characterized by the subsiding of disturbances in body and mind;
their function is the crushing out of disturbances in body and mind; they are manifested as the state of non-excitement and coolness in body and mind;
and their proximate cause is body and mind. They should be understood as being the opposites of defilements such as restlessness, which prevent the subsiding of body and mind.
Lightness of the body is bodily lightness (*kāyalahutā*). Lightness of the mind is mental lightness (*cittalahutā*). These two have the characteristic of the subsiding of heaviness in body and mind;
their function is the crushing out of heaviness in body and mind; they are manifested as the non-sluggishness of body and mind; and they have body and mind as their proximate cause.
They should be understood as being the opposites of the defilements such as stiffness and torpor that produce heaviness in body and mind.

The pliancy of the body is bodily pliancy; the pliancy of the mind is mental pliancy. These two are characterized by the subsiding of rigidity in the body and mind; their function is the crushing out of rigidity in the body and mind;
they are manifested as non-resistance; they have the body and mind as their proximate cause.
They should be understood as being the opposites of the defilements such as views and conceit, which produce rigidity in the body and mind.
The serviceability of the body is bodily adaptability. The serviceability of the mind is mental adaptability.
These two have the characteristic of calming the unserviceability of body and mind; their function is the crushing out of the unserviceability of body and mind;
they are manifested as the attainment of the state of making body and mind fit for their respective objects; their proximate cause is body and mind. Of body and mind...
They should be understood as being the opposites of the remaining hindrances that cause unfitness for action.
They should be understood as bringing about confidence in things that inspire confidence, and as bringing about security in the application of beneficial activities, like the purification of gold.
Bodily fitness is *kāyapāguññatā*; mental fitness is *cittapāguññatā*. These [belong] to the body and mind...

It has the characteristic of having a state free from illness; its function is to crush physical and mental illness; it is manifested as the absence of danger; its proximate cause is the body and mind.
It should be understood as being the opposite of the defilements such as lack of faith that produce physical and mental illness.
Rectitude of the body is bodily rectitude (*kāyujujatā*); rectitude of the mind is mental rectitude (*cittujujatā*). These have the characteristic of straightness of the body and mind.
It has the function of crushing crookedness of body and mind; its manifestation is straightness; its proximate cause is body and mind.
It should be understood as being the antidote to those defilements such as deceit (*māyā*) and fraud (*sāṭheyya*) that produce crookedness of body and mind.

"She remembers" is *sati* (mindfulness). "He understands clearly" is *sampajañña* (clear comprehension); the meaning is that he knows thoroughly and in all modes. This is clear comprehension of purpose (*sātthaka-sampajañña*).

Furthermore, its classification should be understood by way of these four: clarity of comprehension regarding what is suitable (*sappāya-sampajañña*), clarity of comprehension regarding the field of action (*gocara-sampajañña*), and clarity of comprehension regarding non-delusion (*asammoha-sampajañña*). Their characteristics and other attributes should be understood in the same manner as those explained for the faculty of mindfulness (*satindriya*) and the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*).
Thus, these two factors mentioned below have been taken up again in this place by way of their utility.

It is *samatha* because it calms (*sameti*) adverse states such as sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*). It is *vipassanā* because it sees phenomena through various modes, such as impermanence (*anicca*) and so forth.
In terms of their essential meaning, these two are identical with wisdom (*paññā*). The characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and other qualities of these two have already been explained above;
however, here they are taken in the sense of being "yoked together" (*yuganaddha*).
It is "exertion" (paggāha) because it exerts itself toward co-nascent states. It is "non-distraction" (avikkhepa) because it is the opposite of distraction, which is characterized as restlessness.
The characteristics and other qualities of these two are already explained below;
however, it should be understood that this pair is included here for the purpose of joining energy with concentration.
The Explanation of the Remaining Factors:
Furthermore, whatever other conditioned immaterial states exist at that time, these states are wholesome.
These are not only those enumerated in the sequence of the text as "there is contact... pe ... there is non-distraction," but also others.

There are indeed more than fifty such states; however, at whatever time the first great consciousness of the sense-sphere— triple-rooted, accompanied by joy, and unprompted— has arisen, at that time there are also others which,
being associated with those same factors such as contact and so forth, proceed in dependence upon their respective appropriate conditions.

Those that have arisen without the presence of form are "formless" (*arūpino*); all these phenomena (*dhammā*) that are apprehended by way of their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāvato*) are wholesome (*kusalā*).

Having thus illustrated more than fifty-five phenomena included in the Canon by way of the factors of consciousness (*cittanga*), the King of Dhamma further illustrates nine other phenomena by way of the "included" (*yevāpanaka*).
For in various passages of the Suttas, [it is said]: "Desire (*chando*), resolve (*adhimokkho*)..."
“Attention, equanimity, compassion, gladness, abstention from bodily misconduct, abstention from verbal misconduct, and abstention from wrong livelihood”—these nine states are discerned.
Furthermore, within this great consciousness there exists the desire for wholesome states characterized by the wish to act;
however, it is not included in the text as a factor of consciousness (*cittanga*), but is taken here under the category of the "included" (*yevāpanaka*).
There is resolve, there is attention, and there is equanimity. There is the preliminary stage of loving-kindness (*mettā*); when non-hatred is grasped, it is indeed grasped.

There is the preliminary stage of compassion (*karuṇā*), there is the preliminary stage of appreciative joy (*muditā*), and there is the preliminary stage of equanimity (*upekkhā*). However, that [equanimity] is already grasped when equanimity itself is grasped. Right speech (*sammāvācā*).

There is right action; there is right livelihood. However, it is not included in the text by way of being a factor of consciousness (*cittanga*), though it is indeed taken here as an "included" (*yevāpanaka*) factor.
Among these nine, however, only these four—zeal (*chanda*), resolution (*adhimokkha*), attention (*manasikāra*), and equanimity (*tatramajjhattatā*)—occur in a single moment.

The remaining ones are obtained at different moments. For when one abandons wrong speech with this consciousness and fulfills right speech by way of abstinence, then these five—namely, the four beginning with desire (*chanda*) and right speech—are obtained simultaneously.
When one abandons wrong action and fulfills right action by way of abstinence... [and so on] ...wrong livelihood.
One abandons [unwholesome states] and fulfills right livelihood by way of abstention...pe... when one performs the preliminary work for compassion...pe...

when one performs the preliminary work for sympathetic joy (*muditā*), then these five—namely, the four beginning with zeal (*chanda*) and the preliminary stage of sympathetic joy—are obtained in a single moment.
However, apart from this, for one giving a gift or fulfilling virtue (*sīla*) in yoga...pe...
For one performing an action, only four certain factors (apaṇṇakaṅga) are obtained.
Thus, among these nine included states (yevāpanaka-dhamma), "desire" (chanda) is a designation for the wish to act.
Therefore, that desire has the characteristic of wishing to act; its function is the seeking of an object; it is manifested as the need for an object.
That itself is its proximate cause (*padatthāna*). And this should be regarded as the mind’s stretching out of the hand in order to grasp an object.
Resolute determination is *adhimokkha*. It has the characteristic of deciding; its function is non-wavering; it is manifested as certainty; its proximate cause is a state that is to be decided upon.

It should be regarded as a gate-post because of its immovability with respect to the object. Action is *kāra*; action of the mind is *manasikāra*. It is also so called because it makes the subsequent mind different from the preceding mind.
Attention (*manasikāra*). This is of three kinds: that which introduces the object, that which introduces the cognitive process (*vīthi*), and that which introduces the impulsion (*javana*).
Among these, it is called attention because it "places" (*kāra*) [the mind] upon the mind (*manas*); its characteristic is recollecting; its function is to yoke associated states to the object;
its manifestation is the state of being directed toward the object; and it is included within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
By way of leading toward the object, it should be regarded as like a charioteer for the associated states.

However, "leading toward the cognitive process" (*vīthipaṭipādaka*) is a designation for five-door adverting consciousness; "leading toward the impulsion" (*javanapaṭipādaka*) is a designation for mind-door adverting consciousness. These two are not intended here.
Equanimity toward those mental states is "equanimity regarding that" (*tatramajjhattatā*). It has the characteristic of keeping the mind and mental factors in balance.
Its function is to prevent deficiency and excess, or its function is to cut off partiality. It is manifested as the state of neutrality.
It should be regarded as a charioteer who looks on with equanimity at the well-balanced, well-trained horses of the mind and mental factors as they proceed evenly.

“Compassion” and “gladness” will be explained in the description of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*). For the only difference is that those [two] reach absorption (*appanā*) and belong to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), whereas this one belongs to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
“Abstinence from bodily misconduct” (*kāyaduccaritavirati*) means abstaining from bodily misconduct. The same method applies to the other two terms as well.

As for their characteristics and so forth, all three have the characteristic of not transgressing the bases of bodily misconduct and the rest; in other words, they have the characteristic of non-oppression.

Their function is to contract away from the bases of bodily misconduct and the rest; they are manifested as non-action; and their proximate cause consists of such qualities as faith, moral shame, moral dread, and fewness of desires.
They should be understood as being states of the mind that have turned away from unwholesome action (*pāpakiriyā*).
Thus, including the fifty-six factors mentioned by way of inclusion (*yevāpanaka*), there are nine;
so all together, in this section on the enumeration of phenomena (*dhammuddesavāra*), there are sixty-five dharma-terms. Among these, at any given moment, sometimes sixty-one occur, and sometimes...
