The five factors of contact, applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, and one-pointedness of mind; the five faculties; the two powers—namely, the power of moral shame and the power of moral dread;
the two roots—namely, non-greed and non-hatred; and the twelve states beginning with tranquility of body and tranquility of mind:
these constitute thirty mental factors.
Among those thirty factors, eighteen factors are unanalyzed and twelve are analyzed. Which eighteen?
Contact, perception, volition, sustained application, rapture, the life-faculty, and the twelve factors beginning with bodily tranquility—these eighteen are unanalyzed.
Feeling, consciousness, initial application, one-pointedness of mind, and the faith-faculty...
The faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of wisdom, the power of moral shame, the power of moral dread, non-greed, and non-hatred—
these twelve factors are with their respective classifications. Among them, seven factors are classified in two places,
one in three, two in four, one in six, and one is classified in seven places.
How so? These seven—consciousness, applied thought, faith, moral shame, moral dread, non-greed, and non-hatred—are analyzed in two places.
For among these, consciousness is called simply "consciousness" when it reaches the pentad of contact, but it is called the "mind-faculty" when it reaches the faculties.
Applied thought is called "applied thought" when it reaches the factors of jhāna, but it is called "right intention" when it reaches the factors of the path.
Faith, having reached the state of faculties, is called the faith-faculty; having reached the state of powers, it is called the power of faith.
Modesty, having reached the state of powers, is called the power of modesty; having reached the pair of world-protectors, it is called modesty. The same method applies to fear of wrongdoing as well.
Non-greed, having reached the state of roots, is called non-greed; having reached the state of a path of action, it is called non-covetousness. Non-hatred...
It is said that when it reaches the root, it is "non-hatred" (adoso), and when it reaches the path of action, it is "non-ill-will" (abyāpādo). These seven [factors] are thus analyzed in two places.

Feeling (vedanā), however, is said to be "feeling" when it reaches the pentad of contact; it is "pleasure" (sukha) when it reaches the factors of jhāna, and "the faculty of mental joy" (somanassindriya) when it reaches the faculties. Thus, one single phenomenon is analyzed in three places.
Energy (vīriya), moreover, is said to be "the faculty of energy" (vīriyindriya) when it reaches the faculties, and "right effort" (sammāvāyāma) when it reaches the factors of the path.
Having reached the [five] powers, it is called the "power of energy"; having reached the "subsequent dyad," it is called "exertion.

Although it is stated that when reaching the faculties it becomes the "faculty of mindfulness," when reaching the factors of the path it is "right mindfulness," when reaching the powers it is the "power of mindfulness," and when reaching the subsequent dyad it is simply "mindfulness"—thus these two states are analyzed in four contexts.

But concentration (samādhi), having reached the factors of absorption (jhānaṅga), is called "one-pointedness of mind" (cittassekaggatā); having reached the faculties (indriya), it is the "faculty of concentration" (samādhindriya);

having reached the path-factors (maggaṅga), it is "right concentration" (sammāsamādhi). Having reached the powers (bala), it is the "power of concentration" (samādhibala); having reached the subsequent dyad, it is "tranquillity" (samatha) and "non-distraction" (avikkhepa).
Thus, this single state (dhamma) is analyzed into six positions.
But when wisdom reaches the faculties, it is called the faculty of wisdom; when it reaches the path factors, right view;
when it reaches the powers, the power of wisdom; when it reaches the roots, non-delusion; when it reaches the courses of action, right view;
and when it reaches the "back-pair," it is clear comprehension and insight. Thus, a single state is analyzed into seven places.
But if someone were to say: "There is nothing new here; having merely taken what was already stated below, the words have been filled in at various places.
This is a discourse lacking continuity, like goods brought back out of order by thieves, or like grass trampled by a herd of cows;
it was spoken without understanding," one should refute him, saying: "Do not speak thus."
It should be said: "There is no teaching of the Buddhas that is without a logical sequence; it is always sequential. There is nothing spoken without knowing it;
everything is spoken only with full knowledge. For the Perfectly Enlightened One knows the function of each and every phenomenon;
having known that, he applies the analysis according to their functions, [stating] that 'eighteen phenomena have a single function'."
Having understood this, he assigned the grammatical analysis to each individual place. Having understood that seven factors have two functions each, he assigned the analysis to two places each.
Having understood that feeling has three functions, he assigned the analysis to three places.
Having understood that energy and mindfulness each have four functions, he assigned the analysis to four places each.
Knowing that concentration has six functions, he applied its analysis to six points.
Knowing that wisdom has seven functions, he applied its analysis to seven points.
Herein, this is the simile: it is said that a certain wise king, having retired into solitude, thought: "This [treasure] belonging to the royal family..."
"I shall not eat haphazardly; I will increase my craft-appropriate wages.
Having summoned all the craftsmen, he said, "Call for those who know each individual craft.
When thus called, eighteen men arose. Having given each of them a share, he dismissed them. "Two crafts each..."
When he said, "Let those who know seven arts come," seven men arrived; he had two portions of food given to each of them.
When he said, "Let those who know three arts come," only one man arrived; he had three portions given to him.
When he said, "Let those who know four arts come," two men arrived; he had four portions given to each of them.
He caused six portions of meat to be given. When he said, "Let those who know five crafts come," not a single person came.
When he said, "Let those who know six crafts come," only one man came. He caused seven portions of meat to be given to him.
When he said, "Let those who know seven crafts come," only one man came. He caused seven portions of meat to be given to him.
In this context, the peerless Dhamma-king is like a wise king;

the states arisen by way of the various mental factors are like those who have mastered a craft; and the assignment of the specific functions of each of those states is like the increase of wages appropriate to their respective skills.
Furthermore, all these states are analyzed by way of the fivefold contact, by way of the jhāna factors, by way of the faculties, and by way of the path.
There are seventeen groups: by way of strength, by way of root, by way of course of action, by way of world-protector,
by way of tranquility, by way of lightness, by way of malleability, by way of wieldiness, by way of proficiency, by way of rectitude,
by way of mindfulness and clear comprehension, by way of serenity and insight, and by way of exertion and non-distraction.
The exposition of the section on the enumeration of phenomena (*dhammuddesavāra*) is finished.
Now begins the exposition of the section on the detailed explanation (*niddesavāra*) concerning wholesome states of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara-kusala*).

In order to analyze and demonstrate those fifty-six terms that appeared in the section on the enumeration of phenomena, the section on the detailed explanation is commenced by way of the method beginning with: "What, at that time, is contact (*phassa*)? and so forth.

In this regard, first, as for the question, the meaning is as follows: when a great wholesome sense-sphere consciousness arises—accompanied by joy, rooted in three causes, and unprompted—at that time it is said that "contact exists.
By this method, the meaning of all the questions is to be understood: "What is that contact? and so forth.
"Whatever at that time is contact": whatever contact has arisen at that time by way of touching, that is contact.
This is called the "essential-nature term" because it illuminates the essential nature of contact. "Touching" is the mode of touching.

"Impinging" (*samphusanā*) is the same mode of touching, stated with the prefix added to extend the word. "The state of having been impinged upon" (*samphusitatta*) is the condition of having been impinged upon.
This, however, is the application here: that which at that time is contact by way of touching; that which at that time is the act of touching;
that which at that time is the thorough touching; that which at that time is the state of having touched;
or alternatively, that which at that time is contact by way of the mode of touching, and by another method, the act of touching, the thorough touching, and the state of having touched.
It is said: "At that time, this is contact. In the explanations of feeling and the other [mental factors] as well, the construction of the words should be understood by this same method.
However, here is the analysis of grammatical case common to all of them. Regarding those [factors] first taught by the Blessed One as belonging to the sense-sphere...
Having divided and shown the wholesome great consciousness, fifty-two headings are established by way of a matrix (mātikā).
Then, taking each heading one by one, the analysis is applied. As they undergo analysis, they do so by way of three reasons;
as they become diverse, they become diverse by way of four reasons. Furthermore, here is the further elucidation:

It goes to two bases. How? For these [terms] go to their respective case-endings (*vibhatti*) by way of these three causes: by way of the phrasing (*byañjana*), by way of the prefix (*upasagga*), and by way of the meaning (*attha*).
In this regard, "anger" (*kodha*) is the act of being angry and the state of having become angry;

"hatred" (*dosa*) is the act of hating and the state of having become hateful—thus should the going to the case-endings be understood by way of the phrasing. For here, it is indeed one and the same...
Anger (*kodha*) has been analyzed in this way according to its verbal suffixes (*byañjana*).
However, the analysis as "cāra, vicāra, anuvicāra, upavicāra" should be understood as being according to prefixes (*upasagga*).

The analysis as "paṇḍicca, kosalla, nepuñña, vebhabyā, cintā, upaparikkhā" should be understood as being according to meaning (*attha*). Among these, in the description of the term "contact" (*phassa-pada-niddesa*):
Thus these three case endings are obtained here. For the transition to the case ending occurs through the phonetic form (*byañjana*) in the phrase "contact is touching" (*phasso phusanā*);
through the prefix (*upasagga*) in "impinging" (*samphusanā*); and through the meaning (*attha*) in "the state of having touched" (*samphusitatta*).
By this method, the application of case endings should be understood in all word-explanations.

Furthermore, although they are diverse, they are diverse by way of these four reasons: diversity of name, diversity of characteristic, diversity of function, and diversity of opposition. In that context, what is ill-will (*vyāpāda*) at that time?
That which at that time is hatred (*dosa*), being hateful—here, whether it is called "ill-will" or "hatred," both of these are simply anger (*koha*) in name.
"Having reached diversity. Thus, diversity should be understood "by way of the diversity of names.

Furthermore, in the sense of being a heap (*rāsa*), even the five aggregates (*khandhā*) constitute a single aggregate. In this context, however, form has the characteristic of being afflicted (*ruppana*);

feeling has the characteristic of being felt (*vedayita*); perception has the characteristic of perceiving (*sañjānana*); volition has the characteristic of intending (*cetayita*); and consciousness...
"Characterized by cognizing"—by this diversity of characteristics, there are the five aggregates. Thus, diversity should be understood "by way of diversity of characteristics.
The four right efforts: "Here, a bhikkhu [exerts himself] for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states..."
“...for its non-arising... he exerts the mind and strives. Thus, a single energy (vīriya) appears in four places due to the diversity of its functions.
In this way, the diversity [of energy] should be understood “by way of the diversity of its functions.
There are four things contrary to the true Dhamma: respect for anger, not respect for the true Dhamma; respect for slander, not respect for the true Dhamma.

In such cases as "valuing gain rather than valuing the true Dhamma" and "valuing honor rather than valuing the true Dhamma," the diversity [of the factors] should be understood by way of their distinct negations.
Furthermore, these four types of diversity are not found in the contact alone; they are present in all fivefold groups beginning with contact.
They are so obtained. For contact has the name "contact," and so on... consciousness has the name "consciousness. Contact has the characteristic of touching;
feeling has the characteristic of being felt; perception has the characteristic of perceiving; volition has the characteristic of intending; and consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing.

Likewise, contact has the function of touching; feeling has the function of experiencing; perception has the function of perceiving; [volition has the function of intending]; and consciousness has the function of cognizing.
Volition has the function of intending; consciousness has the function of cognizing. Thus, diversity should be understood by way of diversity of function.

There is no diversity of opposition in the pentad beginning with contact. However, in the exposition of non-greed and so forth, it is found in the manner of "non-greed, non-coveting, non-covetousness," and so on;
thus, diversity should be understood by way of diversity of opposition.
Thus, in all the explanations of the terms, the fourfold diversity should be understood according to what is applicable.
Furthermore, the further illustration either serves as a praise of the term's meaning or as a reinforcement; thus it proceeds in two ways.
For when "contact" (phassa) is mentioned once, this term—as if being pressed down by the tip of a staff—is blossomed, adorned, and embellished.

It does not have that name [yet]. However, when it is stated repeatedly—by way of its suffixes, its prefixes, and its meaning—as "contact, touching, contacting, the state of having contacted," it becomes something blossomed, adorned, and embellished.
Just as, for example, after a young boy has been bathed, dressed in beautiful clothes, and adorned with flowers, his eyes...
Having anointed [the forehead], if they were to place only a single drop of *manosilā* on his forehead, it would not yet be called a "mind-painting" (*cittatilaka*).
However, when drops are made surrounded by various colors, it is then called a "mind-painting. This should be understood as being just like that.
This is what is known as "praise of the parts" (*padatthuti*).
Repetition by way of syllables, prefixes, and meanings is indeed what is called "strengthening" (daḷhīkamma).
For instance, when one says only once, "Friend," or "Venerable Sir," or "Yakkha," or "Snake," there is no strengthening.
But when one says, "Friend, friend! or "Venerable Sir, venerable sir! or "Yakkha, yakkha! or "Snake, snake!"—then [there is strengthening].

It is called "strengthening" (daḷhīkamma). In the same way, when the word "contact" (phassa) is uttered only once—as if one were merely pressing down with the tip of a stick—it is not yet called "strengthening.
It is only when it is repeated through the medium of its phonemes, prefixes, and meanings—stated as "contact, touching, full touching, the state of having touched"—that it is called "strengthening."
Thus, the secondary illustration proceeds by way of two points. By means of this as well, the meaning should be understood in all instances of the explanations of the terms as they are obtained.
"At that time there is contact" refers to the time when the first great wholesome sense-sphere consciousness [arises].
When it arises, at that time there is what is called "contact"—this is the meaning.
This, then, is the commentary on the exposition of the term "contact. Regarding the expositions of the subsequent terms beginning with "feeling," we shall explain only their specific distinctions;
the remainder should be understood according to the method already stated here.

3. Regarding the phrase "at that time" (*yasmiṃ samaye*): although it was begun with the question, "What kind of feeling (*vedanā*) is there at that time?", it is stated as "which" (*yaṃ*) by way of the word *sāta*.

In the expression "born of contact with the corresponding mind-consciousness element" (*tajjā-manoviññāṇa-dhātu-samphassajā*), the term "corresponding" (*tajjā*) refers to what is suitable or appropriate for that pleasant happiness (*sāta-sukha*). For this word *tajjā* also carries the sense of being "suitable."
It exists. As it is said: “How does one deliberate upon that which arises from those [objects] and is appropriate to them?
Or, it is called *tajjā* because it is born from those objects such as visible forms (*rūpa*) and so forth, as well as from the conditions for this pleasure.

Mental consciousness itself is the “mental-consciousness-element” (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) in the sense of being a constituent of reality (*dhātu*) by way of its lack of a sentient being. It is “born of contact” (*samphassaja*) because it is born from contact, or born in contact. Because it is dependent on the mind...
It is mental (cetasika). It is pleasant (sāta) in the sense of being sweet. This is what is meant:
that which, at that time, is the mental pleasure born of contact associated with the corresponding mind-consciousness element in the sense already described—this, at that time, is feeling (vedanā).
In this way, the construction should be understood in conjunction with all the terms.
Now, regarding the phrases "mental pleasure" (*cetasikaṃ sukhaṃ*) and so forth:
by the term *cetasika* (mental), bodily pleasure is excluded; by the term *sukha* (pleasure), mental pain is excluded. *Cetosamphassajaṃ* means born from contact with the mind.
*Sātaṃ sukhaṃ vedayitaṃ* means a pleasant feeling, not an unpleasant feeling; a happy feeling, not a painful feeling. Hereafter...
The three terms are stated according to the feminine gender: "pleasant feeling, not unpleasant; happy feeling, not painful.
This indeed is the meaning here.
4. In the description of perception (*saññā*), [it refers to] that which is born from contact with the corresponding mind-consciousness element, which is suitable for that unwholesome perception.
Born from contact with the mind-consciousness element. "Perception" (saññā) is a name for its own intrinsic nature. "Perceiving" (sañjānanā) is the mode of perceiving.
"The state of having perceived" (sañjānitattaṃ) is the condition of having been perceived.
This same method should also be understood in the exposition of volition (cetanā).
In the exposition of consciousness (*cittaniddesa*), it is called *citta* because of its variegated nature (*vicittatā*). It is called *mano* because, measuring out the object, it knows it.
*Mānasaṃ* is simply *mano*. However, in the passage, “The snare that moves through the air, which wanders as the mental (*mānaso*)”—here the associated state (*sampayuttadhamma*) is called ‘mental.
[And]: “How indeed, O Blessed One, is your disciple, delighting in your teaching...”
“A trainee who has not yet attained his heart’s desire might pass away while listening to people.
Here, *arahatta* (Arahatship) is called "the heart" (*mānasa*). But here, "heart" (*mānasa*) means "mind" (*mano*). This word has been expanded by way of its phonetic form (*byañjana*).
"The heart" (*hadaya*) refers to the mind (*citta*). As in the passage: "I will either cast your mind (*citta*) out, or I will split your heart (*hadaya*)," where it refers to the chest (*uro*).
It is called "the heart" (*hadaya*). In the passage, “As if knowing heart by heart, he cleaves it,” it refers to consciousness (*citta*).
In the passage, “The kidney and the heart,” it refers to the physical heart-organ (*hadayavatthu*). But here, it is consciousness itself that is called “the heart” in the sense of being internal.
That very same [consciousness] is “bright” (*paṇḍara*) in the sense of being pure. This is said with reference to the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). As it has been said: “This [mind] is luminous...”
“Monks, it is the mind, and yet it is defiled by adventitious defilements. However, because it has emerged from that [state],
even when unwholesome, it is described as being "pure," just as a river emerging from the Ganges is called the Ganges,
and one emerging from the Godhāvarī is called the Godhāvarī.
Regarding the phrase "mind as mind-base" (*mano manāyatanaṃ*): here, the mention of "mind" is for the purpose of showing that the mind itself possesses the status of a base. By this it is shown:
"This is not called the 'mind-base' because the mind is the base of something else, as in the case of a 'divine base'; rather, the mind itself is the base, thus it is the 'mind-base'.
In this context, [the term "base"] has the sense of an abode, the sense of a mine, and the sense of a meeting place.
Āyatana should be understood in the sense of a place of birth (*sañjāti*) and in the sense of a cause (*kāraṇa*).

For instance, in common usage, in such expressions as "the abode of Īśvara" (*issarāyatana*) or "the abode of Vāsudeva" (*vāsudevāyatana*), the word *āyatana* refers to a dwelling place. In such expressions as "the gold mine" (*suvaṇṇāyatana*) or "the silver mine" (*rajatāyatana*), it refers to a source or mine.
However, in the Teaching (*sāsana*), in such passages as "birds frequent that delightful abode" (*manorame āyatane sevanti naṃ vihaṅgamā*), it refers to a place of assembly or resort.
In such passages as “The southern region is the breeding ground for cattle,” it refers to the place of birth.

In such passages as “He attains the capacity for realization in each respective case, whenever there is a suitable occasion,” it refers to a cause. Here, however, it is appropriate in all three senses: as the place of birth, as the place of convergence, and as a cause.
This is a *āyatana* in the sense of being the place of birth, for it is here that phenomena such as contact (*phassa*) and the rest are born.
It is also an *āyatana* in the sense of being a meeting place, for external forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles converge upon it by way of being its objects.
Furthermore, it is an *āyatana* in the sense of being a cause, because it serves as the cause for contact and the rest by way of being their co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*), and so forth.
This should be understood. The mind-faculty (*manindriya*) has already had its meaning explained.

It cognizes, thus it is consciousness (*viññāṇa*); consciousness itself as an aggregate is the "consciousness-aggregate" (*viññāṇakkhandha*). Its meaning should be understood by way of being a "heap" (*rāsi*) and so forth.
It is reckoned as a "great mass of water. For here, in the sense of a heap, it is an aggregate (*khandha*).

It is spoken of in the sense of a quality in such passages as “the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration,” and so forth. In the passage, “The Blessed One saw a large log of wood,” it is spoken of in the sense of a mere designation. But here, however, “aggregate” (khandha) is spoken of in its conventional usage.

For in the sense of a heap, a single instance of consciousness is but one part of the aggregate of consciousness. Therefore, just as one who cuts down a portion of a tree [is said to cut the tree],...

"One cuts down a tree" is said; in the same way, even a single instance of consciousness that constitutes a portion of the aggregate of consciousness is spoken of as "the aggregate of consciousness" by way of conventional designation (*rūḷhi*).
"The corresponding mind-consciousness element" means the mind-consciousness element that is suitable for those phenomena such as contact and so forth.
For in this term, a single consciousness is spoken of by three names: it is "mind" (*mano*) in the sense of measuring; "consciousness" (*viññāṇa*) in the sense of cognizing;
and "element" (*dhātu*) in the sense of its own-nature or in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being.

Thus, in this pentad beginning with contact, first, contact is indeed contact itself, and not that which is born from the mind-consciousness element produced by those [three]; and as for the mind, it is that mind-consciousness element produced by those [three].
Thus, for this reason, the designation "born of that contact with the mind-consciousness element" was not applied to these two terms.
However, although [terms such as] "applied thought" (*vitakka*) and so forth are applicable, they were not mentioned here because they have been excluded.
Furthermore, having analyzed these phenomena—consisting of contact as the fifth factor—individually and separately, [one should understand them].
The Blessed One performed a difficult feat by rescuing the formal rule (*paññatti*).

For if various waters or various oils were placed in a single vessel and churned for a day, it might be possible to know their difference by seeing, smelling, or tasting the diversity of their color, fragrance, and flavor. Even so, this [rescuing of the rule] is said to be difficult.

But by the Fully Enlightened One, who extracted the designation after having performed a distinct analysis of these immaterial phenomena— mind and mental factors— as they occur with a single object, an exceedingly difficult task was accomplished.
Therefore, the Venerable Elder Nāgasena said:
“It was difficult, Great King, that was done by the Blessed One. “What, venerable Nāgasena, was difficult that was done by the Blessed One?

“It was difficult, Great King, that was done by the Blessed One, that the distinction was declared among these formless mental states—the mind and its concomitants—arising with a single object: ‘This is contact; this is feeling...’”
“This is perception, this is volition, this is consciousness. “Give me a simile, Bhante,” [the king said].
“Suppose, great king, a certain man were to plunge into the ocean in a boat, take up some water in the hollow of his hand, taste it with his tongue, and then know:
‘Great king, would that man be able to discern—this is water from the Ganges, this is water from the Yamunā?’”
“Is this water from the Aciravatī, this water from the Sarabhū, or this water from the Mahī?
“It is difficult to know, Bhante. “Great King, even more difficult than that was what was accomplished by the Blessed One, namely:
‘...of these formless mental states and mental factors... this is mind.’”
7. In the exposition of *vitakka* (initial application of mind): it is *takka* by way of reasoning (*takkanā*).

Its occurrence by way of reasoning should be understood as follows: "He reasoned about a bitter [substance], he reasoned about a jar, he reasoned about a cart, he reasoned about a league (*yojana*), he reasoned about half a league.
This is the term for the intrinsic nature (*sabhāvapada*) of *takka*. It is *vitakka* by way of initial application of mind; this is the name for a stronger form of *takka*.
*Saṅkappa* (intention) is so called by way of being well-constructed (*suṭṭhu kappana*). *Appanā* (absorption) is the one-pointed mind that settles upon the object;
the second word is augmented by means of a prefix. Alternatively, absorption is more powerful, hence it is *byappanā*.

The settling of the mind upon the object, establishing it there, is *cetaso abhiniropanā* (the directing of the mind). It has attained the state of wholesomeness through its quality of leading out (*niyyānikatā*) according to reality (*yāthāvatāya*).
"Wholesome intention" (*sammā-saṅkappo*) means an intention that is praised.

8. In the exposition of investigation (*vicāra*): "movement" (*cāro*) refers to the act of moving upon an object; this is its term for essential nature (*sabhāvapada*). It is "investigation" (*vicāro*) by way of investigating.
It is "sub-investigation" (*anuvicāro*) by way of investigating after having followed along. It is "close-investigation" (*upavicāro*) by way of investigating after having approached.

Alternatively, the words have been expanded by means of prefixes. Because it places the mind upon the object by connecting it, like a string to a bowstring, there is "connecting of the mind" (*anusandhānatā*).
Because it remains as if not looking closely at the object, there is "not-looking-closely" (*anupekkhanatā*).
Alternatively, "not-looking-closely" (*anupekkhanatā*) is the state of not looking closely by way of wandering about.

9. In the explanation of *pīti*, "rapture" (*pīti*) is a term for its intrinsic nature (*sabhāvapada*). The state of one who is gladdened is "gladness" (*pāmojja*). The mode of being delighted is "delight" (*āmodanā*);

the mode of being thoroughly delighted is "thorough delight" (*pamodanā*). Or, just as the unification of medicines, oils, or hot and cold water is called "mixing," so too this rapture is a "mixing" by way of unifying mental states. By virtue of the prefix (*upasagga*),...

But when one has adorned [the mind], it is called "rejoicing" (*āmodanā*) and "delighting" (*pamodanā*). It causes one to laugh, thus it is "laughter" (*hāsa*); it causes one to laugh loudly, thus it is "loud laughter" (*pahāsa*).
This is a designation for the modes of being cheerful and exceedingly cheerful. "Vittī" means "wealth" (*vitta*); this is a name for riches.

However, because it is a condition for mental joy (*somanassa*), it is called "vitti" due to its similarity to wealth. For just as joy arises in a wealthy person depending upon his wealth, so too does joy arise in one possessed of rapture (*pīti*) depending upon that rapture.
Because mental joy (*somanassa*) arises dependent upon it, it is therefore called "elation" (*vitti*).

This is the name for *pīti* when it is established in its essential nature as contentment. However, a person possessing *pīti* is called "exultant" (*udagga*) because of the uplifted and elevated state of their body and mind.

The state of being exultant is "exultancy" (*odagya*). "Serenity of mind" (*attamanatā*) means the state of one’s own mind being pleased; for the mind of one who is dissatisfied is the basis for suffering.
One's own mind does not exist [as a separate entity]; rather, because it is the basis for happiness when one is pleased, it is called "one's own mind.
Thus, being one's own mind is *attamanatā*, which means "being pleased with oneself" (*sakamanatā*). The meaning is the state of being pleased with oneself.
Furthermore, since that is not "one's own mind" belonging to anyone else, it is simply a state of consciousness, a mental factor (*cetasika dhamma*).
Therefore, it is called "gladness of mind. 11.
In the exposition of one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*): it stands upon the object by way of immovability; thus, it is "stability" (*ṭhiti*). The following two terms are expanded by means of prefixes.
Furthermore, it stands by gathering together the associated mental states upon the object; thus, it is "firm stability" (*saṇṭhiti*). The object...
"Having plunged into and entered" means "it stands," thus it is *avaṭṭhiti*. For in the wholesome side, four states plunge into the object:

faith, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. Therefore, faith is called "conviction" (*okappanā*), mindfulness "non-forgetting" (*apilāpanatā*), concentration "steadiness" (*avaṭṭhiti*), and wisdom "thorough penetration" (*pariyogāhanā*).
On the unwholesome side, however, three states [plunge into] the object...
They plunge in—namely, craving, views, and ignorance. For that very reason, they are called "floods" (ogha). Furthermore, one-pointedness of mind is not strong here.

Just as when a dusty place is sprinkled with water and swept clean, the dust settles for only a short time, but as it dries and dries again, it rises up once more to its natural state; even so, on the side of the unwholesome...
One-pointedness of mind is not strong. However, just as when water is poured from jars into a place that has been dug with a spade and then pounded,
kneaded, and rubbed, an image appears in a polished mirror as if it were there even after a hundred years have passed—
as if it had occurred at that very moment— so too, on the side of the wholesome, one-pointedness of mind is strong.
It is "non-distraction" (*avisāhāra*) because it is the opposite of the distracted state that occurs by way of restlessness and doubt.
Indeed, the mind that proceeds by way of restlessness and doubt is said to be "distracted. But since this [state] does not have such distraction, it is "non-distraction" (*avikkhepa*).
Furthermore, by way of restlessness and doubt, the mind is said to be "carried away" (*visāhaṭa*), being drawn hither and thither. This...
Furthermore, the state of a mind that is thus undisturbed is "undisturbed-mindedness" (*avisāhaṭamānasatā*).
"Tranquility" (*samatha*) is threefold: tranquility of mind, tranquility of legal issues, and tranquility of all conditioned formations.
Among these, one-pointedness of mind within the eight attainments is called "tranquility of mind. For by depending upon that, the wavering of the mind [is stilled].
The agitation of the mind is stilled and pacified; therefore, it is called "tranquillity of mind" (*cittasamatha*).

The sevenfold method of settling, beginning with resolution face-to-face (*sammukhāvinaya*), is called "settlement of legal issues" (*adhikaraṇasamatha*); for by resorting to these, various legal issues are settled and pacified, and therefore it is called "settlement of legal issues.
Furthermore, because all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) are stilled by resorting to Nibbāna...
They are stilled; therefore, it is called "the stilling of all formations. In this sense, "mental stillness" (cittasamatha) is intended.

It exercises lordship over the characteristic of concentration, thus it is the "faculty of concentration" (samādhindriya). It is not shaken by restlessness, thus it is the "power of concentration" (samādhibala).
"Right concentration" (sammāsamādhi) refers to concentration as it truly is, liberating concentration, and wholesome concentration.
12. In the exposition of the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*): faith is so called by way of believing in the qualities of the Buddha and others;
or, it is faith because one believes in and places conviction in the Jewels, such as the Buddha. "Believing" (*saddahana*) is the mode of believing.

It is "conviction" (*okappanā*) because it plunges into the qualities of the Buddha and others, as if breaking through and entering them. By means of this, sentient beings become exceedingly confident in the qualities of the Buddha and others.
"Faith itself is the act of placing confidence, thus it is 'confidence' (*abhippasāda*).

Now, since another method has been introduced by means of compound terms such as the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) and so forth, the word-commentary is composed by taking only the initial term—this being the rule (*dhammatā*) in the Abhidhamma—therefore it is stated again: 'faith. Or, just as the faculty of a woman is the 'female-faculty' (*itthindriya*)."
This is not so. Rather, it is faith itself as a faculty that is called the "faith-faculty" (*saddhindriya*).

Thus, the word "faith" is stated again for the purpose of making known the state of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇabhāva*). In this way, the purpose of restating the initial term in all the explanations of the individual members should be understood.

It is the "faith-faculty" because it exercises the function of sovereignty (*indaṭṭha*) regarding the characteristic of resolution (*adhimokkha*). It is the "power of faith" (*saddhābala*) because it does not waver in the face of lack of faith (*asaddhiya*).
13. In the exposition of the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*), the term "mental factor" (*cetasika*) is stated for the purpose of demonstrating that energy is invariably a mental factor.
For this energy is said: "Bhikkhus, whatever is bodily energy, that too is the enlightenment factor of energy;
whatever is mental energy, that too is the enlightenment factor of energy. Thus it is included in the summary."

In such suttas as these, although it is called "bodily" because it arises for one who is walking back and forth and so on, there is no such thing as a "bodily" [state] like body-consciousness; rather, to show that this is purely mental, it is stated as "mental.
"Exertion of energy" (*vīriyārambha*) means exertion characterized as energy. By this, he excludes other types of exertion. For this word "exertion" (*ārambha*) refers to action.
The term *vīriya* occurs with reference to many meanings: in the sense of an offense, an action, energy, and violence, as well as in the sense of agitation.
As it is said: “Whatever suffering arises, all of it has its cause in undertaking (*ārambha*);
through the cessation of undertakings, there is no arising of suffering.”
For here, *kamma* is what has come down as "undertaking" (*ārambha*). In the passage, “He undertakes [the action] and feels remorse,” it refers to an offense (*āpatti*).

In the passage, “Great sacrifices involving great undertakings do not yield great fruit,” it refers to the act of erecting a sacrificial post and so forth. In the passage, “Exert yourselves, strive, apply yourselves to the Buddha’s teaching,” it refers to energy (*vīriya*).
In the passage, “[He slaughtered] a living being for the sake of the ascetic Gotama... [it refers to the taking of life].

In the phrase "they undertake," it refers to violence (*hiṃsā*). In the phrase "he abstains from the destruction of seeds and plants," it refers to the disturbance consisting of cutting, breaking, and so forth.
But here, only energy (*vīriya*) is intended. Therefore he said: "'Exertion of energy' means an undertaking characterized as energy.
For energy is called "exertion" in the sense of being undertaken; this is its term for essential nature (*sabhāvapada*).

*nikkama* is by way of emerging from indolence; *parakkama* is by way of stepping toward higher and higher states; *uyyāma* is by way of exerting oneself after having risen up; *vāyāma* is by way of striving; *ussāha* is by way of enthusiasm;
*ussoḷhi* is by way of supreme enthusiasm; *thāma* is in the sense of firmness; and [it is] by way of sustaining the mind and mental factors, or by way of their proceeding without interruption.
It is called *dhiti* because it sustains the wholesome continuum (*kusalasantāna*).
According to another method: it is exertion for the removal of sensual desires; it is striving for the severing of bonds;
it is effort for crossing over the flood; it is endeavor in the sense of going to the further shore; it is enthusiasm in the sense of being the precursor.
This is "exertion" (*ussoḷhi*) in the sense of being excessive; this is "strength" (*thāma*) because it overthrows obstacles; this is "fortitude" (*dhiti*) because it acts with steadfastness.
When it occurs in the manner of thinking, "Let there remain only skin, sinews, and bone," it is "unrelaxed effort" by way of its unslackened exertion;
the meaning is "firm effort" or "strong effort. And because this energy (*vīriya*)...

In the matter of performing wholesome deeds, one does not lay down the desire, does not lay down the burden, does not let it drop, does not relinquish it, and brings about a state of mind that does not shrink back; therefore, it is said: "having desire not laid down" and "having the burden not laid down.
Just as, for example, when they say to a draft-ox in a place where the ground is saturated with water, "Take up the burden!"...
Just as a bullock, pressing its knees against the ground, bears the yoke and does not allow itself to fall, even so does energy lift up and exert itself in the task of performing wholesome deeds;
therefore it is called "the exertion of the burden. Because it exercises lordship over the characteristic of exertion, it is the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*).
Because it is unshakable by laziness, it is the power of energy (*vīriyabala*).
Right effort is so called because it is wholesome effort that leads to the state of things as they truly are. 14.
In the exposition of the faculty of mindfulness (*satindriya*), mindfulness (*sati*) is defined by way of remembering; this is the term for the intrinsic nature of mindfulness.

It is "recollection" (*anussati*) by way of recollecting again and again. It is "counter-recollection" (*paṭissati*) by way of counter-remembering, as if having gone directly toward [the object] and remembered it.
Or rather, this is merely augmented by a prefix. "The mode of mindfulness" (saraṇākāra) is "mindfulness-ness" (saraṇatā).
However, since "mindfulness-ness" is also a name for the three types of mindfulness, the term *sati* is mentioned again to preclude that [broader sense].

The meaning here is: "mindfulness-ness" as that which is reckoned as mindfulness (*satisaṅkhātā*). It is "retention" (*dhāraṇatā*) because of its state of retaining what has been heard and mastered. By means of what is reckoned as "entering into" (*anupavisana*)...

In the sense of plunging in, the state of not floating is non-floatingness (*apilāpanatā*). For just as the hollow shells of gourds and the like float upon water and do not sink into it, so too this [mindfulness] does not float upon the object when the object is present;
rather, it enters into the object, and therefore it is called "non-floatingness.
It is non-forgetfulness (*asammussanatā*) because of its quality of not forgetting what was done long ago or spoken long ago. Regarding the characteristic of being established...
It is called a faculty (*indriya*) because it exercises lordship (*indaṭṭha*) over its own characteristic mark. The faculty known as mindfulness is the mindfulness-faculty (*satindriya*).

It is the power of mindfulness (*satibala*) because it does not waver in negligence. Right mindfulness (*sammāsati*) is that which is mindful of things as they truly are, which leads to liberation, and which is wholesome mindfulness.
16. In the exposition of the wisdom-faculty (*paññindriya*), it is so called in the sense of making known (*paññāpana*) by way of making each respective object clear.
Wisdom (*paññā*). Alternatively, it is called wisdom because it knows phenomena (*dhamma*) by way of this or that aspect, such as impermanence and so forth;

this is its term for essential nature (*sabhāvapada*). The mode of understanding is "understanding" (*pajānanā*). It is "investigation" (*vicaya*) because it investigates impermanence and so forth; "thorough investigation" (*pavicaya*) is the same term augmented by a prefix.
It is "investigation of phenomena" (*dhammavicaya*) because it investigates the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths. By way of discerning the characteristics of impermanence and so forth...
*Sal-lakkhaṇā*. That same [process], further distinguished by prefixes, is called *upalakkhaṇā* (characterization) and *paccupalakkhaṇā* (re-characterization).
The state of being wise is *paṇḍiccaṃ*; the state of being skillful is *kosallaṃ*; the state of being clever is *nepuññaṃ*.
It is *vebhabyā* (discernment) by way of the discerning of impermanence and so forth; it is *cintā* (reflection) by way of reflecting upon impermanence and so forth. Or, that in which it arises is...

It is called *cintā* because it causes one to reflect upon such things as impermanence (*anicca*). It is called *upaparikkhā* because it investigates such things as impermanence. *Bhūrī* is a name for the earth (*pathavī*).
This [wisdom] is also called *bhūrī* because, in its subtle nature and its vast extent, it is like the earth. Therefore it is said: "The earth is called *bhūrī*.
One who is endowed with wisdom that is equal to the earth—vast and expansive—is called 'one of vast wisdom' (*bhūripañña*)."
Moreover, this is a synonym for wisdom (*paññā*): "vast" (*bhūrī*). It is called "vast" because it delights in the true meaning (*bhūta-attha*).

It is called "intelligence" (*medhā*) because, like a thunderbolt upon a mountain crag, it crushes or destroys the defilements (*kilesa*). Alternatively, it is intelligence in the sense of quick grasping and retention.

That in which it arises carries one across—both in the practice for one's own welfare and in the penetration of the characteristics of things as they truly are (*yathāvalakkhaṇa-paṭivedha*)—through the associated mental states.

*Pariṇāyikā*: It is a guide. *Vipassanā* is so called because it sees phenomena by way of impermanence and so forth. *Sampajañña* is so called because it knows impermanence and so forth in their proper modes.

Like a goad used for the purpose of bringing onto the path a horse that has strayed from the road, it "prods" the crooked mind that is running off-course for the purpose of bringing it onto the path; thus it is like a goad, a *patoda*. [This refers to] the characteristic of seeing.

It exercises lordship, thus it is a faculty (*indriya*). The faculty known as wisdom is the wisdom-faculty (*paññindriya*). It does not waver because of ignorance, thus it is the power of wisdom (*paññābala*).
In the sense of cutting through the defilements, wisdom itself is a sword; thus it is the "sword of wisdom" (*paññāsattha*). In the sense of being preeminent, wisdom itself is a palace;

thus it is the "palace of wisdom" (*paññāpāsāda*). In the sense of illuminating, wisdom itself is light; thus it is the "light of wisdom" (*paññāāloka*). In the sense of radiating brilliance, wisdom itself is an effulgence; thus it is the "effulgence of wisdom" (*paññāobhāsa*).

Wisdom itself is the light in the sense of illuminating; thus it is "wisdom-light. For when one possessed of wisdom sits cross-legged, the ten-thousandfold world-system becomes a single illumination, a single radiance, and a single light; therefore this was said.
Now, although this meaning is established even by a single word among these three terms, as for those [words] beginning with: "Bhikkhus, there are these four..."
“Luminances. Which four? The moonlight, the sunlight, the light of fire, and the light of wisdom. These, monks, are the four luminances.

Among these four luminances, monks, the foremost is this: the light of wisdom. Likewise: “Monks, there are these four radiances... [and so on] ...monks, there are these four lamps,” for the sake of beings.
The discourses were taught according to the underlying inclinations [of those to be trained], and here too, the teaching has been given in accordance with that very principle.
For when the meaning is analyzed through various modes, it becomes well-analyzed; otherwise, one person understands it in one way, while another understands it in another way.

Furthermore, [the Dhamma is so called] in the sense of providing delight, in the sense of bestowing delight, in the sense of generating delight, in the sense of being highly esteemed, and in the sense of its manifestation being rare.
Wisdom itself is the jewel; thus it is the "wisdom-jewel" (*paññāratana*) in the sense of being incomparable and in the sense of being the enjoyment of extraordinary beings.
It is non-delusion (*amoha*) because beings are not deluded by it, or because it itself is not deluded regarding its object.

The term "investigation of phenomena" (*dhammavicaya*) has already been explained. But why is it mentioned again here? It is for the purpose of showing that non-delusion is the direct opposite of delusion. By this, he demonstrates the following:
— This non-delusion (*amoha*) is not merely a state distinct from delusion; rather, it is the antidote to delusion.

Here, what is intended by the term "non-delusion" is that which is designated as the investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicaya*). "Right view" (*sammādiṭṭhi*) is the wholesome view that leads to liberation according to reality.
19. In the description of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*): "That which is the life-span of those immaterial states" refers to the life-span of those associated immaterial states.
That which is "life" (āyu) in the sense of causing to reach [its end]—for when that exists, immaterial phenomena (arūpadhammā) go, proceed, and continue;

therefore it is called "life. This is its term for essential nature (sabhāvapada). However, because these phenomena only abide, persist, endure, move, turn, and maintain themselves when life itself exists, the terms "stability" (ṭhiti) and so forth are stated. This is the etymological explanation (vacanattha).
In this context: by means of this they stand, thus it is *ṭhiti* (stability). They maintain themselves, thus it is *yapanā* (maintenance); likewise, *yāpanā*.

However, in the case of those who awaken [to this], the short vowel is applied in the first term. By means of this they move about, thus it is *iriyanā* (wandering). They proceed, thus it is *vattanā* (proceeding).

They protect, thus it is *pālanā* (protection). That by which they live is *jīvitaṃ* (life). It exercises the function of a lord (*indaṭṭha*) with respect to the characteristic of sustaining, thus it is the *jīvitindriyaṃ* (life-faculty).
30. In the exposition of the power of moral shame (*hiribala*), "at that time" (*tasmiṃ samaye*) means by whatever state [of mind] at that time.
Alternatively, having applied a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*), the meaning should be understood as: "whatever state is at that time.

Regarding "by that which is to be shamed" (*hiriyitabbenā*), this is the instrumental case used in the sense of the accusative. The meaning is: one feels shame for and feels disgust toward those states such as bodily misconduct (*kāyaduccarita*) which are worthy of being shamed.
"Of evil" means of base things. "Of unwholesome states" means of states produced by lack of skill.

"In the attainment": this is also an instrumental case used in the sense of the accusative. The meaning is that one feels shame and disgust toward the attainment, the acquisition, and the possession of those states.
31. In the exposition of the power of moral dread (*ottappabala*), the term "by that which is to be dreaded" (*ottappitabbenā*) is used in the instrumental case to express the sense of a cause.

The meaning is: one feels moral dread (*ottappati*), that is, one fears, by means of bodily misconduct and so forth—which are suitable for being dreaded and serve as causes for moral dread—and by means of the aforementioned meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) which likewise serve as causes for moral dread.

32. In the exposition of non-greed (*alobha*): non-greed is so called by way of not being greedy. It is also non-greed because "one does not become greedy. This is its term for intrinsic nature (*sabhāvapada*).

"Not being greedy" (*alubbhana*) refers to the mode of not being greedy. A person possessing greed is said to be "greedy. One who is not greedy is "non-greedy. The state of being non-greedy is "non-greediness" (*alubbhitatta*).
Because it is the opposite of attachment (*sārāga*), it is "non-attachment" (*asārāga*). "Non-attachment" (*asārajjana*) refers to the mode of not becoming attached.
The mode of being unshaken is *asārajjana*. The state of one who is unshaken is *asārajjitatta*. "Not coveting" (*anabhijjhā*) means the absence of covetousness.
"The wholesome root of non-greed" (*alobha-kusalamūla*) refers to the wholesome root known as non-greed. For non-greed is the root of wholesome states in the sense of a condition;
thus it is a "wholesome root. Furthermore, it is a "wholesome root" because it is both wholesome and a root in the sense of a condition.
33. In the exposition of non-hatred (*adosa*): it is non-hatred by way of not being hateful. It is also non-hatred because "one does not hate. This is its term for essential nature (*sabhāva*).

Non-hatred (*adussanā*) is the mode of not being hateful. The state of one who has not hated is "non-hatred-ness" (*adussitatta*). Because it is the opposite of ill-will (*byāpāda*), it is "not ill-will," thus non-ill-will (*abyāpāda*).

Because it is the opposite of anger and suffering (*kodha-dukkha*), it is "not being afflicted," thus non-affliction (*abyāpajja*). It is the root of the wholesome (*kusalamūla*) designated as non-hatred.
Non-hatred (*adosa*) is a root of the wholesome. Its meaning is exactly as previously stated. 40–41.

Regarding the exposition of bodily tranquility (*kāyapassaddhi*) and so forth: since "body" (*kāya*) here refers to the three aggregates (*khandha*), it is therefore said, "of the feeling aggregate," and so on.
Tranquility (*passaddhi*) is that by which those phenomena become calmed, free from distress, and attain composure.
The second term has been augmented by means of a prefix. "Tranquillizing" (*passambhanā*) refers to the mode of tranquillizing. The second term has been augmented by means of a prefix.
The state of the triad of aggregates that has been thoroughly calmed through the possession of serenity (*passaddhi*) is "thoroughly calmedness" (*paṭippassambhitatta*).
By all these terms, the subsiding of the fever of the defilements (*kilesa-daratha*) of the three aggregates is indicated.
Thus it has been explained. By the second method, the subsiding of the distress of the consciousness aggregate is explained.
42–43. *Lahutā* (lightness) is the mode of lightness. *Lahupariṇāmatā* (light transformability): those phenomena have a light transformation, thus they are "light-transformable" (*lahupariṇāmā*);
their state is "light transformability" (*lahupariṇāmatā*); what is meant is the capacity for rapid, repeated transformation. *Adandhanatā* (non-sluggishness).

This is a term for the negation of heaviness; the meaning is "the state of not being burdensome. "Non-stiffness" means the absence of rigidity due to the lack of the burden of defilements such as conceit.
Thus, by the first [characteristic], the mode of lightness of the three aggregates is described;
by the second, the mode of lightness of the consciousness aggregate is described.
44–45. *Mudutā* means the state of being soft (*mudubhāva*). *Maddavatā*: *maddava* is said to be smooth and polished; the state of being *maddava* is *maddavatā*.
*Akakkhaḷatā* means the state of being non-harsh (*akakkhaḷabhāva*). *Akathinatā* means the state of being non-rigid (*akathinabhāva*).

Here too, according to the former method, the mode of softness of the three aggregates is described, and according to the latter method, it is the mode of softness of the consciousness aggregate that is described.
46–47. *Kammaññatā* means excellence in being workable; the meaning is "fitness for application to wholesome activity. The remaining two terms have been expanded merely for the sake of the phrasing.

For even with these two terms, according to the former method, the mode of workability of the three aggregates is described, and according to the latter method, that of the consciousness aggregate alone.
48–49. *Paguṇatā* means the state of being proficient; it has the sense of being free from illness and free from sickness. The remaining two phrases have been expanded for the sake of the syllables.

Here too, according to the former method, the mode of non-sickness regarding the three aggregates is described, and according to the latter method, it is the mode of non-sickness regarding the consciousness aggregate that is explained.
50–51. *Ujukatā* means straightness; the sense is "proceeding in a straight manner.
*Ujukatā* is the state of the three aggregates that are straight and of the consciousness aggregate. *Ajimhatā* is the negation of the state of being crooked like a cow’s urine stream.
*Avaṅkatā* is the negation of the state of being curved like the crescent moon. *Akuṭilatā* is the negation of the state of being bent like the tip of a plough.
For he who, having indeed committed an evil deed, says, "I did not do it," goes [to hell] and, because of his retreating back, becomes known as "Crooked like Cow-Urine.
He who, while committing an evil deed, says, "I am afraid of evil," mostly becomes known as "Crooked like the Crescent Moon" because of his curvature.
He who, while committing an evil deed, says, "Who would not be afraid of evil?"...
One who is not excessively crooked is called "crooked like the tip of a plough. Alternatively, one whose three doors of action are all impure is called "crooked like a cow's urine-stream.
One whose two [doors] are [impure] is called "crooked like the crescent moon.
One whose single [door] is [impure] is called "crooked like the tip of a plough."

But the Dīgha-bhāṇakas say: A certain bhikkhu who, throughout his entire life, wanders among the twenty-one improper modes of seeking alms and the six improper resorts is called “crooked like a cow’s urination.

One who fulfills the fourfold pure virtue in the first stage of life, being modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training, but remains similar to the former in the middle and final stages of life, is called “crooked like the crescent moon.”
This is the name. One person fulfills the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*) during both the first and middle stages of life;
he is modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training, and remains like the former in the final stage of life. This is called "crooked as the tip of a plough.
The state of such a person—who is thus crooked due to defilements—is called "crookedness," "deviousness," or "insincerity" (*jimhatā*, *vaṅkatā*, *kuṭilatā*).

By way of their negation, [qualities] such as "not crookedness" and so forth are stated. The teaching is given solely with reference to the aggregates (*khandha*). For these qualities, such as not being crooked and so on, belong to the aggregates and not to a person (*puggala*).
Thus, by all these terms, according to the former method, they refer to the three aggregates, and according to the latter method, to the consciousness aggregate (*viññāṇakkhandha*);
[this is said] because of the absence of defilement in these formless phenomena (*arūpī dhammā*).
It should be understood that it is described as having the very form of a straight line.

Now, this section on absorption (appanā) which has been stated under the heading "and so forth" (yevāpanaka), serves as a concise exposition of precisely those "and-so-forth" factors shown in the section on the enumeration of states (dhammuddesa).
The discussion of the section on exposition (niddesa) is concluded.
Thus, the section on the Definition of Dhamma (Dhammavavatthānavāra), adorned with eight chapters—consisting of four chapters in the Section on Enumeration (Uddesavāra):
the Inquiry, the Description of Occasion, the Enumeration of Dhammas, and Absorption; and four chapters in the Section on Exposition (Niddesavāra):
the Inquiry, the Description of Occasion, the Enumeration of Dhammas, and Absorption—is hereby completed.
The Section on Components (Koṭṭhāsavāra) 58–120.
Now, the Section on Compendium (Saṅgahavāra), beginning with the words “At that time, there are four aggregates,” is commenced.
It is threefold by way of enumeration (uddesa), exposition (niddesa), and detailed exposition (paṭiniddesa). Therein, “At that time... [and so forth].
"Four aggregates"—this and so forth is the *uddesa* (enumeration). "Which four aggregates are there at that time?"—this and so forth is the *niddesa* (explanation).
"Which aggregate of feeling is there at that time?"—this and so forth is to be understood as the *paṭiniddesa* (detailed explanation).
Therein, in the section on the enumeration, there are twenty-three sections beginning with "four aggregates. Their meaning is as follows:

It should be understood as follows: at whatever time the first great wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere arises, all those more than fifty states included in the Canon that have arisen at that time by way of being factors of consciousness—excluding the *yevāpanaka* (miscellaneous) factors—are, when subsumed together in the sense of a heap, simply four aggregates (*khandhā*).
This is according to the sense of "base" (*āyatana*) as explained below.
There are two bases. In the sense of intrinsic nature, in the sense of emptiness, and in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being, there are only two elements.
In the sense of nutriment, reckoned as condition, three among these states are nutriments; the remainder are not nutriments.
But are these not conditions for one another, or for the matter originated by them? They are not non-conditions.

However, these [nutriments] exist both in that way and otherwise; thus, although they share the same status as conditions, they are "additional" conditions (*atireka-paccaya*), and for that reason they are called "nutriments" (*āhāra*).

How so? For among these, the nutriment of contact (*phassa-āhāra*) acts as a condition not only for the remaining mental states and mental factors (*citta-cetasika*), but it also brings about the three types of feeling (*vedanā*). The nutriment of mental volition (*manosañcetanā-āhāra*) [acts as a condition] for those...
"It is a condition and it brings about the three existences (bhava). Consciousness as nutriment (viññāṇāhāra) is their condition and it brings about rebirth-linking name-and-form.
"But is that not itself merely fruition (vipāka), whereas this is wholesome consciousness (kusala-viññāṇa)?

"Although it is wholesome consciousness, it is nevertheless called 'consciousness as nutriment' because of its similarity to that [fruition]. Or else, these three are called nutriments in the sense of being supportive."
These are so called because they serve as supporting conditions for associated states, just as physical food is for the material body.
Therefore it has been said: "The immaterial nutriments are a condition, by way of nutriment-condition, for associated states and for the material phenomena originated by them."
Another method: Because they are specific conditions for the internal continuity, edible food and these three states are called "nutriments.
For beings who subsist on edible food, edible food is the specific condition for the material body;

contact is the specific condition for feeling in the mental body; mental volition is the specific condition for consciousness; and consciousness is the specific condition for name-and-form. As it has been said:

“Just as, bhikkhus, this body is sustained by nutriment, it persists dependent on nutriment and does not persist without nutriment; so too, feeling has contact as its condition, consciousness has formations as its condition, and name-and-form has consciousness as its condition.
However, in the sense of predominance, only eight factors are faculties, and not the remainder. Therefore it is said: “There are eight faculties.
In the sense of closely contemplating, only five factors are jhāna-factors. Therefore it is said: “Jhāna consists of five factors.”
In the sense of leading out and in the sense of being a cause, only five factors constitute the path-factors. Therefore it is said: "The path consists of five factors.
For although there is the Noble Eightfold Path, in a mundane state of consciousness three abstinences cannot be obtained at one moment;
therefore it is called "five-factored. [And as for the objection: "But has it not been said: 'As to the so-called "path already traveled"..."?"

In this sutta, with the words, “Bhikkhu, this is a designation for the Noble Eightfold Path,” the meaning is illustrated by the statement that just as the supramundane path is eightfold, so too the preliminary path of insight is likewise eightfold.
Does it follow from this that there must also be a mundane eightfold path? It need not be so.
For this teaching in the Suttas is indeed a teaching by way of a figurative method (pariyāyadesanā). Therefore he said:
"But previously his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood were already quite purified. This, however, is a teaching by way of the non-figurative method (nippariyāyadesanā).
For when the mind is mundane, the three abstinences cannot be obtained in a single moment; therefore it is stated as being "five-factored" (pañcaṅgika) alone.
In the sense of being unshakable, however, there are five states that are powers (*bala*). In the sense of being roots, three states are causes (*hetu*).
In the sense of touching, one state is contact (*phassa*). In the sense of being felt, one state is feeling (*vedanā*).
In the sense of perceiving, one state is perception (*saññā*). In the sense of intending, one state is volition (*cetanā*). In the sense of cognizing, one state is consciousness (*citta*).
In the sense of a heap and in the sense of being felt, the single phenomenon is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-khandha*).
In the sense of a heap and in the sense of perceiving, the single phenomenon is the aggregate of perception (*saññā-khandha*).

In the sense of a heap and in the sense of volitional formation, the single phenomenon is the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhāra-khandha*). In the sense of a heap and in the sense of cognizing, the single phenomenon is the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇa-khandha*).
In the sense of cognizing and in the sense of being a "base" as described above, it is simply the mind-base (*manāyatana*).
In the sense of cognizing and in the sense of being predominant (*adhipati*), it is simply the mind-faculty (*manindriya*).

In the sense of cognizing and in the sense of being empty of intrinsic nature and devoid of a self, it is only the single phenomenon called the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), and not the rest. However, setting aside consciousness itself, according to what has been stated...
In terms of their actual meaning, all remaining phenomena are simply the single base of mental objects (dhammāyatana) and the single element of mental objects (dhammadhātu).
Furthermore, by the phrase "or whatever [states] at that time," even here the aforementioned "whatever-it-may-be" (yevāpanaka) states are included within this absorption section;
and as it is here, so it is everywhere else. Beyond this, we shall not investigate even so much as this.
The meaning should be understood in the same manner as explained previously in the sections on the Exposition (Niddesa) and the Subsequent Exposition (Paṭiniddesa).
The Section on Compendium (Saṅgahavāra) is finished.
"The Section on Divisions" (Koṭṭhāsavāra) is also another name for this very section.
The Section on Emptiness (Suññatavāra), §§121–145.
Now, the Section on Emptiness is commenced with the words, "At that time, however, there are states" (*dhammā honti*).

It is established in two ways: by way of enumeration (*uddesa*) and by way of exposition (*niddesa*). Therein, in the section on enumeration, there are twenty-four sections together with the phrase "there are states."
They exist. And in all the categories, a numerical limit such as "four," "two," or "three" has not been stated.
Why? Because they have already been delimited in the Section on Compendium (Saṅgaha-vāra). Only those phenomena (dhammā) delimited there are mentioned here as well.
For herein neither a being (satta), nor an entity (bhāva), nor a self (attā) is found; these are merely phenomena (dhammā), mere phenomena, devoid of essence and lacking a leader.
These are stated for the purpose of illustrating this emptiness. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as follows:

at whatever time the first great wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere arises, at that time the more than fifty states that have arisen by way of mental factors are simply states (dhammā) in the sense of their own intrinsic nature (sabhāva). There is no other being (satta) or entity (bhāva) whatsoever.

“...or a man, or a person. Likewise, in the sense of a heap, they are simply the aggregates (khandhas). Thus, the application of the meaning in all instances should be understood according to the same method as before.

However, because there is no factor of jhāna other than jhāna itself, nor any factor of the path (maggaṅga) other than the path itself, it is therefore stated here simply: “there is jhāna, there is the path. In the sense of close contemplation (upanijjhāyana),...
For indeed, it is meditation itself that constitutes the path in the sense of being the cause, and not any other being or entity whatsoever.
In this manner, the application of the meaning should be made for all the terms. The section on the exposition is of plain meaning.
The section on emptiness is concluded.
The commentary on the meaning of the first consciousness, which was explained by way of the three major sections, is completed. Now,
the second consciousness.
146. Now, in order to show the second consciousness and the others, the passage beginning with "Which phenomena... is commenced again.

In all of these [subsequent sections], three great sections (mahāvāra) for each should be understood according to the same method as stated for the first consciousness. And it is not only the great sections;
the meaning of all the terms similar to those stated for the first consciousness should also be understood by the same method. Hereafter too...
We shall provide an explanation only of the new terms. First, in this second description of consciousness, the term *sasaṅkhārena* (with volitional effort) is indeed new.
Its meaning is as follows: together with volitional effort (*saṅkhāra*) is "with volitional effort" (*sasaṅkhāra*). The sense is:

by means of that "with volitional effort," which is accompanied by application (*sappayoga*) and method (*saupāya*), [by means of] a collection of conditions. For it is by means of a collection of conditions such as the object (*ārammaṇa*) and so forth that the first great consciousness [arises].
It arises; by that very application and by that very means, this arises. Its arising should be understood as follows:

here, a certain bhikkhu living on the outskirts of a monastery, when the time for sweeping the shrine terrace has arrived, or the time for attending upon the elders has arrived, or the day for hearing the Dhamma has arrived, thinks: "If I were to go..."
Thinking, "If I go back, it will be too far; I will not go," he then reflects again:
"It is indeed improper for a bhikkhu not to go to the shrine courtyard, to attend upon the elders, or to listen to the Dhamma;
I shall go. Thus, whether by his own effort or through another, he understands the danger in the non-performance of duties and the like, and the benefit in their performance.
When wholesome consciousness arises in one who is being exhorted after being shown the benefits, or in one who is being made to act by means of restraint with the words “Come,
do this,” it is said to have arisen through the group of conditions accompanied by volitional effort (*sasaṅkhāra*).
This is the second type of consciousness.
The Third Consciousness (147–148).
In the third [consciousness], it is "dissociated from knowledge" (*ñāṇavippayutta*) because it is dissociated from knowledge.
For this too is thrilled and delighted with respect to its object, yet the discerning knowledge is not present here. Therefore, this is like young children seeing a monk...

In this context, four “infinities” (anantāni) are included. For there are four infinities:
infinite space, infinite world-systems (cakkavāḷāni), the infinite aggregate of beings (sattanikāyo), and the infinite knowledge of the Buddha. For, of space, in the eastern direction...
There is no limit to it in terms of direction—whether east, west, north, or south—nor in terms of distance, such as "it extends this many hundreds of yojanas" or "this many thousands of yojanas.
Even an iron ball the size of Mount Sineru, if cast downward after splitting the earth in two, would simply pass through;
it would find no support. Such is the infinity of space.
There is no limit to the world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), whether by hundreds or thousands.

For even if they were reborn in the Akaniṭṭha heaven, four Great Brahmās— endowed with a speed capable of traversing a hundred thousand world-systems in the time it takes a light arrow from a bow of strong sinew to pass across the shadow of a palm tree— [could not reach the end].
‘We shall see as far as the limits of the world-system (cakkavāḷa),’ they might run with such speed; yet without seeing the limits of the world-system, they would pass away.
Thus, indeed, the world-systems are called infinite.

Moreover, there is no measure for the quantity of beings dwelling in water, on earth, or on dry land within those world-systems. In this way, the category of beings is called infinite. Even beyond that, the Buddha’s knowledge is truly infinite.

Thus, in immeasurable world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), many wholesome consciousnesses—belonging to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), accompanied by joy (*somanassasahagata*), associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta*), and unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*)—arise for a single being; they arise in great numbers even for many beings.
All of these attain unity in terms of their being sense-sphere phenomena, their being accompanied by joy, their being associated with knowledge, and their being unprompted.

There is one great wholesome consciousness accompanied by joy, associated with three roots, and unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*). Likewise, there is a great wholesome consciousness that is prompted (*sasaṅkhārika*)...
and likewise, a prompted consciousness accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from knowledge, and associated with two roots.
In this way, all these sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses arise for immeasurable beings within immeasurable world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).

The Fully Enlightened One, as if weighing them on a great scale, or as if measuring them by placing them in a vessel, defined them with his omniscient knowledge and showed them, having categorized them into exactly eight divisions by way of their similarity, saying: "These are exactly eight.
Furthermore, in this place, what is called the "accumulation of merit" in its sixfold form is included; for there is merit that is self-performed.
There is that done by oneself, there is that done by another, there is that done by command, there is that done intentionally, and there is that done unintentionally.
In this context, what is done by one’s own nature is called "done by oneself" (*sayamkāra*). What is done upon seeing another doing it is called "done by another" (*paramkāra*).
What is done with one's own hand is called "done by one's own hand" (*sāhatthika*). What is caused to be done by giving an order is called "done by command" (*āṇattika*). And the action...

An action performed with conviction in its result is called "done with clear comprehension" (*sampajānakata*). An action performed without knowing either the action or its result is called "done without clear comprehension" (*asampajānakata*).
Among these, even when one performs an action oneself, one does so by means of one or another of these eight wholesome consciousnesses.
This applies equally whether one acts through another, acts with one's own hand, or acts by commanding another.
One performs [the act] by means of any one of these eight wholesome consciousnesses (*kusala-citta*).

However, performing with full awareness (*sampajañña*) occurs through the four types of consciousness associated with knowledge (*ñāṇa-sampayutta*); performing without full awareness occurs through the four types of consciousness dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇa-vippayutta*).
Furthermore, in this context, the four purifications of offerings (*dakkhiṇā-visuddhi*) are included: the lawfulness of the requisites (*paccaya-dhammata*),...

The greatness of volition (*cetanāmahatta*), the excellence of the object (*vatthusampatti*), and the preeminence of qualities (*guṇātirekatā*). Among these, requisites obtained through righteous and equitable means are called "righteous" (*dhammika*).
For one who gives having first placed faith and conviction, there is what is called "the greatness of volition.

The state of being one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) is called "the excellence of the object. The state of having emerged from cessation (*nirodha*) while being one whose taints are exhausted is called "the preeminence of qualities."

When one is able to combine these four [factors] and give them, the wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-kusala*) yields its result within this very lifetime, as in the cases of the merchant Puṇṇaka,

Kākavaḷiya, the garland-maker Sumanā, and others. In brief, all this wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere, taking “consciousness” as its basis, by way of the state of being variegated by consciousness—
It is one only. By way of feeling, it is twofold: accompanied by joy and accompanied by equanimity.

By way of teaching through the analysis of knowledge, it is fourfold. For the great consciousness accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, and unprompted, as well as the great consciousness accompanied by equanimity, associated with knowledge, and unprompted—these are so designated by way of being associated with knowledge and by way of being unprompted.
And it is likewise one alone. Similarly, there is that associated with knowledge and prompted, that dissociated from knowledge and unprompted, and that dissociated from knowledge and prompted.

Thus, within this fourfold classification according to the teaching on the analysis of knowledge, by way of the analysis of the unprompted and prompted, there are eight types: four unprompted and four prompted.

These are wholesome states of consciousness. Having known them as they truly are, the Blessed One—the All-Knowing One, the Chief of the Assembly, the Best of Sages—declares, teaches, proclaims, establishes, reveals, analyzes, and makes plain [them].

Thus, the Blessed One has taught the Four Noble Truths in detail through various methods. This concludes the section on the Four Noble Truths. Now follows the section on the Four Bases of Mindfulness (*cattāro satipaṭṭhānā*). Herein, the four bases of mindfulness are: the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena (*dhammā*). Regarding this, the Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, this is the direct path for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of *nibbāna*—that is, the four bases of mindfulness. What is the purpose of this teaching? It is to show the method for abandoning the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and developing the seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*). How so? Because when the five hindrances are abandoned, the seven factors of enlightenment are developed. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that the four bases of mindfulness are the direct path for abandoning the five hindrances and developing the seven factors of enlightenment. How so? Because when one dwells contemplating the body as a body, the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*) is abandoned.
