When one dwells contemplating feelings as feelings, the hindrance of ill will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*) is abandoned. When one dwells contemplating the mind as mind, the hindrance of sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha-nīvaraṇa*) is abandoned. When one dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena, the hindrances of restlessness and remorse (*uddhaccakukkucca-nīvaraṇa*) and doubt (*vicikicchā-nīvaraṇa*) are abandoned. Thus, the four bases of mindfulness are the direct path for abandoning the five hindrances. Furthermore, when the five hindrances have been abandoned, the seven factors of enlightenment are developed. How so? Because when one dwells contemplating the body as a body, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness (*satisambojjhaṅga*) is developed. When one dwells contemplating feelings as feelings, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga*) is developed. When one dwells contemplating the mind as mind, the enlightenment factor of energy (*vīriyasambojjhaṅga*) is developed. When one dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena, the enlightenment factors of joy (*pītisambojjhaṅga*), tranquility (*passaddhisambojjhaṅga*), concentration (*samādhisambojjhaṅga*), and equanimity (*upekkhāsambojjhaṅga*) are developed. Thus, the four bases of mindfulness are the direct path for developing the seven factors of enlightenment. Therefore, it should be understood that the Blessed One taught the four bases of mindfulness as the direct path for abandoning the five hindrances and developing the seven factors of enlightenment. This concludes the section on the Four Bases of Mindfulness. Now follows the section on the Four Right Strivings (*cattāro sammappadhānā*). Herein, the four right strivings are: the striving to prevent the arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states, the striving to abandon arisen evil unwholesome states, the striving to produce unarisen wholesome states, and the striving to maintain and perfect arisen wholesome states. Regarding this, the Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, there are these four right strivings. What four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states; he makes an effort, exerts his mind, and applies energy. He generates desire for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome states; he makes an effort, exerts his mind, and applies energy. He generates desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; he makes an effort, exerts his mind, and applies energy. He generates desire for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, expansion, and fulfillment by development of arisen wholesome states; he makes an effort, exerts his mind, and applies energy. What is the purpose of this teaching? It is to show the method for abandoning the five hindrances and developing the seven factors of enlightenment. How so? Because when the five hindrances are abandoned, the seven factors of enlightenment are developed. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that the four right strivings are the direct path for abandoning the five hindrances and developing the seven factors of enlightenment. How so? Because when one strives to prevent the arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states, the hindrance of sensual desire is abandoned. When one strives to abandon arisen evil unwholesome states, the hindrance of ill will is abandoned. When one strives to produce unarisen wholesome states, the hindrance of sloth and torpor is abandoned. When one strives to maintain and perfect arisen wholesome states, the hindrances of restlessness and remorse and doubt are abandoned. Thus, the four right strivings are the direct path for abandoning the five hindrances. Furthermore, when the five hindrances have been abandoned, the seven factors of enlightenment are developed. How so? Because when one strives to prevent the arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states, the enlightenment factor of energy (*vīriyasambojjhaṅga*) is developed. When one strives to abandon arisen evil unwholesome states, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga*) is developed. When one strives to produce unarisen wholesome states, the enlightenment factor of joy (*pītisambojjhaṅga*) is developed. When one strives to maintain and perfect arisen wholesome states, the enlightenment factors of tranquility (*passaddhisambojjhaṅga*), concentration (*samādhisambojjhaṅga*), and equanimity (*upekkhāsambojjhaṅga*) are developed. Thus, the four right strivings are the direct path for developing the seven factors of enlightenment. Therefore, it should be understood that the Blessed One taught the four right strivings as the direct path for abandoning the five hindrances and developing the seven factors of enlightenment. This concludes the section on the Four Right Strivings. Now follows the section on the Four Bases of Psychic Power (*cattāro iddhipādā*). Herein, the four bases of psychic power are: the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration due to desire and volitional formations, the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration due to energy and volitional formations, the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration due to mind and volitional formations, and the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration due to investigation and volitional formations. Regarding this, the Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, there are these four bases of psychic power. What four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration due to desire and accompanied by volitional formations; he develops the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration due to energy and accompanied by volitional formations; he develops the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration due to mind and accompanied by volitional formations; he develops the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration due to investigation and accompanied by volitional formations. What is the purpose of this teaching? It is to show the method for abandoning the five hindrances and developing the seven factors of enlightenment. How so? Because when the five hindrances are abandoned, the seven factors of enlightenment are developed. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that the four bases of psychic power are the direct path for abandoning the five hindrances and developing the seven factors of enlightenment. How so? Because when one develops the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration due to desire, the hindrance of sensual desire is abandoned. When one develops the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration due to energy, the hindrance of ill will is abandoned. When one develops the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration due to mind, the hindrance of sloth and torpor is abandoned. When one develops the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration due to investigation, the hindrances of restlessness and remorse and doubt are abandoned. Thus, the four bases of psychic power are the direct path for abandoning the five hindrances. Furthermore, when the five hindrances have been abandoned, the seven factors of enlightenment are developed. How so? Because when one develops the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration due to desire, the enlightenment factor of joy (*pītisambojjhaṅga*) is developed. When one develops the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration due to energy, the enlightenment factor of energy (*vīriyasambojjhaṅga*) is developed. When one develops the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration due to mind, the enlightenment factor of concentration (*samādhisambojjhaṅga*) is developed
In this context, the factors associated with volition (*cetanā*) are called the "path. As stated in such suttas as the *Saṅkhārupapatti Sutta*:
“This, monks, is the path; this is the way,” both volition and the factors associated with volition are called the path.
However, because the word “jhāna” is used here, it is the factors associated with volition that are intended. For jhāna-volition [projects] rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
It draws [toward itself]; therefore, both volition (*cetanā*) and the mental states associated with volition (*cetanā-sampayutta-dhamma*) are indeed included.
"Develops" (*bhāveti*) means generates, produces, and increases. This, first of all, is the meaning of "development" (*bhāvanā*) here.

In other contexts, however, depending on the prefix, the meanings are "cultivation" (*sambhāvanā*), "infusion" (*paribhāvanā*), or "elimination" (*vibhāvanā*); thus, the meaning varies accordingly. In that regard:
“Here, Udāyi, my disciples esteem me thus: ‘The ascetic Gotama is virtuous; he is endowed with the supreme aggregate of virtue’”—this is what is called esteem (*sambhāvanā*);
the meaning is confidence (*okappanā*). “Concentration, when permeated by virtue, is of great fruit and great benefit;
wisdom, when permeated by concentration, is of great fruit and great benefit; [the mind], when permeated by wisdom...”
“The mind is rightly liberated from the taints”—this is called *paribhāvanā*; its meaning is “perfuming.
“Come now, analyze form, analyze feeling… perception… volitional formations… analyze consciousness”—this is called *vibhāvanā*;
its meaning is “making disappear. “Furthermore, Udāyi, the way of practice for my disciples has been declared by me…”
‘Just as my disciples, practicing accordingly, develop the four foundations of mindfulness’—this, however, is called ‘development’ (bhāvanā) in the sense of producing and increasing.
In this context, too, it is precisely this that is intended. Therefore it was said: ‘He develops means he generates, produces, and increases.’”

But why, in this context, has the teaching not been made with the phenomena as the starting point—as was done in the exposition of sense-sphere wholesome states—but instead with the person as the starting point? Because it must be accomplished by means of the path.
For this [wholesome state] is to be accomplished by one of the four paths; unlike the sense-sphere [states], it does not arise without a path. And the path...

In order to show that this [state] exists when there is one who has entered upon the practice, he spoke the words "he develops the path for rebirth in the form realm," giving a teaching preceded by the person (*puggalapubbaṅgama*).
"Quite secluded from sensual pleasures" means having become secluded from sensual pleasures, having been apart from them, having departed from them. As for the word "quite" (*eva*) used here:

Thus, it should be understood that this has the sense of restriction (*niyama*). And because it has the sense of restriction, it demonstrates that even though sensual desires (*kāma*) were not present at the time of entering and abiding in that first jhāna, they constitute the opposite of that first jhāna; furthermore, it shows that its attainment occurs precisely through the relinquishing of sensual desires.
How so? By making the restriction thus: "Quite secluded from sensual desires" (*vivicceva kāmehi*). For when this restriction is made in this way—
It is evident: "Surely sensual pleasures must be its adversaries, for when they are present, this [knowledge] does not occur, just as the light of a lamp does not appear when there is darkness.
Its attainment comes only through the relinquishing of them, just as the reaching of the further shore occurs only through the relinquishing of the near shore.
Therefore, he establishes this certainty.
In this regard, it might be asked: "Why was this stated only in the first member [of the compound] and not in the latter member?
Might one enter and dwell in jhāna even without being secluded from unwholesome states? However, this should not be viewed in such a way.

For it was stated in the first member because that is the escape from them; for this [jhāna] is the transcendence of the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the antidote to sensual lust (*kāmarāga*).
Jhāna is indeed the escape from sensual desires. As it is said: "This is the escape from sensual desires, namely, renunciation.

Furthermore, regarding the word *eva*, just as in the passage, "Bhikkhus, only here is there a recluse; here is the second recluse," the particle *eva* must be supplied [to read *jhānameva*], so too should it be stated here.
For it is not possible that there is an escape from these [desires] by means of anything other than those things known as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
Because it is impossible to enter and dwell in jhāna without being secluded from unwholesome states,

this [seclusion] should be understood in both phrases as "quite secluded from sensual pleasures, quite secluded from unwholesome states. And although in both phrases the common term "secluded" (*vivicca*) includes all forms of seclusion—
such as seclusion by way of factor (*tadaṅga-viveka*) and so forth, as well as physical seclusion (*kāya-viveka*) and the rest— [it is used here specifically in its primary sense].
Although they are included therein, only three types of seclusion should be understood here: seclusion of body, seclusion of mind, and seclusion by suppression.

By the phrase "from sensual pleasures" (kāmehi), those "sensual objects" (vatthukāmā) are referred to which are stated in the Niddesa according to the method beginning with, "What are sensual objects? Agreeable forms," and so on;
as well as those [mental states] mentioned right there in the Vibhaṅga: "Desire is sensual pleasure, lust is sensual pleasure, desire-and-lust..."
“Sensual desire (kāma) is intention (saṅkappa), sensual desire is lust (rāga), sensual desire is intention-and-lust; these are called sensual desires.

Thus, the defilement-sensual-desires (kilesakāma) have been stated, and all of them should be understood as being included therein. This being so, the meaning of “quite secluded from sensual desires” (vivicceva kāmehi) is that one is secluded even from object-sensual-desires (vatthukāma);
by this, bodily seclusion (kāyaviveka) is expressed.
"Secluded from unwholesome states" means it is appropriate to understand this as being secluded from the desires of the defilements (*kilesakāma*) or from all unwholesome states;

by this, mental seclusion (*cittaviveka*) is expressed. Furthermore, because seclusion from the objects of sensual desire (*vatthukāma*) is stated by the former [phrase], the relinquishing of sensual pleasure is clarified;
and because seclusion from the desires of the defilements is stated by the latter, the embracing of the happiness of renunciation (*nekkhammasukha*) is made manifest. Thus...

And because these terms express seclusion from sense-desires as objects and sense-desires as defilements, it should be understood that by the first [seclusion] there is the abandoning of the basis for defilement, and by the second, the abandoning of the defilement itself;
by the first, the relinquishing of the cause of greediness, and by the second, of foolishness;
and by the first, purity of conduct, while by the second, the nourishment of the inner disposition is made manifest. This is so.

The method here is as follows: regarding the term "sensual pleasures" (*kāma*) mentioned in the phrase "by those who are free from sensual pleasures," it refers to the category of *vatthu-kāma* (sensual objects).

However, in the context of *kilesa-kāma* (sensual defilements), the term "sensual pleasure" is intended to mean *kāmacchanda* (sensual desire) itself, which has many divisions such as "desire" (*chanda*) and "lust" (*rāga*).
And although this [sensual desire] is included within the unwholesome states, it is defined by such passages as: "In that regard, what is sensual desire as sensual pleasure? and so forth.
In the *Vibhaṅga*, it is mentioned separately because it is the opposite of meditative absorption (*jhāna*) according to that method.

Alternatively, it is mentioned in the first phrase because it is sensual desire as defilement (*kilesakāma*), and in the second phrase because it is included within the unwholesome (*akusala*). Furthermore, because it has many subdivisions, it is stated as "by means of sensual desires" (*kāmehi*) rather than simply "sensual desire" (*kāmato*).
And although other phenomena (*dhammas*) also exist in an unwholesome state, [it is asked]: "In this context, which are the unwholesome phenomena?"

In the *Vibhaṅga*, by way of the method beginning with "sensual desire" (*kāmacchanda*), they are stated as hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) because they are shown to be the opposites and adversaries of the jhāna factors. For the hindrances are the opposites of the jhāna factors;
it is said that the jhāna factors themselves are their adversaries, destroyers, and obstructors. Thus, it is said: "Concentration is the adversary of sensual desire."
"Joy [is the nutriment] of ill-will, applied thought of sloth-and-torpor, pleasure of restlessness-and-worry, and sustained thought of doubt"—thus it is said in the *Peṭaka*.
In this way, here, by the phrase "quite secluded from sensual desires," the seclusion by suppression of sensual desire is stated;
and by the phrase "secluded from unwholesome states," that of all five hindrances is stated. Furthermore, by the principle of including what has not been explicitly mentioned...

By the first [foundation of mindfulness], there is the abandoning of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*); by the second, of the remaining hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). Likewise, among the three unwholesome roots, by the first there is the abandoning of greed (*lobha*) whose object consists of the fivefold division of the strands of sense pleasure (*pañcakāmaguṇa*);
by the second, of hatred (*dosa*) and delusion (*moha*), whose objects consist of the various bases for resentment (*āghātavatthu*) and so forth.

Or, among the phenomena such as the floods (*ogha*) and so on, by the first there is the abandoning of the flood of sensuality, the yoke of sensuality, the taint of sensuality, the clinging to sensuality, the bodily tie of covetousness, and the fetter of lust for sensuality (*kāmārāga*).
By the second [jhāna], there is the seclusion from the remaining floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), taints (*āsava*), clingings (*upādāna*), ties (*gantha*), and fetters (*saṃyojana*).
It should be understood that by the first [jhāna] there is the seclusion from craving and its associated states, and by the second from ignorance and its associated states.

Furthermore, it should be understood that by the first there is the seclusion by suppression of the eight types of consciousness-arising associated with greed, and by the second, of the remaining four types of unwholesome consciousness-arising.
This, first of all, is the explanation of the meaning of the phrase, “quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome states.
Having thus far shown the factor of abandoning for the first jhāna, the words beginning with “with applied thought, with sustained thought” are now spoken in order to show its factors of association.
Therein, by way of the analysis of the characteristics and so forth mentioned below, [it is associated] through association with absorption (appanā).
It occurs together with both applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) that have attained the state of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*).
Just as a tree is [described] by means of its flowers and fruits, this meditative absorption (*jhāna*) is called "with applied thought and sustained thought" (*savitakka-savicāra*).

However, in the *Vibhaṅga*, it is stated according to the method beginning with, "He is endowed with this applied thought and this sustained thought," which is expressed by way of the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*).
The teaching has been given. However, the meaning there should also be understood in exactly this way.

Regarding the term *vivekaja*: here, *vivitti* (separation) is *viveka* (seclusion). The meaning is the disappearance of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). Or alternatively, *viveka* means that which is separated;
thus the meaning is the mass of states associated with jhāna that are separated from the hindrances. Therefore, "from seclusion" (*vivekā*), or "in that seclusion" (*tasmiṃ viveke*).
"Born" means born of seclusion. Regarding "rapture and pleasure": here, rapture and pleasure have already been explained below.

Among those, that which is the pervading rapture—increasing as the root of absorption-concentration (appanā-samādhi) and having attained association with concentration through the fivefold rapture described above—is the rapture intended in this context. And this is rapture, and this is pleasure.
This jhāna has rapture and happiness, or this jhāna possesses rapture and happiness; thus it is called "rapture-and-happiness" (*pītisukha*).

Alternatively, "rapture-and-happiness" (*pītisukha*) refers to both rapture and happiness, just as in the case of "Dharma and Vinaya" (*dhammavinaya*). This jhāna has rapture and happiness born of seclusion, or in this jhāna there is rapture and happiness born of seclusion;
thus it is also "rapture-and-happiness born of seclusion. For just as with the jhāna itself, so too rapture and happiness are included here.
It is born of seclusion alone, and that [seclusion] exists for him; therefore, it is appropriate to say "joy and happiness born of seclusion" using only a single compound term.
However, in the *Vibhaṅga*, it is stated in the manner of "this happiness is accompanied by this joy," and so forth.
Nevertheless, the meaning there should also be understood in exactly this way.
"First jhāna": here, it is "first" because of numerical sequence; it is "first" because it arises first;
and it is "first" because it is the first to be attained. However, this is not an absolute characteristic.
For one who has mastered his practice and has attained the eight attainments can enter them starting from the beginning all the way to the peak, and likewise from the peak [downward].
Even one who reaches the beginning from the start is able to attain it; even one who enters it intermittently is able to do so.
Thus, in the sense of its first arising, it is called "first.
As for *jhāna*, there are two kinds of *jhāna*: *ārammaṇūpanijjhāna* (contemplation of the object) and *lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna* (contemplation of the characteristics). Of these, the eight...
The meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) are designated as "contemplation of the object" (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*) because they closely contemplate objects such as the earth-kasiṇa and others.
However, insight (*vipassanā*), the path, and the fruit are called "contemplation of characteristics" (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*).

Among these, insight is "contemplation of characteristics" because it closely contemplates the characteristics of impermanence and so forth. The path is so called because it succeeds by means of the path once the task has been performed by insight.
It is "contemplation of characteristics" (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*). However, the fruit contemplates the characteristic of suchness (*tathalakkhaṇa*), which is the truth of cessation;
thus it is called "contemplation of characteristics. Among these, in this context, "contemplation of the object" (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*) is intended.
Therefore, it should be understood as *jhāna* because of its contemplation of the object, or because of its burning away of opposites (*paccanīka*).
“Having attained” (*upasampajja*) means having approached; it is said to mean having reached. Or, it is said to mean having accomplished or having brought to completion.

In the *Vibhaṅga*, however, it is stated: “‘Having attained’ means the gaining, the obtaining, the reaching, the achievement, the touching, the realization, and the full attainment of the first jhāna. Its meaning should also be understood in exactly this way.

"He dwells" (*viharati*) means that, by means of a mode of conduct (*iriyāpatha*) corresponding to that [meditative attainment], having become possessed of the aforementioned kind of jhāna, he effects the moving, the functioning, the protecting, the sustaining, the maintaining, the roaming, and the dwelling of his personal existence (*attabhāva*). For this has been said in the *Vibhaṅga*:
"He dwells means: he moves, he functions, he protects, he sustains, he maintains, he roams, he dwells; therefore..."
“It is said that he dwells.
Regarding “the earth-kasiṇa”: here, even the circle of the earth is called the earth-kasiṇa in the sense of being the whole;
so too is the sign obtained by depending upon it, and also the jhāna obtained in regard to the sign of the earth-kasiṇa. Therein—
In this context, it should be understood that *jhāna* is the earth-kasiṇa. "Having attained and dwelling in the *jhāna* known as the earth-kasiṇa"—this is the concise meaning here.

Now, regarding this earth-kasiṇa, a son of good family who wishes to attain Arahantship should perform the preliminary work (*parikamma*), generate the fourfold and fivefold *jhānas*, and then, with those *jhānas* as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*), develop insight (*vipassanā*).
What is to be done? First of all, having purified the four kinds of virtue— namely, virtue consisting in restraint according to the Pātimokkha,
virtue consisting in restraint of the sense faculties, virtue consisting in purity of livelihood, and virtue consisting in moderation regarding the requisites—

one who is established in perfectly pure virtue should sever whatever impediment exists among the ten impediments such as a dwelling place, and then approach a spiritual friend who bestows the meditation subject.

When one who is examining the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) suitable to his own temperament among the thirty-eight meditation subjects handed down in the Pāli finds that this earth-kasiṇa (pathavikasiṇa) is suitable for him, he should take this very meditation subject,
abandon a monastery that is unsuitable for the development of jhāna, dwell in a suitable monastery, and sever the minor impediments.
One should proceed toward the attainment of jhāna without omitting any of the methods of development, which consist of:

guarding the preliminary sign of the kasiṇa, avoiding the seven kinds of unsuitable things, cultivating the seven kinds of suitable things, and the tenfold skill in absorption. This is the summary here;
the detailed exposition, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the *Visuddhimagga*. And as it is here, so it is elsewhere.

The same applies to what follows hereafter. For the entire method of cultivation for all meditation subjects has been set forth in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*, having been taken from the commentarial tradition (*aṭṭhakathā*).
Why repeat what has already been stated in various places there? Therefore, we shall not elaborate on it again here.
However, without omitting any meaning that has not yet appeared in the preceding portion of the text, we shall provide a continuous word-by-word commentary.
"At that time" means at the time of entering and abiding in the first jhāna. "Contact exists...
non-distraction exists"—these are the fifty-six states occurring in the sequence described for the first wholesome consciousness of the sense-sphere.
For those belong to the sense-sphere, whereas these, by virtue of their different plane, are sublime and belong to the fine-material sphere.
This is the distinction here. The rest is exactly the same. However, only the four factors beginning with desire (*chanda*) are found here among the "additional" (*yevāpanaka*) states.
The sections on the constituents (*koṭṭhāsa*) and the section on emptiness (*suññatā*) remain as they were before.
This is the first.
The Second Jhāna (161–162).

In the exposition of the second jhāna, "with the stilling of applied thought and sustained thought" means: with the stilling—that is, the surmounting—of these two, namely applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*); it is said that they are not manifest at the moment of the second jhāna.
It exists. In this context, although none of the factors of the first jhāna are present in the second jhāna—
for indeed, the contact and other factors in the first jhāna are one thing, while those here are another—

the mention of the overcoming of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) is for the purpose of illustrating that the attainment of the second jhāna and those following it occurs through the surmounting of each successive gross factor of the first jhāna.
It should be understood that this is what is meant by "tranquility. Here, "internal" (*ajjhatta*) refers to one's own internal state (*niyakajjhatta*).
In the *Vibhaṅga*, however, it is stated merely as "internal, personal" (*ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ*). Since one's own internal state is intended here, the meaning is:
"born within oneself," or "arisen in one's own continuity" (*santāna*).
"Serenity" (*sampasādana*): faith is called serenity.
Because it is associated with serenity, the jhāna itself is also "serenity," just as a garment is called "blue" because it is associated with the color blue.

Or else, because that jhāna—by being endowed with serenity and by the subsiding of the agitation of applied and sustained thought—serenifies the mind, it is therefore also called "serenity. And in this interpretation of the meaning, "serenity..."

The connection of the words should be understood as “of the mind” (*cetaso*). However, in the first interpretation of the meaning, the term “of the mind” should be joined with “one-pointedness” (*ekodibhāvena*).

Herein, this is the construction of the meaning: it rises alone, thus it is “one-pointed” (*ekodi*); because it has not ascended upon applied and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*), it is the foremost and best.
The meaning is "having sacrificed, it rises. For even the most excellent person in the world is called "one" (*eka*).

Alternatively, it is appropriate to say that it is "one" because it is solitary, being devoid of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*). Or else, it is "rising" (*udi*) because it causes the associated mental states to rise;

the meaning is that it "causes them to stand up. It is "one" (*eka*) in the sense of being supreme, and it is "rising" (*udi*); thus it is *ekodi*. This is a designation for concentration (*samādhi*). Thus, this...
"He develops and increases unification" refers to this second jhāna as "the state of unification.
Now, since this unification belongs to the mind (*cetaso*), and not to a being (*sattassa*) or a soul (*jīvassa*), it is therefore called "the state of unification of the mind.
But surely this faith (*saddhā*) is present even in the first jhāna, and this concentration (*samādhi*) is also named "unification"; so why [is this alone designated thus]?
Is it said that this very [state] is "serenity of mind" and "unification of mind"? It is replied:

Because that first jhāna is not perfectly serene due to the agitation of applied and sustained thought—like water disturbed by ripples and waves—it is therefore not called "serenity" even though faith is present.
And because it is not perfectly serene, concentration here also is not yet fully established.

It is manifest. Therefore, even the phrase "becoming unified" (*ekodibhāva*) was not stated [in the Sutta]. However, in this jhāna, because the hindrances of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are absent, faith (*saddhā*) gains scope and becomes powerful;
and through the acquisition of such powerful faith as its companion, concentration (*samādhi*) also becomes manifest.
Therefore, it should be understood that this [jhāna] alone is described in this way. In the *Vibhaṅga*, however, it says: "'Sampasādana' means that which is faith, the act of believing..."
"Steadfastness is serene confidence; the singleness of mind is that stability of consciousness...

[and so on] ...right concentration"—only this much was said. However, this commentary on the meaning should be understood in such a way that it does not conflict with what has been stated, but rather harmonizes with it and accords with it.

"Without applied thought and without sustained thought": because it has been abandoned through development (*bhāvanā*), there is no applied thought (*vitakka*) in this [state] or belonging to this [state], thus it is "without applied thought.
By this same method, it is "without sustained thought" (*avicāra*). It is also said in the *Vibhaṅga*:
"Thus, this applied thought and this sustained thought have become stilled, calmed, subsided, passed away, vanished, dissolved, resolved, withered, and utterly dried up."
“...having been brought to an end; therefore it is called ‘without applied thought and without sustained thought.
Here it may be asked: Is this meaning not already established by the phrase “with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought”?
Then why is it stated again as “without applied thought and without sustained thought”? It is replied: This is so; this meaning is indeed established, yet it is not...

This explains its meaning. Did we not say: “But it was stated thus—‘the subsiding of applied and sustained thought’—for the purpose of showing that the attainment of the second jhāna and those following it occurs through the surmounting of each successive gross factor of the first jhāna”?

Moreover, this "tranquility" (*sampasādana*) arises from the subsiding of applied and sustained thought (*vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā*), not from the removal of the turbidity of the defilements (*kilesakālusiyassa*);

and from the subsiding of applied and sustained thought comes "singleness" (*ekodibhāva*), not as in access concentration (*upacārajjhāna*) through the abandoning of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇappahānā*), nor as in the first jhāna through the manifestation of factors (*aṅgapātubhāvā*).
Thus, this statement illustrates the causes for both tranquility and singleness. Likewise...
"With the stilling of applied and sustained thought" means that this [state] is without applied and sustained thought;

it does not mean that they are non-existent as in the case of the third and fourth jhānas or as in the case of eye-consciousness and so forth. Thus, this phrase illuminates the cause for the state of being without applied and sustained thought, rather than merely illuminating the simple absence of applied and sustained thought.
However, that which merely illuminates the absence of applied and sustained thought...
"Without applied thought and without sustained thought"—this is the statement; therefore, even though it was stated previously, it must indeed be stated again.
"Born of concentration" means born from the concentration of the first jhāna, or from the associated concentration.
In this regard, although the first [jhāna] is also born from the associated concentration, nevertheless, this very concentration is what is called "concentration."
It deserves to be so called because it is exceedingly steady and perfectly serene due to its freedom from the agitation of applied and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*).
Therefore, for the purpose of praising this state, it is said: "born of concentration" (*samādhija*). "Rapture and pleasure" (*pīti-sukha*) is in the manner already described.
"Second" (*dutiya*) means second in the sequence of counting; it is also called "second" because one attains this as the second [jhāna]. At that time...
In the passages beginning with "there is contact," the terms *vitakka* and *vicāra* are omitted from the fivefold jhāna, and the term *sammāsaṅkappa* is omitted from the fivefold path.
By means of these omissions, the analysis of the inflected and non-inflected terms should be understood.
In the section on the factors (*koṭṭhāsa*), it is stated that there is a three-factored jhāna and a four-factored path. The rest is exactly the same as in the first jhāna.
The second [section].

163. In the exposition of the third jhāna, regarding the phrase "with the fading away of rapture" (*pītiyā ca virāgā*): "fading away" (*virāga*) means the feeling of disgust toward the aforementioned kind of rapture.
Or it is the surmounting. Between these two, however, the word “and” (ca) has the sense of conjunction;
it either conjoins [the term] “tranquility” (vūpasama) or the “tranquility of applied and sustained thought” (vitakkavicāra-vūpasama).

In that context, when it conjoins only “tranquility,” then the construction should be understood as follows: “from the fading away of rapture, and furthermore, from tranquility. And with this construction—
Dispassion (*virāga*) has the sense of disgust. Therefore, this meaning should be understood as both "disgust for rapture" (*pīti*) and "the subsiding [of applied and sustained thought].

However, when one combines the subsiding of applied and sustained thought (*vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasama*), then the construction should be understood as follows: "and through dispassion for rapture, and furthermore, through the subsiding of applied and sustained thought. And in this construction, dispassion...
It has the sense of surmounting; therefore, this meaning should be understood as "with the surmounting of rapture and the stilling of applied and sustained thought.
Granted that these applied and sustained thoughts were already stilled in the second jhāna itself, [this is stated] for the purpose of illustrating the path of this particular jhāna.
And this was said for the purpose of praising it. For when it is stated, "with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought," this is understood:
"Surely the subsiding of applied and sustained thought is the path to this jhāna.

And just as in the case of the third noble path, although the five lower fetters such as personality-belief have not yet been abandoned, it is nevertheless said, "through the abandoning of the five lower fetters."
When abandonment is thus described, it constitutes a praise that generates enthusiasm in those striving for its attainment;
likewise, here, even though the applied and sustained thought (*vitakkavicāra*) have not yet subsided, the description of their subsiding constitutes a praise.
Therefore, this meaning was stated: “with the surmounting of rapture and with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought.”
"And he dwells in equanimity": here, "equanimity" (*upekkhā*) means that one looks on with composure (*upapattito ikkhati*).

The meaning is that one sees evenly, seeing without falling into partiality. Because he is endowed with that [equanimity] which is clear, vast, and firmly established, the possessor of the third jhāna is called "one who dwells in equanimity."

Equanimity, however, is tenfold: equanimity as a factor of the sixfold sense-restraint (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*), equanimity as a divine abiding (*brahmavihārupekkhā*), equanimity as a factor of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅgupekkhā*), equanimity as energy (*vīriyupekkhā*), equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*), equanimity regarding feeling (*vedanupekkhā*), equanimity as insight (*vipassanupekkhā*), equanimity as neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*), equanimity as a jhāna factor (*jhānupekkhā*), and equanimity as complete purity (*pārisuddhupekkhā*).
In this context, it is said: "Here, monks, having seen a form with the eye, a monk is neither glad nor sad..."

“He dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending”—this is the equanimity that has come down as the state of not abandoning one’s naturally pure disposition when encountering the sixfold course of desirable and undesirable objects at the six sense doors of one whose taints are destroyed; this is called ‘six-factored equanimity.

However, that equanimity which consists in the attitude of neutrality toward beings, as it has come down in the passage, “He dwells having pervaded one quarter with a mind accompanied by equanimity,” is called ‘equanimity as a divine abode.’”

The equanimity that consists in the neutral state toward co-nascent phenomena, as it occurs in the passage: “He develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity, which is based on seclusion,” is called ‘equanimity as an enlightenment factor. However, the equanimity defined as energy that is neither too tense nor too lax, as it occurs in the passage: “From time to time he attends to the sign of equanimity,” is called ‘equanimity of energy. As for the question: “How many kinds of equanimity regarding formations arise by way of serenity? How many kinds of equanimity regarding formations arise by way of insight?”... [text continues] ...it is the equanimity that is the neutrality of mind toward formations. This is called ‘equanimity regarding formations. Furthermore, the equanimity that is the neutrality of mind toward the object, as it occurs in the passage: “With the abandoning of joy, he dwells in equanimity,” is called ‘equanimity of feeling. And the equanimity that is the neutrality of mind toward the body, as it occurs in the passage: “He dwells contemplating the body in the body with regard to internal bodily phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world,” is called ‘equanimity of body. Thus, these four kinds of equanimity should be understood according to their respective characteristics. Among them, the equanimity of feeling and the equanimity of body are mundane; the equanimity of energy and the equanimity regarding formations are both mundane and supramundane; and the equanimity as an enlightenment factor is exclusively supramundane. Regarding the question: “How many kinds of equanimity regarding formations arise by way of serenity?”—there are none. Regarding the question: “How many kinds of equanimity regarding formations arise by way of insight?”—there are two: equanimity as an enlightenment factor and equanimity regarding formations. Regarding the question: “How many kinds of equanimity regarding formations arise by way of both serenity and insight?”—there are none. Regarding the question: “How many kinds of equanimity regarding formations arise by way of neither serenity nor insight?”—there are three: equanimity of feeling, equanimity of body, and equanimity of energy. Thus, these four kinds of equanimity should be understood according to their respective characteristics. Furthermore, the equanimity of feeling and the equanimity of body are included in the aggregate of feeling; the equanimity of energy is included in the aggregate of formations; and the equanimity as an enlightenment factor is included in the aggregate of consciousness. Thus, these three aggregates are associated with equanimity. The equanimity regarding formations is included in the aggregate of formations. Thus, these four aggregates are associated with equanimity. Furthermore, the equanimity of feeling and the equanimity of body are included in the base of mental phenomena; the equanimity of energy is included in the base of mental phenomena; and the equanimity as an enlightenment factor is included in the base of mental phenomena. Thus, these three bases are associated with equanimity. The equanimity regarding formations is included in the base of mental phenomena. Thus, these four bases are associated with equanimity. Furthermore, the equanimity of feeling and the equanimity of body are included in the element of mental phenomena; the equanimity of energy is included in the element of mental phenomena; and the equanimity as an enlightenment factor is included in the element of mental phenomena. Thus, these three elements are associated with equanimity. The equanimity regarding formations is included in the element of mental phenomena. Thus, these four elements are associated with equanimity. Furthermore, the equanimity of feeling and the equanimity of body are included in the sphere of mental phenomena; the equanimity of energy is included in the sphere of mental phenomena; and the equanimity as an enlightenment factor is included in the sphere of mental phenomena. Thus, these three spheres are associated with equanimity. The equanimity regarding formations is included in the sphere of mental phenomena. Thus, these four spheres are associated with equanimity. Furthermore, the equanimity of feeling and the equanimity of body are included in the truth of suffering; the equanimity of energy is included in the truth of the path; and the equanimity as an enlightenment factor is included in the truth of the path. Thus, these two truths are associated with equanimity. The equanimity regarding formations is included in the truth of suffering. Thus, these two truths are associated with equanimity. Furthermore, the equanimity of feeling and the equanimity of body are included in the dependent origination of birth; the equanimity of energy is included in the dependent origination of volitional formations; and the equanimity as an enlightenment factor is included in the dependent origination of consciousness. Thus, these three links of dependent origination are associated with equanimity. The equanimity regarding formations is included in the dependent origination of volitional formations. Thus, these two links of dependent origination are associated with equanimity. Furthermore, the equanimity of feeling and the equanimity of body are included in the nutriment of contact; the equanimity of energy is included in the nutriment of volitional formations; and the equanimity as an enlightenment factor is included in the nutriment of consciousness. Thus, these three nutriments are associated with equanimity. The equanimity regarding formations is included in the nutriment of volitional formations. Thus, these two nutriments are associated with equanimity. Furthermore, the equanimity of feeling and the equanimity of body are included in the clinging to sense-pleasures; the equanimity of energy is included in the clinging to views; and the equanimity as an enlightenment factor is included in the clinging to precepts and observances. Thus, these three clingings are associated with equanimity. The equanimity regarding formations is included in the clinging to views. Thus, these two clingings are associated with equanimity. Furthermore, the equanimity of feeling and the equanimity of body are included in the fetter of envy; the equanimity of energy is included in the fetter of ill will; and the equanimity as an enlightenment factor is included in the fetter of ignorance. Thus, these three fetters are associated with equanimity. The equanimity regarding formations is included in the fetter of ignorance. Thus, these two fetters are associated with equanimity. Furthermore, the equanimity of feeling and the equanimity of body are included in the hindrance of ill will; the equanimity of energy is included in the hindrance of restlessness and remorse; and the equanimity as an enlightenment factor is included in the hindrance of doubt. Thus, these three hindrances are associated with equanimity. The equanimity regarding formations is included in the hindrance of sloth and torpor. Thus, these two hindrances are associated with equanimity. Furthermore, the equanimity of feeling and the equanimity of body are included in the jhāna factor of equanimity; the equanimity of energy is included in the jhāna factor of concentration; and the equanimity as an enlightenment factor is included in the jhāna factor of equanimity. Thus, these three jhāna factors are associated with equanimity. The equanimity regarding formations is included in the jhāna factor of investigation-of-states. Thus, these two jhāna factors are associated with equanimity. Furthermore, the equanimity of feeling and the equanimity of body are included in the path factor of right mindfulness; the equanimity of energy is included in the path factor of right concentration; and the equanimity as an enlightenment factor is included in the path factor of right effort. Thus, these three path factors are associated with equanimity. The equanimity regarding formations is included in the path factor of right view. Thus, these two path factors are associated with equanimity. Furthermore, the equanimity of feeling and the equanimity of body are included in the faculty of equanimity; the equanimity of energy is included in the faculty of energy; and the equanimity as an enlightenment factor is included in the faculty of wisdom. Thus, these three faculties are associated with equanimity. The equanimity regarding formations is included in the faculty of mind. Thus, these two faculties are associated with equanimity. Furthermore, the equanimity of feeling and the equanimity of body are included in the power of equanimity; the equanimity of energy is included in the power of energy; and the equanimity as an enlightenment factor is included in the power of wisdom. Thus, these three powers are associated with equanimity. The equanimity regarding formations is included in the power of mindfulness. Thus, these two powers are associated with equanimity. Furthermore, the equanimity of feeling and the equanimity of body are included in the foundation of mindfulness of feelings; the equanimity of energy is included in the foundation of mindfulness of mental phenomena; and the equanimity as an enlightenment factor is included in the foundation of mindfulness of states. Thus, these three foundations of mindfulness are associated with equanimity. The equanimity regarding formations is included in the foundation of mindfulness of the body. Thus, these two foundations of mindfulness are associated with equanimity. Furthermore, the equanimity of feeling and the equ
"Eight equanimities toward formations arise by way of serenity (samatha), and ten equanimities toward formations arise by way of insight (vipassanā).
This is the equanimity that is characterized by neutrality when grasping at the cessation through reflection upon the hindrances and so forth;
this is what is called "equanimity toward formations" (saṅkhārupekkhā).

However, that equanimity defined as neither-pain-nor-pleasure which occurs in such passages as, "At whatever time a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen accompanied by equanimity," is called "equanimity of feeling" (*vedanupekkhā*).

That equanimity consisting of neutrality in investigation which occurs in such passages as, "He abandons what exists, what has become; he attains equanimity," is called "equanimity of insight" (*vipassanupekkhā*).

But that equanimity which occurs among the miscellaneous factors such as desire (*chanda*), etc., and which consists in the state of evenness toward co-nascent states, is called "equanimity of specific neutrality" (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).
The equanimity that arises as "he dwells in equanimity" and which produces non-partisanship even toward that supreme bliss is called "equanimity of jhāna" (*jhānupekkhā*).

The equanimity that arises as "the fourth jhāna, purified by mindfulness and equanimity," which is completely purified of all adverse factors and remains inactive even while suppressing those adverse factors, is called "equanimity of purification" (*pārisuddhupekkhā*).

Among these, there is the sixfold equanimity, the equanimity of the divine abodes (*brahmavihārupekkhā*), the equanimity of the enlightenment factors (*bojjhaṅgupekkhā*), and the equanimity of specific neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).

The jhāna-equanimity (*jhānupekkhā*), the equanimity of purification (*pārisuddhupekkhā*), and the equanimity of onlooking (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*) are in meaning one and the same—namely, the equanimity of onlooking itself.

However, this distinction exists according to their respective different states, just as there is a distinction in a single being such as a person by way of being a child, a youth, an elder, a general, or a king.
Therefore, among those [types of equanimity], where there is the sixfold equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*), there is not the enlightenment-factor equanimity (*bojjhaṅgupekkhā*) and so forth; and where...
Alternatively, it should be understood that when there is equanimity as a factor of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅgupekkhā*), the sixfold equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*) and the others do not exist therein.
Just as these [other types of equanimity] are identical in meaning, so too are equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) and equanimity of insight (*vipassanupekkhā*).
For this is simply wisdom (*paññā*) divided into two according to its function. Just as, for example, when a man has entered his house in the evening and [sees] a snake...
Just as one who, having taken up a staff with a skull-topped end, while searching for something, sees it lying in a heap of husks and, looking to see whether it is a snake or not,
perceives three auspicious marks (sovatthika), becomes free from doubt; and when he investigates whether it is a snake or not,
there is equanimity— exactly so is it for one who has begun insight, regarding the three characteristics by means of the knowledge of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa).
When, upon seeing the impermanent nature and so forth of formations, a state of equanimity arises, this is "equanimity of insight" (*vipassanupekkhā*).
It is like that man who, having seized the snake firmly with a forked stick, seeks only the manner of releasing it, thinking:
"How might I release this snake without harming it, yet without allowing myself to be bitten by it?"

There is equanimity toward grasping; in the same way, because the three characteristics have been seen, one views the three realms of existence as if they were ablaze, and there is equanimity toward the grasping of formations—this is "equanimity regarding formations" (*saṅkhārupekkhā*).

Thus, when insight-equanimity (*vipassanupekkhā*) is established, equanimity regarding formations is also necessarily established. Furthermore, by this [equanimity], it is characterized as a state of neutrality (*majjhatta*) toward both investigation and grasping.

"It is divided into two by way of function. However, energy-equanimity (*vīriyupekkhā*) and feeling-equanimity (*vedanupekkhā*) are indeed distinct from one another and from the remaining types in terms of their actual meaning.
Among these ten types of equanimity, "equanimity of jhāna" (*jhānupekkhā*) is intended here. It has the characteristic of neutrality and the function of non-exertion (*anābhoga*).
"Its manifestation is non-ill-will, and its proximate cause is the fading away of rapture. Here it may be asked: "Is this not, in meaning, simply equanimity as a specific neutrality?
And since that exists in the first and second jhānas as well, should it not be said there too that 'he dwells in equanimity'?
Why is it not mentioned there? Because its function is not fully evident. For its function is not fully evident [in those stages].

In that case, its function is obscured because it is overwhelmed by applied thought (*vitakka*) and the other factors. Here, however, because it is not overwhelmed by applied thought, sustained thought (*vicāra*), and rapture (*pīti*), it has become clearly manifest in its function, as if with its head held high; therefore, it is said [to be present].
This concludes the explanation of the phrase "and he dwells in equanimity" (*upekkhako ca viharati*).
This concludes the commentary on the meaning [of the preceding section].
Now, regarding the phrase "mindful and clearly comprehending": here, one who remembers is "mindful" (*sato*); one who understands thoroughly is "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāno*).

Thus, both mindfulness and clear comprehension are stated by way of the person. In this context, mindfulness has the characteristic of remembering; its function is non-forgetfulness; it is manifested as protection.
Clear comprehension has non-delusion as its characteristic, investigation as its function, and discrimination as its manifestation. In this regard,
although this mindfulness and clear comprehension exist even in the preceding jhānas— for one who is muddled in mindfulness and lacking clear comprehension does not achieve even access concentration,
let alone absorption— nevertheless, because those jhānas are gross, they do not exist on that [access] plane.
Just as for a man, the movement of the mind is easy; however, in that case, the task of mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*) is not difficult.

But because this jhāna is subtle due to the abandoning of gross factors, like a man walking upon the edge of a razor, the movement of the mind must be accompanied by the support of the tasks of mindfulness and clear comprehension;
therefore, it is stated here alone. Furthermore, just as a calf accustomed to its mother...
Just as a calf that has been taken away from its mother cow, if left unguarded, returns once more to the cow,

so too this bliss of the third jhāna, though removed from rapture (pīti), might— if not guarded by the protection of mindfulness and clear comprehension— return once more to rapture and become associated with it.
Furthermore, beings are attached to pleasure, and this is an exceedingly sweet pleasure.

Beyond that, there is an absence of pleasure. However, it should be understood that this [statement] was spoken right here in order to show this specific point: that in this state, there is no attachment to pleasure by the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*), and not otherwise.

Now, regarding the phrase "he experiences pleasure with the body" (*sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedeti*): although for one possessing the third jhāna there is an application of mind toward the experience of pleasure...

It does not exist; nevertheless, because there is pleasure associated with his mental body (*nāmakāya*), or because his material body (*rūpakāya*) is suffused by an exceedingly refined matter produced by that pleasure associated with the mental body—by virtue of which suffusion he would experience pleasure even after emerging from meditation—it is for the purpose of showing this meaning that [the Buddha said]: "And he experiences pleasure with the body..."
"...experiences [it]," he said. Now,
regarding that which the Noble Ones describe as "dwelling in happiness, mindful and equanimous"— here, because of that jhāna,
for that reason of jhāna, the Noble Ones such as the Buddhas "describe and teach" the person who possesses the third jhāna.
The intention is that they praise [it] by saying: "They describe it, establish it, reveal it, analyze it, make it plain, and clarify it"—how so?
"'Equanimous, mindful, abiding in happiness'—he enters upon and dwells in that third jhāna.
Thus should the construction be understood here.
But why do they praise it in this way? Because it is worthy of praise.
For he is equanimous even in the third jhāna, which has reached the perfection of bliss that is exceedingly sweet; he is not dragged away by attachment to the bliss therein.
And because he possesses mindfulness through the establishment of mindfulness such that rapture does not arise, and because [he possesses] what is dear to the Noble Ones...
He experiences with his mental body that very undefiled happiness cultivated by the noble ones; therefore, he is worthy of praise.

Thus, it should be understood that because he is worthy of praise, the Noble Ones, manifesting those qualities which serve as the grounds for praise, praise him in this way: "He dwells in happiness, equanimous and mindful."
"Third" means third in the numerical sequence; it is also called "third" because one attains this as the third [jhāna].

In the sections beginning with "at that time there is contact," even the term for *pīti* (rapture) has been omitted from the pentad of jhāna factors. The analysis of the terms, both with and without case endings, should be understood according to that [omission] as well.
In the section on the constituents (*koṭṭhāsa*), it is stated that "there is a two-factored jhāna. The remainder is exactly the same as in the second jhāna.
The Third.
Regarding the description of the fourth jhāna:
"With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain" refers to bodily pleasure.
"And with the abandoning of bodily suffering. "Previously" means that this occurs previously, not at the moment of the fourth jhāna.
"With the disappearance of mental pleasure and mental pain" means that these two—mental happiness and mental suffering—also disappear previously;
what is meant is precisely their "abandoning. But when does their abandoning take place?
At the moment of access for the four jhānas: for happiness (*somanassa*), it is abandoned precisely at the moment of access to the fourth jhāna;
for pain (*dukkha*), mental grief (*domanassa*), and pleasure (*sukha*), they are abandoned at the moments of access to the first, second, and third jhānas respectively.
Thus, although their order of abandonment has not been stated here, they are mentioned here as well according to the order of the faculties (*indriya*) as listed in the *Indriyavibhaṅga*.
The abandoning of pleasure, pain, joy, and grief is to be understood.
But if these are abandoned at the very moment of access concentration (*upacārakkhaṇa*) for each respective jhāna, then why [is it said]:
"And where, monks, does the arisen faculty of pain cease without remainder? Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded from..."?
...through the abandoning of sensual pleasures... one enters and dwells in the first jhāna; herein the arisen faculty of pain ceases without remainder.
And where does the arisen faculty of grief... the faculty of pleasure... the faculty of joy cease without remainder?
Here, monks, by the abandoning of pleasure... one enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
“He dwells [therein]. It is here that the faculty of mental joy (*somanassindriya*) ceases without remainder.

Is it thus stated that cessation occurs only in the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*)? Because it is a cessation of a superior degree. For while there is a cessation of a superior degree in the first absorption and so forth, there is not merely cessation [therein].
However, at the moment of access (*upacāra*), there is merely cessation, but not a cessation of a superior degree. For instance, in the case of multiple objects of focus (*nānāvajjana*).

Even for one who has suppressed the faculty of pain during the access concentration (*upacāra*) of the first jhāna, its arising may still occur through contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like, or through the affliction of an uneven seat;
however, this is certainly not the case within the absorption (*appanā*).

Furthermore, although it is suppressed in access concentration, it is not thoroughly suppressed because it has not been struck down by its opposite. But within absorption, the entire body is suffused with bliss due to the pervasion of rapture (*pīti*).
It exists. And for one whose body has descended into bliss, the faculty of pain is thoroughly ceased because it has been destroyed by its opposite.

Furthermore, regarding the faculty of grief—which was abandoned even in the access to the second jhāna through various acts of adverting—it arises when there is physical fatigue and mental affliction, even though these have thought and examination as their conditions;
yet it does not arise at all in the absence of thought and examination.
However, wherever it arises, it does so in the presence of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*);

and since these have not yet been abandoned in the access concentration (*upacāra*) to the second jhāna, its arising might occur there, but certainly not in the second jhāna itself, because its conditions have been abandoned.
Likewise, in the access to the third jhāna, although the faculty of pleasure (*sukhindriya*) has been abandoned, the body is still touched by the sublime matter produced by rapture (*pīti*).
There might be its arising, but certainly not in the third jhāna. For in the third jhāna, the rapture that serves as the condition for pleasure has ceased entirely.

Likewise, in the access to the fourth jhāna, although the faculty of mental joy (*somanassindriya*) has been abandoned, there might be its arising because it is still near and because one has not yet properly transcended it due to the absence of equanimity (*upekkhā*) that has reached absorption. But certainly not [in the fourth jhāna itself].

In the fourth jhāna. And for that very reason, the inclusion of the term "without remainder" (aparisesa) has been made in various places [in the suttas], as in: "The faculty of pain that arose there ceases without remainder.
Here it may be asked: "If these feelings have already been abandoned in the access (upacāra) of each respective jhāna, why are they brought together here?"
‘For the purpose of easy grasping. For that feeling which is described here as “neither-painful-nor-pleasant” is subtle and difficult to discern;
it cannot be grasped easily. Therefore, just as a cowherd, for the sake of catching a bull that is wild and impossible to catch by approaching it in any ordinary way, [drives it] into a single pen...
He gathers all the cows together, and then, as he drives them out one by one, when they arrive in order, he has even that one seized, saying, "This is it; seize it!
In the same way, the Blessed One gathered all these [feelings] together for the sake of easy comprehension.
For having thus shown them gathered together, [he shows that] which is neither pleasure nor pain, neither mental joy nor mental grief—this is...
It is possible to grasp this as "neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Furthermore, it should be understood that these [feelings] are also mentioned for the purpose of showing the conditions for the neither-painful-nor-pleasant liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*).
For the abandoning of pleasure and pain, etc., are its conditions. As it is said: "Friend, there are four conditions for the neither-painful-nor-pleasant..."
“...for the attainment of the liberation of mind through equanimity. Here, friends, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure... [as before] ...enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna;
these, friends, are the four conditions for the attainment of the liberation of mind through equanimity, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Or, just as elsewhere, even though the view of a self-identity and so forth have already been abandoned, they are mentioned again for the purpose of praising the third path.
In that context, these [factors] are said to be abandoned; however, it should be understood that they are mentioned here for the purpose of praising this particular jhāna.
Alternatively, it should be understood that they are mentioned here to demonstrate the extreme remoteness of lust and hatred due to the destruction of their respective conditions.
For among these, pleasure is the condition for joy, and joy for lust; pain is the condition for grief, and grief for...
[This refers] to hatred (*dosa*). Because lust and hatred, along with their conditions, have been destroyed by the destruction of pleasure and so forth, they remain far away.
"Neither-painful-nor-pleasant" (*adukkhamasukha*): it is "not painful" (*adukkha*) due to the absence of pain, and "not pleasant" (*asukha*) due to the absence of pleasure.

By this, he indicates here the third type of feeling which is the opposite of both pain and pleasure, rather than merely the non-existence of pain and pleasure. The third feeling is called "neither-painful-nor-pleasant" (*adukkhamasukhā*).

It is also called equanimity (*upekkhā*). It should be understood as having the characteristic of experiencing what is desirable and undesirable in a neutral way; its function is neutrality; it is manifested as non-manifestation;

and its proximate cause is the cessation of pleasure. "Purity of mindfulness due to equanimity" means the purity of mindfulness produced by equanimity. For in this jhāna, mindfulness is perfectly pure.
There is mindfulness. And that purity of that mindfulness is produced by equanimity (*upekkhā*), not by anything else.
Therefore, this is called "purity of mindfulness through equanimity. It is also said in the *Vibhaṅga*: "This mindfulness becomes clear, pure, and bright by means of this equanimity;
therefore it is called 'purity of mindfulness through equanimity. And by means of which equanimity there is this purity of mindfulness here...
In terms of its meaning, it should be understood as "equanimity toward the middle" (*tatramajjhattatā*).
Not only is mindfulness purified by this [equanimity] here, but all associated mental factors (*sampayutta-dhamma*) are as well; however, the teaching is expressed under the heading of mindfulness.
In this regard, although this equanimity is also present in the three lower jhānas—just as, for example, the radiance of the sun during the day [is obscured] by its overwhelming intensity—
Just as the crescent of the moon, though present by day, is neither pure nor radiant because it lacks the night that is its own kindred and which serves it as a support,
so too this crescent of the moon of equanimity toward the middle state is neither pure nor radiant because it is overwhelmed by the heat of opposing states such as applied thought,
and because it has not yet attained the night that is its own kindred— the feeling of equanimity.
Even though it exists within the various types of the first jhāna and so forth, it is unpurified.

And because it is unpurified, even though mindfulness and the other factors are conascent with it, they too are unpurified—just like the light of an unpurified crescent moon during the day. Therefore, not even one of those [factors] is described as “purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.
However, here, because there is no overcoming by the heat of opposing states such as applied thought (*vitakka*), etc., [it is so described].

And because of the attainment of equanimity as a feeling associated with delight in the meditative state (*sabhāgā*), this crescent moon of equanimity consisting of neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*) is exceedingly pure.
Due to its purity, just like the radiance of a pure crescent moon, the co-nascent factors such as mindfulness (*sati*) and so forth also become pure and radiant.
Therefore, it should be understood that this alone is called "purity of mindfulness through equanimity" (*upekkhāsatipārisuddhi*).
"Fourth": it is the fourth by way of numerical sequence; it is also called "fourth" because one attains this as the fourth.
Regarding the phrases "there is contact," and so forth, within the pentad of contact, "feeling" should be understood as equanimous feeling (*upekkhā-vedanā*).

In the pentad of jhāna factors and the octad of faculties, however, it is already stated that "there is equanimity" and "there is the faculty of equanimity. The remaining factors, which were omitted in the third [jhāna], are present here as well.

They are indeed devoid [of the other factors]. Even in the section on the constituents (*koṭṭhāsa*), "two-factored jhāna" should be understood as being by way of equanimity and one-pointedness of mind alone.
All the rest is exactly like the third [jhāna].
The method of the fourfold system is concluded.
The Fivefold Method (Pañcakanaya) 167. Now, the fivefold method is commenced with the question, "Which states are wholesome? Why?

Both because of the inclinations of the individuals present and because of the elegance of the teaching. It is said that among the assembly of devas seated there, certain devas had this very thought: [text continues]
To some, applied thought appeared gross, while sustained thought, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind appeared peaceful.
According to their suitability, the Teacher divided this into the second jhāna, which has four factors and is without applied thought but with sustained thought alone.
To others, sustained thought appeared gross, while rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind appeared peaceful. According to their suitability, [he taught] the three-factored...
He taught what is called the third jhāna. To some, rapture appeared gross, while bliss and one-pointedness of mind appeared peaceful;
for their benefit, he taught the fourfold jhāna consisting of two factors.
To others, bliss appeared gross, while equanimity and one-pointedness of mind appeared peaceful; for their benefit, [he taught] the fourfold jhāna consisting of two factors.
He analyzed what is called the fifth jhāna. This, first of all, is "the inclination of the person.

Furthermore, that element of phenomena (*dhammadhātu*) which, through being well-penetrated, results in what is called "mastery of teaching"—and which has been thoroughly penetrated by the Tathāgata—therefore, due to the greatness of his knowledge, he is skilled in the methods of teaching and possesses mastery of teaching.
The Teacher determines his teaching in whatever way he desires, according to whichever factors are available; thus,
here he analyzed the first jhāna as having five factors, the second jhāna— which is without applied thought and consists of sustained thought alone—
as having four factors, the third jhāna as having three factors, and [the fourth] as having two factors.
He divided the fourth jhāna and the fifth jhāna, which possesses only two factors. This is called "the elegance of the teaching" (*desanāvilāsa*).

Furthermore, regarding those three concentrations taught by the Blessed One in the Sutta: "Bhikkhus, there are these three concentrations: concentration with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitakkasavicāra*), concentration without applied thought and with sustained thought only (*avitakkavicāramatta*), and concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought (*avitakka-avicāra*)," among these, the first—concentration with applied thought and sustained thought—is...

Concentration without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitakka-avicāra*) has been shown by dividing concentration, but that which consists of sustained thought only (*avitakkavicāramatta*) has not been shown.
It should be understood that this fivefold method (*pañcakanaya*) is undertaken in order to show that [latter].

Therein, in the description of the second jhāna, among contact and the other factors, only applied thought (*vitakkamatta*) is excluded; in the section on the factors (*koṭṭhāsavāra*), it is "four-factored" (*caturaṅgika*).
“Jhāna occurs; the four-factored path occurs”—this alone is the distinction. Everything else is exactly the same as the first jhāna.
Furthermore, those which are the second, third, and fourth in the fourfold system are here the third, fourth, and fifth respectively.
This method should be understood for the purpose of showing the sequence of their attainment:
It is said that a certain son of a minister came from the countryside to the city to attend upon the king.
Having seen the king for only a single day, he squandered his entire fortune through addiction to drink.
One day, while he was intoxicated with liquor, they stripped him naked, covered him with nothing but a worn-out mat, and carried him out of the tavern. As for him—
Seeing him sleeping after lying down upon a heap of refuse, a certain student of physiognomy made this resolution: "This man will become a refuge for the great multitude;
he must be looked after. Having bathed him with clay, dressed him in a pair of coarse cotton cloths, and then bathed him again with scented water, he clothed him in a fine pair of *dukūla* garments.
Having clothed him, led him up to the palace, fed him with choice food, and assigned attendants to him with the instruction, "Serve him in this manner," he departed. Then they laid him upon a couch.
To prevent him from going to the taverns, four men stood pressing down upon his four hands and feet, while one massaged his feet.
One took a palm-leaf fan and fanned him; another sat playing the lute and singing.

Having risen from sleep, his fatigue dispelled by the approach of rest, he woke up and, unable to bear the pressure on his hands and feet, rebuked them, saying, “Who is squeezing my hands and feet? Get away! At that single word, they all departed.
Then, having slept for a short while longer, he woke up; unable to endure the rubbing of his feet, he said, "Who is rubbing my feet?
Go away! At that single word, he departed. Having slept for a short while longer, he woke up;
unable to endure the breeze from the palm-leaf fan, which was like a gale of wind, he said, "Who is this? Let him go away! At that single word, he too departed.
Having slept for a short while longer, he woke up; unable to bear the sound of singing and instrumental music, which was like a piercing pain in his ear, he rebuked the lute-player.

He, too, departed at a single word. Then, having gradually abandoned the afflictions of fatigue, the rubbing and massaging, the blows of the fans, and the disturbances of the sounds of singing and instrumental music, he slept peacefully.
Rising, he went into the presence of the king, who bestowed great sovereignty upon him as well.
Thus, he became a refuge for the great multitude.
In this context, the noble son living in the household who has encountered many calamities and losses should be regarded as being like that minister’s son who had met with the loss of his drink.
The Tathāgata is like the man who was a teacher of the science of bodily marks (*aṅgavijjā*). Of him—
Just as a man forms the conviction, “This person will be a refuge for the multitude;
he deserves to be cared for,” so too does the Tathāgata form the conviction, “This noble son will be a refuge for the multitude; he deserves the going-forth.
Then, just as that minister’s son was bathed with a mere amount of clay, so too did this noble son obtain the going-forth.
Just as he had a coarse cotton cloth for a lower garment, so too does this person have the cloth of virtue consisting of the ten precepts for his lower garment.
Again, just as he had bathing with scented water, so too does this person have the bathing with the scented water of virtue consisting of the restraint of the Pātimokkha and so forth.
Again, just as he had a pair of fine silk garments for a covering, so too does this person have the covering of fine silk consisting of the aforementioned perfection of purification of virtue.

Just as there was the act of placing him upon a palace after he had been clothed in dukūla silk, so too for this [practitioner], who has been clothed in the dukūla silk of purification of virtue (sīlavisuddhi), there is the ascent to the palace of the development of concentration (samādhibhāvanā).

Then, just as there was his partaking of fine food, so too for this [practitioner] there is the enjoyment of the nectar-like qualities such as mindfulness (sati) and clear comprehension (sampajañña), which are conducive to concentration.

And just as there was the placing of him upon a bed by attendants once he had finished eating, so too for this [practitioner] there is [the placing upon the bed] by means of applied thought (vitakka) and the rest.

The application of the access-concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*) is the same. Furthermore, just as a quartet of men who squeeze his hands and feet serves to prevent him from going to a tavern, so too for this [meditation], the thought of renunciation (*nekkhamma-vitakka*)—which squeezes the mind toward the object—serves to prevent it from proceeding toward sensual perceptions (*kāma-saññā*).
Just as the man who rubs his feet, so too for this [meditation], the investigation (*vicāra*)—which rubs the mind over the object—is the same. Of that [man]...
Just as one who provides a fan with a palm-leaf gives coolness, so too does *pīti* (rapture) provide a state of coolness for this mind.
Just as a celestial musician (*gandhabba-purisa*) who attends upon his ears brings him delight, so too does *somanassa* (joy) bring delight to this consciousness.
