And just as one who has relieved his fatigue by lying down on his bed falls into a brief sleep, so too does this [consciousness]—by relying on access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*)—[attain a state of rest].
The attainment of the first jhāna by one who is free from hindrances and fatigue.

Then, just as for someone who has woken from sleep there is the irritation caused by the pressure of hands and feet, and after those irritants have departed, a slight return to sleep; so too it is for this person who has emerged from the first jhāna.

By not enduring thoughts that oppress the mind, one sees the fault in applied thought (*vitakka*); and by abandoning applied thought, one further attains the second jhāna, which possesses sustained thought (*vicāra*) alone.

Then, when he has risen from sleep after falling asleep again and again, by not enduring the rubbing of his feet and so forth according to the aforementioned sequence, there is the successive rebuking of the foot-rubbers and others, and through their respective departures—
Just as falling asleep again and again little by little, so too for this meditator who has repeatedly emerged from the second and subsequent jhānas,

there occurs a successive perception of the faults— namely, applied thought (*vitakka*) and the rest— which he cannot endure. Through the repeated abandoning of each of those [faults], there occurs the attainment of jhānas that are successively free from applied thought and sustained thought (*avitakka-avicāra*), free from rapture (*nippītaka*), and free from joy (*pahīnasomanassa*).

Furthermore, just as for him who has risen from his bed and gone into the presence of the king there is the attainment of sovereignty, so too for this [meditator] who has emerged from the fifth jhāna and entered upon insight, there is the attainment of Arahantship.

Just as that man who has attained sovereignty becomes a refuge for many people, so too should it be understood that he who has attained Arahantship becomes a refuge for many. For to this extent he is indeed called an unsurpassed field of merit.
The Fivefold Method is concluded.

To this extent, the ninefold pure scheme (*suddhikanavaka*), distinguished by the two methods of the fourfold and fivefold [jhānas], has been explained. As for its meaning, however, because the fourfold method is included within the fivefold method, it should be understood as simply the "fivefold jhāna.
The Fourfold Scheme of the Way (*Paṭipadācatukka*, §§176–180).
Now, since this so-called jhāna is accomplished through the sequence of the way (*paṭipadā*), the classification of its ways will therefore be shown.
To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with "Which states are wholesome? is commenced. In that context, "having a painful practice" means it is *dukkha-paṭipada*;
"having sluggish direct knowledge" means it is *dandhābhiñña*. Thus, "painful practice," "sluggish direct knowledge," and "earth-kasiṇa"—all three are names for the jhāna itself.
The same method applies to [the combinations] such as "painful practice with quick direct knowledge" and so forth.

In this context, the development of jhāna that proceeds from the initial application of attention until the access concentration (*upacāra*) of each respective jhāna arises is called the "way" (*paṭipadā*).
However, the wisdom (*paññā*) that proceeds from access concentration until absorption (*appanā*) is called "direct knowledge" (*abhiññā*). Furthermore, for some, this way is painful.
The meaning is that it is difficult and not easy to practice because of the density of the manifestation of opposing states such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
For some, due to the absence of those [hindrances], it is easy. Higher knowledge (*abhiññā*) is also slow, dull, and of non-rapid occurrence for some;
for others, it is quick, not dull, and of rapid occurrence. Therefore, for one who initially suppresses the defilements with difficulty and with effort...
One who suppresses [the defilements] while becoming exhausted through strenuous application has what is called the "painful practice" (*dukkhā paṭipadā*).

However, for one whose defilements have been suppressed and who dwells in the preparatory stage (*parivāsa*) of absorption, but only after a long time reaches the manifestation of the factors [of jhāna], there is what is called "slow direct knowledge" (*dandhābhiññā*).
For one who quickly reaches the manifestation of the factors, there is what is called "swift direct knowledge" (*khippābhiññā*). As for one who suppresses the defilements...
One suppresses [the hindrances] without fatigue through happiness; thus, for him, there is what is called the "pleasant way.

In this regard, concerning those things—suitable and unsuitable factors, preliminary duties such as the severing of impediments, and skillfulness regarding absorption—which have been explained in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on the development of the mind, he who practices what is unsuitable...
The practice is painful and direct-knowledge is slow. For one who cultivates what is suitable, the practice is pleasant and direct-knowledge is swift.

However, for one who cultivated what was unsuitable in the earlier stage but becomes a cultivator of the suitable later on, or who cultivated what was suitable in the earlier stage but becomes a cultivator of the unsuitable later on, a mixed state should be understood. The same applies to the severance of impediments and so forth.
For one who applies himself to meditation without having performed the preliminary duties, the practice is painful; conversely, it is pleasant.
Furthermore, for one who does not achieve proficiency in absorption (*appanā*), direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) is slow; for one who achieves it, it is swift.
Moreover, their classification should be understood by way of craving and ignorance, as well as by way of the respective roles fulfilled by serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
For one overcome by craving, the practice is painful; for one not overcome by it, it is pleasant.

For one overcome by ignorance, direct knowledge is sluggish; for one not overcome by it, it is swift. Furthermore, for one who has not performed the preliminary work regarding serenity (*samatha*), the practice is painful;
for one who has performed it, it is pleasant. But for one who has not performed the preliminary work regarding insight (*vipassanā*), for him—
Higher knowledge is sluggish for one who has not performed the preliminary work, but it is swift for one who has performed it.
Furthermore, their distinction should be understood by way of the defilements and the faculties.

For one with sharp defilements and dull faculties, the practice is painful and higher knowledge is sluggish; however, for one with sharp faculties, higher knowledge is swift. For one with mild defilements...
And for one of dull faculties, the way of practice is pleasant but slow in direct knowledge, whereas for one of sharp faculties, it is quick in direct knowledge.

Thus, among these ways of practice and types of direct knowledge, when a person attains *jhāna* by means of a painful way of practice and slow direct knowledge, that *jhāna* of his is called "painful practice with slow direct knowledge. The same method applies to the remaining cases as well.

In this context, [the attainment occurs] either through the mindfulness described as "mindfulness established in accordance with that" (*tadanudhammatā sati santiṭṭhati*) or through the wisdom characterized by stability (*ṭhitibhāginī paññā*).

The path should be understood as the method for suppressing the attachment to each respective jhāna, and the higher knowledge (*abhiññā*) as the purification of absorption (*appanā*) attained by one who has reached the access concentration (*upacāra*) of each respective jhāna. Furthermore, the path and the higher knowledge also exist by way of their progression;

for instance, having attained the first jhāna that is difficult to practice and slow in its higher knowledge, the second jhāna that follows is likewise of the same nature. This is also the case for the third and fourth jhānas.
The same method applies. Just as in the fourfold scheme, so too in the fivefold scheme, the division into four types should be understood by way of the modes of progress (*paṭipadā*).
Thus, there are four sets of nine stated by way of the modes of progress. Among these, thirty-six consciousnesses are mentioned according to the literal reading;
however, in terms of their actual meaning, because the fourfold scheme is included within the fivefold scheme, they amount to only twenty.
The Tetrad of Ways of Practice.
The Tetrad of Objects (181).
Now, since this so-called jhāna is fourfold according to the distinction of ways of practice, it is likewise fourfold according to the distinction of objects.
It exists. Therefore, in order to show its classification, the passage beginning with "Which states are wholesome? is commenced once again.
In that context, regarding the terms "limited" (*paritta*) and "having a limited object" (*parittārammaṇa*), that which is weak—unable to serve as a condition for higher jhāna—is called "limited.
However, that which [occurs] toward an object the size of a needle-point or a saucer, when it has not yet expanded...
That which has a limited object (*paritta*) as its focal point (*ārammaṇa*) is "limited-object" (*parittārammaṇa*).
That which is familiar and well-developed, capable of becoming a condition for a higher jhāna, is called "immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*).

That which occurs with a vast object is "immeasurable-object" (*appamāṇārammaṇa*) because its object is immeasurable due to its great extent. However, there is also a "mixed method" (*vomisakkanaya*) based on the combination of the characteristics already mentioned.
It should be understood. Thus, four sets of nine have been stated by way of the object as well. Here, the counting of the consciousnesses is exactly as before.
This concludes the tetrad of objects. [Now follows] that which combines the objects with the modes of progress.

186. Now, in order to show the method of the sixteenfold repetition which includes both the object and the mode of progress (*paṭipadā*), the passage beginning "Furthermore, which states are wholesome?

is commenced. Therein, the jhāna described in the first method is inferior for four reasons: because its mode of progress is painful (*dukkha-paṭipadā*), because its direct knowledge is sluggish (*dandhābhiññā*), because it is limited (*paritta*), and because its object is limited (*parittārammaṇa*); whereas the jhāna described in the sixteenth method [is superior] because its mode of progress is pleasant (*sukha-paṭipadā*).
It is sublime for four reasons: because of its quick direct knowledge (*khippābhiññattā*), its immeasurability (*appamāṇattā*), and its immeasurable object (*appamāṇārammaṇattā*).
Among the remaining fourteen [kasinas], their inferiority or sublimity should be understood by one, two, or three of these reasons respectively.
But why was this method taught? Because it is the cause for the arising of jhāna. For, by the Fully Enlightened One, in the earth-kasina...
Pure jhāna has been shown by way of the fourfold method and the fivefold method; likewise pure practice, and likewise pure object.

Therein, for those deities who are able to understand pure jhāna being taught by way of the fourfold method upon the earth-kasiṇa, the fourfold method is taught in regard to pure jhāna as a suitable means for them.
The fivefold method (pañcakanaya) is taught for the benefit of those who are able to understand what is being taught by way of the fivefold method.

For those who are able to understand what is being taught by way of the fourfold method (catukkanaya) regarding the pure practice (suddhikapaṭipadā) and the pure object (suddhikārammaṇa), the fourfold method regarding the pure practice and the pure object is taught for their benefit. For those [who are able to understand] by way of the fivefold method...

The fivefold method (*pañcakanaya*) is taught according to what is suitable for those who are able to understand when it is being expounded. Thus, the teaching has been given below according to the inclinations of individuals (*puggalajjhāsaya*).

Having attained mastery in the elegance of teaching, possessing the four analytical knowledges (*patisambhidā*), the ten powers (*dasabala*), and the lucid knowledge of the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*), [the Buddha]—because he has thoroughly penetrated the true nature and characteristics of phenomena (*dhamma*)—employs whichever method is appropriate due to his skill in the designation of phenomena (*dhammapaññatti*).
He is able to determine the teaching according to each specific case;
therefore, by means of this attainment of skill in teaching, he has presented this earth-kasiṇa meditation by way of the "pure fourfold method" and so forth.

However, since no one who is said to arouse jhāna is able to do so without the object and the preliminary steps, this sixteenfold method is taught because it is the definitive cause for the arising of jhāna.

Up to this point, twenty-five groups of nine have been explained: the pure group of nine, the four groups of nine on the way, and the four groups of nine on the objects—these constitute the sixteen groups of nine. Within each of these groups of nine, there are two methods (naya) by way of the tetrads and pentads;
thus, there are fifty methods in total. Among those, in the twenty-five methods of tetrads, there are one hundred [methods], and in the [twenty-five] methods of pentads...
"Two hundred and twenty-five" means that according to the literal reading (*pāṭhato*), there are two hundred and twenty-five jhāna-consciousnesses.
However, since the fivefold method is included within the fourfold method, in terms of actual meaning (*atthato*), there are only one hundred and twenty-five consciousnesses.

Regarding these two hundred and twenty-five consciousnesses mentioned in the text, in the exposition (*niddesa*) of each one, there are the determination of phenomena (*dhammavavatthāna*) and so forth.
There are three major sections each. However, these have been abbreviated by showing merely the general method in various places.
This concludes the earth kasiṇa.
Now, since these jhānas also arise in the water kasiṇa and the others, [the following is] for the purpose of demonstrating them.
The section beginning with "Furthermore, which states are wholesome? is commenced.

Regarding these, the entire method of the text, the exposition of the meaning, the counting of the consciousnesses, and the summary of the sections should be understood according to the same method as that stated for the earth-kasiṇa.
As for the method of development, it has already been explained in its entirety in the *Visuddhimagga* (starting from Visuddhi 1.91), beginning with the preliminary work for the kasiṇas.
In the Mahāsakuludāyisutta, however, the ten kasiṇas are mentioned. Among these, the consciousness-kasiṇa (viññāṇakasiṇa) pertains exclusively to the immaterial states (āruppa) in every respect;

for it includes both the sublime consciousness occurring in space and the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana-samāpatti) produced by performing the preliminary work upon that [consciousness].
Therefore, it is not discussed in this place.
The space-kasiṇa (ākāsakasiṇa), however, refers to the space itself when the kasiṇa has been removed; it also refers to the aggregates that arise taking that as their object;

and it also refers to the mode of delimitation of the sign to be grasped within a hole in a wall or similar location, as well as to the fourfold and fivefold jhānas that arise taking that as their object.
Among these, the first method belongs to the exposition of the formless attainments (ārūppa).

The final method concerns the teaching on the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*). Thus, because it is mixed, this teaching on the fine-material sphere has not been included [in the previous section].
However, the jhāna produced in the delimiting space (*paricchedākāsa*) is the path to rebirth in the fine-material realm; therefore, that must be taken up.
In that case, only the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arise, but the immaterial jhāna (*arūpajjhāna*) does not arise. Why? Because of the removal of the kasiṇa (*kasiṇugghāṭana*).
Because it is not obtained [as a removal]. For even though it is repeatedly cleared away, it remains as mere space; thus, the removal of the kasiṇa is not possible there.

Therefore, the jhāna arisen therein leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life, serves as a basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā), and serves as a basis for insight (vipassanā), but it does not serve as a basis for cessation (nirodha).
However, the successive cessation here [occurs] up to...
The fifth jhāna is obtained [from this], and it certainly serves as a basis for the round of existence (*vaṭṭapādaka*).
Just as this is so, so too is the jhāna that arises from the preceding kasiṇas; however, the specific distinction here is its status as a basis for cessation (*nirodhapādakabhāva*).
Everything else that ought to be said regarding the space-kasiṇa has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
However, for one who desires the supernormal power of transformation—beginning with “being one, he becomes many”—he should first produce the eight attainments based on the eight kasiṇas.
Then, he should proceed by way of the direct order of the kasiṇas, the reverse order of the kasiṇas, and both the direct and reverse orders of the kasiṇas;
by way of the direct order of the jhānas, the reverse order of the jhānas, and both the direct and reverse orders of the jhānas; and by way of skipping jhānas and skipping kasiṇas.
The mind should be tamed in fourteen ways: by transition from one jhāna to another kasiṇa; by transition between factors; by transition between objects;
by transition between both factors and objects; and by the defining of factors and the defining of objects.
The detailed explanation of these is already given in the *Visuddhimagga*.
However, it is impossible for a beginner practitioner who has not previously developed meditation and has not tamed the mind in these fourteen ways to achieve the transformation of psychic powers.

For a beginner, even the preliminary work on the *kasiṇa* is a heavy burden; perhaps only one in a hundred or a thousand is capable of it. For one who has completed the preliminary work on the *kasiṇa*, the arising of the sign [is possible].

The burden: among hundreds or thousands, only one is able [to accomplish it]. Once the sign has arisen, the burden of increasing it and attaining absorption (*appanā*) is such that, among hundreds or thousands, only one is able [to do so].
For one who has attained absorption, the burden of taming the mind in fourteen ways is such that, among hundreds or thousands, only one is able [to do so].
Even for one whose mind has been tamed in fourteen ways, the supernormal transformation of psychic power (*iddhi-vikubbanā*)—
The ability to perform transformations is a burden; among hundreds or thousands, only one is capable of it.
Even for one who has attained the power of transformation, the state of being quick in response is a burden; among hundreds or thousands, only one is quick in response.

At the Mahāruhana monastery in Therambatthala, when about thirty thousand possessors of psychic power came to attend upon the Elder Mahārohaṇagutta while he was ill, [there was] one who had been ordained for eight years.
It was like the Elder Rakkhita. The entire account has already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Thus ends the discourse on the kasiṇas. Now follows the discourse on the bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*).

204. Having thus demonstrated the fine-material-sphere wholesome state (*rūpāvacara-kusala*) in regard to the eight *kasiṇas*, now—since another fine-material-sphere wholesome state known as the “bases of mastery” (*abhibhāyatana*) also occurs within these same eight *kasiṇas* despite the object being the same, but differing in its cultivation (*bhāvanā*)—the passage beginning with “Which states are wholesome?
is commenced again in order to show that. Therein, *ajjhattam*... [internal]...

"One who is percipient of the formless" means that, due either to not having attained [the higher jhānas] or to having no need for them, he is devoid of the preliminary perception regarding internal form.

"He sees forms externally" means that, because he has performed the preliminary work on the eight kasiṇas externally, he sees those forms externally within the eight kasiṇas by way of both the preliminary stage and absorption. "Limited" means they have not been expanded.

"He overcomes them" means: just as a person who has eaten his fill, having received only a spoonful of food, gathers it together thinking, "What is there to eat here? and makes it into a single mouthful;
even so, a person preeminent in knowledge, possessing clear wisdom, thinks, "What is there to attain in this limited object? This is not for me."
"Having mastered those forms as 'a burden,' he enters [the attainment]"; the meaning is that he produces absorption (*appanā*) right upon the arising of the sign.
By the words "I know, I see," his preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*) is described. However, it is stated in the commentaries on the Agamas:
"By this, however, his mental application (*ābhoga*) is described; and that belongs to one who has emerged from the attainment, not to one within the attainment."

"Infinite" (*appamāṇāni*) means having increased in measure. Regarding "having overcome" (*abhibhuyya*): here, just as a gluttonous man, having received one large portion of food, does not regard it as great, thinking, "Let there be more;
what will this do for me?", even so, a person of superior knowledge with clear wisdom does not think, "What is there to enter into? This is not... [and thus overcomes the perception of magnitude].
Thinking, "It is immeasurable; there is no burden for me in achieving one-pointedness of mind," he overcomes them and enters absorption.
The meaning is that here, appanā is produced simultaneously with the arising of the sign (*nimitta*).

Regarding the phrases "limited with a limited object" and "immeasurable with a limited object," because the term "limited" (*paritta*) is used here, it refers to having an immeasurable object (*appamāṇārammaṇatā*).

They are not taken [as objects] because they have arrived as "immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*) from another [context]; thus, there is the state of having limited objects (*parittārammaṇatā*). However, it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*):
"In this place, instead of taking four objects each, only two are taken. For what reason?
Because if four were taken, the teaching would consist of sixteen instances, and by the Teacher, sixteen instances were already established below."
The teaching is explained in detail, like spreading sesame seeds upon a mat of *kilañja* grass.
At this point, his intention was to deliver the teaching eight times; therefore, it should be understood that only two [sets] were taken up each time.
"Beautiful and ugly colors" refers to pure and impure colors. For blue and other such [pure] colors are "beautiful," while those that are impure are "ugly."
"Unclean and ugly" are what is intended here. However, in the commentaries on the Āgamas, it is said:
"Whether they be beautiful or ugly, these bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana) are taught according to the limited and the measureless.

Among these four, the limited is presented for those whose temperament is dominated by applied thought (vitakkacarita), while the measureless is for those whose temperament is dominated by delusion (mohacarita).
"Beautiful" is by way of one whose temperament is dominated by hatred (*dosacarita*); "ugly" is by way of one whose temperament is dominated by lust (*rāgacarita*).
For these [meditations] are suitable for them. And that suitability for them has been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga* in the "Description of Temperaments" (*cariya-niddesa*).
But why is it not stated here as it is in the Sutta, such as: "One percipient of forms internally sees forms externally, limited," and so forth?
It has been asked: "Why is it that, instead of saying this, 'perception of the formless internally' is stated here for all four bases of mastery?
It is because internal forms are not to be mastered. For whether there [in the first two] or here [in the latter two], only external forms are to be mastered;
therefore, since they must necessarily be mentioned, they are stated both there and here. As for the phrase "perceiving the formless internally": this...

However, this is merely the Teacher’s display of the splendor of his teaching. This concludes, for now, the commentary on the previously unstated terms regarding the four bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*).
As for the classification of the methods according to the pure system (*suddhikanaya*), it should be understood that each base of mastery follows the same method as described for the earth-kasiṇa.
The only difference here is that the tetrad of objects becomes a dyad of objects, and the sixteenfold repetition occurs.

It occurs eight times. The rest is exactly the same. Thus, here in each base of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*), there is one pure ninefold set (*suddhikanavaka*), four ninefold sets of the way (*paṭipadānavaka*), two ninefold sets of the object (*ārammaṇanavaka*), and eight ninefold sets where the object and the way are mixed—making fifteen ninefold sets.
Therefore, it should be understood that across all four bases of mastery, there are sixty-four ninefold sets in total.
246. In the context of the fifth base for mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) and the others, the term "blue" (*nīla*) is stated in an all-inclusive sense.
"Blue-colored" (*nīlavaṇṇa*) is stated by way of color; "blue-appearing" (*nīlanidassana*) is stated by way of appearance.
This means that they are seen as being entirely blue—without visible gaps and with unmixed colors. As for "blue-luminous" (*nīlanibhāsa*), this is stated by way of radiance.
It is said: "Blue-appearing" means endowed with blue radiance. By this, he shows their extreme purity.
For these four bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) are taught by way of extremely pure color.
The meaning in "yellow," and so forth, should be understood in this same manner. One who is learning the blue kasiṇa grasps the sign (*nimitta*) in the blue flower.
Furthermore, the entire procedure for making the kasiṇa, the preliminary work, and the method for absorption regarding "the blue lotus petal," "the cloth," "the color element," and so forth,
has already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. And just as it is with the earth-kasiṇa,
so too in each of these bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*), twenty-five tetrads should be understood.
The Discourse on the Bases of Mastery (Abhibhāyatana-kathā). The Discourse on Liberation (Vimokkha-kathā) 248.
Now, as for this so-called wholesome [kamma] of the fine-material sphere, it is not only [concerned with] the bases (āyatana) in the sense of objects;...
It arises not only by way of the bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) through the act of overcoming, but it also arises by way of liberation (*vimokkha*).
Therefore, in order to show that method as well, the passage beginning "Which states are wholesome? is commenced again.
In what sense, however, should liberation be understood? In the sense of resolute confidence (*adhimuccana*). What is this sense of resolute confidence?
What is its name? It is the sense of being thoroughly liberated from adverse states, and the sense of being thoroughly liberated by way of delighting in the object.
What is meant is that it proceeds toward the object with a state of fearlessness and without restraint, like a child lying on his father’s lap with all his limbs relaxed.
For it is when it possesses such characteristics that it has attained the state of liberation (*vimokkha*).
This method is undertaken in order to demonstrate the wholesome [meditation] of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*).
In this context, "possessing form" (*rūpī*) means that the material jhāna produced internally with respect to the hair and so forth is "form" (*rūpa*); one who possesses that is "possessing form.
For when performing preparatory work on blue internally, one does it either with respect to the hair, the bile, or the pupil of the eye. [Likewise for] yellow preparatory work...
When performing the preparation for black, he does it on the skin, or on the flesh, or in the place of the pupils of the eyes.
When performing the preparation for red, he does it on the flesh, or on the blood, or on the tongue, or on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, or in the place of the red parts of the eyes.
When performing the preparation for white, he does it on the bones, or on the teeth, or on the nails, or in the place of the white parts of the eyes.
Having performed the preliminary work in this way, this was said with reference to one who possesses the jhāna that has arisen.

"He sees forms" means that he sees external forms such as the blue kasiṇa and so forth with the eye of jhāna. By this, the attainment of jhāna regarding kasiṇas based both internally and externally is shown.

"Perceiving no internal forms" means not perceiving forms internally; that is to say, one who has not produced fine-material-sphere jhāna regarding one's own head-hairs and so forth. By this, it is shown that the preparatory work was done externally and the jhāna was obtained only externally.
By the word "beautiful" (*subha*), the jhānas based on the color-kasinas of well-purified blue and so forth are indicated.
Although there is no mental application (*ābhoga*) of "beautiful" within the actual absorption (*appanā*), nevertheless, the object is a well-purified beautiful kasina.

Having done so, he dwells; because he dwells having attained the first *jhāna* [perceiving] "the beautiful" (*subha*), and likewise the second and subsequent *jhanas*, the teaching is thus formulated.
However, in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, it is asked: "How is it that one is intent upon 'the beautiful' as a liberation?
Here, a bhikkhu dwells with a mind imbued with loving-kindness (*mettā*) toward one direction... [and so on]... through loving-kindness."

"Beings whose minds have been developed through loving-kindness (*mettā*) become non-repulsive; through compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekkhā*)—with a mind accompanied by equanimity—one dwells pervading one direction...
[as before] ...beings whose minds have been developed through equanimity become non-repulsive; thus one is resolved upon what is beautiful.
This is called "liberation" (*vimokkha*). However, here in the subsequent text, regarding the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*):

Because it has been handed down [in the texts], that method is rejected; instead, the beautiful liberation is authorized solely by way of the very blue, very yellow, very red, and very white, as well as the pure blue, pure yellow, pure red, and pure white.
Thus, whether called a *kasiṇa*, a *base of mastery* (*abhibhāyatana*), or a *liberation* (*vimokkha*), it is simply a fine-material-sphere absorption (*rūpāvacara-jhāna*).
For that is called a *kasiṇa* in the sense of being "entire" with respect to its object, and it is a *base of mastery* in the sense of mastering the object.
It is said that "liberation" (vimokkha) is so called in the sense of resolving upon an object and in the sense of being liberated from opposing states.
In this context, it should be understood that the teaching on the kasiṇas is according to the Abhidhamma method, whereas the other [teachings] are stated according to the Suttanta method.
This concludes the commentary on the previously unexplained terms here. Now, regarding each individual liberation, just as with the earth-kasiṇa...
By calculating twenty-five times twenty-five, seventy-five groups (navaka) are to be understood.
The Discussion on the Liberations (Vimokkha-kathā). The Discussion on the Divine Abodes (Brahmavihāra-kathā).

251. Now, in order to show the wholesome states of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara-kusala*) as they occur by way of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) such as loving-kindness (*mettā*), the passage beginning "Furthermore, which states are wholesome?
is commenced. Therein, "accompanied by loving-kindness" (*mettāsahagata*) means endowed with loving-kindness.
The same method applies to those accompanied by compassion (*karuṇā*) and so forth that follow. By whatever procedure one has practiced, [one becomes] accompanied by loving-kindness and the rest.
He enters and dwells in the jhānas; all the methods for the cultivation of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] have already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
The meaning of the remaining portion of the text should be understood according to the method stated under the earth-kasiṇa.
For while there are twenty-five sets of nine in the case of the earth-kasiṇa, here, in the first three [immeasurables], they are based on the occurrence of the triple and quadruple jhānas.
There are twenty-five sets of seven; there are twenty-five single units by way of the fourth jhāna with equanimity;

and in the cases of compassion (*karuṇā*) and gladness (*muditā*), these—namely, compassion and gladness together with the four factors beginning with zeal—are also obtainable as "included" (*yevāpanaka*).

Furthermore, the state of having a painful practice (*dukkha-paṭipadā*) and so forth applies here to loving-kindness (*mettā*) by way of the suppression of ill-will (*byāpāda*), and to compassion by way of the suppression of cruelty (*vihiṃsā*).
It should be understood that sympathetic joy functions by way of suppressing discontent, and equanimity functions by way of suppressing lust and aversion.

Furthermore, the state of having a limited object occurs because it does not take many beings as its object, whereas the state of having an immeasurable object occurs because it takes many beings as its object;
this is the distinction. The rest is exactly the same.
Thus, first of all, according to the sequence of the text:
having understood that "these are the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) spoken by the Supreme Brahmā," this further miscellaneous discussion concerning them should also be understood.

Regarding these—loving-kindness (*mettā*), compassion (*karuṇā*), appreciative joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekkhā*)—in terms of their meaning first: it is called *mettā* because it "loves" (*mejjeti*); the meaning is that it "is affectionate.

Alternatively, it is *mettā* because it exists toward friends, or because it proceeds from a friend. It is called *karuṇā* because, when there is suffering in others, it causes the hearts of the virtuous to tremble (*kampana*).

Or else, it is *karuṇā* because it "buys" (*kiṇāti*), that is, it takes pity on, harms [the indifference], or destroys the suffering of others. Or again, it is performed (*kirīyati*) toward those who are suffering.

It is called *karuṇā* (compassion) because it extends itself by way of pervasion. It is called *muditā* (altruistic joy) because those who possess it rejoice through it, or it itself rejoices, or it is merely the act of rejoicing.
It is called *upekkhā* (equanimity) because one looks upon with indifference (*upekkhati*) by abandoning activities such as "May they be free from enmity" and by attaining a state of neutrality.

Furthermore, regarding its characteristics and so forth: *mettā* (loving-kindness) has the characteristic of proceeding in the mode of welfare; its function is to provide welfare; and it is manifested as the subduing of ill-will.

Compassion (*karuṇā*) has as its proximate cause the perception of the endearing nature of sentient beings. Its accomplishment is the pacification of ill-will (*vyāpāda*); its failure is the arising of affectionate attachment.
It is characterized by the manifestation of a mode that removes suffering; its essence is the inability to endure the suffering of others; it is manifested as non-harming (*avihiṃsā*);

and its proximate cause is the perception of the state of helplessness in those overwhelmed by suffering. The pacification of cruelty (*vihiṃsā*) is its accomplishment; the arising of sorrow (*śoka*) is its failure.
*Vipatti* (failure). *Muditā* (appreciative joy) has the characteristic of rejoicing in sentient beings; its function is non-envy; it is manifested as the removal of discontent;
its proximate cause is seeing the success of sentient beings. The cessation of discontent is its success; the arising of derision is its failure.
*Upekkhā* (equanimity) has the characteristic of proceeding with an attitude of neutrality toward sentient beings; its function is seeing beings with impartiality.
It is manifested as the subsiding of aversion and attachment. Its proximate cause is the vision of the ownership of action (*kammassakatā*), which occurs thus: "Beings are owners of their actions;
by whose whim would they become happy, or be released from suffering, or not fall away from the attainment already reached?
Its fulfillment consists in the subsiding of aversion and attachment directed toward the household life.
The failure in equanimity regarding others is its deficiency.
Furthermore, the common purpose of these four divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*) is both the bliss of insight (*vipassanā-sukha*) and success in existence (*bhava-sampatti*);

their individual purposes, however, are the counteracting of ill-will and so forth. Herein, loving-kindness has the purpose of counteracting ill-will; [compassion] has the purpose of counteracting cruelty, aversion, and lust.
The other [is the opposite]. And this has also been said:
"For this, friends, is the escape from ill will, namely, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness;

for this, friends, is the escape from cruelty, namely, the liberation of mind through compassion; for this, friends, is the escape from aversion, namely, the liberation of mind through appreciative joy."
"For this, friends, is the escape from lust, namely, the liberation of the mind through equanimity.
And here, for each one, there are two adversaries according to their proximity and distance.

For in the case of the divine abode of loving-kindness (*mettā-brahmavihāra*), lust is the proximate adversary because of its shared nature in perceiving qualities, just as an enemy who moves about nearby is a threat to a man.
Thus, it quickly finds an opportunity. Therefore, loving-kindness must be well protected from that.
Like a man’s enemy lurking in a thicket of mountains or elsewhere, ill will is a distant adversary due to its inherent dissimilarity.
Therefore, one should practice loving-kindness fearlessly toward it. And it is impossible for one to practice loving-kindness and yet harbor anger.

In the divine abode of compassion (*karuṇā-brahmavihāra*), sorrow arises when one regards the non-attainment of forms cognizable by the eye— which are desirable, lovely, agreeable, charming, and connected with worldly bait—
or when one recollects what was previously attained but is now past, ceased, and changed. Such sorrow as this...

This is called "domanassa associated with the household life," as it occurs in such passages. Because it shares the common characteristic of perceiving misfortune, this domestic *domanassa* is an immediate adversary.
Because its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is dissimilar, cruelty (*vihesā*) is a distant adversary. Therefore, one should practice compassion while being free from fear of that [domestic sorrow].
It is impossible for one to practice compassion and yet inflict cruelty by means of the hands and so forth.

Regarding the divine abode of sympathetic joy (*muditā-brahmavihāra*): when one regards the acquisition of forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, charming, and connected with worldly bait—or when one recollects what was previously acquired in the past, which has ceased and undergone change—a mental gladness arises. Such is the kind of gladness.

This is called "joy connected with the household life," as it has been handed down in such a manner. Joy connected with the household life is an immediate adversary because of its similarity in nature to the perception of success.
Discontent (*arati*) is a distant adversary because of its dissimilarity in nature.
Therefore, one who is fearless of that [joy] should develop sympathetic joy (*muditā*). And being truly joyful, one will dwell in remote lodgings and in highly wholesome states.
And that he would become weary [of it]—that is impossible.

However, regarding the divine abiding of equanimity: "Upon seeing a form with the eye, equanimity arises in the fool, the deluded worldling, who has not conquered the lower realms, who has not conquered the ripening of karma, who does not see the danger, and who is an unlearned worldling."
“Such equanimity as this does not transcend form; therefore, that equanimity is said to be ‘worldly’ (gehassita).
According to this method, the worldly equanimity of ignorance—which is similar [to worldly equanimity] because it lacks investigation into faults and virtues—is an immediate adversary.
Because their intrinsic natures are dissimilar, lust and aversion are distant adversaries. Therefore, one should maintain equanimity, being free from fear of them.
"It will be met with equanimity, and yet it will be delighted in, and it will be repelled"—this is impossible.
For all of these, the desire to act is the beginning, the suppression of the hindrances and so forth is the middle, and absorption (*appanā*) is the conclusion.
As for the object, according to the nature of the phenomena as they are designated, it may be a single being or many beings. In access concentration (*upacāra*),...
Or, once absorption has been attained, there is the extension of the object.

The procedure for this extension is as follows: just as a skilled ploughman delimits the area to be ploughed and then ploughs it, so too, having first delimited a single residence, one [contemplates] the beings therein: "In this residence..."
Loving-kindness should be developed in the manner beginning with, “May beings be free from enmity. Having made the mind pliant and workable therein, one should delimit two dwellings.
Then, by gradual stages, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten;
one street; half a village; a village; a district; a kingdom; and one direction—in this way, as far as...
One should develop loving-kindness toward beings in one world-system, or even beyond that, in various places.
The same applies to compassion and the other [immeasurables]. This is the sequence for expanding the object here.
Just as the formless attainments are the outcome of the kasiṇas, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the outcome of the meditative absorptions (samādhis),...
The outflow of insights is the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*); the outflow of serenity and insight is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*);
likewise, the outflow of the preceding three divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*) here is the divine abiding of equanimity (*upekkhābrahmavihāra*).
For just as it is impossible to place pinnacles and rafters in the air without first erecting a pillar and installing a framework of beams, so too...

Without the third jhāna in the preceding [four bases], it is not possible to develop the fourth. Furthermore, among the kasiṇas, this [fourth] does not arise for one who has already produced the third jhāna, because their objects are of a different nature (visabhāga).
Here it may be asked: "Why are these—loving-kindness, compassion, gladness, and equanimity—called 'divine abodes' (brahmavihāra)? Why..."
And why are there only four? What is their sequence? And why are they called "immeasurables" (*appamaññā*) in the *Vibhaṅga*? It is said:

First, their status as "divine abodes" (*brahmavihāra*) should be understood in the sense of being supreme and in the sense of being faultless. For these abodes are supreme because they constitute the right practice toward sentient beings.
And just as the Brahmās dwell with faultless minds, so too those associated with these [abodes] dwell in that same way.
Because practitioners dwell having become equal to Brahmas, they are called "Brahma-vihāras" in the sense of being supreme and in the sense of being faultless.
As for the question beginning with "And why four?", this is the answer:
"They are four by way of the Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga) and so forth..."
But because they proceed toward immeasurable objects by way of the aspects of "benefit" and so forth,
they are called "immeasurables" (appamaññā) on that account.
For among these, loving-kindness is the path of purification for one who is full of ill-will, compassion for one who is full of cruelty, appreciative joy for one who is full of discontent,

and equanimity for one who is full of lust. Furthermore, because the mental attention directed toward beings is fourfold— consisting of the promotion of welfare, the removal of harm, rejoicing in success, and non-involvement—
and because it is just as a mother [acts] toward her infant, her sick child, her child in the prime of youth, and her child who has gone off to perform his own duties...
Among four sons, a mother desires the growth of the youngest; she desires the removal of illness from one who is ill;
she desires the long endurance of the youthfulness of one who has reached his prime; and she is not occupied with any other task when he is intent on his own duty.

In the same way, one who dwells in the immeasurables (appamaññā) should also abide toward all beings by means of loving-kindness (mettā) and the rest. Therefore, from this point onward, according to the Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga) and other sources:
There are four illimitables (*appamaññā*).

However, since one who wishes to develop all four must first proceed toward sentient beings by way of the manifestation of the aspect of welfare (*hitākāra*), and loving-kindness (*mettā*) has the characteristic of manifesting the aspect of welfare;
therefore, for those beings for whom welfare has thus been wished, [one should consider] their being overwhelmed by suffering...

Having seen, heard, or inferred [the suffering of others], compassion has the characteristic of proceeding in the mode of removing that suffering, because it proceeds in the mode of removing suffering.

Likewise, having seen the success of those for whom one has thus wished for welfare and the removal of suffering as they had wished, sympathetic joy has the characteristic of rejoicing in that success, because it consists in rejoicing in their success. Beyond that, however, there is nothing further to be done.
One should proceed by way of the neutral mode known as equanimity (*ajjhupekkhakatā*), and equanimity has the characteristic of proceeding with that neutral mode.

Therefore, although loving-kindness (*mettā*) was mentioned first here due to its influence through aspects such as "for their welfare," the sequence should be understood as compassion (*karuṇā*), appreciative joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekkhā*).
But because all these operate within an immeasurable range of objects, they are called "immeasurables" (*appamaññā*). For beings who are immeasurable constitute their range of objects;

and since they proceed by way of pervading the whole without taking a limit such as, "Loving-kindness and the rest should be developed toward only this many beings in this much space," it is therefore said:
The fourfold [immeasurables] are by way of the Path of Purification and so forth,
while these five are by way of the aspects of welfare and so on;
and they proceed as immeasurable.
"Because they have that as their object, they are called 'immeasurable' (appamaññā).
Thus, although these four share the single characteristic of having an immeasurable range of objects, the first three consist only of the triad and tetrad of jhānas. Why?
Because they are inseparable from mental joy (somanassa). But why are they inseparable from mental joy? Because [the latter] arises from the subsiding of mental grief (domanassa).

Because they are the escape from ill-will and the other [unwholesome states]. However, the latter [immeasurables] consist only of the remaining single jhāna factors. Why? Because of their association with the feeling of equanimity (*upekkhā-vedanā*).
For the divine abiding of equanimity (*brahmavihāra-upekkhā*), which proceeds with an attitude of neutrality toward sentient beings, does not function without the feeling of equanimity.
Thus ends the discussion on the divine abidings.

263. Now, in order to show the wholesome states of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara-kusala*)—which bring absolute benefit to beings of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*) by proceeding through each individual jhāna upon various objects—the passage beginning "Which states are wholesome? is commenced.

Therein, regarding the phrases "accompanied by the perception of the bloated" (*uddhumātaka-saññā-sahagata*) and so forth: like a bellows filled with air, [the body swells] upwards following the exhaustion of life.
"Distended" (*uddhumātaka*) means being swollen due to the state of bloatedness that has arisen in successive stages. "Distended" itself is "distended-corpse" (*uddhumātaka*).
Alternatively, it is called "distended-corpse" because it is a loathsome, distended thing.

This is a designation for such a carcass. "Discolored" (*vinīlaka*) refers to that which has changed into a bluish color. "Discolored" itself is "discolored-corpse. [It is so called] because of its repulsiveness.
Or, it is "discolored" (*vinīla*) because it is loathsome;

this is a designation for a corpse that is blue-black in color—red-colored in places where flesh has protruded, white-colored in places where pus has accumulated, and predominantly blue-black in color—as if the body were draped in a blue garment.
"Putrefied" (*vipubba*) refers to the pus trickling out from fissured areas; being putrefied is itself "putrefaction" (*vipubbaka*).
Or, because it is loathsome, it is "putrid" (*vipubbaka*), meaning it is putrefying; this is a designation for such a corpse.
"Torn apart" (*vicchiddaka*) refers to that which is split by being cut in two; what is torn apart is itself "torn-apart-ness.
Or, because it is loathsome, it is "loathsome-torn" (*vicchiddaka*); this is a designation for a corpse severed in the middle.
"Here and there, in various ways, it has been eaten and gnawed by dogs, jackals, and other creatures.
That which is gnawed is a *vikkhāyitaka* (the gnawed). Or, because it is loathsome, it is a vile gnawing, thus a *vikkhāyitaka*;
this is a designation for such a corpse with its skin gone. It has been scattered in various ways, thus it is *vikkhitta* (scattered). That which is scattered is a *vikkhittaka* (the scattered)."

Or, because it is loathsome, it is "wickedly scattered," thus it is the "scattered" (vikkhittaka). This is a designation for a corpse that has been scattered here and there, such that one hand is in one place, one foot in another, and the head in yet another.

It is both "struck" (hata) in the manner previously described and "scattered" (vikkhittaka), thus it is the "struck-and-scattered" (hatavikkhittaka). [This refers to a body] where the limbs and members have been cut with a weapon in the shape of a crow's footprint.
"Having destroyed" is a designation for a scattered corpse in the manner already described.
It is called "bloody" (*lohitaka*) because it scatters blood, disperses it, and drips here and there; this is a designation for a corpse smeared with dripping blood.
"Worms" (*puḷava*) refers to maggots. It is called "worm-infested" (*puḷavaka*) because it scatters worms; [this refers to] a corpse filled with maggots.
This is a designation for the physical body. "Bone" (*aṭṭhika*) means simply bone. Alternatively, it is called "bone" because it is a loathsome bone;
thus it is *aṭṭhika*. This is a designation for both a skeleton and a single bone.
Furthermore, these same names apply to the signs that arise based on the bloated corpse and so forth, as well as to the jhānas obtained through those signs.
In this context, the perception that has arisen by way of absorption (appanā) regarding the sign of the bloated corpse is the "perception of the bloated" (uddhumātaka-saññā).
That which is accompanied by that perception of the bloated in the sense of association is "accompanied by the perception of the bloated.

The same method applies to the "perception of the livid" (vinīlaka-saññā) and the others as well. As for the method of cultivation (bhāvanā-vidhāna) that should be stated here, it is explained in its entirety in the *Visuddhimagga*.
This has already been stated. The remaining commentary on the text should be understood according to the method explained below.
For here, just as with the divine abode of equanimity (*upekkhā-brahmavihāra*) by way of the fourth jhāna, there are twenty-five single units for each [meditation subject] by way of the first jhāna.
And because the object of the foul (*asubha*) is not subject to expansion, the sign that arises has its object in a limited place, such as a bloated corpse.

It should be understood that when the object is small, it is a limited object, and when it is large, it is an immeasurable object. This same method applies to the remaining [meditation subjects] as well.
Thus, the one of beautiful qualities whose fame was praised by the Thousand-Eyed One [Sakka], regarding the foul [meditations]...
Having thus understood all those [qualities] which the Ten-Powered One spoke as being causes for each respective jhāna, according to the method of the Pāḷi itself;
In this regard, this further miscellaneous discussion should also be understood.
For among these, one who has attained jhāna anywhere may, because his lust has been well suppressed, behave like one free from lust, devoid of greed.

Nevertheless, it should be understood that this division of the foul (aśubha) which has been stated is both according to the attainment of the body's own nature and according to the divisions of the temperaments characterized by lust.

For the corpse, when arriving at a state of repulsiveness, may have reached the nature of a bloated corpse, or it may have reached the nature of one of the others, such as the livid corpse and so forth.

Thus, in whatever state it can be found, the sign should indeed be grasped as "the repulsiveness of the bloated" or "the repulsiveness of the livid," according to the way the body has reached its particular state; thus it is tenfold by way of the states the body reaches.
It should be understood that the classification of the foul has been stated.
Specifically, among these, the bloated (uddhumātaka) is suitable for one who is lustful toward the shape of the body, because it reveals the corruption of the body’s configuration.
The livid (vinīlaka) is suitable for one who is lustful toward the color of the body, because it reveals the corruption of the skin’s complexion. The festering (vipubbaka)...

The bloated (uddhumātaka) is suitable for one who is lustful toward the body's fragrance, which is produced by means of garlands, perfumes, and so forth, because it reveals the foul odor connected with the physical form.
The fissured (vicchiddaka) is suitable for one who is lustful toward the solidity of the body, because it reveals its internal state of hollowness.

The gnawed (vikkhāyitaka) is suitable for one who is lustful toward the accumulation of flesh in certain parts of the body such as the breasts, because it reveals the destruction of that excellence of fleshly growth.
The "scattered" (vikkhittaka) is suitable for those who are lustful toward the grace of the limbs and members, because it demonstrates the scattering of the limbs and members.

The "mangled and scattered" (hatavikkhittaka) is suitable for those who are lustful toward the excellence of the body's physical form, because it demonstrates the disfigurement resulting from the breaking up of the body's configuration.
The "bloody" (lohitaka) is suitable for those who are lustful toward the beauty produced by ornaments, because it demonstrates the repulsiveness of being smeared with blood.
The "festered" (puḷavaka) is suitable for one who has lust for the body, because it demonstrates that the body is shared by many families of worms.
The "skeleton" (aṭṭhika) is suitable for one who has lust for the perfection of teeth, because it demonstrates the repulsiveness of the bones of the body.
Thus, it should be understood that the tenfold classification of the foul (asubha) has been explained according to the temperament of lust (rāgacarita).
Furthermore, because in all ten kinds of this foulness, just as a boat can only stand still in a river with turbulent waters and a swift current by the power of its rudder—
and cannot be kept stationary without a rudder— so too, due to the weakness of the object,
the mind stands concentrated through the power of applied thought (*vitakka*) alone; it cannot be established without applied thought.
Therefore, only the first jhāna occurs here, not the second and so on. Even when the mental object is repulsive, joy and happiness arise through the perception of its benefits— thinking,
"Surely by this practice I shall be liberated from aging and death"—
and through the abandoning of the fever of the hindrances, just as one might think, "Now I shall receive a large wage."
It is like a scavenger who sees the benefits [of his work] amidst a heap of excrement, or like the process of emetics and purgatives for a sick person suffering from a severe illness.
And although this foulness is tenfold, it is one in its characteristic; for all ten types of it possess the quality of being impure, foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive.

This is the characteristic. By means of this characteristic, it appears not only in a dead body, but also in a living body—just as it appeared to the Elder Mahātissa who dwelt at Cetiyapabbata when he saw the teeth-bone [of the Buddha], and as it appeared to the novice attendant of the Elder Saṅgharakkhita when he was looking up at the king mounted on the back of an elephant. Just as...

For even while this body of mine is thus alive, it is indeed foul; however, its characteristic of foulness is not perceived here because it is concealed by adventitious ornaments. Thus ends the Discourse on Foulness (*asubha-kathā*).
But is it the case that these attainments of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara-appanā) begin with the earth-kasiṇa and end with the perception of bones, or are there others as well?
There are others; for the jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna-jhāna) and the development of mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati-bhāvanā) have not been mentioned here.
Although they were not mentioned, the jhāna of mindfulness of breathing is indeed included when the wind-kasiṇa is taken, and they are included when the color-kasiṇas (vaṇṇa-kasiṇa) are taken.
Bodily mindfulness (*kāyagatāsati*) that arises by way of the fourfold and fivefold jhānas regarding the hair and so forth,
and bodily mindfulness that occurs by way of the jhāna of repulsive attention toward the thirty-two aspects when the ten foul objects (*asubha*) are taken up,

as well as by way of the jhāna on the appearance of the nine charnel-ground corpses, are all included here. Thus, every absorption belonging to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) is indeed explained herein.
The Discussion on Wholesome States of the Fine-Material Sphere is concluded.
Explanation of Wholesome States of the Immaterial Sphere:
The Base of Infinite Space.
265. Now, in order to show the wholesome states of the formless sphere (*arūpāvacara-kusala*), the passage beginning with "Furthermore, which phenomena are wholesome?

is commenced. Therein, "rebirth in the formless" (*arūpūpapatti*) means that the formless existence (*arūpabhava*) is the "formless" (*arūpa*); rebirth in the formless is "rebirth in the formless," and it is for the sake of that rebirth in the formless.
"He develops the path" (*maggaṃ bhāveti*) means he generates and increases the means, the cause, and the reason. "In every way" (*sabbaso*) means in all modes. "Of all" (*sabbāsaṃ*)...
The meaning is "without remainder. "Perceptions of form" refers both to the fine-material-sphere jhānas—which are spoken of by way of their characteristic of perception—and to their objects.
For even the fine-material-sphere jhāna is called "form" in such passages as, "Possessing form, he sees forms," and so on;
and its object is also [called "form"] in such passages as, "He sees external forms, beautiful and ugly," and so on. Therefore, here...
"Perception of form is 'form-perception' (*rūpasaññā*). This is a designation for the fine-material-sphere jhāna described by way of its characteristic of perception.

"Form is its perception" means it is "form-perception"; what is meant is that form is its name. Thus, this should be understood as a designation for the object of that [jhāna], which is distinguished by the earth-kasiṇa and so forth.
"By surmounting" means by way of fading away (*virāga*) and cessation (*nirodha*). What is meant?

It is by the complete and total fading away and cessation of these fifteen kinds of perception of form—reckoned as jhānas by way of wholesome, resultant, and functional—and of these eight kinds of perception of form reckoned as objects by way of the earth-kasiṇa and so forth.
One enters and dwells in the base of infinite space for the sake of dispassion and for the sake of cessation.
For it is not possible to enter and dwell in this state without having completely transcended the perception of form.
In this regard, because there is no transcendence of perception for one who is not dispassionate toward the object, and since the perceptions have been transcended...
The object has indeed been transcended; therefore, without stating the transcendence of the object itself, [it says]:

"In this context, what are perceptions of form (*rūpasaññā*)? The perception, perceiving, and state of having perceived belonging to one who has attained a fine-material-sphere attainment (*rūpāvacara-samāpatti*), or who has been reborn there, or who dwells in happiness in this very life—these are called perceptions of form. One has transcended these perceptions of form."
"He has transcended, he has surmounted it; therefore it is said: 'by completely surmounting perceptions of form.

Thus, in the *Vibhaṅga*, the surmounting of perceptions alone is stated. However, since these attainments are to be reached by surmounting the object—unlike the first jhāna and so forth, which [occur] upon a single object—therefore, this [attainment] is also [described] by way of the surmounting of the object.
It should be understood that the commentary on the meaning has been completed.

Regarding "the subsiding of perceptions of resistance" (*paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamo*): perceptions arisen through the impact of the bases, such as the eye, and their objects, such as visible forms, are "perceptions of resistance.
This is a designation for the perception of visible form and so forth. As it is said: "In this regard..."
“What are perceptions of resistance? Perceptions of forms, perceptions of sounds, perceptions of odors, perceptions of tastes, and perceptions of tangibles—these are called perceptions of resistance.

With the subsiding, abandoning, non-arising, and non-occurrence of all ten perceptions of resistance—the five wholesome resultant and the five unwholesome resultant—[there is the attainment of cessation].
"Having done" is what is meant.
Granted that these do not exist even for one who has attained the first jhāna and so forth— for at that time the mind does not proceed by way of the five doors—
nevertheless, in the case of the fourth jhāna, there is the absence of pleasure and pain that have been abandoned elsewhere.

Just as [the fetters] such as personality-view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) are mentioned in connection with the third path, so too in this jhāna their mention here should be understood as being by way of praise for this jhāna, in order to generate enthusiasm for it.

Alternatively, although these do not exist for one who has attained the fine-material-sphere absorption (*rūpāvacara*), they do not exist because they have been abandoned; for the development of the fine-material sphere is not for the sake of dispassion toward the fine-material realm.
Furthermore, their occurrence depends upon form. This meditation, however, leads to dispassion for form.
Therefore, it is appropriate to say that they are abandoned here. Not only is it appropriate to say so, but it is also entirely proper to maintain this as a certainty.
For it was precisely because they had not been abandoned prior to this that sound was called a "thorn" for one who had attained the first jhāna.
This was said by the Blessed One. And here, it is precisely because of their abandonment that the immovability and the peaceful nature of the formless attainments are stated.
Furthermore, when Āḷāra Kālāma had attained a formless attainment, he neither saw nor heard the sound of about five hundred carts passing by right next to him, one after another.
“Non-attention to perceptions of diversity” means: either perceptions that occur with respect to a diverse object, or diverse perceptions themselves.

For these have been analyzed in the *Vibhaṅga* as follows: “In this context, what are perceptions of diversity? The perception, the act of perceiving, the state of having perceived, of one who has not attained meditative absorption and who possesses either the mind-element or the mind-consciousness-element—these are called perceptions of diversity.”

Those mentioned here are intended [in this context]. In one who has not attained meditative absorption, perceptions comprised within the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element occur with respect to a variety of objects—distinguished by form, sound, and so forth—which possess diverse characteristics.

For these consist of eight wholesome perceptions of the sense sphere, twelve unwholesome perceptions, eleven wholesome-resultant perceptions of the sense sphere, two unwholesome-resultant perceptions, and eleven [neutral] perceptions.
"Perceptions pertaining to sense-sphere functional activity"—thus, these forty-four perceptions are diverse, of different natures, and dissimilar to one another;

therefore, they are called "diverse perceptions. It is through the non-attention, non-orientation toward, non-consideration of, and non-reviewing of all those diverse perceptions that one does not orient oneself toward them, does not attend to them, and does not review them.
Therefore, this is what is meant: because here,
even in the existence produced by this jhāna, the prior perceptions of form and perceptions of resistance do not exist—
let alone at the time of entering and abiding in this jhāna within that existence— it is therefore said, "by the surmounting of these."

By the phrase “with the disappearance,” non-existence itself is stated in two ways. Regarding the "perceptions of diversity," however, it should be understood that what is meant is the non-attention to those twenty-seven perceptions—namely, the eight wholesome perceptions of the sense sphere, the nine functional perceptions, and the ten unwholesome perceptions—which exist in the existence produced by this jhāna. For even there, this jhāna...
While dwelling having attained [the attainment], one dwells precisely by not attending to them. However, one who attends to them has not attained it.
In brief, here, by the phrase “with the surmounting of perceptions of form,” the abandoning of all phenomena belonging to the fine-material sphere is stated.
By the phrase “with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity,”...
It should be understood that the abandoning and non-attention toward all sense-sphere consciousnesses and mental factors are also stated.
Thus, by means of three phrases— “by the surmounting of fifteen perceptions of form, by the disappearance of ten perceptions of resistance,
and by non-attention to forty-four perceptions of diversity”— the Blessed One [described] the attainment of the base of infinite space.
He spoke in praise. If it is asked why, it was for the purpose of generating enthusiasm and for the purpose of enticing the listeners.
For if some who were unwise were to say, "The Teacher says, 'Attain the base of infinite space,' but what is the use of attaining this?
What is the benefit? so that they might not be permitted to speak thus, [he spoke in praise] by means of these...
He spoke in praise of the attainment by way of its characteristics. For upon hearing this, it will occur to them:
“Such indeed is this attainment, so sublime; we shall surely produce it. Thus they will exert effort for the sake of producing it.
And he spoke in praise of it to entice them, like a dealer in poison-thorns. As for the dealer in poison-thorns:
He was called a sugar merchant. It is said that he would take sugar, molasses, candied sugar, granulated sugar, and so forth, by cart to a frontier village and shout, "Take poison! Take poison!
Hearing this, the villagers thought, "Poison is indeed harsh; whoever eats it dies, and even a thorn kills by piercing. Both of these..."

"It is harsh; what benefit is there in this? they thought, and so they bolted the doors of their houses and sent their children away. Seeing this, the merchant thought, "These villagers are skilled in business;
come now, I shall have them take [the goods] by some stratagem. He said, "Take very sweet things, take very delicious things!
Sugar, molasses, and candied sugar are being sold at a low price; even for counterfeit māsakas, counterfeit kahāpaṇas, and the like..."
“...it can be obtained,” he proclaimed. Hearing this, the villagers emerged with joyful hearts and, having paid a great price, took it.
In this regard, the merchant’s proclamation, “Buy poison-thorns! is like the Blessed One’s statement, “Attain the base of infinite space.
“Both of these are harsh; what benefit is there in this?”—this was the thought of the villagers.
The listeners thought: "It is as if the Blessed One were saying, 'Produce the base of infinite space'; what benefit is there in this? We do not know its virtue.

Then, the Blessed One’s proclamation of the benefits, such as the surmounting of perceptions of form, was like the merchant’s words, "Take [the sugar] that is exceedingly sweet," and so forth. Having heard this, they [took] much...

Having given the root [of the teaching], he spoke for the purpose of generating effort and for the purpose of enticing them, thinking: "With their minds enticed by this benefit, like villagers [enticed] by sugar, they will exert great energy and bring about this attainment.
Regarding the phrase "accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite space": that which has no end (*anta*) is "infinite" (*ananta*); infinite space is "space-infinity" (*ākāsānanta*).

"Boundless space" (*ākāsānañca*) is simply space that is boundless. That boundless space is the "base" (*āyatana*)—in the sense of being a foundation—for this jhāna together with its associated states, just as the gods have their own divine base;
thus it is the "base of boundless space" (*ākāsānañcāyatana*). Alternatively, it is the "base of boundless space" because it is both boundless space and a base.
This is a designation for the space remaining after the removal of the kasiṇa. In that base of boundless space...
It is accompanied by perception that has reached absorption, which is to say, accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite space.
However, as it is stated elsewhere, "space is infinite," so here neither "infinite" nor "limited" is grasped. Why?
Because if the infinite is grasped, the limited is not grasped; and if the limited is grasped, the infinite is not.
[If it were] grasped [in that way], then in that case the fourfold set of objects would not be complete, and the teaching would not consist of sixteen repetitions.
Furthermore, it was the Perfectly Enlightened One’s intention to deliver the teaching at this point in sixteen repetitions;

therefore, instead of saying “infinite” or “limited,” he said “accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite space. For when this is the case, both [the infinite and the limited] are indeed included.
It exists. The fourfold set of objects is fulfilled, and the teaching is accomplished in sixteen ways.
The remainder of the meaning of the text is to be understood according to the method already stated below.

Herein, the "painful way" (dukkhā paṭipadā) is due to the suffering involved in the exhaustion of attachment to the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere; and "slow direct knowledge" (dandhābhiññā) is due to the sluggishness of the access to absorption in one who has exhausted that attachment.
The opposite case should be understood as the pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge (*khippābhiññā*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that the jhāna occurring in the space cleared by a limited kasiṇa has a limited object (*parittārammaṇa*), whereas that occurring in the space cleared by an expansive kasiṇa has an immeasurable object (*appamāṇārammaṇa*).
And just as in the case of the divine abiding of equanimity (*upekkhābrahmavihāra*), here too there are twenty-five singlefold [types] by way of the fourth jhāna.
They exist. As it is here, so it is in the subsequent sections as well; we shall, however, explain only their specific differences.
Regarding the base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana):
"Having completely transcended the base of infinite space"—here, first of all, according to the method previously stated, "infinite space" is its base.
"In the sense of resolution": the jhāna itself is the base of infinite space, and the object is likewise so according to the method already stated.

Thus, because this base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana) is to be entered upon and dwelt in only after having transcended both the jhāna and the object—by means of causing their non-occurrence and by means of non-attention—one should consider both together as one.
It should be understood that this was said [in the Sutta] as: “having completely transcended the base of infinite space.

Regarding the phrase “accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite consciousness”: here, it is called *ananta* (infinite) because there is no end (*anta*) to it when one attends to it as being infinite.

That which is infinite is itself *ānañca*. Rather than saying "consciousness is infinite" (*viññāṇam ānañcam*) or "infinite consciousness" (*viññāṇānañcam*), it is called "infinite consciousness" (*viññāṇañca*).
This has been said. Here, this is a conventional term (*rūḷhisadda*). That very "infinite consciousness" (*viññāṇañca*) is the "base" (*āyatana*) in the sense of a foundation for this perception;

thus it is the "base of infinite consciousness" (*viññāṇañcāyatana*). Accompanied by the perception that occurs in that base of infinite consciousness is "accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite consciousness" (*viññāṇañcāyatanasaññāsahagata*).
This is a designation for the jhāna whose object is the consciousness occurring in space.
Herein, the practice leading to the attainment of the base of infinite space is painful because of the suffering involved in exhausting one's attachment to it;

for one whose attachment has been exhausted, direct knowledge is sluggish due to the slowness of the access concentration (*appanā-parivāsa*). Conversely, the practice is pleasant and direct knowledge is swift.
Because it proceeds by taking as its object the space manifested from the removal of the limited kasiṇa, it has a limited object (*parittārammaṇatā*).
By way of reversal, its having an immeasurable object (appamāṇārammaṇatā) should be understood. The rest is exactly as before.
Regarding the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana):

"Having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness" (viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma)—here too, the base of infinite consciousness belongs to this [attainment] according to the method already stated above.
"In the sense of resolution": the jhāna is the base of infinite consciousness, and by the same method stated previously, so too is the object.

Thus, since this base of nothingness is to be entered upon and dwelt in only after having transcended both the jhāna and the object—by means of causing their non-occurrence and by means of non-attention—one should treat both of them together as one.

It should be understood that this is what is meant by the phrase “having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness. Regarding the expression “accompanied by the perception of the base of nothingness”:
here, *akiñcana* means “nothing whatsoever”; it is said that there is not even the slightest residue remaining, such as a mere moment of dissolution.
The state of being *akiñcana* is *ākiñcañña*. This refers to the departure from the consciousness of the base of infinite space.
It is a designation. That nothingness (ākiñcañña) is the "base" (āyatana) for this perception in the sense of being its foundation; thus it is the "base of nothingness" (ākiñcaññāyatana).
"Accompanied by the perception belonging to that base of nothingness" means accompanied by the perception occurring in that base of nothingness.

This is a designation for the jhāna whose object is the disappearance of the consciousness that had occurred in space. Here, [it refers] to the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana).

The painful practice is so called because of the suffering involved in the exhaustion of attachment; for one whose attachment is exhausted, higher knowledge is sluggish due to the slowness of the preparatory stage (*parivāsa*) before absorption (*appanā*).
By contrast, the pleasant practice is characterized by swift higher knowledge.
It has a limited object because its objective support is the consciousness that has arisen in the space cleared by the removal of the limited kasiṇa; by contrast, it has an immeasurable object.
It is to be understood. The remainder is exactly as before.

Regarding the phrase "having completely transcended the base of nothingness, [the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception]," here too, by the same method stated previously, the base of nothingness is its [object].
"In the sense of resolution": the jhāna is the base of nothingness, and by the same method stated above, so too is the object.

Thus, since this base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is to be entered upon and dwelt in only after having transcended both this jhāna and its object by means of making them non-occurent and by not attending to them, therefore both of these together—
It should be understood that this was stated [in the Sutta] as "having completely transcended the base of nothingness.
Regarding the phrase "accompanied by the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception":

first, in order to show what kind of perception one who has entered upon the practice possesses—that perception by whose presence this is called the "base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception"—it says in the Vibhaṅga: "neither percipient nor non-percipient."
