Having emerged from it, he attends to that very base of nothingness as peaceful and develops the attainment with a residue of formations;
therefore it is said, "he is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient. In this context, "he attends to it as peaceful" means:
"Truly peaceful is this attainment, in that it remains even by taking the state of non-existence as its object!"
Thus, by way of its peaceful object, he attends to it as "peaceful. If he attends to it as peaceful, how does there come to be transcendence?
By the absence of desire to advert to it. For although he attends to it as peaceful, he nevertheless thinks:
"I shall advert to this, I shall attain it, I shall resolve upon it, I shall emerge from it, I shall review it."

This [state] lacks application, directed attention, and mental engagement. Why? Because the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is more peaceful and more sublime than the base of nothingness.
For just as a king, mounted on the back of an elephant by means of his great royal majesty, while wandering through the streets of the city, [observes] ivory-workers and others...

Seeing a craftsman wearing a single sturdy cloth as a lower garment, wrapping his head with another, his limbs smeared with tooth-powder and other substances, and fashioning various ivory carvings and such, [the king] thinks:
"Oh, how clever these masters are! They can indeed produce such arts!
Thus he is satisfied by their skill, yet it does not occur to him: "Oh, may I..."
‘Having abandoned kingship, might one become such a craftsman? Why is that? Because of the great benefit of royal splendor.
Yet, having transcended the craftsman, he goes on. In exactly the same way, although he attends to that attainment as peaceful, nevertheless he thinks:
‘I shall advert to this attainment, I shall enter upon it, I shall resolve upon it, I shall emerge from it.’
‘I shall review it’—there is no such mental application, attention, or reflection.

As he attends to that as peaceful, he reaches a perception so extremely subtle that it has attained absorption, by means of which he is said to be ‘neither percipient nor non-percipient,’ and is said to ‘develop the attainment with residual formations.
This is called the ‘attainment with residual formations.’
...the fourth formless attainment, whose mental formations have reached an ultimate state of subtlety.
Now, in order to show the meaning of that which is called the "base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" by way of the perception thus attained, [it is said]:
"The base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception: for one who has attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception..."
"or for one who has been reborn, or for one dwelling in happiness in this very life—the mental states and mental factors.
Among these, it is the mental states and mental factors of one who has attained [jhāna] that are intended here.
As for the meaning of the term: because of the absence of gross perception and the presence of subtle perception, neither does he—along with his associated states—[possess gross perception].

It is perception of the jhāna, yet it is not non-perception; thus it is "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*nevasaññānāsaññā*). And because it is included within the base of mind (*manāyatana*) and the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*), it is a "base" (*āyatana*);
thus it is the "base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*).

Alternatively, the perception that exists here is "not perception" because it is incapable of performing the function of clear perception, and it is "not non-perception" because it exists in a subtle state as a residue of formations (*saṅkhāra*).

Neither-perception-nor-non-perception. It is called the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception because it is both that state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and a base (āyatana) in the sense of being the foundation for the remaining phenomena.
Not only is perception (*saññā*) of this nature here, but feeling (*vedanā*) is also neither-feeling-nor-non-feeling, and consciousness (*citta*) too is neither-consciousness-nor-non-consciousness.
It is not without consciousness; contact, too, is neither contact nor non-contact. This same method applies to the remaining associated states.
However, it should be understood that this teaching was given by way of the term "perception" (*saññā*). And this meaning is to be clarified by such similes as the oil for smearing a bowl:
it is said that a novice monk smeared a bowl with oil and set it aside. At the time of drinking rice-gruel, the Elder...
"Bring the bowl," he said. He replied, "There is oil in the bowl, Bhante. Then, when it was said, "Bring it, novice;

I will fill the tube with oil," he replied, "There is no oil, Bhante. In this regard, because it has been stored inside, there is oil in the sense that it is not allowable [for immediate use] along with the rice gruel; yet, due to the absence of its being used for filling the tube and so forth, there is none.

In the same way, that perception is "neither-perception" because it is incapable of performing the function of clear perception; yet it is not "non-perception" because it exists in a subtle state as a residual formation (*saṅkhārāvasesa*).
What, then, is the function of perception here? It is both the act of perceiving the object and the process of entering the range of insight (*vipassanā*).

It does not produce disenchantment. For just as the fire element cannot perform its function of burning in lukewarm water, this [consciousness] is unable to perform its function of perceiving with sharp clarity.
Just like perception in the other attainments, it is unable to produce disenchantment even after having become an object for insight.
This is because a bhikkhu who has not yet formed a firm conviction regarding the other aggregates [cannot do so] regarding the aggregates of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

There is no one capable of reaching disenchantment merely by reflecting [on the aggregates] in this way. Furthermore, even the Venerable Sāriputta—being of natural insight and possessing great wisdom like Sāriputta himself—could only do so by means of "comprehension by groups" (*kalāpasammasana*), thinking, "Indeed, these phenomena, having not been, come to be;
having been, they vanish," and not by means of "insight into phenomena according to each particular instance" (*anupadadhammavipassanā*).
Thus this attainment has reached such subtlety.
And just as this meaning is to be illustrated by the simile of the oil for greasing a bowl, so too it is to be clarified by the simile of the water on the road.
It is said that while an elder was traveling along a road, a novice monk walking ahead of him saw a small amount of water and said, "Water, Venerable Sir! Sandals!"
"Take it off," he said. Then, when the Elder said, "If there is water, bring me my bathing cloth; I shall bathe," he replied, "There is none, venerable sir.

In this matter, just as water is said to exist in the sense that it is sufficient to moisten sandals, yet is said not to exist in the sense of being enough for bathing, so too, because it was incapable of performing the function of a clear perception, it was neither [existent nor non-existent].
Because it exists by way of the subtle state of residual perception and formations, it is not non-perception.
And this meaning should be clarified not only by these similes, but also by other appropriate ones.

Thus, it is "accompanied by the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" because it is accompanied by the perception occurring in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, or by the perception that constitutes the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception itself.
This is a designation for the jhāna that has the attainment of the base of nothingness as its object.
Herein, because of the suffering involved in the exhaustion of attachment to the attainment of the base of nothingness, the way of practice is painful;

and because of the slowness of the access to absorption in one whose attachment has been exhausted, direct knowledge is sluggish. By contrast, the way of practice is pleasant and direct knowledge is swift.

The state of having a limited object (*parittārammaṇatā*) should be understood as occurring in relation to the attainment whose objective support is the consciousness that has arisen in the space cleared by the limited kasiṇa;
conversely, the state of having an immeasurable object (*appamāṇārammaṇatā*) should be understood through the opposite case. The rest is exactly as before.
The Protector, who is of incomparable form, spoke of the fourfold formless realm (*ārūpya*).
Having understood it thus, the incidental discussion regarding that [matter] should also be understood.
For these four formless attainments occur by way of transcending the object: [text continues].
The wise do not desire the transcending of these factors.

For among them, the first [jhāna] is so called because of the transcending of the sign of form; the second, because of the transcending of space; the third, because of the transcending of the consciousness that occurred in space;
and the fourth, because of the transcending of the disappearance of the consciousness that occurred in space. Thus, in every respect, they are defined by the "transcending of the object."
All four of these should be understood as formless attainments (*arūpasamāpatti*). However, the wise do not admit the transcendence of factors (*aṅgātikkama*) in their case.
For there is no transcendence of factors in these as there is in the fine-material-sphere attainments (*rūpāvacara-samāpatti*);
for in all of them, there are only two jhāna-factors: equanimity (*upekkhā*) and one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*). Even so—
In this context, each subsequent simile is more excellent than the preceding one;
they should be understood through the analogy of the palace floor and the garment.

For just as on the lower floor of a four-storied palace, there are [pleasures] by way of divine dancing, singing, instrumental music, fragrant scents, garlands, delicious drinks, food, beds, coverings, and so forth—
Suppose there were five strands of sensual pleasure present in the first palace, more excellent than those in the second, more excellent still in the third,
and most excellent of all in the fourth. Although all four of these are indeed palace floors and there is no difference between them in their status as palace floors,
yet by virtue of the excellence of the five strands of sensual pleasure, each one is superior to the one below it.
Each successive one becomes more refined.

For example, suppose there were four types of robes made from the spun, coarse, fine, finer, and finest threads of a single woman—namely, those weighing four *pala*, three *pala*, two *pala*, and one *pala*—all equal in length and width.
In that case, although all four robes are equal in length...
They are equal in extent and there is no difference between them in terms of measurement;
however, in respect of their pleasant touch, subtlety, and high value, each subsequent one is more refined than each preceding one.
In the same way, although in all four of these jhānas there are only these two factors—equanimity and one-pointedness of mind—nevertheless, due to the distinction in their cultivation...
It should be understood that among these factors, each subsequent one is more excellent than the preceding because of their progressive refinement.
Thus, in this gradual sequence of ever-increasing excellence:
One clings to a pavilion made of filth, while another leans upon it.
One stands independent of the outside, while another stands depending on each of those [others].
These four persons, standing respectively as described,
should be understood by the discerning one as being equal in their state.
Herein, this is the application of the meaning: It is said that in a certain impure place there was a pavilion.
Then a certain man came and, loathing that impurity, grasped the pavilion with his hands and clung to it; he stood there as if stuck.
Then another came and leaned upon the man who was clinging to the pavilion. Then yet another came and thought: "He who..."
"This one is attached to the pavilion, and this one who depends on him—both of these are poorly situated. It is certain that they will fall when the pavilion collapses;
well then, I shall stand outside. Thus, without relying on the one who depended [on the pavilion], he stood outside.
Then another person arrived and, considering the insecurity of the one attached to the pavilion and the one depending on him, [saw] that the one standing outside was well-situated.
Having reflected thus, he stood relying upon it.
In this context, the space cleared of the kasiṇa should be regarded as a pavilion in an impure place.

Just as a man clinging to the pavilion out of disgust for the filth, so too is the base of infinite space, which takes space as its object, [regarded] due to disgust for the sign of form. Clinging to the pavilion...
The base of infinite consciousness proceeds by taking as its object the base of infinite space, which is like a person supported [by something else].

Having reflected on the insecurity of both of these, one—without relying on that which is fixed to the pavilion, like one standing outside—and without making the base of infinite space the object, takes the base of nothingness, which has the non-existence of that [space] as its object. Of that which is fixed to the pavilion...
Having considered the insecurity of that which depends on it,

and having regarded that which stands outside as "well-established," one should see the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as occurring with reference to the base of nothingness— which stands in the external region consisting of the absence of consciousness— as if standing supported by it. And while occurring in this way—
It indeed takes that as its object, because of the absence of any other [perception];
just as people [take] even a king who has been seen to commit a fault [as their object] for the sake of livelihood.
For this base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception [is thought of thus]: "This attainment has the neighboring base of infinite consciousness as its adversary."
In this way, even though that base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) has the fault of being a [wrong] view, it nevertheless becomes an object because there is no other object available.

How so? "Just as people [serve] even a king who has the fault of being seen, for the sake of their livelihood. For just as one might serve a certain king, lord of all directions, who is unrestrained and harsh in his conduct of body, speech, and mind—thinking, "This man is a harsh practitioner"—so too, even though it has the fault of being a view, [it is taken as an object] elsewhere.
Just as a person who finds no means of livelihood must live by depending on a means of livelihood,
so too this base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, finding no other object despite having seen the fault in that base of nothingness, takes that base of nothingness as its very object.
And while doing so— just as one who has climbed a long ladder must hold onto the side-rail of the ladder;
"Just as one who has ascended to a mountain peak gazes upon the summit of the mountain,
or just as one who has climbed a hill rests his knees upon it—
so too does this [jhāna] proceed by resting upon itself."
The Discussion on Wholesome States of the Formless Realm is concluded. 269.
Now, since all these wholesome states of the three planes proceed according to the classification of inferior and so forth, therefore:
In order to show their classification, the passage beginning with "Which states are wholesome? is commenced. Therein, "inferior" (*hīna*) means base.
It is to be understood by way of its accumulation (*āyūhana*). That which exists between the inferior and the superior is "middling" (*majjhima*).

"Exalted" (*paṇīta*) means brought to a state of preeminence; the meaning is "supreme. These too are to be understood precisely by way of their accumulation. For when, at the moment of accumulation...
If zeal (*chanda*) is deficient, or energy (*vīriya*), or mind (*citta*), or investigation (*vīmaṃsā*), that is called "inferior.
That in which those factors are both middling and sublime is both middling and sublime.
However, that which is exerted by making zeal—consisting of the desire to act—the burden, the chief, and the forerunner, is [the basis] from the predominance of zeal (*chandādhipati*).
Because it has arrived [at the mind], it is called "dominated by zeal" (*chandādhipateyya*).
The same method applies to those dominated by energy (*vīriya*) and so forth. Standing at this point, the methods (*naya*) should be counted.

For first of all, there is one method analyzed as "the inferior," one as "the middling," one as "the sublime," and one as "dominated by zeal. These, then, are the [methods] under that dominated by zeal.
There are five methods (*nayā*). Likewise for those beginning with "predominance of energy" (*vīriyādhipateyya*), there are four sets of five, making twenty.

Alternatively, there is the first single pure method (*suddhikanaya*), the three beginning with "inferior," the four beginning with "predominance of desire" (*chandādhipateyya*), and the twelve beginning with "inferior [method] of predominance of desire";
thus, there are twenty methods in this way as well.
Where are these twenty great methods analyzed? They are analyzed in the *Mahāpakaraṇa* under the triad of the inferior.
However, in this present context, having taken the middle group from the triad of the inferior, three sections should be made according to the inferior, the middling, and the superior.
Furthermore, setting aside the middling group from that as well, nine sections each should be made by taking the inferior and the superior. Within the inferior itself...
Indeed, there is the inferior, there is the middling, and there is the superior. Within the superior as well, there is the inferior, the middling, and the superior.
Likewise, within the inferior-inferior there is the inferior; within the inferior-inferior there is the middling; within the inferior-inferior there is the superior.
Within the inferior-middling there is the inferior; within the inferior-middling there is the middling; within the inferior-middling there is the superior.
"In the inferior and the superior, the inferior; in the inferior and the superior, the middling; in the inferior and the superior, the superior"—this is one set of nine.
Also, in the superior and the inferior, there is what is called the inferior; in the superior and the inferior, the middling; in the superior and the inferior, the superior.
Likewise, in the superior and the middling, the inferior; in the superior and the middling, the middling; in the superior and the middling...
"Exquisite. Within the exquisite, there is the inferior; within the exquisite, there is the mediocre; within the exquisite, there is the exquisite.
This is the second set of nine; thus, two sets of nine make eighteen. These are called the eighteen doors of action (*kammadvāra*).
Because they are manifested by these, and by way of these, there are eighteen kṣatriyas, eighteen brahmins, and eighteen vaiśyas.
Eighteen suttas and forty-eight clans and lineages are to be understood.

Furthermore, among these wholesome states belonging to the three planes, the wholesome of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) may be either three-rooted or two-rooted, depending on whether it is associated with or dissociated from knowledge.
However, the wholesome of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara) are exclusively three-rooted and exclusively associated with knowledge.

Herein, the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) [consciousness] arises both with and without a dominant factor (adhipati). The fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara) [consciousness] arise only when accompanied by a dominant factor.
Furthermore, among the wholesome states of the sense-sphere, two types of dominance are found: objective dominance (ārammaṇādhipati) and co-nascent dominance (sahajātādhipati).
In the fine-material and immaterial spheres, objective dominance is not found; there is only co-nascent dominance.
It is possible. In that context, the mind’s state of being the dominant factor (*cittādhipateyya*) is stated by way of its associated states (*sampayutta-dhamma*).
However, because two minds cannot exist simultaneously, there is no such thing as a "dominant mind" for an associated mind.

Likewise, there are no "dominances of desire" (*chandādhipati*) and so forth for desire and the rest. Yet some say: "If a wholesome state belongs to one who possesses a mind, then [it belongs] to me..."

"Thinking 'it will be,' that previous consciousness which has been made the burden and made the chief, having summoned another wholesome consciousness—of that [subsequent consciousness], that preceding consciousness is called 'the dominance of consciousness' (cittādhipati).
Because it has come from that, this is called 'dominated by consciousness' (cittādhipateyya).
Thus, they maintain that it is called "dominant" (adhipati) even by way of its arrival. However, this method is not found in the Canon (pāḷi).
This is not seen in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). Therefore, the state of predominance (*adhipatibhāva*) should be understood according to the method already stated.
And among these nineteen great methods, the number of consciousnesses, nonads, and textual sections (*pāṭhavāra*) is exactly the same as that stated for the preceding pure method (*suddhikanaya*).

Consequently, the classification of consciousness-nonad-textual-sections should be understood as being twenty times greater than the measure stated for those associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta*).
"In the four types of consciousness dissociated from knowledge, there are sixteen factors. This concludes the miscellaneous discussion on the wholesome states of the three planes.
[End of] Wholesome States of the Three Planes. [Beginning of] Exposition of Supramundane Wholesome States.

277. Having thus shown the wholesome state that produces the attainment of the three planes of existence, the passage beginning with "Furthermore, which states are wholesome? is now commenced in order to show the supramundane wholesome state for the purpose of transcending all existence.

In this context, in what sense is it "supramundane" (*lokuttara*)? It is called supramundane because it crosses over the world (*lokaṃ tarati*); it is called supramundane because it rises above the world (*lokaṃ uttarati*). [It is] the world...

"Having transcended and having overcome, he stands"—this is *lokuttara* (supramundane). "He develops jhāna" means he develops, generates, and increases the absorption-jhāna (*appanā-jhāna*) which lasts for a single moment of consciousness.

It is "leading out" (*niyyānika*) because it leads out from the world and leads out from the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*); or else, it is "leading out" because one goes forth by means of it. One who possesses that [jhāna] is its possessor.
For indeed, a person goes forth by fully understanding suffering, goes forth by abandoning its origin, goes forth by realizing its cessation, and goes forth by cultivating the path.

Furthermore, whereas mundane wholesome states of the three planes are called "leading to accumulation" because they accumulate and increase births and deaths within the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), this [path] is not like that. Rather, it is like a single man...
Just as one might build a wall eighteen cubits high while another, taking a great mallet,

goes along diminishing and destroying the very places where it has been built up; even so, that which goes by way of diminution (*apacayagāmi*) proceeds by diminishing and destroying the rebirth-linkings (*cuti-patisandhi*) built up by the wholesome states of the three planes through the creation of deficiencies in their conditions.

"For the abandoning of the destinations of views" (*diṭṭhigatānaṃ pahānāya*): here, "views" themselves are "destinations of views," just as there are expressions such as "destination of feces" (*gūthagata*) or "destination of urine" (*muttagata*).
Alternatively, they are "destinations of views" because they are included within the sixty-two views; thus, they have "gone into" the views.
Or, they are "destinations of views" because views have gone to them; the meaning is that they have a movement similar to views, or a manifestation similar to views.

But what are they? They are the unwholesome states associated with personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*), and the lust, hatred, and delusion that lead to the states of misery (*apāya*).
For as long as the development of the first path has not yet occurred, these states continue to exist;

thus, because they proceed in a manner similar to views, they are called "destinations of views" (*diṭṭhigata*). Therefore, "views and destinations of views" means "the destinations of views. "For the abandoning of them" means by way of their complete eradication.
For the purpose of abandoning. "The first" means first either by way of enumeration or by way of its initial arising. Regarding "plane" (*bhūmi*):

in such passages as "the immediately preceding plane," this great earth is called the "plane. In such passages as "in the pleasant plane of the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*), it refers to the arising of consciousness.
Here, however, the fruit of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*) is intended; for that [fruit] belongs to its associated states.

It is called "ground" (*bhūmi*) because those phenomena exist there by way of being supported. Alternatively, it is called "ground" because, although the supramundane state is common [to all four paths], it itself comes into being and arises, whereas Nibbāna does not manifest in that same way.
Of that first ground. "For the attainment" means for the sake of attaining the first fruit of recluseship, which is designated as the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).

"For the sake of attainment, for the sake of acquisition"—thus should the meaning be understood here. "Secluded" means having become secluded by way of eradication-seclusion (*samuccheda-viveka*), that is, being apart [from the hindrances].
Now, although even mundane jhāna does not succeed without the path of practice (*paṭipadā*), nevertheless, here it is the pure method (*suddhika-naya*) [that is intended].
Having abandoned supramundane jhāna, because he wishes to teach it together with its path while treating it as weighty, he says:
"difficult progress with sluggish direct knowledge," and so forth.
In this context, one who from the very beginning suppresses the defilements, becoming weary through difficulty, with exertion, and with application—
For one who suppresses [the defilements], the practice is painful;
however, for one who dwells in the retreat of insight while the defilements have been suppressed and only after a long time attains the manifestation of the path, the direct knowledge is sluggish.
Thus, whichever case it may be, it is designated as "painful practice with sluggish direct knowledge."

But which stage did they approve? They approved the stage where, although the defilements that had once been suppressed reappear after being suppressed a second time, when they are suppressed for the third time, they are suppressed in such a way that the Path brings about their total eradication.
Of this stage, it is said: "the painful way with slow direct knowledge."
This is the name given. However, it does not become clear by this much alone. Therefore, the exposition here should be understood starting from the beginning as follows:

For one who, having discerned the four great elements, discerns derived matter and discerns the immaterial, but while discerning “matter and the immaterial,” finds it difficult, laborious, and exhausting to discern—

For him, there is what is called a painful course of practice. However, for one who has discerned both the material and the immaterial, because of the slowness in the manifestation of the path during the preparatory period of insight (vipassanā-parivāsa), there is what is called sluggish direct knowledge (dandhābhiññā).
Furthermore, even for one who, having discerned the material and the immaterial, defines "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) with difficulty, with hardship, and with exhaustion—
Having defined name-and-form, while dwelling in the preparatory stage of insight (*vipassanā-parivāsa*), he is able to arouse the Path only after a long time;
for him, this is called the "painful practice with sluggish direct knowledge" (*dukkhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā*).
Another person, having also defined name-and-form, while grasping the "conditions," proceeds with difficulty, laboriously, and with weariness.
One who grasps at the requisites and, while dwelling in the retreat of insight after having grasped those requisites, arouses the Path only after a long time—
this is called the painful practice with sluggish direct knowledge.
Another person, having also grasped the requisites, while penetrating the "characteristics" (lakkhaṇāni), does so with pain, difficulty, and exhaustion.
One penetrates [the characteristics], and while dwelling in the preparatory stage of insight (*vipassanā-parivāsa*) characterized by such penetration, one arouses the Path only after a long time;
thus, this is called the "painful way with sluggish direct knowledge" (*dukkhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā*).
Another person, having penetrated even the characteristics, [does so] when the knowledge of insight has become sharp, keen, clear, and flowing, and then arouses [the Path].

When one who is consuming the attachment to insight does so with pain, difficulty, and exhaustion, and having consumed that attachment, dwells in the probationary period of insight and only after a long time arouses the Path—this is called the painful practice with sluggish direct knowledge. They approved of this alternative;
this was the name given to this alternative. By this very [method]...
By way of method, the three modes of practice from the perspective of others should be understood.

In the passages beginning with "there is contact," four additional terms are present: the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*), right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
Furthermore, in the section on exposition, within the explanations of applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth, there are terms such as "path factor" (*maggaṅga*).
[These] are additional. The rest is exactly as stated below. However, the distinction here is specifically their supramundane nature (*lokuttaratā*) by way of difference in plane (*bhūmantara*).

In that regard, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*) is the faculty that arises in one who has entered the path with the prior mental application: "In this beginningless cycle of saṃsāra, I shall come to know the Deathless state, or indeed the Dhamma of the Four Truths, which was previously unknown."
Its characteristics and other qualities, however, should be understood in the same manner as those explained below under the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*).
Beautiful or praiseworthy speech is right speech (*sammāvācā*). This is a designation for the abstention from wrong speech (*micchāvācā*) which uproots verbal misconduct.
It has the characteristic of embracing; its function is desisting; it is manifested by the abandoning of wrong speech.

Right action (*sammākammanta*) is beautiful or praiseworthy action. This is the name for the abstention from killing living beings and so forth, which completely cuts off wrong action (*micchākammanta*).
Its characteristic is origination; its function is refraining; it is manifested as the abandoning of wrong action.
Right livelihood (*sammāājīva*) is beautiful or praiseworthy livelihood. This is a designation for the abstention from wrong livelihood. Its characteristic is purification.
Its essence is the manifestation of a livelihood in accordance with the Dhamma; its manifestation is the abandoning of wrong livelihood.
Furthermore, its characteristics and other qualities should be understood here according to what was stated previously regarding the three abstinences.
Thus, by way of these three factors, the fivefold path mentioned above should be understood here as the eightfold path. Among the "included" (yevāpanaka) factors:

And there is the absence of these [other factors]. The same applies to compassion (*karuṇā*) and gladness (*muditā*). For these three states are not included among the "included" (*yevāpanaka*) factors because they do not appear in this specific textual passage (*pāḷi*).
Furthermore, compassion and gladness have sentient beings as their object, whereas these states have Nibbāna as their object;
for that reason, they are not included here. This, then, is the specific meaning in the section on the enumeration (*uddesavāra*).

283. In the section on the detailed explanation (*niddesa*), regarding the phrase "a factor of the path, included in the path" (*maggaṅgaṃ maggapariyāpannaṃ*): first, a factor of the path is a *maggaṅga*;

the meaning is a constituent part of the path. Just as that which is included in a forest is called "included in the forest," so too, that which is included in the path is "included in the path. The meaning is that it is dependent upon the path.
285. *Pītisambojjhaṅga*: here, "the enlightenment factor of rapture" means that rapture itself is the enlightenment factor.

In this context, it is called an "enlightenment factor" (*bojjhaṅga*) because it is a factor (*aṅga*) for enlightenment (*bodhi*) or for one who is enlightened. This is what is meant: when this harmony of states arises at the moment of the supramundane path, it serves as the antidote to sluggishness, agitation, stagnation, striving, devotion to sensual pleasure, devotion to self-mortification, the adherence to annihilationism, eternalism, and so forth.

The Noble Disciple is called "Bodhi" because he awakens by means of the harmony of qualities—consisting of mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity—which serves as the antidote to manifold calamities.
He "awakens" (bujjhati) in the sense that he rises from the sleep of the continuity of defilements, or he penetrates the Four Noble Truths, or he realizes Nibbāna itself. Of that...

It is a "factor of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅga*) because it is a factor of the enlightenment that consists in the harmony of states (*dhammasāmaggī*), just like the factors of jhāna, the factors of the path, and so forth.

Furthermore, it is a "factor of enlightenment" because it is a factor of that enlightenment which is called "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) when applied to the noble disciple who awakens by means of this aforementioned harmony of states, just like the factors of an army or the factors of a chariot. Thus said the teachers of the commentaries.
“The factors of a person who is awakening are ‘awakening-factors’ (bojjhaṅga).
Furthermore: “In what sense are they ‘awakening-factors’? They are awakening-factors because they lead to awakening;

they are awakening-factors because they awaken; they are awakening-factors because they awaken closely; they are awakening-factors because they awaken fully; they are awakening-factors because they awaken completely.”
The meaning of *bojjhaṅga* should also be understood by this same method of analysis for the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). A factor that is praised or beautiful is a *bojjhaṅga*;
thus, joy itself as a factor of enlightenment is the "joy-enlightenment-factor" (*pītisambojjhaṅga*).
The meaning should be understood in this very same way in the descriptions of one-pointedness of mind and so forth.
296. "Of those phenomena" (*tesaṃ dhammānaṃ*) refers to those phenomena of the Four Noble Truths which, at that time, undergo penetration.

"Unknown" (*anaññātānaṃ*): although those phenomena are indeed called "known" by the first path, nevertheless, just as a person who has never before visited a certain dwelling might stand in the middle of that dwelling [and still not know it], so too—by way of their original nature (*pakatiya*)—[they are unknown].
On account of a future state, he says, "I have come to a place where I had never been before";
and just as one who, having previously never worn a garland, wears a garland; having previously never put on a garment, puts on a garment;
having previously never eaten a meal, eats a meal—on account of his previous state of not having eaten—he says, "I have eaten a meal where I had never eaten before."
Just as [the Buddha] speaks thus, so too here, because these states have never before been known by this person through their own nature, they are called "not yet known" (*anaññātānaṃ*).
The same principle applies to "not seen" (*adiṭṭhānaṃ*) and the others as well. In that context: "not seen" means not seen previously by the eye of wisdom;
"not attained" means not attained by way of realization; "not understood" means not made manifest by knowledge; and "not realized" means...
"Of those not yet directly realized. "For the sake of realization" means for the purpose of making them directly realized.

And just as with this phrase, so too should the construction be made with the remaining ones: "for the knowledge of what is not yet known," "for the seeing of what has not been seen," "for the attainment of what has not been attained," and "for the full understanding of what has not been fully understood."
299. Regarding the phrase "by the four misconducts of speech" (*vacīduccarita*) and so forth: "speech" (*vaci*) should be understood as vocal intimation (*vacīviññatti*).
Conduct that is corrupted by any one of the three defilements (*dosa*) is called "misconduct" (*duccarita*). Misconduct proceeding from speech is "verbal misconduct" (*vacīduccarita*);
or, misconduct produced by means of speech is "verbal misconduct. By those verbal misconducts. One who delights in what is remote [from them] is "one who delights in seclusion" (*ārakā ramati*).

*Ārati* means non-delight. *Virati* is so called because one delights without those [unwholesome things]. *Paṭivirati* is so called because, having turned away from this and that, one delights without them;
or rather, the term is expanded by means of a prefix (*upasagga*). All of this is a designation for the very state of abstaining (*oramaṇa*).
*Veramaṇī* is so called because it crushes (*maṇati*) or destroys (*vināseti*) enmity (*vera*); this too is a synonym for abstaining. Furthermore, by means of which volition (*cetanā*)...
When one speaks such things as false speech, it is called "doing"; this is the abstention from the supramundane path.
Because, having arisen, it does not allow that action to be performed and cuts off the path of action, it is "non-doing" (*akiriya*).
Likewise, because it does not allow that doing to be performed and cuts off the path of doing, it is "non-doing" (*akaraṇa*). And by means of which volition the fourfold verbal misconduct—

One who is speaking is said to "transgress. This [state], having arisen, does not allow one to transgress in that way; thus it is "non-transgression" (*anajjhāpatti*). Regarding "non-exceeding of the limit" (*velānatikkamo*):
here, in such phrases as "at that time" (*tāya velāyā*), "limit" (*velā*) refers to time. In "he dwells at Uruvelā," it refers to a heap or collection.
In "the established nature does not overstep its limit," it refers to a boundary. Here too, it is a boundary in the sense of being something not to be exceeded.
Indeed, the four types of verbal good conduct (*vacīsucarita*) are intended here as the "time" (*velā*).

Thus, that volition (*cetanā*) by which one who utters the four types of verbal misconduct is said to "transgress the time"—this [volition], having arisen, does not allow that time to be transgressed; therefore it is called "non-transgression of time" (*velā-anatikkama*).
Alternatively, *velā* means that which "causes to move" (*velāyati*), in the sense that it "shakes" or "destroys. What does it cause to move?

There are four kinds of verbal misconduct. Thus, it is called "a limit" (*velā*) because of its boundary. Furthermore, it is called "non-transgression" (*anatikkama*) because it proceeds without overstepping what is beneficial and pleasant for a person.
In this way, the meaning should be understood here even by means of these two terms.

It is "a breach of the bridge" (*setughāta*) because it destroys the bridge; the meaning is that it is the destruction of the foundation and the destruction of the conditions for the four kinds of verbal misconduct.
For here, "condition" (*paccaya*) is intended in the sense of a "bridge" (*setu*). Its etymological meaning is as follows:

it is called a "bridge" (*setu*) because it binds (*sinoti*) or fetters a person within the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), acting as the condition for the four types of verbal misconduct beginning with greed. The "destruction of the bridge" (*setughāta*) is the destruction of that bridge; this is a designation for the abstention (*virati*) that uproots the conditions for verbal misconduct.
Furthermore, this abstention, known as right speech (*sammāvācā*), exists in various states of consciousness during the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*).
It is obtained. For one abstains from false speech with one consciousness, and from malicious speech and so forth with another.
However, at the moment of the supramundane path, it is obtained within a single consciousness alone.
For when one performs the analysis of the words of the fourfold volition of verbal misconduct, filling out the path-factor (*maggaṅga*), only a single abstinence (*virati*) arises.
300. "By bodily misconduct" means by misconduct such as killing living beings, which proceeds from the body or is produced by the body.
The remainder should be understood in the same manner as before. This abstinence, termed right action, is also obtained in various states of consciousness during the preliminary stage.
For one abstains from killing living beings with one state of consciousness, and from taking what is not given and sexual misconduct with another.
However, at the moment of the supramundane path, it is obtained in a single consciousness alone.
For when one analyzes the phrase "threefold volition of bodily misconduct," there arises only a single *virati* (abstinence) that fulfills the factor of the path. 301.

In the description of right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*), regarding the terms "non-action" (*akiriya*) and so forth: it refers to that volition by which, while living a wrong livelihood (*micchā-ājīva*), one performs action...
It is called "action" (karoti); it is called "non-action" (akiriya) because, having arisen, it does not allow that action to be performed.
The application [of these terms] should be understood according to this method. Furthermore, livelihood (*ājīva*) is not a separate category;
it is already included when speech and bodily actions are taken up, as it belongs to their side. However, it is extracted from those and shown separately by way of its constant practice. Thus...
When it is present, right livelihood does not fulfill its own function, and the eight path-factors are not fulfilled.
Therefore, right livelihood must be made to fulfill its own function, and the eight path-factors must be fulfilled. Herein, this is the method:
when livelihood is analyzed, it is analyzed only in terms of the doors of body and speech; there is no such thing as a division of livelihood in the mind-door. Even while fulfilling [the path],...
It is fulfilled in those same two doors [the body and speech]. In the mind-door, there is no such thing as "fulfilling one's livelihood" (ājīvapūraṇa).
However, in the body-door, transgression exists both for the sake of livelihood and not for the sake of livelihood; likewise in the speech-door.
In that regard, when kings, royal ministers, or great officials, being addicted to sport, display their prowess by killing deer or plundering travelers on the road—
Or when they commit adultery with another's wife, this is called unwholesome bodily action (*akusala-kāyakamma*). Abstinence from that is also called "right action" (*sammākammanta*).
Furthermore, the fourfold verbal misconduct that people utter not for the sake of livelihood is called unwholesome verbal action (*akusala-vacīkamma*).
Abstinence from that is also called "right speech" (*sammāvācā*).

Furthermore, when hunters, fishermen, and others kill living beings, take what is not given, and engage in sexual misconduct for the sake of their livelihood, this is called wrong livelihood (*micchājīva*).

Abstinence from that is called right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*). Moreover, when one takes bribes and speaks falsehoods, or engages in slander, harsh speech, and idle chatter, this too is called wrong livelihood. From that...
Abstinence is called right livelihood.

However, the Elder Mahāsīva said: “Whether a transgression through the doors of body and speech is caused by livelihood or not, it is reckoned simply as unwholesome bodily or verbal action. Abstinence from that, too, is right action.”

"It is precisely right speech that is so called. But when asked, "What is livelihood? he replied: "It is the acquisition and enjoyment of the four requisites by relying on the three bases of hypocrisy. This, however, is the extreme form of wrong livelihood.
Abstinence from it is what is called right livelihood.

This right livelihood is also obtained in various states of consciousness during the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*); for one refrains from transgressions of the bodily door by means of one state of consciousness, and from transgressions of the verbal door by another.
However, at the moment of the supramundane path (*lokuttaramagga*), it is obtained in a single state of consciousness alone.
This is because, regarding the doors of body and speech, there exists a volition termed misconduct (*dussīlya*)—namely, wrong livelihood—which arises by way of the seven courses of kamma.

While performing the division of words (*padapaccheda*) and fulfilling the factors of the path (*maggaṅga*), only a single abstinence (*virati*) arises. This is the distinction in the section on the exposition (*niddesavāra*).

As for the fact that the "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" faculty (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*) was expanded among the faculties, and right speech and so forth among the path-factors—it is by virtue of these that it is stated in the section on inclusion (*saṅgahavāra*): "nine faculties, the eightfold path. The section on emptiness (*suññatavāra*) remains exactly as before.
This, then, is the distinction regarding the plain way of practice (*suddhikapaṭipadā*).

343. Hereafter, there is this classification of the teaching: the plain emptiness (*suddhika-suññatā*), the way of practice of emptiness (*suññatapaṭipadā*); the plain wishlessness (*suddhika-appaṇihitā*), and the way of practice of wishlessness (*appaṇihitapaṭipadā*).
In that context, "emptiness" (*suññata*) is a name for the supramundane path (*lokuttara-magga*). For it is so called from the perspective of its arrival...
It receives its designation by way of three causes: by way of its qualities, and by way of its object. How so?

Here, a bhikkhu, having adhered [to formations] as non-self, sees formations as non-self. However, since the emergence from the path does not occur merely by seeing them as non-self, it is necessary to see them also as impermanent and as suffering;
therefore, [one contemplates them as] "impermanent, suffering, and non-self."
Having applied the threefold contemplation, he proceeds practicing in synthesis.
However, his insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā) perceives even the conditioned phenomena of the three planes as emptiness alone. This insight is called "emptiness" (suññatā).
Standing in the position of the approach, it bestows the name "emptiness" upon its own path. Thus, the path receives the name "emptiness" from the perspective of its approach.
It receives [the name] because it is empty of lust and the other defilements; therefore, it receives the name "emptiness" by its own quality alone.

Nibbāna is also called "emptiness" because it is empty of lust and the other defilements. Because it arises having made that [Nibbāna] its object, the Path receives the name "emptiness" from the perspective of its object.
In this context, according to the method of the Suttanta, it receives its name both from its quality and from its object;
for that is a teaching by way of a figurative approach (*pariyāya-desanā*). However, discourse on the Abhidhamma is a teaching not by way of a figurative approach (*nippariyāya-desanā*).
Therefore, here it does not receive its name either from its quality or from its object, but only from its source of arrival (*āgamana*). For the source of arrival alone is primary. That is twofold:
"Vipassanā-coming" means the coming of the path. In that context, where the path is the subject, the coming of insight (vipassanā) is primary;
where the fruit (phala) is the subject, the coming of the path is primary. Here, because the path is the subject, the coming of insight alone is primary.
"Appaṇihita": here too, "appaṇihita" is a name for the path itself. This name [is applied] to the path in three ways.
One attains it by means of causes. How? Here, a bhikkhu, from the very beginning, fixes his attention on [formations] as suffering and sees formations as suffering.
However, since the emergence of the path does not occur merely by seeing them as suffering, it is necessary to see them also as impermanent and as non-self;
therefore, he contemplates them in the three ways as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self."

Having applied contemplation, he proceeds practicing by means of comprehension. However, his insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā), having dried up and exhausted aspiration toward the formations of the three planes, relinquishes them.
This insight is called "the wishless" (appaṇihitā).
Standing in the position of the approach, it bestows the name "wishless" upon its own path. Thus, the path is [defined] "by way of the approach."

It receives the name “wishless” (appaṇihita). Because there is no wishing (paṇidhi) for lust, hatred, or delusion therein, it receives the name “wishless” by its very quality. Nibbāna is also called “wishless” due to the absence of those wishes;
and because the Path arises having that as its object, it receives the name “wishless.”
In this context, according to the method of the Suttantas, it receives its name both from its quality and from its object; for that is a teaching by way of a figurative approach (*pariyāya-desanā*).
However, the discourse of the Abhidhamma is a teaching not by way of a figurative approach (*nippariyāya-desanā*).
Therefore, here it does not receive its name either from its quality or from its object, but only from its source of arrival (*āgamana*). For the source of arrival alone is primary. That is twofold:
"Insight-arrival is path-arrival. In that context, at the stage where the path arrives, insight-arrival is primary;
at the stage where the fruit arrives, path-arrival is primary. Here, because it is the path that has arrived, insight-arrival alone has become primary.
But is it not the case that "void," "signless," and "desireless" are three names for the path? As it is said: "Bhikkhus, there are these three..."
“The liberations are: the void liberation, the signless liberation, and the desireless liberation.
Among these, why is the signless [liberation] not included here when two paths are being taken up? Because there is no arrival [of it].
For signless insight, standing in its own place as that which is to be arrived at, is unable to give its name to its own path. The Fully Enlightened One...
But [he spoke] to his own son, the Elder Rāhula:
“Cultivate the signless and abandon the underlying tendency to conceit;
then, through the full comprehension of conceit, you shall wander at peace.”
He taught insight into the signless (*animittavipassanā*).
For insight dispels the sign of permanence, the sign of stability, the sign of pleasure, and the sign of self; therefore, it is called "signless.
And although it dispels those signs, it itself moves among phenomena that possess signs; thus, it remains "with signs" (*sanimittā*) itself. Therefore, in its own proper sphere...
Having stood [there], it is unable to give a name to its own path. Another method:
the Abhidhamma is the teaching on the ultimate sense (paramattha). And for the signless path, there is indeed an absence of a cause from the standpoint of the ultimate sense.
How so? For the signless liberation is explained by way of the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā). And by that liberation...

The faculty of faith is predominant; however, it does not constitute even a single factor of the Noble Path, and because it is not a path-factor, it cannot truly be given the name "path" in the ultimate sense.
As for the other two, the void liberation is explained by way of the contemplation of non-self, and the desireless liberation is explained by way of the contemplation of suffering.

Among those, the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*) is predominant through the liberation of emptiness (*suññatavimokkha*), and the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*) through the liberation of the wishless (*appaṇihitavimokkha*).
Because these constitute factors of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*), they are able to give their own name to the path in the ultimate sense.

For even in the triad of objects of the path (*maggārammaṇattika*), when classifying the states dominated by the path (*maggādhipati*), at the time when desire (*chanda*) or consciousness (*citta*) is dominant, those states are not considered factors of the path precisely because they are not factors of the path.
The state of having the Path as its dominant influence (*maggādhipatibhāva*) has not been mentioned. This should be understood as being of a similar nature.
This is the decision of the intellect of one teacher, handed down outside the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathāmuttaka*).
Thus, in every respect, insight into the signless (*animittavipassanā*), standing at the point where it must come of its own accord, [confers] the name upon its own Path.
"He is unable to give" means that the signless path has not been grasped. However, some have said:
"Although the signless path does not receive its name from its arrival [at fruition], it receives its name according to the Suttanta method by way of its qualities and its object.
Those who say this are refuted as follows: if the signless path were to receive its name by way of its qualities and its object, [it would follow that...]
The paths of emptiness and the signless would also receive their names here on account of their qualities and on account of their objects;
yet they do not receive them. For what reason? This so-called "path" receives its name for two reasons:
by way of its own essence and by way of its opposite; that is to say, by way of its intrinsic nature and by way of its counteragent. In this regard, the paths of emptiness and the signless—

They receive their names both from their intrinsic nature (*sarasato*) and from their opposition (*paccanīkato*). For the void (*suññatā*) and aimless (*appaṇihita*) paths are called "void" because they are empty of lust and so forth, and "aimless" because they are free from the longing for lust and so forth; thus they receive their names from their intrinsic nature.

Furthermore, the void path is the opposite of the adherence to a self, and the aimless path is the opposite of longing; thus they receive their names from their opposition. As for the signless (*animitta*) path:
However, it receives its name from its own intrinsic nature due to the absence of the signs of lust and so forth, as well as the sign of permanence and so on, rather than from its opposition to them.
For it is not the opposite of the contemplation of impermanence which has the sign of formations as its object; rather, the contemplation of impermanence stands in a state of conformity with it.
Thus, in every respect, according to the method of the Abhidhamma, there is no such thing as a "signless path."
But according to the Suttanta method, this has been brought forward and explained as follows:

For in whichever turn the emergence of the path occurs, the three characteristics come into range as if by a single advertence; yet there is no such thing as the simultaneous coming into range of all three together.
This was said for the purpose of showing the clarity of the meditation subject. For initially, wherever—

Let there be adherence to any one [of the three characteristics]; however, insight leading to emergence, having emerged by means of whichever [characteristic] it has comprehended, gives its own path a name by standing at the point of arrival according to that very [characteristic]. How so?

For among the impermanent and the rest, having adhered to any one, it is indeed necessary to see the other two characteristics as well. It is not by the mere seeing of a single characteristic [that the path is defined].

For there is no such thing as "emergence from the path" [in isolation]; therefore, a bhikkhu who has resolved upon impermanence emerges not only from impermanence, but also from suffering and non-self. The same principle applies to one who has resolved upon suffering or non-self.
Thus, regardless of where the initial resolution may lie, insight leading to emergence—whatever it may be—[emerges from all three].
Having emerged from the contemplation of whichever [aspect] he has practiced, he stands at the point of arrival according to that very same aspect and gives a name to his own path.
In this regard, for one emerging by way of impermanence, the path is called "signless" (animitta); for one emerging by way of suffering, it is "desireless" (appaṇihita);
and for one emerging by way of non-self, it is "emptiness" (suññatā). Thus it is explained by bringing it forward according to the method of the Suttas.

But what is the object of insight leading to emergence? It has the characteristics as its object. Now, the "characteristics" are not to be described as entities that fall under conceptual designation (*paññatti*);

rather, they are the actual phenomena themselves. For one who discerns the three characteristics—impermanence, suffering, and non-self—the five aggregates become like a corpse tied around one's neck. Knowledge that has formations as its object [arises] from those very formations.

He emerges. For just as a certain bhikkhu, desiring to buy an alms-bowl, might see one brought by a bowl-seller and, being overjoyed, think "I shall take it," yet upon examining it, he sees three flaws;

he does not settle his attachment on the flaws, but settles his attachment on the bowl itself—in the same way, having observed the three characteristics within conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), [he emerges].
He becomes homeless. It should be understood that he emerges from formations by means of knowledge that has formations as its object. The same method applies to the simile of the cloth as well.
Thus, while classifying supramundane jhāna, the Blessed One brought forward two methods—the fourfold method and the fivefold method—by way of the pure path, the void path, and the wishless path.
Likewise [he did so] for the pure voidness, the path of voidness, and the pure wishless.

"Regarding the way of practice that is wishless (appaṇihita-paṭipadā). Why was it brought forward in this way? It is due to both the inclination of the individual (puggalajjhāsayena) and the elegance of the teaching (desanāvilāsena).
Both of these should be understood according to the method already stated below.

Thus, in the phrase "one develops supramundane jhāna," there are two methods based on the fourfold and fivefold [formulas] for the plain way of practice (suddhika-paṭipadā), and likewise for the remaining ones; thus, in all of them...
The ten methods have been distributed among the five sections.
This is the miscellaneous discussion on supramundane wholesome states;
herein is the miscellaneous [treatment]:
"Internally and externally, among the five [aggregates] both material and immaterial, one who has entered upon the way perceives the sign as the transformation of seven or eight factors.
For the supramundane path, having applied its attention internally, emerges internally; having applied its attention internally...
It emerges externally; having adhered externally, it emerges externally; having adhered externally, it emerges internally.
Having adhered to forms, it emerges from forms; having adhered to forms, it emerges from the formless.
Having adhered to the formless, it emerges from the formless; having adhered to the formless, it emerges from forms—all at once.
One emerges by means of the five aggregates.
Regarding the phrase "the transformation of seven or eight factors," this path may consist of eight factors or seven factors.
The factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) may be either seven or six. Furthermore, jhāna may consist of five factors, four factors, or three factors.
Or it may be sixfold or fivefold. The meaning is that the transformation of seven, eight, and so on factors should be understood in this way.

Regarding the phrase “the sign and the progress”: “the sign” refers to that from which emergence occurs; “the progress” refers to the movement or non-movement of both the progress and the dominant influence (*adhipati*).
In this context, concerning such passages as “having entered within, he emerges within,” first of all, here a certain person, from the very beginning, [directs his mind] internally...
He becomes attached to the five aggregates; having become attached, he views them as impermanent and so forth.

However, since the emergence of the path does not occur through the mere vision of one's own internal [aggregates] alone, but must also be seen externally, he therefore views the aggregates of another person and even non-clung-to formations as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. At that time...
"One contemplates internally at the proper time, externally [at the proper time].

As he contemplates in this way, when he is contemplating internally, his insight (vipassanā) joins with the path (magga). Thus, having applied himself to the internal, it is said that he "emerges from the internal.
However, if his insight joins with the path while he is contemplating externally, then in the same way—
Having adhered internally, one is said to emerge externally. The same method applies when emerging both externally and internally after having adhered externally.
Another person adheres to form from the very beginning; having adhered, he delimits primary form and derived form.

He sees [them] as impermanent and so forth; however, since emergence does not occur through the mere sight of form alone, but the formless must also be seen, he therefore takes that form as his object and, having delimited the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness arisen therein as "this is the formless," he sees them as impermanent and so forth.
At times he contemplates form, and at times...
It is formless. As he thus comprehends, when the time comes for the comprehension of form, insight joins with the path;

thus, having focused on form, one is said to "emerge from form. But if, at the time of comprehending the formless, insight joins with the path, then having focused on form, one is said to "emerge from the formless. This is the method.
Having adhered to the formless, one emerges from both the formless and the forms.

Having adhered thus: "Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation," at the very time of emergence, one is said to emerge all at once by means of the five aggregates. This is for one who possesses sharp insight.
This is the insight of a bhikkhu of great wisdom.
For it is as if a man who was famished were to have a ball of excrement placed before him in the middle of a bowl filled with various kinds of choice food;
while sorting through the condiments with his hand, he would see that ball of excrement and think, "What is this?"
When asked, if told it was a lump of excrement, he would say, "Shame, shame! Take it away! and would have no attachment even to his food or his bowl.
This should be understood as being exactly like that.
For just as there was a time when he was delighted at the sight of his food and bowl, so too was this monk in the stage of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).
The time of grasping at the five aggregates as "I" and "mine" is like the time of seeing a lump of excrement;
it is like the time of observing the three characteristics. It is like the time when one is free from attachment to both the food and the bowl;
for a bhikkhu of great wisdom with sharp insight, [the realization occurs] regarding the five aggregates that "whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation."
The time of emergence in a single moment should be understood.
Regarding the phrase "the transformation of the seven or eight factors," this transformation of the factors as previously classified should be understood according to how it occurs.
For it is precisely the knowledge of equanimity toward formations that constitutes the specific distinction of the factors of enlightenment, the path-factors, and the jhāna-factors of the Noble Path.
It determines. However, some elders say that the preliminary jhāna determines the distinction between the factors of enlightenment, the factors of the path, and the factors of jhāna.
Some say that the aggregates which have become the object of insight determine it. Some say that the individual’s inclination determines it.
In all these views, it is this very preliminary insight leading to emergence, known as equanimity regarding formations, that [determines it].
It should be understood that [the path] "determines" [the object].
Herein, this is the progressive exposition: by way of the determination of insight, for one who practices bare insight (sukkha-vipassaka), even the path arisen [is determined];

and for one who attains meditative absorption (samāpatti), even the path arisen without making jhāna the basis (pādaka) is determined; and for one who makes the first jhāna the basis, it is determined with respect to miscellaneous formations (pakiṇṇaka-saṅkhāra).

Even for one who has generated the path after having practiced comprehension, it possesses only the first jhāna factors. In all these cases, there are seven enlightenment factors, eight path factors, and five jhāna factors.

For their preliminary insight—whether accompanied by joy or accompanied by equanimity—upon reaching the state of equanimity regarding formations at the time of emergence, becomes accompanied only by joy.

In the Pañcakanaya (Fivefold System), when the paths are produced by taking the second, third, and fourth jhānas as their bases, the jhāna in each case respectively possesses four factors, three factors, and two factors. However, in all of them there are seven path-factors, while in the fourth there are six enlightenment-factors.
This distinction arises from both the restriction of the base-jhāna and the restriction of the insight.
And it is so for them as well; for their preliminary insight (pubbabhāga-vipassanā) may be accompanied by either joy (somanassa) or equanimity (upekkhā).
That which leads to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī) is accompanied by joy alone.
However, in the path (magga) produced by taking the fifth jhāna as its basis, there are two jhāna factors by way of equanimity and one-pointedness of mind (cittakaggatā).
The factors of enlightenment and the factors of the path are six and seven respectively. This distinction also arises by way of the double restriction.
For in this system, preliminary insight is accompanied either by joy or by equanimity, whereas the path leading to emergence is accompanied by equanimity alone.
The same rule applies to the paths produced by taking the formless jhānas as the basis. Thus...
Emerging from the access concentration (pādakajjhāna) and having reflected upon any formations whatsoever,
the attainment that has arisen in the proximate stage to the path brings about a state of similarity with itself, just as the color of the ground [blends] with the color of a lizard.
However, according to the second Elder’s doctrine, emerging from whichever attainment and having reflected upon whichever attainment-phenomena, [the path arises].
The path that has been generated becomes similar to whichever attainment it corresponds to; the meaning is that it is similar to the attainment in which the object was comprehended.

However, if one comprehends states belonging to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), it is associated with the first jhāna. In that case as well, the rule regarding insight (*vipassanā*) should be understood according to the method already stated.
In the third Theravāda interpretation, the path that is generated—

whether by taking as its basis whichever jhāna accords with one’s own inclination, thinking, “O, may I attain the sevenfold path,” or “may I attain the eightfold path,” or by contemplating whichever jhāna-factors—
resembles that very jhāna. However, it is neither the basic jhāna nor the contemplated jhāna [that constitutes the path].
Without that, it does not succeed by intention alone. This matter should be illustrated by the Nandakovāda Sutta. For it is said there:
“Bhikkhus, just as on the fifteenth day of the uposatha, when there is no doubt or uncertainty among many people as to whether the moon is waning or waxing, yet it is simply known as the full moon;”
"In the same way, monks, those bhikkhunīs were delighted by Nandaka’s teaching of the Dhamma and their intentions were fulfilled.
Among those five hundred bhikkhunīs, monks, even the one who was the last [to attain realization] became a stream-enterer,
no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and destined for full enlightenment."
For among those bhikkhunīs, whichever one had the necessary support (upanissaya) for the fruit of stream-entry fulfilled her intention by that very fruit of stream-entry...
[and so on] ...whichever one had the support for arahantship fulfilled it by that very arahantship.
In the same way, according to their own inclinations, having made this or that jhāna the basis, or having reflected upon these or those dhammas of jhāna, the Path was brought forth.

He becomes similar to whichever specific jhāna he practices. However, that [supernormal power] does not succeed through mere intention alone without either the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*) or the jhāna of insight-comprehension (*sammasitajjhāna*).
Here too, the rule regarding insight (*vipassanā*) should be understood according to the method already stated.
In this regard, the pupils of the Elder Cūḷanāga, who maintained that "only the foundational jhāna determines [the result]," said:
They asked: “Venerable sir, where there is a foundation-jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*), let it be determined by that.
But in that formless existence (*arūpabhava*) where there is no foundation-jhāna, what determines it? “Friends, even there, it is the foundation-jhāna itself that determines it.
For a bhikkhu who has attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*), having made the first jhāna his foundation, [attains] the paths and fruits of stream-entry.”
Having been reborn and without falling away from jhāna, he passes away and is reborn in the formless realm (*arūpabhava*).
Emerging from the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*) associated with the first jhāna, he establishes insight (*vipassanā*) and realizes the three higher paths and fruits;

for him, these are likewise associated with the first jhāna alone. The same method applies to those associated with the second jhāna and so forth. In the formless realm, the triad and tetrad of jhānas arise, and that too—
"It is supramundane, not mundane. Thus, even there, it is the foundational jhāna itself that determines [the result], friend. "Well explained, Bhante, was the question," he said.
But the pupils of the Elder Mahā Datta, who dwelt at Moravāpi, argued: "The aggregates that serve as the object for insight determine [the result];
for whichever of the five aggregates one emerges from after having comprehended them, the Path becomes similar to that very aggregate."
They said: “Venerable sir, a fault appears in your doctrine—for a bhikkhu who has emerged after having comprehended form, there ought to be a path that is indeterminate and similar to form;

and for one who has emerged after encompassing the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception by way of method, there ought to be a path that is similar to it and has reached the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. “No,” [he replied].
"Friend, it is so. For there is no supramundane path that has not reached absorption; therefore, for one who has emerged after contemplating form, the eightfold path is accompanied by joy.

But for one who has emerged after contemplating the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it is not exactly like that in every respect; rather, the sevenfold path is accompanied by equanimity."
They recounted the argument of the Elder Cūḷa-Abhaya, who maintained that “the individual’s inclination determines [the type of rebirth],” to the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷa-Nāga.
He said: “In the case of one who possesses the foundational jhāna, their individual inclination may determine [the rebirth];
but for one who lacks it, what inclination could possibly determine anything? It is like a poor man seeking a means of livelihood.”
Having brought this matter forward, they recounted it again to the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷābhaya. He said, "Friends, this was spoken by one who possesses the foundational jhāna (pādakajjhāna).
However, it should be understood that the same applies to one who possesses the jhāna attained through comprehension (sammasitajjhāna).
For when one emerges from the fifth jhāna and comprehends the first jhāna and so forth, the path that arises is designated by the term "the first elder" (paṭhamattheravāda).
[The first position holds that it] belongs to the fifth jhāna. According to the second position, it falls under the first jhāna and so forth; thus, these two positions contradict each other.
However, according to the third position—that "it belongs to whichever jhāna one desires"—those positions do not contradict one another, and the underlying intention becomes meaningful.
Thus, all three elders were indeed wise, competent, and endowed with intelligence.

Therefore, they established their doctrine by making that [text] their authority. Here, however, having extracted only the meaning, it is shown that in all three of these doctrines, it is insight alone that determines [the path].

Now, regarding the phrase "the sign conforms to the way," at the time of the arising of the path—which possesses the transformation of its factors—the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) [consciousness occurs].
From what does one emerge? From where does the path emerge? First, change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu*) emerges from the sign (*nimitta*), but it is unable to cut off the process of existence (*pavatta*);
for it is an emergence from one side only. The path emerges from the sign and also cuts off the process of existence;
for it is an emergence from both sides. This is the method of their arising: in whichever turn the emergence of the path occurs, in that very turn there is conformity (*anuloma*).
It is neither one nor five. For it does not receive repetition; and because the fifth is close to the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), it falters.
At that time, the impulsion (*javana*) is said to have fallen away. Therefore, it is neither one nor five.
However, for one of great wisdom, there are two conformities (*anuloma*), the third is change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*), the fourth is the path-consciousness (*maggacitta*), and there are three fruits.

Then there is the emergence from the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). For one of medium wisdom, there are three moments of conformity (*anuloma*), the fourth is the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*), the fifth is the path-consciousness (*magga-citta*), and two moments of fruition (*phala*); then there is the emergence from the life-continuum.

For one of dull wisdom, there are four moments of conformity, the fifth is the change-of-lineage, the sixth is the path-consciousness, and the seventh is the fruition; then there is the emergence from the life-continuum.
In this context, one should explain it not by way of those with great wisdom or limited wisdom, but by way of one of medium wisdom.

For in that turn [of consciousness] when the emergence of the path occurs, the functional root-causeless mind-consciousness element, accompanied by equanimity, acts as the mind-door adverting consciousness;
having made the aggregates within the range of insight its object, it turns back toward the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
Immediately after that, having seized the aggregates already grasped by that same adverting [consciousness], the first impulsion arises as the knowledge of conformity (*anuloma-ñāṇa*).
Having proceeded toward those aggregates as "impermanent," or "suffering," or "non-self," it dispels the increasingly gross darkness that conceals the Truths,
so that the three characteristics become more and more evident.
Having done so, it ceases. Immediately thereafter, the second conformity (dutiyānuloma) arises. Among these, the former is without repetition (anāsevana).
For the latter, the former serves as its repetition (āsevana). Because that [second conformity] has also acquired repetition, it becomes sharp, keen, and clear;
having proceeded toward that same object in that very same manner, it is of medium magnitude and dispels the darkness that obscures the Truths.
Having dispelled the three characteristics and made them increasingly manifest, [the insight] ceases. Immediately following that, the third conformity (tatiyānuloma) arises.
Its repetition is the second [moment]. Because it has attained such repetition, it becomes sharp, keen, and clear;
having proceeded toward that same object in that same manner, it dispels the remaining darkness that accompanies even the subtlest [defilements] which obscures the Truths.
Having dispelled [the obscurations] without remainder and having made the three characteristics increasingly evident, [the insight] ceases.
Thus, when the state of obscuring the truths has been dispelled by the three conformities, immediately thereafter the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) arises,
taking Nibbāna as its object.

In this regard, there is this simile: A certain man with sight, thinking "I shall know the conjunction of the stars," went out during the night and looked upward to see the moon. Because it was concealed by clouds, the moon was not visible to him.
Then a wind arose and dispersed the thick clouds; another [wind] dispersed the medium-sized ones; and another dispersed the fine ones.
Then, that man, seeing the moon in a cloudless sky, recognized its conjunction with the constellations.
