In this analogy, the three clouds are like the thick, medium, and subtle darkness of the defilements that obscure the truth.
The three winds are like the three conformable thoughts. The man with sight is like the knowledge of the change-of-lineage (gotrabhu-ñāṇa). The moon is like Nibbāna.
Just as each wind successively disperses the three kinds of clouds,
so too does each corresponding (anuloma) consciousness dispel the darkness that conceals the Truths. Just as that man sees the pure moon in a cloudless sky, so too,
when the darkness concealing the Truths has vanished, the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhu-ñāṇa) takes perfectly purified Nibbāna as its object.
For just as those three winds are able only to disperse the clouds that obscure the moon, but not to see the moon itself,
so too the conformable [knowledges] are able only to dispel the ignorance that obscures the Truths,
but not to take Nibbāna as their object. Just as that man is able to see the moon itself, but not to disperse the clouds.
In this way, the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) is able to take only Nibbāna as its object, but it is not yet able to dispel the darkness of the defilements.
Thus, the conformity (anuloma) has conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) as its object, while the change-of-lineage has Nibbāna as its object.
For if the change-of-lineage were to take the same object grasped by the conformity, the conformity would follow after it once again.

There would be no emergence from the path at all. However, the change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhu-ñāṇa), without taking the object of conformity (anuloma) as its own object and making that [conformity] its immediate predecessor, ceases as if giving a signal to the path, saying "Be born thus," even though it itself lacks advertence (āvajjana); it stands, as it were, in the place of advertence.
And the path, not letting go of the signal given by that [change-of-lineage], [proceeds].

Following that knowledge by way of an uninterrupted succession, as if piercing and shattering the mass of greed, the mass of hatred, and the mass of delusion—which had never before been pierced or shattered—one is reborn.
Here is a simile for this: it is said that a certain archer, having had a hundred shields placed at the distance of a hundred bow-lengths, [aimed] with a cloth...
Having covered his face and fixed an arrow, he stood at the edge of the wheel.
Another man, having turned the wheel, gave a signal with a staff when the hundred boards were facing the archer;
the archer, without even releasing the signal of the staff, shot the arrow and pierced through the hundred boards. In this context, the "signal of the staff" refers to—
The knowledge of change-of-lineage is like the archer; the knowledge of the path is like the arrow.

Just as the archer’s piercing of the hundred planks without letting go of his perception of the target-stick, so too the knowledge of the path—without letting go of the perception given by the knowledge of change-of-lineage—takes Nibbāna as its object and pierces and shatters the mass of greed and so forth, which had never before been pierced or shattered.
This same point is also expressed as "the uprooting of the white bridge already gained. For the path has only one function:
the abandoning of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*). Thus, while abandoning those underlying tendencies, it is said that he "emerges from the sign" and "severs the process.

"Sign" refers to the signs of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. "Process" likewise refers to the very process of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

That [consciousness] is twofold: acquired (*upādinnaka*) and unacquired (*anupādinnaka*). Regarding these, having stated that the shadow of emergence from the Path is seen as being unacquired, they said, "He emerges from the unacquired.
For by means of the Stream-entry Path, there are five types of consciousness: those associated with the four views and that accompanied by doubt.

They are abandoned. They give rise to material form; that is the aggregate of non-clung-to matter (*anupādinnaka-rūpakkhandha*). Those consciousnesses are the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*);
the associated feeling, perception, and mental formations are the three immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*).
In this regard, if the path of stream-entry had not been cultivated by a stream-enterer, those five types of consciousness would have become obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) regarding the six objects.

[They] would reach [them]. However, the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga), by preventing their manifestation and effecting the uprooting of the bridge—the state of being incapable of arising—is said to emerge from the unclung-to (anupādinnaka).

By means of the once-returner path (sakadāgāmimagga), [the fetters] associated with the four types of views and the two types accompanied by grief—namely, those consisting of gross sensual lust and ill will—are [abandoned].

Six types of consciousness are abandoned. By the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*), those same six types of consciousness are abandoned by way of latent attachment to sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and ill will (*byāpāda*).

By the path of arahantship (*arahattamagga*), five unwholesome types of consciousness are abandoned: the four dissociated from views (*diṭṭhigatavippayutta*) and that accompanied by restlessness (*uddhaccasahagata*).
In this regard, if those noble ones (*ariya*) had not developed those paths, [the defilements would remain].
Those states of consciousness might reach the stage of obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) regarding the six objects.

However, those paths, by preventing the attainment of obsession and effecting the destruction of the bridge—thereby rendering them incapable of arising—are said to "emerge from the unclung-to" (*anupādinnaka*).
Having stated that the shadow of emerging from the clung-to is seen, they also said that one emerges from the clung-to. If...

For if the path of stream-entry had not been cultivated by the stream-enterer, the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra-vaṭṭa*)—consisting of the process of appropriation within the beginningless round of births—would have continued beyond seven existences. Why? Because the causes for its continuation would still have existed.
However, these five defilements—the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the underlying tendencies of views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) and doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*)—the path of stream-entry [abandons].

As it arises, it eradicates [them]. Now, from where could the cycle of existence consisting of appropriated formations continue for a stream-enterer, setting aside the seven births within the beginningless round of saṃsāra?
Thus, the path of stream-entry, by making the cycle of appropriated formations non-existent, is said to "emerge from what is appropriated."
If the once-returner’s path of the once-returner had not been cultivated, the occurrence of the acquired [kamma] would have continued in five more births instead of being limited to two.
Why? Because of the presence of the causes for its continuation.
However, the coarse fetters of sensual lust and ill will, as well as the coarse underlying tendencies of sensual lust and ill will—these...

That path, as it arises, eradicates the four defilements. Now, having set aside two more births for the once-returner, how could the turning of the cycle of existence based on what has been acquired proceed for five more births?
Thus, by making the turning of the cycle of existence based on what has been acquired non-existent, the path of the once-returner is said to "emerge from what has been acquired."
If the non-returner’s path to non-returning had not been developed, then—setting aside one existence—the karmic process of clinging would continue into a second existence.
Why? Because of the presence of the causes for its continuation.
However, these four—the fetters of sensual lust and aversion that remain as subtle traces, and the underlying tendencies of sensual lust and aversion that remain as subtle traces—[are abandoned].

That path, upon arising, utterly eradicates the defilements. Now, from where could the second round of existence involving the appropriated [kamma] proceed for a non-returner, except for one remaining birth?
Thus, by making the round of existence involving the appropriated not proceed, the path of non-returning is said to "emerge from the appropriated."
If the path to Arahantship had not been cultivated for an Arahant, the conditioned process of existence in the fine-material and immaterial realms would continue.

Why? Because the causes for its continuation would still exist. However, as that path arises, it simultaneously eradicates these eight defilements: lust for the fine-material realm, lust for the immaterial realm, conceit, restlessness, ignorance, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, and the underlying tendency to ignorance.
It eradicates. Now, from where could the process of the appropriated [existence] proceed again for one whose taints are destroyed?
Thus, the path of Arahatship, by making the process of the appropriated non-occurrent, is said to "emerge from the appropriated.

And herein, they say that the stream-entry path emerges from the plane of misery; the once-return path, from a portion of the happy sensual-sphere existence; the non-return path, from the sensual-sphere existence; and the path of Arahatship emerges from the fine-material and immaterial existences, and thus from all existences.
To clarify this meaning, the following text is given: “By means of the knowledge of the path of stream-entry and through the cessation of volitional consciousness,
name-and-form— which would otherwise arise within the beginningless round of saṃsāra, setting aside the seven [remaining] existences—
cease, subside, come to an end, and become tranquil right here.”
‘By means of the knowledge of the path of once-returning, through the cessation of volitional consciousness,
name-and-form— which would have arisen in five more existences, setting aside two— cease, subside, come to an end, and become tranquil herein.
By means of the knowledge of the path of non-returning, through the cessation of volitional consciousness, [name-and-form] in the sense-sphere realm, setting aside one existence...’
Whatever name-and-form might arise in the two realms of existence, these cease, are stilled,
come to an end, and subside therein—
either in the form realm or the formless realm through the cessation of volitional consciousness by means of the knowledge of the path of arahantship.
Or whatever [states] might arise— name and form, wherein these cease, are stilled, go to their end, and subside.
With the cessation of final consciousness in an Arahant passing away into the Nibbāna-element without residue,
wisdom, mindfulness, name, and form— wherein these cease, are stilled, and go to their end— [subside].
“They go forth and subside. This, first of all, is the analysis of the sign (*nimitta*).
Regarding the phrase “one who has entered the path” (*paṭipadāpatī*): does the path waver here or not? It wavers.
For while for the Tathāgata and the Venerable Sāriputta, all four paths were of pleasant progress and quick direct knowledge (*khippābhiññā*), for the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna...
The first path is easy to practice and possesses swift direct knowledge; the three higher paths are difficult to practice but possess swift direct knowledge.
Why? Because he was overcome by sleep. It is said that for seven days the Perfectly Enlightened One attended upon the Elder like a young boy.
On one day, the Elder sat down and fell asleep. Then the Teacher said to him: "You are nodding off..."
“Moggallāna, you are not nodding; Moggallāna, you are not dozing.
Even for a disciple who has attained such great direct knowledge (mahābhiññā), the practice (paṭipadā) may falter; how much more so for others?
For some bhikkhus, all four paths are of difficult progress and slow direct knowledge; for some, they are of difficult progress and quick direct knowledge; for some...

There is the pleasant way with sluggish direct knowledge; for some, there is the pleasant way with swift direct knowledge. For some, the first path is difficult to practice and sluggish in direct knowledge; the second path is difficult to practice and swift in direct knowledge;
the third path is pleasant to practice and sluggish in direct knowledge; the fourth path is pleasant to practice and swift in direct knowledge.

And just as the way of practice wavers, so too does the dominant influence (adhipati) waver. For to some bhikkhu all four paths have desire as their dominant influence; to some, energy; to some, consciousness; and to some, investigation.
Furthermore, for some, the first path has desire as its dominant influence, while the second has energy as its dominant influence.
The third has consciousness as its dominant influence; the fourth has investigation as its dominant influence.
The miscellaneous discussion is finished.
This concludes the first great method of the twentyfold path.
357. Now, when one develops supramundane wholesome [consciousness], one does not develop only jhāna in the sense of close contemplation;

rather, one also develops the path in the sense of escape, the foundations of mindfulness in the sense of establishing, the right efforts in the sense of exertion, the bases of power in the sense of succeeding, the faculties in the sense of predominance, and the powers in the sense of unshakability.
It is power in the sense of awakening; it is a factor of awakening in the sense of being enlightened; it is a truth in the sense of suchness; it is serenity in the sense of non-distraction;
it is a phenomenon in the sense of emptiness; it is an aggregate in the sense of a heap; it is a sense base in the sense of a door;

it is an element in the sense of being empty, of its own nature, and of non-existence; it is nutriment in the sense of a condition; it is contact in the sense of touching; it is feeling in the sense of being felt.
One develops perception in the sense of perceiving, volition in the sense of intending, and consciousness in the sense of cognizing.
Therefore, in order to show these nineteen terms, it was said again: "Which states are wholesome? and so forth.
Thus, by way of both the inclination of the individual and the elegance of the teaching, it is stated: "This too he develops; this too he develops."

Twenty methods have been taught. For those in the assembly of devas seated to hear the Dhamma who understand when the supramundane is called “jhāna” in the sense of close contemplation, it is called “jhāna” for their benefit... and so on, up to:
for those who understand when “citta” is spoken of in the sense of cognizing, it is called “citta” for their benefit.
This, in this context, is the "inclination of the individual.

However, the Fully Enlightened One, by virtue of his own perfect awakening as a Buddha, possesses the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the six unique knowledges;
thus, he displays the teaching by determining it according to his own wish. Wishing [to teach], he does so in the sense of close contemplation (*upanijjhāyana*).
It shows that it is "supramundane absorption" (lokuttara-jhāna); for one who desires [it], it is "supramundane consciousness" in the sense of leading out...
[and so on] ...in the sense of cognizing. This is called "the elegance of the teaching" (desanā-vilāsa).

In this regard, just as ten methods (nayā) are analyzed for the phrase "supramundane absorption," those same [methods] should be understood for the path (magga) and so forth as well. Thus, in twenty places, there are ten...
Having performed the tenfold analysis, two hundred methods have been explained.
Now, in order to demonstrate the classification according to predominance (*adhipati*), the passage beginning "Which states are wholesome? is commenced once again.
In that context, supramundane (*lokuttara*) jhāna produced by making desire (*chanda*) the burden, the chief, the eldest, and the forerunner, is called "predominant in desire" (*chandādhipateyya*).

[This is] the name. The same method applies to the remaining [factors] as well. Thus, having analyzed by means of one thousand two hundred methods—two hundred methods for the first pure [factor], and two each for those dominated by desire and so forth—the Dhamma King demonstrated the first path.
The first path is finished.
The Second Path. 361.
Now, in order to show the second path and so forth, the section beginning with “Which states are wholesome? is commenced again.
Therein, “for the thinning out of sensual lust and ill will” means for the purpose of making these defilements thin. Therein—
The state of attenuation should be understood by two reasons: by its infrequent arising and by the weakness of the obsessions.
For in the case of a once-returner, unlike the common worldling who follows the round of existence, the defilements do not arise frequently;
they arise only occasionally. Even when they do arise, they do so in a sparse manner, like sprouts sown in a field with sparse planting.
Even when they arise, they do not arise as something that crushes, spreads, covers, or creates darkness for the great masses of people who follow the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
Rather, because they have been abandoned by two paths, they arise only very slowly;
they arise in a subtle form, like a layer of clouds or like flies on a wing.
Regarding this, some elders say: "Although the defilements of a once-returner arise only after a long time, they nevertheless arise in abundance;
for indeed, his sons and daughters are seen. But this is not a valid measure. For sons and daughters come about even by the mere touching of one's limbs and members.
However, [the once-returner is so called] because [those defilements] have been abandoned by two paths.
There is no density of defilements. The attenuation of his defilements is to be understood by two reasons alone:
by their infrequency of arising and by the mildness of their obsession.

"In the second" means second both in terms of numerical order and in terms of its second occurrence. "For the attainment of the plane" means for the sake of obtaining the fruit of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*). The same method applies to the third and fourth as well; we shall, however, state only the specific difference.
The faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*) is the faculty that fully understands.
It is said to be the faculty that understands those very same Four Noble Truths already known by the first path, without overstepping the boundary of what has been known by that path.

Its meaning should be understood in this same manner during the section on the exposition (*niddesavāra*). In the section on the constituents (*koṭṭhāsavāra*), there are nine faculties when this is added to the previous ones.
The remainder is to be understood in the same manner as before.
The second path is finished.
[Now follow] the third and fourth paths.

362. "In the third [path], for the sake of abandoning without remainder" means for the sake of abandoning without exception those very fetters that had been attenuated by the path of the once-returner (*sakadāgāmi*).

"In the fourth, for the sake of abandoning without remainder lust for the fine-material realm, lust for the immaterial realm, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance" means for the sake of abandoning without exception these five higher fetters (*uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*).
Therein, "lust for the fine-material realm" (*rūparāga*) is the desire and lust for existence in the fine-material realm.

"Attachment to the formless" (arūparāga) is the desire and lust for existence in the formless realm. "Pride" (māna) refers specifically to that pride which is abandoned by the path of arahantship; likewise for restlessness and ignorance.
In these two paths as well, there is only the ninth faculty, the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya). This constitutes one thousand methods of the four paths.
In all the paths, there are sixty-four steps according to the sequence of the words; with the four *apaṇṇaka* factors, they become sixty-four.
However, from the perspective of non-distinction, there are thirty-three. The sections on the divisions (*koṭṭhāsa-vāra*) and emptiness (*suññata-vāra*) remain as they were before.
And just as it is for the first path, so it is for the second and subsequent paths; thus, there are exactly one thousand methods for each of the four paths.
The Dhamma King divided [the teachings] and showed them.
Furthermore, in the *Saccavibhaṅga*, sixty thousand methods pertaining to the supramundane (*lokuttara*) were set forth by means of these very [categories].
In the *Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga*, twenty thousand methods pertaining to the supramundane [were set forth], and in the *Sammappadhānavibhaṅga*, twenty [thousand].
In the *Vibhaṅga* on the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), there are thirty-two [thousand methods]; in the *Vibhaṅga* on the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), thirty-two;
and in the *Vibhaṅga* on the factors of the path (*maggaṅga*), twenty-eight thousand supramundane methods are set forth by means of these very [factors].
However, here, in the four paths, there are only four thousand methods. Among those, in the first path of the first jhāna—
The eight factors are distributed [among the paths]; likewise for the second and subsequent paths. In that context, in the first path, right view abandons wrong view, thus it is called "right view.
Right intention and the others should also be understood in the sense of abandoning wrong intention and so forth.
This being so, since the sixty-two types of views have already been abandoned by the first path alone, [what remains to be abandoned] by the three higher paths?
“There is no such thing as a view that is to be abandoned. In that case, how can there be the designation ‘right view’?
“Just as whether poison exists or not, it is still called an ‘antidote,’ so too, whether wrong view exists or not, this is indeed called ‘right view.’”
‘If this were merely a matter of name, then it would follow that right view has no function in the three higher paths, and the path-factors would not be fulfilled;
therefore, right view must perform its own function and the path-factors must be fulfilled.
And here, right view performing its own function should be illustrated according to the principle of whatever is obtained. It is to be abandoned by the three higher paths.
Indeed, there is one kind of conceit (*māna*) which stands in the place of wrong view (*diṭṭhi*). Right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) abandons that conceit; thus it is called right view.

For in the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*), right view abandons wrong view. However, for the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), there remains a conceit to be abandoned by the path of once-returning (*sakadāgāmi-magga*), which stands in the place of wrong view.
Right view abandons that conceit; thus it is called right view. Of that very [person]...

There is intention co-arising with the seven unwholesome consciousnesses. With those same consciousnesses, there is the instigation of vocal action, there is the instigation of bodily action, there is the enjoyment of requisites, there is co-arising effort, and there is the state of non-attention.
There is also co-arising one-pointedness of mind. These, namely wrong intention and so forth, become right intention and so forth on the path of the once-returner through their abandonment.
Right intention and the others are to be understood in this way. Thus, the eight factors arrive having performed their respective functions on the path of the once-returner (*sakadāgāmi*).
For the once-returner, there remains conceit (*māna*) which is to be abandoned by the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmi*); that [conceit] stands in the place of view (*diṭṭhi*).

The intentions and so forth that are co-nascent with those very seven consciousnesses [of the once-returner] are abandoned through the abandonment of those [defilements]. By that abandonment, the eight factors [arise] on the path of the non-returner.
The performance of their respective functions is to be understood. For the non-returner, there exists conceit that is to be abandoned by the path of arahantship;
this stands in the place of [wrong] view. Furthermore, there are his five unwholesome consciousnesses, with which volition and the other factors are co-nascent.
Through the abandoning of these, the performance of the functions of the eight factors in the path of arahantship is to be understood.
Among these four paths, the Four Truths are seen by the first path.

Regarding the question, "Does one see what has already been seen by the three higher paths, or does one see what has not yet been seen?", the teachers' consensus is that "one sees only what has already been seen.
However, the caviller says, "One sees what has not yet been seen. He should be asked: "In the first path, which faculty [is it]?"
"Should it be classified [as such]? Knowing this, he will say, "It is the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' (anaññātaññassāmītindriya).
When asked, "Which of the higher paths? even then he will say, "It is the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya). He should be told:

"Since there is the seeing of truths not yet seen, you must classify it as the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' even in the higher paths. In this way, your question will be resolved. But as for the defilements, they are different...
“Does one person abandon [defilements] while another abandons those already abandoned? “One person abandons, and another abandons.

“If it is one person and another, then he abandons defilements that have not been abandoned, and he sees truths that have not been seen. A person who holds such a view should be asked: “How many truths are there?
Knowing, he will say, “Four. He should then be told: “In your doctrine, there are sixteen [truths].”
“They fall into [contradictory] truths. You see what has not even been seen by the Buddhas!
You are called a ‘Master of Many Truths. Do not hold such a view. There is nothing new in the vision of truth; rather, it abandons the defilements that have not yet been abandoned.
Regarding the absence of anything new in the vision of truth, the “Chest Simile” is cited: it is said that there was once a man who had four chests of jewels.

They were placed inside the heart of the core. During the night, when his business arose regarding the baskets, he opened the door, lit a lamp, and once the darkness was dispelled by the light and the contents of the baskets became visible, he performed his task within them, closed the door, and departed.
Darkness enveloped them again. He did exactly the same on the second and third occasions. On the fourth occasion—
While he was investigating, thinking, "The boxes are not visible because the door is open and it is dark," the sun rose;
when the darkness was dispelled by the light of the sun, he performed his task regarding the boxes and departed.
In this context, the four boxes are like the Four Noble Truths. When the need arose for those [truths], the time of opening the door is like...
This is the time for directing insight toward the path of stream-entry. Darkness is like the gloom that conceals the truths; the light is like the illumination of the path of stream-entry.
Just as the contents of the boxes become manifest to that man when the darkness has been dispelled, so too do the truths become manifest through the knowledge of the path.
Furthermore, these truths are made manifest by the knowledge of the path to one who possesses that path.

These become manifest to the person. The time when the stream-entry path has ceased after abandoning the defilements to be abandoned by oneself is like the time when one has finished the work inside a chest and departed.
The spreading of darkness once more is like the darkness that conceals the truths which are the objects of abandonment for the three higher paths.
The time when insight is directed toward the second path is like the time when the door is opened a second time. The light of the lamp—

The light [of the first flash] is like the path of once-returning (sakadāgāmimagga). The time when one has gone after performing the task within the caskets is like the time when the path of once-returning has ceased after abandoning the defilements to be abandoned by itself.
Again, the spreading of darkness is like the darkness that conceals the truths which are the objects of the two higher paths.
The time of opening the door on the third occasion is like the time of directing insight toward the path of non-returning (anāgāmimagga). The light of the lamp...

The radiance is like the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*). The time spent having performed the task within the caskets is like the cessation of the path of non-returning after it has abandoned the defilements to be abandoned by itself.
Again, the spreading of darkness is like the darkness that conceals the truths which are the targets of the higher path of arahantship (*arahattamagga*).
The time of opening the door on the fourth occasion is like the moment the path of arahantship brings forth insight (*vipassanā*). The rising of the sun...
It is like the arising of the path to Arahantship. The dispelling of darkness is like the removal of the obscurations to the truths by the path to Arahantship.
Just as the contents of those boxes become manifest when the darkness has been dispelled, so too do the four truths become manifest to the knowledge of the path to Arahantship.
What is manifest to knowledge is necessarily manifest to the person. Having performed the task regarding the boxes...
Just as the passing of time [is the cause] for the removal of all defilements by the path of Arahantship, so too, from the moment the path of Arahantship arises,
there is no longer any state of darkness that obscures the truths, just as light continues to exist from the moment the sun rises.
This, first of all, is the simile for the non-existence of the truths' being previously unseen.
For one sees only what has been seen. Regarding the statement, "But one defilement abandons another," the simile of the lye is taken here.
A certain man gave a soiled cloth to a dyer.

The dyer applied three kinds of lye—alkaline lye, ash-lye, and cow-dung lye—and having recognized that it had been treated with these lyes, he washed it in water, [removing] the coarsest [impurities].
He washed away the impurity. Since it was not yet completely pure, he gave it alkaline solution a second time as well, rinsed it in water, and then washed away an even finer impurity.
Since it was still not completely pure, he gave it alkaline solution a third time, rinsed it in water, and then washed away an even more subtle impurity. Since it was still not yet completely pure...
A fourth time, she gave him caustic alkali, rinsed it in water, and having washed away every trace of impurity even from within the fibers, she returned it to her husband.
He placed it in a perfumed casket and wore it whenever he desired.
In this context, the mind accompanied by defilements is like the soiled cloth; the time of applying the three kinds of alkali is like the [three watches of the night].
The time for the application of the task is during the contemplations.
Just as washing in water removes gross impurities, so too does the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) cast out the five defilements.
Just as there would be no further addition of those alkaline salts, so too, thinking "this mind is not yet completely purified," one applies the task again within those same three contemplations.
Then, like the removal of a stain that is not too soft, there is the casting off of the two gross fetters by means of the path of once-returning.

Then, as if giving a third application of lye because "the cloth is not yet perfectly clean," there is the setting in motion of the work through those same three contemplations because "this mind is not yet perfectly pure. Then, there is the removal of a stain that is even softer.
Just as the removal of the two subtle fetters by the path of non-returning, so too, just as one gives salt three times [to a cloth] thinking,
"The cloth is not yet pure," so one applies the practice to those same three contemplations thinking,
"This mind is not yet pure. Then, by washing, having washed away the dirt that had entered the fibers, the cloth becomes pure.
Just as one might put on a cloth resembling a silver plate kept in a perfumed casket at any desired moment, so too,

because the eight defilements have been exhausted by the path of arahantship, one who possesses a perfectly pure mind with taints destroyed (khīṇāsava) may spend time in the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) at any desired moment.
This is what is meant by "one [person] abandons defilements that are different [from himself]."
Here is an analogy. And this has also been said:
"Suppose, friends, there were a cloth that was soiled and stained; its owners would hand it over to a dyer.
The dyer would scrub it with alkaline salt, or lye, or cow dung, and then rinse it in clear water. Even though..."
That cloth becomes pure and bright; yet there remains within it a subtle lingering odor of ammonia, or alkaline salt, or cow dung that has not been removed.
The washerman returns it to its owners.
The owners place it in a casket perfumed with fragrances. Whatever subtle lingering odor of ammonia there may be in it—
Or the smell of dung, or the smell of cow-dung, even if not yet removed, that too goes to complete eradication.
In the same way, friends, although the five lower fetters have been abandoned by a noble disciple,
there still remains within him a subtle residual conceit of "I am," a desire of "I am," and a latent tendency toward the five aggregates of clinging.
The underlying tendency of "I am" not having been eradicated, he dwells at a later time contemplating the arising and passing away of the five aggregates of clinging:
"Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away; such is feeling...
such is perception... such are formations... such is consciousness, such its origin, such its passing away."
"As he dwells contemplating the arising and passing away of these five aggregates of clinging,
whatever subtle underlying tendency of the conceit 'I am,' the desire 'I am,' and the latent tendency 'I am' that remained unuprooted within those five aggregates of clinging—
that too goes to its total eradication."
Therein, by the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*), the five unwholesome states of mind are abandoned together with the evil qualities that arise by way of their mental factors (*cittaṅga*).
By the path of once-returning (*sakadāgāmi-magga*), the two types of grief-accompanied consciousness become attenuated together with the evil qualities that arise by way of their mental factors.
By the path of non-returning (*anāgāmi-magga*), those very same [unwholesome states] are abandoned together with their associated phenomena (*sampayutta-dhamma*).
By means of the path of arahantship, the five unwholesome consciousnesses are abandoned along with the evil states that arise by way of their mental factors.
From the moment these twelve unwholesome consciousnesses are abandoned, for one whose taints are destroyed,
there is no longer any defilement that can subsequently arise by way of their mental factors.
In this regard, there is this simile: It is said, O Great King, that a certain monarch, having established a guard at the frontier, dwelt enjoying sovereignty in the great capital city.

Then his frontier became disturbed. At that time, twelve chief bandits, together with many thousands of men, were plundering the country. The high ministers living on the frontier [thought], "The frontier is in revolt."
They sent word to the king. The king sent back this message: “Seize them at your pleasure; I shall do for you what must be done.
At the very first assault, they had the five chief bandits executed along with many thousands of men.
The remaining seven men, taking each his own followers, entered the mountain. The ministers—
They sent word of that occurrence to the king.
The king sent wealth back, saying, "I shall know what is appropriate for you to do;
seize them as well. By means of a second assault, they struck the two chief thieves and rendered their followers weak. They—
They all fled and entered the mountain. The ministers sent word of that occurrence to the king.

Again, the king sent wealth with the message, "Let them seize them freely. With the third dispatch, they had the two chief thieves killed along with their accomplices and sent word of that occurrence to the king.
Again, the king sent wealth with the message, "Let them seize the remainder freely. With the fourth dispatch, [they seized] them together with their retinues...
They had the five chief bandits executed. From the time the twelve chief bandits were put to death, there was no longer anyone who could be called a "bandit.
The people of the countryside lived as if they were cradling their own children upon their breasts.
Surrounded by warriors who had returned victorious from battle, the king sat in his magnificent palace and enjoyed great prosperity.
In this context, the Dhamma-king is like a great king; the noble sons who are practitioners of yoga are like the border-dwelling ministers;
the twelve unwholesome states of mind are like the twelve chief thieves; and the evil qualities that arise by way of mental factors are like the many thousands of men who are their companions.
It is like the time when the king’s border region has risen in revolt and he sends forth his forces.
When defilements arise regarding an object, it is the time to inform the Teacher, saying: "Venerable Sir, a defilement has arisen in me.
Just as one might give wealth with the words, "Take them freely," so too does the Dhamma-King point out the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), saying, "Bhikkhus, restrain the defilements!
This is like the time when the five chief bandits, along with their retinues, were executed by the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) for those [defilements] associated with it.
The abandoning of the five unwholesome states of consciousness is like the king’s dispatching of the messenger.
The proclamation of the qualities attained by the Fully Enlightened One is like the report sent back to the king.
And the Blessed One’s teaching of insight for the path of once-returning is like the further gift of wealth, saying, “Let the others take it as well.”

Just as the second assault weakens the two chief thieves along with their retinue, so too does the path of the once-returner (sakadāgāmimagga) cause the attenuation of the two types of mental states associated with grief (domanassa).
Then, just as the king’s dispatching of his emissaries, there is the proclamation by the Teacher of the qualities he has attained: “Let them take it with confidence!”
Furthermore, the Blessed One’s teaching on insight for the path of non-returning is like the gift of wealth;

the destruction of the two chief thieves along with their retinues by the third blow is like the abandonment of the two types of displeasure-consciousness together with their associated factors by means of the path of non-returning.
The Tathāgata’s announcement of the qualities he had attained is like the king’s dispatching of his messenger.
The Blessed One’s teaching of insight (vipassanā) as the path to Arahatship is like the second gift of wealth, saying, “Let them take it with confidence.
From the time of the execution of the five chief thieves along with their retinue by the fourth blow, the country was in a state of security.
Just as when the five unwholesome states of consciousness associated with the path to Arahatship have been abandoned,
from the moment those twelve unwholesome states are relinquished, there is an absence of any unwholesome dhamma arising again by way of the factors of consciousness.
This is like a king who has won a battle, surrounded by his assembly of ministers, experiencing great prosperity in his magnificent palace.

It should be understood that for the King of Dhamma, surrounded by those whose taints are exhausted, there is the experience of the bliss of attainment— whether it be the bliss of the attainments distinguished as emptiness (*suññatā*),
signlessness (*animitta*), or wishlessness (*appaṇihita*)— and the bliss of attaining whatever fruit is desired at will.
The commentary on the phrase "wholesome states" (*kusalā dhammā*) is concluded.
The Section on Unwholesome States: Discussion of the Enumeration of Phenomena;
First Consciousness.
365. Now, in order to analyze and demonstrate the section on unwholesome states (*akusaladhammapada*), the passage beginning with "Which states are unwholesome? is commenced.

Herein, the classification of the sections such as the "Determination of States" (*dhammavavatthāna*) and the analysis of the meaning of the terms already encountered should be understood according to the method explained above.
However, we shall describe only the specific distinctions found in each respective place.

In that context, regarding the determination of the occasion (*samaya-vavatthāna*), because there is no division of planes for the unwholesome as there is for the wholesome, this [consciousness], although it is exclusively of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), is not called "sense-sphere" [in the specific definition].

Here, in the phrase "associated with views" (*diṭṭhigata-sampayutta*), "view" itself is "gone-to-view" (*diṭṭhigata*), just as in expressions such as "gone-to-excrement" (*gūthagata*) or "gone-to-urine" (*muttagata*). This is because there is nothing further to be gone to [once a view has been established].
Or, it is called "a resort of views" (*diṭṭhigata*) because it is merely gone into a view. That which is associated with this is "associated with a resort of views" (*diṭṭhigatasampayutta*).

In this regard, the arising of this wrong view—termed a "resort of views"—should be understood through such causes as hearing false doctrines, associating with unwholesome friends, having no desire to see the Noble Ones, and improper attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*).
For those false doctrines associated with views, there is [the fault] of listening preceded by great esteem, which transcends the middle way and lacks investigation;
and for those who are corrupted by views— namely, unwholesome friends (akalyāṇamitta)— there is the state of being an unwholesome friend consisting in intimacy with them,
and the lack of desire to see the Noble Ones such as the Buddhas and other true persons, regarding the divisions of the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth.

It arises through lack of skill in the noble Dhamma; by means of improper attention—which is permeated by those very same causes—consisting in the failure to observe the discipline known as the various types of restraint (namely, restraint of the Pātimokkha, restraint of the sense faculties, restraint of mindfulness, restraint of knowledge, and restraint of abandoning) regarding both the noble Dhamma and the Dhamma of the true person;
and through being intent upon superstitious omens, auspicious signs, and the like.
This should be understood. Furthermore, the state of being without volitional effort (*asaṅkhāra*) regarding this consciousness is to be understood by the same method explained below.

In the section on the "indication of phenomena" (*dhammuddesa*), "contact" (*phassa*) refers to contact co-arising with unwholesome consciousness. The same principle applies to feeling (*vedanā*) and the other factors.

Thus, these consist solely of the unwholesome; this is their distinction from the preceding [categories]. "There is one-pointedness of mind" (*cittassekaggatā hoti*): even in the case of killing living beings and so forth, there is one-pointedness of mind due to its undistracted state.
For people, having concentrated their minds and being undistracted, strike weapons at the bodies of living beings without faltering;
being well-concentrated, they carry off the property of others; and with a mind of a single flavor, they engage in sexual misconduct.
Thus, even in the occurrence of unwholesome states, there is one-pointedness of mind.
*Micchādiṭṭhi* (wrong view) means a view that is not according to reality; or, because it grasps things erroneously, it is a false view, thus *micchādiṭṭhi*.
It is also called *micchādiṭṭhi* because it is a view loathed by the wise due to its bringing about what is harmful.
The same method applies to *micchāsaṅkappa* (wrong intention) and the others as well. Furthermore, they see wrongly by means of it, or it itself sees wrongly; it is merely a wrong seeing.

"Or these" refers to wrong view. It has the characteristic of irrational insistence, the function of misapprehension, the manifestation of false adherence, and its proximate cause is the lack of desire to see the Noble Ones and so forth. It should be regarded as the "supreme fault.
In the case of wrong intention and the others, the only distinction is the word "wrong. The rest should be understood according to the method already stated in the section on the wholesome.

Regarding the terms *ahirikabalaṃ* (the power of shamelessness) and *anottappabalaṃ* (the power of fearlessness of wrongdoing): the meaning of "power" (*bala*) in this context will be made clear in the section on the exposition (*niddesa*).
As for the others: one who does not feel shame is *ahiriko*; the state of being such is *ahirikaṃ*. That which is not dread [of wrongdoing] is *anottappaṃ*.
Among these, *ahirikaṃ* has the characteristic of lacking disgust toward bodily misconduct and so forth, or it has the characteristic of lack of shame. *Anottappaṃ*...
It has the characteristic of not shrinking away from what is base, or the characteristic of fearlessness. Shamelessness itself is the power of shamelessness (*ahirikabala*);
recklessness itself is the power of recklessness (*anottappabala*). This is the summary meaning here. The detailed explanation, however, should be understood by way of the opposites as stated above.
Lobha is so called because by means of it they become greedy, or it itself becomes greedy, or it is merely the state of greed.
Moha is so called because by means of it they become deluded, or it itself becomes deluded, or it is merely the state of delusion.

Among these, lobha has the characteristic of seizing upon an object, like the smearing of a monkey; its function is clinging, like a piece of meat thrown onto a hot pan; its manifestation is non-renunciation.
Like the dye of *añjana* oil, its proximate cause is the perception of gratification in things that lead to fetters.
It should be understood that as it increases by way of the river of craving, like a river with a swift current, it carries one away toward the great ocean—that is, toward the states of misery alone.
Delusion is characterized by the blindness of the mind or by ignorance; its function is non-penetration, and its function is the obscuring of the true nature of the object.
Alternatively, it is manifested as wrong practice or manifested as darkness; its proximate cause is unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*).
It should be regarded as the root of all unwholesome states.
It is called *abhijjhā* because one covets by means of it, or because it itself covets, or because it is merely the act of coveting.
It has the characteristic of desiring one’s own agency regarding the success of others; its function is seeking in that manner; it is manifested as being directed toward the success of others;
and its proximate cause is delighting in the success of others. For it manifests only when directed toward the success of others, and it occurs when there is delight in them;
it should be regarded as like the stretching out of the hand of the mind toward the successes of others.

In the phrases "there is tranquility" (*samatha*) and so forth: it is "tranquility" because it pacifies distraction regarding other duties. It "exerts" the mind against the occurrence of unwholesome states, thus it is "exertion" (*paggāha*). It does not become distracted, thus it is "non-distraction" (*avikkhepa*).
In this consciousness, the following factors are not included: faith, mindfulness, wisdom, and the six pairs. Why?
Because there is no such thing as "clarification" (*pasāda*) in a mind devoid of faith; therefore, for that reason, faith is not included. But what about those who hold wrong views (*diṭṭhigatika*)?
"Do they not have faith in their own respective teachers? "They do have faith. But that which is called "faith" is not [true] faith;
it is merely the acceptance of words. In substance, it is either a lack of investigation or a view (*diṭṭhi*).

However, because there is no mindfulness in a mind devoid of mindfulness, it was not included [among the faculties]. "Do those who follow views not remember the kamma they themselves have performed? "They do remember."
But that is not what is called mindfulness (*sati*). It is merely the occurrence of an unwholesome state of consciousness in that particular mode.
Therefore, it is not included [among the factors of the path]. Why, then, is it called "wrong mindfulness" (*micchāsati*) in the Suttas?

Because that state is devoid of mindfulness among the unwholesome aggregates, and because it is the opposite of mindfulness, it is taught there figuratively for the purpose of completing the factors of the wrong path and wrongness.

[This] has been explained. However, in the ultimate sense (nippariyāya), this [wisdom] does not exist; therefore, it was not included. Furthermore, it was not included because wisdom does not exist in the mind of a blind fool.
Is there no "deceptive wisdom" (vañcanā-paññā) among those who hold wrong views? There is. But that is not wisdom; it is called "illusion" (māyā).
In its actual meaning (atthato), it is simply craving (taṇhā). This mind, however, is full of longing, heavy, burdensome, and harsh.
"Stiff" means unworkable, sick, crooked, and distorted. Therefore, the six pairs beginning with serenity (*passaddhi*) were not included.

Having thus far shown the thirty-two terms that have entered the Canon by way of the factors of consciousness according to the sequence of the text, he now says "or whatever other [states] at that time," etc., in order to show the miscellaneous states (*yevāpanaka-dhamma*). Therein, in all unwholesome consciousnesses...

Desire (chanda), resolve (adhimokkha), attention (manasikāra), conceit (māna), envy (issā), avarice (macchariya), sloth (thīna), torpor (middha), restlessness (uddhacca), and worry (kukkucca)—these ten are indeed the "accessory" (yevāpanaka) states;
they are said to be included in the suttas and are seen in the sections of the discourses.
However, in this particular consciousness, desire, resolve, attention, and restlessness—these four alone are the accessory states, reckoned as the "infallible factors" (apaṇṇakaṅga).
In this context, zeal (*chanda*) and the other factors should be understood according to the method already explained below. For while those [factors] are wholesome, these are unwholesome.
Furthermore, agitation (*uddhacca*) is the state of one who is agitated. Its characteristic is the lack of tranquility in the mind, like water stirred by the impact of the wind;
its function is instability, like a banner or a flag fluttering in the wind; it is manifested as wavering.
Just as ashes scattered by the impact of a stone, unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) is the proximate cause for the lack of tranquility of the mind;
it should be understood as mental distraction (*cittavikkhepa*).
Thus, the thirty-two factors beginning with contact, together with the four mentioned by way of inclusion, constitute all the factors in this section on the exposition of phenomena (*dhammuddesa*).
There are thirty-six factors of the Dhamma. Excluding the four "infallible" factors (*apaṇṇakaṅga*), those included in the canonical text (*pāḷi*) are exactly thirty-two.

However, by including those not explicitly mentioned here, there are sixteen factors: the fivefold contact (*phassapañcaka*), applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), rapture (*pīti*), one-pointedness of mind (*cittassekaggatā*), the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*), the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*), lack of moral shame (*ahirika*), lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), greed (*lobha*), and delusion (*moha*).
Among those sixteen, seven factors are undifferentiated and nine are differentiated. Which seven?
Contact, perception, volition, sustained application, rapture, the life-faculty, and delusion—these seven are undifferentiated.
Feeling, consciousness, initial application, one-pointedness of mind, the energy-faculty, wrong view, lack of moral shame, lack of moral dread, and greed—these nine are differentiated.
Among those, six factors are analyzed in two places, one in three, one in four, and one in six. How so?
Consciousness (citta), applied thought (vitakka), wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi), lack of moral shame (ahirika), lack of moral dread (anottappa), and greed (lobha)—these six are analyzed in two places.
For among them, consciousness is first stated as "consciousness" when it reaches the pentad of contact, and as "mind-faculty" (manindriya) when it reaches the faculties.

Applied thought (*vitakka*), having reached the factors of absorption (*jhānaṅga*), is called "applied thought," but having reached the factors of the path (*maggaṅga*), it is called "wrong intention" (*micchāsaṅkappa*).

Wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*) is simply "wrong view" both among the path factors and among the courses of action (*kamma-patha*). Shamelessness (*ahirika*), having reached the powers (*bala*), is called the "power of shamelessness";
having reached the pair of world-destroyers (*lokanāsaka-duka*), it is called "shamelessness. The same principle applies to lack of dread (*anottappa*).
Having reached the root, greed is called "greed"; having reached the path of action, it is called "covetousness. These six are thus analyzed in two places.

Feeling, however, having reached the pentad of contact, is called "feeling"; having reached the factors of jhāna, it is called "pleasure"; and having reached the faculties, it is called the "faculty of mental joy. Thus, a single dhamma is analyzed in three places.
Energy, moreover, having reached the faculties, is called the "faculty of energy"; and having reached the path factors, it is [called] "wrong effort."
Regarding the term "occurs": having reached the powers, it is called the power of energy; having reached the pair of the bases, it is called exertion.
Thus, this single dhamma is analyzed in four places.
Concentration, however, having reached the factors of jhāna, is called one-pointedness of mind; having reached the faculties, it is called the faculty of concentration.
Upon reaching the path-factors, it is "wrong concentration"; upon reaching the powers, it is "the power of concentration.

Upon reaching the second dyad, in the first instance of that dyad, it is "serenity" by way of the single factor; in the third, it is "non-distraction. Thus, this single state is analyzed in six places.
Furthermore, all these states [are analyzed] by way of the pentad of contact, by way of the jhāna-factors, by way of the faculties, and by way of the path-factors.
There are nine groups: by way of strength, by way of roots, by way of courses of kamma, by way of world-destroyers, and by way of the back-pain group.
Regarding these, whatever needs to be said has already been stated in the exposition of the first wholesome consciousness.
The discussion on the section of the enumeration of states is finished.
Niddesavārakathā 375.

Regarding the exposition of one-pointedness of mind (*cittassekaggatā*) in the section of the detailed explanation (*niddesavāra*): first, as for "stability" (*saṇṭhiti*) and "steadiness" (*avaṭṭhiti*), these two are merely synonyms for "abiding" (*ṭhiti*).
However, that which is stated in the exposition of the wholesome (*kusala*)—namely, "it is steadiness because it stands having plunged into and entered the object"—is [also included].
That [meaning] is not found here. For it has already been explained below that, in the unwholesome state, the one-pointedness of mind is weak.
(384) Furthermore, the meaning of "not wandering" (*avisāhāra*) as the opposite of the "wandering" (*visāhāra*) that occurs by way of restlessness and doubt is also not found here.
However, it is "not wandering" (*avisāhāra*) in the sense that it does not wander among co-nascent states (*sahajātadhamma*); that is, it does not distract.
Non-distraction (*avikkhepa*). The state of a mind that is not scattered due to unwholesome one-pointedness of mind is "non-scattered-mindedness" (*avisāhaṭamānasatā*).

It is called the "power of concentration" (*samādhibala*) because it does not waver among co-nascent phenomena. As for "wrong concentration" (*micchāsamādhi*), it should be understood here as meaning "concentration that is not according to reality" (*ayāthāvasamādhāna*). 385.

In the exposition of the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*), the method stated below—beginning with “This is the exertion for the removal of sensual desires”—is not applicable here. The power of energy (*vīriyabala*) should be understood precisely in the sense of being unshakable among co-nascent phenomena.
386. In the exposition of wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*): it is wrong view in the sense of seeing things as they are not.
It is "gone among views" (*diṭṭhigata*) because this seeing has entered into the sixty-two types of views. Its meaning has already been stated above.
It is a "thicket of views" (*diṭṭhigahana*) because the view itself is difficult to transcend, just like a thicket of grass, a thicket of forest, or a thicket of mountains.

It is like a wilderness of views in the sense that it is full of danger and fear, just as there are wildernesses of robbers, wildernesses of wild beasts, wildernesses of deserts, wildernesses without water, and wildernesses of famine.
It is a "thicket of views" in the sense of piercing through and in the sense of being contrary to right view;
for when wrong seeing arises, it pierces through and contradicts right seeing—sometimes [viewing things] as eternal, sometimes...
Because it wavers in an improper manner due to grasping at annihilationism, it is called "the vacillation of views" (*diṭṭhivipphandita*).
For one who follows a wrong view cannot remain established in a single position; sometimes he falls into eternalism, and sometimes into annihilationism.
View itself is called the "fetter of views" (*diṭṭhisaṃyojana*) in the sense of being a bond.
It is "grasping" (gāha) because it seizes its object firmly, like the crocodile (susumāra) and others seizing a man.

It is "fixation" (paṭiṭṭhāha) because of its establishing; for this [craving] seizes by having established itself through its state of powerful occurrence. It is "adherence" (abhinivesa) because it adheres by way of permanence and so forth.

It is "misapprehension" (parāmāsa) because, having transcended the true nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva), it touches upon them as other than they are by way of permanence and so forth. Because it brings about what is harmful...
A bad road, or the road to the miserable states of existence (apāya), is a "wrong road" (kummagga). It is a "false path" (micchāpatha) because it is not the true path.

For just as a person who has lost his way may take a path thinking, "This is the road to such-and-such a village," yet it does not lead him there, so too a view held by one who holds to wrong views—though taken to be the path to a happy destination (sugati)—does not lead to a happy destination; thus, it is a false path because it is not the true path.
It is a wrong path. It is "wrongness" (*micchatta*) because its intrinsic nature is wrong. It is a "ford" (*tittha*) because fools cross over there by wandering about in that very place.

It is a "ford-basis" (*titthāyatana*) because it is both a ford and a basis for misfortunes. Alternatively, it is a "ford-basis" because it is the dwelling place of the sectarians (*titthiya*) in the sense of being their birthplace and their residence. It is a perverted grasp, due to perversion.
"Or grasps erroneously" means a perverted grasp; the meaning is "a distorted grasp. 387–388.

In the descriptions of shamelessness (*ahirika*) and lack of dread (*anottappa*), the meaning should be understood by reversing the description of moral shame (*hiri*) and moral dread (*ottappa*). Furthermore, among co-nascent states, the power of shamelessness and the power of lack of dread should be understood in the sense of being unshakable.
389. In the descriptions of greed (*lobha*) and delusion (*moha*): it is greed because one is greedy; "greediness" refers to the mode of being greedy. A consciousness associated with greed...
A person is greedy; the state of being greedy is greediness (*lubbhitattaṃ*). One is lustful, thus it is lust (*sārāga*); the mode of being lustful is lustfulness (*sārajjanā*);
the state of one who is lustful is lustfulness (*sārajjitattaṃ*). It is covetousness in the sense of coveting. Furthermore, the reason for using the term "greed" has already been stated.
It is both unwholesome and a root, or the root of unwholesome states; thus, it is an unwholesome root (*akusalamūla*).

390. Ignorance (*aññāṇa*) is non-seeing (*adassana*) because it is the opposite of knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassana*). It is "non-realization" (*anabhisamaya*) because, being turned away, it does not accord with or meet the Dhamma face-to-face.
It is "non-awakening" (*ananubodha*) because it is the opposite of awakening to the Dhamma in accordance with its nature.
It is "non-enlightenment" (*asambodha*) because one does not awaken by connecting [the mind] with impermanence and so forth. It is non-existent and unequal.
It is called "non-awakening" because one does not awaken. It is called "non-penetration" because one does not penetrate the Dhamma of the Four Truths.

It is called "non-comprehension" because one does not comprehend even a single phenomenon among form and the rest by way of its common characteristics such as impermanence. It is called "non-plunging" because one does not plunge into that very same Dhamma.
It is called "non-contemplation" because one does not look upon things with equanimity. It is called "non-reflection" because one does not reflect upon the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
Because of its contrary engagement with wholesome and unwholesome kamma, or because of the absence of grasping their true nature, not even a single instance of kamma is evident to it;
nor does it itself bring any kamma to direct perception. Thus, it is "kamma beyond direct perception" (*appaccakkhakamma*).
That which, if this [defilement] were not to arise, would cause the mental continuum to be neutral, pure, and cleansed—that [continuum] becomes corrupted.
That which is difficult to overcome by means of this [wisdom] is *dummejjha*. The state of fools is *bālya*. One is deluded, thus it is *moha*.
Delusion that is more powerful is *pamoha*. One is deluded all around, thus it is *sammoha*. Because it is the opposite of true knowledge (*vijjā*), it is "not-knowledge," *avijjā*.
Its meaning as a flood (*ogha*) and a yoke (*yoga*) has already been stated. It underlies in the sense of being firmly established, thus it is an *anusaya*. It obsesses the mind; it overcomes it.
*Pariyuṭṭhānaṃ*. Because of the absence of grasping for what is beneficial, one is unable to proceed toward the beneficial;
rather, one merely limps—thus it is called *laṅgī*; the meaning is that one limps (*khañjati*). Or, in the sense of being difficult to remove, it is *laṅgī*.

For just as a threshold-bar (*laṅgī*) known as a great bolt is difficult to remove, so too this [hindrance] is like a threshold-bar, thus it is called *laṅgī*. The rest is self-evident. The sections on the Bases of Accomplishment (*saṅgahavāra*) and Emptiness (*suññatavāra*) are also [to be understood in the same way].
It should be understood according to the meaning in the same manner as stated below.
Regarding the second consciousness:
in the phrase "with volitional effort" (*sasaṅkhārena*), that term is the specific distinction. Its meaning is also exactly as stated below. However, this...
Although this consciousness arises in one who is gladdened by any of the six objects and who, having generated greed, misapprehends [the object] in such a manner as "a being,
a being," it nevertheless arises with volitional effort, through application and means—
just as when a clansman desires the daughter of a family with wrong view, and they [say], "They hold a different view..."
They do not give the girl to you. Then other relatives, saying, "She will do exactly what you are doing," cause her to be given.
He approaches those heterodox teachers together with them. From the very beginning, he is full of doubt.
As time passes, he comes to find pleasure in the conviction that their practices are agreeable; he adopts their view—at such a time as this.
It should be understood that this is what is obtained.

Among the yevāpanaka factors, however, sloth-and-torpor (*thinamiddha*) is additional here. In that regard, the state of being slothful is "sloth" (*thina*); the state of being torpid is "torpor" (*middha*);
the meaning is a lack of exertion and a loss of capability. Sloth and torpor together constitute "sloth-and-torpor" (*thinamiddha*).
In this context, *thīna* (sloth) has the characteristic of lack of exertion; its function is the dispelling of energy; it is manifested as a state of sinking.
*Middha* (torpor) has the characteristic of unworkability; its function is shrouding; it is manifested as a state of sluggishness, or as drowsiness and sleep.
Both have inappropriate attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) as their proximate cause, occurring in such states as boredom, languor, and yawning.

The Third Consciousness (400). The third [consciousness] belongs to one who, feeling joy regarding the six objects, has generated greed but does not misapprehend them by way of such thoughts as “a being, a being,” and so forth;
it belongs to one who is intent on watching Nārāyaṇa wrestling matches, boxing bouts, theatrical performances, and the like, or on listening to pleasant sounds and so on.
Or it arises. Here, there are five infallible factors together with conceit (*māna*). In this context, "he conceives" (*maññati*) is "conceit" (*māna*).
It has the characteristic of loftiness, the function of grasping at excellence, and is manifested as the desire for self-display. Its proximate cause is greed dissociated from views;
it should be regarded as like madness.
The Fourth Consciousness (402). When, among the aforementioned instances, they spit phlegm on his head or sprinkle dust from their feet upon him, then—
while watching with enthusiasm at intervals for the sake of avoiding him as the royal dramas unfold— the fourth consciousness arises.
It arises in such contexts as "while a proclamation is being made" or "of those looking through various openings," and so forth.
However, in this case, there are only seven concomitants (yevāpanaka), including sloth and torpor. In both instances, wrong view is excluded.
The enumeration of the factors should be understood according to the remaining ones, setting that aside.
The Fifth Consciousness (403).
The fifth arises in one who, through the mode of feeling toward any of the six objects, generates equanimity and, by way of such expressions as "a being, a being," clings [to it].
However, in place of joy (*somanassa*), there is here the feeling of equanimity (*upekkhā-vedanā*).
[The first jhāna] exists; the factor of rapture (*pīti*) falls away. All the rest is exactly the same as in the first consciousness. Regarding the sixth consciousness and so forth (409–412):
the sixth, seventh, and eighth [consciousnesses] are also formed by substituting the feeling (*vedanā*) and omitting the factor of rapture from the second, third, and fourth [jhānas].

These should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. In these eight types of greed-accompanied consciousness, both types of predominance—conascence-predominance (*sahajātādhipati*) and object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*)—are found.
As for the ninth consciousness...
413. The ninth [type of consciousness] arises in one who generates resistance (*paṭigha*) toward the six objects, being depressed.
First, regarding the section on the determination of its occasion: "The mind is bad" (*duṭṭhu mano*), or because it is a base feeling, it is a "corrupt mind" (*kucchitaṃ mano*);

thus it is *dummano*. The state of being *dummano* is depression (*domanassa*). That which is accompanied by this is "accompanied by depression" (*domanassasahagata*). By way of the state of not finding pleasure...
It strikes against an object (*ārammaṇa*), thus it is *paṭigha*. That which is associated with that is "associated with resistance" (*paṭighasampayutta*).
In the summary of states (*dhammuddesa*), only the feeling of displeasure (*domanassavedanā*) is mentioned in all three places. Among these, the term for feeling has already been explained.

Likewise for the terms "pain" (*dukkha*) and "displeasure" (*domanassa*): however, from the perspective of its characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), displeasure has the characteristic of experiencing an undesirable object.
Whether in this way or that, its essence is the experience of an undesirable form; its manifestation is mental affliction; and its proximate cause is exclusively the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*).
Just as it was stated in the preceding states of consciousness regarding the fundamental courses of action that "there is greed" and "there is covetousness," so too here it is said:
"there is hatred" and "there is ill will. In this context, one hates by means of it, or it itself hates, or it is merely the act of hating.
Or rather, hatred (*dosa*) should be regarded as having the characteristic of ferocity like a struck venomous snake; the function of spreading [corruption] like the application of poison;
the function of burning its own support like a forest fire; the manifestation of malice like an enemy who has found an opening;
and its proximate cause being the objects of resentment like putrid urine mixed with poison.
The mind is corrupted (*byāpajjati*) by it, it reaches a state of putrefaction, or it corrupts (*byāpādayati*) such things as discipline, conduct, physical beauty, excellence, welfare, and happiness;
thus it is called ill-will (*byāpāda*). In terms of its essential meaning, however, this is simply hatred (*dosa*). Here, there are twenty-nine terms according to the sequence of the words.
By including those not explicitly mentioned, there are fourteen. According to these, the classification into groups with and without case endings should be understood.
Among the "sometimes-occurring" (yevāpanaka) factors, desire (chanda), resolution (adhimokkha), attention (manasikāra), and restlessness (uddhacca) are fixed.

However, envy (issa), avarice (macchariya), and worry (kukkucca) arise together with any one of these others, making five each time. Thus, these three factors are called the "sometimes-occurring indeterminates.
Among them, "envy" means "to envy"; its characteristic is resentment toward the prosperity of others, and its function is dissatisfaction with that very [prosperity].
It should be understood as a fetter (*saṃyojana*) manifested as a state of aversion, having the excellence of others as its proximate cause.
Stinginess (*macchariya*) is the state of being stingy. Its characteristic is the concealment of one’s own acquisitions—whether already obtained or yet to be obtained.
Its function is the inability to endure sharing those very acquisitions with others. It is manifested as contraction and manifested as harshness and rigidity.
Or rather, it has self-perfection as its proximate cause. It should be understood as a state of mental deformity. That which is badly done is "badly done" (*kukata*);

the state of that is "remorse" (*kukkucca*). Its characteristic is subsequent regret; its function is to sorrow over what has been done and left undone; it is manifested as remorse; its proximate cause is what has been done and left undone.
It should be regarded as like slavery. This, then, is the distinction in the section on the enumeration.
415. In the section on the exposition (*niddesa*), within the exposition of feeling (*vedanāniddesa*), "unpleasant" (*asāta*) is to be understood by way of being the opposite of "pleasant" (*sāta*).

418. In the exposition of hatred (*dosa*): it "hates," thus it is hatred (*doso*). "Hating" (*dussanā*) is the mode of hating. "The state of having hated" (*dussitattaṃ*) is the condition of having hated.
In the sense of abandoning one's natural state, there is "affliction" (*byāpajjana*) and "affliction" (*byāpatti*). "Afflicting" (*byāpajanā*) is the mode of afflicting. It "resists," thus...

"Contradiction" (*virodha*). "Repeatedly contradicting" is "counter-contradiction" (*paṭivirodha*). Or rather, this is stated by way of the mode of being contradictory and the mode of being counter-contradictory.
One who is fierce is called "fierce" (*caṇḍa*), meaning a stubborn person; the state of such a person is "fierceness" (*caṇḍikka*).
Because speech uttered by such a person is not well-spoken, but is ill-spoken and incomplete, it is "not well-spoken" (*asuropa*). At the time of anger...
Indeed, there is no such thing as a "complete" word; even if someone were to use one, it would be of no authority.

Others, however, say it is "displeasure" (*assuropo*) because it does not produce tears (*assu*) and because it is associated with tears (*assu*). That is not a valid reason, for it also produces tears in the case of joy (*somanassa*).
It is "non-pleasure" (*anattamanatā*) because it is the opposite of the aforementioned mental gladness (*attamanatā*). Furthermore, since that [non-pleasure] belongs to the mind alone—

It does not belong to a being; therefore, it is said to belong to "the mind. The rest here should be understood according to the method already explained in the sections on inclusion and emptiness below.
The Tenth Consciousness (421):

This arises in one who is incited by others because of their volitional effort (*saṅkhāra*), or in one who has been reminded of an offense committed by others, or in one who becomes angry by himself after recollecting an offense committed by others.
Here too, according to the sequence of the words, there are twenty-nine; however, by taking only those not already included, there are fourteen words.

Furthermore, among the "miscellaneous" (yevāpanaka) factors, sloth-and-torpor (thinamiddha) is also found. Therefore, here—excluding envy, avarice, and worry—there are four "infallible" (apaṇṇaka) factors and sloth-and-torpor;
these six, together with any one of the others beginning with envy at the time of their arising, constitute the seven miscellaneous factors.
They arise in a single moment. All the rest is exactly like the ninth [consciousness] in all the sections.

However, in these two types of grief-consciousness, only co-nascent predominance (*sahajātādhipati*) is found, not object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*). For one who is angry does not hold anything in high esteem.
This is the eleventh consciousness.
422. The eleventh [type of consciousness] arises at the time when doubt occurs in one who is indifferent toward the six objects by way of feeling.
In its definition of the occasion, the phrase "associated with doubt" (*vicikicchā-sampayutta*) is new. Its meaning is as follows:
"associated with doubt" means associated with doubt. In the enumeration of phenomena (*dhammuddesa*), the specific distinction is simply the phrase "there is doubt."

In this context, "vicikicchā" means that which is devoid of investigation (*vicikicchā*). Alternatively, it is called *vicikicchā* because one suffers and becomes weary while investigating its intrinsic nature.
It has the characteristic of doubt; its function is to waver; it is manifested as indecision, or as the grasping of multiple alternatives;
its proximate cause is improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*). It should be understood as an obstacle to progress in practice.

Here, in the sequential order of the words, there are twenty-three terms. By including those not previously mentioned, there are fourteen. Based on these, the determination of the groups with and without case endings should be understood. *Manasikāra* (attention) and *uddhacca* (restlessness) are the only two [factors] included among the *yevāpanaka* (residues). 424.

In the section on the exposition (*niddesavāra*), regarding the exposition of one-pointedness of mind (*cittassekaggatā*), because this weak mind here exists merely as a state of occurrence, the single term “stability” (*ṭhiti*) alone was stated for the mind, without mentioning “establishment” (*saṇṭhiti*) and so forth. For that very reason...
And for this reason, even in the section on the summary (uddesavāra), the term "concentration faculty" (*samādhindriya*) and so forth was not mentioned.

425. In the exposition of doubt (*vicikicchā*), it is "doubt" (*kaṅkhā*) by way of doubting. "Doubting-coming" (*kaṅkhāyanā*) means the coming of doubt; for a preceding doubt indeed brings about a subsequent doubt.
Or else, this is stated by way of its formal characteristic (*ākāra*): a consciousness possessing doubt [is so called] because of doubt.
Because it wavers, it is called "wavering" (*kaṅkhāyita*); the state of that is "wavering-ness" (*kaṅkhāyitatta*). "Doubt" (*vimati*) means it inclines [toward various sides].
"Perplexity" (*vicikicchā*) has already been explained in its meaning. In the sense of shaking, it wavers in two ways, thus it is "double-dealing" (*dveḷhaka*).

Because it obstructs the path of practice, it is like a forked road, thus it is "a double-path" (*dvedhāpatha*). It occurs in the form of such thoughts as, "Is this permanent, or is it impermanent? and so forth.
It is called *saṃsayo* because it lies down all around due to an inability to settle. It is called *anekaṃsaggāho* because it does not grasp a single side due to an inability to take up one position.
It is called *āsappanā* because, being unable to reach a decision, it retreats from the object.
It is called *parisappanā* because, being unable to plunge in, it creeps all around. It is [called *pariyogāha*] due to an inability to fathom thoroughly.
Non-penetration. It is a state of rigidity due to the inability to proceed toward the object with decisiveness;
the meaning is a stiffened condition of the mind. For doubt, having arisen, makes the mind rigid.
Furthermore, because it, upon arising, seizes the object and as if scratches the mind, it is called "scratching of the mind" (*manovilekho*). The rest...
The meaning is clear throughout. Regarding the twelfth consciousness (427):
in the determination of its occasion, it is "associated with restlessness" because it is associated with *uddhacca* (restlessness). Thus, it is "restlessness-associated."
For this consciousness, having become neutral with respect to the six objects by way of feeling, becomes agitated.
