Here, in the exposition of phenomena (*dhammuddesa*), "restlessness" (*uddhacca*) is mentioned in the place of "doubt" (*vicikicchā*). There are twenty-eight terms according to their sequential order;
there are fourteen by taking them in groups of two. Based on these, the arrangement of the groups with and without case endings is established.
This should be understood. Resolve and attention are the only two [mental factors] included among the evens (yevāpanaka).
429. In the section on the exposition, regarding the exposition of restlessness (*uddhacca*): "of the mind" means not of a being, nor of a person.
"Restlessness" is the mode of being agitated. "Not calming" is non-calming. "The mind is distracted" is mental distraction (*cetaso-vikkhepa*). It is a state of wavering.
“Of the mind” means the state of wavering of the mind, like a wavering carriage or a wavering ox and so forth.
By this, the quivering within a single object itself is described. For restlessness (uddhacca) quivers within a single object, whereas doubt (vicikicchā) [quivers] among various objects.
The remainder in all sections should be understood according to the method already stated below.
Now, there follows an incidental analysis concerning these two types of consciousness.
If it is asked, "How many types of consciousness are said to 'proceed' upon an object?", one should reply, "These two alone.

Among them, that accompanied by doubt proceeds exclusively [without a firm basis], whereas that accompanied by restlessness proceeds having gained a foothold because it has obtained a degree of conviction (*adhimokkha*). Just as...
For instance, when two gems—one round and one square—are placed on a sloping surface and released, the round gem rolls away exclusively, while the square gem rolls only by repeatedly coming to rest;

this should be understood as being exactly like that. Furthermore, no distinction such as "inferior" and so forth has been mentioned for all [the types of predominance], because they are all invariably inferior. Co-nascent predominance (*sahajātādhipati*).

Even though it is obtainable, it has not been extracted because the method for doing so has already been shown below. Furthermore, because of the absence of knowledge (*ñāṇa*), there is no "predominance of investigation" (*vīmaṃsādhipati*) here.
In the final two dyads, the remainder is likewise absent. Why? Because no state is made the primary factor (*dhura*) and subsequently arises, and because it is prohibited in the *Paṭṭhāna*.
When karma is accumulated by these twelve unwholesome consciousnesses, eleven of them— excluding that accompanied by restlessness—

induce rebirth-linking. Why does that accompanied by restlessness, which is strong and has obtained conviction, not induce rebirth-linking when the two accompanied by doubt, though weak and lacking conviction, do induce it?
Because it is not something to be abandoned by vision (*dassanena pahātabba*).
For if it were to be drawn [into the category], it would appear in the analysis of the term "to be abandoned by vision"; therefore, setting that aside, the remaining eleven are drawn.

For when any one of those karmas is accumulated, rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) occurs in the four states of misery (*apāya*) by means of that volition (*cetanā*). Among the unwholesome resultant states, it is associated with the rootless mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity (*ahetuka-manoviññāṇadhātu-upekkhāsahagatā*).
It takes rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). For the other [type of consciousness] as well, the giving of rebirth-linking would occur in this very same way.
However, since that is not the case, it does not appear in the word-analysis (*padavibhaṅga*) for the phrase "to be abandoned by seeing.
The commentary on the phrase "unwholesome states" (*akusalā dhammā*) is concluded.
The Section on the Indeterminate (*Abyākatapada*). 431.
Now, in order to analyze and demonstrate the section on the indeterminate, the passage beginning with "Which phenomena are indeterminate? is commenced.

Therein, the indeterminate (avyākata) is fourfold: resultant (vipāka), functional (kiriya), material form (rūpa), and Nibbāna. Among these, it is the resultant-indeterminate. Within the resultant-indeterminate, it is wholesome-resultant.
Within that, it is limited-resultant. Within that, it is rootless. Within that, it is the fivefold sense-consciousness.
Within that, according to the sequence of the doors, it is eye-consciousness. Of that too, setting aside the common conditions such as the door and the object, etc., [it arises].
In order to demonstrate arising by way of the condition of uncommon kamma alone, it is said: "because of having performed wholesome kamma of the sense-sphere," and so forth.

Therein, "having been performed" (*katattā*) means because of the cause of having been done. "Having been accumulated" (*upacitattā*) means because of being heaped up; that is, because of the cause of having been increased.
"Eye-consciousness" (*cakkhuviññāṇaṃ*) means the consciousness of the eye which serves as its cause, or that which proceeds from the eye, or [that which exists] in the eye.
"Consciousness dependent on the ear," etc., refers to eye-consciousness (*cakkhu-viññāṇa*). The same method applies to the subsequent ear-consciousness and so forth.
Therein, eye-consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing visible forms in dependence on the eye; its function is to have mere visible form as its object;
it is manifested as being directed toward visible form; and its proximate cause is the subsiding of the functional mind-element that had visible form as its object.

The ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousnesses—characterized by the cognition of sounds and so forth that have come from outside and are dependent upon the ear and other sense bases—have as their flavor the mere objective field of sound and so forth;

they are manifested by the state of being directed toward sound and so forth; and they serve as the footing for the disappearance of the functional mind-elements (*kriyā-manodhātu*) whose objects are sound and so forth.

Here, there are ten terms according to their sequential order; by omitting those already mentioned, there are seven. Among these, five are without case endings (*avibhattika*) and two are with case endings (*savibhattika*).
Of these, consciousness (*citta*) undergoes analysis in two places—by way of the pentad of contact (*phassapañcaka*) and by way of the faculties (*indriya*);

feeling (*vedanā*) undergoes analysis in exactly three places—by way of the pentad of contact, the factors of jhāna (*jhānaṅga*), and the faculties. The groups (*rāsi*) are also [to be understood] in this manner.
These are exactly three. The one [factor] included as "and so forth" (yevāpanaka) is simply attention (manasikāra). 436.

In the section on the exposition (niddesa), eye-consciousness is described as "pure" (paṇḍara) by way of its basis (vatthu). For the wholesome (kusala) is called pure due to its own intrinsic purity; the unwholesome (akusala) is so called through the outflow of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga-nissanda); and the resultant (vipāka) is so called because of the purity of its basis. 439.
In the exposition of the one-pointedness of mind (cittassekaggatā), only the single term "stability of mind" (cittassa ṭhiti) is stated. For this too is weak.
In this case, only the mere persistence of the process of consciousness is obtained;
it is not able to reach the state of "stability" or "establishment. In the section on the Compendium, the factors of absorption (jhānaṅga) and the factors of the path (maggaṅga) are not mentioned.

Why? Because what is called "absorption ending with initial application" (vitakkapacchimaka) and what is called "the path ending with its cause" (hetupacchimaka)—in a natural mind that is without initial application (avitakka), the factors of absorption are not found.

And in the rootless consciousnesses, there are no path-factors. Therefore, neither of these has been mentioned here. Furthermore, the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) is analyzed here as having only four factors.
The section on emptiness (suññatavāra) remains exactly as before. The descriptions of ear-consciousness and the others should also be understood by this same method;
for in the case of eye-consciousness and the rest, "equanimity" (upekkhā) is analyzed, while in body-consciousness, "pleasure" (sukha) is. This is the distinction here.
This is the distinction. Furthermore, it should be understood that this [distinction] occurs by way of impact (*ghaṭṭana*).

For among the four doors beginning with the eye-door, it is only derived matter (*upādārūpa*) that impacts derived matter; when only derived matter impacts derived matter, the sound produced by the impact is not strong.
This is like placing four balls of cotton wool upon four grinding stones and [striking] only the balls of cotton wool.
It lasts only as long as it takes for a blow to be struck. Feeling remains in a state of neutrality.

However, at the door of the body, the external great elements, having struck the internal sensitivity of the body which has the great elements as its object, rebound against those great elements that serve as the conditions for that sensitivity.
This is like the case of one who places a tuft of cotton wool on the surface of a grindstone and strikes it with a hammer.
Just as when one cuts a tuft of cotton wool and takes it to the grinding stone, the friction is powerful, so too the friction of impact is powerful.
Upon a desirable object, a body-consciousness accompanied by pleasure arises;
upon an undesirable object, one accompanied by pain arises.
However, for these five types of consciousness, the physical bases, doors, and objects are fixed;

there is no shifting of the bases and so forth here. For instance, wholesome-resultant eye-consciousness takes the sensitive eye-faculty as its base and performs the function of seeing desirable or desirable-neutral objects consisting of fourfold-originated matter at the eye-door.

It ripens by remaining [in its respective door]. Ear-consciousness and the others, having made the ear-sensitivity and so forth their physical basis, perform the functions of hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching with respect to sounds and other objects that are desirable, undesirable, or neutral; they ripen by remaining in the ear-door and so forth.
In this context, however, sound has only two types of origination.
455. In the exposition of the mind-element (*manodhātu*): in the sense of its intrinsic emptiness and lack of a self-entity, the mind itself is the element; thus it is the mind-element.

It has the characteristic of cognizing visible forms and so forth immediately after eye-consciousness and the rest; its function is the reception of visible forms and so forth; it is manifested as such a state of being;

and its proximate cause is the cessation of eye-consciousness and the rest. Here, in the enumeration of phenomena (*dhamma*), there are twelve terms. By way of including what was not previously included...

Nine. Among these, seven are without case endings and two are with case endings. Resolve (*adhimokkha*) and attention (*manasikāra*) are the two factors included in the "yevāpanaka" (miscellaneous) category.

The exposition of initial application (*vitakka*) is established by bringing it to the state of "directing onto" (*abhiniropana*). However, because this consciousness is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, it is not described as either "right intention" (*sammā-saṅkappa*) or "wrong intention" (*micchā-saṅkappa*). Although it is found in the section on inclusion (*saṅgaha-vāra*), [it is not mentioned here].
The jhāna-factor has fallen into and entered the stream of the fivefold sense-consciousness. However, because the path-factor is not obtained there, it is not mentioned.
The section on emptiness is exactly as before. For this consciousness, the physical basis is fixed; it is the heart-basis alone. The doors and objects are unfixed.
Although the doors and objects shift therein, the location [of the basis] remains constant.
One [consciousness]. Its function is precisely that of receiving. For this [consciousness] ripens by acting as the recipient with respect to the five objects in the five doors.

When the eye-consciousness and the others among the wholesome-resultants have ceased, it immediately follows them and receives those very same objects, such as visible forms, which have now reached their respective positions.
469. In the explanations of the mind-consciousness elements (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), the term "rapture" (*pīti*) is additional in the first mind-consciousness element.
Feeling there is also feeling of mental joy (*somanassa*), for this [consciousness] occurs only with respect to a desirable object.

The second mind-consciousness element has a desirable-neutral object; therefore, feeling there is equanimity (*upekkhā*). The other terms are exactly the same as in the explanation of the mind-element (*manodhātu*).

In both cases, the factors of jhāna (jhānaṅgāni) are not mentioned because [the mind] has fallen into and proceeded along the stream of the fivefold sense-consciousness; the factors of the path (maggaṅgāni) are not mentioned simply because they are not obtained.
The rest is to be understood everywhere according to the method already stated.

Furthermore, from the perspective of its characteristics and so forth, this mental-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu)—of both types—is rootless-resultant (ahetuka-vipāka), characterized by the cognition of the six objects, having investigation (santīraṇa) and so forth as its function (rasa), and manifested as such a state of being.
It should be understood that its proximate cause is the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*). Among these, the first ripens in two places.

For, at the five doors, immediately after a wholesome resultant eye-consciousness and so forth have ceased, having received that object by means of the resultant mind-element (*vipākamanodhātu*), it performs the function of investigating (*santīraṇa*) that very same object.

When it is being accomplished, it ripens while standing at the five doors. However, when there is a powerful object at the six doors, it ripens by becoming an "object-attaining" (tadārammaṇa) consciousness.

How so? Just as when a boat is traveling crosswise in a violent current, the water, having cut off its path, follows the boat for a short distance and then flows back according to the current; even so, when there is a powerful object at the six doors—
When an object has come into range and is enticing, the impulsion (javana) runs its course. When that has run its course, it is the turn of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

However, this consciousness does not allow the life-continuum its turn; instead, having seized the object grasped by the impulsion, it proceeds for one or two thought-moments and then sinks back into the life-continuum itself.
Even in the case of crossing a river on a raft, the simile should be expanded in exactly this way.

Thus, this [kamma-resultant consciousness], having taken an object by means of the impulsion (javana), becomes "having that as its object" (tadārammaṇa) because it has grasped that very object, and then it matures.

However, the second type matures in five places. How so? First, in the human world, at the moment of seizing rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), it matures as rebirth-linking for those who are blind from birth, deaf from birth, mentally deficient from birth, insane from birth, hermaphrodites, and eunuchs. After the rebirth-linking has passed, [it matures] for the duration of their lifespan...

It ripens by becoming the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). It ripens in these five instances: as investigation (santīraṇa) in the cognitive process of the five sense objects regarding desirable or neutral objects;
as registration (tadārammaṇa) at the six doors regarding powerful objects; and as death (cuti) at the time of dying.
This concludes the exposition of the two types of mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu).
Commentary on the Eight Great Resultant Consciousnesses (Aṭṭhamahāvipākacittavaṇṇanā). 498.
Now, in order to show the eight great resultant consciousnesses, the passage beginning with "Which states are indeterminate? is commenced again.
Therein, having shown merely the method in the Pāḷi, all the sections are abbreviated. Their meaning is to be understood according to the method already stated above.
It should be understood. To show the distinction that exists here, it is said: "Non-greed is an indeterminate root," and so forth.

That which was not mentioned there should be understood as follows: for that division consisting of doors of action, courses of action, and bases for meritorious deeds which was described in the context of sense-sphere wholesome states does not exist here.
Why? Because they do not produce intimation (*viññatti*), because they are not subject to ripening (*avipākadhamma*), and because they do not function in that manner.

Furthermore, those very factors of compassion (*karuṇā*) and gladness (*muditā*) mentioned among the "included" (*yevāpanaka*) states do not exist among the resultants (*vipāka*), because they have sentient beings as their object.
For resultants of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) invariably have limited objects. Not only do compassion and gladness not exist there, but the abstinences (*virati*) also do not exist;
for it is said that "the five training precepts (*sikkhāpada*) are exclusively wholesome."

In this context, the classification of the spontaneous (*asaṅkhāra*) and prompted (*sasaṅkhāra*) [kamma] should be understood both in terms of their moral quality (*kusala*) and their specific conditions.
For the result of a spontaneous wholesome [kamma] is itself spontaneous, while that of a prompted one is prompted.

Furthermore, what arises through powerful conditions is spontaneous, whereas the other arises through the remaining [conditions]. Even regarding the classification into inferior and so forth, these [results] correspond to the inferior, middling, and superior [causes].
Because they are not produced by means of zeal (*chanda*) and the other [factors], they are not called inferior, medium, or superior.
However, the result of an inferior wholesome state is inferior, that of a medium one is medium, and that of a superior one is superior. Furthermore, there are no predominances (*adhipati*) here.
Why? Because it is not to be produced by making zeal and the others the primary factor. All the rest is exactly as described for the eight wholesome [states].
Now, the place where these eight great resultant consciousnesses ripen should be understood.
For they ripen in four places: at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), the death-moment (*cuti*), and as the object-attaining consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*).
How so? First, among humans and among the sense-sphere deities, for those possessing merit who are endowed with two or three roots, at the time of taking rebirth-linking—

They ripen by becoming rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). When rebirth-linking has passed away, they ripen during the course of existence (pavatta) for sixty or eighty years, or even for an incalculable period of life, by becoming the life-continuum (bhavaṅga);
at the six doors when there is a powerful object, by becoming registration (tadārammaṇa);
and at the time of death, by becoming the death-moment (cuti). Thus, they ripen in four ways.

In that regard, all omniscient Bodhisattvas, when taking their final rebirth-linking, take that rebirth-linking by means of the first great resultant consciousness—accompanied by joy, with three roots, and unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*). That, moreover, is the result of a state of mind preceded by loving-kindness (*mettā*).
By means of the rebirth-linking bestowed by that [consciousness], there is an incalculable lifespan. However, it comes to an end according to the power of time. But the Elder Mahāsīva said:
—“That which is accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*) is stronger than that which is accompanied by joy (*somanassa*). By means of it, one takes rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

For those who have taken rebirth-linking by means of it possess great aspiration; they do not become distracted even by divine objects, like the Elder Cūḷanāga, the master of the Three Piṭakas, and others.
However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), it says: “This is the elder’s wish,” “There is none... [and so on].

Having rejected this [objection] with the words "this is so," it is stated: "The service rendered for the benefit of omniscient Bodhisattvas is powerful; therefore, they take rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) with a three-rooted, spontaneous, sense-sphere wholesome resultant consciousness accompanied by joy, preceded by loving-kindness (mettā).
This concludes the Discussion on the Extraction of the Resultant.
Now, the matrix for the discussion on the extraction of resultant consciousness should be established. First, the Elder Cūḷanāga of the Tipiṭaka said:
"From a single wholesome volition, sixteen resultant consciousnesses arise; herein are included both the twelvefold path-consciousness and the eight rootless [resultants].
However, the Elder Mahādatta, resident of Moravāpi, said: "From a single wholesome volition, twelve resultant consciousnesses arise."
They arise. In this very context, there is also the tenfold path and the eightfold rootless [consciousnesses].
The Elder Tipiṭaka Mahādhammarakkhita said: "From a single wholesome volition, ten resultant consciousnesses arise; in this very context, there are the eight rootless ones.
At this point, they took up what is called the Sāketa Question. It is said that at Sāketa, lay followers sat in a hall and asked: "What..."
"Now, when a single kamma is accumulated by a single volition, is there one rebirth-linking or many?
Having raised this question, being unable to reach a decision, they approached the Abhidhamma masters and asked them.
The elders convinced them, saying, "Just as only a single sprout emerges from a single mango seed, so too there is only a single rebirth-linking."
Then one day, having raised the question, "Are the rebirth-linkings diverse when various volitional karmas are accumulated, or are they one?
and being unable to reach a decision, they questioned the Elders. The Elders made them understand:
"Just as when many mango seeds are planted, many sprouts emerge, even so there are many rebirth-linkings."
Furthermore, in this context, what is called the "exposition of predominance" (ussadakittana) is included.

For among these beings, greed (lobha) may be predominant, as may hatred (dosa) or delusion (moha); likewise, non-greed (alobha), non-hatred (adosa), and non-delusion (amoha) may be predominant. What determines this state of predominance in them? It is determined by past causes (pubbahetu).
The differentiation occurs at the very moment of the accumulation of kamma. How so? For one who, at the moment of accumulating kamma—
Greed is strong and non-greed is weak; hatred and delusion are strong while non-hatred and non-delusion are weak.
In such a case, his weak non-greed is unable to overcome greed, but his strong non-hatred and non-delusion are able to overcome hatred and delusion.
Therefore, having been reborn through the rebirth-linking granted by that kamma, he is greedy, yet he is of a pleasant disposition and free from anger.
“But he is wise, possessing knowledge like a thunderbolt. However,
for one at the moment of accumulating kamma whose greed and hatred are strong while non-greed and non-hatred are weak, and whose delusion is strong while non-delusion is weak,
he is likewise— according to the previous method— both greedy and hateful, yet he is wise, possessing knowledge like a thunderbolt.
Like the Elder Dattābhaya:

"But for one at the moment of accumulating kamma whose greed, hatred, and delusion are strong while the others are weak, he is, by the same method as before, both greedy and dull, yet he is of a pleasant disposition and free from anger.

Likewise, for one at the moment of accumulating kamma whose three—greed, hatred, and delusion—are strong while non-greed and the others are weak, he is, by the same method as before, both greedy, hateful, and deluded."

"But he for whom, at the moment of accumulating kamma, non-greed, hatred, and delusion are strong while the others are weak, is—by the same method as before—one with few defilements; even upon seeing a divine object, he remains unshaken, yet he is corrupt and slow-witted.

But he for whom, at the moment of accumulating kamma, non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are strong while the others are weak, is—by the same method as before—both free from greed and of pleasant character, yet he is slow-witted."

“Likewise, when at the moment of accumulating kamma non-greed, non-hate, and non-delusion are strong and the others are weak, that person—by the same method as before—is both non-greedy and wise, yet he is also hateful and prone to anger.

But when at the moment of accumulating kamma all three, beginning with non-greed, are strong and greed and the rest are weak, he is non-greedy, non-hateful, and wise, like the Elder Mahā-Saṅgharakkhita.
Furthermore, in this context, what is called the “explanation of the roots” is included; for a kamma possessing three roots may itself possess three roots or two roots.
It also gives fruit that is without roots. Karma with two roots does not give fruit with three roots; it gives the other [fruits].

By means of karma with three roots, rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) is either with three roots or with two roots; it is never without roots. By means of [karma] with two roots, rebirth-linking is either with two roots or without roots;
it is never with three roots. Wholesome [karma] that is unprompted (asaṅkhārika) gives fruit that is either unprompted or prompted.
It gives a result (vipāka). Whether it is prompted (sasaṅkhārika) or unprompted (asaṅkhārika), it gives a prompted or an unprompted result.
Feeling (vedanā) should be exchanged according to the object (ārammaṇa); the registration (tadārammaṇa) should be determined by the impulsion (javana).
Now, regarding the assertions of each Elder, the sixteen paths and so forth should be understood. [This is] similar to the first sense-sphere wholesome (kāmāvacara-kusala).

Indeed, for one who has taken rebirth by means of the first great resultant consciousness (*mahāvipākacitta*) and has reached a state capable of establishing restraint or non-restraint after emerging from the womb-dwelling,

there is no limit to the objects that pass away before the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) has even turned back when a desirable object enters the range of the eye-door via the functional mind-element (*kiriyamanodhātu*). Why is this?
Is it thus? Because of the weakness of the object. This, first of all, is one instance of futility.

But if it turns back toward the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), then once the life-continuum has been turned back by the functional mind-element (kiriyamanodhātu), it will turn back in the interval without even reaching the determining consciousness (voṭṭhabbana);
that is to say, it will turn back after having stood merely at eye-consciousness, or at reception, or at investigation. This is not so.
There is such a possibility. However, having stood by way of determining (voṭṭhabbana), one or two moments of consciousness proceed.
Then, having received repetition (āsevana), they stand in the position of impulsion (javana) and again descend into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga);
this too occurs solely due to the weakness of the object. This stage, moreover, is found at the time when one says, "It is as if I have seen it," "It is as if I have heard it," and so forth.
This is the second section on the futile.

It is said that when the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) of another person has been turned back by a functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu), the cognitive series arise and the impulsion (javana) occurs.
However, at the conclusion of the impulsion, it is the turn of the registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa). Even before that has arisen, the process lapses back into the life-continuum.

In this regard, there is this simile: just as when a dam is built across a river and the water is directed toward a great irrigation trench, the water flows and fills the fields on both banks, and then, overflowing, escapes through cracks, drains, and so forth, and returns once more into the very same river—so too should this be understood.
For here, the time of the water's flow in the river is [the initial stage].

The time for the occurrence of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and the cognitive process (vīthi) is like the time when [the water] flows freely. The time when the life-continuum is turned back by the functional mind-element (kiriyamanodhātu) is like the time when the flow is obstructed by a dam.
The occurrence of the consciousnesses of the cognitive process is like the flowing of the water through the great channel. The javana is like the filling of the field on both banks.
The crossing of the river by the water again after having fled by way of the crab-paths and so forth is like [the return to the life-continuum].

Just as a swift horse gallops on, even before the registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa) has arisen, there occurs again the sinking back into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). Thus, there is no way of counting even the moments of consciousness that descend into the life-continuum.
And this happens precisely because of the weakness of the object. This is the third section on futility.
However, if a powerful object enters the range of the senses, the life-continuum is turned back by the functional mind-element (kiriyamanodhātu), and then the eye-consciousness and the others arise.
They arise. However, at the stage of impulsion (*javana*), the first sense-sphere wholesome consciousness acts as the impulsion;

having impelled for six or seven moments, it yields its turn to the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*). When the registration consciousness establishes itself, a great resultant consciousness (*mahāvipākacitta*) similar to it establishes itself.
This [resultant consciousness] receives two names: because of its similarity to the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*), it is called the "root life-continuum" (*mūlabhavanga*).
And it is called "having that as its object" (*tadārammaṇa*) because it takes as its object that same object which was grasped by the impulsion (*javana*).
At this point, four resultant consciousnesses—the eye-consciousness, the receiving, the investigating, and the "having that as its object"—are included in the count.
However, when the second wholesome consciousness functions as impulsion, then only the second resultant consciousness, which is similar to it, [arises].

Having that [object] as its object, it becomes established. And this receives two names: because it is unlike the rebirth-linking consciousness, it is called "the adventitious life-continuum" (*āgantuka-bhavanga*);
and by the same method as before, it is called "registration" (*tadārammaṇa*). Together with this, there are four or five [types of consciousness] preceding it.
But when the third wholesome consciousness becomes the impulsion (javana), then a similar third resultant consciousness establishes itself as the registration (tadārammaṇa).
This too receives two names—“guest bhavaṅga” and “registration”—in the same manner already described.
Together with this, there are six [consciousnesses] including the previous five.
But when the fourth wholesome consciousness is the impulsion (javana), then a corresponding fourth resultant consciousness establishes itself as the registration (tadārammaṇa).
This too receives two names—“guest bhavaṅga” and “registration”—in the same manner already described. Together with this, there are six or seven [resultant types].
But when an "agreeable-neutral" object comes into range at that door, there too the three "vain" sections are obtained in the same manner as described.
Since feeling turns according to the object, therefore, in that case, there is investigation accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā-sahagata-santīraṇa*).
And at the conclusion of four great wholesome javanas accompanied by equanimity, there are precisely four great resultant consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity.

They establish themselves by having that [object] as their object (*tad-ārammaṇa*). These too receive two names according to the method already stated: "guest life-continuum" (*āgantuka-bhavanga*) and "that-object" (*tad-ārammaṇa*).
They are also called "subsequent life-continuums" (*piṭṭhi-bhavangāni*).
Thus, these five together with the previous seven make twelve. In this way, there are twelve in the eye-door, and twelve each in the ear-door and the others.
There are sixty in total. Thus, when a single kamma has been accumulated by means of a single volition (*cetanā*), sixty resultant consciousnesses (*vipākacitta*) arise.
By including what was not previously included, there are twelve in the eye-door and sixteen in the ear, nose, tongue, and body consciousnesses (four each).
At this point, they took up the simile of the mango: it is said that a certain man, at the foot of a flowering mango tree, [placed his head]...

Having put on his robes, he lay down and fell asleep. Then, one mango fruit, detaching from its stalk, fell to the ground with the sound "tham," as if brushing against his ear-ornament. Waking at that sound, he opened his eyes and looked.
Then, reaching out his hand, he took the fruit, crushed it, smelled it, and ate it.
In this context, the time when that man is sleeping at the foot of the mango tree is like the period of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
The time when the mango fruit, having detached from its stalk, strikes the earring as he wipes it is like the time when the object strikes the sensitive matter (*pasāda*).
The time when he awakens due to that sound is like the time when the functional mind-element (*kiriyamanodhātu*) turns back the life-continuum. Having opened [his eyes]...
The moment of looking is like the moment when visual consciousness performs its function of seeing.

The moment of grasping by stretching out the hand is like the moment when the resultant mind-element receives the object. The moment of crushing after having grasped it is like the moment when the resultant mind-consciousness element investigates the object.
The moment of smelling is like [the moment] for the functional mind-consciousness element regarding the object...
This is the time of determining. It is like the time of experiencing the flavor of the object for the impulsion (javana), similar to the time of eating.
What does this simile illustrate? The function of the object is merely to strike the sensitive matter (pasāda).

When that sensitive matter has been struck by it, there is merely the turning back of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) by the functional mind-element (kiriyamanodhātu); there is merely the seeing by the eye-consciousness; and there is merely the receiving of the object by the resultant mind-element (vipākamanodhātu).

The function of the resultant mind-consciousness element is merely the investigation of the object, while the function of the functional mind-consciousness element is merely the determination of the object.
This demonstrates that it is the impulsion (javana) alone that exclusively experiences the flavor of the object.
And herein: "You be the life-continuum (bhavaṅga); you be the adverting consciousness; you be the seeing; you..."
"There is no agent or instigator who can say, 'Be you reception,' 'Be you investigation,' 'Be you determining,' or 'Be you impulsion.
However, at this point, they recognized five kinds of natural order (niyāma): the natural order of seeds, the natural order of seasons, the natural order of karma," and so forth.
"The fixed order of phenomena, the fixed order of the mind. In this context, there is the upward growth of the *kulattha* bean stalk,
the climbing vine’s circling around the tree to the right, the sunflower’s orientation toward the sun, the *māluva* creeper’s movement toward the tree,
and the presence of a hole at the top of the coconut— these are the respective inherent tendencies of those seeds.
The "law of the seed" (bījaniyāma) refers to the yielding of fruits corresponding to each respective seed.

The "law of the season" (utuniyāma) refers to the simultaneous taking up of flowers, fruits, and foliage by various trees at their respective times. For instance, kamma with three roots (tihetuka) yields a result that may have three roots, two roots, or no roots;
kamma with two roots yields a result that may have two roots or no roots, but it does not yield a result with three roots—such is its [nature].
The "law of karma" (*kammaniyāma*) refers precisely to that specific action's yielding of a result corresponding to itself.
Furthermore, there is another law of karma based on the principle of a result similar to the action. To illustrate this, they relate the following story:
During the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One, a village at the gate of Sāvatthī was consumed by fire. From that place, a burning bundle of straw—
As the crow rose and flew through the air, she fastened it around its neck. Crying out, it fell to the ground and died.
In the great ocean as well, a ship came to a standstill. Seeing no cause for the obstruction below, they drew lots for ill fortune (*kāḷakaṇṇisalāka*).
The lot fell into the hands of the laywoman who was the ship’s captain. Then—
"Lest all should perish for the sake of one, let us cast her into the water," they said.
The boatman, thinking, "I shall not be able to look upon her floating in the water," had a jar filled with sand tied around her neck and cast her in.
At that very moment, the ship sped away like a discharged arrow. A certain bhikkhu was living in a cave. A great mountain peak—
Having fallen, it closed the door. On the seventh day, it opened by itself.
While the Perfectly Enlightened One was seated in Jeta’s Grove preaching the Dhamma, they reported these three matters to him all at once. The Teacher said, “This was not done by others;
it was indeed the result of the karma performed by them,” and he spoke, bringing forth a past account to demonstrate this.
In a previous existence, this crow was a human being who, unable to tame a rogue ox, tied a bundle of straw around its neck and set it on fire.
The ox died from that very act. Now, even though he is traveling through the air, that karma has not released him from its consequences.
That woman, too, was a woman in her previous existence; she had become intimate with a certain dog.
Having made the offering, he went along with her as she was going to the forest, and he returned with her alone.
People mocked them, saying, "Now our dog-hunter has gone out!
She, being distressed by this and unable to stop the dog, tied a jar of sand around its neck and threw it into the water. That deed [caught up with her] in the middle of the ocean.
He did not release it. That monk, too, in a previous existence, having been a cowherd, blocked the entrance of a hole with a handful of broken branches for a lizard that had entered it.
Then, on the seventh day, he himself came and opened it. The trembling lizard emerged;
out of compassion, he did not kill it. That karma followed him as he entered between the mountains.
“He did not grant release to one who was seated. Having combined these three instances, he spoke this verse:
“Neither in the sky, nor in the midst of the ocean, nor by entering a cleft in the mountains,”
“There is no place in the world where one, while remaining there, could be freed from evil kamma.
This too is indeed called the fixed order of kamma (kamma-niyāma). Other such instances should also be recounted.

Furthermore, for Bodhisattas at the moment of taking rebirth-linking, upon emerging from the mother’s womb, at their full enlightenment, at the Tathāgata’s turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, at the relinquishing of the life-formations, and at the final Nibbāna, there is a natural law known as the "shaking of the ten-thousandfold world-system.
However, when the sensitive matter (pasāda) is struck by an object, [the following occurs]: "You shall become adverting consciousness... you shall become impulsion consciousness," and so forth.
There is no agent or instigator whatsoever;

rather, by the very nature of each respective phenomenon, from the moment the sense-faculty is struck by the object, the functional mind-element (kiriyamanodhātu) turns back the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), the eye-consciousness fulfills its function of seeing, and the resultant mind-element (vipākamanodhātu) fulfills its function of receiving. The resultant mind-consciousness-element...

The investigating consciousness (santīraṇa) accomplishes the function of investigation; the functional mind-consciousness element (kiriyamanoviññāṇadhātu) accomplishes the function of determining (voṭṭhabbana); and the impulsion (javana) experiences the flavor of the object.
This is what is called the "fixed order of consciousness" (cittaniyāma), and it is this that is intended here.

[This applies] even to wholesome states with three roots accompanied by volitional effort (sasaṅkhārika), as well as to wholesome states accompanied by equanimity, whether they are without volitional effort (asaṅkhārika) or with volitional effort (sasaṅkhārika).
The same method applies to the rebirth-linking that is taken up by resultant consciousnesses similar to that [kamma] when kamma has been accumulated.
Regarding the two types accompanied by equanimity, however, one should first show their occurrence "by way of a desirable-neutral object" and afterwards show it "by way of a desirable object.
Thus, there are twelve for each door, making sixty in total. By including what was not previously mentioned, sixteen resultant consciousnesses arise.
At this point, they took up the simile of the five sugar-cane presses.
It is said that at the time of pressing sugar cane, eleven press-drivers departed from a certain village;
seeing a sugar-cane field and knowing it was fully ripe, they approached the owner of the field and announced, "We are press-drivers. He replied, "I shall seek you out myself."
Taking a cartload of sugarcane, he went there. Having prepared a sugar-mill there, they said, “We are eleven men; it is necessary to get one more. Take him for a wage.
The owner of the sugarcane said, “I myself shall be the companion,” and filling their cart with sugarcane, he became their companion. Each of them...
Having performed their tasks— when the sugarcane juice had been boiled by the boilerman, when it had been formed into lumps by the sugar-maker,
and when the owner of the sugarcane had weighed it and distributed the shares— they each took their own portion, entrusted the sugarcane shed to the owner,
and departed after performing work in the same manner in four other sheds as well.
In this context, the five sensitive organs (pasāda) are to be seen as like five sugar-pressing sheds; the five sense objects as like five sugar-cane fields;
the eleven resultant consciousnesses as like the eleven workers who operate the pressing machines; and the five types of sensory consciousness as like the owners of the five sugar-cane fields.
When twelve people, including the owner, are together in the first shed...

Just as it is the time for the partners to receive their shares of the work, so too is it the time when the eleven resultant consciousnesses, having come together with eye-consciousness, perform their respective functions at the eye-door regarding a visible-form object.
Just as it is the time for the owner of the hall to receive [the benefit] in the hall, so too is it the non-transference of the door by the eye-consciousness. Second, third, fourth...
Just as it is the time for twelve people who have acted together in the fifth hall to receive their respective shares,
so too is it the time for eleven resultant consciousnesses to act in concert with body-consciousness at the body-door regarding a tangible object, each performing its own specific function.
Just as it is the time for the owner of the hall to receive [the benefit] in the hall, so too is it the non-transference of the door by the body-consciousness.
This should be understood. Up to this point, the section has been explained wherein rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is three-rooted (*tihetuka*) by means of a three-rooted kamma.
However, the rebirth-linking that occurs through that [same kamma] as two-rooted (*duhetuka*) has passed while remaining concealed.

Now, the section must be explained wherein rebirth-linking is two-rooted by means of a two-rooted kamma. For, by means of a two-rooted consciousness accompanied by joy (*somanassa-sahagata*) and unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*):

When a desirable object comes into the range of the eye-door for one who has taken rebirth-linking by a two-rooted resultant consciousness similar to that [kamma], there are three "vain" sections according to the method already described.

At the conclusion of a spontaneous (asaṅkhārika) javana accompanied by two roots and associated with joy, there is a registration (tadārammaṇa) consciousness similar to that, known as the root-bhavanga. At the conclusion of a prompted (sasaṅkhārika) javana, it is similar to that.

The registration [consciousness] consists of the adventitious bhavaṅga; it has that same object. In the case of "desirable-neutral objects," at the conclusion of two javanas accompanied by equanimity, two such registrations arise.
Here, calculating eight for each door, there are forty-eight consciousnesses.
However, by not including those already mentioned, there are eight at the eye-door, and [the corresponding] ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousnesses.
The four [types of consciousness] become twelve. Thus, when a kamma has been accumulated by means of a single volition, twelve resultant consciousnesses arise.

The discourse on the fivefold determination, using the simile of the mango, remains as it was before. This same method applies even to one who has taken rebirth-linking with a resultant consciousness similar to the remaining three types of double-rooted consciousness.
However, according to the simile of the machine-operator, there are seven machine-operators here; by means of them, therein—
When the "yanta" [mechanism] is prepared, the eighth section concerning the owner of the house should be understood by applying the method according to what has been stated.
Up to this point, the section explaining that a two-rooted rebirth-linking occurs through a two-rooted kamma has been discussed.
Now follows the discussion on rootless rebirth-linking: for, by means of any one of the four two-rooted wholesome consciousnesses...

When karma has been accumulated, for one who has taken rebirth-linking by means of a rootless mind-consciousness element associated with equanimity and accompanied by wholesome kamma-result, it cannot be said that the rebirth-linking is similar to the karma. For the karma is double-rooted, whereas the rebirth-linking is rootless.
When that [karma] has reached growth and a desirable-neutral object enters the range at the eye-door, then, in the same manner as before, three [moments of consciousness arise].

It should be understood as having futile results. However, at the conclusion of any one of the four double-rooted wholesome javanas, a rootless consciousness establishes itself as the object-attaining (tadārammaṇa) state.

That [consciousness] receives two names: "root-life-continuum" (mūla-bhavanga) and "object-attaining" (tadārammaṇa). Thus, in this case, there is eye-consciousness, reception, and equanimity-accompanied investigation.
Since even the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) in those cases is accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*), taking one from among them, there are exactly three that come under counting.
However, in the case of a desirable object, both the investigating consciousness (*santīraṇa*) and the registration consciousness are accompanied by joy (*somanassa*).
Taking one from among these, the preceding three become four. Thus, having counted four for each of the five doors, with one [remaining]—
It should be understood that when karma is accumulated through volition (*cetanā*), twenty resultant consciousnesses (*vipākacitta*) arise.
By including what was not previously mentioned, there are eight—namely, the four types of sense-consciousness (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body) at the eye-door and so forth.
This is called the "rootless group of eight" (*ahetuka-ṭṭhaka*). This is included within the human world.
However, it is found in the process [of consciousness] within the four states of misery (*apāya*).

For when the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, having manifested a lotus in hell, sat upon the pericarp of that lotus and delivered a discourse on the Dhamma to the denizens of hell, at that time, as they beheld the Elder, a wholesome-resultant eye-consciousness arose; and as they heard his voice, an ear-consciousness arose.
The nose-consciousness at the time of smelling the fragrance of his robe after he had sat for his midday rest in a sandalwood grove;
the tongue-consciousness at the time of giving water after causing the rain-god to send down rain to extinguish the fires of hell;

and the body-consciousness at the time of raising a very gentle breeze—thus there are the five [consciousnesses] beginning with eye-consciousness, one receiving consciousness, and two investigating consciousnesses.
The group of eight rootless [consciousnesses] is obtained. Even for nāgas, supaṇṇas, beings of the celestial mansions (vaimānika), and petas, rebirth-linking occurs through unwholesome [kamma].
During the course of existence, wholesome [kamma] ripens. The same applies to the auspicious elephants, horses, and so forth of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti).
This, then, is the method of exposition regarding the wholesome javanas with respect to desirable, undesirable, and neutral objects.

When a desirable object has been impelled by four unwholesome consciousnesses accompanied by joy (*somanassa-sahagata-akusala-citta*), the wholesome-resultant rootless consciousness accompanied by joy (*kusalavipāka-somanassasahagatāhetuka-citta*) takes that as its object (*tadārammaṇa*).

When a moderately desirable object has been impelled by four [unwholesome consciousnesses] associated with greed and accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā-sahagata-lobhasampayutta*), the wholesome-resultant rootless consciousness accompanied by equanimity takes that as its object. As for that which was [impelled] by the impulsion (*javana*)...
It should be understood that when it is said, "the registration [consciousness] must be determined," this is stated with reference to wholesome [kamma].
What arises as the registration consciousness arising immediately after a javana accompanied by mental displeasure? It is the unwholesome-resultant, rootless mind-consciousness element that arises.
But what determines whether this javana is for the sake of the wholesome or for the sake of the unwholesome? Both the adverting consciousness and the determining consciousness.
For it is impossible that, when turning has been done properly by adverting and determining has been done properly by apprehending, the impulsion will be unwholesome.

It is also impossible that, when turning has been done improperly by adverting and determining has been done improperly by apprehending, the impulsion will be wholesome. However, when both have been done properly by turning and determining...
And it should be understood that the impulsion is wholesome;

whereas, when one is doubting or agitated regarding a desirable object, it should be understood as unwholesome. But what is the registration consciousness for one who is doubting or agitated toward a desirable object?

Whether one doubts or does not doubt, whether one is agitated or not, the registration consciousness in respect of a desirable object is exclusively a wholesome-resultant, rootless, joyful consciousness.
It is thus: "In the case of a desirable-neutral object, it is 'accompanied by wholesome-resultant rootless equanimity'.
This, however, is the exposition of the meaning in brief known as the doctrine of the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita.
For when a javana accompanied by joy has occurred, five registration-moments (*tadārammaṇa*) are to be sought; likewise when a javana accompanied by equanimity has occurred.
"Six things are to be sought. Now,
when one who has a rebirth-linking consciousness accompanied by joy (somanassa) produces jhāna during the course of existence, and then, having fallen away from that jhāna through negligence,
reflects, "A sublime state has been lost to me," and sorrow arises due to remorse (vippaṭisāra), [that is the first thing to be sought].
Then what arises? For it is prohibited in the *Paṭṭhāna* that "after joy there is grief, and after grief there is joy.

And when a sublime state (*mahaggata-dhamma*) is taken as the object and a functional consciousness (*javana*) occurs, is it also prohibited in that same context for a registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) to arise?
[It is] either a wholesome-resultant or unwholesome-resultant mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity and rootless (*ahetuka*).
“It arises; what, then, is its function of adverting? “It has no function of adverting, just as there is none for the life-continuum or the adverting consciousness.
“Let these [other states] arise because of their own inclination, habit, and manifestation; but how does this one arise?
“Just as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the immediate condition for cessation, so from cessation...”

For one emerging [from attainment], the consciousness of the fruition-attainment (*phalasamāpatti*), the noble path-consciousness (*ariyamaggacitta*), and the fruition-consciousnesses immediately following the path arise;
thus, even in the absence of an act of adverting (*āvajjana*), it arises by virtue of its habitual practice and inclination.
For while consciousness arises without an act of adverting, it does not arise without an object (*ārammaṇa*). "Then what is its object? "It is among forms and so forth..."

"Any one among the limited states (parittadhamma). For it should be understood that this consciousness arises by taking as its object whichever among these has at that time come into the range of perception.
Now, this miscellaneous method is stated for the purpose of making all these types of consciousness clear.
The Thread, the Gatekeeper, the Village Boy, the Mango, and the Koliyan;
the one born blind, the cripple, and the grasping for sense-objects, and the supporting condition as the goal.
In this context, regarding the "Thread": there was once a spider on a path that, having stretched out thread in the five directions, made a web.

It lies down in the middle. When the thread stretched toward the first direction is struck by an insect, a moth, or a fly, it moves away from its place of rest, goes along following the thread, drinks its fluid, and returning once more, lies down right there.
It acts in exactly the same way when the threads in the second direction and so forth are struck.
In this context, the five sensitive organs (pasāda) are like a thread stretched out in the five directions;
the mind (citta) is like a spider lying in the middle; the time when the sensitive organ is struck by an object is like the time when the thread is touched by insects and the like;
and the movement of the spider lying in the middle is like the functional mind-element (kiriyamanodhātu) taking up the object that struck the sensitive organ.
The time when the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is turned back is like the time of setting out according to the instructions of a sutta;
the occurrence of the cognitive process (vīthicitta) is like the act of walking. The time when the impulsion (javana) rushes toward the object is like drinking broth after piercing the head;
the mind’s proceeding by depending solely on the heart-base (hadayavatthu) is like returning once more and lying down in the middle.

What does this simile illustrate? It illustrates that when the sensitive matter is struck by an object, the consciousness based on the material heart-base arises prior to the consciousness based on the sensitive matter as its physical basis.
It also illustrates that a single object enters the range of two pairs of doors.
As for the "gatekeeper": there was a king who, having gone to his bed, was sleeping. His attendant sat massaging his feet.
The deaf doorkeeper stood at the gate. Three porters were stationed there in succession.
Then a man from the borderlands arrived carrying a gift and knocked on the gate.
The deaf doorkeeper did not hear the sound. The foot-massager gave him a signal. Following that signal, he opened the gate and looked out. This was the first porter.
Having taken the gift, he gave it to the second; the second gave it to the third; the third gave it to the king. The king consumed it.
In this context, the king should be regarded as the impulsion (javana); the foot-massager as the adverting consciousness (āvajjana); the deaf doorkeeper as the eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa);
the three gatekeepers as the three process-consciousnesses beginning with the receiving consciousness (sampaṭicchana); and the border-dwellers...
The striking of the sense-faculty by the object is like the knocking at the door after one has arrived bringing a gift.

The moment when perception is provided by the "rubber of the feet" (the preliminary mental process) is like the time when the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is turned back by the functional mind-element (kiriyamanodhātu).
The moment when the eye-consciousness accomplishes its function of seeing the object is like the deaf doorkeeper opening the door upon being given the signal by that [functional element].
The moment the object is received by the resultant mind-element (vipākamanodhātu) is like the time the gift was accepted through the first miracle.
The moment the object is investigated by the resultant mind-consciousness-element (vipākamanoviññāṇadhātu) is like the time the second [gift] was handed over by the first.
The moment the object is determined by the functional mind-consciousness-element (kiriyamanoviññāṇadhātu) is like the time the third [gift] was handed over by the second.
The moment of voṭṭhabbana is like the time when [the gift] is handed over to the king by the third person;
the moment of the javana is like the time when the king experiences the flavor of the object.
What does this simile illustrate? It shows that the function of the object is merely to strike the sensitive organ (pasāda), while the functional mind-element (kiriyamanodhātu) [perceives it].
The functions of eye-consciousness and the others are merely the seeing, receiving, investigating, and determining [of the object];
it is shown that only the impulsion (javana) exclusively experiences the flavor of the object.
"The village boy": many village children were playing with sand in the middle of the street. There, one...
A coin struck against his hand. He said, "It has struck my hand; what indeed is this? Then one said, "This is pale.
Another grasped it firmly along with the dust. Another said, "This is broad and square.
Another said, "This is a kahāpaṇa coin. Then, having brought it, he gave it to his mother. She set it to work.
In this context, the occurrence of the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*) is to be seen as like the time when many children are sitting and playing in the middle of an alleyway.
The moment the sense-faculty is struck by the object is like the moment a coin strikes the hand.
The moment one says, "What is this? after having grasped that object, is like the functional mind-element (*kiriyā-manodhātu*) [arising] toward the life-continuum.
The time of turning [the object] around is like the time when it is said, "This is white"—it is the time when the function of seeing has been accomplished by eye-consciousness.
The time when the object is firmly grasped together with the dust is like the time when the resultant mind-element (vipākamanodhātu) receives the object.
The time when it is said, "This is broad and four-cornered," is like the time when the resultant mind-consciousness-element (vipākamanoviññāṇadhātu) [perceives the object].

This is the time of investigation (*santīraṇa*). It is like the time when it is said, "This is a kahāpaṇa coin"; it is the time when the object is determined by the functional mind-consciousness element (*kiriyamanoviññāṇadhātu*).
The experiencing of the flavor of the object by the impulsion (*javana*) should be understood as being like the time when the mother has presented the work to be done.

What does this simile illustrate? The functional mind-element (*kiriyamanodhātu*) turns back the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) even without having seen [the object], whereas the resultant mind-element (*vipākamanodhātu*)...
The resultant mind-consciousness element (vipākamanoviññāṇadhātu) apperceives without having seen; the functional mind-consciousness element (kiriyamanoviññāṇadhātu) defines without having seen;
and the impulsion (javana) experiences the flavor of the object without having seen. However, it is demonstrated that eye-consciousness alone fulfills the function of seeing exclusively.
‘Both the mango-gatherer and...’—this was said with reference to the mango simile and the simile of the owner of the sugar-cane shed mentioned above.
‘The man blind from birth and the cripple’—both of them, it is said, were sitting in a hall at the city gate.
There, the cripple said: “O blind man, why do you wander about here wasting away? Such-and-such a place has abundant food.”
“There is plenty of food and drink there; why should it not be fitting for you to go there and live in comfort?
“I have been told by you what it is like, but as for you, why should it not be fitting for you to go there and live in comfort?
“I have no feet to go. “I have no eyes to see. “If that is so, then your feet [are useless].”
"Let there be eyes for me," he said; both of them, having agreed by saying "Very well," the one born blind placed the cripple upon his shoulder.
Seated on his shoulder, the cripple encircled the other's head with his left hand and, with his right hand, directed him:
"A root stands here blocking the path; here is a rock; let go of the left and take the right."
"Release the right hand; take the left," he says, thus defining and pointing out the path.
In this way, the birth-blind man’s feet and the cripple’s eyes—both through their union—reached the desired destination and lived happily.
In this context, the physical body (*rūpakāya*) is like the birth-blind man, and the immaterial body (*arūpakāya*) is like the cripple. Without the cripple, the birth-blind man...

Just as there is no time when the volitional formation of going to travel toward a direction has not yet been produced, so too matter is incapable of undergoing appropriation, grasping, or movement without the immaterial.

Just as a cripple cannot go toward a direction or produce the volitional formation of going without a person born blind, so too the immaterial does not function without the five-aggregate materiality. This is due to the association of both.
Just as one reaches a desired place and lives there in comfort, so too, through the mutual conjunction of material and immaterial phenomena, there arises the occurrence of all functional activities.
This question has been explained by way of existence in the fivefold plane (*pañcavokāra-bhava*).
Regarding the phrase "the grasping of objects": the eye grasps the object of visible form; the ear and the other [senses] grasp their respective objects, such as sound and so forth.
‘By way of decisive support and by way of meaning’: that is, both ‘by way of decisive support’ (upanissayato) and ‘by way of meaning’ (atthato).

Therein, because the eye is unimpaired, because visible forms have come into its range, and being dependent on light and caused by attention, eye-consciousness arises by way of four conditions, together with its associated mental states. In that regard, even for one who has died, the eye becomes impaired.
Even in a living person, that which has ceased, or is obstructed by bile, phlegm, or blood, and is thus unable to become a condition for eye-consciousness, is called "obstructed" (*sambhinna*).
That which is able [to do so] is called "unobstructed" (*asambhinna*). The same principle applies to the ear and the other sense-faculties.
However, even when the eye is unobstructed, if an external visible object does not come into the range of perception, [eye-consciousness does not arise].
Eye-consciousness does not arise. Even when that [object] has come into the range of perception, it does not arise if there is no dependence on light.

Even when that [light] is present, it does not arise if the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) has not been turned toward the functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu). It arises only when [the life-continuum] has been turned.
When it arises in this way, it arises together with its associated mental states (sampayutta-dhamma). Thus, these four—
Having obtained the conditions, eye-consciousness arises.

Due to the non-deficiency of the ear, the arrival of sounds within its range, its dependence on space, and having attention as its cause, ear-consciousness arises together with its associated mental states through four conditions. In this context, "dependent on space" means:
It arises only by depending on space, not without it; for auditory consciousness does not occur in one whose ear-channels are closed.
The rest should be understood in the same manner as previously explained. And just as it is here, so it is in the subsequent cases as well. We shall, however, state only the specific differences.
Because the nose is unobstructed and because odors have come into its range, [olfactory consciousness] depends on air and has attention as its cause.
Olfactory consciousness arises by way of four conditions, together with its associated mental states.
In this context, "dependent on air" means that it arises only when air enters the nostril; the meaning is that in the absence of that [air], it does not arise.
Because the tongue is unimpaired, because tastes have come into range, and because of attention as the cause, it is dependent on water. By way of these four...
Tongue-consciousness arises by means of conditions, together with its associated mental states.
In this context, “dependent on water” means that it arises only after obtaining the water-element within the tongue; it does not arise without it.
For indeed, in the case of those with dry tongues, even when dry food is placed upon the tongue, tongue-consciousness simply does not arise.

Due to the non-disruption of the body, the arrival of tangible objects within its range, its dependence upon earth, and having attention as its cause, body-consciousness arises by way of four conditions, together with its associated mental states.

In this context, "dependent on earth" means that it arises only after obtaining the support of earth, which is the condition for the sensitivity of the body; it does not arise without that. For, in the door of the body—
Having struck the internal bodily sensitivity (*kāyapasāda*) with an external great element as its object, it rebounds against the great elements that serve as the conditions for that sensitivity.

Because the mind is unimpeded and because mental objects have come into its range, mind-consciousness arises together with its associated states by means of four conditions—dependent upon the physical base and caused by attention. In this context, "mind" refers to...

The life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅgacitta*). Even though it has ceased, if it is incapable of becoming a condition for the adverting consciousness (*āvajjanacitta*), it is called "confused" (*sambhinna*) even while proceeding in a weak state.
However, that which is capable of being a condition for the adverting consciousness is called "unconfused" (*asambhinna*).

Regarding the phrase “because the mental objects have come into the range,” this means when the mental objects (*dhammārammaṇa*) have entered the range. “Supported by a physical basis” (*vatthusannissita*)—means...
It arises only by depending upon the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*), and not without it. This question, too, is stated with reference to existence in the fivefold plane (*pañcavokārabhava*).
"Having attention as its cause" means that it arises only when the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) has been turned back toward the functional mind-consciousness element (*kriyā-manoviññāṇadhātu*).
This, then, is the commentary on "support by way of decisive support" (*upanissaya*) within the phrase "support by way of meaning."

As for the meaning (*atthato*): the eye has the purpose of seeing, the ear the purpose of hearing, the nose the purpose of smelling, the tongue the purpose of tasting, the body the purpose of touching, and the mind the purpose of cognizing.
In this context, "seeing" is its purpose; because that [seeing] is to be accomplished by means of it, it is called "having seeing as its purpose.
The same method applies to the others as well. Thus far, according to the doctrine of the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷanāga.
The section on the sixteenfold path, together with the twelvefold path and the group of rootless [consciousnesses], is concluded.

Now follows the discussion of the twelvefold path according to the doctrine of the Elder Mahādatta, the resident of Moravāpi. In this regard, the Sāketa-question, the exposition of the "excess" (ussada), and the exposition of the roots are the same as before.
However, this elder, seeing a fault in both the unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*) and prompted (*sasaṅkhārika*) [paths], [asserts] the unprompted...
He said: "It yields only unprompted (asaṅkhārika) result, not prompted (sasaṅkhārika); and even when prompted, it yields only a prompted result, not an unprompted one.
Furthermore, he does not define the determination of consciousness by means of the impulsion (javana), but rather defines the determination of feeling by means of the object (ārammaṇa).

Therefore, in his exposition of the results (vipākuddhāra), there arises what is called the "twelvefold path" (dvādasakamagga). The "tenfold path" (dasakamagga) and the "rootless eightfold" (ahetukaṭṭhaka) are also included therein.

In this regard, the method is as follows: when a deed has been accumulated by means of a triple-rooted, unprompted consciousness accompanied by joy (*somanassa*), and rebirth-linking has been taken by a resultant consciousness of the same type, then for one who has reached growth, when a desirable object comes into range at the eye-door, there are three "vain" (ineffective) moments according to the method explained below.
From that wholesome state, four [resultant moments] accompanied by joy arise.
At the conclusion of a process impelled by any one of these thirteen consciousnesses— namely, the four unwholesome, the five functional,
the joy-accompanied unprompted triple-rooted consciousness, or the double-rooted consciousness—

the registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa) becomes established. Thus, in the eye-door, there are three [consciousnesses] beginning with eye-consciousness and two registration consciousnesses, making five in total.
The thoughts are accompanied by counting. However,

having replaced the feeling [of joy] with the object, at the conclusion of a javana consisting of any one of the twelve equanimity-accompanied consciousnesses— four wholesome, four unwholesome, and four functional— an equanimity-accompanied, triple-rooted, spontaneous resultant [consciousness] may also arise.

Even the double-rooted spontaneous resultant [consciousness] arises as registration (*tadārammaṇa*). Thus, for this person at the eye-door, there is the equanimity-accompanied investigating consciousness;
these two are the registrations. Therefore, there are three types of consciousness that enter the count. Together with the five preceding ones, there are eight.
In the ear-door and so forth, there are likewise eight each; thus, when a single kamma is accumulated, there are forty-eight types of consciousness.
They arise. By taking what has not yet been taken [into account], there are eight in the eye-door and four beginning with ear-consciousness, making twelve.

Therein, the "state of being the root life-continuum," the "state of being the adventitious life-continuum," and the "discourse on the mango simile" should be understood according to the method already stated.
The same method applies even when karma is accumulated by means of a wholesome consciousness accompanied by joy, rooted in three causes, and prompted;

and also when karma is accumulated by means of consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity, rooted in three causes, whether unprompted or prompted. In this regard, the analogy of the oil-press is exactly as before.

Up to this point, the section has been explained wherein rebirth-linking with three roots occurs through karma rooted in three roots. Now, [the case where] rebirth-linking with two roots occurs through karma rooted in three roots:
But the turn [of the mind] passed away while concealed.

Now follows the discussion on rebirth-linking with a two-rooted kamma. For when a kamma is accumulated by a two-rooted, joy-accompanied, unprompted consciousness, and rebirth-linking has been grasped by a resultant consciousness of that same type, then for one who has reached growth, at the eye-door—

When a desirable object comes into range, there are three "vain" (mogha) sections according to the method explained below. However, for one of two-rooted (duhetuka) consciousness, there is no functional (kiriya) impulsion.

Therefore, at the conclusion of an impulsion by any one of these eight—four accompanied by joy from the wholesome side and four from the unwholesome side—it is only the two-rooted, joy-accompanied, unprompted (asaṅkhārika) [consciousness] that arises.

That becomes the object of registration (*tadārammaṇa*). Thus, for him, there are four types of consciousness that reach the count: the three beginning with eye-consciousness, and this registration-consciousness.

However, when the object is desirable-neutral, at the conclusion of a javana by any one of the eight—namely, the four wholesome states accompanied by equanimity and the four unwholesome states—it is necessarily double-rooted (*duhetuka*) alone.
The registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa) is accompanied by equanimity and is unprompted (asaṅkhārika).

Thus, for such a person, there are two types of consciousness that reach the count: the investigation consciousness accompanied by equanimity and this registration consciousness. These, together with the four preceding ones, make six.
Since there are six each in the ear-door and so forth, thirty consciousnesses arise when a single kamma has been accumulated through volition (cetanā).

By taking the foremost [of each category], there are ten: six in the eye-door and four in the ear-consciousness and so forth. The discussion regarding the simile of the mango is just as it was previously.
It was stated that the simile of the machine does not apply here.

Even when a wholesome consciousness accompanied by joy, having two roots, and prompted (sasaṅkhārika) has accumulated kamma, [the result arises] through [consciousnesses] accompanied by equanimity, having two roots, and unprompted (asaṅkhārika) or prompted.
The same method applies when karma is accumulated with two roots. Up to this point, the section explaining how rebirth-linking with two roots occurs through karma with two roots has been stated.
However, the section explaining how rebirth-linking occurs without roots (ahetuka) should be understood as follows:

when karma is accumulated from the wholesome side by means of the four types of consciousness dissociated from knowledge, rebirth-linking occurs through the wholesome-resultant rootless mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity.
When [a thought] has been grasped, it cannot be said that the rebirth-linking is similar to the kamma.

From this point onward, one should explain according to the method stated below, and understand the occurrence of consciousness regarding both the desirable and the intermediate-desirable. For, according to the doctrine of this Elder, the "alms-gathering impulsion" (piṇḍajavana) impels.
As for the rest, there is the discussion beginning with: "But what determines whether this impulsion is for the sake of the wholesome or for the sake of the unwholesome? etc.
All [the details] should be understood according to the method already explained below.
Up to this point, in the doctrine of the Venerable Mahādatta, resident at Moravāpi, the twelvefold path has been concluded together with the tenfold path and the rootless group of eight.
Now follows the discussion of the tenfold path in the doctrine of the Venerable Mahādhammarakkhita. In that regard, there are the questions from Sāketa and the enumerations of the ussadā (excesses).

They are indeed natural. However, there is this distinction in the exposition of the causes: a three-rooted (*tihetuka*) kamma gives rise to a three-rooted, two-rooted (*duhetuka*), or even rootless (*ahetuka*) resultant.
A two-rooted kamma does not give rise to a three-rooted resultant, but gives rise to the others.
Through a three-rooted kamma, rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is exclusively three-rooted; it is never two-rooted or rootless. Through a two-rooted kamma, [rebirth-linking] is two-rooted or rootless.
It is with roots, but it is not three-rooted. Spontaneous (asaṅkhārika) kamma yields only spontaneous resultant, not prompted (sasaṅkhārika).
Prompted kamma also yields only prompted resultant, not spontaneous. Feeling should be changed according to the object.
The impulsion (javana) impels as a single impulsion. The states of consciousness should be explained starting from the beginning.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: One person accumulates karma with the first wholesome consciousness (*paṭhamakusalacitta*) and takes rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) with that very same first resultant consciousness (*paṭhamavipākacitta*). This is a rebirth-linking similar to the karma.

When that person has reached maturity and a desirable object enters the range of the eye-door, there are three "vain sections" (*moghavāra*) occurring in the manner already described. Then, for him, of those mentioned below...
At the conclusion of any one of the thirteen impulsion moments accompanied by joy, the very first resultant consciousness takes that same object.
It receives two names: "root-life-continuum" (*mūla-bhavanga*) and "registration" (*tadārammaṇa*).
Thus, for this [process], there are four reckoned consciousnesses: the three beginning with eye-consciousness and this registration consciousness. [This occurs] when the object is desirable-neutral.

At the conclusion of any one of the twelve types of javanas accompanied by equanimity mentioned above, a three-rooted (tihetuka) mind-moment accompanied by equanimity and unprompted (asaṅkhārika) arises as the registration (tadārammaṇa).
