This receives two names: "adventitious bhavaṅga" and "registration. Thus, there are two [types of consciousness]: the investigation accompanied by equanimity and this registration.
The [seven] consciousnesses associated with counting. Together with the previous four, these make six.
Thus, when a kamma has been accumulated by means of a single volition, thirty mental states arise at the five doors.
By including what was not previously included, there are ten: six at the eye-door and the four beginning with ear-consciousness. The discussion regarding the mango simile remains as it was before.
Even when karma is accumulated by means of the second, third, and fourth wholesome consciousnesses, there are exactly this many resultant consciousnesses.
The same principle applies even when karma is accumulated by means of the four consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity. Here, however, first the desirable-neutral object must be shown;
afterwards, the feeling should be exchanged for a desirable object. The discussion regarding the mango simile remains as it was before.

Thus it is; no further simile can be found. From the point where it says, "But when one of the four types of wholesome [kamma] dissociated from knowledge has been accumulated," all should be explained in detail starting from there as the "Set of Eight Without Roots" (*ahetukaṭṭhaka*).
Up to this point, according to the doctrine of the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita, the "Path of Tens" (*dasakamagga*), together with the "Set of Eight Without Roots," is completed.
Now, which of these three elders’ doctrines should be accepted? Not exclusively any one of them.

Rather, what is appropriate among all their doctrines should be accepted. For in the first doctrine, the distinction between "with effort" (*sasankhāra*) and "without effort" (*asaṅkhāra*) is intended by way of the difference in conditions.
Thus, herein, the result of a wholesome state without effort that arises through weak conditions is [termed] "with effort."

Having taken both the spontaneous (*asaṅkhārika*) resultant that arises through strong conditions from the prompted (*sasaṅkhārika*) wholesome, and having set aside the functional (*kiriya*) impulsions even though they are obtainable, one determines the feeling by means of the object and the wholesome impulsion as the registration (*tadārammaṇa*).

Thus, the sixteenfold path is explained according to the categories of trainees (*sekkha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*). However, in this context, at the conclusion of an unwholesome impulsion, there occurs only a rootless (*ahetuka*) resultant.

That object-of-registration [consciousness] has been shown there, but it was not shown at all in the other cases. Therefore, that which was stated there—namely, the resultant consciousness with roots—is indeed obtainable here as well.

This is the method: for when unwholesome consciousness occurs in the intervals between wholesome impulsions (*javana*), then at the conclusion of the wholesome, it is exactly like the habitual [object]; but at the conclusion of the unwholesome, it is the object-of-registration with roots.

This is logical. When there is exclusively unwholesome [consciousness] without interval, then it is rootless (*ahetuka*). Thus, first of all, in the first position, this should be understood as logical.
However, in the second position, the distinction between "with effort" (*sasaṅkhāra*) and "without effort" (*asaṅkhāra*) regarding the wholesome is intended.

Therefore, here, having taken the resultant of wholesome consciousness without effort to be only without effort, and the resultants of wholesome consciousness with effort to be only with effort, by means of the impulsion (*javana*)—

Without establishing a fixed rule regarding that registration (tadārammaṇa), the twelvefold path was taught here by way of the javana of the alms-round for all—whether they be trainees (sekkha), those beyond training (asekkha), or worldlings (puthujjana).
However, at the conclusion of a javana with three roots (tihetuka), a registration with three roots is appropriate;
whereas at the conclusion of a javana with two roots (duhetuka) or a rootless (ahetuka) javana, it is not stated because [the registration] is divided accordingly.
Thus, in the second position, what is logical should be accepted.
In the third position as well, the distinction between the volitional (*saṅkhāra*) and non-volitional (*asaṅkhāra*) [kamma] is intended precisely from the standpoint of skillfulness (*kusala*).

However, because of the statement: “Three-rooted kamma gives rise to three-rooted, two-rooted, and rootless resultant [rebirth],” for one who has obtained a three-rooted rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) through non-volitional [kamma],...
There must also be a resultant consciousness with that [wholesome state] as its object even when it is unprompted and double-rooted.

That was not shown; rather, only a resultant consciousness similar in roots was shown. This does not accord with the previous claim regarding the attainment of roots. It was stated merely for the purpose of illustrating the tenfold path.
However, the other type is certainly obtainable as well. Thus, in the third position as well, what is logical should be accepted. And this entire...
The discussion regarding that object refers specifically to the result of the very same karma that produces rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

However, because of the statement, “A bhavaṅga with roots is a condition for a bhavaṅga without roots by way of proximity-condition (*anantarapaccaya*),” it follows that even for one who has a rootless rebirth-linking through a different karma, a resultant state with roots can arise as an object-of-attainment (*tadārammaṇa*). The method of its arising will be made clear in the *Mahāpakaraṇa*.
The discussion on the wholesome and resultant states of the sense-sphere is concluded.
Now, in order to show the resultant states of the fine-material and immaterial spheres, the section beginning with "Which states are indeterminate? is commenced once again. (499)
In this context, because sense-sphere resultant [consciousness] is both similar and dissimilar to its own corresponding wholesome [state],

it was not analyzed by following the pattern of the wholesome. However, because fine-material-sphere and immaterial-sphere resultant [consciousness] is exactly similar to its own corresponding wholesome state—
just as the shadows of elephants, horses, mountains, and so forth are identical to the elephants and so forth themselves— it follows the pattern of the wholesome.
Having made [this distinction], it was divided. Sensuous-sphere karma gives its result at any time whatsoever;
however, fine-material-sphere and immaterial-sphere karma gives its result without obstruction, in the very next existence. This too was divided by following the same method as for the wholesome.
The remainder should be understood in the same manner as stated for the wholesome. This, however, is the distinction: the classification according to the path of practice (*paṭipadā*) and so forth.
Furthermore, their inferior, superior, or middling nature should be understood from the way these jhānas are entered.
However, because they cannot be produced by making any one of desire and so forth the primary factor, these are indeed without a dominant influence (niradhipatika).
The discussion on the resultant consciousness of the fine-material and immaterial spheres is concluded.
505. The discussion on supramundane resultant (lokuttara-vipāka) is also classified as following the pattern of the wholesome (kusala), because it resembles the wholesome.
However, since wholesome states of the three planes accumulate and expand the round of existence by way of death and rebirth-linking, therefore, in that regard—

It is said, "because of having been done and accumulated. However, as for the supramundane [path], although it accumulates by means of that [kamma], it also dismantles what has been accumulated; furthermore, it does not itself accumulate by way of death and rebirth-linking.
Therefore, instead of saying here "because of having been done and accumulated," it is said, "because of having been done and developed.
Regarding the terms "emptiness" and so forth, first, the "path" receives its name through three reasons: from its arrival, from its qualities, and from its object.

"Obtains [a name]"—this has been explained in detail above in the section on the wholesome (*kusala*). In that context, according to the method of the Suttantas, it receives its name both from its quality (*saguṇa*) and from its object (*ārammaṇa*); for this is a teaching by way of a figurative method (*pariyāya-desanā*). However, the discourse of the Abhidhamma is a teaching not by way of a figurative method (*nippariyāya-desanā*).
Therefore, here it does not receive its name either from its quality or from its object, but receives it only from its source (*āgamana*). It is precisely its source [that determines the name].
Indeed, there is a burden. That is twofold: the approach by way of insight (vipassanā) and the approach by way of the path (magga).
Therein, at the stage where the path arrives, the approach by way of insight is the burden;

at the stage where the fruit (phala) arrives, the approach by way of the path is the burden—this too has already been stated below. Of these, this is the stage where the fruit arrives; therefore, here it is the approach by way of the path.
It should be understood that this path receives the name “emptiness” (suññatā) from its mode of arrival;
yet, because of its own qualities and its object, it is also called “signless” (animitta) and “desireless” (appaṇihita).
Therefore, standing in the position of the arrival itself, it bestows three names upon its own fruit. How so? For this [path] receives its name solely by way of pure arrival.
The “emptiness path” (*suññatāmārga*), standing in its own place of arrival and bestowing a name upon its own fruit, gave it the name “emptiness” (*suññata*).

The “signless emptiness path” (*suññatānimittamārga*), standing in its own place of arrival and bestowing a name upon its own fruit, gave it the name “signless” (*animitta*). The “emptiness wishless path” (*suññatāppaṇihitamārga*), standing in its own place of arrival...
Standing there, as if giving a name to its own fruit, it bestowed upon it the name "Appanihita" (the Wishless).

These three names, however, are obtained by this same method only in the fruition-consciousness immediately following the path, and not in the fruition-attainment (*phalasamāpatti*) that occurs at a later time.

At a later time, one is able to practice insight (*vipassanā*) by means of the three insights, such as impermanence and so forth. Then, by way of the successive insights that have arisen, [the practitioner...]
The three fruits known as the signless, the desireless, and the void arise; their objects of focus are those same formations.
The knowledges consisting of the contemplations of impermanence and so forth are called "conformity-knowledge" (*anuloma-ñāṇa*).
This is what was stated regarding the path of the void; the same method applies to the path of the desireless as well. For this too, by way of pure arrival—
The path named “the wishless” (appaṇihita), standing at its own place of arrival and bestowing a name upon its own fruit, gave it the name “wishless.

The path “the signless wishless” (appaṇihita-animitta), standing at its own place of arrival and bestowing a name upon its own fruit, gave it the name “signless. The path “the emptiness wishless” (appaṇihita-suññata) [did likewise].
Standing in its own place of arrival and giving a name to its own fruit, it made the name “emptiness” (suññatā).

These three names are also obtained by this same method only in the fruition-consciousness immediately following the path, and not in the subsequently experienced fruition-attainment (phalasamāpatti).
Thus, in this exposition of fruition, [there are] three times as many [fruition moments] as there are wholesome consciousnesses.
The resultant consciousnesses are to be understood.
However, whereas the wholesome states of the three planes are unable to cause their own resultants to obtain predominance, the supramundane wholesome states are not so.
Why? Because for the wholesome states of the three planes, the time of accumulation is one thing and the time of ripening is another.
Therefore, those [worldly wholesome states] are unable to cause their own result to become predominant.

However, supramundane states—due to that faith, that energy, that mindfulness, that concentration, and that wisdom which have not yet subsided—obtain their result immediately after the path, unfailing and unerring;
thus, they cause their own result to become predominant.
They are able to cause [the fire] to be obtained.
For just as in the place where a small fire has gone out, as soon as the fire is extinguished, there is no trace of heat remaining;
but when a great, blazing mass of fire is extinguished, even if a coating of cow-dung is applied, [the heat remains].

The state of heat remains unappeased; even so, in the wholesome states of the three planes, the moment of kamma is one thing and the moment of its result is another, like the time when the heat has subsided in a small fire. Therefore, it is unable to cause its own result to obtain predominance.
But in the supramundane, by that faith... [and so on] ...by that wisdom which remains unappeased, [it does attain predominance].
The fruit arises immediately after the path; therefore, it should be understood that it causes its own result to obtain predominance.
Thus the ancients said: "There is no predominance over the result, except for the supramundane.
555. In the description of the fourth fruit, "the faculty of one who has already known" refers to one who has completed the task of knowledge regarding the four truths.

It is a faculty (*indriya*) because it exercises lordship (*indaṭṭha-sādhana*) within the states of those who have become "knowers of the unknown" (*aññātāvī*), that is, those who have completed their task regarding the four truths and stand having known and penetrated the four truths.
In its section of exposition (*niddesa-vāra*), the term "of those who have become knowers of the unknown" means "of those who stand having fully understood.
"Of the states" means within the associated states. "Knowing" (*aññā*) is full understanding; it is wisdom (*paññā*).

The terms "understanding" (*pajānana*) and so forth have already had their meanings explained. Regarding "a factor of the path" (*maggaṅga*) and "included in the path" (*maggapariyāpanna*): the meaning is that it is a factor of the fruition-path and is included within the fruition-path.
Furthermore, there is this incidental point here: one faculty goes to one place; another [faculty] goes to six places.
It goes; it goes to one specific place. For the single faculty known as "the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'" goes to one place:
the path of stream-entry. The single faculty known as "the faculty of final knowledge" goes to six places: the three lower fruits and the three higher paths.
The single faculty known as "the faculty of one who has already known" goes to one place: the fruit of arhatship.
In all the paths and fruits, eight faculties each in terms of their actual meaning (attha) are taught, thus making sixty-four supramundane faculties (lokuttarindriya).
However, according to the canonical text (pāḷi), they are seventy-two, as nine are counted for each.

It is said that what is a path-factor (maggaṅga) in the path is also a path-factor in the fruit; what is an enlightenment factor (bojjhaṅga) in the path is also an enlightenment factor in the fruit. At the moment of the path, there are "abstinence" (ārati) and "refraining" (virati).

It is stated that even at the moment of the fruit (*phalakkhaṇa*), there is "abstinence" (*ārati*) and "refraining" (*virati*). In this context, the path (*magga*) is called a "path" precisely by virtue of its being a path; however, the fruit (*phala*) is called a "path" only in dependence upon the path. It is also appropriate to say that a factor of the fruit is "included within the fruit.

It is a "factor of full enlightenment" (*sambojjhaṅga*) because it is a factor for one who awakens to the path; it is a "factor of full enlightenment" because it is a factor for one who has awakened to the fruit. By way of delighting in and refraining from the path...
Abstention and non-abstention. Regarding the fruit, however, it is by way of abstention and non-abstention.
The discussion on supramundane resultant [kamma] is finished.
The discussion on unwholesome resultant [kamma].
556. Beyond this are the unwholesome-resultants—namely, the fivefold consciousnesses of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body, one element of mind, and one element of mind-consciousness;
these seven types of consciousness are similar, both according to the text and in meaning, to the corresponding wholesome-resultant consciousnesses mentioned above.

For those [previously mentioned] are conditions for wholesome kamma, whereas these are conditions for unwholesome kamma. Those operate upon desirable, desirable-neutral, and neutral objects, while these operate upon undesirable, undesirable-neutral, and neutral objects.
Furthermore, in that case, body-consciousness is accompanied by pleasure;
here, it is accompanied by pain. And in that case, the mind-element accompanied by equanimity occurs among humans who are blind from birth and so forth.
It ripens in five ways, beginning with rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

Here, however, when unwholesome kamma has been accumulated by any of the eleven types of unwholesome consciousness, it takes one of the objects—either the kamma itself, the sign of the kamma (*kamma-nimitta*), or the sign of the destination (*gati-nimitta*)—as its object and ripens as rebirth-linking in the four woeful states.
From the second moment onwards, until the end of the life-span, it functions as the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) with an undesirable, desirable, or neutral object.
Having served as investigation (*santīraṇa*) in the cognitive process of the fivefold sense-consciousness, having served as registration (*tadārammaṇa*) at the six doors when the object is powerful,
and having served as death (*cuti*) at the time of dying— it thus ripens in these five places alone.
The discussion on unwholesome resultant [kamma] is concluded.
Commentary on the Functional-Indeterminate:
Mind-element Consciousness. 566.
Now, in order to classify and demonstrate the functional-indeterminate, the passage beginning with "Which states are indeterminate? is commenced once again.
In this context, "functional" (*kiriya*) means mere activity. For among all functional consciousnesses, that which has not reached the state of impulsion (*javana*) is like a flower in the air.
That which has reached the state of impulsion is fruitless, like a flower on a tree whose roots have been cut;
yet, because it proceeds by accomplishing its respective task, it is merely an activity. Therefore, it is called "functional."

It has been stated. Regarding the phrases "neither wholesome nor unwholesome" and so forth: they are "neither wholesome" because of the absence of a wholesome cause, which is to say a root of the wholesome;

they are "neither unwholesome" because of the absence of an unwholesome cause, which is to say a root of the unwholesome; and they are "neither wholesome nor unwholesome" because of the absence of the wholesome and unwholesome conditions, which consist of wise attention and unwise attention respectively.
[This refers to the absence] of the generative cause, which consists of what is termed wholesome or unwholesome.
Because they are non-existent, there is no ripening of kamma.
Here too, in the description of one-pointedness of mind, only the mere occurrence and persistence [of consciousness] is obtained.
Among these seventeen—the two fivefold sense-consciousnesses, the three mind-elements, the three mind-consciousness-elements, and that accompanied by doubt—
Due to the weakness of these consciousnesses, stability, steadiness, and so forth are not obtained.
All else should be understood according to the method already explained in the exposition of the resultant mind-element (*vipākamanodhātu*), with the exception of the place of its arising;

for that [resultant] consciousness arises immediately after the fivefold sense-cognitions. This [functional mind-element], however, arises prior to all others at the time of the functioning process within the five doors.

How so? First, at the eye-door, when any one of the sense-faculties is struck by a visible object—whether desirable, desirable-neutral, undesirable, or undesirable-neutral—an adverting consciousness arises, preceded by that [adverting], taking hold of that object and turning back toward the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
This same method applies to the ear-door and the others as well.
The functional mind-element consciousness is finished.
Regarding the functional mind-consciousness-element consciousnesses (568): "The mind-consciousness-element has arisen... accompanied by joy"—this consciousness is not shared with others.
This is exclusively for one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava). It is obtained at the six sense doors.

For instance, having seen a place suitable for striving at the eye door, the one whose taints are destroyed becomes gladdened by this thought: “Such greed-and-craving as that has been abandoned by me.

At the ear door, having reached a place where goods are being distributed and loud noise is made while greedy people are seizing them, he thinks: “Such greed-and-craving as that has been abandoned by me.”
With this mind, one becomes joyful. At the door of the nose, while worshipping a cetiya with fragrances or flowers, one becomes joyful with this mind.
At the door of the tongue, having received alms-food endowed with excellent flavor and partaking of it after sharing it, one becomes joyful with this mind, thinking:
"Truly, the quality of being consoling has been fulfilled by me. At the door of the body...
While performing the duties of proper conduct (*abhisamācārika-vatta*), one is gladdened by the thought, "I have fulfilled my duty regarding the door of the body.
Thus, it first occurs in the five doors.
However, in the mind-door (*manodvāra*), it arises with reference to the past or the future. For instance, during the time of the young Brahmin Jotipāla, King Maghadeva, and the ascetic Kaṇha.
Reflecting on the cause, the Tathāgata manifested a smile. That, however, was the function of the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*).
When these two knowledges have reached their limit of mastery, this mind arises, gladdening [the heart].
Regarding the future, he manifested a smile [thinking], "Tanti-sara Mudiṅga-sara will become a Paccekabuddha. That too—

It is the function of the knowledge of future existences (*anāgataṃsañāṇa*) and the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). However, this consciousness arises gladdening the mind at the conclusion of what has been practiced by those two knowledges.

In the section on the exposition (*niddesavāra*), because it is more powerful than the remaining rootless consciousnesses (*ahetukacitta*), its one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*) attains the status of the power of concentration (*samādhibala*).

It was set aside. Even energy, having been brought to the state of the power of energy, is not called "power" in this context because it has not yet arrived at the section on the summary (uddesavāra), where it says, "there is the power of concentration, there is the power of energy.
Since these two do not possess the full sense of power, they are not called power here.
However, because it is "neither wholesome nor unwholesome," it was set aside after being called "power"; and because it is not [power] in the primary sense (nippariyāya).

Because of that power, it is not stated even in the section on the factors of comprehension (saṅgahavāra) that "there are two powers. All the rest should be understood according to the same method explained in the exposition of the mind-element accompanied by joy and without root-cause (somanassasahagatāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu). 574.
"Accompanied by equanimity" (upekkhāsahagatā): this consciousness is common to all sentient beings possessing minds within the three realms of existence (bhava).
For no one possessing a mind does it fail to arise. When it arises, it is *voṭṭhabbana* (determining) in the five sense-doors and *āvajjana* (adverting) in the mind-door.
Even the six types of uncommon knowledge grasp only that which has been grasped by this [consciousness].
This consciousness is like a great elephant; for it, there is nothing that is not an object. "Even the non-omniscient knowledge is of the same nature as omniscient knowledge."
When it is asked, "What is its name?", one should say, "This. The rest here should be understood according to the method already stated for the preceding consciousness.

For there, because it was accompanied by rapture (*sappītika*), the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) was analyzed as ninefold; here, because it is without rapture (*nippītika*), it is eightfold.

Now, as for those eight great wholesome consciousnesses (*mahācitta*) which become functional (*kiriya*) in an arahant due to the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsava*), they should be understood according to the method stated in the description of the wholesome.
Standing here, the laughing consciousnesses (*hasana-citta*) should be synthesized. How many are there? It is said: thirteen.
For worldlings (*puthujjana*), they laugh by means of eight consciousnesses—four wholesome accompanied by joy (*somanassa-sahagata*) and four unwholesome.
For those in training (*sekkha*), they laugh by means of six consciousnesses—four wholesome accompanied by joy and two unwholesome dissociated from views (*diṭṭhigata-vippayutta*).

"Accompanied by joy": they laugh with six types of consciousness. It is said that those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) laugh with five types of functional consciousness accompanied by joy. Regarding the functional consciousnesses of the fine-material and immaterial spheres (rūpāvacara-ārūpāvacara-kiriya):

in the explanations of the functional consciousnesses of the fine-material and immaterial spheres, "dwelling in happiness in this very life" (diṭṭhadhamma-sukhavihāra) refers to the present life (diṭṭhadhamme).

In this very selfhood, it is merely a pleasant abiding. In that regard, for one whose taints are destroyed, the attainment produced during the time of being an ordinary person remains wholesome until the moment he enters it; at the time of entering, it is functional (*kiriya*).

However, the attainment produced during the time when he is one whose taints are destroyed is exclusively functional. The rest is all similar to that, as explained in the description of the wholesome.
"It should be understood in the manner already stated.
Thus ends the Exposition of the Section on the Arising of Consciousness in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, the Commentary on the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*.
However, the section on the indeterminate (abyākatapada) has not yet been completed.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness (Cittuppādakaṇḍa) is finished.
2. The Chapter on Material Form (Rūpakaṇḍa).
The Commentary on the Summary:
Now, in order to explain the Section on Matter by dividing it up, the passage beginning "Which states are indeterminate? is commenced.

Therein, although in the preceding Section on the Arising of Consciousness (*cittuppādakaṇḍa*) both the resultant-indeterminate (*vipākābyākata*) and the functional-indeterminate (*kiriyābyākata*) were treated exhaustively, [they are not repeated here].
The [resultants] have been analyzed; however, the unmanifest form and the unconditioned nibbāna—these indeterminate (abyākata) states—were not mentioned.

To explain them, he says "the results of wholesome and unwholesome states," etc., presenting all four kinds of the indeterminate together. Therein, "of wholesome and unwholesome states" refers to both the wholesome and unwholesome states of the four planes.
Thus, first, the resultant-indeterminate (vipākābyākata) has been explained.
It is shown by way of two terms—namely, as wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant—which encompass it.

However, since all of that belongs either to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) or to one of the others such as the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), it is therefore shown by the method beginning with “belonging to the sense-sphere” (kāmāvacara), which encompasses that very same indeterminate resultant by way of its different planes (bhūmantara). And because...
That is also the aggregate of feeling... [and so on] ...the aggregate of consciousness; therefore, it is shown again by way of the four associated aggregates.
Thus, the indeterminate resultant has been explained by way of the wholesome and unwholesome, by way of the different planes, and by way of the associated aggregates.

Having shown [the categories] by way of the three methods (naya), he spoke the passage beginning with “And those states which are functional” (*kiriyā*) in order to further demonstrate the functional indeterminate (*kiriyābyākata*).

In that context, one might have expected it to be stated as: “The aggregate of feeling belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere... up to ... the aggregate of consciousness.
However, since these were already included below, he set them aside after showing that method. Now, in order to show what has not yet been analyzed:

And he said: “all form and the unconditioned element. Therein, by the phrase “all form,” it should be understood that the twenty-five types of form and the ninety-six divisions of form are included without exception.
By the phrase “and the unconditioned element,” Nibbāna is included without exception. To this extent, the category of “indeterminate phenomena” is completed.
584. Regarding that, why is the phrase "what is all form" included here? Previously, form as indeterminate was explained in brief.
Now, this is included in order to demonstrate it by dividing it in detail according to the categories of single, dyads, triads, tetrads...
up to... elevenfold. Its meaning is as follows: that which was stated as "all form and the unconditioned element."
Regarding those two terms, [the question] "What is called 'all form'? is now being answered; thus he says, beginning with "the four great elements" (*cattāro mahābhūtā*).
Therein, "four" is a delimitation by number. By this, he precludes their being fewer or more than that. The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of inclusion.
By it, he includes "derived form" (*upādārūpa*), showing that form is not merely "the four great elements" alone, but that there is something else as well.
Regarding the term *mahābhūtāni* (great primaries): here, their status as "great primaries" is to be understood through such reasons as their "great manifestation" and so forth.

Indeed, these are called "great primaries" (*mahābhūtāni*) for the following reasons: because of their great manifestation, because of their commonality with the great elements, because of their great maintenance, because of their great transformation, and because they are great beings (*mahantabhūtattā*). In this context, "because of their great manifestation" means that even in the unclung-to (*anupādinnaka*) continuity...

Even in the continuity of what is grasped (*upādinnaka*), these appear on a vast scale. Their appearance on such a vast scale in the continuity of what is not grasped (*anupādinnaka*) should be understood as follows:
for one world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) measures, in length and breadth, twelve hundred thousand, three thousand, four hundred, and fifty yojanas; as for its circumference—
The entire circumference is three million six hundred and ten thousand four hundred and fifty [yojanas].
Therein—
Two hundred thousand and forty nahutas—
this much, by its thickness, is reckoned this earth.
Its supporter is as follows:
Four hundred thousand and eighty thousand [yojanas]—
to this extent is the water established upon the wind in thickness.
And its supporter is—
Nine hundred thousand leagues, and sixty thousand as well, does the wind rise up into the sky;
such is the established structure of the world.
And within this established order, the measurements in yojanas are as follows:
Sineru, the supreme mountain, plunges eighty-four thousand [yojanas] deep into the great ocean and rises above it by exactly that same measure. From there,
its dimensions decrease by half and half again, respectively.
Sublime peaks rising deep within, variegated with diverse jewels:
Yugandhara, Īsadhara, Karavīka, Sudassana, Nemindhara,
Vinataka, Assakaṇṇa, and the vast mountain Brahā.
These seven great rocky mountains surround Sineru;
they are the abodes of the Great Kings, frequented by gods and yakkhas.
The Himavat mountain is five hundred yojanas in height.
Three thousand yojanas in length and breadth,
it is adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks;
the city known as Nagavhayā has a circumference of three or five yojanas at its base.
Its trunk and branches extend fifty yojanas on all sides;
it is a hundred yojanas wide and rises to that same height—
the Jambu tree by whose power Jambudīpa is made known.
Whatever is the size of the Jambu tree, that same is the size of the Cittapāṭali tree of the asuras,
the Simbali tree of the garuḷas, the Kadamba tree in Aparagoyāna, the Kappa tree in Uttarakuru, the Sirīsa tree in Pubbavideha,
and the Pāricchattaka tree among the Tāvatiṃsa devas. Thus said the ancients:
The *pāṭalī*, the *simbalī*, the *jambū*, the *pāricchattaka* of the gods,
the *kadamba*, the *kapparukkha*, and the *sirīsa* is the seventh.
It plunges eighty-two thousand [yojanas] down into the great ocean.
“Just as high as it is, the mountain range of the world-sphere stands encircling this entire world-system.

Even within the continuity of what is clung-to (*upādinnaka*), these [elements] appear on a vast scale by way of the bodies of fish, turtles, devas, dānavas, and so forth. For this was said by the Blessed One: “Bhikkhus, there are individual existences (*attabhāva*) in the great ocean that are even a hundred yojanas long,” and so on.
‘By way of the commonality of the great elements’: for just as a magician displays water that is not a gem as a gem, or a clod of earth that is not gold as gold;
and just as he himself, while being neither a *yakkha* nor a bird, displays both the state of a *yakkha* and the state of a bird—so too, while being himself not blue, [he displays] the blue.
They display derived form (*upādārūpa*): though not yellow... not red... and not white, they display white derived form.
Thus, the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are so called because of their commonality with the great elements of a magician.
And just as when yakṣas and others seize a great element, neither its being inside them nor its being outside them is perceived, yet they do not exist without depending upon it.
In the same way, these [great elements] are not perceived as existing either inside or outside one another, yet they do not exist without depending upon one another.
Because they are an inconceivable state and because they share the common nature of great beings such as *yakkhas*, they are called "great elements" (*mahābhūtāni*).
And just as the great elements known as *yakkhinīs* manifest their own terrifying nature through pleasing colors, shapes, and movements, [so too do these elements].
Just as [certain people] deceive beings by concealing [their true nature], even so these [elements] also deceive foolish folk by concealing their own essential characteristics—
such as hardness and so forth— behind the pleasing color of the skin on the bodies of women and men, the pleasing configuration of the limbs and members,
and the pleasing movements of the hands, feet, fingers, and eyebrows; they conceal their own intrinsic nature.

They do not allow one to see them. Thus, they are called *mahābhūta* (great elements) because they share the common characteristic of being *yakkhinīs* (female spirits) or great beings in the sense of being deceptive.

Regarding the phrase "because of great maintenance": it is because they must be maintained with great requisites. For these are called *mahābhūta* because they are sustained by great food, clothing, and so forth, as they must be provided for day after day.
Alternatively, they are called *mahābhūta* because they are beings (*bhūta*) that require great maintenance.

‘From great transformation’ means from the great transformation of the primary elements (*bhūta*). For these [elements] undergo great transformations whether they are appropriated (*upādiṇṇa*) or unappropriated (*anupādiṇṇa*).

Among these, the magnitude of the transformation of the unappropriated becomes manifest at the end of an eon (*kappa*), while that of the appropriated becomes manifest at times when the elements are disturbed. Thus it is said:
Rising from the earth, it spreads as far as the Brahma-world;
a flame from a blazing fire consumes the world with its heat.
A single world-system of a hundred thousand koṭis dissolves away.
When the world is destroyed by water through the wrath of the [deity],
a hundred thousand times ten million world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) are scattered;
when the world is destroyed by the upheaval of the wind element, [the same occurs].
The body becomes rigid, as if bitten by a woodpecker, due to the provocation of the earth element; it becomes like that very woodpecker.
The body becomes putrid, as if bitten by a putrid-mouthed creature.
Through the provocation of the water element, he becomes like one with a putrid mouth;
his body becomes scorched, as if bitten by the mouth of fire.
Through the provocation of the fire element, he becomes like one with a fiery mouth.
The body is cut, or it is pierced by the edge of a weapon;
through the disturbance of the air-element, it becomes as if by the edge of a weapon.
Thus, because the primary elements undergo great transformations, they are called "great elements" (mahābhūtāni).

‘And because they are great beings’: for these are “great” (*mahanta*) because they must be grasped with great effort, and they are “beings” (*bhūta*) because they exist; thus, because they are great beings, they are the “great primary elements” (*mahābhūtāni*). In this way, they are called “great primary elements” due to reasons such as their great manifestation.

“And derived form based on the four great primary elements”: here the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative. The meaning is: form that proceeds by depending on, relying upon, and not relinquishing the four great primary elements. This is called “all form. This...
The four great elements and the twenty-three derived material phenomena, as set forth in their sequential order, constitute all materiality, which is divided into twenty-seven types.

Now, in order to demonstrate that in detail, the author establishes the table of contents (*mātikā*) by means of eleven groupings beginning with "of one kind," and states: "All materiality is not a root-cause," and so forth.

In this context, the phrase "all form" (*sabbaṃ rūpaṃ*) should be joined with all the subsequent phrases, such as "all form is not a cause" (*sabbaṃ rūpaṃ na hetu*) and "all form is rootless" (*sabbaṃ rūpaṃ ahetukaṃ*). All these forty-three phrases, beginning with "not a cause," have been enumerated.
Among them, forty phrases have been established by taking them in order from the matrix (*mātikā*), while three remain at the end.
"Those not included in the matrix. Thus, first of all, the determination of the text should be understood for the first compendium. Likewise for the second compendium and the others.
Regarding the Compendium of the Two Kinds of Matter, this is the method: in the second compendium there are four hundred and two dyads. Therein, "matter exists as derived," etc.
There are fourteen dyads beginning with "there is matter that is not derived" (*noupāda*), which are called miscellaneous dyads (*pakiṇṇaka-duka*) because they lack mutual relationship.

Following those, there are twenty-five dyads beginning with "there is matter that is the basis for eye-contact," which are called basis dyads (*vatthu-duka*) because they proceed by way of examining what is a basis and what is not a basis. Then there are [dyads] beginning with "there is matter that is the object of eye-contact."
The twenty-five [pairs] are called "object-pairs" (*ārammaṇa-duka*) because they function by way of investigating what is an object and what is not an object.

Following that, there are ten [pairs] beginning with "there is form, the eye-base," which are called "base-pairs" (*āyatana-duka*) because they function by way of investigating what is a base and what is not a base.
Following that, there are ten [pairs] beginning with "there is form, the eye-element," which [function] by way of investigating what is an element and what is not an element.

Because they proceed by way of the elements and the pairs, these are called the "Element-Pairs. Following that, there are eight beginning with "There is material form, the eye-faculty," which are called the "Faculty-Pairs" because they proceed by way of examining the faculties and non-faculties.
Then there are twelve beginning with "There is material form, body-intimation," which are called the "Subtle-Form Pairs" because they proceed by way of examining the very subtle forms.
This is the determination of the text in the Second Compendium.
The Compendium of the Threefold Form (Tividharūpasaṅgaha) 585. In the third compendium, there are three sets of threes.
Therein, by combining one of the fourteen miscellaneous dyads mentioned in the second compendium—namely, the internal dyad—with the remaining thirteen, whatever form is internal is derived (upādā).

Regarding that external form, there are thirteen miscellaneous dyads (pakiṇṇaka-duka) established by way of such formulations as "there is [form] derived" and "there is [form] non-derived. Then, having combined that very dyad with the remaining dyads:
"That form which is external is not the basis for eye-contact; that form which is internal is the basis for eye-contact."
The remaining triads are established by way of such methods as: "There is a basis for eye-contact; there is no basis for eye-contact," and so forth.

Their names and their enumerations should be understood according to those same [categories] beginning with the "basis-duad" (vatthudukā). This is the determination of the text in the Third Compendium. [Now follows] the compendium of the fourfold and other kinds of material phenomena.

586. In the fourth compendium, there are twenty-two tetrads. Among them, the very last one—beginning with "There is matter derived" and "There is matter not derived"—is placed here without reference to the matrix (mātikā) stated in this work. The others, however, are placed by referring to that matrix. How so?
First, regarding the three dyads among the miscellaneous items in the two-fold compendium presented here, each one of them...

Having taken that form which is "clung-to" (*upādiṇṇa*) and that which is "not clung-to" (*anupādiṇṇa*), and having combined it with five dyads (*duka*) each according to this method—beginning with "there is [form] that is clung-to, there is [form] that is not clung-to"—fifteen tetrads (*catukka*) based on the three dyads are established at the beginning.
Now, as for whichever tetrad is the "visible" dyad (*sanidassanaduka*): since that form which is visible exists...

Because of the absence of a corresponding meaning, the absence of a sequential order, and the absence of a distinguishing characteristic, it does not form a dyad (duka) with others—either with those such as "with resistance" (*sappaṭigha*) and "without resistance" (*appaṭigha*), or with those such as "derived" (*upādā*) and "non-derived" (*noupādā*).
For instance, there is no such thing as "visible" (*sanidassana*) that is "without resistance" or "non-derived"; thus, it lacks a corresponding meaning.

"It does not go with the *yoga*. However, there is that which is both appropriated (*upādiṇṇa*) and non-appropriated (*anupādiṇṇa*); because of the absence of sequence (*kamābhāva*), it does not go with the *yoga*.
For all the [negative] terms are indeed joined only with each subsequent one. This is the sequence here. But as for the absence of sequence with the preceding ones, [it is said]:
'When the meaning exists, the absence of sequence is no reason; therefore, it should be joined with the term "appropriated" and the others.'"
No, because there is no distinction. For the terms "appropriated" (*upādiṇṇa*) and so forth are joined with this [term].
In that context, when it is said, "either the appropriated is visible, or the visible is appropriated," there is no distinction;

thus, due to the absence of a distinction, it does not form a conjunction. Therefore, without taking up that fourth dyad, [the text proceeds] with the subsequent ones, such as "there is matter that is impinging" (*sappaṭigha*), and so on.
Together with three pairs, by way of such formulations as "That matter which is impinging is either a faculty or not a faculty;
that matter which is non-impinging is either a faculty or not a faculty," six tetrads have been established after joining each pair of two.
And just as this fourth dyad does not form a logical connection [with the first], so too the initial dyad does not form a connection with it.
Why? Because non-derived matter (*anupādā-rūpa*) is exclusively non-demonstrable (*anidassana*).
For when one considers that "of that matter which is non-derived, some is demonstrable and some is non-demonstrable," it does not form a connection when joined with the fourth dyad in this manner.
Therefore, having passed over that, it is joined with the fifth. Thus, it should be understood which [factor] enters into conjunction with which, and which does not.
This is the establishment of the text regarding the fourth compendium (*saṅgaha*).
Hereafter, however, the seven compendia beginning with the fivefold compendium are entirely unmixed. Thus, for the entire matrix (*mātikā*)...
The determination of the text should be understood. 594.
Now, in order to explain its meaning by way of analysis, the passage beginning "All matter is not solely with cause" is commenced.
But why is the question “Which of that all-form is not a root-cause? not asked here? Because there is no differentiation.

For just as in the case of the dyads and so forth, there is both derived form and non-derived form, so too here there is no such differentiation as “root-cause” and “not a root-cause,” or “with root-cause” and “without root-cause”;
therefore, it was analyzed without asking the question. In this context, “all” means...
"Entirely," "without remainder. "'Matter' (rūpa)" is a description of its general characteristic (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*), illustrating its state of being "mattered" (*ruppana*) by cold and so forth.
"Not this very cause" is a description that negates a common cause (*sādhāraṇahetu*).

In that regard, there are four kinds of causes: the causal cause (*hetuhetu*), the conditional cause (*paccayahetu*), the supreme cause (*uttamahetu*), and the common cause (*sādhāraṇahetu*). Among these, "three..."
“The three wholesome roots, the three unwholesome roots, and the three indeterminate roots”—this is called “cause-as-cause.
“Bhikkhu, the four great elements are the cause and the four great elements are the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of form”—this is called “condition-as-cause.
“Wholesome and unwholesome [kamma] in their own place of ripening, and a supreme, desirable object...”
"In the case of wholesome kamma-result, it is the highest desirable object; in the case of unwholesome kamma-result, it is the highest undesirable object"—this is called the "supreme cause.
As it is said: "He understands, as it really is, the result of the undertaking of kamma in the past, future, and present, according to its basis and its cause";
and: "This is the cause, this is the condition for volitional formations, namely, ignorance. This is ignorance.
Because it fulfills the function of a condition by acting as a common cause for volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), it is called the "common cause" (*sādhāraṇahetu*).

Just as the essence of earth and the essence of water are conditions for both sweet and non-sweet things, so too ignorance (*avijjā*) is a common condition for both wholesome volitional formations and unwholesome volitional formations.
However, in this context, the term "cause-cause" (*hetuhetu*) is intended.

Thus, having determined the state of being a cause for matter as it appears in the matrix (mātikā) under the heading "states that are causes" and "states that are not causes," he rejects it by saying, "it is not a cause at all.
In this manner, both the exposition of rejection and the exposition of non-rejection should be understood for all the terms.
Furthermore, the meaning of the words for all these terms has already been stated in the commentary on the matrix.

Regarding the phrase "only with conditions": here, that which is produced by kamma has only kamma as its condition, while those produced by nutriment and so forth have only nutriment and so forth as their conditions;
thus the meaning should be understood according to these four conditions stated for matter alone. Regarding "matter alone":
this negates the state of being immaterial mentioned in the matrix (mātikā) as "material phenomena" and "immaterial phenomena. It is arisen...
"By the six consciousnesses" means that only present form is to be experienced by the six [consciousnesses], beginning with eye-consciousness.
However, the restriction is made with reference to eye-consciousness and the others; for they do not cognize what is past or future.
Mental consciousness, however, cognizes both the past and the future. Since it falls within the stream of these five consciousnesses, it is indeed included within that stream.
It has gone after having been sacrificed. Furthermore, in the sense of non-existence after having been sacrificed, it is simply impermanent.
Because its nature is such that it must be overcome by aging, it is "overcome by aging. Or, because aging is manifest in the material body, for that reason too it is said to be "overcome by aging.
Thus, regarding the phrase "the inclusion of matter in one way," here the word *vidhā* is seen in the senses of measure, shape, and portion.
In such passages as “The conceit ‘I am superior’ is a mode; the conceit ‘I am equal’ is a mode,” *vidhā* means conceit (*māna*).
In such passages as “Of what kind do they say one is virtuous? Of what kind do they say one is wise? it means shape or configuration (*saṇṭhāna*).

For the meaning of the term “of what kind” (*kathaṃvidha*) is “of what shape” (*kathaṃsaṇṭhāna*). In such passages as “A basis for knowledge by way of one mode, a basis for knowledge by way of two modes,” it means category or classification.
“Division” (*koṭṭhāsa*) means a classification (*vidhā*). Here too, it is specifically a division that is intended.
The word “group” (*saṅgaha*) is also fourfold, according to genus, birth, action, and number. Among these, [examples are]:
“Let all the khattiyas come; let all the brāhmaṇas, all the vessas, and all the suddas come,” and “Friend Visākha, whatever...”
“Right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these states are included within the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha).
This is called “grouping by genus. For here, as in the expression “let those of the same genus come,” all have entered into a single grouping by way of their genus.
[As in: “Let all the people of Kosala come; let all the people of Magadha come; let all the people of Bharukaccha come.”
"Let them come. "And, friend Visākha, whatever is right effort, whatever is right mindfulness, and whatever is right concentration—these states are included in the aggregate of concentration.

This is called "inclusion by place of birth" (*sañjātisaṅgaha*). For here, just as in the passage where it is said, "Let those born and grown in one place come," all [states] are included by way of the place where they were born—that is, the space occupied.

They have come together into a single collection. “Let all elephant-riders come, let all horse-riders come, let all charioteers come,” and “That which, friend Visākha, is right view and that which is right intention—these states are included within the aggregate of wisdom”:
this is called ‘collection by action. For all these have come together into a single collection by virtue of performing their own respective actions. “The eye-base...”
To which aggregate does it belong in its enumeration? The eye-base belongs in the enumeration of the form aggregate.
If the eye-base belongs in the enumeration of the form aggregate, then indeed, friend, you must say: "The eye-base is included within the form aggregate.
This is called "inclusion by enumeration. This is what is intended here. By way of a single category...
"Enumeration of form" (rūpagaṇanā) is the meaning here. This same method applies everywhere.
The commentary on the exposition of the dyads (*dukaniddesa*), the discussion on the analysis of derived matter (*upādābhājanīyakathā*).

595. Now, regarding the two kinds of inclusion and so forth, since there exists a distinction such that "there is matter which is derived (upādā)" and "there is matter which is non-derived (noupādā)," he says, beginning with "What is that matter which is derived?
in order to show the word-commentary preceded by a question. In this context, it is called "derived" (upādā) because it is derived from [the elements];
the meaning is that it proceeds by depending upon the great primary elements (mahābhūta), having grasped them and not released them.
Now, showing its classification, he says: "The eye-base," and so forth.
(596) Having thus briefly enumerated the twenty-three kinds of derived matter (*upādārūpa*), and further explaining that same [matter] in detail, he says:
"What is that matter which is the eye-base? and so forth. Therein, the eye is twofold: the fleshly eye (*maṃsacakkhu*) and the wisdom-eye (*paññācakkhu*).
Now, among these, the fivefold eye of wisdom consists of the Buddha-eye, the universal eye, the knowledge-eye, the divine eye, and the Dhamma-eye.
Among them, the so-called "Buddha-eye" is that [passage] which says: "Monks, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, I saw beings with little dust in their eyes...
[and so on] ...difficult to instruct. The "universal eye" is said to be—
“Omniscient knowledge”—this is called the universal eye (*samantacakkhu*). “The eye arose, knowledge arose”—this is called the knowledge-eye (*ñāṇacakkhu*).
“I saw, monks, with the purified divine eye”—this is called the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
“On that very seat, the dustless, stainless Dhamma-eye arose”—this is...
The knowledge comprised by the three lower paths is called the Dhammacakkhu.
The flesh-eye (maṃsacakkhu) is twofold: the sensitive eye (pasādacakkhu) and the eye as a physical aggregate (sasambhāracakkhu).
Among these, that which is situated in the eye-socket—below by the bone of the socket, above by the brow-bone, and on both sides by the eye-ridges—[is the physical aggregate].
It is a mass of flesh delimited internally by the brain and externally by the eyelashes and eyebrows. In brief, it consists of fourteen components:
the four elements, color, odor, taste, nutritive essence, origin, shape, life-force, state, bodily sensitivity, and visual sensitivity.
In detail, it consists of the four elements, along with the color, odor, taste, nutritive essence, shape, and origin dependent upon them.
Thus, these ten, because they arise from four [origins], amount to forty. Life, existence, the clarity of the body, and the clarity of the eye—these four are exclusively produced by kamma.
By way of these forty-four material phenomena, there is the "forty-fourfold aggregate.
That which the world perceives as "the eye"—white, wide, spread out, and extensive—is not the eye.
One perceives; one perceives the physical basis through the eye. That lump of flesh is situated in the eye-socket, bound to the brain by a thread of sinew.
In it there is white, black, and red; there is earth, water, fire, and air.
It is white because of the predominance of phlegm (*semha*), black because of the predominance of bile (*pitta*), and red because of the predominance of blood (*lohita*).
When there is an excess of earth, it becomes solid; when there is an excess of water, it trickles; when there is an excess of fire, it burns;
when there is an excess of air, it quivers—this is called the eye as a composite of material elements (*sasambhāra-cakkhu*).

However, that which is dependent on this, bound to this, and derived from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as a sensitive surface (*pasāda*)—this is the eye as sensitive surface (*pasāda-cakkhu*).
This [eye-consciousness] resides in the middle of that black circle (kaṇhamaṇḍala), which is surrounded by a white circle (setamaṇḍala) and constitutes the physical eye with its constituent parts;
it is located within the visual field (diṭṭhimaṇḍala)—the place where the shape of bodies appears to those standing directly in front.

It pervades the seven layers of the eye (khipaṭala), just as oil poured onto seven cotton-wick layers permeates those layers. It performs the functions of maintaining, cleansing, adorning, and opening [the eye].
Like a noble prince attended by four nurses, it receives assistance from the four elements whose functions are supporting, binding, maturing, and moving;
it is sustained by temperature, consciousness, and nutriment; it is protected by vitality; it is surrounded by color, odor, taste, and so forth;
in measure, it is the size of the tip of a louse's head; and it serves as the respective basis for eye-consciousness and the other types of consciousness.
It remains establishing itself as the state of being the door to the physical basis (vatthu). And this was said by the General of the Dhamma:
"That clarity of the eye by which one perceives forms—this is limited and subtle, comparable to the head of a louse."

"The eye and that base" is the "eye-base" (*cakkhāyatana*). In the phrase "the eye which is sensitivity derived from the four great elements," the genitive case is used here in the sense of the accusative;
the meaning is "sensitivity that has arisen having taken up the four great elements.
By this, he takes only the sensitive eye and excludes the remaining types of eye. As for what is stated in the *Indriyagocara Sutta*...

“Sensitivity derived from one great primary element is included within the earth element, and within the water element, the fire element, and the air element”—thus it is stated in the *Catuparivatta Sutta*. [And:
“Sensitivity derived from two great primary elements is included within the earth element and the water element, and within the fire element and the air element.”
And as for what was said, “and of the air element,” that was stated by way of a figurative method (pariyāya). For this discourse on the Suttanta is indeed a teaching by way of a figurative method.

Whatever sensitivity is derived from the four great elements, it is described there by way of this figurative method: even though it is given for each one of them individually, it is simply sensitivity belonging to both together.
However, the Abhidhamma is called a teaching not by way of a figurative method. Therefore—
Here it is said: "derived from the four great elements, it is translucent.
Because it is grasped by foolish people as "this is my self," it is called *attabhāva* (selfhood), referring both to the physical body and to the pentad of aggregates (*khandhapañcaka*).
That which is included within that [selfhood] and dependent upon it is "included in selfhood" (*attabhāvapariyāpanna*), and it cannot be seen by eye-consciousness.

“Sakka” means “non-indicative. It is called “sappaṭigha” (with resistance) because a clash or impact arises therein. Regarding the passage beginning with “by which,” this is the summary of the meaning:
by means of that eye acting as the instrument, this being either saw such a form as described in the past, sees it in the present, or will see it in the future, provided it is not impaired.
If the eye were to exist, then one might see a visible form that has come into its range;

or else, one might have seen a past form with a past eye, sees a present form with a present eye, or will see a future form with a future eye—provided that form should come into the range of the eye, one would see that form with the eye. This is the hypothetical statement used here.
In the sense of being the guide for seeing, this is the eye; in the sense of being a meeting place for those of similar birth, this is the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*);
in the sense of being empty, devoid of a self, this is the eye-element (*cakkhudhātu*). It exercises lordship over the characteristic of seeing, thus it is the eye-faculty (*cakkhundriya*).
In the sense of breaking up and dissolving, this is the world (*loka*); in the sense of a means of access, these are the doors; in the sense of being unfathomable, this is the ocean.
In the sense of being utterly pure, it is white. In the sense of being the place where contact and the other factors are born, it is a field.
In the sense of being their foundation, it is a site. In the sense that it leads one’s personal existence (attabhāva) toward what is even or uneven, it is a guide.
In that same sense, it is a leader. In the sense of being included within personality-view (sakkāya), it is this shore. In the sense of being shared by many, it is...
“And a village is empty in the sense of being ownerless.

Up to this point, it should be understood that four methods of defining the eye-base have been stated by applying the fourteen names, beginning with “the eye itself,” to the four phrases beginning with “he saw. How so? For here, by means of which...
"With the invisible, impinging eye, one sees visible form that is both visible and impinging; this eye is also [invisible and impinging]...pe...
this village is empty; this is that visible form, the eye-base"—this is one method. The rest should be understood in the same way. 597.
Now, at times such as when lightning flashes, even for one who does not wish to look, the visible form strikes the sensitivity of the eye.
Therefore, in order to show that mode [of activity], the second section of the exposition is commenced.
Therein, "in which eye" means in which eye acting as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). "Visible form" (*rūpa*) is a term in the nominative case. Therein, "has struck" expresses the past sense;
"strikes" expresses the present sense; "will strike" expresses the future sense; and "might strike" [expresses the potential].
The meaning is "supposition. For past form was indeed said to have struck against the past eye; present [form] is said to strike against the present [eye];
and future [form] will be said to strike against the future [eye].
If that form were to come within the range of the eye, it would strike against the eye—that is the supposition here. As for its actual meaning:

However, it is precisely when striking against the translucent materiality (pasāda-rūpa) that visible form (rūpa) is said to be "impinged. Here too, the four methods of defining [the sense base] should be understood in the same manner as previously described.
598. Now, when one who desires to look at a visible form directs the eye toward that form by his own will, the eye [is related] to the visible form...
It strikes back; therefore, in order to show that mode [of reaction], the third section of the exposition has been commenced. Its meaning is indeed evident.
Here, however, the eye is said to "strike back" against the visible object precisely while it is receiving the objective field.
In this case as well, the four methods of definition should be understood according to the same method as before.

599. Following this, ten sections are presented: five by way of showing the arising of [consciousness] with contact as the fifth, and five by way of showing the arising of those same [consciousnesses] bound to their respective objects.
Therein, "dependent on the eye" means having the eye as its support, making it a condition.
"Taking form as object" means coming upon, referring to, and depending on the objective field of form. By this, [the consciousnesses] based on the sensitive matter of the eye...

In the first section, the conditionality of matter is shown by way of the pre-arising condition (*purejāta-paccaya*) for contact and so forth included within the cognitive process of the eye-door, and by way of the object-dominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*) and object-strong-dependence (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*) conditions.

In the remaining five sections, the conditionality is shown solely by way of the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), in the sense that "matter is its object" (*rūpam assa ārammaṇam*), thus it is called "having matter as its object" (*rūpārammaṇo*). Just as in the first three [sections], so too...
In these ten sections as well, four methods of definition are to be understood for each.

Thus, in order to show in various ways that "this is it"—referring to the eye which was raised as the answer to the question "Which is that material form called the eye-base?"—thirteen explanatory sections have been presented:
the first three and these ten. And herein, within each one, there are four [methods].
It should be understood that because it has come down through the methods of definition (*vavatthāpana*), it is shown as adorned with fifty-two methods.
This same method applies to the subsequent descriptions of the ear-base (*sotāyatana*) and so forth. However, the specific distinction here should be understood as follows:

it hears, thus it is the "ear" (*sota*). That [ear] is located inside the ear-cavity together with its constituent parts, having the shape of a finger-stall (*aṅgulivedhaka*) and being covered with fine, reddish-brown hairs.
In its location, it remains performing its function as a basis and door for ear-consciousness and so forth, as appropriate, having been assisted by the elements of the kind already described,
being supported by temperature, consciousness, and nutriment, being maintained by vitality, and being surrounded by color and the other [characteristics].
It is called the nose (*ghāna*) because it smells. It resides within the nasal cavity along with its constituent tissues, in a location shaped like a goat’s hoof-print;
there, acting as a support, a maintenance factor, and a surrounding protection of the aforementioned type, it establishes itself as the appropriate basis and door for nose-consciousness and the rest.
The tongue (*jivhā*) is so called in the sense of tasting. It is located above the middle of the tongue together with its constituent tissues, in a place shaped like the tip of a lotus petal.
Having become supported, maintained, and accompanied by the aforementioned kinds of assistance,
it remains establishing itself as the appropriate basis and door for tongue-consciousness and the rest.
Furthermore, wherever there is what is called "clung-to matter" (upādiṇṇaka-rūpa) in this body, there exists the body-base (kāyāyatana) throughout, like the surface of a cotton pad.

Like moisture, it remains as a support, maintenance, and accompaniment for the aforementioned types of assistance, establishing the status of being the respective bases and doors for body-consciousness and so forth. This is the distinction here.

The rest—the classification of the text and the meaning—should be understood according to the method already stated in the Description of the Eye (*Cakkhuniddesa*). For here, in place of the term "eye," [the term "body" is used].
In place of the word *sota* (ear), words such as *rūpa* (form) appear; in place of the word *rūpa*, words such as *sadda* (sound) appear;

and in place of words such as *passati* (sees), words such as *suṇāti* (hears) have come down. Furthermore, because of the absence of the two terms “this is a net” (*nettaṃ petaṃ*) and “this is a guide” (*nayanaṃ petaṃ*), there are twelve names for each [sense faculty].
The rest is exactly the same as what was stated everywhere else.

In this regard, it might be argued: "If, to whatever extent there is 'appropriated matter' (upādiṇṇaka-rūpa) in this body, the body-base (kāyāyatana) exists everywhere—like moisture throughout a cotton pad—then it follows that there is a confusion of characteristics. [Reply: "It does not follow. "Why?
"Because one thing does not exist in another place. "If that is so, then the body-base does not exist everywhere? [Reply: "Not at all."
In the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*), [the characteristic] is present everywhere. However, it is impossible to point out its specific distinction by separating it [from the other elements];

therefore, it was stated thus. For just as visible form, taste, and so forth, are said to be mutually pervasive because they cannot be separated—like grains of sand or dust—yet in the ultimate sense there is no taste within visible form. If there were [such a thing], then by the very perception of visible form...

The apprehension of taste would likewise proceed. Thus, even the body-base (*kāyāyatana*), from the ultimate standpoint (*paramatthato*), neither exists everywhere nor is it entirely non-existent, because it cannot be separated [from its own specific characteristics]. In this way, it should be understood that there is no confusion of defining characteristics (*lakkhaṇasammissatā*) here.
Furthermore, their unmixed nature should be understood through the determination of their characteristics and so forth:

among these, the eye has as its characteristic the sensitivity of the primary elements capable of being struck by visible forms, or the sensitivity of the primary elements originated by kamma rooted in the desire to see; its function is to seize upon visible forms;
it is manifested as the state of being the support for eye-consciousness; and its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to see.

The ear has the characteristic of being a sensitivity of the primary elements capable of striking against sounds; or, it has the characteristic of being a sensitivity of the primary elements originated by kamma rooted in the desire to hear.
Its function is to apprehend sounds. It is manifested as the basis for ear-consciousness. Its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to hear.

The nose has the characteristic of being a sensitivity of the primary elements capable of striking against odors; or, it has the characteristic of being a sensitivity of the primary elements originated by kamma rooted in the desire to smell.

Or else, the nose has the characteristic of drawing [the object] toward itself among odors; its manifestation is the state of being the support for nose-consciousness; its proximate cause is the kamma-born primary elements resulting from the desire to smell.

Or else, the tongue has the characteristic of sensitivity as the primary element capable of being struck by tastes; or it has the characteristic of sensitivity as the primary element originated by kamma resulting from the desire to taste;

its function is to draw [the object] toward itself among tastes; its manifestation is the state of being the support for tongue-consciousness; its proximate cause is the kamma-born primary elements resulting from the desire to taste.

The body has as its characteristic the sensitivity of the primary elements capable of being struck by tangible objects, or alternatively, the sensitivity of the primary elements originated by kamma rooted in the desire to touch;

its function is to reach out toward tangible objects; it is manifested as the state of being the support for body-consciousness; and its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to touch.

Some, however, maintain that the sensitivity of the primary elements in which fire predominates is the eye, while the sensitivities of the primary elements in which air, earth, and water predominate are [the other sense organs].

They say that the ear, nose, tongue, and body [faculties] belong to all [beings]. Others say: "The eye faculty is the sensitivity of those in whom fire is predominant; the ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties are the sensitivities of those in whom space, air, water, and earth are predominant respectively.
They should be told: "Produce a scriptural passage [to support this].
Certainly, they will not find any such passage. However, some here provide the following reason: "Because they are sustained by the qualities of fire and so forth, namely, visible form and the rest."
They say this. And they should be asked: “Who, indeed, says that visible form and the rest are qualities of fire and the other elements?
For when material phenomena are inseparable, it is impossible to say, ‘This is the quality of this,’ or ‘That is the quality of that. Furthermore, they might argue:

“Just as in various combinations of constituent parts, due to the predominance of this or that primary element, there occur the functions of supporting and so forth belonging to earth and the others...”
If you maintain that "we desire these functions because we observe an excess of form and so forth in those constituent elements where fire and the others predominate;
therefore, it must be accepted that form and the rest are their qualities," they should be told:

"We would accept this if, in water which has a preponderance of cohesion, its odor were more intense than that of the fermented liquor which has a preponderance of cohesion, and if in hot water which has a preponderance of fire, its color were likewise more intense."

The color of the water of the Sītā [River] would diminish. However, since neither of these two [conditions] exists here, one should therefore abandon this postulation of a distinction among those [elements] that serve as the support.

Just as, even in the absence of any distinction, the visible form, taste, and so forth of the primary elements within a single group are mutually dissimilar, so too are the eye-sensitivity and the others; thus it should be understood that there is no other cause for their distinction.

But what is it that makes them unique to one another? Karma alone is their distinguishing cause. Therefore, the distinction between these [faculties] is due to a distinction in karma, not a distinction in the primary elements (*bhūta*).
For if there were a distinction in the primary elements, the sensitive matter (*pasāda*) would not arise at all.

"The sensitive matter belongs to those who are equal, not to those who are unequal," so say the ancients. Thus, among these which possess distinctions due to a distinction in karma, the eye and the ear—

The [faculties of] nose, tongue, and body grasp objects that have reached them; because they are causes of consciousness with respect to objects that adhere to their own bases and do not adhere to bases other than themselves.

The nose, tongue, and body are graspers of objects that have reached them, because they are causes of consciousness with respect to objects that adhere to their own bases both by way of their support and by themselves.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is said: "An object is called 'attained' simply because it has come into the range [of the eye].
For the color of the moon’s disk and the sun’s disk, which stand at a distance of forty-two thousand yojanas, strikes the sensitivity of the eye.
Although they are perceived while standing far away, they are indeed called 'attained. Because that is its field of activity, the eye is said to have only an attained field of activity."
It is said: "Even for woodcutters cutting a tree at a distance, or for washermen washing clothes at a distance, the bodily movement is discerned from afar;
but sound, having arrived through a succession of elements (dhātu-paramparā) and struck the ear, proceeds to gradual definition.
In this context, although it is said that the object is "attained" because it has come into the range [of the senses], nevertheless, the color of the moon's disk and so forth—

The eye perceives its object even while standing at a distance without having reached it. As for sound, if it were to arrive slowly, that which has arisen at a distance would be heard only after a long time;
furthermore, having arrived by successive impact and striking the ear, it would not be discerned as "coming from such-and-such a direction.
Therefore, these two have non-attained objects as their domain.

And these are things that are disagreeable, like a snake. For just as a snake does not delight in a place that has been sprinkled and swept clean, but rather enters into refuse heaps, thickets of grass and leaves, or ant-hills, and finds delight and attains one-pointedness while lying there, even so the eye does not delight in smooth surfaces such as golden walls and the like;
it does not even wish to look at them, but [finds delight] only in representations of forms such as paintings of flowers, creepers, and fruits.
But he delights in it. For in such places, even when their vision fails them, they wish to look about with their mouths wide open.
Even the crocodile, having emerged from the water, sees nothing to seize; he wanders about with his eyes closed.
But when he has plunged into water a hundred fathoms deep, entered his lair, and is lying down, then his mind—
It becomes one-pointed and sleeps happily; in the same way, the ear makes its basis solely in the cavity of the ear-hole, which is situated within the hollow of the skull and dependent upon space.
That very space within the ear-hole is the condition for the hearing of sound. Even the unobstructed space suffices;
for when recitation is being performed inside a cave, the sound does not break through the roof of the cave.
When it goes out, having emerged through the openings of the doors and windows, it proceeds by striking the successive series of elements until it strikes the ear-sensitivity (*sotappasāda*).
At that time, those sitting on the roof of the cave know, "So-and-so is reciting.
This being so, there is the state of having a present object (*sampattagocarata*). [Question: "But what is this 'having a present object'? [Answer: "Yes, it is having a present object."
“If that were so, when drums and such are being struck at a distance, there would be no cognition of the sound as being ‘far away,’ would there? “No, it is not so.
For when the physical basis of the ear is stimulated, there arises a mode of cognition corresponding to whether the sound is far or near, or on the opposite bank or this side;
this is simply the nature of things (*dhammatā*). “What is the use of this ‘nature of things’? From whichever opening [the sound enters]...”
"From here and there it hears, like the seeing of the moon, sun, and so forth; thus, this [nose] does not reach its object.

Even a bird finds no delight in a tree or on the ground; but when it has flown beyond one or two throws of a clod into the cloudless sky, it then attains one-pointedness of mind. In the same way, the nose also has a disposition toward space.
