Its objective domain is odors dependent on wind. For instance, when it has rained recently, cows repeatedly sniff the ground and, facing toward the sky, draw in the wind.
Even when taking a mass of fragrance between the fingers and smelling it, one who does not draw in the wind does not perceive that odor at all.
Even a cock, while wandering outside, does not see a place of safety and is harassed by blows from clods of earth and other such things.
But when it has entered the village and lies down after piling up ashes at the site of the hearth, it is at ease;

in the same way, the tongue also has its inclination toward the village and takes as its object the flavor dependent upon water. For thus, throughout the three watches of the night, [one should practice] the duty of a recluse.
Even after doing so, one must still enter the village early in the morning, taking bowl and robes.
Furthermore, it is not possible to know the flavor of dry solid food unless it has been moistened with saliva.
Even a jackal, wandering about outside, finds no pleasure until it lies down after eating human flesh in a raw charnel ground.
Just as that [couch] becomes comfortable for him, so too the body has a grasping-impregnated inclination (*upādiṇṇakajjhāsaya*) and takes as its object tangible things dependent on earth.
For, failing to obtain other grasped objects, beings lie down placing their heads upon the very palm of their own hands.
And both internal and external earth serve as conditions for the apprehension of its object. For even in the case of a well-spread bed, [the body rests upon it].
Nor is it possible for one who is neither sitting nor pressing to know the hardness or softness of fruits held in the hand.
Thus, both internal and external earth serves as a condition for this sensitive body-faculty in the cognition of tangible objects.
In this way, their unmixed nature should be understood through the determination of their specific characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth; for the sensitive eye-faculty is indeed something else.

The eye-base and the others are indeed unmixed [with one another] by way of their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), functions (*rasa*), manifestations (*paccupaṭṭhāna*), proximate causes (*padaṭṭhāna*), spheres (*gocara*), inclinations (*ajjhāsaya*), and supports (*nissaya*), as they are distinct from the ear-sensitivity and so forth.
Furthermore, this simile should be understood to illustrate their unmixed nature:
just as when five-colored banners are raised, although their shadows appear as if joined together, each shadow remains distinct from the others.

And just as when a wick is made from five-colored cotton and a lamp is lit, although the flames appear to be joined together as one, the flame of each individual strand is actually distinct and unmixed;
even so, although these five sense-bases are gathered together within a single personal existence, they remain entirely unmixed with one another. Not...
And these five alone, as well as all other material phenomena, are unmixed. For in this body there are three sections:
the lower part of the body, the middle part of the body, and the upper part of the body. Therein, from the navel downwards is called the lower part of the body.
In that [section] are the decad of the body, the decad of sex, eight born of nutriment, and [eight] born of temperature.

There are eight [material qualities] originating from consciousness; thus, there are forty-four material qualities. From the navel upwards as far as the throat is called the middle part of the body (*majjhima-kāya*).

Therein are the body-decad (*kāya-dasaka*), the sex-decad (*bhāva-dasaka*), the base-decad (*vatthu-dasaka*), and three octads consisting of those originating from nutriment and so forth—thus, there are fifty-four material qualities. Above the throat is called the upper part of the body (*uparima-kāya*). Therein...
The eye-decad, the ear-decad, the nose-decad, the tongue-decad, the body-decad, the sex-decad,
and the three octads beginning with those produced by nutriment— these are the eighty-four material phenomena. Among these,
the conditions for the sensitive eye are the four great elements, visible form, odor, flavor, nutritive essence, and the life-faculty.
"Eye-sensitivity": this refers to what is called the "eye-decad," consisting of ten produced material phenomena that are entirely inseparable.
The remaining [decads] are to be understood in the same manner. Among these, the matter of the lower part of the body is unmixed with the matter of the middle and upper parts of the body;
likewise, the matter of the other two parts of the body is also unmixed with the others. For example:
Just as at the time of sunset the shadows of the mountain and the shadows of the trees, though appearing as if joined together, are nonetheless unmixed with one another,
so too, within these bodies, the forty-four, fifty-four, or eighty-four types of material phenomena,
though appearing as if joined together, are nonetheless entirely unmixed with one another.
616. In the exposition of the visible-object base (*rūpāyatana*), "color" (*vaṇṇa*) itself is "color-appearance" (*vaṇṇanibhā*); or, it is called "appearance" (*nibhā*) because it appears.

The meaning is that it is manifest to eye-consciousness. Color itself as appearance is "color-appearance. "With demonstration" (*sanidassana*) means together with demonstration; the meaning is that it is to be seen by eye-consciousness.
"With resistance" (*sappaṭigha*) means together with resistance; it is that which generates impact and collision.

The meaning is as follows: among blue and the others, "blue" is like the flax flower; "yellow" is like the *kaṇikāra* flower; "red" is like the *bandhujīvaka* flower; "white" is like the morning star. "Black" is like extinguished charcoal; "madder-red" (*mañjiṭṭhaka*) is a dull red, like the *sinduvāra*, *karavīra*, or *makuḷa* flowers. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the desire for green, gold-colored, and moon-faced [complexions]," although the word "green" (*hari*)— [...is used here... "Gold" has been mentioned; however, since it is already included by the term "precious metal" (*jātarūpa*) further on, here it refers specifically to what one has personally carried.
These seven items are shown in their own nature without touching upon other categories.
"The color of gold" means the color of green grass. "The color of a mango sprout" means having a color identical to that of a mango sprout. These...
Two [characteristics] are shown by touching the physical basis. The twelve, beginning with long and so forth, are shown by way of conventional usage (*vohāra*).

And this conventional usage of theirs is established both by comparison (*upanidhāya*) and by specific configuration (*sannivesa*). For the long and so forth are established by comparison to one another, while the circular and so forth are established by a particular configuration.
In that regard, compared to the short, that which is higher than it is long; that—
Having compared it with something lower, it is short; having compared it with something thick, it is minute;
having compared it with that, it is thick and larger. That which is shaped like a wheel is circular (*vaṭṭa*); that which is shaped like a hen’s egg is oval (*parimaṇḍala*).
That which is joined with four sides is quadrangular (*caturaṃsa*). The same method applies to hexagons and so forth. "Low" means sloping down; "high" means rising up.
In this context, since length and so forth can be known by touching them, whereas blue and so forth cannot be known in that way,

length and shortness are not the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) in an absolute sense. However, it should be understood that what is spoken of here as the sense-sphere of visible form is simply the object itself situated in such a way—
relative to this or that [other object]— that it is designated by the conventional terms "long" or "short."
"Shadow and sunlight"—this is defined by their mutual exclusion; likewise with light and darkness.

The four items beginning with "clouds and mist" are shown by way of the physical basis (*vatthu*) itself. Therein, "clouds" (*abbhā*) refers to rain-clouds (*valāhaka*); "mist" (*mahikā*) refers to frost (*hima*).
By these four, the colors of the clouds and so forth are shown. By the phrases "the color and luster of the moon's disk" and so on, the colors of their respective radiances are shown.
In this regard, the distinction between the bases such as the moon’s disk should be understood as follows:
the celestial mansion of the divine son Canda, known as the moon’s disk, is made of jewels and covered with silver;
it is forty-nine yojanas in length and breadth. That of the divine son Suriya is made of gold and covered with crystal; it is fifty yojanas in length and breadth.

The celestial mansion is named the Solar Orb (*sūriyamaṇḍala*). The mansions of those respective sons of gods, made of the seven precious gems and measuring seven, eight, ten, or twelve *yojanas* in length and breadth, are named the Star-Forms (*tārakarūpa*).
Therein, the moon is below and the sun is above; the distance between the two is one *yojana*. From the lower limit of the moon...
The upper limit of the sun is one hundred yojanas. On both sides, the lunar mansions and stars move.
Among these three, the moon moves slowly, the sun moves swiftly, and the lunar mansions and stars move most swiftly.
At times they are ahead of the moon and sun, and at times they are behind them.
"A mirror-disk" means made of bronze. "Jewel" refers to all varieties other than beryl, such as the *jotirasa* and so forth.
"Conch" refers to the sea conch. "Pearl" includes both those from the sea and others. "Beryl" is a gemstone the color of bamboo. "Gold" is said to be the color of a sword-blade;
for the Teacher is gold-colored, and gold is also the color of a sword-blade. "Silver" is what is called...
"Kahāpaṇa" refers to the copper māsaka, the wooden māsaka, and the lacquer māsaka; everything that is said to "enter into commerce" is included here.

By the phrase "or whatever else," all other forms—excluding those mentioned in the canonical text—are included, such as the various types of coins (taṭṭika), rags (pilotika), ear-ornaments (kaṇṇika), and so forth; for all of these are comprised within the "miscellaneous items" (yevāpanaka).
Thus, although this material form is divided by distinctions such as blue and so forth, it is entirely non-different in its characteristics and other attributes.
For all of this is material form characterized by resistance to the eye; its function is to be the objective field of eye-consciousness; its manifestation is as the domain of that very consciousness;
and its proximate cause is the four great elements. And as this is so, so too are all derived material forms. However, where there is a distinction:
There is something there we shall explain. The rest here should be understood according to the same method as stated in the exposition of the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*).
For while in that [exposition] the description is preceded by the "eye," here it is preceded by "form" (*rūpa*).
Therein, there were fourteen names beginning with “This too is the eye,” whereas here there are three beginning with “This too is form. The rest is exactly the same. Just as with the four...
Thirteen sections were stated for defining the eye after it had been adorned with the four methods; here too, they are stated in exactly the same way. 620.

In the description of the sound base (*saddāyatana*), "the sound of a drum" (*bherisadda*) refers to the sound of drums struck by large drums. The sounds of the *mudiṅga*, conch, and *paṇava* drums are also sounds produced by such conditions as the *mudiṅga* and so forth.
"The sound of singing" (*gītasadda*) is the sound designated as song. For the remaining instruments mentioned, such as the lute (*vīṇā*) and others, which are strung with wires...

The sound of musical instruments (*vāditasaddo*). The sound of clapping (*sammasaddo*) refers to the sound of bronze cymbals, hand-claps, and wooden clappers. The sound of hand-clapping (*pāṇisaddo*) refers to the sound of striking with the hands.
The sound of the clamor of beings (*sattānaṃ nigghosasaddo*) refers to the sound of the indistinct utterances of many people gathered together.
The sound of the collision of elements (*dhātūnaṃ sannighātasaddo*) refers to the sound of trees rubbing against one another, the clashing of bells, and so forth. Of the wind...
The sound of wind is "wind-sound. The sound of water as it flows or strikes against something is "water-sound.
The sound of human conversation and so forth is "human-sound. With the exception of these, all other sound is "non-human-sound. By these two phrases, every kind of sound is encompassed.
Even so, in cases such as the splitting of bamboo or the tearing of rags, etc., [the term "sound" still applies].
It should be understood that the word *yevāpanaka* (included) occurring in the text refers to whatever has been mentioned.
Thus, although this sound is divided by distinctions such as the sound of a drum and so forth, it is nevertheless non-different in its characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and other qualities.
For all such sound has the characteristic of impinging upon the ear; its function is to be the objective domain of ear-consciousness, and its manifestation is as the range of that very consciousness.

The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated in the exposition of the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*). For here too, thirteen sections are presented, adorned by four sets of four methods each.
Their meaning can be understood according to the method already stated, so it has not been elaborated upon.

In the exposition of the odor-base (*gandhāyatana*), "root-odor" (*mūlagandha*) refers to any odor produced in dependence on a root. This also applies to "heartwood-odors" (*sāragandha*) and so forth.
The same method applies here. The odor of demons (*ḍāka*) and the like who have not yet attained or have poorly attained [their state] is the "raw odor" (*āmaka-gandha*).

The odor of fish, dried meat, putrid flesh, and defiled ghee and so forth is the "stench" (*vissa-gandha*). "Fragrant" (*sugandha*) means a desirable odor; "foul-smelling" (*duggandha*) means an undesirable odor. By these two terms, every odor whatsoever is encompassed.
Even though this is so, odors such as those of *kaṇṇaka* flowers and rags are mentioned in the Canon (*pāḷi*).
It should be understood that all future odors as well have entered the category of "miscellaneous" (yevāpanaka).
Thus, although this odor is divided by distinctions such as root-odors and so forth, it is indeed non-different in terms of its characteristic and other properties.
For all of it has the characteristic of striking the nose, the function of being the objective domain for nose-consciousness, and the manifestation of being the resort for that same consciousness.

The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated in the exposition of the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*). For here too, thirteen sections adorned with fifty-two methods have been set forth; these are indeed evident in their meaning.
In the exposition of the taste-base (*rasāyatana*), "root-taste" (*mūlarasa*) is any taste produced in dependence upon a root. The same applies to trunk-taste (*khandharasa*) and so forth.
The same principle applies here. "Sour" refers to sour gruel and the like. "Sweet" refers exclusively to cow’s ghee and the like.

However, honey that has been kept for a long time becomes astringent when combined with astringent substances. Treacle that has been kept for a long time becomes bitter when combined with bitter substances.
But ghee, even after being kept for a long time—even if it loses its color and fragrance—does not lose its taste; therefore, it alone is exclusively sweet.
"Bitter" refers to neem leaves and the like. "Pungent" refers to ginger, black pepper, and the like. "Salty" refers to sea salt and the like.

"Astringent" refers to the shoots of the vātiṅgaṇa plant and the like. "Acid" refers to jujube, myrobalan, kapiṭṭha, sāla-vā, and the like. "Astringent" (in the sense of a decoction) refers to yellow myrobalan and the like.

All these tastes are mentioned here according to their respective substances (*vatthu*). However, it is the taste itself that is distinguished from its various substances by terms such as "acid" and so forth.
It should be understood that [the term] is expressed by these names. "Tasty" means a desirable flavor; "untasty" means an undesirable flavor.

By these two terms, every flavor is fully encompassed. Nevertheless, it should be understood that all flavors not mentioned in the Canon—such as the flavor of a clod of earth, the flavor of a wall, or the flavor of a rag—are included within the category of "and so forth" (yevāpanaka).
Thus, although this taste is divided into various types such as root-juice and so forth, it is nevertheless non-different in its characteristics and other attributes.

For all of this taste has the characteristic of impinging on the tongue; its function is to serve as the objective field for tongue-consciousness; and its manifestation is as the range of that same consciousness.

The rest should be understood in the same manner as stated in the description of the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*). Here too, just as there, thirteen sections adorned with the fifty-two methods have been set forth.

632. In the exposition of the femininity faculty (*itthindriya*), the word “by which” (*yena*) is an instrumental expression. The meaning here is: by whatever cause the feminine characteristics and so forth of a woman exist.
In that context, “characteristic” (*liṅga*) refers to shape (*saṇṭhāna*).
For the shape of a woman’s hands, feet, neck, chest, and so forth, is not like that of a man. Indeed, the lower body of women is slender, while the upper body is... [the text continues].
"Not distinct" means that the hands and feet are small, and the mouth is small. "Sign" refers to the perception [of these features]. For in women, the flesh of the chest is not distinct;
the mouth is without beard and without prominent teeth; and even the binding of the hair or the grasping of a cloth is not like that of men.
"Action" refers to behavior. For women, when young, play with dolls and pestles, and with painted wooden boards.
They play; they spin what is called a thread with clay yarn. "Demeanor" (ākappa) refers to the manner of walking and so forth.
For when women walk, they walk without ostentation; when standing, reclining, sitting, eating, or consuming food, they do so without ostentation.
Indeed, seeing even a man who is without ostentation, a woman walks, stands, and lies down just as she would for a woman.
They say that one "sits," "eats," and "enjoys.

"Femaleness" (*itthatta*) and "the state of being female" (*itthibhāva*) both have the same meaning; the sense is "the essential nature of a woman" (*itthisabhāva*). This [nature] is born of karma and originates from rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
However, the female sex-signs (*liṅga*) and so forth arise during the course of existence (*pavatta*) dependent upon the female faculty (*itthindriya*). For just as when there is a seed...
Just as, depending on a seed and with the seed as condition, a tree grows, becomes endowed with branches and twigs, and stands filling the sky;
even so, when the female faculty (itthindriya)—which is designated as the state of being female—is present, the female characteristics and so forth come to be.
For the female faculty is like the seed, and the female faculty is like the tree that, having grown depending on the seed, stands filling the sky.
Depending [on the heart-base], the female sex-signs and so forth arise during the course of existence. Among these, the female faculty (*itthindriya*) is not cognizable by eye-consciousness;
it is cognizable only by mind-consciousness. The female sex-signs and so forth are cognizable both by eye-consciousness and by mind-consciousness.

This material form is called the "female faculty" because, unlike the eye-faculty and so forth which belong to males as well, this is specifically the faculty of a female; thus, by way of restriction, it is the "female faculty."

633. The same method applies to the male faculty (*purisindriya*) as well. However, the male characteristics (*purisaliṅga*) and so forth should be understood as being the opposites of the female characteristics (*itthiliṅga*).
For the configuration of a man’s hands, feet, neck, chest, and so on, is not like that of a woman.
Indeed, the upper body of men is robust, while the lower body is not; their hands and feet are large, and their face—
The chest is large, the flesh is ample, and the beard and teeth grow.
The binding of the hair and the wearing of clothes is not like that of women. In childhood, they play with toy chariots, plows, and the like;
having made mounds of sand, they dig what they call ponds; their gait and other movements are distinct. Even in women, the gait and other such traits are performed with distinctness.
Having seen [it], they say, "He walks like a man," and so forth. The rest is exactly as described for the femininity faculty (*itthindriya*).

Therein, the femininity faculty has the characteristic of the female state; its function is to manifest as "woman"; it is manifested as the cause of the female gender, marks, gestures, and deportment.
The masculinity faculty has the characteristic of the male state; its function is to manifest as "man."
It has the manifestation of being the cause for the male gender, signs, postures, and modes of conduct. Both of these arise during the course of existence (*pavatta*) for those of the first eon;
at a later stage, they arise at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). Even that which arises at rebirth-linking fluctuates and changes during the course of existence, as it has been said:
“Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu’s female characteristics appeared; and at that same time, a certain bhikkhunī’s male characteristics appeared.
Of these two, the male characteristic is superior and the female characteristic is inferior.

Therefore, the male characteristic disappears through powerful unwholesomeness, while the female characteristic is established through weak wholesomeness. As for the female characteristic disappearing—

The female characteristic disappears through weak unwholesomeness, while the male characteristic becomes established through strong wholesomeness. Thus, it should be understood that both disappear through unwholesomeness and are established through wholesomeness.
But as for the hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanaka*), does he have one faculty or two? It is one; and that belongs to the female hermaphrodite.
The female faculty (*itthindriya*) [belongs to a female], and for one who possesses both sets of sexual characteristics (*purisaubhatobyañjanaka*), the male faculty (*purisindriya*) [belongs].
"If this is so, it follows that there is an absence of the second set of sexual characteristics. For it has been stated that the faculty is the cause of the sexual characteristic, yet he lacks it.
"The faculty is not the cause of his sexual characteristic. "Why? "Because of its constant absence. For when, in the case of a female who possesses both sets of sexual characteristics..."
When a woman’s mind of lust arises, at that very moment the male characteristic becomes manifest and the female characteristic becomes concealed and hidden;
likewise for the other in the case of the former.
And if their faculty were the cause of the second characteristic, both characteristics would persist at all times.
But it does not remain [as such]. Therefore, it should be understood that its physical characteristics (*byañjana*) are not the cause of that [sexuality].

Rather, in this case, the mind of lust accompanied by karma is the cause. And because he possesses only one sexual organ (*indriya*), the hermaphrodite (*itthi-ubhatobyañjanaka*) both conceives a fetus himself and causes another to conceive.
The male hermaphrodite (*purisa-ubhatobyañjanaka*) [causes] another to conceive a fetus.
[He] causes [another] to take it up, but does not take it up himself.
634. Regarding what should be said in the exposition of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), that has already been stated above in the section on the immaterial life-faculty.
For there, it was said "of those immaterial phenomena," whereas here, because it is the material life-faculty, it is said "of those material [phenomena]."
The distinction here is simply the word "of phenomena" (*dhammānaṃ*). Its characteristics and so forth should be understood as follows:

the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) has the characteristic of maintaining conascent material phenomena; its function is to cause them to proceed; its manifestation is the stabilization of those very same phenomena; and its proximate cause is the primary elements that are to be sustained. 635.
In the description of bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*), regarding the phrase "bodily intimation": first, for those who make their own state known by means of the body—
Because the state of this [action] is understood from its being grasped by following the seizing of the body—whether by animals of men, or by men of animals—it is called ‘intimation’ (*viññatti*).
Alternatively, it is called ‘intimation’ because it is understood by itself through the seizing of the body.
And in such passages as “Restraint by body is good,” the body itself, which is reckoned as *copana*, is ‘bodily intimation’ (*kāyaviññatti*).

Because it is the cause for making one’s intention known through the movement of the body, and because it is itself to be understood in that way, it is called "bodily intimation" (*kāyaviññatti*), meaning "intimation by means of the body.

Regarding the phrase "of a wholesome consciousness," and so forth: it arises from nine types of wholesome consciousness—namely, the eight sense-sphere wholesome states and the consciousness of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*)—as "of a wholesome consciousness";
or from twelve unwholesome consciousnesses as "of an unwholesome consciousness"; or from the eight great functional (*mahākiriyā*) consciousnesses.

By means of eleven functional consciousnesses—namely, two rootless functionals, one functional consciousness of one who has attained direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), and one fine-material-sphere functional—the indeterminate mind arises. Indeed, no other types of consciousness produce intimation (*viññatti*).

However, for those in training (*sekkha*), those beyond training (*asekkha*), and worldlings (*puthujjana*), intimation occurs only through these many consciousnesses; thus, they are shown "by way of cause" through the three terms beginning with "wholesome" (*kusala*).
Now, in order to show [the result] "by way of the fruit" through six phrases, it is said: "for one who is stepping forward," and so forth.

For since stepping forward and the rest occur by way of intimation (*viññatti*), they are called the "fruit of intimation. Therein, "for one who is stepping forward" means for one who is bringing the body forward;
"for one who is stepping back" means for one who is drawing it back; "for one who is looking ahead" means straight ahead.
"Of one looking": *vilokentassa* means of one looking here and there. "Of one contracting": *samiñjentassa* means of one bending the joints. "Of one extending":
*pasārentassa* means of one stretching out the joints.
Now, in order to show [the body] "by way of its intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvato*) through six terms, "stiffening of the body," and so forth, was said. Therein, "of the body" (*kāyassa*)...
Of the body. It stiffens and makes rigid the body, thus it is "stiffening" (*thambhanā*).

By adding a prefix to that very term, it is called "rigidification" (*santhambhanā*). Or, stiffening that is more powerful is "rigidification. "Rigidified-ness" (*santhambhitatta*) is the state of being rigidified.
Intimation (*viññatti*) is by way of making known. "Intimating" (*viññāpanā*) is the mode of intimating. The state of having been intimated is "intimated-ness" (*viññāpitatta*).
Whatever needs to be said here has already been stated below in the Discourse on the Doors (Dvārakathā). The same applies to verbal intimation (vacīviññatti).
However, the meaning of the term "verbal intimation" and its explanatory phrases were not stated there; it should be understood as follows:
[it refers to] those among animals who make their own state known by speech to men, or those among men who make it known to animals.

It is called *viññatti* because its existence is made known by means of the apprehension of speech; it is also called *viññatti* because it itself is made known by means of the apprehension of speech.
Furthermore, in such passages as “Restraint of speech is good,” speech itself—which is reckoned as *copana* (impelling)—is *viññatti*;
thus it is “vocal intimation” (*vacīviññatti*). This is because it is the cause for making one’s intention known through the sound of speech, and because it is itself to be understood in that way.
“Intimation by speech” (*vacīviññatti*) means that which is intimated by speech. It is called “speech” (*vācā*) because it is spoken in such contexts as “speech” (*vācā*) and “voice” (*girā*).

It is called “voice” (*girā*) because it is uttered. A “mode of expression” (*byappatha*) is a division of sentences. It is called a “mode of expression” because it is both a sentence and a path for those who desire to know and those who desire to make known the meaning.

It is called “utterance” (*udīraṇa*) because it is uttered. It is called “sound” (*ghosa*) because it resounds. It is called “action” (*kamma*) because it is performed. Thus, sound itself is the action.
*Ghosakamma*: the meaning is "a sound produced in various ways. *Vācībhedo* (verbal expression) is the differentiation of speech.

However, that is stated as "speech which is verbal expression" (*vācā vacībhedo*) for the purpose of making it known that it is not merely the breaking [of sounds], but rather speech that has reached differentiation.
By all these terms, "sound-speech" (*saddavācā*) alone is shown. Now, having connected it with that speech, [the following applies] to the meanings stated below:
In order to show its intrinsic nature through three modes by means of the terms "intimation" (*viññatti*) and so forth, it was said: "That which is the intimation by that speech," and so on.
Since this follows the method explained below, its meaning is already clear.
Now, for the sake of avoiding confusion regarding the consciousnesses that originate intimation, [the numbers] thirty-two, twenty-six, nineteen, and sixteen...
"Last" (pacchimāni) should be understood as follows: this is an incidental point (pakiṇṇaka).

For thirty-two types of consciousness originate matter, sustain the postures (iriyāpatha), and produce both kinds of intimation (viññatti). Twenty-six types do not produce intimation, but perform the other two functions.
Nineteen types originate matter only, while performing the other two functions [of sustaining postures and producing intimations].
They do not perform them. Among these three [categories], they do not perform even one of the sixteen.

Therein, "thirty-two" refers to those already mentioned below: the eight wholesome consciousnesses of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), the twelve unwholesome ones, the ten functional (* kiriya *) consciousnesses, the superknowledge-consciousness (*abhiññā-citta*) of trainees (*sekkha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*), and the superknowledge-consciousness of those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*).
"Twenty-six" refers to the five wholesome consciousnesses of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), the five functional (* kiriya*) consciousnesses of the fine-material sphere,

the four wholesome consciousnesses of the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*), the four functional consciousnesses of the immaterial sphere, the four path-consciousnesses (*magga-citta*), and the four fruition-consciousnesses (*phala-citta*). "Nineteen" refers to the eleven resultant consciousnesses from the wholesome and unwholesome categories of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*),

the two resultant consciousnesses from the unwholesome category, the functional mind-element (*kiriyamanodhātu*) from the functional category, and the five resultant consciousnesses of the fine-material sphere.
The sixteen are: the two fivefold sensory consciousnesses; the rebirth-linking consciousness of all beings; the death-consciousness of those whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava);
and the four resultant consciousnesses in the formless realm. These sixteen do not produce even a single instance of materiality among the postures or intimation.
Furthermore, many other consciousnesses arising in the formless realm do not originate materiality because they have no spatial location. It is not only these that [fail to do so].
There are also bodily and vocal intimation. 637.
In the description of the space element (*ākāsadhātu*): it is not scraped, nor is it pared away; because it cannot be scraped, cut, or broken, it is called "space" (*ākāsa*).

That which has gone into space is "that which has gone into space" (*ākāsagata*), just as [one speaks of] that which has gone into saliva and so forth. Alternatively, "that which has gone into what is called space" is "that which has gone into space."

It is called *agha* because it cannot be struck; the meaning is that it is "unassailable. That which is simply *agha* is *aghagata*. It is a "cavity" (*vivara*) in the sense of being a void. That which is simply a cavity is *vivaragata*.
"Untouched by the four great elements" means it is described as being like space, free from the tangle of those [elements].
Furthermore, from the perspective of its characteristic and so forth, the space element has the characteristic of delimiting matter; its function is to manifest the boundaries of matter.
Material form has the manifestation of being noble, or it has the manifestation of the state of being untouched and the state of having gaps and openings;
its proximate cause is delimited material form, by means of which there arises the notion regarding delimited forms: "This is above this, below this, or across this.
638. From here on, the exposition of the lightness, etc., of material form should be understood in the same manner as that stated for the lightness, etc., of consciousness.
Regarding the characteristics and so forth here: the lightness of matter has the characteristic of non-sluggishness; its function is the removal of heaviness from material phenomena;
it is manifested as quick transformation; and its proximate cause is light matter. The plasticity of matter has the characteristic of non-stiffness;
its function is the removal of stiffness from material phenomena; it is manifested as non-obstruction in all activities; and its proximate cause is plastic matter.
The plasticity of matter has the characteristic of being wieldy, in accordance with bodily activity; its function is the removal of unwieldiness;
it is manifested as a state of non-weakness; and its proximate cause is plastic matter.
These three, moreover, do not abandon one another. Even so, that lightness of matter which is like that of one who is healthy—

The lightness of matter (*rūpassa lahutā*) is a mode of non-heaviness characterized by easy turning; it arises from conditions that counteract the disturbance of the elements which cause the heaviness of matter.
It is the softness of material phenomena, like well-tanned leather, the state of being directed according to one's own will, the state of being wieldy, and the mode of gentleness;
it arises from conditions that counteract the disturbance of the elements which cause the rigidity of matter.
That alteration of matter which is the plasticity of matter is ‘the malleability of matter.

Furthermore, that state of workableness in material phenomena—like well-polished gold—which consists in their being suitable for bodily activities, and which arises from conditions opposed to the disturbances of the elements that are unsuitable for bodily activities, is that alteration of matter called ‘the wieldiness of matter.
In this way, the distinction between these two should be understood.
But even these three are unable to perform the work; it is the nutriment and so forth that perform it.
For thus do practitioners say: "Today we have obtained suitable food; our body is light, supple, and fit for work. And they say: "Today we have obtained a suitable climate;
today our mind is one-pointed; our body is light, supple, and fit for work."
641. In the explanations of accumulation (*upacaya*) and continuity (*santati*), "of the bases" (*āyatanānam*) refers to the eight and a half material bases.
"Accumulation" (*ācaya*) means arising. That which is the accumulation of the bases—the repeated arising of those [bases]—is itself called the accumulation of matter;
the meaning is "growth. That which is the accumulation of matter is the continuity of matter.
The further increase of material phenomena that have been accumulated in this way during the period of their occurrence is called the "continuity" (*santati*) of matter;
the meaning is "occurrence. For example, the time when water rises in a well dug on a riverbank is like "origination" (*ācaya*);
the time when it is full is like "accumulation" (*upacaya*); and the time when it overflows and flows away is like "continuity" (*santati*).
It should be understood as "occurrence. What, then, is stated by this?
By means of the base (*āyatana*), accumulation (*ācaya*) is stated; by means of accumulation, the base is stated.
Thus, accumulation itself is stated, and the base itself is stated. What, then, is stated by this? The materiality of the four continuities (*catusantatirūpa*).

Accumulation (*ācaya*), heaping-up (*upacaya*), arising (*nibbatti*), and growth (*vaḍḍhi*) have been mentioned. For in meaning, both of these are synonyms for the materiality of birth (*jāti-rūpa*) itself.

However, because there is no difference in meaning here, the Teacher provided a summary teaching by using the terms "heaping-up" and "continuity" (*santati*) according to their different modes and to suit those to be trained;
thus, in the detailed exposition (*niddesa*), it is said: "That which is the accumulation of the sense-bases (*āyatana*) is the heaping-up of materiality."
It is said: "That which is the accumulation of form is the continuity of form.
And since both of these are designations for the very same birth-form, therefore, in this context, the accumulation of form has the characteristic of heaping up;
its function is to cause forms to emerge from the past; its manifestation is as directing and as the state of fullness.

Or, it has the state of accumulated material form as its proximate cause. The continuity of matter should be understood as having the characteristic of occurrence, the function of uninterrupted succession, the manifestation of non-interruption, and the proximate cause of uninterrupted material form.

In the description of aging (*jaratā*): aging by way of the process of growing old is here the description of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). The mode of growing old is the state of growing old (*jīraṇatā*).
*Khāṇḍicca*, and so forth, are three descriptions of functions occurring upon the passing of time. The latter two are descriptions of its natural state (*pakati*).
For this [aging] is illuminated by the term "old age" (*jarā*) according to its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*); therefore, this is its description of intrinsic nature.

By the term "decaying" (*jīraṇatā*), it is shown according to its mode (*ākāra*); therefore, this is its description of mode. By the term "brokenness" (*khāṇḍicca*), it is shown according to the function of causing the teeth and nails to become broken upon the passing of time.
By the term *pālicca* (greying), it is indicated through the function of causing the hair and body hair to turn grey.
By the term *valittacatā* (wrinkling of the skin), it is explained through the function of causing the flesh to wither and the skin to become wrinkled.

Thus, these three—*khaṇḍicca* (brokenness) and so forth—are descriptions of its functions at the time of the passing of age. Through the perception of these transformations, aging becomes manifest as "manifest aging" (*pākaṭajarā*).

It has been shown. For just as the path traversed by water or fire—by means of the crushing or destruction of grasses, trees, and so forth, or by their being scorched—is manifest, yet that traversed path is not those very waters and so on themselves;
even so, the path traversed by aging through the brokenness of the teeth and so forth is manifest, and it is apprehended even when one opens one's eyes.
Nor is aging merely broken teeth and so forth. For aging is not something cognizable by the eye.

However, by these terms—"waning of the life-span" and "ripening of the faculties"—the natural process known as the exhaustion of the life-span and the ripening of the eye and other faculties is illustrated specifically at the time of the passing away of the [normal] period. Therefore, these latter two...

These should be understood as a description of their intrinsic nature (*pakatiniddesa*). In this context, because the life-force (*āyu*) of one who has reached old age diminishes, aging (*jarā*) is described by way of a metaphorical application of the result (*phalūpacāra*) as "the destroyer of life-force.
Furthermore, because the faculties such as the eye, which were very clear and capable of easily grasping even subtle objects during youth, become fully ripened for one who has reached old age...

They become agitated and non-transparent, and even coarse objects are unable to be grasped by them; therefore, "the ripening of the faculties" is also spoken of by way of a metaphorical designation for the fruit.
This aging, thus described in its entirety, is twofold: manifest and concealed. Therein—
In material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*), aging is called "manifest aging" because it is seen in states such as the breaking off of teeth and so forth.

In immaterial phenomena (*arūpa-dhamma*), however, aging is called "concealed aging" because no such transformation is visible. Furthermore, it is also twofold: "uninterrupted" (*avīci*) and "with interruption" (*savīci*).
Among these, [aging] is like that of gems, gold, silver, coral, the moon, the sun, and so on; and in those with weak faculties, such as the ten-year-olds and others...

Just as with living beings, and just as with non-living things such as flowers, fruits, and sprouts, aging is called "uninterrupted aging" (*avīcijarā*) because the various changes in color and so forth are difficult to discern from moment to moment;

the meaning is that it is continuous aging. On the other hand, in the case of other [non-living] things mentioned above, aging should be understood as "interrupted aging" (*savīcijarā*), because the various changes in color and so forth are easily discernible from time to time.

The aging of matter (*rūpa-jaratā*) should be understood as follows: its characteristic is the maturation of matter even from the perspective of its specific marks (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth; its function is to lead [matter] toward decline; its manifestation is the departure from newness despite the non-departure of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*);

and its proximate cause is matter that is undergoing maturation, like the state of rice becoming old. In the description of impermanence (*aniccatā-niddesa*): "decay" (*khaya*) is by way of going to destruction; "waning" (*vaya*) is by way of going to disappearance; and "breaking up" (*bhedo*) is by way of dissolution.
Alternatively, because matter, having reached that state, decays, wanes, and breaks up, it is said: "it decays in this."
‘Khayo’ means destruction; ‘vayo’ means that which disintegrates; ‘bhedo’ means that which breaks apart. By prefixing a preposition (*upasagga*), the word is expanded from *bhedo* to *paribhedo*.
In the sense of non-existence after having existed, it is not permanent, thus it is *anicca* (impermanent).
The state of that is *aniccatā* (impermanence). It is *antaradhāna* because things disappear therein. For once death is reached, material form (*rūpa*) disappears.
It goes to non-appearance. And it is not only material form alone; rather, all five aggregates are likewise.
Therefore, it should be understood that this very characteristic belongs to the impermanence of all five aggregates.

Furthermore, from the perspective of its characteristic and so forth, the impermanence of material form should be understood as having the characteristic of disintegration, the function of sagging away, the manifestation of destruction and fall, and the proximate cause of material form in the process of breaking up.
Below, birth was taken up and aging was taken up; at this point, death is taken up.
These three phenomena are like an enemy with a raised sword for these beings.
For just as if a man had three enemies wandering about seeking an opportunity [to strike him], one of them might say: "Having led him out, his entry into the forest is my [task]."
"Let it be my burden," thought the first. "Beating me and throwing me down upon the ground when we have entered the forest—that is my burden," thought the second.
"From the moment we have reached the ground, the cutting off of my head with a sword—that is my burden," thought the third.
Such are these things, beginning with birth. Having been brought out, birth here is like an enemy who leads one into the forest; in each respective place...

Because it causes [beings] to be produced. Aging is like an enemy who strikes down one gone into the wilderness and casts them to the ground, because it renders the produced aggregates weak, dependent on others, and destined for the bed.
Death is like an enemy who cuts off the head with a sword when one has reached the earth, because it brings about the destruction of the life-force of the aggregates that have reached aging.
645. In the exposition of physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*): it is called *kabaḷīkāra* because it is made into mouthfuls (*kabaḷaṃ karīyati*).

It is called *āhāra* because it is taken in (*āharīyati*); the meaning is that it is swallowed after being made into mouthfuls. Alternatively, it is also called *āhāra* because it nourishes matter (*rūpaṃ āharati*).

Having thus extracted the name by way of its basis, the passage beginning with "boiled rice, boiled bean-soup" was stated to show its classification again by way of its basis. [The items] such as boiled rice...
Indeed, there are twelve bases for the food intended here, ending with molasses.
Roots, fruits, and so forth, which are not mentioned in the text, are included under the category of "and so on" (*yevāpanaka*).
Now, in order to show what should be done regarding those roots, fruits, and so forth, he says: "In whichever country," and so on. Therein:
That which is to be eaten and consumed with the mouth is "mouth-food" (*mukhāsiya*). That which is to be chewed with the teeth is "tooth-chewing" (*dantavikhādana*).
That which is to be swallowed by the throat is "throat-swallowing" (*galajjhoharaṇīya*). Now, to show this by way of its function, he says: "distending the belly.
For when roots, fruits, and so forth, or boiled rice, sour gruel, and so forth, have been swallowed, they distend the belly. This is its [function].

The function (*kicca*). Having shown nutriment together with its basis by means of all the preceding phrases—namely, "by which nutritive essence beings subsist"—this [verse] is now stated to show the very nutritive essence produced [from that basis].
But what here is the function of the basis? And what is the function of the nutritive essence? [They are] the removal of danger and protection. The bases [remove] danger...
The *harati* (remover) is unable to protect, while the *ojā* (nutritive essence) is unable to remove dangers. When these two are combined, they are able both to protect and to remove dangers.
What, then, is this so-called "danger"? It is the fire born of karma (*kammaja-tejo*).
For when there is no material basis such as boiled rice within the belly, the fire born of karma arises and seizes the lining of the stomach.
He makes [the being] say, “I am hungry; give me food. At the time of eating, it releases the skin of the belly and seizes the underlying flesh.
Then the being becomes one with it.
For just as the Shadow-Rākṣasa, having seized the shadow that has entered [his body], binds it with a divine chain and [makes it his own].
Delighting in his abode, he comes during the time of drought and bites on the head. Having been bitten, the person cries out.
Hearing that cry, people come from here and there, thinking, "Someone has fallen into suffering here. Seizing each person as they arrive, he eats them and delights in his abode.
This should be understood as being exactly like this: for the heat born of karma is like the shadow-demon (chāyārakkhasa).
The abdominal membrane is like a being bound and placed there by a divine chain; the rice and other foodstuffs are like people who have returned;
the grasping of the abdominal membrane by the kamma-born heat when it has emerged from its source is like descending and biting on the head;
the time of crying out after being bitten is like the time of saying, "Give me food"; and having taken what comes and goes with that perception...

Just as it is the time for enjoyment after eating in a palace, so too, when the abdominal membrane is released by the heat of kamma-born fire and the food is taken into the stomach, there is one-pointedness of mind.
In that regard, the nutritive essence (*ojā*) is weak when the food is coarse; it is strong when the food is subtle.
For after eating coarse foods such as millet porridge, one becomes hungry in just a moment; whereas for one who has drunk ghee and the like, even after staying for a whole day, hunger does not arise.
It is pleasing. And here, the relative grossness and subtlety should be understood by taking each subsequent stage as a reference.
For the food of peacocks is subtle compared to the food of crocodiles; it is said that crocodiles swallow stones, which dissolve upon reaching their stomachs.
Peacocks eat creatures such as snakes and scorpions. Compared to the food of peacocks, however, [the food] of hyenas...
Their food is subtle. It is said that they eat horns and bones discarded three years prior;
these, merely moistened by their saliva, become as soft as bulbous roots for them.

Compared even to the food of hyenas, the food of elephants is subtle, for they eat the branches and other parts of various trees. Compared to the food of elephants, [the food] of the gavaya, the gokaṇṇa deer, and others...
Their food is subtle; it is said that they eat the sapless leaves and such of various trees. Even compared to their food, the food of cattle is more subtle;
they eat green and dry grass. Compared to their food, the food of rabbits is more subtle.
Compared to the food of rabbits, the food of birds is more subtle. Compared to the food of birds, the food of those living in border regions is...
Subtle. Compared to the food of those living in the borderlands, the food of village overseers is subtle. Compared to the food of village overseers, the food of royal ministers is subtle.
Compared to their food, the food of a wheel-turning monarch is subtle. Compared to the food of a wheel-turning monarch, the food of the earth-dwelling devas is subtle.
Compared to the food of the earth-dwelling devas, the food of the devas of the Four Great Kings is subtle.
It is subtle. In this way, the nutriment of the gods up to those who wield power over the creations of others should be detailed; however, their nutriment is concluded simply as "subtle.

Furthermore, it should be understood from the perspective of its characteristics and so forth that edible nutriment has the characteristic of nutritive essence (*ojā*), the function of providing material form, the manifestation of support, and the proximate cause of being taken after having been made into mouthfuls.

646. In the description of "not derived" (*noupādā*): just as derived matter (*upādārūpa*) is itself derived and is not derived by anything else, so too this [nutriment] is not derived at all; thus it is "not derived."
647. "To be touched" means *phoṭṭhabba*. The meaning is: that which is to be known by touching. It is the sense-sphere (*āyatana*) of the tangible, thus it is the *phoṭṭhabbāyatana*.
And since it is water in the sense of having the nature of being devoid of a sentient being and empty, it is the *āpodhātu* (water element).
Now, because three kinds of form are to be known by touching, in order to show them by dividing them up, [the text asks]: "What is that form..."
Regarding the sense base of the tangible, he says: "The earth element," and so forth. Therein, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness;
its function is to provide a foundation; it is manifested as receiving. The fire element has the characteristic of heat;
its function is to mature; it is manifested as the provision of softness. The air element has the characteristic of distension; its function is to cause motion; it is manifested as conveying.
The first, however, the water element, has the characteristic of trickling, the function of moistening, and is manifested as cohesion.
It should be understood that each one here has the remaining three as its proximate cause.
"Hard" means stiff; "soft" means not stiff; "smooth" means polished; "rough" means coarse; "pleasant to touch" means...

A desirable tangible object is the condition for pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*). An undesirable tangible object is painful contact (*dukkhasamphassa*), meaning it is the condition for painful feeling.
"Heavy" means burdensome; "light" means not burdensome, which is to say very light.
And here, by the terms "hard," "soft," "smooth," "rough," "heavy," and "light," the earth element itself is analyzed. "When this..."
In the Sutta it is also said: “When the body is accompanied by vitality, accompanied by heat, and accompanied by consciousness, then it becomes lighter, more pliant, and more wieldy.
This was stated specifically with reference to the earth element having become light and pliant.
However, by the two phrases “pleasant contact” and “painful contact,” all three great primary elements (mahābhūta) are distributed [among the sense bases].
For the earth element is both pleasant to touch and painful to touch; likewise for the fire element and the air element.

Therein, the earth element that is pleasant to touch, when a young person massages soft and tender hands and feet, causes them to repeatedly experience pleasure and utter the words, “Massage me, dear one! Massage me, dear one! The fire element that is pleasant to touch...
In the cold season, having brought a bed of coals, he warms his limbs; repeatedly relishing this, he makes gestures as if saying, "Warm me, dear one!

Warm me, dear one! Or, in the hot season, when the young monk is perfect in his duties, he repeatedly relishes the air-element of pleasant touch as it fans him with a fan, making gestures as if saying, "Fan me, dear one! Fan me, dear one!"
He does so. But when a young person with stiff hands massages his feet, it feels as if his bones are breaking;
he too must be told, "Go away! During the heat of the season, when a charcoal brazier is brought near, one must say, "Take it away from me!
During the cold season, when someone is fanning him with a fan, one must say, "Go away, do not fan me! Such is the case with these [sensations].
The pleasant contact and the painful contact are to be understood.

However, the thirteen sections adorned with four methods each—beginning with "the tangible that is non-manifest and impinging"—are to be understood in the same manner as explained previously for the base of visible form and the others.
But do these three great primary elements come into the range of perception simultaneously, or not? They do come.
Do those [objects] that have thus arrived strike the body-sensitivity or not? They strike it.
Does body-consciousness arise by taking them as its object all at once, or does it not arise? It does not arise.
For the taking of them as objects occurs either through the process of bending toward them or through their predominance.

In that regard, first, by way of "taking up" (*ābhujita*): when a bowl has been filled with boiled rice and one takes up a single grain while examining whether it is hard or soft, although there is also the fire element and the air element therein, one takes up only the earth element.
When one lowers the hand into hot water and examines it, although there is also the earth element therein—
There is air as well, yet one inclines toward the fire element alone.

During the heat of the day, having opened a window and standing while letting the wind strike the body, even though earth and fire are also present there when a gentle breeze blows, one inclines toward the air element alone.
In this way, by virtue of such inclination, it is said that one takes it as an object.
But when one stumbles, or strikes his head against a tree while eating, or bites on a pebble,
although there is both fire and air present there, he takes the earth element alone as his object because of its predominance.
Even when one steps on fire, although there is both earth and air present there, [he takes it as such] because of its predominance.

However, it takes the fire element alone as its object. When a strong wind strikes the eardrum and causes deafness, although earth and fire are also present there, one takes the air element alone as the object because of its predominance.
For one who takes any element as an object, body-consciousness does not arise simultaneously. [This is illustrated by] a cluster of needles...
When pierced by a single blow, the body is struck. However, body-consciousness arises in whichever part of the body the sensitivity (kāyapasāda) is most prominent;
furthermore, it arises first in whichever place the friction and impact are strongest. When a wound is being washed with a chicken feather, drop by drop...
It strikes the sensitive body-element (*kāyapasāda*). Wherever the sensitive element is predominant, there alone does body-consciousness arise.
Thus it takes the object by way of predominance. And it is precisely by way of predominance that body-consciousness is said to arise.
But how does the transition of consciousness from one object to another occur? It occurs in two ways: either through inclination (*ajjhāsaya*) or...
Or, due to the intensity of the object. For instance, one who has gone with the underlying intention (ajjhāsaya) such as, “I shall pay homage to those various shrines and images,
and I shall look upon the works of ivory-carving and painting,” even after having paid homage to or looked upon one,
proceeds to pay homage to or look upon another by forming the resolve to do so.
Thus it is said that [the mind] "transfers" by way of inclination (*ajjhāsaya*).

Furthermore, even one standing while gazing at the Great Cetiya, which resembles the peak of Mount Kelāsa, may later—when all musical instruments are played—abandon the visible object (*rūpārammaṇa*) and transfer to the audible object (*saddārammaṇa*). This also occurs with flowers or fragrances that possess pleasant scents.
Or, having relinquished the sound-object among those [objects], it passes over to the odor-object. Thus it is said to "pass over" by way of the predominance of the object. 651.

In the description of the water element (*āpodhātu*), "water" (*āpo*) is a designation for its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). Water itself is "wateryness" (*āpogataṃ*). By way of cohesion, it is "cohesion" (*sineha*);

cohesion itself is "cohesiveness" (*sinehagataṃ*). "The state of binding of matter" refers to the quality of being a binder for the primary matter (*bhūtarūpa*) such as the earth element and so forth.
For the water element, having bound together things such as lumps of clay, makes them firm. Because they are bound by it, they are called "bound.
The same principle applies to stones, mountains, palm trunks, elephant tusks, cow horns, and so forth.
For all these, the water element alone binds them together and makes them firm; it is precisely because they are bound by the water element that they are firm.
But does the earth element serve as a support for the remaining elements or not? Does it do so by touching them or without touching them?
And as for the water element binding the others, does it bind by touching or without touching?
First, the earth element serves as a support for the water element without touching it, but for the fire element and the air element, it does so by touching them.
The water element, moreover, binds together even without touching the earth element or the fire and air elements.
If it were to bind by touching them, it would have to be called the sense base of the tangible (phoṭṭhabbāyatana).
The same principle applies to the fire and air elements in performing their respective functions among the remaining elements. For the fire element—
Having touched the earth element, it burns it; yet that [earth element] does not burn by becoming hot.
If it were to burn by becoming hot, it would indeed have the characteristic of heat. However, it heats the water element without even touching it.
Even while heating, it does not heat by becoming hot. If it were to heat by becoming hot, it would indeed have the characteristic of heat. [The same applies to] the air element...
But it heats only after having made contact. Even as it heats, it does not heat by becoming hot itself.
If it were to heat by becoming hot itself, it would have the characteristic of heat. The air element supports the earth element after making contact with it;
likewise, the fire element supports the water element, but without making contact with it at all.
When sugarcane juice is boiled and being made into a mass of molasses, does the water element become stiff or not?
It does not. For that [water element] has the characteristic of trickling. The earth element has the characteristic of hardness.

However, when the water is deficient and the earth is predominant, it becomes such that it loses its state of existing in the form of juice, yet it does not lose its characteristic. [This applies to] the mass of molasses.
Even when melting away, the earth element does not vanish. For the earth element has the characteristic of hardness, while the water element has the characteristic of trickling.
However, when the earth is deficient and the water becomes predominant, the earth loses its state of existing as a solid mass, though it does not lose its characteristic.
For there is only a change in the mode of being of the four great elements.
There is no alteration of their characteristics. Their impossibility is illustrated by the *Aṭṭhānaparikappa Sutta*. For it is said:

"Ānanda, there might be an alteration of the four great elements—the earth element... [and so on] ...the air element; but there could never be an alteration in a noble disciple who possesses verified confidence in the Buddha.
This is the meaning here: Ānanda, the earth element, characterized by hardness, might turn into the water element, characterized by trickling... [and so on].

It might be called the water element; however, for a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka), there is no such thing as "changeability" (aññathatta). Thus, in this context, the consideration of impossibility (aṭṭhānaparikappa) has been presented. 652.

Regarding the subsequent explanations of appropriated form (upādiṇṇarūpa) and so forth, the meaning of terms such as "appropriated" (upādiṇṇa) is to be understood according to the method already stated in the discussion on the Schedule (mātikākathā).
It should be understood. The sense bases of the eye and so forth have already been explained in detail below; however, we shall mention only their specific distinctions here and there.
First, in the description of "clung-to" (*upādiṇṇa*), the sense bases of the eye and so forth are mentioned because they are exclusively clung-to.
But since the sense base of visible form and the others are both clung-to and not clung-to, they are shown briefly by the phrase "or whatever else," and then again...

They have been explained in detail by way of the method beginning with “the sphere of visible form due to the performance of kamma,” and so forth. By this means, the meaning should be understood in all the [categories of] “included” (yevāpanaka) states.

But why, in the exposition of both “due to the performance of kamma” and “not due to the performance of kamma,” are “aging and impermanence” not included, whereas they are included in the expositions of “not acquired by clinging” (anupādiṇṇa) and the rest? Not due to kamma...

Regarding the term *katattā* (by having been done): here, first of all, that which originates from conditions other than karma is included. In the phrase “by having done an action” (*kammassa katattā*), only that which originates from karma is meant.
These two types of matter do not arise either from karma or from any other condition that produces matter;

therefore, they are not included. And their non-arising will be made clear later. Regarding the terms *anupādiṇṇa* (not grasped) and so forth: [The text continues with the analysis of these categories.]

However, by the mere mention of "not grasped" (*anupādiṇṇa*) and so forth, the state of being originated from karma and the like is excluded, but the state of being originated from other conditions is not permitted.
Therefore, it should be understood that these are included therein.

In the description of what is originated by consciousness (*cittasamuṭṭhāna*), the pair consisting of bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*) and verbal intimation (*vacīviññatti*) is exclusively originated by consciousness.

It is manifested by depending upon the primary elements; therefore, it has been so stated. However, in the ultimate sense, its supporting primary elements are themselves mind-originated, because it is dependent upon them.
Just as the aging and death of impermanent matter are called "impermanent," so too this [matter] is designated as "mind-originated."

668. This same method applies to the exposition of what is co-existent with consciousness (*cittasahabhū*). Since wisdom (*paññā*) is manifest as long as consciousness exists, only these two are mentioned. However, this pair does not arise together with consciousness in the manner of the primary elements (*bhūta*), nor like volition (*cetanā*) and the other mental factors.

670. This same method applies to their being concomitant with consciousness (*cittānuparivatti*). Because they are manifest as long as consciousness exists, these two are said to be "concomitant with consciousness. 674.

"Gross" (*oḷārika*) means coarse, because it must be grasped by way of contact due to its nature as the physical basis (*vatthu*) and the object (*ārammaṇa*). By the reversal of what was stated, the "subtle" (*sukhuma*) should be understood.
676. Because it cannot be grasped by way of contact, even though it is situated nearby, it is "distant" due to its state of being difficult to discern.
The other, however, because it can be grasped by way of contact, is "near" due to its state of being easy to discern, even though it is situated at a distance.
The detailed explanation of the eye-base and so forth should be understood according to the method already stated above. This, first of all, is [the classification] by way of two kinds.
In the compendium of form (*rūpa-saṅgaha*), there is merely a distinction. The threefold compendium is of obvious meaning.
966. Commentary on the Exposition of the Fourfold:
At the conclusion of the fourfold compendium, because there is no further division for the final term of "seen" and so forth, [the exposition] begins from the beginning.
It has been stated that without even asking, the visible-form base (rūpāyatana) is "seen" and the sound base (saddāyatana) is "heard," and so forth.

In that context, because the visible-form base can be looked at and perceived by means of the eye, it is termed "seen. Because the sound base can be heard and known by means of the ear, it is termed "heard.
As for the triad beginning with the odor base (gandhāyatana), they are to be grasped after being reached by the nose, tongue, and body respectively.
That which is "thought" (muta) is so called in the sense of being known by means of reflection (munitvā).

It is also said to be "thought" because it is a cause for the arising of consciousness through contact (phusitvā). Furthermore, since all material form is to be known by mind-consciousness, it is thus "cognized by the mind" (manasā viññātaṃ).
Commentary on the Exposition of the Pentad.
967. In the exposition of the fivefold inclusion: *kakkhaḷa* means stiff. *Kharagata* means simply hard; the meaning is "rough.
The other two [terms] are also merely expositions of their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). *Ajjhatta* means internal to oneself. *Bahiddhā* means external.

*Upādiṇṇa* does not refer exclusively to what is originated by kamma; rather, this is a general inclusion of that which consists of the eight factors of the body. For the "eightfold body" (the four primary elements and the four derived forms) is...
Whether it be clung-to (*upādiṇṇa*) or not-clung-to (*anupādiṇṇa*), everything is called "clung-to" by way of being taken up, grasped, and adhered to. 969.

*Tejogataṃ* means the characteristic of heat that has entered into all fiery elements; or, because the fire itself has attained the state of fire, it is called "that which has gone to fire" (*tejogataṃ*).
*Usmā* is the mode of heat. *Usmāgataṃ* means having gone to the state of heat; this is simply a name for the mode of heat itself.
*Usumanti* means possessing heat. *Usumagatanti* means that which has reached the state of heat, namely heat itself. 970. *Vāyoti* is wind by way of its blowing (*vāyanaka*).

*Vāyogatanti* means that which has reached the state of wind, because it has attained the nature of wind itself. *Thambhitattanti* refers to the stiffened state of matter, like that of lotus stalks, leather, and so forth, when they are filled with air.
[End of] Commentary on the Description of the Sixfold Base (*Chakkādiniddesavaṇṇanā*).

972–4. Regarding the three groups beginning with the "sixfold" (chabbidha), because there is no variation in the concluding term, the exposition is given starting from the beginning without asking questions.
Therein, that which can be known by eye-consciousness is "to be cognized by the eye" (*cakkhuviññeyya*)...

[and so on] ...that which can be known by mind-consciousness is "to be cognized by the mind" (*manoviññeyya*). That which can be known by the three-fold mind-element is "to be cognized by the mind-element" (*manodhātuviññeyya*).

Regarding the phrase "all form" (*sabbaṃ rūpaṃ*): because there is not even a single form that cannot be known by the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), it is therefore said to be "all form.
Indeed, once the Perfectly Enlightened One had mastered the Abhidhamma, there was no place where a method (*naya*) ought to be applied that he did not apply.
And this [is the case] regarding even a single form that is unknowable to the mind-consciousness element.
There is indeed a place where it is appropriate to apply a method by way of non-existence; therefore, applying the method, he said, "all form.

(974) "Pleasant contact" is the condition for the acquisition of pleasant feeling. "Painful contact" is the condition for the acquisition of painful feeling. Here too, this method is given because of the existence of pleasure and pain within the objective field of the tangible. [End of] the commentary on the description beginning with the "new" (navaka).
975. However, in the *Navaka* (Nines), the method is given for the existence of the materiality of the sense faculties (*indriyarūpa*).

In the *Dasaka* (Tens), the method is given for their state of being with or without resistance (*sappaṭigha-appaṭighatā*). In the *Ekādasaka* (Elevens), eleven and a half bases (*āyatana*) are analyzed.
Their sections of exposition (*niddesavāra*) should be understood in detail according to the method stated below. The remainder is everywhere of obvious meaning.

**Miscellaneous Discussion:** Regarding these material phenomena (*rūpa*), for the purpose of non-confusion, one should understand this "miscellaneous discussion" (*pakiṇṇaka*) concerning their combination, their origination, and their production by conditions (*parinipphanna-saṅkhata*).
Therein, "combination" (*samodhāna*) refers to all this material form when combined: the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*)... [and so on] ... edible food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*).

Food, the tangible base, and the water element—these constitute twenty-five [types of materiality]. Together with the basic materiality (*vatthurūpa*), they should be understood as numbering twenty-six.
There is no materiality other than these. However, some claim that there is such a thing as "sleep-materiality" (*middharūpa*).
They say: "Surely you are a sage, a perfectly enlightened one; for you, there are no hindrances," and so forth.
The notion that there is no such thing as the material quality of torpor (*middharūpa*) must be refuted.

Others say that there are twenty-seven material qualities together with the material quality of strength (*balarūpa*), twenty-eight together with the material quality of cohesion (*sambhavarūpa*), twenty-nine together with the material quality of birth (*jātirūpa*), and thirty together with the material quality of disease (*rogarūpa*).
These views also must be rejected by demonstrating that those [qualities] do not exist separately from them. Regarding the air element (*vāyodhātu*):
For when the water element is grasped, the materiality of strength is indeed grasped; there is no such thing as "materiality of strength" apart from that.

When the water element is grasped, the materiality of production is grasped through its arising, accumulation, and continuity; and when decay and impermanence are grasped, the materiality of disease is indeed grasped. There is no such thing as "materiality of disease" apart from that.
Even an affliction such as an ear disease is merely the elements themselves arisen from unfavorable conditions.
There is no other thing called "disease" there; thus, when taken together, there are exactly twenty-six material phenomena.

Regarding "origination": how many material phenomena have how many origins? Ten have one origin; one has two origins; three have three origins; nine have four origins; and two do not originate from anything.
Therein, the eye-sensitivity … [and so on] … the life-faculty—these eight originate exclusively from kamma.
The dyad consisting of bodily intimation and verbal intimation arises exclusively from consciousness; thus, these ten are called “arisen from one.

Sound arises both from temperature and from consciousness; thus, this one is called “arisen from two. Therein, sound that is without consciousness arises from temperature, while sound that is with consciousness arises from consciousness.
Furthermore, the triad beginning with lightness (lahutā) arises from temperature, consciousness, and nutriment.
The three [material qualities] are called "arising from three. The remaining nine material qualities arise from those [three] and from kamma;
thus, these nine are called "arising from four. However, decay and impermanence do not arise from even one of these;
thus, these two are called "not arising from anything. Why? Because they are not born. For these two are not born. Why?
Because that which is born is subject to ripening and dissolution. For it must necessarily be admitted that once matter has arisen, it decays and breaks up;
indeed, no matter or non-matter that has arisen is ever seen to be indestructible. It is established, therefore, that as long as it does not break up, there is its ripening.
As for the phrase "because that which is born is subject to ripening and dissolution," if those [material qualities] were to be born, they too would be subject to ripening and dissolution.

[They] would [so] exist. But since what has been born undergoes ripening and disintegration, these two do not themselves arise; for there is no ripening or disintegration of that which has already arisen.

Herein, it might be argued: "Just as in the explanations such as 'due to the performance of kamma,' by the expressions 'accumulation of matter' and 'continuity of matter,' it is accepted that 'birth' itself arises, so too let 'ripening' also ripen and 'disintegration' also disintegrate."

“In that context, it is not accepted that ‘birth itself is born. However, because birth is the state of the actual production of those phenomena that are generated by karma and other causes, the conventional designation of birth as their condition is permitted. But in the ultimate sense, birth itself is not born;
for birth is merely the act of being produced in that which is being born.”

In this regard, it might be argued: "Just as birth (jāti) receives the designation of 'origination' (abhinibbatti) and the designation of 'condition' for those phenomena whose origination it is, so too let the various maturations (pākabhedā) receive the designation of 'condition' and the designation of 'origination' for those phenomena whose maturation they are.
In this way, these two [types of matter] should also be said to be originated solely by karma and so forth. To this we say: "No."
They receive that designation according to their specific mode of maturation. Why? Because they do not exist at the moment when the efficacy of the productive conditions is present.
For the efficacy of productive conditions exists only at the very moment of the arising of the dhamma to be produced, and not beyond that.
And at the moment of the dhamma produced by them, birth being manifest receives the designation of "conditionality" and the designation of "production"; at that moment—
Because of its actual existence; the other two [characteristics] do not, because they are absent at that moment. Therefore, it should be said: "This does not arise.
If it is argued that these two also arise because it is stated, "Bhikkhus, aging-and-death is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen," we say:
No, because it was taught by way of a figurative method (*pariyāya*). For in that context, regarding phenomena that have arisen dependently...
It is said that, in a figurative sense, because it possesses aging and death, that [conditioned state] is dependently originated. If it is argued:
“If that is so, then this too does not exist—being unarisen like a hare’s horn—or else it must be permanent like Nibbāna,” we say no;
for its existence is dependent upon a support. For when the supports, such as earth and the rest, exist, the triad of birth and the others [aging and death] occurs.
Because it is perceived, it is not non-existent. And because it is not perceived when those [conditions] are absent, it is not permanent.
This too was said—namely, "Bhikkhus, aging-and-death is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen"—solely in order to refute that adherence.
