By such methods as these, it should be understood that those two kinds of form do not arise from anything whatsoever.

Furthermore, there is this other meaning here for the term “origination” (*samuṭṭhāna*). Its summary table (*mātikā*) is as follows: “born of kamma, conditioned by kamma, originated by temperature conditioned by kamma;
originated by nutriment, conditioned by nutriment, originated by temperature conditioned by nutriment;
originated by temperature, conditioned by temperature, originated by temperature conditioned by temperature; originated by consciousness, conditioned by consciousness.”
"Conditioned by mind, arisen from temperature.
In this context, the eightfold materiality beginning with eye-sensitivity, together with the heart-base, is called "born of kamma.

Hair of the head, hair of the body, tusks of an elephant, manes of a horse, and tails of a yak, and so forth, are called "conditioned by kamma. The wheel-treasure [of a universal monarch] belongs to the deities.
Gardens, celestial mansions, and so forth—such as these are called "originated by kamma-conditioned temperature" (*kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhāna*).
That which has arisen from nutriment, the pure octad (*suddhaṭṭhaka*), is called "nutriment-originated" (*āhārasamuṭṭhāna*).

Edible nutriment is a condition for both types of material continuity: that which is originated by nutriment and that which is clung-to (*upādinnaka*). [This applies] to that which is originated by nutriment...

Being a producer, it becomes a condition; being a protector of that which is born of kamma—this is what is called "nutriment-condition" (*āhāra-paccaya*) for kamma-born materiality sustained by nutriment.
When one consumes unwholesome food and goes out into the heat, freckles, black moles, leprosy, and so forth arise;
this is called "arising from both nutriment-condition and temperature" (*āhāra-paccaya-utu-samutthāna*).
The pure octad arisen from temperature is called "temperature-originated. When that temperature gives rise to another octad, this is called "conditioned by temperature.
When that [second] octad also gives rise to another octad, this is called "temperature-originated conditioned by temperature.
In this way, it is able to connect only three successions.
Not beyond that. This meaning may also be illustrated by means of what is not clung-to (*anupādinnaka*).

A cloud is called "temperature-originated" (*utusamuṭṭhāna*). Rain showers are called "conditioned by temperature" (*utupaccaya*). When it rains, seeds sprout, the earth releases its fragrance, mountains appear blue, and the ocean rises; this is called "temperature-originated conditioned by temperature."
The pure octad arisen from consciousness is called "consciousness-originated" (*cittasamuṭṭhāna*).

"Post-nascent states of consciousness and mental factors are a condition for this pre-nascent body by way of post-nascence condition" (*pacchājāta-paccaya*)—this is called the "consciousness-condition" (*cittapaccaya*).
In the sky, in the atmosphere, he displays even an elephant, he displays a horse, he displays a chariot, and various [other things].
“‘Displaying an array of troops’—this is what is called ‘originated by temperature conditioned by mind.
“‘Fully accomplished’: fifteen material phenomena are called fully accomplished; ten are called unaccomplished.
‘If they were unaccomplished, they would have to be unconditioned. [Objection: But there is indeed bodily change of those very same material phenomena.”
‘Bodily intimation’ means a modification of the body; ‘verbal intimation’ means a modification of speech; ‘the space element’ means a fissure or aperture;
‘lightness’ means the state of being light; ‘malleability’ means the state of being soft; ‘wieldiness’ means the state of being workable;
‘arising’ means growth; ‘continuity’ means the process of occurrence; ‘ageing’ means the mode of decaying.
"Having been sacrificed [into non-existence], its mode of being is 'impermanence' (aniccatā). Thus, everything that is fully accomplished is indeed conditioned (saṅkhata).
The commentary on the Matter Section (Rūpakaṇḍa) of the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, the commentary on the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, is finished.
3. The Section on Deposition (Nikkhepakaṇḍa). Discourse on the Deposition of Triads (Tikanikkhepakathā): 985.
Up to this point, the triad of the wholesome has been explained in detail by way of the analysis of the words for all wholesome and other phenomena.

It exists. Furthermore, because this method of analysis for the wholesome triad has been stated, this same method of analysis applies to the remaining triads and dyads as well—just as it is here, so too [one asks]: "Which states are associated with pleasant feeling?
At whatever time a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen that is accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge..."
"Or the visible-object base... pe... or whatever other conditioned immaterial states there are at that time, excluding the feeling aggregate—these states are associated with pleasant feeling.
In this way, by following the sequence through all the triplets and dyads, the wise can discern the method of classification; therefore, that detailed exposition [is omitted].

Having set this aside, in order to show the analysis of all the pairs of phenomena (*dhamma*) by means of a method that is neither too concise nor too prolix, the "Section on Enumeration" (*Nikkhepakaṇḍa*) is commenced with the question:

"Which phenomena are wholesome? For the "Section on the Arising of Consciousness" (*Cittuppādakaṇḍa*) is a detailed exposition, while the "Commentarial Section" (*Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa*) is a concise exposition;
this "Section on Enumeration," however, follows upon the "Section on the Arising of Consciousness."
The summary is based on the *Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa*, while the detailed exposition is based on the rest; thus, it consists of both the concise and the detailed portions.

This should be understood as the *Nikkhepakaṇḍa* (the Section on Presentation) because it is taught by setting aside the detailed instruction, and also for the reasons stated below. For this has been said:
Because it is taught by setting aside [the subject] from the perspective of its root, its aggregates, its doors, its planes, its meaning, its phenomena, its names,
and its characteristics, it is called "setting aside" (nikkhepa).
For this has been taught by way of its roots, beginning with "these three wholesome roots," and so forth.
It is taught by way of the aggregates as "the aggregate of feeling associated therewith. It is taught by way of the doors as "bodily action originating therefrom";
for action that proceeds through the bodily door is called "bodily action. It is taught by way of the planes as "in the plane of happiness, in the sense-sphere realm."
It should be understood that it is taught as "taught by way of meaning, etc. because it is taught in various places according to the categories of meaning, phenomena, names, and genders.
In that regard, first, in the exposition of the wholesome factors (*kusala-pada*), "three" is the delimitation by number. They are both "wholesome" and "roots";
or alternatively, they are "roots" in the sense of being the cause, condition, source, producer, originator, and generator of wholesome phenomena.
The roots of the wholesome. Having thus shown them by way of their meaning, he now said, "Non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion," in order to show them by way of their names.

To this extent, because there is no such thing as a wholesome state that is devoid of a root, the King of Dhamma demonstrated the wholesomeness of the four planes by encompassing it within the three roots. "Associated with those" means associated with those [roots], namely non-greed and so forth.
Therein, among the formations-aggregate associated with non-greed, both non-hate and non-delusion are included within the very reckoning of the formations-aggregate associated with non-greed.

This same method applies even when they are associated by way of the other two [factors]. Thus the Dhamma-King demonstrated the wholesome states of the four planes, having further encompassed them by way of the four aggregates associated with them.
"Originated from those" means originated from those [states] such as non-greed and so forth. By this also...
By this method, the Dhamma King demonstrated that very same wholesome [consciousness] of four planes by way of the three doors of action.
Thus, first of all, the wholesome has been demonstrated by being categorized in three places.
986. The same method applies to the unwholesome as well. For among the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses, not even one is called "rootless."
The Dhamma King demonstrated that there is nothing beyond the root [consciousness] by means of the four aggregates associated with it;
he showed that there is no such thing as "unwholesome" apart from those twelve unwholesome consciousnesses themselves, which comprise the four aggregates.
Furthermore, because these states occur by way of bodily action and so forth, the Dhamma King [classified them] according to the doors of kamma.

Having exhausted [them], the Dhamma King showed them. As for what was said here, beginning with "and those defilements associated with that," therein, that which exists in a single consciousness or in a single person is called "associated" (*ekaṭṭha*). Among these, that which exists in a single consciousness is called "naturally associated" (*sahaja-ekaṭṭha*);
that which exists in a single person is called "associated by abandonment" (*pahāna-ekaṭṭha*). By means of that greed and so forth...

Or, that which stands together with what has been specified here and there as being associated with it is "associated with that" (*tadekaṭṭha*). In this regard, [it is said] in the *Saṃkiliṭṭhattika*:
"Which phenomena are defiled and subject to defilement? The three unwholesome roots—greed, hatred, and delusion—and the defilements associated with them.
And: "Which phenomena are inferior? The three unwholesome roots—greed, hatred..."

Regarding the *Vipāka-ttika* (Triplet of Resultants), although material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*), like immaterial phenomena (*arūpa-dhamma*), are indeed originated by kamma, they are not included here. This is because they are not associated with consciousness (*citta-sampayutta*) and do not arise together with consciousness (*citt’ekuppāda*). Furthermore, since they are not themselves results (*vipāka*), they are excluded from this classification. As for the immaterial phenomena that are results, they are classified as such because they are produced by wholesome or unwholesome kamma; they are not, however, wholesome or unwholesome themselves. This is because they lack the characteristic of volition (*cetanā-lakkhaṇa-rahita*). For it is volition alone that is called "kamma," and it is that which is wholesome or unwholesome. Since these resultant states are the fruits of that volition, they are designated as "resultants" (*vipāka*). Thus, the term "resultant" is applied to them by way of their being the fruit of kamma. It is in this sense that the immaterial phenomena are included in the *Vipāka-ttika*. As for the material phenomena, they are included in the *Vipāka-ttika* by way of their being the fruit of kamma, even though they are not themselves kamma or resultants. This is because they are produced by wholesome or unwholesome kamma. Just as a tree is called "sweet" because its fruit is sweet, or "bitter" because its fruit is bitter, so too these material phenomena are called "resultants" because they are the fruit of kamma. Therefore, they are included in the *Vipāka-ttika*. However, they are not included in the *Kusala-ttika* (Triplet of the Wholesome) or the *Akusala-ttika* (Triplet of the Unwholesome) because they lack the characteristic of volition. It is only volition that possesses the characteristic of kamma, and thus only volition is wholesome or unwholesome. Since these material phenomena are merely the fruit of that volition, they are not classified as wholesome or unwholesome. Consequently, they are not included in the *Kusala-ttika* or the *Akusala-ttika*. But because they are the fruit of kamma, they are included in the *Vipāka-ttika*. They do exist; however, because they lack an object (*anārammaṇa*), they are not similar to kamma.

Therefore, it is said that only immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) which possess an object (*sārammaṇa*) are "fruits" (*vipāka*) due to their similarity to kamma, just as a fruit is similar to its seed.
For when a rice seed has been sown, even though sprouts, leaves, and so forth emerge, it is not called a "rice fruit. But when the rice head has ripened and matured, [it is then called so].

In that case, the paddy itself, which resembles the seed, is called "the fruit of paddy. However, the sprouts, leaves, and so forth, being born from the seed and produced from the seed, are called "seed-born";
in the same way, it is appropriate to say that material form (*rūpa*) is either "kamma-born" or "clung-to" (*upādiṇṇa*). 994.

Regarding the triad of "clung-to," although the aggregates (*khandha*) of one whose taints are exhausted [are not clung-to], they may still be referred to as "our Elder Mātula" or "our Elder Cūḷapitu."
For those who speak thus, [the aggregates] become conditions for clinging; however, the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna are not grasped, are not adhered to, and are indeed not subject to clinging.

For just as a red-hot iron ball during the day is not a condition for flies to alight upon it, so too, because they are preponderantly fiery, they are not a condition for grasping by way of craving, conceit, or views.
They do not become conditions. Therefore it was said: "These states are not acquired and are not subject to acquisition.
998. This same method applies to those that are undefiled and non-defiling as well.

1003. In the triad of "accompanied by joy" (*pītisahagata*), joy and the other factors, having bestowed upon the co-nascent phenomena their state of being "accompanied by joy" and so forth, themselves become like the back-bone.

And when these five categories are not obtained, it is called "liberated.
In the triad of fetters to be abandoned by vision, "fetters" means bonds. "Sakkāyadiṭṭhi" (personality-belief):

it is "belief in a body" because the view exists toward the body, which is the designation for the pentad of aggregates (*khandha-pañcaka*) in the sense of being present; or, since the view itself is present in that body, it is "sakkāyadiṭṭhi."

The adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*) is the grasping of the undertaking [of the thought]: "One can be purified by virtue, one can be purified by observances, one can be purified by both virtue and observances.
Here, *idha* is a particle used to indicate location. This [term] is sometimes used with reference to the world, as it has been said:
“Here the Tathāgata appears in the world. In some instances, it refers to the Teaching, as it is said: “Right here, monks, is the ascetic;
right here is the second ascetic. In some instances, it refers to a location, as it is said:
“While standing right here, even though I have become a god...”
“Furthermore, O dear sir, my life has been regained; know this thus.

In some instances, [the particle] is used merely for the completion of the meter, as it is said: “In this case, monks, I would have finished eating and been invited to stop. However, here it should be understood as being stated with reference to the world.

Regarding the phrase “an uninstructed worldling,” it should be known that one is called “uninstructed” due to the absence of scriptural learning (*āgama*) and realization (*adhigama*). For one whose...

Because he lacks mastery, inquiry, and discernment regarding the aggregates, elements, bases, conditions, the foundations of mindfulness, and so forth, he possesses neither "scripture" (āgama) as it negates wrong views, nor "realization" (adhigama) because he has not attained that which is to be attained through practice.
Thus, "due to the absence of scripture and realization, he should be known as one who has not heard [the Dhamma]. And this person—
A "puthujjana" (worldling) is so called because of causes such as the generation (*janana*) of manifold things, or because this person is included among the multitude (*puthu*).
For he is a worldling due to causes such as the generation of manifold defilements (*kilesa*) and so forth. As it has been said:
“They generate various defilements, thus they are *puthujjana*s. They possess various unshaken views of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), thus they are *puthujjana*s.
They look toward the faces of various teachers, thus they are *puthujjana*s. They have not emerged from various destinies, thus they are *puthujjana*s.
They perform various volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*), thus they are *puthujjana*s. They are swept away by various floods (*ogha*), thus they are *puthujjana*s.”

They are called *puthujjana* because they are tormented by various and manifold fevers (*santāpa*). They are called *puthujjana* because they are consumed by various and manifold burning pains (*pariḷāha*).
They are called *puthujjana* because they are attached, greedy, infatuated, muddled, clinging, stuck, and obstructed by various and manifold objects of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).
They are called *puthujjana* because they are shut in, covered, enveloped, and hemmed in by various and manifold hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

"Ordinary people (puthujjana) are those who are covered over and shut in. Alternatively, they are called "ordinary people" because they are included among the multitude (puthu)—those who have passed beyond the path of counting, who are turned away from the noble Dhamma, and whose conduct consists of base qualities.

Or, this person is "ordinary" (puthu) because he has gone into a separate reckoning, being distinct and unassociated with the Noble Ones (ariya) who are endowed with virtues such as morality and learning; thus he is a "person of the multitude" (puthujjana). In this way, by these [reasons]...

By the two words ‘the uninstructed worldling’ (assutavā puthujjana), those who have been described by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun, as: “Two kinds of worldlings are spoken of by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun:
one is the blind worldling, and the other is the noble worldling.”
Two types of worldlings (puthujjana) have been mentioned; it should be understood that among them, the "blind worldling" is the one being discussed here.

Regarding the passage beginning with "one who does not see the Noble Ones" (ariyānaṃ adassāvī): they are called "Noble Ones" (ariya) because they are far removed from defilements (ārakattā), because they do not proceed in what is not the right way (anaye na iriyanato), because they proceed in the right way (aye iriyanato), and because they are worthy of being approached by the world together with its devas (sadevakena lokena ca araṇīyato).
Thus, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha are so designated.
Or, in this context, only Buddhas are "noble ones" (*ariya*). As it is said: "Bhikkhus, in the world with its devas... the Tathāgata is called 'noble'.
However, here "true persons" (*sappurisa*) should be understood as both Paccekabuddhas and disciples of the Tathāgata;
for they are "true persons" because they are beautiful persons due to their possession of supramundane qualities. Or rather, all these [categories] are stated in both ways.
For Buddhas, noble ones, and true persons—whether Paccekabuddhas or disciples of the Buddha—are likewise [worthy of offerings]. As it is said:
“The wise man who is grateful and mindful of benefits, who possesses virtuous friends and firm devotion;”
“He respectfully performs what is necessary for one who is suffering;
such a person they call a true man.
By this much—namely, by the qualities of gratitude and so forth—one is called a disciple of the Buddha, provided he possesses “a good friend and firm devotion.”

"Paccekabuddhas and Buddhas. Now, one who is by nature not disposed to see those noble ones and does not perform well in seeing them should be understood as "one who has not seen the noble ones" (*ariyānaṃ adassāvī*).
He is twofold: one who has not seen with the eye, and one who has not seen with knowledge (*ñāṇa*).

Of these two, it is the one who has not seen with knowledge who is intended here. For even if the noble ones are seen with the fleshly eye or the divine eye, [they are still not seen in the true sense].
They are indeed "not seen," because those eyes grasp only the mere color-form (*vaṇṇamatta*), and not the domain of noble being (*ariyabhāvagocara*).
Even jackals, dogs, and the like see the Noble Ones with their eyes, yet they are not seers of the Noble Ones.
Here is an illustration of this: it is said that there was an elderly renunciant who was the attendant to an elder monk whose taints were destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) living on Mount Cittala.
One day, having walked for alms with the Elder and returning behind him while carrying the Elder’s bowl and robes, he asked the Elder:
“Venerable sir, what indeed are those called ‘Noble Ones’ (ariya) like? The Elder replied:

“In this case, a certain elderly man, though walking together with the Noble Ones while carrying their bowls and robes and performing his duties of service, does not recognize them as Noble Ones at all.”
"Thus, friends, the noble ones understand. Even when this was said, he did not yet know. Therefore, seeing with the eye is not "seeing";
rather, it is the vision of knowledge (*ñāṇadassana*) alone that is "seeing. As it was said: "What, Vakkali, is the use of seeing this putrid body?
He who sees the Dhamma, Vakkali, he sees me. Therefore, even one who sees with the eye—

One who does not see with wisdom the characteristics of impermanence and so forth as perceived by the Noble Ones, and who does not attain the Dhamma attained by the Noble Ones—because he has not seen the qualities that make one noble nor the state of being noble—he is to be understood as "one who has not seen the Noble Ones.
"Unskilled in the Noble Dhamma" means unproficient in the Noble Dhamma distinguished by the foundations of mindfulness and so forth. Regarding "undisciplined in the Noble Dhamma," here:
The discipline (*vinaya*) is twofold, and each of these two is fivefold here.
Because one lacks that [discipline], one is called "undisciplined" (*avinīta*).
Indeed, this discipline is twofold: the discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-vinaya*) and the discipline of abandonment (*pahāna-vinaya*). And within these two types of discipline, each individual...

The Vinaya is fivefold. For the Vinaya of restraint is fivefold: the restraint of virtue, the restraint of mindfulness, the restraint of knowledge, the restraint of patience, and the restraint of energy. The Vinaya of abandonment is also fivefold:
abandonment by substitution of opposites, abandonment by suppression, abandonment by cutting off, abandonment by subsiding, and abandonment by escape.

In this context, “he is endowed with, fully endowed with, this restraint of the Pātimokkha” refers to the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*). “He guards the eye faculty; he attains restraint over the eye faculty” refers to the restraint of mindfulness (*sati-saṃvara*).
“Whatever streams there are in the world, O Ajita,” said the Blessed One, “mindfulness is their dam.”
“I call it the restraint of the streams;
by wisdom they are closed.
This is called the restraint of knowledge (*ñāṇasaṃvara*). “He is patient with cold and heat”—this is the restraint of patience (*khantisaṃvara*). “When [a thought] has arisen... [and so forth].
“He does not tolerate thoughts of sensual desire”—this is restraint by energy.

Furthermore, this entire restraint is called “restraint” (saṃvara) because it restrains the bodily misconduct and so forth that ought to be restrained, and it is called “discipline” (vinaya) because it disciplines them.
Thus, first of all, it should be understood that “restraint-discipline” (saṃvaravinaya) is divided fivefold.
Likewise, because they act as opposites to the various types of insight-knowledge such as the discernment of name-and-form,
each specific insight-knowledge abandons its corresponding disadvantage, just as the light of a lamp dispels darkness— for example,
personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) by means of the definition of name-and-form, and the views of no-cause and wrong cause by means of the discernment of conditions.
Subsequently, by means of the overcoming of doubt, [he abandons] the state of being perplexed; by means of the comprehension of groups, the grasping at "I" and "mine";
by means of the discrimination between the path and what is not the path, the perception of a path where there is no path; by means of the vision of arising, the view of annihilationism;
by means of the vision of passing away, the view of eternalism; by means of the vision of danger, the perception of safety in what is dangerous; and by means of the vision of disadvantage...
The abandoning of the perception of gratification by means of the contemplation of disenchantment; the abandoning of the perception of delight by means of the knowledge of the desire for deliverance;
the abandoning of non-equanimity by means of the knowledge of equanimity; the abandoning of the contrary state toward the stability of phenomena and Nibbāna by means of conformity;
and the abandoning of the grasping at the sign of formations by means of change-of-lineage—this is called "abandoning by substitution of opposites" (*tadaṅga-pahāna*).
Furthermore, the abandoning of those various states such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), by means of concentration— distinguished as access (*upacāra*) and absorption (*appanā*)—
which prevents the occurrence of existence just as a blow from a jar [removes] moss from the surface of water, is called "abandoning by suppression" (*vikkhambhanappahāna*).
[And] that which, through the cultivation of the four noble paths, occurs within the continuum of one who possesses each respective path, regarding the various views (*diṭṭhigata*)...

The abandonment of the mass of defilements belonging to the side of origination—which is described by the method beginning with “for the sake of abandoning”—by way of their absolute non-occurrence, is called ‘abandonment by cutting off’ (samucchedappahāna).
Furthermore, that state of the defilements being subsided at the moment of the fruit (phala) is called ‘abandonment by subsidence’ (paṭippassaddhippahāna).
That which has abandoned all conditioned things because it has escaped from all the conditioned is [the abandonment] of all the conditioned.
Nirvana—this is what is called "abandonment as escape" (*nissaraṇa-pahāna*).

And because all this abandonment is abandonment in the sense of relinquishing (*cāga*) and discipline (*vinaya*) in the sense of leading away (*vinayana*), it is therefore called "discipline as abandonment" (*pahāna-vinaya*).
Alternatively, it is called "discipline as abandonment" because each specific discipline arises for one who possesses its respective abandonment. Thus, discipline as abandonment is also fivefold.
It should be understood that it "breaks. Thus, this Vinaya is twofold in brief, and tenfold when analyzed;
because of the breaking of restraint and because of the non-abandonment of what ought to be abandoned, it does not exist for this uninstructed worldling. Therefore, due to its absence in him—

The same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates as well.
In that context, “one regards form as self” means that pure form alone is stated to be the self. Or:
“the self possesses form,” or “form is in the self,” or “the self is in form”; [likewise] one regards feeling as self... perception... [and so on].
In these seven instances— “one regards volitional formations … consciousness as self”— it is stated that “the formless is the self. Or,

by way of three permutations for each of the four aggregates— “the self possesses feeling,” “feeling is in the self,” or “the self is in feeling”— it is stated in twelve instances that “the self is a mixture of form and formlessness.”
In this context, the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*) is stated in these five instances: "one regards form as self," "feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness as self.
In the remaining cases, it is the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*).
Thus, there are fifteen views of existence (*bhavadiṭṭhi*) and five views of non-existence (*vibhavadiṭṭhi*) here. All of them are obstacles to the Path, not obstacles to heaven.
It should be understood that [this person] is to be abandoned by the first path.
"He doubts the Teacher" means he doubts either the Teacher’s physical body, his qualities, or both.
Doubting the physical body, he wonders: "Does a body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man exist, or does it not?"
He doubts. Doubting regarding the qualities, he doubts: "Does the omniscient knowledge capable of knowing the past, future, and present exist, or does it not? Doubting in both respects, he [doubts]:

"Having penetrated the omniscient knowledge capable of knowing all that is to be known, [is the Blessed One] endowed with the perfection of the physical body, adorned by the eighty minor marks and the fathom-wide radiance?"
He doubts whether "there exists one called a Buddha, a world-deliverer, established [in the world]," or "does he not exist?

This is called doubting in both respects because he doubts regarding either his own person or his qualities. "Is skeptical" (*vicikicchati*) means that, being unable to determine the object, he is troubled and exhausted.
"Does not resolve" (*nādhimuccati*) means that he does not obtain conviction (*adhimokkha*) in that very same thing. "Does not become serene" (*na sampasīdati*)...
Having made the mind turbid, one is unable to have confidence; one does not have confidence in the qualities.

Regarding such passages as "one doubts the Dhamma," [it refers to] the four noble paths which abandon the defilements, the four fruits of recluseship in which the defilements have been pacified, and that which is called the deathless Great Nibbāna, which serves as the object-condition for the paths and fruits.
One who doubts, thinking "Does it exist or does it not exist?", and one who doubts, thinking "Is this Dhamma leading to liberation or not leading to liberation?", is said to doubt the Dhamma.

One who doubts, thinking "Do these four who stand on the paths and four who stand on the fruits—the Jewel of the Saṅgha—exist or do they not exist?", and one who doubts, thinking "Is this Saṅgha practicing rightly or practicing wrongly? [is said to doubt the Saṅgha].
Even one who doubts, thinking, "Is there indeed a fruit of ripening for what is given to this Jewel of the Saṅgha, or is there not?
is said to doubt the Saṅgha. Even one who doubts, thinking, "Do the three trainings exist, or do they not?
or "Is there indeed a benefit resulting from the condition of training in the three trainings, or is there not? is said to doubt the training.
The "past" refers to the past aggregates, elements, and bases. The "future" refers to those yet to come.
In this context, one who doubts whether the past aggregates and so forth "did exist or did not exist" is said to doubt regarding the past.
One who doubts whether the future aggregates and so forth "will exist or will not exist" is said to doubt regarding the future. One who doubts in both respects...
One is said to be "doubting about the past and the future. One who doubts, thinking, "Does this twelvefold cycle of conditions exist or not?
is said to be doubting regarding those phenomena that have arisen dependently through specific conditions (*idappaccayatā-paṭiccasamuppanna*). Herein, this is the etymological meaning:
the conditions for these [phenomena] such as aging-and-death are "specific conditions" (*idappaccaya*). The state of being specific conditions is "specific-conditionality" (*idappaccayatā*).
Or, "conditionality" (*idappaccayatā*) is simply the state of having this as its condition; it is a designation for birth and so forth.
Because they have arisen in dependence upon and by coming to those respective factors among birth and so forth, they are called "dependently arisen" (*paṭiccasamuppanna*). This is what is meant:
he doubts both regarding conditionality and regarding dependently arisen phenomena.
1009. By "virtue" (sīlena) is meant cow-virtue and so forth. By "observance" (vatena) is meant cow-observance and so forth. By "virtue-and-observance" (sīlabbatena) is meant both of these together.
"Purity" (suddhi) refers to purity from defilements; or it refers to Nibbāna itself, which is ultimate purity.

"Associated with that" (tadekaṭṭhā) here means associated with the task of abandoning. And in this passage, only two types of defilement are mentioned: the defilement of views and the defilement of doubt. Greed, hatred...
Delusion, conceit, sloth, restlessness, lack of moral shame, and lack of moral dread— these eight, however,
have not yet been mentioned and must be brought forward for explanation. For here, when wrong view and doubt are being abandoned,
all these— greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, sloth, restlessness, lack of moral shame, and lack of moral dread— which are factors to be abandoned together with them, are also abandoned.
However, it should be illustrated by bringing forward the term "conascent-to-be-abandoned" (*sahajekaṭṭha*).
For, by means of the stream-entry path (*sotāpatti-magga*), five types of consciousness are abandoned: the four associated with views (*diṭṭhi*) and that associated with doubt (*vicikicchā*).

Among these, when the two types of spontaneous (*asaṅkhārika*) view-consciousness are abandoned, the defilements—namely greed (*lobha*), delusion (*moha*), restlessness (*uddhacca*), shamelessness (*ahirika*), and fearlessness of wrongdoing (*anottappa*)—are abandoned by way of being conascent-to-be-abandoned (*sahajekaṭṭha-vasena*) with them.
The remaining defilements of wrong view and the defilement of doubt are abandoned by way of being abandoned together with [the path].

Even when the impulsions associated with views are abandoned, the defilements of greed, delusion, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness that are co-nascent with them are abandoned by way of being abandoned together with their co-nascent factors. The remaining defilements of wrong view...

And the defilement of doubt are abandoned by way of being abandoned together with [the path]. Thus, since "being abandoned together" (pahānekaṭṭha) itself implies "arising together" (sahajekaṭṭha), they brought forward and elucidated this "arising together.
"Associated with those" means associated with those eight defilements which are abandoned together with [the path]. Or, having made a distinction:
By that greed and by that hatred—in this way, association with each one individually should be illustrated.

Therein, when greed is taken, delusion, conceit, sloth, restlessness, lack of moral shame, and lack of moral dread—this group of defilements within the aggregate of mental formations is called "associated with greed.
When hatred is taken, delusion, sloth, restlessness, lack of moral shame, and lack of moral dread—this [group]...
The group of defilements associated with hatred consists of greed, conceit, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing.

When delusion is taken [as the primary factor], this group of defilements—consisting of greed, hatred, conceit, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing—is called "associated with delusion. When conceit is taken [as the primary factor], the group of defilements consisting of greed, delusion, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing that arise together with it is called "associated with conceit."

By this method, the construction should be made as follows: "associated with that [state] which is associated with that greed, that restlessness, that lack of moral shame, and that lack of moral dread.
Regarding "originated by that": the meaning is "arisen from that greed... [and so on] ...up to that lack of moral dread."
Regarding the statement, “These states are to be abandoned by seeing”: here, “seeing” refers to the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*);
the meaning is that they are to be abandoned by means of that [path]. But why is the path of stream-entry called “seeing”? Because it is the first [moment] of seeing Nibbāna. [Objection:
But does not the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu*) see even earlier? [Reply: It is not that it does not see; however, although it sees, the task still remains to be performed.
He does not act [in this way] because he has not abandoned the fetters (*saṃyojana*). Therefore, it cannot be said that "he sees.

In this regard, the illustration is a countryman who, although he has seen the king somewhere and presented him with a gift, says, "Even today I have not seen the king," because he has not witnessed the fulfillment of his purpose.
1011. “The remainder of greed” means that which remains after what has been abandoned by vision. The same method applies to hatred and delusion as well.
For it is only those [defilements] leading to the states of misery (apāya) that are abandoned by vision. However, this was said in order to show others besides those;
thus, “associated with them” refers to the five defilements that are associated with, and abandoned together with, the three defilements mentioned in the text. Nor...

The phrase "by seeing, not by cultivation" is stated with reference to the fact that [certain defilements] cannot be abandoned by those paths, just as is the case with the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth.

However, it has been said: "By the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, through the cessation of volitional consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa*), name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa*)—which would otherwise arise throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra-vaṭṭa*) setting aside the seven [remaining] existences—cease right here," and so on.

It should be understood that by way of this method, the abandoning of even wholesome states and so forth is also permitted; however, this was stated with reference to this specific approach: that those [states] which would arise because those paths have not been developed are "abandoned" because the defilements that serve as their decisive support conditions (*upanissaya-paccaya*) have been abandoned. 1013.
In the triad of "states whose roots are to be abandoned by vision," having determined that "these states have roots to be abandoned by vision,"...

Furthermore, after showing those things to be abandoned by means of the passage beginning "the three fetters," it was stated in order to show that, by virtue of being associated with them (*tadekaṭṭha*), they are both causes and possessed of causes. In this regard, although among the causes to be abandoned by vision,

delusion accompanied by greed is possessed of a cause by way of greed, delusion accompanied by hatred is possessed of a cause by way of hatred, and both greed and hatred are possessed of a cause by way of delusion— these are all included under the category of "causes to be abandoned."

They are included [in the category of states with roots]. However, delusion accompanied by doubt is itself a root because of the absence of any other associated root, and thus it is not "with-root" (sahetuka).
To show its abandonment, it is said: "These states have roots to be abandoned by vision.
In the second phrase, to show the abandonment of delusion accompanied by restlessness, it says: "These states [are to be abandoned] by cultivation."
It is said, "having roots that are to be abandoned. For that [delusion], having made the states associated with itself possessive of roots, becomes like a "back-bone" (piṭṭhivaṭṭaka);
because it lacks any other root associated with it—being like that which is accompanied by doubt—it does not partake of the category of "having roots that are to be abandoned.
In the third phrase, the term "unwholesome" is mentioned again for the sake of including the remaining unwholesome states, namely those accompanied by doubt and restlessness.

This has been done for the purpose of grouping the delusions (*moha*). For they, due to the absence of an associated cause (*sampayutta-hetu*), are not called "having a cause to be abandoned" (*pahātabba-hetuka*).
1029. In the triad of limited objects (*paritta-ārammaṇa*): *ārabbha* means having made an object.

Whether they themselves are limited or sublime, those that have arisen having made limited phenomena their object are "limited-object" (*paritta-ārammaṇa*); those that have made sublime [phenomena] their object...
Those that arise having a sublime object are *mahaggatārammaṇā*; those that arise having made an immeasurable object are *appamāṇārammaṇā*.
These, moreover, may be limited (*paritta*), sublime (*mahaggata*), or immeasurable (*appamāṇa*). 1035.
In the triad concerning wrongness, "immediate" (*ānantarika*) means those that yield their fruit without interval; this refers to such deeds as matricide and so forth.
This is a synonym. For among those [karmas], even when a single deed has been performed, it prevents another deed from finding an opportunity for its own fruition.

Indeed, even if one were to construct a golden stupa the size of Mount Sineru, or cause a monastery with a wall made of jewels as large as a world-system to be built and fill it, and then sit there before the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha—
Even for one who provides the four requisites throughout their entire life, that merit is not able to avert the ripening of these [other] karmas.
And as for "wrong view that is fixed," this refers to any one among the doctrines of non-causality (*ahetukavāda*), non-action (*akiriyavāda*), or nihilism (*natthikavāda*).
For even a hundred Buddhas or a thousand Buddhas cannot awaken a person who stands firm having grasped such a view.

1038. In the triad on the path as object (*maggārammaṇattika*), "having taken the noble path as an object" means having made the supramundane path the object. These [mental states] are both limited (*paritta*) and sublime (*mahaggata*).

1039. In the description of the path as cause (*maggahetuka-niddesa*), by the first method, the state of being with-cause (*sahetuka*) of the aggregates associated with the path is shown by way of the causal condition (*paccayaṭṭha*).
By the second method, the remaining path factors are [shown to have their state of being with-cause] by way of the cause consisting of right view, which is the path itself.
The state of being with a cause has been shown. By the third method, it should be understood that the state of right view having a cause is shown by means of the causes arisen in the path.
"Making it the predominant factor" means making it the objective-predominant factor (*ārammaṇādhipati*); and these, moreover, are only limited states (*parittadhammā*).
For noble disciples, when they reflect upon their own path while holding it in high esteem, the predominance of the object (*ārammaṇādhipati*) is obtained.

However, when a noble disciple reflects upon another’s path by means of the knowledge of penetration of minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*), even though he holds it in high esteem, he does not esteem it as highly as the path he himself has realized.
[This is like] regarding the Tathāgata performing the Twin Miracle...
"Having seen it, does he revere that path or not? He does revere it, but not as he does his own path.
An Arahant does not revere any phenomenon except for the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna. Here too, this is the meaning.
"Predominance of investigation"—this is stated to show co-nascent predominance (*sahajātādhipati*). For having made desire (*chanda*) the foremost...
For one developing the path with zeal as the dominant factor, it is called "zeal-dominant," not the path.
The remaining factors are also called "zeal-dominant," not "path-dominant. The same principle applies to the mind (citta).
However, for one developing the path by making investigation (vīmaṃsā) the preeminent factor, it is both "investigation-dominant" and the "path"; the remaining factors are "path-dominant."

...are the names [of these states]. The same method applies to energy (*vīriya*) as well. 1041. In the exposition of the "arisen triad" (*uppanna-ttika*): "arisen" (*jātā*) means produced (*nibbattā*), having acquired a state of being (*paṭiladdhattabhāvā*). "Become" (*bhūtā*) and so forth are synonyms for those very same terms.

For it is precisely that which has arisen which, through the attainment of its own nature, is "become. Because it has arisen through the conjunction of conditions, it is "fully arisen" (*sañjātā*). Because it has attained the characteristic of production, it is...
*Nibbattā*. By adding a prefix to the word, it is said to be *abhinibbattā* (reborn).
*Pākaṭībhūtā* means manifested. *Uppannā* means risen from the past. By adding a prefix to the word, it is said to be *samuppannā* (arisen together).
In the very sense of being reborn, it is *uṭṭhitā* (standing up); when combined with a suffix, it is *samuṭṭhitā* (fully arisen). Again...

The reason for using the term "arisen" (uppanna) should be understood in the same manner as explained below. "Included by the arisen portion" means they have been counted by way of the category of the arisen.
"Form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness"—this is the demonstration of their intrinsic nature (sabhāva).
The description of the second term should be understood by way of the method of negation already stated. The description of the third term is indeed plain in meaning.
This triad, however, is presented by way of two time periods. For the ripening of karma that has found an opportunity is twofold:
that which has reached its moment (*khaṇappatta*) and that which has not yet reached it (*appatta*). Therein, "that which has reached its moment" is called "arisen.

"That which has not yet reached it" may arise either in the immediate next moment of consciousness or even after the passing of a hundred thousand eons. In terms of being a stable condition, there is no difference between them.
There is no such thing as "non-arising"; rather, there are phenomena called "arising. For instance, it is said:
"At this very moment, Poṭṭhapāda, the formless self consisting of perception remains. Then, for this person, one perception arises and another perception ceases.

Herein, even at the time when perceptions of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) are occurring within the formless realm (ārūpa), although the perception of the root-life-continuum (mūlabhavanga) [remains].
However, at the time when the perception of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara-saññā*) has ceased, that [perception] will necessarily arise;

thus, not being reckoned as a self consisting of the formless (*arūpa*), it is understood as "it simply remains. In exactly the same way, the result of karma that has found its opportunity is twofold...
[omission] ...in the sense of being a stable condition (*dhuvapaccaya*), it is not called "non-existent," but rather it is known as "states that are subject to arising" (*uppādino dhammā*).
If, however, all accumulated wholesome and unwholesome karma were to yield its result immediately, there would be no opportunity for other [karma].
That [karma] is of two kinds: that with certain ripening (*dhuvavipāka*) and that with uncertain ripening (*adhuvavipāka*).

Among these, the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*), the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and the four noble paths (*ariyamagga*) are called "with certain ripening. Furthermore, even when that [certain ripening] has reached the moment [of fruition],...
It exists, even though it has not yet arrived. In this context, that which has reached its moment is called "arisen. That which has not yet arrived is called "unarisen.
Whether its result arises in the immediate succession of the mind or only after the passing of a hundred thousand eons, in the sense of being a stable condition, it is not called "unarisen";
rather, it is said that phenomena which are destined to arise have been born. This refers to the path of the Bodhisatta Metteyya.
"Unarisen" means that only those phenomena (dhammas) which are subject to arising have come into being as the fruit.
In the exposition of the triad of the past: "Past" means having transcended the three moments. "Ceased" means having reached cessation.
"Departed" means having gone to non-existence, or having vanished. "Transformed" means having undergone change through the relinquishing of their original nature.

"Gone" (*gatā*). "Gone to the goal known as cessation" (*nirodha-saṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ gatā*) means they have reached their end (*atthaṅgatā*). "Completely gone" (*abbhatthaṅgatā*) is a phrase expanded by means of a prefix (*upasagga*).
"Having arisen, they have vanished" (*uppanjitvā vigatā*) means having been produced, they have disappeared.

The reason for using the past tense here has already been stated below. This same method applies to the future and so forth hereafter. "Included within the past" (*atītaṃsena saṅgahitā*) means by way of the past category (*atītakoṭṭhāsena*).
They have been enumerated. Which are they? Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. The same method applies to the subsequent sections on the future and so forth. 1047.

In the exposition of the triad of objects with past referents, regarding the phrases "having taken past phenomena as object" and so forth, only limited (*paritta*) and sublime (*mahaggata*) phenomena are to be understood. For these arise having taken the past and other [time periods] as their objects. 1050.
In the exposition of the triad of internal states, the two phrases "of those various" encompass all sentient beings. *Ajjhattaṃ* (internally).
“Individual” (*paccatta*) is a designation for both [the internal and the personal]. “Inherent” (*niyata*) means born within oneself.
“Belonging to each individual” (*pāṭipuggalika*) means belonging to each distinct person. “Clung-to” (*upādiṇṇa*) means residing in the body.
For whether they are produced by kamma or not, they are here called “clung-to” in the sense of having been taken up, grasped, and adhered to.
1051. *Parasattānaṃ* means of all beings other than oneself. *Parapuggalānaṃ* is a synonym for that same term. The rest is exactly as stated below. *Tadubhayaṃ* means both of those. 1053.

In the first clause of the triad of internal objects (*ajjhattārammaṇattika*), limited (*paritta*) and sublime (*mahaggata*) states are to be understood. In the second, the immeasurable (*appamāṇa*) are also included.
In the third, only the limited and sublime are included; however, the immeasurable are at times external and at times internal.
They do not take it as an object. The exposition of the "visible-with-form triad" (sanidassanattika) is indeed already clear.

1062. Regarding the exposition of the pairs (duka), in the description of non-hatred (adosa): it is *metti* by way of the act of loving-kindness (*mettāyana*). The mode of loving-kindness is *mettāyana*. For one who has acted with loving-kindness...

The state of a mind possessed of loving-kindness (*mettā*) is "loving-kindliness" (*mettāyitatta*). It is called "compassionate" (*anuddā*) because it feels compassion; the meaning is that it protects.

The mode of being compassionate is "compassionateness" (*anuddāyanā*). The state of one who has become compassionate is "compassionateness" (*anuddāyitatta*). The desire for welfare (*hitesitā*) arises through the seeking of what is beneficial. Compassion (*anukampā*) arises through the mode of pitying.
By all these terms, only loving-kindness (*mettā*) that has reached the stages of access (*upacāra*) and absorption (*appanā*) is expressed.
By the remaining terms, non-hatred (adosa) is described as both mundane and supramundane. 1063.
In the description of non-delusion (amoha), "knowledge regarding suffering" refers to wisdom (paññā) concerning the truth of suffering.

The same method applies to the phrases "regarding the origin of suffering," and so forth. Furthermore, in this context, knowledge regarding suffering pertains to hearing, comprehension, penetration, and review. Likewise...
Regarding the origin of suffering; regarding cessation, however, it consists only in hearing, penetration, and reviewing.

Likewise regarding the way leading thereto. Regarding the past means in the past section. Regarding the future means in the future section. Regarding both the past and the future means in both those sections.
"Knowledge of things as they have arisen dependently upon this or that condition" means: "This is the condition; this is the dependently arisen."
"Depending on this, that arises"—such is the knowledge regarding conditions and the phenomena arisen from conditions.
In the exposition of greed (*lobha*), the meaning of the terms not yet explained below is as follows: it is *rāga* (lust) by way of coloring (*rañjana*).

It is *sārāga* (passion) in the sense of intense coloring. It is *anunaya* (adherence) because of its inclining toward sense objects for sentient beings. It is *anurodha* (indulgence) because one is "fond of" (*anurujjhati*); the meaning is that one desires.
“Delight” (*nandī*) is that by which beings rejoice in any state of existence whatsoever, or that which itself rejoices.
This delight, in the sense of being a coloring (*rañjana*), is “lust-delight” (*nandī-rāga*). In this context, craving (*taṇhā*) that arises once toward a single object is called “delight”;
when it arises again and again, it is called “lust-delight. It is the “coloring of the mind,” which—as stated previously—is a powerful coloring in its essential nature.
It is called "attachment" (*sārāga*); the meaning is that it is not the attachment of a being, but rather the attachment of the mind itself.

It is "desire" (*icchā*) because by means of it they desire objects. It is "infatuation" (*mucchā*) because by means of it living beings become infatuated due to the state of having abundant defilements.
It is "clinging" (*ajjhosāna*) in the sense of grasping after having swallowed and fully digested [the object]. By this, beings are "greedy" (*gijjhanti*), meaning they fall into greed.
*Gedha* means greed; or, in the sense of density, it is *gedha*. For it is said, “greed or a thicket of trees,” precisely in the sense of density.
The following term is expanded by means of a prefix (*upasagga*). Or, greed on every side is *paligedha*. It is called *saṅga* because one is attached by means of it;
or, in the sense of clinging, it is *saṅga*. In the sense of sinking down, it is *paṅka*. In the sense of dragging along, it is *ejā*.
“For craving drags this person along toward the production of this or that state of existence,” so it is said.

It is called *māyā* (deceit) in the sense of deception; it is called *janikā* (the progenitor) in the sense of generating beings within the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). For it is said: “Craving generates the person;
his mind runs hither and thither. Thus, by yoking beings to suffering within the round of existence, it generates them.
It is "generative" (*sañjananī*). In the sense of joining together, it is "sewing" (*sibbinī*).

For this [craving] sews and joins beings within the round of existence by way of death and rebirth-linking, just as a tailor joins one piece of cloth to another; therefore, it is called "sewing" in the sense of joining.
It is "net-like" (*jālinī*) because it possesses a net of manifold objects, or because it has a net characterized by the agitation and settling of craving.
It is called *saritā* (a stream) in the sense of drawing [toward objects], like a river with a swift current; or it is *saritā* in the sense of being moist. For this has been said:
"The streams and the moistenings of a person are the joys. Here, the meaning is that they are both moist and sticky.
It is *visatā* (clinging) in the sense of clinging (*visatta*). It is *visatā* in the sense of spreading (*visaṭa*). It is *visatā* in the sense of being extensive (*visāla*).
It clings (*visakkati*), thus it is clinging (*visattikā*). It deceives (*visaṃvādikā*), thus it is clinging. It scatters apart (*visaṃharati*), thus it is clinging.
It has poison as its root (*visamūlā*), thus it is clinging. It has poison as its fruit (*visaphalā*), thus it is clinging. It is the enjoyment of poison (*visaparibhogā*), thus it is clinging.

Or else, that craving is called clinging because it spreads out (*vitthātā*) over forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, mental objects, families, and social groups. In the sense of leading to misfortune and ruin...
It is called a "thread" (*sutta*) because it is like a thread that binds a tortoise. For this has been said: "A 'thread,' monks, is a designation for delight-and-lust.

It is "spread out" (*visaṭā*) in the sense of being extended over forms and so forth. It is "entangling" (*āyūhinī*) because it causes beings to strive (*āyūheti*) for the sake of obtaining this or that.
It is a "companion" (*dutiyā*) in the sense of providing assistance by not allowing one to become disenchanted. For this [craving] is... of beings.
It does not allow one to become weary of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*), but causes one to delight in every place one goes, like a dear friend. Therefore it is said:
“Accompanied by craving, a person wanders through the long course of existence;
In this state or another, he does not transcend the cycle of rebirth.”
Aspiration is so called by way of its act of aspiring. "The lead-rope of existence" (*bhavanetti*) means the rope of existence.
For by this, beings are led to whatever place they desire, like oxen bound by the neck with a rope. It is called *vana* because it seeks (*vanati*), frequents, or clings to various objects;
or alternatively, it is called *vana* because it seeks or entreats. The term *vanatha* is a word formed by the addition of a suffix.
It is called "the forest" (*vana*) because it is like a forest in the sense of being a source of misfortune and suffering, and in the sense of being a dense thicket;
this is a name for powerful craving (*taṇhā*). But that which is even denser than that, being more powerful, is called "the jungle" (*vanatha*). Thus it was said:
"Cut down the forest, not the tree; from the forest, fear is born."
“Having cut through both the forest and the undergrowth, become free from the forest, O bhikkhus!
*Santhava* (familiarity) means by way of intimacy; the meaning is “association. It is twofold: intimacy through craving (*taṇhā-santhava*) and intimacy through friendship (*mitta-santhava*).

Of these, it is intimacy through craving that is intended here. *Sineha* (affection) is by way of endearment. One “looks back with longing” (*apekkhati*) by way of making a dwelling-place (*ālaya-karaṇa*).
Longing (*apekkhā*). And this has also been said: "O King, here are these eighty-four thousand cities, with Kusāvatī as the capital.
O King, generate desire for these; place your longing (*apekkha*) on life. Here, the meaning is "make an attachment" (*ālayaṃ karohi*).
It is called a bond (*paṭibandhu*) because it binds to each respective object. Or, it is individual (*pāṭiyekka*) in the sense of being a kinsman (*ñātaka*).
"Bandhūti" means "a close relative. For there is no kinsman for sentient beings equal to craving (*taṇhā*) in the sense of being a constant support.

It is called "longing" (*āsā*) because it does not abandon its objects; the meaning is that it both overwhelms and consumes them without reaching satiety. It is "longing" (*āsisanā*) by way of desiring;
"the state of longing" (*āsisitattaṃ*) is the abstract quality of that which has longed. Now, [the text describes] the sphere of its occurrence.

To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with "craving for forms" (*rūpāsā*) was spoken. Therein, taking the meaning of "craving" (*āsā*) as "longing" (*āsīsana*), one should understand the nine terms in the same way:
craving for forms is "craving for forms" (*rūpāsā*). Among these, the first five are stated by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
The sixth is by way of greed for requisites (*parikkhāra-lobha*), which specifically pertains to those who have gone forth. The three following that are—
[This is] by way of the objects of non-contentment for householders. For there is nothing dearer to them than wealth, children, and life.
It is called *jappā* because it causes beings to long, thinking, “This is mine, this is mine,” or “This was given to me by so-and-so, this was given to me.
The following two terms are augmented by prefixes. After that, [it is explained] in another manner.
Because it was begun to be analyzed, it is stated again as "jappā. The manner of longing is *jappanā*.
The state of having longed for is *jappitattaṃ*. That which repeatedly seizes or draws toward an object is *lolupo*.
The state of being greedy is *loluppaṃ*. The manner of greed is *loluppāyanā*. The state of one possessing greed is *loluppāyitattaṃ*.

"Tail-wagging" (*pucchañjikatā*) is the name for that craving by which one wanders about trembling in places where gains are obtained, like dogs wagging their tails; it is the craving characterized by such trembling.
"One who desires well" (*sādhukāmo*) is so called because he desires objects that are pleasant and agreeable; the state of being such a person is "the desire to do well" (*sādhukamyatā*).
"Unrighteous lust" (*adhammarāgo*) is lust for improper objects, such as one's mother or maternal aunt; [it is also lust] even for proper objects—
Having become strong, greed that has arisen is "uneven greed" (*visamalobha*).

Alternatively, according to such statements as "lust is uneven," the desire and lust (*chandarāga*) that arises—whether in an appropriate place or an inappropriate place—should be understood as "unrighteous lust" (*adhammarāga*) in the sense of being contrary to the Dhamma, and as "uneven greed" in the sense of being uneven.
Inclination (*nikanti*) is by way of longing for objects; the mode of longing is "longing" (*nikāmanā*); it is "aspiration" (*patthanā*) by way of yearning.
*Pihanā* (craving) is by way of longing (*pihāya*). *Sampatthanā* (aspiration) is an excellent longing (*suṭṭhu patthanā*). Craving for the five strands of sensual pleasure is *kāmataṇhā*.
Craving for existence in the realms of form and formlessness is *bhavataṇhā*. Craving for non-existence, reckoned as annihilation (*uccheda*), is *vibhavataṇhā*.
Craving specifically for a pure existence in the realm of form is *rūpataṇhā*. Craving for the formless realm is *arūpataṇhā*. [Craving] accompanied by the view of annihilation...
Lust is lust for views. Craving for cessation is craving for cessation. Craving for form is craving for form; craving for sound is craving for sound.
The same method applies to craving for odors and so forth. The terms "floods" (ogha) and the rest have already been explained in meaning.
It is called an obstruction (āvaraṇa) because it obstructs wholesome states; it is a covering (chādana) by way of concealing; it binds beings to the round of existence (vaṭṭa).
It is a bond (*bandhana*). It is called a secondary defilement (*upakkilesa*) because, having approached the mind, it defiles it and makes it impure.
It is called a latent tendency (*anusaya*) because it lies dormant in the sense of being firmly established. It is called an obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) because, as it arises, it overpowers the mind;

the meaning is that it seizes the course of wholesome states by not allowing them to arise. This is seen in such expressions as, "Thieves have obsessed the road," or "Scoundrels have obsessed the road."
The meaning is: "Indeed, they took the path. Thus, here too, *pariyuṭṭhāna* (obsession) should be understood in the sense of grasping.
It is called a *latā* (creeper) because it is like a creeper in the sense of entwining. Even in the passage where it says, "The creeper stands breaking through," this craving is called a creeper.

It is called *veviccha* (diversity of views) because it desires various objects. It is the root of the suffering of saṃsāra, thus it is the "root of suffering" (*dukkhamūla*). Of that very [craving]...
The source of suffering (*dukkhanidāna*): it is the cause of suffering. It is the origin of suffering (*dukkhappabhava*) because suffering arises from this.
In the sense of being a bond, it is like a snare (*pāsa*); thus it is a "snare. It is the "Mara-snare" (*mārapāsa*). In the sense of being difficult to swallow, it is like a hook (*baḷisa*);
thus it is a "hook. It is the "Mara-hook" (*mārabaḷisa*). Those overcome by craving do not transcend the domain of Mara; over them—
"Māra’s domain" (māravisaya) means that it is the domain of Māra by way of this method: "Māra exercises his power over it. Craving itself is a river in the sense of flowing;
thus it is the "craving-river" (taṇhānadī). Craving itself is a net in the sense of overwhelming; thus it is the "craving-net" (taṇhājāla).
Just as dogs bound by a leash are led wherever one wishes, so too are beings bound by craving; thus, it is in the sense of being a firm bond.

"Like a leather bag" means a leather bag (*gaddula*). Craving itself is the leather bag; thus, it is the "craving-leather-bag" (*taṇhā-gaddula*). In the sense of being difficult to fill, craving itself is the ocean; thus, it is the "craving-ocean" (*taṇhā-samudda*). In the description of hatred (*dosa*):
"He acted for my harm" means he brought about my lack of progress. By this method, [the meaning] applies to all the terms.

The meaning should be understood. Or, "ill-will in an improper place" means anger without cause—for some one becomes angry thinking, "It rains too much," or becomes angry thinking, "It does not rain";
he becomes angry when the sun is scorching, or becomes angry when it is not scorching;
he becomes angry when the wind is blowing, or becomes angry when it is not blowing; and being unable to sweep, he becomes angry with the Bodhi-tree leaves.
This was said with reference to the fact that one who is unable to put on his robe becomes angry at the wind, or stumbles and becomes angry at a tree stump—thus:

"Or else resentment arises toward what is not a proper object. In this context, in the nine instances mentioned below, because they arise directed toward sentient beings, there is a breach of the course of kamma (*kammapatha*).
However, resentment toward what is not a proper object, arising toward formations (*saṅkhāra*), does not constitute a breach of the course of kamma.
It does not act [thus]. That which arises as a state of resentment toward the mind is "mental resentment" (*cittassa āghāto*).

Resentment (*paṭighāto*) is stronger than that. It is "repulsion" (*paṭighaṃ*) by way of striking back. It is "opposition" (*paṭivirodho*) because it opposes. It is "anger" (*kopo*) by way of being provoked.

"Provocation" (*pakopo*) and "complete provocation" (*sampakopo*) are terms expanded by means of prefixes. It is "hatred" (*doso*) by way of being corrupt. "Corruption" (*padoso*) and "complete corruption" (*sampadoso*) are [terms expanded] by means of prefixes.
The footing has been increased. "Corruption of the mind" means the mind's state of being corrupted, its mode of perversion. "Malice of mind" (manopadosa) arises as that which defiles the mind.
Anger is so called by way of being angry; the act of being angry is "angering" (kujjhanā);
the state of one who is angry is "angry-mindedness" (kujjhitattaṃ).
Now, in order to show the method explained in the description of the unwholesome (*akusala*), it is said: "hatred, being hateful," and so forth.

Therefore, that which was stated here as "whatever such resentment of the mind... up to ...the state of being angry," and which was stated previously by way of the sequence "hatred, being hateful," etc., is called hatred (*dosa*).
In this way, the construction should be made here. For when it is thus, the fault of tautology (*punarukta-dosa*) is avoided.
[The section on] delusion (*moha*) should be understood by way of the opposite method to that stated in the description of non-delusion (*amoha*).
Furthermore, this will be made clear in all its aspects in the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*. 1079.

Regarding those phenomena which "are with roots" (*sahetuka*) by means of those [other] phenomena: this refers to those other root-phenomena [or associated factors] distinct from those root-phenomena themselves.
Nor are those states without cause (ahetudhammā) themselves accompanied by a cause (sahetukā). This same method applies even to the category of "rootless" (ahetuka). Herein, a root is simply a root;
or, when three or two [roots] arise together, it is "accompanied by a root. However, delusion (moha) associated with doubt (vicikicchā) or restlessness (uddhacca) is a root that is itself rootless.
This same method applies in the exposition of the dyads on "associated with a root" (hetusampayutta).

1091. In the exposition of the dyad of the conditioned (*saṅkhata-duka*), with reference to the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*) mentioned in the first dyad, the singular designation "that which is this dhamma" was employed.
However, because the question in the first dyad was raised using the plural form, the plural was used here in accordance with the method of following the sequence of the question:
"These dhammas are without conditions. The same principle applies to [the questions] such as "These dhammas are visible," and so forth.
1101. In the exposition of the dyad "cognizable by someone": "cognizable by the eye" means to be known by eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*).

The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. And here, "cognizable by someone" means to be known by one or another among the eye-consciousnesses, ear-consciousnesses, and so forth—namely, by either eye-consciousness or ear-consciousness. "Not cognizable by anyone" [means] not by that very same eye-consciousness or ear-consciousness... [and so on].

Or they are not to be known. Since it was stated previously that "this constitutes a dyad because, such being the case, there is a difference in meaning between the two terms," the dyad "those phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness are not those phenomena cognizable by ear-consciousness" does not exist.
However, taking the sense that "visible form is cognizable by eye-consciousness, whereas sound is not cognizable by eye-consciousness," [the dyad] "those phenomena... [is established].
‘Those phenomena cognizable by the eye are not cognizable by the ear, and those phenomena cognizable by the ear are not cognizable by the eye’—
this should be understood as one pair. Thus, having formulated four pairs based on each individual faculty,
it should be understood that twenty pairs have been analyzed.
But is it not the case that there is nothing "to be cognized by mental consciousness" and "not to be cognized by anything"? Is it for this reason that the dyads are not mentioned here?
No, they are not absent; rather, they are not mentioned because of the absence of a definitive distinction.

For there is no such definitive distinction as "these are not to be cognized by eye-consciousness," and likewise none regarding mental consciousness; thus, due to the absence of such a distinction, these [dyads] are not mentioned here.
Pairs have not been stated. However, there is this point: by means of mind-consciousness, some things are cognizable and some are non-cognizable.

Therefore, although that has not been explicitly stated, it should be understood according to what is available. For, among those sense-sphere phenomena (kāmāvacara-dhamma) that fall under the category of "mind-consciousness," some sense-sphere phenomena themselves are cognizable by some [mental factors] and non-cognizable by others.
By those same [mental factors], even fine-material-sphere (rūpāvacara) and other phenomena are [likewise treated].

Some are cognizable by some, and some are not cognizable by others. Even among those belonging to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), some belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) are cognizable by some and not cognizable by others.
By those same [beings], even those belonging to the fine-material sphere and so forth are cognizable by some and not cognizable by others.

However, for those belonging to the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*), those belonging to the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the unconditioned (*apariyāpanna*) are not cognizable at all. But as for those belonging to the immaterial sphere, by some...
They are cognizable by some and incognizable by others. And even among those, some are cognizable by some and incognizable by others.

As for those not included [in the mundane], the sense-sphere and so forth are neither cognizable nor incognizable by those [not included]. However, because the states not included [in the mundane] are incognizable by means of Nibbāna, they are cognizable by some and incognizable by others.
Furthermore, because they are incognizable by means of the paths and fruits, even among those [not included], some are cognizable and some are incognizable.
1102. In the exposition of the taints (*āsava*): lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure is called the taint of sensuality (*kāmāsava*).

Lust and desire for the fine-material and immaterial realms, attachment to meditative absorption (*jhāna*), and lust co-arising with the eternalist view, together with the aspiration based on existence, is called the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*).
The sixty-two views are called the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*). Ignorance regarding the eight points is called the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*). In each respective instance...
However, when they have been introduced, their classification into one kind and so forth should be understood for the sake of non-confusion.
In terms of meaning, these are indeed of one kind, being "outflows" (āsava) by virtue of having flowed on for a long time. In the Vinaya, however, they are presented in two ways:
"for the restraint of outflows pertaining to the present life, and for the warding off of outflows pertaining to future lives. In the Sutta, first, regarding the six sense bases:
“Friends, there are these three taints: the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance”—thus they are presented as threefold.
In the *Nibbedhika-pariyāya*: “Bhikkhus, there are taints leading to rebirth in hell; there are taints leading to rebirth in the animal realm;
there are taints leading to the sphere of hungry ghosts; there are taints leading to the human world; and there are taints leading to the world of the devas.”
It has come down in five ways. In the *Āhuneyyasutta* of the *Chakkanipāta*: "There are taints to be abandoned by restraint;
there are taints to be abandoned by avoidance; there are taints to be abandoned by endurance;
there are taints to be abandoned by evasion; there are taints to be abandoned by removal; there are taints to be abandoned by development"—thus it is sixfold.
[The term] has appeared [in the texts]. In the *Sabbāsavapariyāya*, it appears in seven ways together with [the defilements] "to be abandoned by vision.
Here, however, these appear in four ways according to the division into the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) and so forth. In this regard, the etymological meaning is as follows:

the taint regarding sensual pleasures (*kāma*), which are comprised of the five strands of sense pleasure, is the "taint of sensual desire" (*kāmāsava*). Regarding existence (*bhava*), which is twofold—consisting of both the realm of form (*rūpa*) and the formless realm (*arūpa*), and being of two kinds through both karma and rebirth—[the taint therein is the taint of existence].

The taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) and the taint of non-existence (*vibhavāsava*). View itself is the taint; thus it is the "taint of views" (*diṭṭhāsava*). Ignorance itself is the taint; thus it is the "taint of ignorance" (*avijjāsava*). 1103.

"In sensual pleasures" means in the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*). "Sensual desire" (*kāmacchanda*) refers to desire characterized by sensuality, not the desire for action, nor the desire for the Dhamma.

By way of longing for and being stained by sensual pleasures, sensual pleasure itself is lust; thus it is "lust for sensual pleasures" (*kāmarāga*). By way of longing for... [the rest of the sentence continues].
And because of delighting in them, desire itself is "delight in desire" (*kāmanandi*). Thus, having understood the meaning of "desire" (*kāma*) in all instances, it should be understood that:

in the sense of flowing toward, it is "craving for desire" (*kāmatanha*); in the sense of endearing, it is "affection for desire" (*kāmasineha*); in the sense of burning, it is "fever of desire" (*kāmaparilāha*);

in the sense of infatuation, it is "infatuation with desire" (*kāmamuccha*); and in the sense of swallowing and thoroughly consuming, it is "clinging to desire" (*kāmajjhosāna*). This is what is called...
This is called the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*), analyzed by way of eight terms.

(1104) “Craving for existence regarding the [various] existences” (*bhavesu bhavachando*) means the desire that proceeds by way of longing for existence within the realms of form and formlessness; this is “craving for existence. The remaining terms should also be understood according to this same method.
(1105) The various types of views have been stated by way of ten modes, beginning with “the world is eternal. Among these, “eternal”...

Regarding the term "the world" (*loka*): here, taking the five aggregates (*khandha-pañcaka*) as "the world," the view that arises in the mode of grasping "this world is eternal, permanent, and everlasting" is the view of eternalism (*sassata*).
The view that arises in the mode of grasping annihilation—that very same world "is cut off and perishes"—is the view of nihilism (*asassata*).
"Finite" (*anta-vā*) refers to one who has attained the limited kasiṇa (*paritta-kasiṇa*).

The view that arises in the mode of grasping “the world is finite” belongs to one who has attained a kasiṇa meditation of the size of a saucer or a bowl, and who perceives both the material and immaterial phenomena occurring within that attainment as the “world,” and who—by way of the kasiṇa’s boundaries—grasps it as being “finite.
That view is both an eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi) and an annihilationist view (ucchedadiṭṭhi). However, for one who has obtained a vast kasiṇa... [in that...]

For one who has attained a kasiṇa, the view that arises in the mode of grasping that "the world is infinite"— grasping the material and immaterial phenomena occurring within the attainment as "the world" by way of the kasiṇa's boundary and as "infinite" by way of its extent—
is a view that occurs in the form of the apprehension "the world is infinite. That [view] is both an eternalist view and an annihilationist view.
The view that "the soul is the same as the body" arises from the mode of grasping at annihilationism, because the term "soul" is applied only to the body—
which is subject to disintegration— and thus one thinks, "When the body is destroyed, the soul is also destroyed. In the second phrase, because a soul distinct from the body is grasped,
it arises from the mode of grasping at eternalism, thinking, "Even when the body is destroyed, the soul is not destroyed."
