Regarding "view": in such statements as "The Tathāgata exists after death," the term "Tathāgata" refers to a sentient being.

For one who grasps that "he exists after death," this is the first view, eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*). For one who grasps that "he does not exist," it is the second view, annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*).

For one who grasps that "he both exists and does not exist," it is the third view, partial-eternalism (*ekaccasassatadiṭṭhi*). For one who grasps that "he neither exists nor does not exist," [it is the fourth view, neither-nor].

The fourth is the view of the Eel-Wriggler (*amarāvikkhepa*). These phenomena are called "outflows" (*āsava*): these four phenomena—namely, the outflow of sensuality (*kāmāsava*), the outflow of existence (*bhavāsava*), and the outflow of views (*diṭṭhāsava*)—are grouped together as one by way of passion (*rāga*), making three in brief and four in detail.
Furthermore, whatever desire and lust (*chandarāga*) arises toward the celestial palaces, wish-fulfilling trees, and ornaments of the Brahmās, that is the outflow of sensuality.
Is it not present? It is not present. Why? Because greed for the five strands of sensual pleasure has been abandoned right here.

However, upon reaching the group of causes (*hetu-gocchaka*), greed is called a cause (*hetu*). Upon reaching the group of ties (*gantha-gocchaka*), it is called the bodily tie of covetousness (*abhijjhā-kāya-gantha*).

Upon reaching the group of defilements (*kilesa-gocchaka*), greed is called a defilement (*kilesa*). But is the greed co-arising with wrong view (*diṭṭhi-sahajāta*) the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) or not? It is not.
There is [the taint of] lust for views. For this has been said: "A gift given to a person who is stained by lust for views is not of great fruit, nor does it have great benefit.
Now, these taints may be cited according to the sequence of the defilements (*kilesa*) as well as according to the sequence of the paths (*magga*). According to the sequence of the defilements:

The taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) is abandoned by the path of non-returning; the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) by the path of arahantship; the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*) by the path of stream-entry;

and the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*) by the path of arahantship. According to the sequence of the paths, the taint of views is abandoned by the path of stream-entry, the taint of sensual desire by the path of non-returning, and both the taint of existence and the taint of ignorance by the path of arahantship.
1121. In the exposition of pride (*māna*) among the fetters (*saṃyojana*): “I am superior” pride is the pride that has arisen in the sense of being pre-eminent, thinking “I am superior.
“I am equal” pride is the pride that has arisen in the sense of being exactly the same, thinking “I am equal.
“I am inferior” pride is the pride that has arisen in the sense of being base, thinking “I am inferior. Thus is the pride of superiority.
“Equal,” “inferior”—these three types of conceit arise in three kinds of persons.

For even in one who is superior, three conceits may arise: “I am superior,” “I am equal,” and “I am inferior. Likewise for one who is equal, and likewise for one who is inferior. Among these, in the case of the superior person, only the conceit “I am superior” is a conceit in accordance with reality (*yāthāvamāna*);
the other two are conceits not in accordance with reality. In the case of the equal person... [and so on] ...in the case of the inferior person.

"Inflated pride" (*hīnamāna*) is conceit regarding what is inferior; "conceit as it really is" (*yāthāvamāna*) is conceit regarding what is equal; the other two are conceits regarding what is superior.

What is stated by this? It is stated that three types of conceit arise in one person. However, in the *Khuddakavatthuka*, in the first section on the classification of conceit (*mānabhājanīya*), it is stated that one type of conceit arises in three kinds of persons.
Pride (*māna*) is so called by way of making oneself great. "Conceiving" (*maññanā*) and "the state of conceiving" (*maññitatta*) are designations for its mode and its manifestation.
It is "haughtiness" (*unnati*) in the sense of being uplifted. It is "arrogance" (*unnamo*) because it makes the person who gives rise to it stand upraised, as if lifting them up.

It is a "banner" (*dhaja*) in the sense of being hoisted high. It is "exaltation" (*sampaggāho*) because it thoroughly lifts up the mind in the sense of tossing it upward. A "pinnacle" (*ketu*) is said to be the foremost among many banners.
Accuggatadhajo (one with a raised banner): Pride (*māna*), arising again and again by depending on successive [bases], is like a banner (*ketu*) in the sense of being raised high;
thus it is called “banner. One who desires a banner is “desirous of a banner” (*ketukamyam*); the state of being such is “desire for a banner” (*ketukamyatā*).
However, that belongs to the mind, not to the self. Therefore it is said: “Desire for a banner of the mind. For the mind associated with pride desires a banner.
He desires it. And his state of being so is *ketukamyatā*; it is pride (*māna*) designated as a "banner" (*keta*).

1126. In the exposition of envy (*issā*): "envy regarding the gains, honors, respect, esteem, veneration, and worship of others"—envy has the characteristic of disparaging the success of others regarding these gains and so forth, thinking, "What has this person got to do with these? In that regard:
"Gain" (*lābha*) means the obtaining of the four requisites, such as robes and so forth. A person who is envious (*issukī*) reviles another's gain, thinking, "What has this person to do with this?";
he does not desire it. "Honor" (*sakkāra*) means the obtaining of those same requisites when they are well-made and beautiful.
"Veneration" (*garukāra*) means the act of holding in high esteem, the making of something weighty. "Reverence" (*mānana*)...

"Acting with kindness" means acting in a way that is pleasing to others. "Vandana" (reverence) is reverence performed by prostrating on all five limbs. "Pūjanā" (worship) is worship with perfumes, garlands, and so forth.
"Issā" (envy) is by way of the act of envying. The state of envying is "issāyanā. The condition of having envied is "issāyitattaṃ. Terms such as "usūyā" (malice) are synonyms for envy and the like.
Furthermore, the characteristic of this envy—namely, disparaging—should be illustrated by both the householder and the homeless renunciant. The householder...

For indeed, by relying on his own manly effort through one or another livelihood such as farming or trade, a certain person obtains an excellent vehicle, a mount, or a treasure. Another, desiring that [same] gain, is not satisfied with that acquisition;
he thinks: "When will this man fall away from this prosperity and wander about in poverty?"
Having reflected, he becomes pleased when that person falls away from such success for one reason or another.
Likewise, a certain houseless one who is envious, seeing the success in gains and so forth arising in another by virtue of their own learning, mastery of the scriptures, and so on, thinks:
"When indeed will this person fall away from these gains and so forth? And when, for one reason or another, that person—
When he sees another fallen [from prosperity], he is pleased. Thus, envy (*issā*) should be understood as having the characteristic of disparaging the success of others.

1127. In the exposition of stinginess (*macchariya*), the passage beginning with “five kinds of stinginess: stinginess regarding residence” (*āvāsamacchariya*) and so forth is stated for the purpose of showing stinginess by way of its objects. Therein, stinginess regarding a residence is “stinginess regarding residence. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
A “residence” (*āvāsa*) refers to the entire monastery (*ārāma*), a courtyard (*pariveṇa*), a single cell (*ekovara*), or places such as night-quarters and day-quarters. Among these—
In the spring, they dwell happily and obtain the necessary requisites.
However, a certain monk does not wish for the arrival of a well-behaved and virtuous monk there; even when such a one has arrived, he thinks, "Let him depart quickly.

This is what is called "avarice regarding the dwelling-place" (*āvāsamacchariya*). On the other hand, there is no such thing as "avarice regarding the dwelling-place" when one does not desire the residence of those who cause quarrels and the like.
"Families" refers to both families of supporters and families of kinsmen. In that regard, family stinginess consists in not wishing for another person to approach those families.

However, one who does not wish for an evil person to approach them is not called "stingy," for such a person acts to prevent the destruction of their faith. It is only for a bhikkhu capable of protecting that faith that [family stinginess] exists there.
One who is unwilling to approach [others] is called a miser.

"Gain" refers specifically to the gain of the four requisites. When another person who possesses virtue receives such gain, the thought "May he not receive it" constitutes the miserliness regarding gain (*lābha-macchariya*).
Furthermore, one who squanders what has been given in faith through such means as non-enjoyment or improper enjoyment [is also characterized by this].
There is no such thing as stinginess in one who destroys [the gift], nor in one who does not give it to another even when it is becoming putrid; for when seeing that, one thinks:
"If he does not get this, perhaps another virtuous person might get it and make use of it.
As for "beauty," there is both the beauty of the physical body and the beauty of virtues. Regarding the beauty of the physical body, a stingy person thinks: "Another is handsome..."

When it is said, "possessing beauty," he does not wish to speak of that. Being envious of the praise of virtues, he does not wish to speak of the praise of his virtue, ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*), way of progress, or conduct.
"Dhamma" refers both to the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*) and the Dhamma of realization (*paṭivedha-dhamma*). In this regard, noble disciples [speak of] the Dhamma of realization...
They do not harbor stinginess; they desire that others in the world, including the devas, should realize the Dhamma they themselves have realized.

Furthermore, they desire that others should know of that realization. However, it is only regarding the Dhamma within the "threads" (the scriptures) that there is what is called "stinginess regarding the Dhamma.
A person endowed with that [stinginess] conceals whatever secret text or method of discourse they know.

He does not wish to make another understand. However, one who, having examined a person, does not give [teaching] for the sake of supporting that person with the Dhamma, or having examined the Dhamma, does not give it for the sake of supporting that person, is not called "one who is stingy regarding the Dhamma.
In this regard, a certain person is fickle; at one time he is a śramaṇa, at another time a brāhmaṇa, and at another time a nigaṇṭha.

For when a bhikkhu does not give [the teaching], thinking, "This person will disrupt the subtle and delicate internal Dhamma by breaking the tradition handed down through the lineage," this is called not giving out of consideration for the person and support for the Dhamma.
But when [a teacher thinks], "This Dhamma is subtle and delicate; if this person were to grasp it, he would declare himself [to have attained] another [state]," [he withholds it].
If one does not give [the teaching] thinking, "He will perish after revealing it," this is called not giving out of a desire to benefit the individual after having examined the Dhamma.
However, if one does not give thinking, "If he takes up this Dhamma, he will be capable of breaking our tradition," this one is called a miser regarding the Dhamma.
Among these five types of stinginess, first, by way of stinginess regarding one's dwelling (*āvāsamacchariya*),
one becomes a *yakkha* or a *peta* and wanders about carrying the refuse of that very dwelling on one’s head. By way of stinginess regarding one’s family (*kulamacchariya*),
seeing others performing acts of giving, honoring, and so forth within that family, one thinks, "This family has surely been divided from me," and blood even flows from one’s mouth.
It comes up; there is also purging from the stomach, and even the intestines come out in pieces.
Having been stingy regarding gains belonging to the Saṅgha or a group, and having used them as if they were one's own private property, one is reborn as a *yakkha*, a *peta*, or a great python.
[This occurs] through stinginess regarding the beauty of one’s body and the excellence of one’s qualities.
Through stinginess regarding the Dhamma of the scriptures, one praises one's own reputation while disparaging the reputation of others by saying things such as, "What kind of reputation is this?
and by refusing to give any portion of the scriptural Dhamma to anyone, one becomes ugly and deaf-mute.
Furthermore, through stinginess regarding dwellings, one is cooked in an iron house; through stinginess regarding families, one obtains little gain; and through stinginess regarding gains...
One is reborn in the Excrement Hell. Due to stinginess regarding physical beauty, one who is reborn in various states of existence lacks beauty.
Due to stinginess regarding the Dhamma, one is reborn in the Kukkuḷa Hell.
It is "stinginess" (*macchariya*) by way of the act of being stingy. The manner of being stingy is "the state of being stingy" (*maccharāyanā*). For one who has become stingy through stinginess...
The state of one possessing avarice (*macchara*) is the quality of being avaricious (*maccharāyitatta*).

One who does not wish to share any of his own successes with others, thinking, “Let these belong to me alone, not to another,” is *viviccha*. The state of such a person is *veviccha*; this is a name for mild avarice.
A *kadariya* is said to be one who is disrespectful. The state of such a person is *kadariya*; this is a name for stubborn avarice.
Indeed, a person endowed with such qualities even prevents others from giving to those who give. And this has been said:
"The miserly one, evil in intention, Holding wrong views and lacking respect, Prevents those who are giving food To those who are begging."
One who bends or contracts the mind out of a sense of bitterness upon seeing a beggar is called *kaṭukañcuka*. The state of being such is *kaṭukañcukatā*.
According to another method: *kaṭukañcukatā* refers to "taking with a ladle" (*kaṭacchuggāha*).
For when taking rice from a cooking pot filled to the brim, one takes it using the tip of the ladle contracted on all sides; this is done so as not to take it after filling [the ladle] to the top.
He is unable [to give]; thus the mind of a stingy person contracts.
When that has contracted, the body likewise contracts, shrinks back, turns away, and does not extend itself; therefore, stinginess is called "bitter rigidity" (*kaṭukañcukatā*).
"Non-extension of the mind" means that it does not extend itself toward performing a service for others by way of giving and so forth.

Such is the state of the mind when it is obstructed and grasping. Furthermore, because a person who is miserly (maccharipuggala) desires not to give what belongs to himself to others, but desires to take what belongs to others, its characteristic consists in concealing one's own excellence and seizing one's own excellence, by way of the mental process: "May this wonder belong to me alone; let it not belong to another."
Or it should be understood thus. The rest of this group [of suttas] has a meaning that is already clear.
Furthermore, these fetters (saṃyojana) may be cited according to the sequence of the defilements (kilesa) or according to the sequence of the paths (magga).

According to the sequence of the defilements, the fetters of sensual lust (kāmarāga) and aversion (paṭigha) are abandoned by the non-returning path (anāgāmimagga), and the fetter of conceit (māna) is abandoned by the path of arahantship (arahattamagga).

The fetters of views, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances are abandoned by the path of stream-entry; the fetter of lust for existence is abandoned by the path of arahantship; envy and avarice are abandoned by the path of stream-entry;

and ignorance is abandoned by the path of arahantship. According to the sequence of the paths: views, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, envy, and avarice are abandoned by the path of stream-entry;
sensual lust and ill will are abandoned by the path of non-returning; and conceit, lust for existence, and ignorance are abandoned by the path of arahantship.

1140. In the *Ganthagocchaka*, it is called the "body of knots" (*nāmakāya-gantha*) because it knots together; it joins one to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) by way of death and rebirth-linking, hence it is a "knot of the body.
Having rejected even the speech of the Omniscient One, one adheres in this manner: "The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is vain"—this is "adherence to 'this is the truth'.
Furthermore, as for the distinction between covetousness (*abhijjhā*) and sensual lust (*kāmarāga*):

Since this is the case, therefore, in the word-commentary on the bodily tie of covetousness (*abhijjhākāyagantha*), it is not stated as "whatever desire for sense-pleasures (*kāmacchanda*) or lust for sense-pleasures (*kāmarāga*)," but rather it is said:

"whatever lust (*rāga*), intense lust (*sārāga*)," and so forth. By this, that which was stated below—that "the desire and lust (*chandrarāga*) for the celestial palaces (*vimāna*) of the Brahmās and such is not the outflow of sense-desire (*kāmāsava*), but upon reaching the group of ties (*ganthagocchaka*), it becomes the bodily tie of covetousness"—is [confirmed].

It should be understood as "well-spoken. The same method applies to the subsequent group of defilements (*kilesagocchaka*). Regarding the phrase "except for the misapprehension of rules and observances" (*ṭhapetvā sīlabbataparāmāsaṃ*):

because the misapprehension of rules and observances does not adhere in the manner of "this alone is the truth," etc., but rather adheres specifically in the manner of "purity comes through rules," etc., he said "except for" in order to exclude it, even though it is a form of wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*).

1162. In the explanation of sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*) within the group of hindrances (*nīvaraṇagocchaka*): "Unwieldiness of mind" (*cittassa akallatā*) is the state of sickness of the mind. For one who is sick is called "unwell. It is also said in the Vinaya: "Venerable sir, I am not unwell. "Inflexibility" (*akammaññatā*) is simply the mode of inflexibility consisting of the sickness of the mind. "Sluggishness" (*olīyanā*) is the mode of sluggishness. For the mind pertaining to the postures (*iriyāpathika-citta*)— [The text continues: ...is sluggish. "Languor" (*līnatta*) is the state of languor. It is the state of being weighed down by the heaviness of the mind. "Stolidity" (*thina*) is the state of stolidity. It is the state of being stiffened by the rigidity of the mind. "Torpor" (*middha*) is the state of torpor. It is the state of being overcome by sleep. "Drowsiness" (*niddā*) is the state of drowsiness. It is the state of being overcome by the power of sleep. "Sleep" (*suppa*) is the state of sleep. It is the state of being overcome by the power of sleep. "Dreaming" (*supina*) is the state of dreaming. It is the state of experiencing various objects while asleep. "Sleeping" (*soppa*) is the state of sleeping. It is the state of being overcome by the power of sleep. "Yawning" (*vijambhitā*) is the state of yawning. It is the state of stretching out the limbs while overcome by sleep. "Distaste for food" (*bhattasammada*) is the state of distaste for food. It is the state of being overcome by the heaviness of the stomach after eating too much. "Unwieldiness of body" (*kāyassa akallatā*) is the state of sickness of the body. For one who is sick is called "unwell. It is also said in the Vinaya: "Venerable sir, I am not unwell. "Inflexibility of body" (*kāyassa akammaññatā*) is simply the mode of inflexibility consisting of the sickness of the body. "Sluggishness of body" (*kāyassa olīyanā*) is the mode of sluggishness. It is the state of being weighed down by the heaviness of the body. "Languor of body" (*kāyassa līnatta*) is the state of languor. It is the state of being weighed down by the heaviness of the body. "Stolidity of body" (*kāyassa thina*) is the state of stolidity. It is the state of being stiffened by the rigidity of the body. "Torpor of body" (*kāyassa middha*) is the state of torpor. It is the state of being overcome by sleep. "Drowsiness of body" (*kāyassa niddā*) is the state of drowsiness. It is the state of being overcome by the power of sleep. "Sleep of body" (*kāyassa suppa*) is the state of sleep. It is the state of being overcome by the power of sleep. "Dreaming of body" (*kāyassa supina*) is the state of dreaming. It is the state of experiencing various objects while asleep. "Sleeping of body" (*kāyassa soppa*) is the state of sleeping. It is the state of being overcome by the power of sleep. "Yawning of body" (*kāyassa vijambhitā*) is the state of yawning. It is the state of stretching out the limbs while overcome by sleep. "Distaste for food of body" (*kāyassa bhattasammada*) is the state of distaste for food. It is the state of being overcome by the heaviness of the stomach after eating too much. "Unwieldiness of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa akallatā*) is the state of sickness of both body and mind. For one who is sick is called "unwell. It is also said in the Vinaya: "Venerable sir, I am not unwell. "Inflexibility of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa akammaññatā*) is simply the mode of inflexibility consisting of the sickness of both body and mind. "Sluggishness of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa olīyanā*) is the mode of sluggishness. It is the state of being weighed down by the heaviness of both body and mind. "Languor of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa līnatta*) is the state of languor. It is the state of being weighed down by the heaviness of both body and mind. "Stolidity of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa thina*) is the state of stolidity. It is the state of being stiffened by the rigidity of both body and mind. "Torpor of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa middha*) is the state of torpor. It is the state of being overcome by sleep. "Drowsiness of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa niddā*) is the state of drowsiness.

It is the state of being overcome by the power of sleep. "Sleep of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa suppa*) is the state of sleep. It is the state of being overcome by the power of sleep. "Dreaming of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa supina*) is the state of dreaming. It is the state of experiencing various objects while asleep. "Sleeping of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa soppa*) is the state of sleeping. It is the state of being overcome by the power of sleep. "Yawning of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa vijambhitā*) is the state of yawning. It is the state of stretching out the limbs while overcome by sleep. "Distaste for food of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa bhattasammada*) is the state of distaste for food. It is the state of being overcome by the heaviness of the stomach after eating too much. "Unwieldiness of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa akallatā*) is the state of sickness of both body and mind. For one who is sick is called "unwell. It is also said in the Vinaya: "Venerable sir, I am not unwell. "Inflexibility of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa akammaññatā*) is simply the mode of inflexibility consisting of the sickness of both body and mind. "Sluggishness of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa olīyanā*) is the mode of sluggishness. It is the state of being weighed down by the heaviness of both body and mind. "Languor of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa līnatta*) is the state of languor. It is the state of being weighed down by the heaviness of both body and mind. "Stolidity of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa thina*) is the state of stolidity. It is the state of being stiffened by the rigidity of both body and mind. "Torpor of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa middha*) is the state of torpor. It is the state of being overcome by sleep. "Drowsiness of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa niddā*) is the state of drowsiness. It is the state of being overcome by the power of sleep. "Sleep of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa suppa*) is the state of sleep. It is the state of being overcome by the power of sleep. "Dreaming of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa supina*) is the state of dreaming. It is the state of experiencing various objects while asleep. "Sleeping of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa soppa*) is the state of sleeping. It is the state of being overcome by the power of sleep. "Yawning of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa vijambhitā*) is the state of yawning. It is the state of stretching out the limbs while overcome by sleep. "Distaste for food of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa bhattasammada*) is the state of distaste for food. It is the state of being overcome by the heaviness of the stomach after eating too much. "Unwieldiness of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa akallatā*) is the state of sickness of both body and mind. For one who is sick is called "unwell. It is also said in the Vinaya: "Venerable sir, I am not unwell. "Inflexibility of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa akammaññatā*) is simply the mode of inflexibility consisting of the sickness of both body and mind. "Sluggishness of both body and mind" (*kāyacittassa olīyanā*) is the mode of sluggishness.
Being unable to maintain its posture, it sinks down like a bat clinging to a tree, or like a pot of molasses stuck to a wooden post.
It is with reference to this mode that "sinking" (*olīyana*) is said. The second term is augmented by means of a prefix.
"Stagnant" (*līna*) means contracted due to a lack of expansion. The other two terms are descriptions of the modes of cultivation. "Sloth" (*thina*)...
It stands in a state of density due to its lack of expansion, like a lump of ghee. *Thiyana* is a designation for a mode of being;
*thiyitabhāvo* is "the state of having become firm," meaning stiffness by way of non-expansion. 1163.
*Kāyassa* refers to the mental body (*nāmakāya*), which is comprised of the three aggregates. *Akallatā* is unworkability, as explained below.
It is exactly as previously stated. It "overwhelms" (onāha) the body like a cloud [overwhelming] the sky; thus it is an "overwhelming" (onāha).
An overwhelming from every side is a "complete overwhelming" (pariyonāha). It "shuts up within" (samorundhati); thus it is "shutting up within" (antosamorodha).

For just as when a city has been besieged and captured, the people are not permitted to go outside, so too the mental states (dhammā), being shut up by torpor (middha), are unable to go out by way of expansion.
They do not obtain [it]. Therefore, it is said "internal confinement" (*antosaṃvarodho*). It is called *middha* because it "stupifies" (*medhati*);

the meaning is that it injures by way of making one unfit for action. It is called *soppa* because "one sleeps by means of it. It is called *pacalāyikā* because it causes the eyelids and so forth to become heavy (*pacala*).
The terms *supana* and *supitatta* are designations of its mode and its state of being. As for the word *soppa* mentioned before them, its repetition [is for the sake of emphasis].
The reason has already been stated. This is called the hindrance of sloth and torpor (*thinamiddhanīvaraṇa*);
that is, sloth and torpor taken together are called the "hindrance of sloth and torpor" in the sense of being an obstruction.

That which generally arises for trainees (*sekkha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*) before and after sleep is completely eradicated by the path of Arahantship. For those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), [it does not arise].
However, due to the weakness of the body born of karma, there occurs a crossing over into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
While that remains unmixed [with other states], they sleep; that is what is called their "sleep. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"I recall, Aggivessana, in the last month of summer, having spread out my outer robe folded fourfold, lying on my right side, mindful and clearly comprehending..."
"Having fallen asleep. Now, this weakness of the physical body composed of the four great elements (*karaja-kāya*) is not something to be abandoned by the Path;
it is found both in what is clung-to (*upādinnaka*) and in what is not clung-to (*anupādinnaka*).

When it is found in what is clung-to, it occurs at such times as when one whose taints are exhausted has traveled a long distance, or when one is exhausted after having performed some kind of labor. When it is found in what is not clung-to—
It is found in leaves and flowers. For the leaves of certain trees expand in the heat of the sun and contract at night;
lotus flowers and the like bloom in the heat of the sun and contract again at night.
However, this drowsiness (*middha*), being unwholesome (*akusala*), does not occur in those whose taints (*āsava*) have been destroyed.
In this regard, it might be argued: "Torpor is not unwholesome. Why? Because it is material form (*rūpa*). For material form is indeterminate (*abyākata*), and this [torpor] is material form.
For that very reason, the term 'body' is used here in the phrase 'the body's lack of fitness and unwieldiness.

If this were material form merely because the word "of the body" (*kāyassa*) is stated, then states such as bodily tranquility (*kāyapassaddhi*) and so forth would also have to be material form. Furthermore, "pleasure..."

If it were said, “He experiences with the body” and “He realizes the ultimate truth with the body,” then both the experience of pleasure and the realization of the ultimate truth would have to occur by means of the material body (*rūpakāya*) alone.
Therefore, it cannot be said that “matter is torpor. For here, what is called “body” is the mental body (*nāmakāya*).
If it is the mental body, then why is it said, “sleeping and nodding”? It is not the mental body that sleeps.

"And it does not nod" means: just as the "marks" (*liṅga*) and so forth are said to be the results of the female faculty (*itthindriya*), because they are its effects—just as these marks, signs, gestures, and appearances are stated to be the results of the female faculty—so too, falling asleep and so forth are stated to be the results of this drowsiness (*middha*), which is defined as the languor of the mental body (*nāmakāya*). Regarding drowsiness:

For when that [sleep] exists, those [states] come to be. By way of metaphorical designation (*phalūpacāra*), even though torpor (*middha*) is formless (*arūpa*), it is spoken of as "sleeping," "drowsiness," "slumbering," and "the state of having slept.
Furthermore, this meaning is established by the etymological definition: "It causes the eyelids and so forth to become drowsy (*pacala*); thus it is *pacalāyikā*."
Torpor is not matter (*rūpa*). Its immaterial nature is indeed demonstrated by its being a "constriction" (*onāha*) and so forth.
For matter cannot be a "constriction, a constriction around, or a confinement within" for the mental body (*nāmakāya*). [Objection: "But is this not itself matter precisely because of this reason?
For that which is immaterial cannot be a constriction, a constriction around, or a confinement within for anything. [Response: If that were so, then obstruction (*āvaraṇa*) would also [be matter].

It would not be so. Therefore, just as desire for sense-pleasures (*kāmacchanda*) and the other [hindrances] are immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) that are called "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*) in the sense of being obstructions, so too this [state] should be understood as having the nature of a "shrouding" (*onāha*) and so forth, in the sense of shrouding and the rest.
Furthermore, it is immaterial because of the statement: "Having abandoned the five hindrances, which are defilements of the mind and weaken wisdom. For form (*rūpa*) is not a defilement of the mind.
"It does not cause weakness of wisdom.
Why does it not do so? Has it not been said:

"There are, bhikkhus, some recluses and brahmins who drink fermented liquor and spirits, who are not abstinent from drinking fermented liquor and spirits; this, bhikkhus, is the first defilement of recluses and brahmins"?
Furthermore, it has been said: “Householder’s son, there are these six dangers in the practice of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants as a basis for negligence:

loss of wealth visible here and now, increase of quarrels, a breeding ground for diseases, the cause of ill repute, the exposure of one’s private parts, and the weakening of wisdom—this is the sixth point. This is also established by direct experience.

Just as when liquor has entered the stomach, the mind becomes defiled and wisdom becomes weak, so too, like liquor, torpor might be both a defilement of the mind and a cause of weakness for wisdom. This is not so, because of the description of its condition.
For if liquor were itself a defilement, it would have been included [in the list] with the words: "Having abandoned these five hindrances, the defilements of the mind."

Or again: "In the same way, monks, there are these five defilements of the mind, by which defilements the mind being defiled is neither malleable, nor wieldy, nor luminous, but is brittle and does not become rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints (*āsava*). What are the five? Sensual desire, monks, is a defilement of the mind..."

Or it would come under the definition of "corruption" (*upakkilesa*) in such passages as: "And what, monks, are the corruptions of the mind? Covetousness and improper greed are a corruption of the mind," and so forth.
However, when that [liquor] is drunk, corruptions arise which are both defilements of the mind and causes of weakness for wisdom.
Therefore, because it serves as a condition for them, it is described as a "condition" (paccaya) in that way.
But as for torpor (*middha*), it is itself both a defilement of the mind and a weakening of wisdom; thus, torpor is purely immaterial (*arūpa*).
Furthermore, this is evident from the mention of its association: "The hindrance of sloth-and-torpor is a hindrance by means of the hindrance of ignorance."
For it is said: "And associated with the hindrances. Therefore, because of this statement regarding association, this is not matter (rūpa).
For matter does not receive the designation of being "associated. Now, it might be argued: "This was stated according to what is available. For example:
'Even the shells and pebbles, even the schools of fish—whether moving or stationary.'"

Thus, having grouped them together, this was stated according to their availability. For gravel and pebbles remain still and do not move, whereas the other two [the ocean and the river] both remain still and move.
Likewise here too, *middha* (torpor) is only an *nīvaraṇa* (hindrance) and not associated [with consciousness], while *thina* (sloth) is both a hindrance and associated;
thus, having grouped all these together according to their availability, it is said: "It is both a hindrance..."

And it is said: “It is also associated with the hindrances. However, torpor (*middha*) is merely a hindrance and not associated [with other mental factors], just as gravel or pebbles simply remain stationary and do not move.
Therefore, torpor is just a material phenomenon (*rūpa*). No; for its status as a material phenomenon is not established.
For the fact that gravel or pebbles do not move is established even without a sutta. Therefore, in that case, the meaning is according to what is available.
Let it be so. However, that torpor (*middha*) is material form (*rūpa*) is unproven. It is not possible to establish its status as material form by means of this sutta;

therefore, since the material nature of torpor is not established, this [sutta] was not spoken according to whatever [classification] might be available, and thus torpor is indeed non-material (*arūpa*).
Furthermore, because of the statement beginning with "due to the absence of the self" (*cattattā*), etc., in the *Vibhaṅga*: "‘Free from sloth and torpor’ (*vigatathinamiddho*)... [refers to] its...
“Because of its being abandoned, vomited out, released, relinquished, and cast off, it is therefore called ‘one who has departed from sloth and torpor’”;
and “This mind cleanses, purifies, thoroughly purifies, liberates, releases, and completely liberates itself from this sloth and torpor;
therefore it is said that ‘he thoroughly purifies the mind of sloth and torpor’”—thus [it is stated].

The passage beginning with “because of its non-material nature” (cattattā) has been stated. However, it is not *rūpa* alone that is spoken of in this way; therefore, torpor (*middha*) is indeed non-material (*arūpa*).

No, [it is not so], because of the statement regarding the impossibility of its being mind-born (*cittaja*). For torpor is threefold: mind-born, temperature-born (*utu-ja*), and nutriment-born (*āhāra-ja*).

Therefore, regarding that which is mind-born among them, its impossibility [in the formless realm] was stated in the *Vibhaṅga* in relation to the jhāna-consciousnesses; it was not its lack of materiality (*arūpa-bhāva*) that was meant.
"It is established that sleep (*middha*) is indeed material form (*rūpa*). No, because the existence of sleep as material form has not been proven.

For it would be possible to accept this only if the material nature of sleep were established; however, its impossibility as something born of mind (*cittaja*) has already been stated there, and that very point is not proven.

Therefore, sleep is indeed non-material (*arūpa*). Furthermore, because of the mention of its abandonment: for the Blessed One said, "Bhikkhus, having abandoned six things, one is capable... [and so on].
To enter and dwell in the first jhāna; which six? Sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt;
and furthermore, the danger in sensual pleasures has been clearly seen by him with right wisdom. And:
“Having abandoned these five hindrances, with powerful wisdom, for his own benefit or for the benefit of others...”

In such passages as “...or he will know,” the abandoning of even *middha* (torpor) is mentioned. Yet, form (*rūpa*) is not to be abandoned. As it has been said: “The aggregate of form is to be directly known, to be fully understood;
it is not to be abandoned, not to be developed, and not to be realized. [If you argue that] because of this statement regarding its abandoning, *middha* must be non-material, [we reply:

no, for there are also statements regarding the abandoning of form. “Form, ...[is to be abandoned]. (A III 416) [Thus, the presence of such statements does not prove that *middha* is exclusively non-material.]
“Monks, that is not yours; abandon it. For here, the abandoning of form (*rūpa*) itself has indeed been stated. Therefore, this [objection] is not a valid reason.
No, because it was stated otherwise. For in that sutta, the abandoning of form is stated by way of the abandoning of desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*), as in:
“Monks, whatever is the removal of desire and lust regarding form, that is its abandoning there,” and not in the manner [you suggest].
In the passage, “Having abandoned six things, having abandoned the five hindrances,” it is stated that [torpor] is something to be abandoned;

because it is stated otherwise [than as a material thing], torpor is not material form (*rūpa*). Therefore, by these suttas—such as “Having abandoned these five hindrances, the defilements of the mind”—and by other suttas as well, it should be understood that torpor is exclusively immaterial (*arūpa*). For instance:
“Bhikkhus, there are these five hindrances, obstructions, mental obsessions that weaken wisdom. Which five?

Sensual desire, bhikkhus, is a hindrance, an obstruction... lethargy and drowsiness, bhikkhus, is a hindrance, an obstruction, a mental obsession that weakens wisdom. And: “The hindrance of lethargy and drowsiness...”
“...monks, it creates blindness, it creates lack of vision, it creates ignorance, it obstructs wisdom, it belongs to the side of affliction, and it does not lead to Nibbāna”;
and, “In the same way, brahmin, at whatever time one dwells with a mind obsessed by sloth and torpor, overwhelmed by sloth and torpor”;
and, “For one who attends to things unreasonably, monks, [unarisen states do not arise]...”

"...and sensual desire arises... and unarisen sloth and torpor arise," and, "Bhikkhus, this entire heap of the unwholesome consists of these five hindrances"—many such suttas have been spoken that indicate its immaterial nature. And because this is immaterial...
Therefore, it also arises in the formless realm (ārūpa). For this was stated in the *Mahāpakaraṇa Paṭṭhāna*:
"Dependent on a state that is an hindrance (nīvaraṇa), a state that is an hindrance arises, but not by way of the prenascence condition (purejāta-paccaya). In its analysis (vibhaṅga):

"In the formless realm, dependent on the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa), [arise] sloth and torpor... restlessness... and the hindrance of ignorance (avijjā-nīvaraṇa)"—all of this should be expanded in detail.
Therefore, one should reach the conclusion here that *middha* (torpor) is indeed formless (*arūpa*).
In the description of *kukkucca* (worry), the phrases "perceiving what is unallowable as allowable" and so forth are stated for the purpose of showing the root of worry.
For when an offense has been committed through such a perception, and the transgression of the object has been finalized, even if mindfulness arises again—
"This arose for one who regrets in this way, thinking, 'I have done wrong,' by way of subsequent remorse.
To show its root, it was said: 'The perception of what is allowable in what is not allowable,' and so forth.
Therein, one consumes food that is not allowable while perceiving it as allowable; one consumes meat that is not allowable while perceiving it as allowable meat; [or] the flesh of a bear..."

He eats pork, or the meat of a leopard, or the meat of a deer; when the time has passed, he perceives it as being within the time; after having invited others to stop, he perceives that they have not stopped;
and when dust has fallen into his bowl, he perceives it as having been properly received—thus one commits a transgression by perceiving what is unallowable as allowable.
Furthermore, eating the meat of a pig while perceiving it to be the meat of a bear...
Furthermore, one who eats at the wrong time perceiving it as the right time commits a transgression through "perceiving what is allowable as unallowable.

Likewise, one who performs some blameless act perceiving it as blameworthy, or a blameworthy act perceiving it as blameless, commits a transgression through "perceiving what is blameless as blameworthy and what is blameworthy as blameless. Since this [is so], "what has not been done..."
"Alas for me! I have not done what is auspicious; I have not done what is wholesome; I have not created a refuge from fear; I have committed evil;
I have committed cruelty; I have committed sin. When a transgression is thus committed through perceiving the blameless as blameworthy, it arises.
Therefore, permitting another basis for that [transgression], he said: "Whatever is of such a kind," and so forth.
In this context, the term *kukkucca* has already been explained. The mode of being remorseful is *kukkuccāyanā*. The state of one who is remorseful is *kukkuccāyitatta*.
Regarding the phrase "remorse of the mind" (*cetaso vippaṭisāro*): the turning toward what has been done or left undone, or what is blameworthy or blameless, is called "remorse" (*vippaṭisāro*).
Furthermore, because it does not allow for the repetition of evil that was committed, nor the performance of what was not done [but should have been].
Or, having failed to do what is good, one does not do it; therefore, it is a deformed or loathsome remorse, hence "remorse" (*vippaṭisāra*).
Furthermore, it is stated as "remorse of the mind" (*cetaso*) in order to indicate that it belongs to the mind and not to a sentient being.
This is the description of its intrinsic nature. However, when arising, remorse scratches the mind even as it arises, like a sharp point on a bronze plate.
It arises; therefore it is called "mental remorse" (*manovilekho*). This is its description in terms of function.

As for the "remorse" mentioned in the Vinaya—"Then the Venerable Sāriputta, being anxious because the Blessed One had prohibited repeatedly staying over to partake of alms-food from a rest-house," and so on—it was not that [mental remorse] which is an hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*).
For an Arahant has no such remorse as "I have done this badly. However, this so-called *vinayakukkucca* (scruple regarding discipline) is merely a semblance of an hindrance;
it consists of the investigation as to whether something is "allowable" or "unallowable.
Regarding the explanation of the phrase, "Which states are both hindrances and associated with hindrances," since—

Dullness and drowsiness do not abandon one another; therefore, the hindrance of dullness-and-drowsiness is described without being separated from the hindrance of ignorance, as it is both a hindrance and associated with the hindrance.
However, because restlessness arises even in the absence of remorse—since there is no remorse when restlessness is present—it is described by separating it [from ignorance].
Furthermore, that which does not enter into association with something else should be understood as not being conjoined with it.
As for these hindrances, they may be cited according to either the sequence of the defilements or the sequence of the paths.
According to the sequence of the defilements, sensual desire and ill will are abandoned by the non-returning path, while lethargy-and-drowsiness and restlessness are abandoned by the arahant path.
Remorse and doubt are abandoned by the path of stream-entry; ignorance is abandoned by the path of arahantship. According to the sequence of the paths:
remorse and doubt are abandoned by the path of stream-entry; sensual desire and ill will by the path of non-returning;
and sloth-and-torpor, restlessness, and ignorance by the path of arahantship.
1182. In the *Parāmāsa-gocchaka*, the plural form is used in accordance with the nature of the question: "having set aside those states. 1219. In the exposition of clinging (*upādāna*):

"It clings to sense-pleasures (*kāma*) reckoned as the objective basis (*vatthu*)," thus it is "clinging to sense-pleasures" (*kāmupādāna*). It is also "clinging to sense-pleasures" in the sense that "it is both sense-pleasure and clinging.
"Clinging" (*upādāna*) means firm grasping. For here the prefix *upa-* has the sense of firmness, as seen in such terms as *upāyāsa* (affliction) and *upakaṭṭha* (near).
Likewise, it is "clinging to views" (*diṭṭhupādāna*) because it is both a view and a clinging. Or, it is "clinging to views" because one clings to a view.
For in such cases as "the self and the world are eternal," a subsequent view clings to a preceding view.

Similarly, it is "clinging to rules and observances" (*sīlabbatupādāna*) because one clings to rules and observances. It is also "clinging to rules and observances" because it is both rules and observances and a clinging. [This refers to] such things as the cow-vow and the ox-vow.

Indeed, because of the adherence [to the view] that "this alone is purity," these are themselves the clingings (*upādāna*). Likewise, it is called "discourse" (*vāda*) because one speaks by means of it;
it is called "clinging" (*upādāna*) because one clings by means of it. What does one speak of, or what does one cling to? One's self (*atta*).

Or, the clinging to the discourse of a self is "clinging to the discourse of a self" (*attavādupādāna*); or, it is called "clinging to the discourse of a self" because one clings to it [thinking], "The self is merely the discourse of a self."

1220. Regarding the phrase "whatever sensual desire there is for sense-pleasures," here too it is precisely the objects of sense-pleasure (*vatthukāmā*) that are intended as "sensual pleasures" (*kāmā*) without exception.

Therefore, sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) toward those objects of sense-pleasure is what is meant here by "clinging to sense-pleasures" (*kāmupādāna*). Consequently, this is established even for a non-returner (*anāgāmin*); for such a person, sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) itself, which has the five strands of sense-pleasure as its basis, no longer exists.

1221. In the exposition of the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*): "There is no giving. [One] knows that there is indeed such a thing as giving—that it is possible to give something to someone—but one grasps [the view] that there is no fruit or result of what has been given. "There is no sacrifice.

A "sacrifice" (*yiṭṭha*) refers to a great offering (*mahāyāga*). One knows that it is possible to perform such a sacrifice, yet one grasps [the view] that there is no fruit or result of the sacrifice.
He accepts [the view]: "There is no *huta*," meaning there are no offerings, hospitality rites, or auspicious ceremonies;
he accepts this because he knows that while it is possible to perform them, they have no fruit or result (*vipāka*). Regarding the phrase "there is no well-done or ill-done":

here, the ten courses of wholesome action (*kusalakammapatha*) are called "well-done deeds," and the ten courses of unwholesome action (*akusalakammapatha*) are called "ill-done deeds. He accepts the non-existence of these.
One knows the fruit, yet one grasps that there is no ripening. Thinking "this world does not exist," while standing in the next world, one grasps that this world does not exist.
Thinking "the next world does not exist," while standing in this world, one grasps that the next world does not exist.
Thinking "there is no mother, there is no father," one knows the existence of parents, yet [denies] anything resulting from the conditions performed toward them.
He holds that there is no fruit and no ripening of kamma. He holds that there are no beings of spontaneous birth, meaning he holds that there are no beings who pass away and are reborn.
He holds that there are none in the world who have fared rightly or practiced rightly—those who have entered the conformable way, the righteous recluses and brahmins.
[He denies those] who, having personally realized through direct knowledge this world and the world beyond...
"Proclaims": one grasps that there is no so-called "Omniscient Buddha" capable of proclaiming [the truth] after having known this world and the other world by means of his own preeminent knowledge.

Furthermore, it is appropriate to present these types of clinging either according to the sequence of the defilements (*kilesa*) or according to the sequence of the paths (*magga*). According to the sequence of the defilements...
Sensual clinging (*kāmupādāna*) is abandoned by the four paths; the remaining three [types of clinging] are abandoned by the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*).
According to the sequence of the paths, views-clinging (*diṭṭhupādāna*) and the others are abandoned by the path of stream-entry, while sensual clinging is abandoned by all four paths. 1235.
In the group of defilements (*kilesagocchaka*), the defilements themselves are the bases for defilement (*kilesavatthu*). Or else, beings whose taints (*āsava*) are not yet exhausted dwell therein.
They are called "bases" (*vatthu*) because they are established upon greed and the other [defilements].

They are "bases of defilement" (*kilesavatthu*) because they are both defilements and the bases for those [defilements] in sentient beings. Furthermore, since the defilements themselves also abide here by way of being immediate conditions (*anantara-paccaya*) and so forth, they are thus called "bases of defilement" (*kilesavatthu*).
1236. Therein, what is greed (*lobha*)? That which is lust (*rāga*), infatuation (*sārāga*)—this greed is explained by more than a hundred additional terms in three places:

in the "Cluster of Causes" (*hetugocchaka*), in the "Cluster of Bonds" (*ganthagocchaka*), and in this "Cluster of Defilements" (*kilesagocchaka*). In the clusters of taints (*āsava*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), and clinging (*upādāna*), it is explained by eight terms each.
This same [greed] is also explained by eight [terms] in the place where it was explained by more than a hundred additional terms.
It should be understood that even in the places defined by the eight categories (*pada*), craving is taken in its entirety (*nippadesato*).

Among those [categories]—the groups of fetters (*gantha*), hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), clingings (*upādāna*), and defilements (*kilesa*)—craving, which is to be abandoned by the four paths, stands as a single division. However, among the taints (*āsava*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), floods (*ogha*), and yokes (*yoga*), even that which is to be abandoned by the four paths stands as two divisions.
How so? Among the taints, there are the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) and the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*); among the fetters, there is the fetter of sensual lust (*kāmarāga-saṃyojana*).

The fetter of lust for existence (*bhavarāga-saṃyojana*), among the floods (*ogha*) is the flood of sensual desire (*kāmogha*) and the flood of existence (*bhavogha*); among the yokes (*yoga*) it is the yoke of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*) and the yoke of existence (*bhavayoga*).
Furthermore, these bases of defilement may be cited according to the sequence of the defilements or according to the sequence of the paths. According to the sequence of the defilements:
greed is abandoned by four paths; hatred by the non-returning path; and delusion and conceit by the path of Arahatship.

Views and doubt are abandoned by the path of stream-entry; stiffness and the rest [of the hindrances] are abandoned by the path of arahantship. According to the sequence of the paths: views and doubt are abandoned by the path of stream-entry;
hatred by the path of non-returning; and the remaining seven by the path of arahantship.
(1287) In the exposition of the sense-sphere, "below" means the lower portion. Or, [it refers to] the Avīci hell or the flames of fire.
Because there is no interval (*vīci*), gap, or opening between the painful feelings of sentient beings here, it is called *Avīci*.

Because there is no pleasure (*ayo*)—which is reckoned as happiness—here, it is called *Niraya*. It is also called *Niraya* in the sense of "absence of delight" (*nirati*) and in the sense of "lacking essence" (*nirassāda*).

"Having made that the limit" means having made that hell known as *Avīci* the boundary. "Above" means by way of the upper portion. "The devas who wield power over the creations of others" (*Paranimmitavasavatti*).
"Devas" refers to those so designated because they exercise mastery over objects created by others (*paranimmita-kāma*). "Including within" means having placed them inside.

"In this interval" means in this space. By the word "ranging therein" (*etthāvacarā*), it is stated that although others also range within this interval at times and in certain places due to their occasional arising, they are not included [among the devas]; thus, the term "ranging" (*avacara*) is used.
By this, those who have plunged into this interval and move about there, existing everywhere and at all times due to their continuous occurrence;
and those who move in the lower region below the Avīci hell by way of the continued existence of primary and derived matter—their inclusion is effected.
For they move having indeed plunged down, and they move only in the lower region; thus they are "those who move" (*avacarā*). By the phrase "included herein,"...
However, because these [factors] range over this [sphere] and also range over others, yet are not included within those [other spheres], they are therefore defined as ranging over others as well.

Now, in order to show these factors included herein by way of their state as a collection, as emptiness, and as conditions, as well as by way of their intrinsic nature, he says: "The aggregates," and so forth.
1289. In the description of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), "the Brahmā-world" refers to the plane of Brahmā, which is comprised of the first jhāna level.
The rest here should be understood according to the same method as stated in the description of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).

Regarding the phrases "of one who has attained," and so forth, it should be understood that by the first term the wholesome jhāna (*kusala-jhāna*) is mentioned; by the second, the resultant jhāna (*vipāka-jhāna*); and by the third, the functional jhāna (* kiriya-jhāna*) is mentioned.

1291. In the exposition of the formless realm (*arūpāvacara*), "one who has gone to the base of infinite space" (*ākāsānañcāyatanūpaga*) means one who has gone to the existence known as the base of infinite space. The same method applies to the second term as well. The remainder should be understood according to the method explained below.

1301. In the exposition of the dyad of "with root" (*saraṇa*): that which is delusion (*moha*) among the three unwholesome roots is "with root" through greed when associated with greed, and it is "with root" through hatred when associated with hatred. However, delusion associated with doubt or restlessness [is "with root"] through [the unwholesome root of] wrong view (*diṭṭhi*).

Furthermore, because it stands together with the abandonment of the battle of lust known as attachment to the fine-material realm (*rūparāga*) and attachment to the immaterial realm (*arūparāga*), it should be understood as "with-battle" (*saraṇa*) and "with-lust" (*saraja*).
[End of] the Discourse on the Exposition of the Pairs in the Suttas (Suttantikadukanikkhepakathā) 1303.
In the exposition of the matrix (*mātikā*) among the pairs in the Suttas, since these have been analyzed according to their meaning, here are their explanatory passages (*niddesapada*):
Since these too are easy to understand by the same method explained below, they are for the most part self-evident. However, this much is the specific distinction here:
regarding the simile of the lightning-flash first, it is said that a man with good eyesight set out on a path at night in the darkness of a cloud.
Because of the darkness, the path was not discerned. A flash of lightning broke forth and dispelled the darkness.
Then, with the disappearance of the darkness, the path became visible. He set out on his journey for a second time.
Again, darkness enveloped him; the path was not discerned. A flash of lightning burst forth and dispelled it. When the darkness had vanished, the path became visible.
He set out on his journey for a third time. Darkness enveloped him; the path was not discerned.
A flash of lightning, having burst forth, dispels the darkness.
In this context, the commencement of insight (vipassanā) by a noble disciple for the sake of the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) is like a sighted person setting out on a path in the dark.
The time when the path is not discerned in the darkness is like the gloom that obscures the truths. By means of the lightning...

Having emerged, it is like the time when darkness is dispelled; having arisen with the radiance of the stream-entry path (*sotāpatti-magga*), it is the time when the darkness that obscures the truths is removed.
Just as the path becomes manifest once the darkness has vanished, so too the four truths become manifest through the stream-entry path.
Furthermore, what is manifest to the path is indeed manifest to the person possessing that path. This is the second application of the effort for going.

The commencement of insight for the sake of the once-returning path is like the beginning of a journey in darkness. The time when the path is not discerned in the darkness is like the darkness that obscures the truths.

The second flash of lightning, having burst forth and dispelled the darkness, is like the moment the light of the once-returning path arises and removes the darkness that obscures the truths. When the darkness has vanished...
The time when the path becomes manifest is like the time when the Four Truths become manifest through the Once-returning Path.

Furthermore, what is manifest to the path is indeed manifest to the person who possesses that path. The undertaking of insight for the sake of the Non-returning Path is like the setting forth on the third journey.
The darkness that obscures the truths is like the time when the path is not perceived in the dark. Third.

Just as the time when darkness is destroyed by the flashing forth of lightning, so too is the time when the veil obscuring the truths is dispelled by the arising of the light of the non-returning path (*anāgāmimagga*).

Just as the time when the path becomes manifest once the darkness has vanished, so too is the time when the four truths become manifest through the non-returning path. Furthermore, what is manifest to the path is indeed manifest to the person who possesses that path (*maggasamaṅgipuggala*).
For a diamond, however, there is no stone or gem that is called "indestructible. Wherever it falls, it pierces right through.
It hurls away everything except for another diamond. The path traversed by a diamond never returns to its former state.
In the very same way, for the path of Arahatship, there is no defilement that is called "unslayable. It pierces through all defilements.
Like a diamond: the path of arahantship also destroys the defilements, exhausting them without remainder.
Just as there is no returning to the natural state for a path traversed by a diamond, so too there is no recurrence of the defilements abandoned by the path of arahantship. 1307.
In the exposition of the dyad on fools (*bāla*), lack of shame (*ahirika*) and lack of dread (*anottappa*) are prominent among fools, and they are the roots of the remaining qualities of fools.
For one who is shameless and lacks moral dread does indeed do nothing that is unwholesome. These two [factors] were stated separately at the very beginning.
This same method applies to the white side as well. Likewise for the black dyad. 1311.
In the exposition of the dyad on burning, burning should be understood both from what has been done and from what has not been done. [These refer to] bodily misconduct and so forth.

For they burn because of what has been done, and do not burn because of bodily good conduct and so forth that has not been done. Thus, a person burns thinking, "Bodily misconduct was committed by me," and burns thinking, "Bodily good conduct was not performed by me.
He burns thinking, "Verbal misconduct was committed by me"... [and so on] ...he burns thinking, "Mental good conduct was not performed by me.
The same method applies even to those things that do not cause burning. For a person who performs wholesome deeds...
“I have performed good conduct of body,” he does not burn with remorse; “I have not performed misconduct of body,” he does not burn with remorse...
pe ... “I have not performed misconduct of mind,” he does not burn with remorse.
In the explanation of the pair of designations (*adhivacanaduka*), the phrase “of those various phenomena” includes all phenomena. It is called “reckoned” (*saṅkhāyati*).
*Saṅkhā*: the meaning is "it is conceptualized. How is it conceptualized? It is conceptualized in many ways such as:
"I," "mine," "another," "another's," "a being," "an entity," "a person," "an individual," "a man," "a youth," "Tissa," "Datta";
or "bed," "bench," "cushion," "bolster," "monastery," "courtyard," "door," "window"—thus it is conceptualized in these and other various modes.
‘Concept’ (*saṅkhā*). It is a designation (*samaññā*) because it is designated (*samaññāyati*). How is it designated? It is designated as “I,” and so forth, up to “window”;
thus it is a “designation. It is a description (*paññatti*) because it is made known (*paññāpiyati*). It is a conventional expression (*vohāra*) because it is uttered (*vohariyati*).
How is it uttered? It is uttered as “I,” and so forth, up to “window”; thus it is a “conventional expression.”
Names are fourfold: the common name (*sāmaññanāma*), the name based on qualities (*guṇanāma*), the name based on reputation (*kittināma*), and the spontaneous name (*opapātikanāma*).
Among these, the name of the king was "Mahāsammata" (Greatly Elect) because he was established by being elected by the great multitude among those of the first eon;
this is what is called a "common name. It is with reference to this that it was said: "Because he was elected by the great multitude, Vāseṭṭha, he is called Mahāsammata."

“Indeed, this very first syllable was produced. A name derived from such qualities—such as “Dhammakathika,” “Paṃsukūlika,” “Vinayadhara,” “Tepiṭaka,” “Saddha,” or “Pasanna”—is called a “name based on qualities” (*guṇanāma*).
The hundreds of names of the Tathāgata, such as “Bhagavā,” “Arahaṃ,” and “Sammāsambuddho,” are likewise all names based on qualities. Therefore it is said:
“Countless are the names of the Great Sage according to his qualities;
even from among a thousand names, one name should be selected on account of his virtue.
Furthermore, on the day the newborn prince’s name was taken, after performing honors for those worthy of offerings, [he was brought] into their presence...
Relatives, having deliberated and reflected, establish a name saying, "This one is named so-and-so";

this is what is called a "designative name" (*kittimanāma*). Furthermore, when a prior designation falls into a subsequent designation, and a prior usage falls into a subsequent usage—for example, in previous eons the moon was indeed called "the moon," and even now it is still "the moon"—so it was in the past.
The sun... the ocean... the earth... and a mountain—just as it was called a "mountain" in the past, so too even now it is indeed a mountain;
this is what is called a "conventional name" (*opapātika-nāma*). All these four kinds of names are, in this context, simply "names" (*nāma*).

"Naming" (*nāmakamma*) is the act of giving a name. "Designation" (*nāmadheyya*) is the establishing of a name. "Etymology" (*nirutti*) is the linguistic derivation of a name. "Phrasing" (*byañjana*) is...
It is the "manifestation of the name. It is stated thus because it manifests that meaning. "Expression" refers specifically to the expression of the name.

All phenomena (dhammā) are the path of designation; there is no phenomenon that is not the path of designation. One phenomenon subsumes all phenomena, and all phenomena subsume one phenomenon. How so? For this is the conceptual designation of "name" (nāma-paññatti).
There is one dhamma that applies to all dhammas of the four planes. Neither a sentient being nor a conditioned formation exists apart from a name.
Even a tree in the forest or on a mountain is a burden to the people of the country; for when they are asked, "What is this tree called?
they reply with the name they know it by, such as "khadira" or "palāsa. And even that whose name they do not know—
"They say 'the nameless one' (*anāmaka*)," they say; yet even that remains as his very designation. The same principle applies to fish, turtles, and so forth in the ocean.
The other two dyads have exactly the same meaning as this one. 1316.
In the dyad of "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), it is called "name" (*nāma*) in the sense of naming (*nāmakaraṇa*), in the sense of bending (*namana*), and in the sense of inclining (*nāmana*). Therein—

First, the four aggregates are called “name” (nāma) in the sense of being that which bends (namana). For just as Mahā Sammata received the name “Mahā Sammata” because he was highly esteemed by the great multitude;
or as parents give their son a descriptive name such as “Let him be named Tissa,” or “Let him be named Phussa”; or as one is called a “Dhamma-preacher” or a “Master of Discipline.”
A name comes into being by way of its qualities (*guṇa*), but this is not the case for feeling (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates.
For feeling and the rest arise having already established their own names, just like the great earth and so forth. When they have arisen, their names are already established.
Indeed, when feeling arises, no one says, "You shall be called 'feeling'. Nor does there exist any function of assigning a name to it.
It exists. Just as when the earth has arisen, there is no need for the act of giving it a name by saying, "You shall be named Earth";

and when the world-system, Sineru, the moon, the sun, and the constellations have arisen, there is no need for the act of giving them names by saying, "You shall be named the world-system," or "You shall be named a constellation"—the name simply exists as such within the conventional designation of spontaneous birth (*opapātika-paññatti*).
When feeling arises, there is no need for the act of assigning a name by saying, “You, feeling, must become ‘feeling’”;
rather, as soon as it has arisen, it is already possessed of the name “feeling. It falls under the designation of “spontaneous birth” (opapātika).
The same principle applies to perception and the other aggregates. For even in the past, feeling was simply feeling; perception... formations... consciousness was simply consciousness.
In the future as well, and in the present as well. But Nibbāna is always Nibbāna itself. In the sense of "making a name" (*nāmakaraṇa*), it is called "name" (*nāma*).
Furthermore, in the sense of "bending" (*namana*), the four aggregates (*khandha*) are also "name," for they bend toward their objects. In the sense of "bending," everything is "name";
for the four aggregates bend one another toward the object. Nibbāna [is so called] by way of being the dominant condition (*adhipatipaccaya*) for the object.
He inclines [the mind] toward a faultless state within himself.
(1318) Ignorance and craving for existence are mentioned here in order to demonstrate the active manifestation of the root of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
(1320) Taking the five aggregates as "self and world" in the sense of "there will be self and world," he [regards] that...

The eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*) is established in the mode of grasping [the thought], ‘I shall exist. The second is the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*), established in the mode [of thinking], ‘I shall not exist.
“Concerning the past” means taking the past portion as the object. By this, those [views] included in the *Brahmajāla Sutta* are indicated.
The eighteen views concerning the past (*pubbantānudiṭṭhiyo*) are included. "With reference to the future" (*aparantaṃ ārabbha*) means taking the future portion as an object;
by this, the forty-four views concerning the future (*aparantānudiṭṭhiyo*) mentioned in that same [text] are included. 1332.

In the description of "obstinacy" (*dovacassatā*), regarding the phrase "when being spoken to by those who speak according to the Dhamma" (*sahadhammike vuccamāne*): "those who speak according to the Dhamma" (*sahadhammika*) refers to those whom the Blessed One...
When a training rule has been laid down, and after showing the basis for it and charging him with an offense, he is told:
"You have fallen into such-and-such an offense; come now, confess it, emerge from it, and make amends.

In the context of the terms *dovacassatā* and so forth, when one who is thus reproved responds with counter-reproach or obstinacy (*appadakkhiṇagāhitā*), the formal act against that ill-spoken person is *dovacassiya*. That very same thing is also called *dovacassanta*.
It is so called. Its state is *dovacassiya* (refractoriness). The other term is a synonym for that very same thing.

"Adverse grasping" (*vippaṭikūlagāhitā*) means contrary grasping. One who has pleasure (*sāta*) through the contrary [attitude] known as adverse grasping is "one who finds pleasure in contrariety" (*vipaccanīkasāta*).
This refers to one who, having taken up a grasping like a shield, makes it soundless with a single stroke—thus obtaining ease.

It is a designation (*adhivacana*). Its state is constant opposition (*vipaccanīkasātatā*). Disrespect (*anādariya*) is the state of non-regard (*anādara*) due to not accepting instruction; the other term is a synonym for that same thing.
Or, disrespect is the mode of not accepting. The state of lack of reverence (*agāravatā*) is the state of irreverence (*agārabhāva*) arising from not living in the dwelling of one who is venerable.
The state of lack of deference (*appaṭissavatā*) is the state of non-deference arising from not living in the dwelling of one who is senior.
"Unyieldingness. This is called such-and-such "difficult-to-correctness" (*dovacassatā*).
In terms of its actual meaning, however, it consists of the four aggregates (*khandha*) occurring in that particular mode, or simply the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) alone.

The same principle applies to "having evil friends" (*pāpamittatā*) and so forth. For there are no separate mental factors (*cetasika-dhamma*) named "difficult-to-correctness," "having evil friends," and the like.
1333. They are "faithless" (assaddhā) because they have no faith; the meaning is that they do not believe in the objects [of faith] such as the Buddha.
"Immoral" (dussīla): there is no such thing as a "bad name" for virtue; the meaning is that they are devoid of virtue. "Of little learning" (appassuta):

those bereft of learning. "Miserly" (maccharino): those who possess the five kinds of miserliness. "Lacking wisdom" (duppañña): those devoid of wisdom. "Cultivation" (sevanā) is so called by way of practicing or associating with.
*Balavasevanā* means intense service. *Sabbatobhāgena sevanā* means service on all sides;

or, the term has been expanded by means of a prefix (*upasagga*), yet it is still described as simply "service" (*sevanā*) by all three [terms]. *Bhajanā* means approaching. *Sambhajanā* means approaching on all sides;
or, the term has been expanded by means of a prefix. *Bhattī* means firm devotion. *Sambhattī* means [devotion] on all sides.
*Bhatti*. Alternatively, the word is expanded by means of a prefix (*upasagga*). By both [terms], firm devotion (*daḷhabhatti*) itself is expressed.
*Tamsampavaṅkatā* means the state of being completely devoted to those persons both in body and in mind; the meaning is being inclined toward them, leaning toward them, and tending toward them.
1334. The exposition of the dyad on being easy to speak to (*sovacassatā*) should also be understood by way of the opposite of what has been stated.
1336. "The five classes of offenses" refers, by way of the exposition of the matrix (*mātikā*), to these five offenses:
*pārājika*, *saṅghādisesa*, *pācittiya*, *pāṭidesanīya*, and *dukkaṭa*. "The seven classes of offenses" refers, by way of the exposition of the discipline (*vinaya*), to:
*pārājika*, *saṅghādisesa*, *thullaccaya*, *pācittiya*, *pāṭidesanīya*, *dukkaṭa*, and *dubbhāsita*.
These are the seven offenses. In this context, the wisdom that knows the delimitation of those offenses together with their underlying bases is called "skill in offenses.
Furthermore, the wisdom that knows the delimitation of the emergence from an offense together with the formal ritual proclamation (*kammavācā*) is called "skill in the emergence from offenses."

It is called *samāpatti* because it is to be attained (*samāpajjitabbato*). Furthermore, the wisdom that knows the delimitation of absorption (*appanā*) together with its preliminary work (*parikamma*) is called skill in attainment (*samāpattikusalatā*).

Skill in emerging from attainment (*samāpattivuṭṭhānakusalatā*) exists by virtue of the presence of the wisdom that emerges at that very moment without fail, thinking: "When the moon, the sun, or a constellation has reached this much distance, I shall emerge."

1340. Wisdom consisting in the learning, attention, hearing, retention, delimitation, and knowing of the eighteen elements is called proficiency in the elements (*dhātu-kusala-tā*). Wisdom consisting in the learning, attention, and knowing of those very same [elements] is called proficiency in attention (*manasikāra-kusala-tā*).
1342. Wisdom consisting in the learning, attention, hearing, retention, delimitation, and knowing of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) is called proficiency in the bases (*āyatana-kusala-tā*).
Or, in all three types of proficiency, there are learning, attention, hearing, comprehension (*sammasana*), and penetration (*paṭivedha*).
"Reviewing" (paccavekkhaṇā) includes everything. Among these, hearing, grasping, and reviewing are mundane; penetration is supramundane;

and attention consisting of comprehension is a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane. "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," and so forth, will be clarified in the *Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga*.
However, the wisdom that knows, "By means of this condition, this comes to be," is [supramundane].
Skill in dependent origination. 1344.
In the exposition of the dyad on skill in what is possible and impossible, both "cause" (*hetu*) and "condition" (*paccaya*) are synonyms for one another.
For the sensitivity of the eye is both the cause and the condition for the arising of eye-consciousness that occurs by taking visible form as its object.
Likewise, the ear-sensitivity and so forth are conditions for ear-consciousness and so forth; and mango seeds and so forth are conditions for mango fruits and so forth.
In the second method, "whatever states" is an illustration of states that are dissimilar conditions. "Of whatever [states]" is an illustration of the states arisen from those dissimilar conditions.
"Neither causes nor conditions" refers to the eye-sensitivity in relation to the ear-consciousness that arises having sound as its object.

There is neither cause nor condition. Likewise, the ear-sensitivity and so forth are not causes for the remaining consciousnesses and their concomitants; and mango trees and so forth are not causes for the arising of palmyra trees and so forth—this is how the meaning should be understood.
In the description of "straightforwardness and gentleness" (*ajjava-maddava*), the only difference is the phrase "a humble mind. Its meaning is: by way of the absence of conceit (*māna*).

One whose mind is low is "low-minded" (*nīcacitta*). The state of having a low mind is "low-mindedness" (*nīcacittatā*). The remainder [of the definitions] for mental rectitude (*cittujukatā*) and mental malleability (*cittamudutā*) has already been presented in the word-analysis (*padabhājanīya*).
In the exposition of patience (*khanti-niddesa*):
patience (*khanti*) is so called by way of being patient. The mode of being patient is "patience-ness" (*khamanatā*). By means of this, one endures (*adhivāsenti*).
"Endurance" (*adhivāsanatā*) means that they allow [insults] to be placed upon themselves and endure them; they do not ward them off, nor do they stand in opposition to them.
