"Non-anger" (*acaṇḍikkaṃ*) is the state of one who is not fierce. "Not a speaker of harsh words" (*anasuropo*): a "speaker of harsh words" (*asuropo*) is so called because of speaking ill-spoken speech due to being improperly composed;
by contrast, "not a speaker of harsh words" means one who speaks well-spoken words. Thus, in this context, the cause is indicated by way of a metaphorical designation of the effect.

“Satisfaction of mind” (*attamanatā cittassa*) means the state of being agreeable to the mind by way of joy; it is the very nature of one’s own mind, not a state of a corrupted mind—this is the meaning.
(1349) In the description of “moral restraint” (*soracca*), “bodily non-transgression” refers to the threefold bodily good conduct. “Vocal non-transgression” refers to...
Virtuous verbal conduct is fourfold. By the phrase "bodily and verbal," this includes the morality of the eightfold livelihood arising from the doors of body and speech.
"This is called gentleness" (soracca): it is called gentleness because one has thoroughly retreated (orata) from evil.
"The entire restraint of virtue" (sīlasaṃvara): this is because one does not practice misconduct merely through body and speech, but also through the mind.
He indeed practices [it]; therefore, it is stated in order to demonstrate the mental virtue (*mānasika-sīla*) by exhausting its full extent.

1350. In the exposition of gentleness (*sākhalya*): "pustules" (*aṇḍaka*)—just as pustules arise on a tree that has a disease, so too, due to the presence of fault, "pustules" are produced by words such as reviling and disparaging. "Harsh" (*kakkasa*)—it is like a rotten tree.
It is rough, with its powder falling away; thus it is "rough. It enters as if striking the ear.
Therefore it is called "rough. "Painful to others" means painful for others, unpleasant, and provocative of hatred.
"Provocative of hostility toward others" means that, like a crooked thorny branch, it pierces the skin and provokes hostility in others, preventing even those who wish to go from going.

"One who clings without giving. "In the vicinity of anger" means close to anger. "Not conducive to concentration" means not conducive to either absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*) or access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*).
Thus, all these are synonyms for speech accompanied by hatred.
"Having abandoned such speech"—this refers to that which occurs intermittently even for one who has not yet abandoned harsh speech.
“Gentle speech” (*saṇhavācā*) is stated for the purpose of illustrating that which is indeed not harsh speech (*asaṇhavācā*).

“Neḷā”: *eḷa* is said to mean fault (*dosa*). That which has no *eḷa* is *neḷā*; the meaning is “faultless. It is like the word *neḷa* used in the phrase, “The chariot with faultless limbs and a white canopy.
“Pleasant to the ear” (*kaṇṇasukhā*): it is pleasant to the ears because of the sweetness of its phonemes (*byañjana*), unlike the piercing of a needle.
It does not produce earache as it were. Because of its sweetness of meaning, it produces affection rather than irritation in the body;
thus, it is "endearing" (*pemanīyā*). It goes to the heart, entering the mind easily without being obstructed;
thus, it is "heart-reaching" (*hadayaṅgamā*). Because it is full of virtues, it is "urban" (*porī*); or, like a woman raised in a city, it is "refined" (*porī*). Of the city...
This too is "polished" (*porī*); the meaning is "the speech of city-dwellers. For city-dwellers are speakers of refined speech.
They say "father" for one who is merely a father, and "brother" for one who is merely a brother. Such speech as this is "dear to many people" (*bahujanakantā*).

Precisely because it is dear, it is "pleasing to many people" (*bahujanamanāpā*), meaning it is agreeable to many people and increases their mental well-being. "That which is there... (*yā tattha*)... [and so forth].

That which pertains to that person: "Gentle speech" means smooth speech. "Affable speech" means soft speech. "Non-harsh speech" means speech that is not rough. 1351. In the description of hospitality (*paṭisanthāra*):

"Hospitality with material things" (*āmisa-paṭisanthāra*) is the extending of welcome through material gifts in such a way that the deficiency of others, together with oneself, becomes closed and concealed by means of those material things. "Hospitality with the Dhamma" (*dhamma-paṭisanthāra*)... [is]...
Just as one covers and conceals a flaw in oneself with the non-attainment of the Dhamma so that it is hidden from others, such is the welcoming with the Dhamma.
He is a "welcomer" because there are only two flaws in worldly existence, and he is a welcomer of those two: either by the welcoming of material things or by the welcoming of the Dhamma.
By means of these two kinds of hospitality, one is hospitable, one extends hospitality, and one acts continuously.
Herein, this is the discourse starting from the beginning:
when a monk who is hospitable sees a visitor approaching, he should go out to meet him, take his bowl and robe, give him a seat, and fan him with a palm-leaf fan.
Having washed his feet, they should be massaged; if there is ghee or molasses, medicine should be given; he should be asked if he needs drinking water;
and the dwelling should be looked after. In this way, hospitality with material things is said to be performed in part.
However, even if one is junior, if the senior has not yet come to attend upon him, one should go to him, sit down, and...
One should not ask a question regarding a subject that is outside of one's scope; rather, having asked about their specific field of expertise, one should pose a question within that domain.
Without first asking, "Which reciter (*bhāṇaka*) are you? one should instead ask, "Which texts do your teachers and preceptors (*ācariya-upajjhāya*) employ?
and then pose a question on a subject for which they are capable. If they are able to explain it, that is well. If they are not able, one should explain it oneself.
It should be given. In this way, a partial welcome in accordance with the Dhamma is considered performed.
If he is living near you, you should take him along and go regularly for alms.
If you wish to depart, on the day before your departure, you should take him along to a village that lies on your route, go there for alms, and then dismiss him.
If monks have been invited in another direction, one should go taking that monk with him if he wishes to go.
If he does not wish to go, thinking, “This direction is not familiar to me,” one should send the other monks on and then go for alms taking him along.
Whatever food one has obtained oneself should be given to him. In this way, it is said that “hospitality with material goods” has been performed.
Regarding one who distributes material gifts (*āmisa-patisanthāraka*), to whom should what he has received be given? First, it should be given to a guest.
If there is anyone who is ill or lacking in requisites, it should also be given to them. It should be given to the preceptor (*ācariya*) and the teacher (*upajjhāya*).
It should be given to the storekeeper (*bhaṇḍagāhaka*). Furthermore, by one who fulfills the qualities of cordiality (*sārāṇīya-dhamma*), even a hundred times or a thousand times—
It should be given to those who arrive, starting from the seat of the senior elder. Furthermore, the host should give to each person who has not received anything.
Having gone outside the village, if one sees an elderly person, a destitute person, a bhikkhu, or a bhikkhunī, one should give to them as well.

In this regard, there is this story: It is said that when the village of Gutta-sālā was attacked by bandits, at that very moment an elder nun who had destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*) emerged from cessation (*nirodha*).
Having had a young bhikkhunī take her belongings, she set out on the road with a great crowd of people.
At midday, having reached the gate of the village of Nakula-nagara, she sat down at the foot of a tree. At that time, [there lived] one who resided in the Kāḷavalli bower...
The Elder Mahānāga, having walked for alms in the village of Nakulanagara and coming out, saw the elder nun and asked her about her meal.
She replied, "I have no bowl. The Elder said, "Eat with this very one," and gave it to her along with his own bowl.
After the nun had finished her meal and washed the bowl, she gave it back to the Elder and said, "For today at least, [let us go] by way of alms-round."
“You will become weary; from now on, dear ones, there will be no such thing as a mere pittance for you in alms-food.
From that time forth, not even an alms-meal worth less than a kahāpaṇa had ever before arisen for the elder. This is what is called “hospitality with material things.
Having performed this hospitality, the monk, standing on the side of support, [should provide] that monk’s meditation subject.
One should speak [the Dhamma], the Dhamma should be recited, remorse should be dispelled, and whatever duty has arisen should be performed.

The acts of rehabilitation (*abbhāna*), emergence from probation (*vuṭṭhāna*), penance (*mānatta*), and the period of probation (*parivāsa*) should be granted. One who is worthy of going forth should be ordained;

one who is worthy of full admission (*upasampadā*) should be fully admitted. For a bhikkhunī who desires full admission in one’s presence, the formal ritual statement (*kammavācā*) [should be recited].
It is proper to do so. This is called "welcoming with the Dhamma" (*dhammapaṭisanthāra*).

Through these two kinds of welcoming, a monk who practices welcoming generates unarisen gain, makes arisen gain stable, and protects his own life in a place of danger—just as one would by grasping the hand of a robber-king.
It is like an elder who, taking the tip [of the food], scatters the meal from his very bowl. Regarding the production of gain not yet obtained,

there is the account of the Great Medicinal Gift established for life at the Setamba courtyard by the Mahānāga king, who had fled from here to the other shore, received patronage from a certain elder, returned, and was re-established in his kingdom.

It should be told. Regarding the making of what has arisen into a permanent gain, the story concerning how the goods were not plundered by thieves at Cetiya Pabbata after receiving hospitality from the hands of the Elder Dīghabhāṇaka Abhaya should be told. 1352.
In the description of the lack of guarding the doors of the sense faculties, "having seen a form with the eye" refers to the eye by way of its causal function.
Having seen a visible form with eye-consciousness, which is capable of seeing forms by way of conventional designation. However, the ancients have said:
"The eye does not see the form, because it is devoid of consciousness; the mind does not see, because it is devoid of the eye;

rather, one sees by means of a consciousness based on the sensitive organ (*pasāda*), through the impact of the door and the object. But this [expression] is like [the phrase] 'one shoots with a bow' and so forth."
This is called a discourse on the requisites. Therefore, the meaning here is simply: "having seen a form with eye-consciousness.

One who seizes upon signs (*nimittaggāhī*) seizes upon a sign that has become a basis for defilement—such as the sign of a woman or a man, or the sign of beauty and so forth—by way of desire and lust;
he does not settle for the mere sight of it. One who seizes upon secondary characteristics (*anubyañjanaggāhī*) [seizes upon] the defilements...

One takes up the "manner" (ākāra), which is designated by the term *anubyañjana* because it makes [the internal state] manifest through its secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*), and which is divided into gestures of the hands and feet, smiling, speaking, looking forward, looking around, and so forth.
In the passage beginning with "on account of which," the word "which" (*yaṃ*) refers to the cause—
that is, the lack of restraint of the eye-faculty— by reason of which that person, having failed to restrain the eye-faculty with the door of mindfulness, leaves the eye-door unshut.
While he is dwelling thus, these states such as covetousness might flow in after him, follow him, and overwhelm him.
"He does not practice for its restraint" means he does not practice for the purpose of closing the door of mindfulness upon that eye-faculty.
And being just such a person, he does not guard the eye-faculty; he is said to "not attain restraint over the eye-faculty."
In this regard, although there is neither restraint nor non-restraint in the eye-faculty—
for mindfulness or forgetfulness does not arise dependent upon the sensitive materiality of the eye— nevertheless, when a visible object comes into the range of the eye,
after the life-continuum has arisen and ceased twice, the functional mind-element performs the function of adverting.

Having arisen, it ceases. Thereafter, eye-consciousness arises and ceases, performing the function of seeing; thereafter, the resultant mind-element arises and ceases, performing the function of receiving;

thereafter, the resultant rootless mind-consciousness-element arises and ceases, performing the function of investigating; thereafter, the functional rootless mind-consciousness-element arises and ceases, accomplishing the function of determining. Immediately following that, the impulsion (javana) occurs.
Even there, neither restraint nor non-restraint exists during the moment of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) or during any of the moments such as adverting (āvajjana).
However, at the moment of impulsion (javana), if immorality, negligence, ignorance,
intolerance, or laziness arises, there is non-restraint.

When this occurs, it is called "non-restraint of the eye-faculty. Why? Because when that non-restraint exists, not only is the door unguarded, but the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and the process-consciousnesses (vīthicitta), such as adverting and so forth, are also unguarded. How is this so?
It is just as when the four gates of a city are left unguarded, even though the inner houses, gate-towers, chambers, and so on may be well-guarded.
Nevertheless, all the goods within the city remain unprotected and unguarded; for once thieves have entered through the city gate, they may do as they please.

In the same way, when misconduct and other such faults arise in the "swift course" (javana), if there is that lack of restraint (asaṃvara), then the door is unguarded, as are the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and the cognitive processes beginning with the adverting consciousness (āvajjana).
The same method applies to the phrases "having heard a sound with the ear," and so forth. "That which belongs to these" means:

for one who does not attain such restraint, that which is the lack of guarding, the lack of protection, the lack of defense, and the lack of restraint regarding these six sense-faculties; the meaning is "that which is not closing off" or "not sealing.
In the description of "immoderation in food": "here, a certain person" means a certain person in this world of beings. "Without reflection" means...
"Without knowing through the wisdom of reflection (paṭisaṅkhāna-paññā) and without having investigated. "Improperly" means by an unskillful means (anupāya).
"Food" refers to that which is swallowed, such as what is eaten, drunk, and so forth. "Eats" means consumes or swallows. "For sport," etc., is stated for the purpose of showing the unskillful means;
for one who eats by an unskillful means eats for the sake of sport, for intoxication, for adornment, or for beautification, and not with the aim of this [noble] purpose.
"Dependent upon": that which therein is "lack of contentment" (*asantuṭṭhi*) means the state of non-contentment, the condition of not being satisfied with that improper utilization of food.
"Lack of moderation" (*amattaññutā*) means the state of not knowing the measure; it is the failure to recognize the measure defined as the proper limit.
"This is called": this lack of moderation in food, which occurs by way of consuming without reflection, is what is called "lack of moderation in food."
1354. In the exposition on guarding the doors of the sense faculties, "the eye," and so forth, should be understood according to the method already stated.
"He does not seize upon the sign" means that he does not grasp the sign in the manner described under the influence of desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*).

The remaining phrases should likewise be understood by way of their respective opposites as previously explained. And just as it was stated below: "When misconduct and so forth have arisen in the course of impulsion (*javana*), and there is non-restraint therein..."
It was said: "The door is unguarded, as are the life-continuum and the process-thoughts such as adverting.
In the same way, when those virtues and so forth have arisen here, the door is guarded, as are the life-continuum and the process-thoughts such as adverting.
How is this so? Just as when the city gates are well-shut, even though the interior houses and so forth may be unshut.

Nevertheless, just as all the goods within a city remain well-guarded and well-protected when the city gates are closed—since there is no entry for thieves—the same applies when the impulsion (javana) has arisen regarding virtue and so forth:
the doors are guarded, as are the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and the cognitive-process consciousnesses such as adverting (āvajjana).
Therefore, even though it arises at the moment of impulsion, it is called "restraint in the eye-faculty."
It has been said. The same method applies to such passages as "having heard a sound with the ear," and so forth. 1355.

In the exposition on moderation in eating, the phrase "he consumes food with wise reflection" means that having understood through the wisdom of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhā-paññā*), he partakes of food by means of a proper method. Now, in order to show that method, it is said: "Neither for sport," and so forth.
Therein, "neither for sport" means he does not consume food for the sake of amusement. In this regard, actors, acrobats, and the like [consume food] for the sake of amusement.

They indeed consume. For that food which, after having eaten, seems to a man like a festival consisting of dancing, singing, poetry, and verse recitation—that food they consume by seeking it through unrighteous and improper means. But this bhikkhu does not consume in such a way.
"Not for intoxication" means he does not consume it for the purpose of increasing the intoxication of pride and the intoxication of manhood. In this regard, kings, royal ministers, and...
They indeed eat for their own sake; for they consume choice foods such as rice porridge and other delicacies for the purpose of increasing their own pride, intoxication, and manly arrogance.
But this bhikkhu does not consume food in this manner.

"Not for the sake of adornment" means he does not consume it for the purpose of adorning the body. In this regard, women who subsist on physical beauty, such as those in the royal harem and others, [act otherwise].

And they drink ghee and molasses; for they consume food that is unctuous, soft, and mild, thinking, “In this way our limbs will remain well-proportioned, and the complexion of our skin will become radiant.
But this bhikkhu does not consume food in such a manner.
"Not for the sake of beautification" means he does not consume food for the purpose of beautifying the flesh of the body.

In this regard, wrestlers, boxers, and the like nourish the flesh of their bodies with very succulent fish, meat, and so forth, thinking, "In this way our flesh will become well-developed for the sake of enduring blows.
But this bhikkhu does not consume food in such a manner for the sake of beautifying the flesh of the body.

"Only as long as" (*yāvadeva*) indicates the limitation and determination of the purpose for taking food. "For the maintenance of this body" (*imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā*) means he takes food for the sake of sustaining this body composed of the four great elements and derived matter.

This is the meaning: "This is the purpose for his taking of food. "For its endurance" (*yāpanāya*) means he takes food for the sake of maintaining the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). "For the allaying of affliction" (*vihiṃsūparatiyā*): affliction (*vihiṃsā*) is... [text continues]
Hunger is that which arises with non-eating as its condition. He eats for the purpose of its cessation and pacification. "For the support of the holy life" (*brahmacariyānuggahāya*):
the holy life (*brahmacariya*) consists of the three trainings and the entire teaching; he eats for the purpose of supporting it.
"Thus" (*iti*) is a demonstration of the means; the meaning is, "by this means. "In order to ward off old feeling": old feeling...
“New feeling” refers to the feeling that arises due to the condition of over-eating; one consumes food thinking, “I shall ward off that [feeling].
Furthermore, “new feeling” refers to the feeling that would arise due to the condition of under-eating; one consumes food thinking, “I shall not give rise to that new feeling.
Alternatively, “new feeling” refers to the feeling that does not arise due to the condition of having eaten [properly]; one consumes food so that this [feeling] does not arise.
He consumes food solely for the purpose of non-arising [of afflictions]. "There will be sustenance for me" means there will be maintenance for me.
Regarding "blamelessness": herein, there is that which is blameworthy and there is that which is blameless.

In this context, unrighteous seeking, unrighteous acceptance, and unrighteous enjoyment—this is called "blameworthy. Having sought in accordance with the Dhamma and accepted in accordance with the Dhamma...
Consuming [food] after having reflected upon it is called "blameless. Yet, some person commits what is blameworthy even when it is blameless;
thinking "I have received it," he consumes beyond measure. Unable to digest it, he suffers from purging upwards, purging downwards, and so forth.
All the monks in the monastery exert themselves in attending to his body and seeking medicine for him.
They fall into [this state]. When asked, "What is this?", they say, "The belly of such-and-such a person is bloated," and so forth.
They criticize and revile him, saying, "This man is always of such a nature; he does not even know the measure of his own stomach.
This is called committing what is blameworthy when it is actually blameless. Not acting in this way, one consumes food with the thought, "There shall be blamelessness."
"And a comfortable dwelling": here too, there is what is a comfortable dwelling and there is what is not a comfortable dwelling.

In this regard, the food of these five types of brahmins—namely, the "food-bearer," the "hand-bringer," the "ample-portion," the "crow-peck," and the "eater-until-satiated"—is called a non-comfortable dwelling.
For among them, the one called the "food-bearer" eats much for himself...
Being unable to rise by his own nature, he says, "Bring me a hand. One called *alaṃsāṭaka* is so utterly bloated and loathsome that even when he has risen, he is unable to put on his garment.
One called *tatthavaṭṭaka* is unable to rise and merely rolls about right there.
One called *kākamāsaka* is such that it can be pecked at by crows all the way up to the opening of the mouth.
He eats. One who has "eaten until full" is one who, being unable to hold it in his mouth, vomits right there. Not acting in that way, he eats with the thought:
"There will be a comfortable dwelling for me. A "comfortable dwelling" means having the stomach less than half-full by four or five mouthfuls.
For after eating this much and drinking water, the four postures can be maintained with ease.
Thus they proceed. Therefore the Dhamma-Senāpati said:
“Having eaten four or five mouthfuls, one should drink water;
this is sufficient for a bhikkhu of resolute self to dwell in comfort.”
In this context, however, the factors should be brought together: “Neither for amusement” is one factor;
“not for intoxication” is one; “not for adornment” is one; “not for beautification” is one; “only for the maintenance and sustenance of this body” is one;
“for the cessation of affliction and for support of the holy life” is one; and “thus [to avoid] past... [and future suffering]” is one.
"One part is: 'I shall endure existing sensations and shall not give rise to new sensations';
another part is: 'There will be sustenance for me. In this context, the benefit of eating is blamelessness and a comfortable dwelling.
However, the Elder Mahāsīva said: 'The four parts mentioned above are called prohibitions; the eight parts mentioned subsequently, however, are to be combined together.'"
In this regard, “only for the maintenance of this body” is one factor; “for its sustenance” is one; “for the cessation of affliction” is one;
“for the support of the holy life” is one; “so that I may ward off old feelings” is one;
“and I shall not give rise to new feelings” is one; “and there will be for me sustenance” is one; and “faultlessness” is one.

And this is one [benefit]. Furthermore, a comfortable dwelling (*phāsuvihāra*) is the benefit of food. Thus, one who consumes food endowed with these eight factors is called "one who knows the proper measure in eating" (*bhojane mattaññū*).

"This is called" means that this reflective consumption (*paccavekkhitaparibhoga*), which proceeds by way of knowing the appropriate measure in seeking, receiving, and consuming, is called "moderation in eating."
1356. In the exposition of forgetfulness (*muṭṭhassacca*): "unmindful" (*asati*) refers to the four aggregates devoid of mindfulness.

"Lacking recollection" (*ananussati*) and "lacking presence of mind" (*appaṭissati*) are terms expanded by means of prefixes. "State of being without a refuge" (*asaraṇatā*) is the mode of having no refuge. "Inability to retain" (*adhāraṇatā*) is the incapacity to hold [in mind].
For a person endowed with that is unable to reach a state of firm retention or endure being placed in storage. It is like a gourd-bowl in water.
It "floats away" (pilāpeti) upon the object, thus it is "floating away" (pilāpanatā). "Forgetfulness" (saṃmusanatā) is the state of having lost one's mindfulness.
For a person endowed with that is like a crow that has dropped its food, and like a jackal that has dropped its meat.

In the description of the power of development (bhāvanābala): "of wholesome states" refers to the states conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhammā). "Cultivation" (āsevanā) means repeated practice. "Development" (bhāvanā) means increasing. "Making much of" (bahulīkamman) means doing again and again.
1368. The exposition of failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*) should be understood as the opposite of the exposition of success in virtue (*sīlasampadā*).

The exposition of failure in view (*diṭṭhivipatti*) is the opposite of the exposition of success in view, and the exposition of success in view is the opposite of the exposition of the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*).
Although the exposition of purification of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*) is identical to the exposition of success in virtue, it nevertheless pertains there to that which brings about such purification.
The virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha has been explained; here, however, it is virtue that has attained purification.

Furthermore, by means of these six dyads: mindfulness and clear comprehension; the power of reflection and the power of cultivation; serenity and insight; the sign of serenity and the sign of exertion;
exertion and non-distraction; and the perfection of virtue and the perfection of view.
Even those phenomena belonging to the four planes are described as being both mundane and supramundane. 1373.
In the exposition of purification of view, "knowledge of the ownership of kamma" is the wisdom that discerns: "This kamma is one's own;
this is not one's own. In this context, whether performed by oneself or by another, all unwholesome kamma is "not one's own."
Why? Because it destroys welfare and generates harm. Wholesome kamma, however, is called "one's own" because it destroys harm and generates welfare.

In this regard, it is just as if a man possessing wealth and resources were to set out on a long journey and, while on the road, when a festival was proclaimed in villages, market towns, and so forth, he thought: "I am a stranger; whom indeed shall I rely upon?"
Just as one who plays with constellations does not think, "I shall play with the constellations," but rather plays with the constellations in whatever manner he desires,
thereby crossing the wilderness with ease; even so, by standing upon this knowledge of the ownership of kamma, these beings,
having accumulated much kamma leading to the round of existence, experience happiness through happiness and reach the state of Arahantship beyond counting.
"Transcended. "Knowledge in conformity with the truths" (*saccānulomika-ñāṇa*) is the insight-knowledge that conforms to the four truths.
"Knowledge of one possessing the path" and "knowledge of one possessing the fruit" are simply the knowledge of the path and the knowledge of the fruit.

In the exposition of the phrase "Purification of View," the four knowledges previously mentioned—beginning with the knowledge of the ownership of action (*kammassakata-ñāṇa*)—are analyzed by means of the terms "wisdom" (*paññā*), "understanding" (*pajānanā*), and so forth.

1375. Regarding the explanation of the phrase “exertion according to one’s view,” the energy described by such words as “the arousal of mental energy” and so forth is entirely under the guidance of wisdom (*paññā*).
For it should be understood that through wisdom, it is mundane when in a mundane state, and supramundane when in a supramundane state.

1376. In the exposition of the pair on spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*): "fear of birth" is the knowledge established by seeing birth as fear. The same method applies to the fear of aging, death, and so forth.

1377. By the phrases beginning with "of unarisen evil states," the striving for the means by one who desires to be liberated from birth, aging, sickness, and death—having seen birth and the rest as fears—is explained.
However, the meaning of the word-commentary (*padabhājanīya*) will be made clear in the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*.
1378. Regarding the phrase “lack of contentment with wholesome states,” the term *bhiyyokamyatā* means the desire for distinction.

For instance, someone here might initially give only a meal on the fortnight (*pakkhika*), or a ticket-meal (*salākabhatta*), or a meal on the Uposatha day, or a meal on the first day of the lunar half-month (*pāṭipadika*);
being dissatisfied with that, he further gives a meal for the head of the community (*dhurabhatta*), a meal for the Saṅgha (*saṅghabhatta*), or a meal for the rainy season retreat (*vassāvāsika*).
He builds a dwelling and provides the four requisites.
Even there, being dissatisfied, he takes the refuges and undertakes the five precepts. Even there, being dissatisfied, he goes forth into homelessness.
Having gone forth, he masters one collection, then two collections, and eventually the entire word of the Buddha consisting of the three baskets; he develops the eight attainments and insight.
Having increased [these qualities], one attains *arahatta*. From the moment of attaining *arahatta*, one is called "greatly contented.
Thus, the desire for distinction up to the stage of *arahatta* is what is meant by "the desire for more" (*abhiyyokamyatā*).
Regarding the explanation of the phrase "and non-retrogression in striving," because of the superior skill in remote lodgings (*pantasenāsana*), [one does not fall back].
One who is weary of the cultivation of wholesome states is said to abandon their striving;
one who is not weary does not abandon it. Therefore, in order to demonstrate that method, the passage beginning with "of wholesome states" was spoken.
In this context, *sakkaccakiriyatā* means performing wholesome deeds with thoroughness. *Sātaccakiriyatā* means performing them constantly. *Aṭṭhitakiriyatā* means...
"Without breaking off" means not leaving it unfinished; "without setting it aside. "Unflagging conduct" means a life that is not sluggish, or a mode of existence that is not sluggish.
"Undiminished desire" means the non-abandonment of the desire for what is wholesome. "Undiminished burden" means the non-laying down of the burden of energy in the performance of what is wholesome.
1380. Regarding the statement, “Knowledge of recollection of past lives is true knowledge (*vijjā*):

here, “past lives” (*pubbenivāsa*) refers both to the aggregates (*khandhā*) in which one previously dwelt and to whatever is associated with those aggregates. Recollection of past lives is “recollection of past lives” (*pubbenivāsānussati*).

Knowledge associated with that [recollection] is “knowledge of recollection of past lives” (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*). This [knowledge] is the dispeller of the darkness that conceals the aggregates in which one previously dwelt.
It pierces, thus it is *vijjā* (clear vision). Having pierced that darkness, it makes those aggregates known and manifest; thus, in the sense of making them known, it is also *vijjā*.
"Knowledge of passing away and rebirth" means knowledge regarding both death (*cuti*) and rebirth (*upapāta*).

This too is *vijjā* because it pierces the darkness that conceals the passing away and rebirth-linking of beings. Having pierced that darkness, the passing away and rebirth-linking of beings become known and manifest.
It is "clear vision" (*vijjā*) also in the sense of making known. "Knowledge of the destruction of the taints" (*āsava-kkhaya-ñāṇa*) is knowledge at the moment of the destruction of all defilements.
This very [knowledge] pierces the darkness that obscures the Four Noble Truths; thus it is "clear vision.
Having pierced that darkness, it makes the Four Noble Truths known and manifest; thus it is "clear vision" also in the sense of making known.

1381. Regarding the phrase “the mind’s resolve and Nibbāna”: here, in the sense of being resolved upon an object and in the sense of being well-freed from opposing states, the eight attainments (samāpatti) are called the mind’s resolve.
As for the other, it is Nibbāna because “there is no craving (vāna) termed thirst (taṇhā) herein,” or “it has gone out from that craving. Among these, the eight attainments...
It is called "liberation" because it is liberated from the defilements that have been suppressed; however, Nibbāna is called "liberation" because it is absolutely liberated from all defilements.
(1382) "Knowledge of one possessing the path" refers to the four knowledges of the paths. "Knowledge of one possessing the fruit" refers to the four [knowledges of the fruits].
The knowledges of fruition (*phala-ñāṇa*). Therein, the first path-knowledge arises casting out, stopping, pacifying, and subsiding five defilements;
thus it is called "knowledge of destruction" (*khaye-ñāṇa*). The second path-knowledge [casts out] four defilements.
Likewise for the third path-knowledge. Furthermore, the fourth path-knowledge arises casting out, stopping, [and subsiding] eight defilements.
Because it arises as they are being stilled and completely subsided, it is called "knowledge of destruction. Furthermore,
because that respective knowledge of the path and fruit arises while those respective defilements are reaching their end, ceasing, being stilled, completely subsiding, not arising again,
and no longer occurring, it is called "knowledge of non-arising."
The commentary on the Nikkhepakaṇḍa of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā, the Aṭṭhasālinī, is completed. 4.
The Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa.

Commentary on the Extraction of the Meaning of the Three Sections (Tika-atthuddhāravaṇṇanā) 1384. Now, the turn has come for the commentary on the Section on Exegesis (Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa), which was established immediately after the Section on Enumeration (Nikkhepakaṇḍa).
But why is this called the "Section on Exegesis"? It is because it extracts the meaning of the Buddha’s word contained within the Three Piṭakas.

Because it has been established. For in all three Piṭakas, when another point of Dhamma has come down in the text, it is only by means of the *Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa* (the section on the commentary) that it becomes properly delimited, determined, and well-determined.

Even for one who does not perceive the method-path in the entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka, nor the extraction of questions, nor the course of enumeration in the *Mahāpakaraṇa*, it is appropriate to reconcile these matters from the *Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa* alone.
But from what source does this originate? It originates from the Elder Sāriputta.

For the Elder Sāriputta, having explained the *Aṭṭhakathā-kaṇḍa* (the Commentary Section), gave it to one of his own co-residents who was unable to discern the summary of meanings (*atthuddhāra*) in the *Nikkhepa-kaṇḍa* (the Section on Enumeration).
However, this [tradition] having been rejected in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* (Great Commentary), the following was stated: "The Abhidhamma..."
This is not within the domain of a disciple, nor is it the range of a disciple; this is the domain of a Buddha, the range of a Buddha.
However, when the Dhammasenāpati was questioned by his resident pupil, he took him to the presence of the Teacher and related it to the Perfectly Enlightened One.
The Perfectly Enlightened One, having explained the *Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa* (the section on commentary), gave it to that bhikkhu. How so?

The Blessed One indeed asked, “Which phenomena are wholesome? The meaning is that he was considering, “What are those things called wholesome phenomena? Then, while he remained silent, [the Blessed One thought]:

“Is it not the case that I have already shown the wholesome according to the distinction of planes, by way of such passages as: ‘At whatever time a wholesome consciousness pertaining to the sense-sphere has arisen’? Thus, all of it...

Having explained it by way of extracting the meaning—showing the wholesome and other states by forming clusters, groups, and bundles according to this method: "That which is wholesome in the four planes; these states are wholesome"—he gave [the text].
Therein, "in the four" means in the sense-sphere, fine-material-sphere, immaterial-sphere, and the unincluded (unconditioned) planes. "Wholesome" refers to the classification beginning with contact.
"Wholesome": all these phenomena—contact and the rest—that have been described in their respective planes are called "wholesome.
Regarding the unwholesome, however, because there is no division by way of plane, it is said that there are "twelve unwholesome consciousness-arising types.

In this context, "arising" (uppāda) means that which arises; consciousness itself is the arising, hence "consciousness-arising" (cittuppāda). This is merely a conventional term for the teaching. Just as, for example:

When it is said, “The king has arrived,” the arrival of his ministers and others is already implied; likewise, when “arising of consciousness” (cittuppāda) is mentioned, the mental states associated with it are also included.

It should be understood that in all instances, by the term “arising of consciousness,” consciousness together with its associated states is meant. Hereafter, for all the terms in the analysis of triplets and dyads—such as “resultant” (vipāka) in the four planes—[the same principle applies].

The meaning [of these terms], as well as the fact that pleasure and the other [feelings] cannot be predicated [as such] in the "Triad of Feeling" and so forth, should be understood by investigating the meaning of the Canon according to the method already stated above.
We shall, however, state only the specific differences. 1420.
Regarding the "Triad of Limited Objects," first, in the phrase "all resultants of the sense-sphere," this refers to the two sets of fivefold sense-cognitions (*pañcaviññāṇa*).

The eye-sensitivity and the others arise invariably by depending on objects such as visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles—whether desirable or undesirable—and thus they have limited objects (*parittārammaṇa*).

Furthermore, the two types of resultant mind-elements, both wholesome and unwholesome, arise invariably immediately after eye-consciousness and the rest by depending on the heart-base, taking only visible forms and so forth as their objects; therefore, they too have limited objects.

The wholesome-resultant rootless mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy occurs, as a rule, by way of investigation at the five doors and by way of registration at the six doors, taking only the six limited objects such as visible forms and so forth;
thus, it has a limited object (*parittārammaṇa*). The two rootless mind-consciousness elements—both wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant—occur at the five doors by way of investigation.
In the six doors, by way of registration, it necessarily occurs taking only the six limited objects such as visible forms and so forth as its object.
Even when occurring by way of rebirth-linking, limited kamma takes as its object either the sign of the kamma or the sign of the destination;
likewise, when occurring during the course of existence by way of the life-continuum, or at the end by way of death.
It has a limited object because it takes that very same object as its support.

Furthermore, the eight types of resultant consciousness accompanied by roots proceed only with respect to limited phenomena, functioning as registration (*tadārammaṇa*), rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), and death (*cuti*), according to the method already explained.

The functional mind-element (*kiriyamanodhātu*) proceeds by taking visible forms and so forth as its objects through the five doors. The functional mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy and unaccompanied by roots (*somanassasahagatāhetukakiriyamanoviññāṇadhātu*)...

In the six doors, when directed toward limited phenomena such as visible forms and so forth—whether present, past, or future—at the mind-door, these states occur in those whose taints are destroyed by assuming a joyful mode; thus, they have limited objects.
In this way, these twenty-five types of consciousness should be understood as having exclusively limited objects.

1421. The states of the base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception have sublime objects because they arise by taking their respective lower attainments as their object. Likewise, the states of the Path and the Fruit have immeasurable objects because they take Nibbāna as their object.

As for the eight types of consciousness dissociated from knowledge—four wholesome and four functional—at the time they arise in the learners, worldlings, and those with taints exhausted while taking sense-sphere phenomena as their object during careless reflection on giving, listening to the Dhamma, and so forth, they have limited objects.

At the time of reviewing the highly proficient first jhāna and so forth, they have a sublime object (*mahaggatārammaṇa*). At the time of reviewing the conceptualized signs of the kasiṇas and so forth, they have an indeterminate object (*navattabbārammaṇa*).

Among the unwholesome states, the four types of consciousness associated with wrong view have a limited object (*parittārammaṇa*) at the time of misapprehending, relishing, and delighting in the fifty-five sense-sphere phenomena as "a being, a being."
In that same manner, when they occur with reference to the twenty-seven sublime states (*mahaggata-dhamma*), they have a sublime object (*mahaggatārammaṇa*).
When they occur with reference to conceptualized states (*paṇṇatti-dhamma*), they may have an indeterminate object (*navattabbārammaṇa*).

For those dissociated from views, when they occur with reference to those same states solely through relishing and delighting, or for those associated with aversion through mental grief (*domanassa*), [they have an indeterminate object].

The state of having a limited, sublime, or indeterminate object during the occurrence of a consciousness-moment associated with doubt should be understood by way of its leading to the undesirable, and that of a consciousness accompanied by restlessness by way of distraction and lack of tranquility.
However, not even a single factor among these is able to occur directed toward an immeasurable object; therefore, they do not have immeasurable objects.

The eight types of consciousness associated with knowledge— four wholesome and four functional— belonging to trainees (*sekha*), worldlings (*puthujjana*), and those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), have limited, sublime,
or indeterminate objects when they arise in relation to such phenomena as careful giving, reflection, or hearing the Dhamma, as previously described.
At the time of the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*) and at the time of reflecting on supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*), [they have supramundane objects].
And their state of having an immeasurable object should be understood.

Furthermore, this fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere consists of: the fourth jhāna based on all bases, the fourth jhāna of the space-kasina, the fourth jhāna of the light-kasina, the fourth jhāna of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra), the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna), the fourth jhāna of the supernormal powers (iddhividha), and the fourth jhāna of the divine ear (dibbasota).

With the knowledge of penetration into others' minds as the fourth, the knowledge of rebirth according to karma as the fourth, the knowledge of the divine eye as the fourth, the knowledge of past lives as the fourth, and the knowledge of future existences as the fourth—thus there are twelve types, both as wholesome and as functional.
Among these, that which is called "the fourth based on all bases" refers to the fourth jhāna in relation to the eight kasiṇas; for that [jhāna] is also [the basis] for insight.
It serves as a basis for direct knowledge, for cessation, and indeed for the round [of saṃsāra] as well; therefore, it is called "the basis for all.
However, the fourth [meditation] on the space-kasiṇa and the light-kasiṇa serve as bases for insight, for direct knowledge, and for the round, but they do not serve as bases for cessation.
The fourth [meditation] on the divine abodes and the mindfulness of breathing serves as a basis for insight...
They serve as the basis for the mundane (*vaṭṭa*) but do not serve as the basis for the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) or for cessation (*nirodha*).

In this regard, all ten kinds of kasiṇa-jhāna proceed by taking the designation of the kasiṇa as their object; the fourth of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) proceeds by taking the designation of a being as its object;

and the fourth of the mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*) proceeds by taking the sign (*nimitta*) as its object; thus, they are classified according to the categories of limited (*paritta*) and so forth.

Because its object is a state that cannot be defined [as either mundane or supramundane], it is called "having an indefinable object. The fourth base of psychic power has a limited or sublime object. How so?
For when, wishing to go with an invisible body by making the body dependent on the mind, one transforms the body through the power of the mind—[this occurs] in a sublime consciousness.
When one merges and superimposes [the mind] upon the physical body, then, considering that the object is obtained through application,

it becomes a limited-object (parittārammaṇa) because its object is the physical body. And when, desiring to go by means of the visible body, one makes the mind dependent on the body and transforms the mind according to the body—
merging and superimposing the foundational jhāna-consciousness upon the physical body— [it becomes a limited-object].
In that case, since the object is obtained through application, it is an exalted object because its object is an exalted consciousness.

The fourth [knowledge], the divine ear, has exclusively a limited object because it proceeds by taking sound as its basis. The fourth [knowledge], knowledge of the penetration of minds, has limited, exalted, and measureless objects.
How so? For when it knows another’s sense-sphere consciousness at the time of knowing it, [it takes a limited object].

It has a limited object when it knows sense-sphere consciousness; it has a sublime object at the time of knowing fine-material-sphere or immaterial-sphere consciousness; and it has an immeasurable object at the time of knowing the path and fruition.

Furthermore, in this context, an ordinary person does not know the mind of a stream-enterer, nor does a stream-enterer know the mind of a once-returner, and so on up to the arahant. However, an arahant knows the minds of all.
Furthermore, this distinction should be understood: that the higher [knowledge] is different from the lower.

When the fourth knowledge, the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their deeds (*yathākammupagañāṇa*), knows sense-sphere karma, its object is limited (*paritta*); when it knows fine-material or immaterial sphere karma, its object is exalted (*mahaggata*).

The fourth knowledge, the divine eye (*dibbacakkhuñāṇa*), has exclusively a limited object because its object is material form. The fourth knowledge, the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*)...

It has an object that is limited, sublime, immeasurable, or indescribable. How so? For when recollecting the aggregates belonging to the sense-sphere, it has a limited object. When recollecting the aggregates belonging to the fine-material sphere or the immaterial sphere, it has a sublime object.
And when recollecting the path developed or the fruit realized by oneself or others in the past, it has an immeasurable object.
In the past, the Buddhas cultivated the path, realized the fruit, and attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna;
thus, by means of recollecting the breaking of the cycle of rebirth (*vaṭumaka*), even through the reviewing of the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna, it has an immeasurable object.
In the past, there was a Blessed One named Vipassī. His city was named Bandhumatī, and his father was Bandhumā...

When one recollects such things as name, clan, the earth, and signs in the manner beginning with, “The father was named King [so-and-so], the mother was named Bandhumatī,” the object is not something that can be described [as existing in the present].

The same method applies to the fourth type of knowledge, the knowledge of future existences (*anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa*). In that case as well, one knows: “In the future, this person will be reborn in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*”).

At the time of knowing [that one will be reborn in the sense-sphere realm], the object is limited (*paritta*). At the time of knowing, "One will be reborn in the fine-material sphere or the immaterial sphere," the object is exalted (*mahaggata*).
At the time of knowing, "One will cultivate the Path, realize the Fruit, and attain final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna," the object is immeasurable (*appamāṇa*).
Regarding the future: "The Blessed One named Metteyya will arise; Subrahmā..."
At the time of knowing the name and clan— according to the method beginning with “The father will be a brahmin named Nāma, and the mother will be a brahmin woman named Brahmavatī”—

the object is not to be designated. However, I shall explain the fourth immaterial-sphere attainment and the fourth attainment of the destruction of the taints at the very places where they appear in the Canon.
The functional root-cause mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity is the precursor to all these wholesome, unwholesome, and functional consciousnesses.

Its classification of objects should be understood according to the method already stated for them. However, in its occurrence as determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*) at the five sense doors, it has exclusively limited objects.
As for the fine-material-sphere triplets, the fourfold jhānas, and so forth, they are [classified] by way of their limited nature and so on.

"Objects that cannot be described" refers to those states that have arisen in relation to things that cannot be described. Herein, the fine-material-sphere [consciousnesses] occur with respect to the earth-kasiṇa and so forth;
the base of infinite space occurs with respect to the space cleared by the removal of the kasiṇa; and the base of nothingness occurs with respect to the disappearance of consciousness.
1429. Regarding the triad of objects that are the Path, the eight types of consciousness associated with knowledge mentioned at the beginning belong to both trainees and non-trainees.
At the time of reviewing the path realized by oneself, they have the path as their object; however, because they are not co-nascent with the path, they do not have the path as their cause (*hetuka*).
At the time of reviewing the path realized by oneself while esteeming it, they have the path as their dominant influence (*adhipati*) by way of objective dominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*).
At times when they have other phenomena as their objects, they cannot be described as either having the path as their object or having the path as their dominant influence.
The four noble paths are invariably path-rooted (*maggahetuka*) because of the presence of either the cause designated as "path" or the cause associated with the path.

However, when either energy (*vīriya*) or investigation (*vīmaṃsā*) is made predominant during the cultivation of the path, they may be path-predominant (*maggādhipati*) due to co-nascent predominance (*sahajātādhipati*).
But when either desire (*chanda*) or consciousness (*citta*) is made predominant, they cannot be described as path-predominant.

Among the twelve types of fine-material-sphere fourth jhānas, the nine beginning with the "all-basis" (sabbatthapādaka) fourth jhāna have neither the Path as their object, nor the Path as their cause, nor the Path as their predominance.

However, the fourth jhānas associated with the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa), the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa), and the knowledge of future states (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa) do have the Path as their object at the time when noble ones know the mind of one on the Path; yet, because they are not co-nascent with the Path, they do not have the Path as their cause or predominance.
They do not have the Path as their cause because they do not arise by making the Path an object of esteem; nor do they have the Path as their predominance-condition.
But why do these [states] not esteem the Path? Because of their own sublime nature (*mahaggatatā*).
For just as the whole world esteems a king, but one’s mother and father do not, so too these states do not esteem the Path; for they do not rise from their seats upon seeing the king.
They perform acts such as joining their palms in reverence, and they converse according to the manner used during childhood.
Thus, because of their own loftiness, these states do not regard the Path as weighty.
Even the functional, rootless mind-consciousness element, at the time when Noble Ones review the Path, [does not regard it as weighty] because it precedes that reviewing.

It has the Path as its object, but because it is not co-nascent with the Path, it does not have the Path as its cause (*magga-hetuka*); and because it does not proceed by making the Path its preeminent condition (*garu*), it does not have the Path as its predominance (*adhipati*).
Why does it not make it its preeminent condition? Because of its own lack of a cause, its inferiority, and its dullness.
For just as the whole world holds a king in high esteem, yet his own attendants—such as hunchbacks, dwarfs, and servants—do not.

Just as people do not show great respect to one who lacks wisdom because of his own ignorance, so too this consciousness, due to its lack of cause, its inferiority, and its dullness, does not hold the Path in high esteem.

It should be understood that wholesome states and the like dissociated from knowledge—both because of the absence of knowledge and because they have mundane phenomena as their object—do not attain the status of having the Path as their object and so forth; rather, they simply have an "indeterminate" (navattabba) object.

1432. In the triad of past objects, the phenomena of the base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—which arise by taking as their object a past attainment below them—are exclusively those with past objects.
1433. Regarding the rule that there are none with future objects: by this restriction, there is no separate state of consciousness called "with future object.
But is it not the case that knowledge of the future is exclusively one with future objects, and that knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*) is also [concerned with] the future?
Does it arise by taking [the future] as its object? No, it does not so arise. However, this is not a single, independent consciousness.
Because it is comprised within the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), it is mixed with other sublime states of consciousness (mahaggata-citta).
Therefore, it is said: "Necessarily, there is none that has the future as its object."
1434. The two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness and the three mind-elements (manodhātu) are said to have present objects because they proceed with respect to present visible forms and so forth.

Regarding the "ten types of consciousness": first, the eight types accompanied by roots, when occurring at the moment of taking rebirth-linking for gods and humans, have past objects, taking either kamma or the sign of kamma as their object. This is also the case at the moments of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and death.

The same method applies here. However, when apprehending rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) by taking the sign of destiny as its object, as well as subsequently during the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) period, it has a present object.

Likewise, in the occurrence of the five sense doors by way of registration (tadārammaṇa), it has a present object. In the mind door, however, because it occurs after the mind-door adverting consciousness has grasped the object of impulsions (javana) that have past, future, or present objects, it has past, future, or present objects.
The same method applies to the wholesome-resultant mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity and without root-cause (*kusalavipākāhetukaupekkhāsahagatamanoviññāṇadhātu*).

The only difference is that it serves as the rebirth-linking for those born blind and so forth among human beings; furthermore, in the case of the five sense doors, it also functions as investigation, thus having a present object—this is the distinction here.
However, that which is “accompanied by joy” (*somanassasahagatā*) [functions] in the five sense doors by way of investigation and by way of registration (*tadārammaṇa*).

And it has a present object. In the mind-door, by way of registration (*tadārammaṇa*), they should be understood as having past, future, and present objects, just like the resultant states accompanied by roots.
However, the "unwholesome-resultant rootless mind-consciousness element" shares the same destiny as the wholesome-resultant [rootless] consciousness accompanied by equanimity;
for it occurs solely as the rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death-moment for those destined for the woeful planes.

This is the distinction here: the "functional rootless mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy" (kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu) of those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), when manifesting a state of exhilaration at the five sense doors, has a present object.
When it occurs in the mind door by way of the arising of a smile directed toward phenomena belonging to the past and so forth, it has objects that are past, future, or present.

Regarding "wholesome states of the sense sphere" (*kāmāvacara-kusala*) and so forth: first, among the wholesome states, there are four types of consciousness-arising associated with knowledge (*ñāṇa-sampayutta-cittuppāda*).

For those in training (*sekkha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*) who are comprehending or reviewing the aggregates, elements, and bases (*khandha-dhātu-āyatana*) classified as past and so on, these states have past, future, and present objects.

In the reviewing of concepts (*paṇṇatti*) and Nibbāna, they have objects that are not to be specified (*navattabba-ārammaṇa*). The same method applies to those [consciousnesses] dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇa-vippayutta*).
For they lack only the reviewing of the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna. This alone is the distinction here.

Among the unwholesome states, the four types of consciousness associated with wrong view have the past and other [time-periods] as their objects at the time of relishing, delighting in, and adhering to the aggregates, elements, and bases, whether past or otherwise.
This is so for one who relishes them by taking a conceptual designation (paññatti) as the object.
For one who delights in them and, having misapprehended them, grasps them as "a being, a being," these become objects that are not to be designated [as such].
The same method applies even to those consciousnesses dissociated from views; however, there is simply no grasping through misapprehension by them.

The two types of consciousness associated with aversion, when directed toward phenomena classified as past and so forth, have the past and so forth as their object; for those who are depressed when directed toward a conceptual designation (paññatti), [the object] is that designation.

[The remaining states] have objects that cannot be specified as past, future, or present. Those [states] associated with doubt and restlessness proceed with respect to those same phenomena by way of their state of being undesirable and their state of being agitated;
thus, they have objects that cannot be specified as past, future, or present.
Of the functional [consciousness], the eight types of root-cause consciousness follow the same course as the wholesome types of consciousness. The functional root-cause mind-consciousness element...
Accompanied by equanimity, [this consciousness] has only a present object during its occurrence as the determining (voṭṭhabbana) process in the five doors.

In the mind door, at the time when it acts as the precursor to impulsions (javana)— whether those impulsions have past, future, or present objects, or have concepts (paññatti) or Nibbāna as their object—
it has past, future, present, or indeterminate objects.
Among the aforementioned classifications of fine-material-sphere jhāna, these five— the fourth jhāna based on all bases (*sabbatthapādaka*),

the fourth jhāna of the space-kasiṇa, the fourth jhāna of the light-kasiṇa, the fourth jhāna of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), and the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*)— have only indeterminable objects.

As for the "fourth jhāna of the modes of psychic power" (*iddhividha*), it arises for one who transforms the mind by means of the body, taking as its object the past jhāna-consciousness that served as the basis.

It has a past object because it arises from what has already occurred. For those who resolve upon a future object—such as the Elder Mahākassapa and others when they established the Great Relic Treasury—it has a future object. It is said that while the Elder Mahākassapa was constructing the Great Relic Treasury, he resolved:
"In the future, for two hundred and eighteen years, may these perfumes not dry up; may the flowers..."
He resolved, "May the lamps not go out," and everything happened exactly so.
Seeing the Saṅgha of bhikkhus eating dry food at the Vattaniya monastery, the Elder Assagutta resolved, "May the water-trough have the taste of curd every day before the meal.
Consequently, the curd-taste that had been taken before the meal [appeared].

After the meal, it becomes just as it was before. However, when one makes the body dependent on the mind and travels by means of an invisible body, or when performing another miracle, [the divine eye] has a present object because it occurs with reference to the body.
The "divine ear, fourth," has a present object because it occurs only with reference to sounds that are currently existing.

The fourth, the knowledge of penetrating the minds of others (*cetopariyañāṇa*), has both past and future objects when one knows the minds of others within seven days in the past or within seven days in the future. However, once those seven days have elapsed, one is unable to know them;
for this is the domain of the knowledge of past and future recollection (*pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa* and *anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa*). It is not [the domain] of this [knowledge] at the time it knows the present.
However, it has a present object.
And this "present" is threefold: the momentary present (*khaṇapaccuppanna*), the serial present (*santatipaccuppanna*), and the temporal present (*addhāpaccuppanna*).
Therein, that which has reached the stages of arising, presence, and dissolution is the "momentary present. That which is included within one or two moments of the seventy-five-fold [process]...
‘The present as continuity. In this context, for one who has been sitting in darkness and then goes to a place of light, the object does not become manifest immediately;
rather, it should be understood that there are one or two moments of the seventy [mind-moments] in the interval until it becomes manifest.
Likewise, for one who has wandered about in a place of light and then enters a small inner room, the visible form does not become manifest all at once; rather, until—
That becomes manifest; within this interval, one or two hundred cycles should be understood.
Furthermore, even after seeing from a distance the movements of the washermen’s hands and the striking of gongs, drums, and so forth, one does not yet hear the sound;
until that sound is heard, within this interval as well, one or two hundred cycles should be understood. Such is the view of the Majjhimabhāṇakas.

The Saṃyutta reciters, however, having stated two continuities—“material continuity” and “immaterial continuity”—explain: for one who has stepped into water, [the continuity lasts] until the line made by the water where he stepped on the bank has subsided;
for one who has come from a journey, [it lasts] until the heat in the body has subsided;
and for one who has entered a womb after coming from the sunlight, [it lasts] until the state of darkness [is dispelled].

"It does not disappear: when one has attended to the meditation subject inside the inner chamber and looks out through the window with the shutters open during the day, as long as the flickering of the eyes has not subsided, this is called the continuity of form (rūpa-santati);
two or three impulsion-moments (javana) are called the continuity of the immaterial (arūpa-santati).
Having said this, they declare that both of these together are called 'present by way of continuity' (santati-paccuppanna)."
However, that which is delimited by a single existence is called the temporal present (*addhā-paccuppanna*). With reference to this, it is said in the *Bhaddekaratta Sutta*:
"Friend, whatever is the mind and whatever are mental phenomena—both of these are the present.
If consciousness is bound to desire and lust for that which is present, then because consciousness is bound to desire and lust, one delights in it; delighting in it..."

It is said: “One is shaken regarding present phenomena. Herein, the “present as continuity” (santati-paccuppanna) is mentioned in the Commentaries, while the “present as duration” (addhā-paccuppanna) is mentioned in the Suttas.
Regarding this, some say that “mind as momentary present (khaṇa-paccuppanna) becomes the object of the knowledge of penetration into others’ minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa).”
What is the reason? Because the minds of both the one possessing psychic power and the other arise at the same moment.

And this is their simile: just as when a handful of flowers is thrown into the air, inevitably one flower pierces the stalk of another, and stalk pierces stalk, so too, with the thought "I shall know the mind of another," [the practitioner perceives] a great multitude by way of a mass.
When a mind has been adverted to, one mind necessarily penetrates the mind of another—
at the moment of its arising, its presence, or its dissolution. Furthermore, for one who adverts to [a past object] even for a hundred years or a thousand years,

there is no simultaneous occurrence of the two positions— that of the mind by which one adverts and that by which one knows— due to the non-coexistence of the adverting consciousness and the impulsive (javana) consciousnesses.
In the commentaries, it is rejected as being "inappropriate" because of the fault of falling into the state of having various objects in an undesirable situation.
However, it should be understood that the object is both the present continuity (santati-paccuppanna) and the present duration (addhā-paccuppanna).
In this context, [the object] exists during the time measured by two subsequent thought-moments (javana-vīthi), reckoned from the past and future relative to the currently occurring thought-moment.
Another’s consciousness—all of that is indeed called "present by way of continuity" (*santatipaccuppanna*).

However, as for what is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) that "the present by way of duration" (*addhāpaccuppanna*) should be illustrated by means of a cognitive process (*javanavāra*), that is well said. Herein is the illustration: one possessing psychic power (*iddhimā*), desiring to know another’s consciousness, adverts (*āvajjeti*).
Having made the momentary present (*khaṇapaccuppanna*) adverting consciousness its object, together with that very [adverting],...

It ceases. Then there arise four or five impulsion moments (*javana*), the last of which is the supernormal power consciousness (*iddhicitta*), while the remaining ones belong to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
For all of them, that very same ceased mind becomes the object. They do not have different objects;
because they take as their object the present by way of the duration of the moment, they have a single object. Even though they have a single object, [the subsequent moments]...
And by means of the supernormal power of mind, one understands only another's mind, not the others; just as at the eye-door, visual consciousness sees only visible form, not the others.
Thus, this has a present object by way of both the present of the continuum (*santati-paccuppanna*) and the present of duration (*addhā-paccuppanna*).
Or rather, because even the present of the continuum is indeed the present of duration.
It falls [into the past]; therefore, it should be understood that this has a present object by way of the present of duration (*addhā-paccuppanna*).

Regarding the fourth [knowledge], the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa*): when recollecting names and clans, and when reviewing the sign of Nibbāna, its object is "not to be defined" (*navattabba*);
at all other times, it has only a past object. Likewise, the fourth [knowledge], the knowledge of the destination according to deeds (*yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa*), has only a past object. In that regard:

Although both the knowledge of past lives and the knowledge of others' minds have the past as their object, nevertheless, for the knowledge of past lives, there is no past aggregate or anything connected to the aggregates that is not its object.
For that [knowledge] shares the same range as omniscient knowledge regarding those phenomena connected to the past aggregates and their constituents.
And as for the knowledge of others' minds, it [perceives] what has occurred within seven days in the past.

The mind itself is the object. For it does not know another aggregate (*khandha*) or anything connected with an aggregate; however, because its object is the mind associated with the Path, it is figuratively called "having the Path as its object.

Furthermore, for the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa*), only past volition (*cetanā*) is the object; whereas for the knowledge of the destiny according to deeds (*yathākammupaga-ñāṇa*), only past volition is the object.

This distinction should be understood. This is the method of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) here. But since [the text says], "Wholesome aggregates are the object of the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*)... [the following applies].

It is stated in the *Paṭṭhāna*: “The four aggregates are related to knowledge of the penetration of others’ minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*), knowledge of recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa*), knowledge of the destination according to deeds (*yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa*), and knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa*) by way of object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*). Therefore, all four aggregates are objects for knowledge of the penetration of others’ minds and knowledge of the destination according to deeds;
however, among those, only the wholesome and unwholesome [aggregates] are objects for knowledge of the destination according to deeds.
The fourth [knowledge], the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*), has only the present as its object because it takes existing visible forms as its objective support.

The fourth, the knowledge of future destinies (*anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa*), has only the future as its object. For that, regarding phenomena connected with the aggregates of the future, is of the same range as the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*), just like the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa*).
In this regard, although the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*) also has the future as its object, [it does not extend to all future things].
However, that [consciousness] takes as its object only the consciousness arising within the interval of seven days.
This includes even consciousness arising in a hundred thousand future eons, as well as the aggregates and things associated with the aggregates.

It should be understood that the fine-material-sphere triplets, quadruples, jhānas, and so forth, have exclusively "inexpressible objects" (anavattabbārammaṇa), because they do not occur by taking even a single dhamma from among the past, future, or present as their object.
1435. In the triad of the internal (*ajjhatta*), both non-faculty-bound matter and Nibbāna are "external" (*bahiddhā*).

Just as that which is bound to the faculties, even when said to be "external" in the continuum of another person, is nonetheless "one's own internal" (*niyakajjhatta*) because it is included within one's own continuum, so too these two are not "internal" by any method whatsoever;
thus, they are excluded from the category of "one's own internal."
"External" (bahiddhā) is stated [in this context] because there is no possibility of a mere internal state belonging to oneself (niyakajjhatta).
However, it is with reference to the mere impossibility of a state belonging to oneself that "having an external object" (bahiddhārammaṇatā) is stated in the triad of internal objects.
Precisely because of the departure from internal states, the object of the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) may be considered internal, external, or both internal and external.
It was stated that, without exception, even the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) should not be said to have an internal object,
and so forth. In this regard, not only that [base] itself has an indeterminate object (*navattabbārammaṇa*),

but its advertence (*āvajjana*), its access consciousnesses (*upacāracitta*), its reviewing consciousnesses regarding that object, and even the unwholesome consciousnesses that arise by way of relishing that very [base] are likewise so.

[They] have only objects that should not be spoken of (*navattabbārammaṇa*). However, since those [objects] are already mentioned when that [state] is mentioned, they are not mentioned separately. How are they already mentioned?

For this sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) and whatever precedes it—which occurs by way of adverting (*āvajjana*), access concentration (*upacāra*), and so forth—would share the same object as that.
All of that is included in the triad of "having past objects" (*atītārammaṇa*) under "sense-sphere wholesome" (*kāmāvacarakusala*).
Because it has been admitted that these types of consciousness— namely, the unwholesome, the nine types of functional consciousness, and the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere—
as mentioned above, have an "indefinable object" (*navattabbārammaṇa*) according to the method beginning with the statement,
"They may not be said to have a past object," and because the base of nothingness and the four paths not included in the mundane world [are also defined in this way].
And because it is stated that "the four fruits of recluseship—

these states are not to be called 'having a past object'," it is thus described as "having an indeterminate object" due to being spoken of as having exclusively an indeterminate object. Now, even when this is mentioned within the triad of internal objects,

since it was previously considered— even in reference to its state of having a single common object with those— together with the wholesome states of the sense-sphere and so forth, [it is included here].
The state of having an indeterminate object has been stated; therefore, here too it indicates that their objects are of an indeterminate nature.

For what obstacle could there be to those things that share the same object as that [indeterminate consciousness] also having an indeterminate object? Thus, when that has been stated, it should be understood that they are indeed already "stated.
The rest here is clear from the text regarding the triad of internal objects.

Regarding the classification of objects (*ārammaṇa-vibhāga*), it should be understood that for these six types of consciousness-arising— namely, the wholesome, the resultant, and the functional of the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*) and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*)—
there is an internal object because they proceed by taking as their object the lower attainment connected to one's own continuity.
And herein, the functional space-infinity base (*ākāsānañcāyatana*) [serves as the object] only for the functional consciousness-infinity base.

It is the object of one [consciousness], but not of the other. Why? Because for one who possesses the functional consciousness of the base of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana-kiriyasamaṅgin*), there is no wholesome or resultant consciousness of the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*). However, the wholesome [consciousness] is the object of all three: the wholesome, the wholesome-resultant, and the functional [consciousnesses]. Why?
Because for one who has produced and remains in the wholesome consciousness of the base of infinite space, [thereafter arises] the threefold [consciousness] of the base of infinite consciousness.
This is because of the possibility of the arising of the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*). However, the result (*vipāka*) does not become an object for anything. Why?
