Because once one has emerged from the result, it is impossible for the mind to direct itself toward it. The same principle applies even when the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*) is made an object.
For all the fine-material-sphere jhānas, such as the triads and tetrads, [the result] exists externally to its own internal domain.
Its status as having an external object should be understood as arising by taking external elements, such as the earth-kasiṇa and so forth, as its basis.

All wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states pertaining to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), as well as the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*)—here, first, regarding the wholesome:
for one who reviews one’s own aggregates and so forth, there are four types of consciousness-arising associated with knowledge.
They have internal objects. When reviewing the aggregates and so forth of others, or when reviewing designations and Nibbāna, they have external objects.
By way of both, they have internal-external objects. This same method applies even to those consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge;
for them, however, there is no reviewing of Nibbāna. From the unwholesome, there are four types of consciousness associated with views.
When it occurs at the time of relishing, delighting in, misapprehending, and grasping one’s own aggregates and so forth, it has an internal object;
when it occurs in the same way toward another’s aggregates and so forth, as well as toward non-sensory-bound matter and the kasiṇas, it has an external object;
and by way of both, it has an internal-external object. This same method applies even to those dissociated from views; for indeed, only...
There is no grasping through misapprehension for them. Both types associated with aversion have internal objects when they consist of dejection toward one’s own aggregates and so forth;
they have external objects when directed toward another’s aggregates and so forth, as well as toward non-sensory material phenomena and concepts;
and they have both internal and external objects by way of both these modes. The same applies to those associated with doubt and restlessness among the aforementioned types.
The state of having internal and other objects should be understood by way of the occurrence [of consciousness] through the wavering and state of doubt regarding phenomena.

Thirteen types of consciousness—namely, the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness and the three mind-elements—have internal objects when they occur taking one's own visible forms and so forth as their object;
they have external objects when they occur with respect to another's visible forms and so forth; and they have both [internal and external] objects accordingly.

[These consciousnesses] have internal and external objects. The rootless resultant mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy, during its occurrence, has internal objects when it functions as investigation or registration with respect to its own five [sensory] phenomena such as visible form at the five doors, and also with respect to other internal sense-sphere phenomena at the mind door through the mode of registration alone; however, with respect to the phenomena of others...
When occurring with external objects, they have external objects; by way of both, they have internal-external objects.

This same method applies to the two types of resultant mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity and rootless. However, these also occur among the internal and other divisions in relation to kamma and so forth, by way of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death in both happy and miserable destinies.
The eight great resultant consciousnesses (*mahāvipākacitta*) also share the same destiny as these two [types of investigating consciousness]. However, they do not function by way of investigation;
rather, they occur only by way of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death, and only within the happy destinies (*sugati*).

The rootless functional consciousness accompanied by joy (*somanassasahagata-ahe tukakiriya*) occurs in the five doors by way of producing a state of exhilaration directed toward its own visible forms and so forth; it has internal objects.

Those occurring with respect to the form and other [objects] of another are external objects. Those occurring in the mind-door (manodvāra) by way of the arising of a smile when the Tathāgata reviews actions performed by himself at times such as those of the youth Jotipāla, King Magha, and the ascetic Kaṇha, are internal objects.
[Examples include] the performance of deeds by Queen Mallikā, the minister Santati, and the garland-maker Sumana, and so forth.
At the time of their occurrence directed toward an object, they have external objects. By way of both, they have internal-external objects.

The functional, rootless mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity has internal and other types of objects during its occurrence as the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*) in the five doors and as the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*) in the mind door.

The eight great functional consciousnesses follow the same pattern as the wholesome consciousnesses; for these arise only in those whose taints are exhausted, whereas the wholesome ones [arise in others].
The only difference here is between those who are still in training (*sekkha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*).

In the aforementioned fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), all five jhānas—beginning with the "universal basis" (*sabbatthapādaka*) fourth jhāna—find their place in this triad. For these have external objects (*bahiddhārammaṇa*), since they take as their object the sign of the conceptualized kasiṇa (*kasiṇapaṇṇatti-nimitta*).
As for the "fourth jhāna of the modes of psychic power" (*iddhividha*), at the time of transforming the mind by means of the body, or the body by means of the mind, one's own...
At the time of creating emanations such as the form of a youth, it has an internal object because one takes one's own body and mind as its object;
at the time of seeing external elephants, horses, and so forth, it has an external object; at times it has an internal object and at times an external object;
thus, in its course of occurrence, it has both internal and external objects.
The fourth [base], the divine ear, has an internal object at the time of hearing sounds within one’s own belly; it has an external object at the time of hearing the sounds of others;
and by way of both, it has an internal-external object. The fourth, the knowledge of penetration of minds, has only an external object because its object is the minds of others.
However, there is no purpose for that [knowledge] in knowing one’s own mind.
There is none. When recollecting one’s own aggregates during the "previous births as the fourth" [knowledge], it has an internal object;
when recollecting another’s aggregates, non-sensory-bound matter, and the three types of designations, it has an external object;
and by way of both, it has an internal-external object.
The "divine eye as the fourth" has an internal object at the time of seeing forms such as those within one's own womb;
it has an external object at the time of seeing remaining forms; and it has both internal and external objects by way of both.

The "knowledge of future states as the fourth" has an internal object at the time of recollecting one's own future aggregates, and [it has an external object] at the time of [recollecting] another's future aggregates.
At the time of recollecting form that is not bound up with the faculties, it has an external object; by way of both, it has an internal-external object.
The reason why the base of nothingness has an indeterminable object has already been stated above.
Commentary on the Extraction of the Meaning of the Dyads.

1441. In the exposition of the group on causes (hetugocchaka), after showing the causes by way of the method beginning with "the three wholesome causes," it is further stated that "they arise in the wholesome states of the four planes" in order to show those same causes from the perspective of their point of origin.
By this same method, the manner of teaching should be understood for the remaining groups as well.
1473. Regarding the statement, "Where two or three taints (*āsava*) arise together," here the simultaneous arising of the taints should be understood in three ways.

In that context, among the four [consciousnesses] dissociated from views, the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) arises together with the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*); and among those associated with views, it arises together with both the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*) and the taint of ignorance;
thus, the taint of sensual desire arises together in two ways. As for the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*), in the four [consciousnesses] dissociated from views...

"Along with the taint of ignorance" means it arises in one way, that is, simultaneously. And just as it is here, so too wherever two or three fetters arise simultaneously, there the arising of the fetters would likewise be tenfold in one way.
In that regard, sensual lust arises simultaneously in four ways, aversion in three ways, conceit in one way, and likewise doubt.
And attachment to existence (*bhavarāga*). How so? First, sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) arises together with four [factors]:

with the fetter of conceit (*māna-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of ignorance (*avijjā-saṃyojana*), with the fetter of views (*diṭṭhi-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of ignorance, with the fetter of adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbata-parāmāsa*) and the fetter of ignorance, and with the fetter of ignorance alone;

thus it arises together in four ways. Furthermore, resentment (*paṭigha*) arises together with the fetter of envy (*issā-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of ignorance, and with the fetter of stinginess (*macchariya-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of ignorance.

And [it arises] together with the fetter of ignorance alone; thus it arises in three ways collectively. Conceit arises in only one way collectively, together with the fetters of existence-attachment and ignorance.
Doubt is likewise; for it arises in only one way, together with the fetter of ignorance.
The same principle applies to existence-attachment as well. Thus, in this context, two or three fetters arise collectively.

1511. Furthermore, regarding that which was stated in the *Nīvaraṇagocchaka*—"where two or three hindrances arise together"—therein too, the simultaneous arising of the hindrances should be understood as eightfold.
For among these, sensual desire arises together in two ways, ill will in four ways, and restlessness in one way. Likewise for doubt. How so?

First, sensual desire arises together with the hindrance of restlessness and the hindrance of ignorance in unprompted consciousnesses, and with the hindrances of sloth-and-torpor, restlessness, and ignorance in prompted consciousnesses; thus it arises in two ways.
As for what was stated as "two or three," that was said by way of the minimum limit. Therefore, all four arise together.
The statement is indeed appropriate. However, ill-will (*vyāpāda*) occurs in four ways together with other hindrances:

in an unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*) consciousness, it occurs together with the hindrances of restlessness (*uddhacca*) and ignorance (*avijjā*); in a prompted (*sasaṅkhārika*) consciousness, it occurs together with the hindrances of sloth-and-torpor (*thinamiddha*), restlessness, and ignorance; and in an unprompted consciousness alone, it occurs together with the hindrances of restlessness, worry (*kukkucca*), and ignorance;
and in a prompted consciousness alone, it occurs together with the hindrances of sloth-and-torpor, restlessness, worry, and ignorance. Thus, it is fourfold in combination.
It arises. Restlessness, however, arises in one way together with the hindrance of ignorance alone.
It arises in one way together with the hindrances of doubt, restlessness, and ignorance. 1577.
Regarding that which was stated in the "Cluster of Defilements" (Kilesagocchaka) concerning where two or three defilements arise together: therein...
The meaning should be understood thus: "Two defilements arise together with others, or three defilements arise together with other defilements.
Why? Because it is impossible for only two or only three to arise simultaneously.
In that regard, there is a tenfold simultaneous arising of defilements; for here, greed arises simultaneously in six ways.

Aversion is twofold; likewise, delusion is to be understood [as twofold]. How so? First, greed occurs with the unprompted (asaṅkhārika) type when dissociated from views, accompanied by delusion, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing;

with the prompted (sasaṅkhārika) type, it is accompanied by delusion, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing; with the unprompted type alone, it is accompanied by delusion, conceit, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing;
and with the prompted type alone, it is accompanied by delusion, conceit, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing.

Furthermore, in the case of a spontaneous (asaṅkhārika) consciousness associated with wrong view, it arises together with delusion, restlessness, wrong view, lack of shame, and lack of fear of wrongdoing—thus in six ways;
whereas in the case of a prompted (sasaṅkhārika) consciousness, it arises together with delusion, wrong view, sloth, restlessness, lack of shame, and lack of fear of wrongdoing.

As for aversion (paṭigha), however, in the case of a spontaneous consciousness, it arises together with delusion, restlessness, lack of shame, and lack of fear of wrongdoing; whereas in the case of a prompted consciousness, it arises together with delusion, sloth, restlessness, lack of shame, and lack of fear of wrongdoing.

"Along with" (*saddhim*) means that it arises together in two ways: delusion (*moha*) arises together with doubt (*vicikicchā*), restlessness (*uddhacca*), shamelessness (*ahirika*), and fearlessness of wrongdoing (*anottappa*) when associated with doubt;
and it arises together with restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing when associated with restlessness.
The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the *Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa* of the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā*,
known as the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, is completed.
The words of the conclusion.
And to this extent— the mind and matter, their classification, the extraction of meaning, and that which is delightful—
the Lord of the World, distributing [the teaching], taught the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*.
Having summarized the Abhidhamma exhaustively according to its doctrines,
this commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*) which I have undertaken was composed for that [work] while it stood firm.
Because the meanings are presented without confusion, it is called the *Aṭṭhasālinī*.
Thus, by name, this work has reached its conclusion. It was brought to completion by me,
who was concluding it from the recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*) of the thirty-nine discourses (*pāḷi*),
for the sake of the long endurance of the Dhamma.
By the power of whatever merit has been attained, may all living beings,
having understood the Dhamma that brings happiness from the King of the True Dhamma,
reach the practice that leads to purity and bliss.
May there be freedom from sorrow and distress, the supreme bliss of Nibbāna.
May the True Dhamma endure for a long time; may all beings have reverence for the Dhamma;
and may the rain god send rain in due season upon all living beings.
Just as the ancient, righteous kings protected [their subjects],
so too should this king protect his own people according to the Dhamma,
O people! [He who is] adorned with the most purified faith, wisdom, energy, and fortitude, and endowed with a multitude of virtues such as virtue, conduct, gentleness, and humility...
To the one endowed with the analytical clarity of wisdom capable of penetrating and fathoming his own school’s tenets as well as those of other schools;
to the great expounder whose unimpeded radiance of knowledge shines throughout the Teacher’s Dispensation—the scriptures of the Three Piṭakas together with their commentaries;

to the foremost of debaters who speaks with fitting and excellent words, sweet and noble, flowing forth from the bliss produced by perfection of skillful means; to the great poet adorned with the various virtues such as the six supernormal powers and surrounded by the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).

This is the commentary on the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* called the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, composed by the Elder named Buddhaghosa— a name bestowed upon him by his teachers— who was an ornament to the lineage of the Mahāvihāravāsī Elders, who were lamps of the Elder tradition and possessed wisdom well-established in the superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*), and whose intellect was vast and purified.
May he remain as long as possible in the world for those seeking to cross over the world,
showing to noble sons the method for the purification of wisdom—
even so long as the mere name "Buddha" exists for that one of pure mind who is such-like.
"In this world, the Great Seer proceeds as the eldest in the world.
The commentary on the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, titled the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, is completed.
